cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: THE ULTIMATE FORD BE/MOATES EFI TUNING GUIDE? Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon May 20, 2024 6:24 am My guess is the most official information is going to be both in the helpfiles of BE (and EA). However those are written very generically and don't include a lot of the learned practices and behaviors that might be shared on forums, tech docs, and FAQs on sites like this. So if you are looking to train an AI, you'll need to figure out if you can get the AI to scrape forums like this one (and others) for all the various types of problems people have along with the found solutions (where the OP posted the solution). AIs, just like humans, have to be given a lot of context and scenarios. Where AIs excel above humans is with memorization and recognizing patterns. The dangers here are a lot of the information may have been red-hearings or the actual fix was not as posted in the thread. These kinds of issues will certainly be reasons why the AI gets it wrong sometimes. But for all the useful data, it's possible an AI could identify common problems and suggest reasonable solutions for how to improve some of the more annoying and frustrating issues people have with DIY tuning. It might even be able to do things like suggest values that need to be changed. However without the AI being able to open up def files, make sense of them, and apply them to bin files, it's not likely you are going to get an AI to generate modified BIN files for you. I'm not saying it is impossible, but there'd be a LOT of behind-the-scenes developer training necessary. And as complex as tunes are, I don't think you'd find anybody with tuning experience willing to blindly trust such a tune. Novice users that wouldn't know what to look for would definitely want to have an experienced person compare that AI-generated tune against a known good tune just to make sure the AI didn't hallucinate and inject some REALLY bad information in a dangerous area of the tune. And then, you'd have to trust the AI wasn't making edits to areas of the tune it shouldn't (i.e. areas not explicitly described by the def file). But if you could pull this off, it'd be interesting to feed into the AI all the details about the Intel 8061/5 processors and the various sub-processors to see just how well it could write a custom tune (including executable code) and then generate a def file for that tune. My experience with AIs generating low-level assembly has not been great. I tried to get a ChatGPT to generate some code capable of running on a TI PRU (Programmable Runtime Unit) within my BeagleBone AI64, and it didn't work. The syntax was surprisingly close, but the GPT failed to understand the nature of special I/O registers, what they were used for, and how to use configure for them which is a fairly fundamental detail of the PRU. Point is, Intel 8061/5 processors have numerous memory mapped peripherals to co-processors, which appear to the code, as special registers or as external memory. Add to that, Ford wrote the bins in somewhat bizzarre ways, for example, directly manipulating the stack in areas that generally only the hardware should be in charge of. But those Ford programmers predated using coding patterns, clean-code conventions, and the like. Also I suspect a huge part of their motivation was execution efficiency, performance, and determinism. They were inventing their own conventions to solve problems that didn't have industry standard ways of being done yet. Not to mention, the 8061/5 wasn't an industry standard chip. It was an Intel variant that was ONLY used by Ford. It would be AT LEAST another decade before the concept of programming patterns and anti-patterns would be recognized and articulated to the development world. So it'd be easy for an AI to try applying modern programming conventions to deciphering that old code and get it wrong. And worse, Chatbots have a bad history of being "confidently wrong" meaning they'll spin all kinds of logic together that, to a laymen, seems perfectly reasonable, but is absolute BS when actually analyzed. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

title: No apparent O2 signal as viewed from CalCon - EECTuning.org

posts.author: SHO037
posts.content: SHO037 Gear Head Posts: 4 Joined: Sat Oct 28, 2023 10:35 am No apparent O2 signal as viewed from CalCon Quote Post by SHO037 » Sat Nov 04, 2023 3:15 pm Hi all, I will say up front that I am new to CalEdit/CalCon, and EEC and the Tweecer. And to the engine I am working on, for that matter, so just assume I don't know anything... Engine is 1994 SHO 3.0, but it's not in a Taurus. I have the Tweecer connected and I am getting readings from it in CalCon for everything but the O2 sensors. I have gone through the wiring, I have continuity from the "signal" pin on the O2 sensors to pins 29 and 43 at the ECU. I have pin 6 at the ECU grounded, as it appears to be the ECU's ground for the O2 sensors. I have new O2 sensors installed. I have verified good ground and 12v at the heater wires on the sensors. In CalEdit/CalCon, I have selected the O2 sensors as part of the payload, and downloaded that to the Tweecer. As I said I can see other signals from the gauges moving around in CalCon, but the vertical HEGO1/HEGO2 O2 bars don't read anything, nor does the horizontal "AFR (Gasoline) " bar. I have tried everything I can think of to show the AFRs on CalCon. I have to believe that if they are not showing on CalCon, then the ECU is not seeing the signal from them either. I have a separate PLX wideband sensor hooked up as well. It starts in the 14s, but if I let the engine idle, as it warms up, it starts drifting upward to some marginally alarming numbers, 15, 16 or 17. To me that is proof that the ECU is not seeing the O2 signals, since it would correct them back down to where they should be if it did. But I'm not 100% sure my reasoning there is sound. Blipping the throttle sends them back down to the 13/14 range, but if I let the engine idle, it will go very lean. Thanks in advance for any help or insights you can give me! Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Re: 35lbs to 42lbsinjectors Quote Post by sailorbob » Wed Apr 12, 2017 10:19 am Changing the VAF transfer to adjust for injector size changes often doesn't work as the vane is usually fully open before the airflow reaches it's peak on VAF equipped engines. The VAF transfer is showing considerable air flow increases over the stock values. If the engine is not flowing that amount of air it will run richer. Also, the 'Air - SD Airmass VE Multiplier' scalar has been set to its maximum value and, whilst I'm not convinced it's naming is correct, if the description of its effects are correct then this will be another reason for it running rich as it's almost 3 times the stock value. As an aside, the rev. 9 version of the definition contains an error; do not alter the 'Air - SD Engine Displacement' parameter as it has the wrong address and corrupts the last entry in the 'Failed - Air Mass estimate (failed VAF)' table. posts.author: RideADV
posts.content: RideADV Gear Head Posts: 34 Joined: Sun Jan 08, 2017 2:58 am Re: 4R70W Shift Tuning, SUV to Car Quote Post by RideADV » Wed Jan 18, 2017 1:15 pm decipha wrote: unless youve correctly calculated nvbase then dont worry about how it shifts unless you want to cross calculate the corrections, if so more powah to you Reading through a document eectuninginfo.doc that I googled: Tranny Shifting For the trans shifting early problem, you need to change the trans_base_RPM/VSS parameter, which should equal ((axle ratio*336)/tire diameter). I had the same problem with OD and my 3.73 gears. BTW, with my 3.73's, the rpm/vss parameter worked out to 49, but yours may be different if you're using a different sized rear tire than me (275/40-17). Also, for WOT, you should match your WOT_RPM shift point to the MPH you're running at that WOT_RPM. For instance, my WOT_RPM for 1st gear is 5800, so my UPSHIFT_SPEED_VS_TP_1_2 @ WOT ( 4.98047, 41.8 ). Assuming trans_base_rpm/vss is the nvbase you're talking about, is it? Of course, that doesn't say what units to use, but assuming inches (25 for my 225/45R17)... ((3.73*336)/25) = 50.1312 That's on par with what the document says, but my Explorer with 29" tires (235/75R15) had a value of 21 loaded, where that calculation says it should be ((3.73*336)/29) = 43.2166 1998 Volvo V90 Explorer 5.0/4R70W EEC-V Swap (XDT2/CQAB1) Ford Racing GT40X Heads & E303 Cam. title: Why are there limits on NIOLD? - EECTuning.org

posts.author: Pontisteve
posts.content: Pontisteve Regular Posts: 78 Joined: Mon May 16, 2011 12:33 pm Location: FL Why are there limits on NIOLD? Quote Post by Pontisteve » Fri Mar 18, 2016 2:16 am Looking in GUF1 at parameters NIOLD (Neutral Idle Open Loop Delay) and NIHYS (hysteresis), the description in the def warns "Do NOT set to a value of 0". I'm trying to figure out why have this warning. Setting it to 0 would seemingly force open loop every time you entered closed throttle. That could be handy with a big cammed car to use that. So why not set this to 0 in that case? Is there some reason we can't set it to 0, or is it more about the PCM constantly flopping into open loop every time you let off the gas for a split second? Since the Closed Throttle Neutral Timer (CTNTMR) is clipped to NIOLD + NIHYS, that would prevent FN180 (Idle Spark Subtractor) and FN880 (Idle RPM Adder based on time in neutral) from being functional, since the CTNTMR would never upcount if you set NIOLD to 0. But that's equally as true if you set it to 1 or 2 seconds, or anything under about 240 seconds really. Any input greatly appreciated. Thanks! If it's worth doing, it's probably not easy. Top

posts.author: Stengun
posts.content: Stengun Regular Posts: 185 Joined: Sat Oct 15, 2011 2:19 pm Re: No start on new CDAN4 tune Quote Post by Stengun » Thu Apr 24, 2014 10:37 am Howdy Shaker, Actually mine's a stroked 414W. Like your's it has ran with a carb, but has new heads (AFR 205 ) and new AFM N-71 cam and if course EFI. No spark? Gee, of all the issues I've had I've always had spark, except when the case wasn't grounded. I have finally solved my rich condition. My MAF setup was temporary and I placed the MAF directly over the TB ( this is how Mass Flo does their 4bbl style EFI assembly ) and the sampling port of the slot was directly over one of the primary butterfly valves and was drawing a large volume of air through the port which made the ECU believe the engine was using 2-3Xs as much air as it was actually using. As a result the ecu was injecting enough fuel for this volume of air which caused the engine to run very rich. No matter what I did I could not get the engine to run anywhere near stoich. I made a new MAF tube ( 4" od 3.76"ID ), a new adaptor so I could connect a 4" flex hose to the TB and the MAF tube, plus another 2 feet of flex hose connected to the inlet side of the MAF tube. I this helped to lower the MAFV and kg/hr at the same RPM and load but was still rich. I recalculated my MAF transfer and reduced it by 10% but I haven't tried it yet. If it's not raining when I get home I'll try it this evening. I feel that this will solve my rich condition. I look at this "project" as a marathon not a sprint. posts.author: Stengun
posts.content: Stengun Regular Posts: 185 Joined: Sat Oct 15, 2011 2:19 pm Re: No start on new CDAN4 tune Quote Post by Stengun » Thu Apr 24, 2014 1:09 pm Howdy Shaker, Are you using Decipha's ZXA5 basic tune? I am and it seems a lot easier than the calibration from Saliorbob which is a totally stock, unedited 4.6 T-bird tune. As far as the Cranking Fuel PW I used Decipha's write up. Here it is: FN 348A Crank PW Multiply the Y-axis as a percentage of the stock 281 cubic inch and 19 lb/hr injectors values by doing, 19/(new injector size) * (new engine size)/281= 0.xxx For my combo: (19/60) x (414/281)=? .31667 X 1.473 = .467 I took the value that was in each column of the Cranking Fuel PW vs ECT table and multiplied it by .467 and edited the table. I was still having a starting issue so I lowered each column by .1 and this helped. I always felt that the initial timing was too slow with the stock T-bird calibration and it seems to be better with Decipha's tune. 10 degrees is normal for a 4.6 but as soon as it starts it will jump to +20 degrees. Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Apr 04, 2013 7:43 am 96lt4c4 wrote: ...The first thing I did was change the Engine Displacement SARCHG, obviously to 300 CID... The difference from 302 to 300 will be minuscule, but you are correct. SARCHG is one of those things that normally needs to be changed. And for clarity, keep it at 300. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...The description led me to the other scalers that need to be changed. Some of them are pretty straight forward others I may need help with... I'm glad to see NUMCYL's comments led you to all these things. I was wondering how someone would know what to change and if there was something I could add to the def file to help out. So I was glad to see it was already there. Obviously, someone has run into this before and thus documented what needed changing in order for it to get documented right into the def file. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...'Injector Output Port' (aka FN1327) Not sure ? ... This has to do with whether you setup the engine with 1 or 2 banks. If you run the 2-header setup and thus run 2 HEGOs (the preferred option), then you'll need to setup say cylinders 1-3 on Bank 1 and 4-6 on Bank2. However if you run a single header with a single HEGO, then all cylinders will be on Bank 1. This is the simpler option and likely your only option if you run a turbo. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...'Manifold Fast Fill Constant' (aka FKARC1) Not Sure ? 'Manifold Slow Fill Constant' (aka FKARCH) Not Sure ? ... It'd be nice to find a def file and tune for a 300L6 and see if you can find these values. Otherwise, setting these might be a bit of trial-n-error to find numbers that work well. These values are used to help with transient fueling, I believe. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...'Number of PIPs Between Injector Outputs' (aka PIPOUT) Not sure but changed to 6 ? ... I believe that is correct. This is to setup for 1 injector pulse per cylinder intake. I believe some strategies experimented with firing the injector more than once per intake. I don't know why that was seemed useful, but someone thought it was a good idea to fire the injector on a closed intake valve, then fire it again later probably while the intake valve was opening. I'm speculating here, but regardless, keep it at 6 unless you hear otherwise from somebody more informed. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...'PIPs per Rev' (aka ENGCYL) Not sure but changed to 3 ? ... Correct. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...'Signature PIP Multiplier Highest Value' (aka SIGKLU) Not Sure ... Purely based on the comments, you want 1.99996 for this value to correspond with 30% signature PIP duty cycle as explained in MHPFD. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...'Signature PIP Multiplier Lowest Value' (aka SIGKLL) Not Sure ... Again purely based on the comments, you want 1.42857 for this value to correspond with 30% signature PIP duty cycle as explained in MHPFD. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...Also so what part number is the ECM that I am looking for?... Go to eBay, junkyard, or wherever and find one of the many GUFx EECs such as a GUFB/A9L. For an extensive list of GUFx EECs, go to the EEC Analyzer website and note all the tune file names in each of the 3 GUFx def folders. The *.bin tune file names correspond to the catch codes on the EECs they were extracted from. In the GUFB folder, you should find a stock tune for an A9L, X3Z, A9M, A3M, A3M1, A3M2, and perhaps a few others I'm not thinking of right now off the top of my head. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...As far as the harness goes, are most of or all the Ford EEC's of this era all pinned out the same or will I need to be swapping wires around?... For the most part, that's true. However if the truck was originally speed-density, it's quite possible pins could be different. And of course your existing wiring harness isn't going to have pins for the MAF. So you'll need to add those and get a connector to connect to a MAF. I'd recommend using a slot style MAF. If you purchase a used one off eBay, you can usually get the connector included. But you'll need to fabricate a housing for it. Here's how I did just that: Custom intake track for slot style MAF sensor Again, be absolutely sure by getting the pinout of your EEC and the pinout of an 89-93 Mustang GT EEC. From there, compare pin-by-pin to ensure your wiring harness has the right wires on the right pins. If this engine used to be EEC-V/OBD-II, make sure your wiring harness is pin-compatible at all. Ford upgraded from 60pin EEC-IVs to 104 pin EEC-Vs. Notice: The EEC-IVs has 3 rows of 60 much thicker pins as compared to the EEC-Vs: The newer EEC-Vs have 4 rows of 104 pins: 96lt4c4 wrote: ...I am also thinking that this truck would benefit from running a MAF?... If you go with a GUFx EEC, a MAF is a requirement, not an option. And tuning a Ford MAF EEC is much easier than tuning a Ford SD EEC. It's not to say that SD tuning isn't a good way to tune. It's just Ford's SD EECs are not as easy to tune as MAF-based EECs. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...If I load the tune onto a Moates https://www.moates.net/f3-ford-memory-a ... l?cPath=63 and slide it into the ECM already in his truck, will that work? Granted we install the MAF... First off, when you start tuning, you need datalogging. So you'll want a Moates Quarterhorse and BinaryEditor to tune this thing. Once you have a tune you like and works well, you can burn that perfected tune to a Moates F3 chip. This is all true. However the EEC has to be able to support the hardware the tune is describing. I don't believe SD-EECs have the hardware to support monitoring a MAF or the other sensors a MAF wants. So while it MIGHT work, I wouldn't expect it or plan for it at all. Plan to replace the EEC with an EEC you know will do what you are trying to do. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...I will be going by my friends house tomorrow night to see if this is the route he wants to go. I will also take a look at his distributor and see if is the correct one, but I am pretty sure it is. Let us know. If you do wind up going this route and all the things mentioned above do wind up working for you, then I'd be glad to spend some time updating the GUFx def files with comments and enumerations to choose the right options easier without the confusion you've expressed. But being I've never actually done this nor have I ever received a perfected GUFx 6 cyl or 4 cyl tune to compare to, I have been reluctant to do any more with the def files than what's done. Ultimately if you find that this project is a huge success that you recommend this route, then I want to help smooth the path for others walking behind you where I can. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

Not sure how it compares to the Mustang MAF, or what we would need to do to install the Mustang MAF... My recommendation would be to begin with the MAF you plan to use with the turbo. That way upgrading the turbo has 1 less thing to worry about. I wouldn't trust that the stock MAF for any F150 except maybe the Lightning is going to be sufficient once you get the turbo on there. Running it for the time being on a stock 300L6 should be fine. But even the GT MAFs are undersized for the job when you start talking boost of any amount...even small levels like 5-6PSI. So I'd recommend you plan for an upgraded MAF now even though the stock engine isn't going to need it. If the stock 96 F150 MAF is anything similar to the 97 Ford Explorer 5.0L MAF, it definitely is on the small side when you include boost. Also if the 96 airbox has the 4-bolt holes, then there's a chance the 90mm LMAF might mount to it. After all the LMAF is the F150 Lightning MAF. Although I believe there are 3 different MAF bolt patterns for the various Ford 4-bolt MAFs. So don't just assume because you have a 4-bolt MAF airbox and the LMAF is a 4-bolt MAF that they are the same bolt pattern. You'll need to research that. I'm fairly sure the dimensions of the LMAF are published on the Internet somewhere. So it's just a matter of measuring your box's bolt pattern and comparing. However as I mentioned earlier, my recommendation would be to consider the slot style MAF. Then you can control how "big" the MAF is by adjusting the diameter pipe you stick it in. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...He is going to get the harness and wiring we need to install the MAF as well. I am bidding on a couple ECM's on Ebay right now. One of them comes with a Mustang MAF... Don't pay over $100 for an eBay EEC. You can buy them for $100 at AutoZone. Although you'll need to take them a core to swap out. The core doesn't even have to be any good. They just need the aluminum frame & pin connector basically. Although I suspect they do reuse the circuit boards where possible when they remanufacture those things. And again, if the MAF that comes with the EEC is a stock GT MAF, that'll work for the stock engine, but I wouldn't trust it'll have the flow capacity necessary once you add boost. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...As far as the turbo we are thinking about using, its the one off of a chevy 6.5 liter diesel. There are a few posts on other forums floating around on the internet where guys have had good success with this Turbo on the 300 6... I've heard from others saying that turbo is a good one to use in other projects. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...As far as running boost on the A9L, what needs to be done?... There are FAQs that talk to this topic. Start with the one talking about Scaling Functions. Understanding how Scaling Functions work is KEY to configuring for boost. If you have further questions about this, post as new threads. Although what you'll need to adjust for boost is not going to be related to the fact that you are running a V8 EEC on an L6. So while that's interesting info, it's not likely to be necessary info to that discussion. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...Will we still be using a MAP at all or is it straight MAF? I have seen something about a BAP sensor?... MAF-based EECs don't use MAP as a MAP sensor at all. Although the BAP (aka BARO) sensor is the same exact sensor as a MAP sensor. So the EEC will reuse the sensor you now call a MAP. It'll just be used as a BAP sensor when you do the conversion. And the sensor will no longer be connected to the manifold. It will be used to reference atmospheric pressure, not manifold pressure. That's probably the most important thing to remember. 96lt4c4 wrote: ...Also what is the name of the main MAF table in the A9L.bin? I can not find it for anything. Not MAF table. MAF function. FN036 is the PID name of the MAF transfer function in the GUFx stuff. Just seek for FN036 and ye shall find. BTW, FN036 is NOT FN36 . cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: MAF and throttle body tuning - which one first Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Dec 04, 2012 2:04 pm My very inexperienced opinion is MAF tuning is far more important. MAF tuning is tuning almost every aspect of the engine running condition. The only part of engine management that the MAF isn't involved in is cranking and MAF failure scenarios. TB tuning is more fine tuning of transient fueling. The computer needs to have an idea of how much more/less air is being aspirated in as the throttle plate changes position. The amount of change is based on the initial blade position, rate of change, and the RPM/Load at the time of change. I'm not intimately familiar with newer strats and transient fueling, but the GUFx era tunes break out blade movement enrichment with Load change enrichment. Blade movement based on the TPS is handled by the Accel Enrichment controls. Only opening movements have an affect on fueling. The blade position and the rate of change are used to come up with an amount of fuel enrichment to be added to the next firing injectors. Enrichment addition ends the moment the blade stops moving. This enrichment accounts for air aspiration changes before they are detected by the MAF. Even after the MAF detects the change in airflow, there are still additional transient fueling needs associated with wall wetting. As throttle increases, you inject more fuel to accommodate the higher engine load. That's more wall wetting. The more wetness on the walls, the less is getting into the cylinders. Transient enrichment accounts for increases in Load to ensure that the AFR going into the cylinders isn't going lean. If anything, you want transients to ensure a slightly richer-than-commanded mix just to be on the safe side. Although as you back off on throttle, now you have a build-up of wet walls that evaporate off and cause a rich decel when load drops off. So transient enrichment compensates by pulling fuel on drops in engine Load. Because transient fueling is controlled by changes in load, and only indirectly due to changes in throttle body size, upgrading to a larger throttle body shouldn't affect how much transient fueling the tune gives. But I'm not 100% sure just how true this is in practice. I simply don't have the experience to know this. Although if I was put in this position, this is where I'd defer to one of decipha's attitudes on tuning. Give'er what she wants. If you determine that more enrichment is needed and it is needed in a condition that only transient enrichment can satisfy, then tune to fix the problem. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: reef93lx Gear Head Posts: 28 Joined: Tue Feb 28, 2012 10:21 pm Location: Edmond, OK Re: a9l2 kamrf Quote Post by reef93lx » Sun Aug 19, 2012 1:56 pm I'm still getting my feet wet and far from an expert on this, but what I've been doing is: I try to vary the RPM and load, yet stay in a steady-state cruise for 10 secs at a time. I typically drive around for 20-30 mins of mixed driving: city, highway, easy cruise, WOT, etc. When I get back, I filter the logs and I filter out anything with a TPS value <1.25, AEFUEL flag, and EFTRFF (Decel I believe?) flag. I also start by filtering out all open loop. This leaves me with steady-state closed loop values only. Using the average KAMRF values, I tweak the MAFV points in my curve. I go back to the unfiltered log and filter again, this time filtering out the closed loop. Then, I focus on the LAMBSE and AFR (Wideband) values, tweaking the MAFV points along the curve. Once that's done, I've been running it through EA's MAF fitting tool to smooth the curve out slightly. However, I must be doing something wrong, as the EA generated curve is missing the 15.998V point and it hoses the bottom of the curve also. So, watch out for that if you decide to do the MAF Fitting tool. I'm amazed at how well mine is running. Its a 331ci with a nasty camshaft, yet idles along nice and smooth and part-throttle drivability is very nice. I have a couple minor issues to contend with, but I'm very happy with the tune, considering how little time I've actually spent logging and tweaking. Thanks to decipha, we've all got a head start with the a9l2 bin... The other thing I've started doing and its helped tremendously is keeping a log. I have a txt document on my desktop where I make a chronological list of the date, the tune name, and my impressions. If I make any changes, I add those to the list. There was a point where I was making too many changes at once and losing track of where I was. I also travel a lot for work, so I may go a week or more in between tuning sessions. I would get home and nt be able to remember what the last tune change I made was. Lol Good Luck and hope some of my rambling helps a little! cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: decel lean concern Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 01, 2012 9:00 am I had a similar problem except for me, it was rich decel. On decel, the LAMBSEs would work themselves up trying to fight a rich condition. Then for about 10 seconds after I got to neutral, the LAMBSEs had to work their way back down to a stoic mix. And if during that time, I needed to take off (a stop sign that I approached, stopped, at and wanted to go again) before the LAMBSEs had settled, I'd be tipping-in lean which is where my driveability issues were seen. The problem never was that the decel was rich or that idle was lean. The engine seemed to idle OK lean. It was on the tip-in while LAMBSEs were still working their way down that caused all my issues. Before I discovered DFSO, I solved this by purposely running my MAF curve lean at decel flow rates and idle. This way when the decels happened, the LAMBSEs didn't go as lean. I also sped up Closed Loop behavior by mucking with the HEGO functions so Closed Loop responded to lean conditions faster than it did rich conditions. Some might read that and wonder why I didn't just use HEGO Bias. The problem with HEGO Bias is you can't speed up lean response without slowing down rich response. I wanted rich response as responsive as it was, but lean response faster. To get that, I had to mess with the HEGO jump to/from and ramp rate functions. And when I was done, I got much faster response times from Closed Loop. So what used to take about 10 seconds for LAMBSEs to stabilize from was only about 3 seconds. Add in my MAF hacks to lean out low flow conditions and I pretty much had my lean tip-ins licked. Then Clint told me about the X3Z tune which had this magical thing called DFSO activated by default. Keep in mind, all this investigation was going on before there was a completely broken out GUFB def and most of us were still using TunerPro to tune and CalEdit/CalCon to write and datalog our TwEECers so we didn't have the same abilities we have with BE and the QH today. What DFSO got me was the ability to shut off the injectors (the ultimate lean condition) and force open loop which set the LAMBSEs at values I wanted them to be at when fuel was reactivated. It eliminated the problem caused by overly lean or overly rich decel by preventing the Closed Loop wind-up. It wasn't until a bit later that Clint got BE to write and datalog the TwEECer and we discovered the flaw in CalCon's conversion of Injector PWs. It was close enough to be believable, by far off enough that EEC Analyzer never calculated slope/bp values correctly leading many people to not trust EA...and at the time for good reason. But one Derek discovered this flaw, GUFx def files for BE were updated and suddenly EA calculated Injector Slope/BP exactly as it was supposed to allowing me to see and properly correct the overly rich condition with proper slope/bp/offset values. Even though the original problem is pretty much solved, I keep all my optimized settings for Closed Loop, DFSO, and MAF curve hacks purely because I think they still work better. Do I recommend others do what I do? No. But they've been working for me for many years now, so I'm not at all interested in changing it. Since all that, I made further tweaks to the HEGO functions and HEGO Bias to get me a very lean cruise which improved my fuel economy by 2 MPG points over stock settings. And as of last year, a member showed interest in using MFA (lean cruise) mode and we discovered more things in the GUFx defs that needed updating. Ever since then, I've been running MFA mode as well. While MFA may improve my fuel economy a little, it is just barely noticeable over my already leaned out Closed Loop settings I ran. But for the average person running stock values, I expect they should get the same 10% fuel economy improvement from MFA cruise too. No guarantees, but for anybody interested in better fuel economy, it's worth a shot trying. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: decel lean concern Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Apr 07, 2012 11:18 am There are 2 other possibilities for a misfire that are not spark related. Wrong fuel mix. Excessively rich or excessively lean mixes can also cause misfires or severely weakened combustion. All fuels have a characteristic refereed to as their limits of flammability. Fuel can only burn if the air-fuel ratio is in a certain range. When the mix is too lean, it can't sustain a flame to continue the combustion. This is where having a multi-spark ignition comes in handy. When the fuel is on edge, multiple attempts to fire off the fuel might mean the difference between a false-start and a just barely successful lite-off. You can also relate to this concept when you turn on a gas grill or gas stove. Before it lights, you often smell gas, but when it finally catches, the flame is only around the burner. If you let it run 15-20 seconds before igniting, it'll make a ball of gas around the pan, but you can smell the gas strong. Obviously there's gas all around including in your nose and lungs, but the flame only lights around the stove because Natural Gas and Propane have a fairly narrow limit of flammability on the lean side. The flame only travels as far as that limit of flammability exists. Likewise if there's too much fuel, the fuel won't burn even if there is oxygen present. For gasoline, this is usually because the fuel must be atomized to burn. Liquid gasoline DOES NOT burn. It's only the surface of the liquid that burns as it evaporates into the air. The liquid doesn't have enough oxygen within it to combust. As this relates to an engine if the fuel is the right amount, but entering the combustion chamber in floods or large droplets, not as atomized fuel, then it just won't burn right. The air mix around the plug is lean, but the fuel splashed everywhere is too rich. Now in a warm engine, even at decel, this is rather difficult to do since even whole droplets of fuel hitting hot valves & pistons isn't likely to stay liquid long at all. But you could still have the fuel too rich or too lean for it to combust. It's up to you to figure out which it is if you are confident this isn't an ignition problem. Possible problems are wrong Injector Offset function and/or too high of a low slope. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: decel lean concern Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Apr 07, 2012 12:11 pm If you feel like you are burning too much fuel even at cruise, then what cam are you running? You may be firing the injectors too early and loosing some of your fuel out the exhaust if you are running a "big" cam. On the other side, if the cam is mild (less than 220/220 duration 110-115 LSA) then you might benefit by trying different injector timing values. With smaller injectors that take a while to spray their payload of fuel, you often benefit by starting the spray before the intake valve opens but time it such that the spray is still happening after the valve is open and flowing air into the cylinder. However with BIG injectors, I also see the possibility that you are spraying TOO MUCH fuel at one time not giving it enough time to vaporize or simply spraying too much to evaporate off the valve and walls thus this trick can't be used and instead you need to hold off on spraying until the airflow is at max...that's at about 470 crank degrees. So with big injectors, you might experiment with moving timing around. Try it late, try it early and see if that helps any. At least, see if it makes any detectable difference in how much the WB reports. If the WB gets richer, you know you are going in the right direction. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: decel lean concern Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Apr 07, 2012 4:06 pm If there are voltage fluctuations, that might be alternator or it might be crappy grounds. Since the mid 90s, Ford started installing decently powered alternators in their vehicles. My 89 Ranger had a 40A alternator that couldn't hold the voltage above 12.5v with the brights and the blower motor on. If I was also cranking the stereo (big woofers), the headlights would dim to the bass. The 97 Explorer 5.0L I replaced the stock engine with has a 140A alternator. While it does still drop voltage a tad when I cranking the bass with the headlights and blower motor running, it doesn't drop nearly as much. And from what I understand, there's a 200A option I could upgrade to and be guaranteed to eliminate power source problems. But the 140A is good enough for me so I stick with it. Assuming your alternator is one of the newer style 3-bolt 140A alternators typical on serpentine setups, the problem is more likely caused by bad grounds. If in doubt, go overkill with additional grounds around the body, frame, to the engine and up to the battery. Ground loops are bad, but when you can't avoid them, the best way to get rid of their negative effects is to tie all ground sources together with lots of copper to ensure all critical ground lugs are being maintained at the same voltage...the voltage of the negative battery terminal. In review, install overkill grounds to the engine to the frame to the body and to battery. At that point, if you are still getting fluctuations in voltage, you know it isn't from gremlins in the ground. It's just a weak alternator. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Max Injector Duty Cycle Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Dec 09, 2011 7:58 am I wouldn't call them junk, but if you are referring to the older fat-body single pintle injectors, they certainly are not going to be as nice of a spray pattern and as accurate at fuel delivery as the modern day multi-hole injectors are like the Siemens Deka or the newer Bosch. Thus if you are buying new, I wouldn't waste my time on those older generation injectors. The older fat-body injectors are the ones people would pay extra for to get "flow-matched" because even brand new out of the box, they were notorious for being off their spec by 5-10%. That's according to one of the injector flow experts at Fuel Injector Connection (FIC) that I talked to. The newer injectors (both Siemens and Bosch) he said are so accurate out of the box, they'll be closer to each other than what he sells as flow-matched sets...usually within 1% of their rated spec. I took my set of 36lb Bosch used injectors in to FIC to test to make sure I didn't have any leakers or any that were poor performers. They are the newer style (skinny) injectors that have the 4 holes in the bottom. While testing, he said all 10 of the injectors I brought in were still right on spec and while there was some slight differentiation between them looking at the test-tubes, I had to get down level with the test-tubes to see it. He said the difference I was seeing was maybe 1% and thus they were close enough that if they were his injectors, he could easily pack them up and resell them as a flow-matched set as-is. It's easy to think that all injectors are the same. Their only difference is the rated fuel delivery. But as soon as you get them on a flow bench, you see immediately the difference in quality between older injectors and new purely by the spray patterns they produce. Older injectors tend to make more of a stream of fuel that may or may not be straight. Newer injectors tend to make a cone-shaped mist or fog rather than a semi-solid stream. Pull up some Youtube videos and see it for yourself. It's quite interesting to see just how different the spray patterns can be from brand to brand. So, if you are buying used or getting a good deal on someone's never-installed injectors, that's a different story. How much better will the modern injectors be? I couldn't really say without seeing the 42s you had in mind on a flow bench. But I do know the newer generation injectors are more accurate as well as much better fuel atomization...both characteristics that improve idle quality, fuel economy, and overall AFR stability. Does that mean the older style injectors are junk? You decide... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

They ASSUME you have a base of 10 degrees. Here's some example scenarios. If you have a 30 for spark advance in your tune, you should see a 30 with the timing light. I don't recall what the WOT function timing values are in an A9P (or an A9L for that matter) since I quit using that function quite some time ago. But if the A9P has a 22 for spark advance@3500, then that is correct. Also keep in mind the stock tunes are designed for 87 octane engines with a varied range of compression (they weren't as tight on tolerances back then). That's a big reason why 2 identical cars of the same make/year/model/engine/trans could perform noticeably different right off the showroom floor. For the past 30 years, engines have been gradually improving in tolerances bringing the performance variance of "identical" engines much closer together. I'd be very surprised if there is a 5% difference in performance for engines rolling off the assembly line today. I expect any variance in performance of "identical" new vehicles today has far more to do with the gas in the tank than with engineering/production tolerances of the engine and trans. But back to your topic, what a lot of people do is eliminate the WOT spark function altogether and tune spark purely out of the sealevel spark table. It became a popular thing to do on these older EECs, so I wrote an FAQ about how it is done along with other popular spark related tune mods to simplify spark tuning in GUFx EECs: FAQ->Simplifying timing on 89-93 Mustang 5.0L (GUFx) EECs ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: TexasRoadster
posts.content: TexasRoadster Gear Head Posts: 17 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2010 8:19 pm Location: Houston Re: EA Cam Spec Injector Timing table cell values Quote Post by TexasRoadster » Thu Jul 07, 2011 7:49 pm I think I have it figured out. Depending on which firing event is chosen (do you want your injectors to start firing when intake valve opens, exhaust valve closes, etc.) the values in the cells represent where in timing the injectors should fire. For example, if I set my injector events to start firing when the intake opens, and at .050 lift, my table value is calculated to be 24 degrees for 75% load at 5000 rpms. However, if I want my injectors to start firing when the exhaust valve closes, my timing value for the same load and rpm is now 84. At intake close, the value is 304. In simpleton terms, depending on when you want your injectors to start firing - intake open, exhaust close, TDC, etc. - affects where in the crank rotation (720 degrees total) your injectors need to start squirting fuel. With the 2003 Cobra 39lb injectors my AFR's were a mess; two weeks of hacking and I never got the tune dialed in. But there was some confusion about the use of yellow since the SAE standard color for Diesel was yellow. What added to the confusion is that so many gas stations display diesel with a green pump and green handle dispensers. Since the advent of E85, gas stations can no longer install green diesel pumps. All new diesel signs, pumps, and handles should now show diesel as yellow. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Understanding a "Rich idle" problem Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Sep 26, 2010 9:01 am I would think that being that high would be an indication that the CATs are toast. That's about the levels that the engine runs at without CATs. If you search around, you can find graphs of what typical engine emissions look like without CATs. As you would expect at rich conditions, the HC and CO is high. At lean conditions the NOx is high. Around stoic, both are lower than they are at rich/lean conditions, but still pretty significant...much much higher than what will pass a test. As soon as you put CATs on the car, the levels drop 5-10x non-CATed levels. Most pushrod engines with fairly hefty aftermarket cams just aren't efficient enough to burn off all the fuel that was fed to it. But newer engines with VVT can do a better job of burning off more of the fuel. The result is better fuel economy and lower HC emissions even before the CATs. So I'd say as much as you might not want to, cut the CATs out and look down into them. Make sure they don't look like this: In this pic, 2/3rds of the CAT batting is gone. And what's left shows the obvious signs of overheating due to running too rich for too long. Or worse: This was from the driver's side and was completely blown out. Even looking around the edges of this CAT housing had no batting what so ever. All this guy was doing was being a resonator in the exhaust line. As for your cam, a 70° overlap @.006" does sound like a lot. Cams this high at .006" are generally going to have a few degrees of overlap @.050" which is another source of HC loss due to scavenging out the exhaust port. Something you can try is delaying your Injector Firing until TDC or until after your exhaust valve has closed. If you do have scavenging of air/fuel out the exhaust, this will minimize the amount of raw fuel that is being scavenging. It won't eliminate it, but it will minimize it as much as possible. Also if you have scavenging of air and fuel into the exhaust, that would explain why you are showing a lean condition, when you may actually be running the engine rich. This could also explain CAT failure. CATs are designed to either finish the combustion of HC in an oxygen-starved environment (rich) or convert NOx back into O2 (oxygen) and N2 (nitrogen) in a lean burn condition. However when you throw raw fuel AND a bunch of unburned oxygen at the CATs, they will light up like gasoline on a bonfire and can overheat. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

That's the condition where a heavy overlap cam is going to have the worst effect on emissions. At least a loaded condition in the 1500-2500RPM range, you'll have enough exhaust to fill the void between the overlap. Lightly loaded like idle, is also when WBs are the most easily fooled by overlap cams. The biggest thing I can recommend is to shift your injector timing to sometime after TDC. Then probably force OL and lean it out further. You are probably running richer than the WB is indicating and you won't be able to sustain AFRs like that in Closed Loop. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Converting Bronco to SEFI Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon May 31, 2010 6:56 pm You'll need to hope real hard on that. Chances are you will have issues. They may not be major issues, but a 400M is not a 302 Cobra. Spark advance needs, displacement, expectation of EGR, warm-up enrichment needs, WOT enrichment needs, its all going to be different. Add to that, the EEC is going to be measuring the air and calculating that to an engine load value to determine spark advance, fueling, and a few other things. The amount of air the 400 can take in is going to be much higher than a 302 so the EEC is going to calculate engine load much higher than it actually is on the engine. The negative side-effect is that as you increase the throttle, the EEC will force Open Loop sooner and pull spark advance further than it really should for the actual engine load condition BOTH of which could severely hinder fuel economy and performance at non WOT conditions. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

The QH can do pretty much anything a TwEECer RT can and MORE for cheaper than you can get a new TwEECer RT. Although if you are getting a sweet deal on a TwEECer RT, then go for it. Just make sure what you are getting is a TwEECer RT and not a TwEECer Base. If it is a TwEECer Base, don't bother with it unless it is $50 or less. The TwEECer Base isn't going to get you datalogging, which is what you need to solve driveability issues. A TwEECer Base can be upgraded to a TwEECer RT, but it can only be done by Mike Glover and I believe he charges somewhere around $150 for it. Between that and buying a TwEECer Base, you'd be better off spending your money on the QH. All this is explained in that FAQ about what you need to know BEFORE buying a TwEECer or QH. title: CBAZA stock adaptive load scaling wrong - EECTuning.org

posts.author: decipha
posts.content: decipha CBAZA stock adaptive load scaling wrong Quote Post by decipha » Sun Jul 04, 2010 11:56 am The load scaling function for adaptive learning is not setup to max rows for the non cobra calibrations. Both the cobra and the Cobra R are scaled correctly using the 7th row as the maximum value. This doesn't pose a problem since you can't exceed 200 load but it sure is stupid. Just an observation that I thought would be an interesting read. T4M0 200.00 6 75.00 6 15.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 S4M1 200.00 6 75.00 6 15.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 FCL0 200.00 6 75.00 6 15.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 U4P0 200.00 6 75.00 6 15.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 J4J1 200.00 7 75.00 7 60.00 6 10.00 1 5.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 ZAO 200.00 7 75.00 7 60.00 6 10.00 1 5.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 0.00 0 Because of the 7th row not being accounted for in the scaling function the 7th row is the lowest value for row 6 divided by 2, so in the non-cobra bin's row 7 is 37.5 (75/2) above row 6 at 75, the adaptive update table looks like this non-cobra SPECIAL IDLE CELLS 37.5 75 65 55 45 35 25 15 COBRA SPECIAL IDLE 75 60 50 40 30 20 10 5 I recommend everyone use the COBRA scaling for FN021A, and also since adaptives are almost disabled at idle in the CBAZA strat, go 1 out the whole adaptive learning table FN1325 Top

Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jun 01, 2010 8:52 am My engine takes a good .75-1 second to crank. I've often wondered if I could increase this, but haven't found where the EEC is at fault for it taking this long. Spark and fueling are in as BASIC of a routine as can be during crank. Spark is fixed at 10°, and fueling is based on ECT, is generally VERY rich, and the injectors fired in a batch-fire scenario. There's not much to control. However something that caused my cranking to extend way out was when I upgraded my FPR to an aftermarket adjustable FPR. The stock FPR was capable of holding fuel pressure for hours after the fuel pump had turned off. However the adjustable FPR would bleed off fairly quickly. It couldn't hold fuel pressure more than about a second after the pump turned OFF. With a stock-sized pump, the fuel pump couldn't prime the system as fast as I could get the engine to turn over with the key. What I had to do to prevent long crank times was to turn the key ON and OFF a few times before actually cranking to prime the fuel lines. Then the engine would crank over like normal. I eventually got tired of doing that and replaced my stock 88lph fuel pump with an aftermarket 255lph fuel pump. That solved the long-crank issue for me, but created another problem that is almost as annoying. The higher flow fuel pump sucks fuel down too fast. So when my fuel level gets to about 1/4, I can't take sharp turns while accelerating. Doing so will cause the fuel to slosh to one side and to the back of my fuel tank. Truck gas tanks are thin and long with the fuel pump dead-center. The little bit of fuel held by the contours on the bottom of the tank are just not sufficient and the fuel pump runs right in the middle of the turn. And of course the engine falls flat until the fuel works its way back to the center of the tank and the pump reprimes. First couple of times it did this, I thought there was something electrically wrong. It wasn't until about the 10th time of it doing this that I associated hard accels, turns, and low fuel level as being the cause. Now it is quite predictable, but still annoying. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: EGR delete question Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 29, 2010 11:10 am I'm 99% sure the hot wire to the EGR is not controlled by the EEC. I think it is hard-wired power that gets supplied right along with all the other components on the same line like the TPS, Injectors, etc. Turning off the EGR logic simply tells the code to ignore that input and don't do control based on it. Although I would expect the amount of current the fan is pulling would be WAY too much for the EGR hot line to supply. That's intended to be a low load line...certainly not intended to supply the multiple amps needed to run a fan. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

I will probe for a suitable 12v power source to reconnect it that is not part of the main EFI harness. Thanks for the replies! Scott The EEC basically provides a ground to turn on the fan relay. So you run a fused battery hot to the relay, then a key on hot. The relay has a ground on the other side of the key on hot basically so the relay is the only thing you are feeding with the EEC ground. So if your fan controller requires a small ground to activate you can probably just use that. - This assumes the fan has it's own ground to the chassis. Do not confuse the two as it can damage the EEC to connect the fan to the EEC wire that provides the switched ground. PIN 41 is what you want for that on the EEC. see this for instructions http://www.fordfuelinjection.com/?p=20 A direct link for the sheet. http://www.fordfuelinjection.com/files/ ... posts.content: decipha Re: EGR delete question Quote Post by decipha » Sun May 16, 2010 11:50 am that's because the code was written in for vehicles that did come equipped with electric fans like the 89+ supercoupes, the mustang already had a mechanical fan so there was no point in spending all that money to adapt an electric fan to it, since ford likes to update all their ecu's as they go, the mustangs inherited the code for it and even the hardware if you have any questions about ford just look at the thunderbird its fords R&D vehicle it gets all the good stuff before put into production for example: it was their first supercharged car and in 95 they made a few with the 4.6 supercharged that they later put in the cobra's EXACT REPLICA of what the thunderbird had in 92 ford put a cbaza based strategy in the ecu's which wasn't released to the mustang crowd until 94-95 in 89 Henry put the independent rear suspension in the back of the thunderbird which is THE SAME IRS in the 99+ cobra's in 2001 ford came back with the thunderbird after dropping the line in 97, the new thunderbird was a retro designed to mimic the 50s and 60s thunderbirds, based off the success and sales of the thunderbird they later designed the 2005 mustang to be a retro and mimic the 60s mustangs what most people fail to realize is that the thunderbird is the mustangs older brother, thunderbirds were made in 1955 to compete with the corvette's the mustang wasn't released until 1964-1/2 Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: MAF question Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Dec 02, 2009 7:51 pm Relying on the calibration between the MAF and Injectors is never recommended when you have the ability to tune the EEC. The MAF/Injector calibration is used as a poor-man's tune. When upgrading from 19s to 24s, the effects are fairly benign. But as the upgrade gets more and more significant, the negative effects are more noticeable. The main downside to relying on the calibration is that the EEC's calculation of Load is wrong. The EEC will be calculating load at say 40% when actual load is well above that, but the EEC will continue to command the spark it associates to 40% which is not often what you want. Same is true of every other Load-based adjustment the EEC makes. This is particularly important for EECs that control an automatic transmission. Having the EEC believe the engine load is at 40% when the actual engine load is much higher will burn up a stock transmission because the EEC won't firm up the shifts to correspond with the actual engine load. The fact that the engine's output capabilities are higher than stock (hence the need for larger injectors) further endangers a stock or near-stock tranny. In contrast, when the EEC knows the actual MAF curve and actual Injector size, you remove the "calibration" relationship and allow the EEC to know about the actual amount of air being aspirated and thus the EEC can calculate a more accurate Load. If the displacement of the engine has increased, then the actual torque output for a given Load percentage will be higher and thus you'll need to modify the tranny shifting parameters in the tune to firm up the shifts at lower Loads even if you put the correct MAF/Injector info into the tune. But even with the Injector Slope/BP values in the tune, often the EEC doesn't get it right either because the MAF curve isn't quite right and/or the Injector parameters need some attention or you've forgotten to change something in the tune like the Injector Offset curve. So yes, replacing the stock MAF curve and Injector parameters takes more time-n-effort to get dialed in, but it is the right way to do it...assuming you care. If you don't care and are happy with the way running the stock MAF curve and Slopes runs things, then do whatever you think is best for your setup based on your intentions. After all, you are the one that has to drive and maintain the car, not me or anybody else on the forum. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: MAF question Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Dec 04, 2009 9:06 am When you have the ability to tune the EEC, the whole concept of "calibrated" MAFs goes right out the window. Don't even think about it anymore. Just use the actual MAF curve and actual Injector parameters. However knowing an aftermarket MAF's intended "calibration" can be useful just for the reassurance that the MAF will not be undersized for the injectors you are running. Thus if you run 42s and get a MAF cal'd for 42s, you can be confident that the MAF will be properly sized to work with 42s, even though you won't be taking advantage of the "calibrated" aspect. And yes the LMAF is a common meter because it works well with 42s. Even though it isn't "calibrated" for them, its max flow is in the range of 42lb injectors making an LMAF and 42lb injectors a good match for an application that will get a custom tune. Since you will have a datalogging device and a WB, you'll be able to sort out most any AFR issues you have over time. The main things you want from the dyno guy are: The AFR, with reference to your WB, that your engine produces HP at best. The Spark Advance that your engine produces MBT (Max Brake Torque) at. For #1, I say use your WB as a reference because you won't have his WB when you leave. So if he finds that his WB displays 12.6 AFR when your engine produces the best, but your WB indicates 12.3, then in the future, you know you need to be targeting 12.3. The number his WB was saying is irrelevant. For #2, MBT is something you can't detect easily without a dyno. People often associate the max possible advance without ping as the engine's MBT, as though you ALWAYS get more power with more spark. With low grade gas or a high compression engine, that can be an acceptable method of tuning spark. But with higher octane fuel, you can actually over-advance the spark beyond MBT and loose performance that you would've had commanding a lower spark advance. To find MBT without ping getting in the way, you'll need to go to the dyno with a high octane fuel. If the highest octane you ever plan to run is 93 pump gas, then go there with that. If the tuner hits ping before hitting MBT, then so be it. You know what the max torque you can produce with the fuel you plan to use is. But if you ever plan to run E85 or some high octane racing gas, then you'll want it tuned with that so he can find MBT without the engine pinging before he can get to MBT. If this will be a frequently driven vehicle that you would like to get good fuel economy with, then you'll also want the tuner to find MBT for non-WOT conditions as well so he'll need to run the engine at say 30% Load from idle to ~4000 RPMs to find the spark advance that produces the best torque output while maintaining a 30% Load on the datalog. Then do that again for 40%, 50%, and 60% Load (the common loads attained while cruising in Closed Loop). Once you've gotten the Closed Loop cruising MBT spark values, you can be certain the engine will get the best possible fuel economy that can be gotten from spark tuning. Later on, you can test the engine with lower octane fuels to see how they run on your tune. It's quite possible that 89 octane mid-grade will suffice without pinging too badly. But you will likely find that 87 octane pings with the tune you got at the dyno using the high octane gas. So to run 87, you can always adjust the advance DOWN to avoid ping for cheaper gas. This will lower the performance and responsiveness of the engine if you have to pull much spark, but at least you get to run the cheaper gas. But what you'll need to find out is if the cheaper gas is really cheaper on your wallet. When you can't run an MBT spark advance due to ping, you loose fuel economy because the engine can't produce as much torque for the same amount of fuel going in. What you'll need to determine is if the cheaper price at the pump is worth the fuel economy loss. Ultimately what you want is the best Mile/$, not necessarily the best Mile/Gallon. So lets analyze a theoretical scenario just to see how its done. Lets say you get: 20 MPG with 87 octane 22 MPG with 93 octane With 87 octane at $2.50/gal and 93 octane at $2.80/gal, which is really the best Mile/$? 20 MPG / ($2.50/gal) = 8 Miles/$ 22 MPG / ($2.80/gal) = 7.86 Miles/$ With current gas prices, the 87 octane fuel is best even though the MPG is lower. But what if gas was $4.00 for 87 and $4.30 for 93? 20 MPG / ($4.00/gal) = 5 Miles/$ 22 MPG / ($4.30/gal) = 5.11 Miles/$ Suddenly the fuel economy benefits of running 93 actually make sense and make driving cheaper even though you pay more per gallon at the pump. Hopefully at this point it is obvious that as the price of gas goes higher, the cheaper premium becomes. Also notice I'm putting a $.30 spread between regular and premium because that's what it is here in Atlanta. If you live in an area where the spread is only $.20 between regular and premium, then premium becomes the better deal at an even lower price point for you. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: POPSRACING
posts.content: POPSRACING Professional Tuner/Shop Owner Posts: 620 Joined: Fri Mar 20, 2009 11:58 am Location: Rochester, NY Contact: Contact POPSRACING Website Re: Problems with reading eec from 98 Mark VIII Quote Post by POPSRACING » Sun Jan 24, 2010 8:20 am You have listed CMBA0 whick is 4 bank strategy and CZAJL which is 1 bank strategy, 98 processors generally are 4 bank (with the excepption of a few that are 2bank). If you load a single bank calibration in a 4 bank strategy most values will appear maxed due to null data (FF FF FF FF and so on). There is a chance Ford disabled the J3 port on the processor as many 98-99 processors had this issue. If that's the case, pop open the EEC V processor and look on the backside near the J3 port after removing the mainboard from the housing. At this point you may see two sets of contacts that need to be soldered together, doing this will enable the port. Feel free to give me a shout at 585.802.6911. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Needing some afr advice Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Aug 18, 2009 7:22 am A Stoic burn is what you aim for on injected vehicles when the engine can handle it at idle, cruising, and moderate acceleration. The HEGOs feed back info about whether the mix is above or below stoic, and the computer just keeps trimming and responding the fuel mix to keep the HEGO(s) bouncing between slightly rich and slightly lean. When you can tweak the computer, you can dictate whether the EEC favors slightly rich or slightly lean. By default, the older computers favor the rich side and make up the difference with a smog pump to "lean it out" for the CATs. But the newer computers tend to favor lean since that gets better fuel economy. The problem is that running on the lean side generally causes higher NOx emissions, but EGR, better CATs, ethanol in the fuel we burn, and new engine designs have helped reduce the NOx. The problem with EFI control on "built" engines is that at idle, a heavy overlap cam can leak unburned intake air into the exhaust causing the exhaust at idle to always appear leaner than it really is. This confuses the EEC and causes the EEC to run the engine way richer than it should often resulting in idle instability. The most common solution for this is to simply run the idle RPMs high enough that this doesn't happen. But this is wasteful with fuel so people that have access to their EEC's tune will often force Open Loop while idling and manually command the fuel mix that runs the engine smooth. The HEGOs and even a Wideband O2 (aka WB) will scream that the mix is running lean, but it isn't. It's just the cam screwing with them at low RPMs. With a carb, you don't have this kind of real time positive feedback to control the AFRs so precisely. So the best you can do is tune carb to idle the engine smooth without rich-idle hunting and setup the carb as close to stoic as you can while cruising. As long as you aren't intermittently going so lean that the engine surges and hesitates on accels or while floating the engine (i.e. going down hills or deceling to a stop), most people will never notice that the engine is running slightly rich or slightly lean. In the carb world, close enough is good enough 99% of the time. Now at heavy acceleration and WOT, you generally run richer than stoic because a richer burn produces better max power and also runs the burn cooler at a time when the heat production in the engine is at its peak. Most naturally aspirated engines will run between 12.0-13.0 AFR depending on the engine. The vast majority of engines produce max power at 12.5 AFR. To know for sure what the optimal AFR is, you need a dyno to give you instant feedback as to whether enriching or leaning the mix is producing more or less power. But generally the minor gains you get from "fine tuning" AFR is not going to get you more than a few HP as compared to just getting the AFR to 12.5 and leaving it at that. You generally run forced induction engines in the 10.5-12.3 AFR range depending on how much boost is being applied. Lightly boosted engines can stay on the high side of 11s and possibly even low 12s. But when you start getting much above about 5 PSI, you are pretty much required to be in the mid 11s. Once boost is in the 10-15 PSI range, you tune for lower 11s. In all these cases, you are not tuning AFRs for max HP, but rather for combustion cooling. Leaning out the mix could actually produce more power but runs the combustion temps way too high for safety. Thus the added fuel is being used purely for combustion temp control. This is why anybody that adds an aftermarket supercharger to their engine and is planning on more than a few PSI of boost should have a WB as part of their arsenal of tools and gadgets to make sure the engine is burning at the right mix. Ideally, boosted applications would have an exhaust temp sensor too, but its been proven time and time again that gasoline burning boosted engines can maintain adequate exhaust temps purely by controlling the AFR, so having a WB is sufficient as long as you have access to the vehicle's fuel control and actually tune the engine for "safe" AFRs. And of course, if you are in doubt about whether the AFR is safe for your engine at WOT, run it richer rather than leaner. Running richer wastes gas, but running leaner burns exhaust valves and melts pistons. Note, all this is my interpretation of things I've read from other members of this forum and various articles over the years. Hopefully this info is what you need, but some of it may be bogus. I'll leave it to the others on this forum to point out whats legit and what's engine folklore. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

That's been one of the biggest reasons we've been so reluctant to consider an ARM for our hardware because our entire platform is based on Big Endian processing. Although I have heard that the Motorola PowerPCs can be setup for Little Endian. I guess it would make sense that ARMs could be configured for Big Endian. Yeah the only time endian even comes into play is when you are dealing with network communications OR with unions. Generally Big Endian is easier to work with in embedded devices that are heavy on network communications because most all network streams are in Big Endian format. Thus Big Endian processors will layout data in memory in the same order as the data is streamed in/out over a network. On a little endian platform, every byte-pair has the bytes in reverse order as compared to a networked byte-stream. So if you stream out data to a network byte-by-byte, you have to take the "endian" into account just as you found. If there was 1 thing in the Computer Science world I wish industry would standardize on, it would be to have 1 endian standard for processors as well as network com. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: HEGO Bias, understanding what I'm seeing Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Jun 19, 2009 1:07 pm donc wrote: Question 1: The "Load" values (75.00 down to 5.00 on the left hand side of the table) Are these actual load as shown in the data log or load% as shown in the data log? According to the GUFB doc, it is Load, not Load%. Although I would've thought it would be Load% since this is a fuel-related parameter. But I won't argue with the GUFB doc in this matter. donc wrote: Question 2: The values in the table I would assume that 0.0000 represents no bias but I don't know what the + and - represent. Do they represent values above(+) and below(-) stoich (around 4.25 in the data log)? What do the values themselves (example 0.1000 or -0.1000) represent? Are these values Volts added to or subtracted from the ~4.25 stoich or do they represent some other value? They represent average AFR from stoic. So a bias of 0 should result in an average AFR of stoic. However a value of say .25 should average about .25 points above stoic (14.64 + .25) or biasing lean. Likewise a -.25 value would bias rich (14.64 - .25). This only holds true at stabilized driving conditions. But the purpose of HEGO Bias is far more than just the average AFR that is to be targeted during stabilized conditions. The real need for bias is to cover for transient conditions when the EEC returns to Closed Loop from a rich OL/WOT condition or gets all messed up and the mix is bad rich or bad lean. Unless you are idling, most people never notice a rich condition in progress except maybe at the pump if it lasts long enough. However you are quick to notice when things get too far lean. Much over about 15.5 AFR, and you start feeling the engine loosing power. Once you are above 16 AFR, you start feeling the hesitation and bucking. From about 18 and up, you can get popping up the intake. The HEGO Bias is strategically assigned to communicate to the EEC which mix you really want corrected for quick. So at idle, you might actually prefer a lean bias since the engine can idle OK at 16 AFR, but idles like crap at 13 or below. Although the engine runs like crap when at positive thrust and it goes lean. And of course, pure decels don't matter if they are rich or lean to the driver. So HEGO Bias is an indication as to how aggressively the EEC should effort to correct a Rich or Lean condition. With a HEGO Bias of 0 (no bias), the EEC will effort to correct a lean mix just as fast as it efforts to correct a rich one. The catch is at 0 Bias, it doesn't really effort very fast to correct either one with stock HEGO function settings. If the EEC is biasing rich at some point and the HEGO indicates Lean, then the EEC will lower the LAMBSEs much faster than it would raise the LAMBSEs if the HEGO was indicating rich since a rich bias indicates you'd rather be rich than lean. The stronger the bias towards rich, the FASTER the EEC will correct for a lean condition AND the SLOWER it'll correct a rich condition. Vice-versa with a lean bias. The trouble with this method is you can't speed up the EEC's response to a lean condition without slowing the rich condition response using only HEGO Bias. To get that, you have to delve into the HEGO functions which get complicated, cryptic, and difficult to understand. But I've done the best I can explaining them in the comments sections. Its also worth mention that the narrow band HEGOs are only responsive from around 14.3-15 AFR. I wouldn't expect HEGO Bias values that would result in an average outside this range or even close to this range's limits to be accurate. Putting in a value to target say 12 AFR is certainly useless. The EEC has no way to know if it is hitting 11, 12, 13 or 14 AFR. To the EEC, it's all "rich" with no indication of severity. The true table is the normal HEGO Bias table that follows very specific formulas in the EEC as defined by the GUFB document. The HEGO Bias (AFR View) is an alternate view of the same exact table. Thus changes you make in one will be seen in the other. The AFR View is approximation of average AFRs and quickly becomes inaccurate/unreliable as you target AFRs farther from stoic. But it was left in because people can relate to it a little easier than they can the normal table. donc wrote: Question 3: How much is a little or a lot? Reading other posts on the HEGO Bias they make reference to "bias towards rich or lean". What constitutes a significant change in the values? Would changing a value from -0.1000 to -0.1500 be a significant change and, referring to question 2 above, would it tend to make CL run richer or leaner? As for what's a lot of bias. the -.1 to -.15 is a slight bias. A HEAVY Bias is anything in the -.3 to .-4 range. Likewise a slight lean bias is .1 to .15. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top
