cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: HEGO Bias, understanding what I'm seeing Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Jun 19, 2009 6:23 pm donc wrote: Does HEGO bias effect only CL or are the values used in OL as well? HEGO Bias only has a direct effect on things at Closed Loop. Since HEGOs are ignored in OL, none of the HEGO controls do anything at Open Loop. Now the influences HEGO Bias, and the other HEGO controls have at Closed Loop, can have an effect on OL via the KAMRFs...but VERY little effect. Nothing of great significance at all. I certainly wouldn't go looking in the HEGO controls for the cause of a problem in Open Loop. donc wrote: ...Assuming everything else is normal and the engine is running lean at a given range, would altering the HEGO Bias work as a factor in correcting that condition? It could, but not without a good bit of tinkering and understanding. 99% of people tune and have never touch any of the HEGO controls or if they touch something, it's only the HEGO Delay table to adjust for Long Tune Header propagation delays. I would even go so far as to say if you are doing much more than HEGO Delay and minor changes in the HEGO Bias table, you have some other problem you are trying to tune around instead of fixing. However if you are having very specific problems that you think Closed Loop can help solve, as I did, then it is possible you can fix a problem by retasking HEGO Bias, Amplitude, Delay, and the HEGO functions in a way that will correct a leanout by allowing Closed Loop to be faster on the reaction to Lean conditions, but without sacrificing the snappiness that the EEC responds to rich conditions. But to do this effectively is not an easy task and pretty much requires hours of trial-n-error messing around with things until you get a clear picture as to what problems can be fixed and caused by changing HEGO parameters. I'm not discouraging anybody from messing with these parameters. I'm just saying that most of the time, a Closed Loop leanout can be solved in other ways. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: question on ZA0 bin Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Jun 03, 2009 2:28 pm When the slopes are equal, the breakpoint has no meaning. Breakpoint becomes more active in the mix the further different the high and low slopes get. So if you have slopes of say 42H/46L, the breakpoint will have little effect. You could change the breakpoint by whole numbers and it wouldn't have that much effect. But if you had say 19H/46L, the breakpoint would be much more significant and SLIGHT adjustments to the breakpoint by .1 could make noticeable differences in fueling. The whole concept of how breakpoint plays out is very complicated and difficult to wrap your mind around. I've taken a stab at explaining this and put it in the Tech Docs section for when this question comes up. posts.content: bender460 Tuning Addict Posts: 393 Joined: Thu Sep 07, 2006 12:29 am Re: Need help understanding some tuning points Quote Post by bender460 » Thu Mar 26, 2009 1:18 pm Your idle tuning needs a little refining. First it is not the lowest rpm the engine will stay running at. It is guessing here but 100-150rpm below the idle you have set in the tune. Depends on many factors and key components "tuned in". Here is a cut and paste of the procedure I use with good results it should get you going in the right direction. There is a better procedure I will try to find it. The throttle body airflow idle scalar is the amount of air flowing through the throttle body when closed without added air from the ISC. To adjust the parameter, I warmed the car up, disconnected the ISC, pulled the spout connector and set timing to 18* (because I want 18* timing at idle) in order to lock in timing. I then turned the throttle set screw to the lowest possible idle my car would maintain.Usually 100-150 below setting in tune. I then set the TPS to .95. Then I datalogged the airflow for about 1 min. I opened the datalog with Excel and averaged the idle speed and MAF flow, converted the result from kg/hr to lb/min, and input that parameter. The ISC function is the amount of air flowing through the ISC at XX duty cycle. What I did here was write down each duty cycle shown in the ISC transfer function. The first DC that flows air in my table was .28, so I input .28 into the entire column so I would have .28 DC no matter what the EEC tried to do. Again with the SPOUT disconnected and timing locked in I datalogged airflow with the ISC connected. This gave me my total airflow at .28 DC. I then repeated this for every DC in the function. Once I had all the data I averaged the idle again, then averaged the airflow. I converted to lb/min, and subtracted the throttle body base airflow from the result. This gave me the airflow in lb/min of the ISC at each duty cycle. I then populated the ISC function with my results. After this is done, you can take the total airflow number for both the TB and ISC with your averaged RPM and populate the neutral and drive idle air functions. Now the EEC knows how much air is flowing through the TB and how much extra air each duty cycle of the ISC will result in. stock block 347, highports, CI TLSR C-4 8" 4500 stall, 3.90 8.8 Super victor efi intake, 03 cobra 39lb injectors 4500 Wilson TB Speed density setup with a Map-Ecu 1 3/4 kooks- 3" dumps, a9lL/Map-Ecu, Tweecer Techedge wideband 11.19 at 120.... Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Mar 18, 2009 11:23 am There are some Ford strategies that did try to do away with the 2-slope strategy. But they brought it back. So it had use and merit. The reason for the low slope was to adjust for a non-linear behavior of the injectors at low PW conditions. The easiest way to handle this was to simply treat the injector as a smaller or larger injector when the commanded fuel weight was a less than a certain amount. However the Injector Offset curve also does a similar thing. It compensates for differences in injector behavior over a voltage range. Naturally since injectors are mechanical devices, they will behave differently when given 14v (running) vs given 11v (bad battery and/or heavily loaded electrical system). So the Injector Offset curve makes up for this. However this curve CAN also make up for the other differences seen with injectors. Although I expect the low slope was kept in the mix just because it is easier to correct for small PW differences using a low slope and BP than it is to adjust the Injector Offset curve up and down. I'd really love to know more about Ford's procedures and testing methods to come up with accurate Slope/BP/Offset parameters for production injectors. That info could go a long way towards helping us. But for now, we have dataloggable devices and EEC Analyzer to analyze the logs from those devices and guide us on how to adjust the Slopes and Injector Offset curves. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: EV6 24lb inj slopes, voltage offset, breakpoint? Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Mar 18, 2009 1:24 pm The Injector Offset is nothing more than an adder to the calculated Injector PW. The purpose here is as stated before to compensate for differences in Injector behavior as voltage changes. However that's all it is supposed to do is make up the DIFFERENCE in behavior between various voltages. Thus it's the shape of the curve that really is important when dealing with Injector Offset. However because the lowest PW value (the value at the highest voltage) on the Injector Offset curve is not 0, there's a "constant" adder component to the Injector Offset curve that you can increase or reduce. I call it a constant adder because it is always there regardless of voltage. That adder component to the Injector Offset curve is adding additional ON time to the final calculated Injector ON time, which is adding more fuel obviously. As the Injector PW ON time gets smaller, the more significant that adder becomes which makes the injectors seem larger than they really are at lower PWs...because more fuel is getting added than was calculated thanks to that fixed PW adder. It's that component that I believe the low slope is trying to "cancel out". However if you just manually reduce all points on the Injector Offset curve by the same amount, you reduce that "adder" component and thus reduce the amount the low slope needs to be compensating for which brings the low slope closer to the high slope. Ideally each point on the Injector Offset curve will only be large enough to make up for the mechanical delay between when the EEC commanded the injector ON and when the injector actually began spraying it's rated fuel flow as well as compensate for any additional fuel the injector might spray AFTER the EEC commanded the injector OFF. And as discussed, the amount of PW compensation is dependant on the voltage going to the injectors at any given moment. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

However it by itself isn't going to cause driveability problems, it just won't make torque where a smaller intake would. The thing that will make the biggest effect on your driveability will be your cam. Next would be your MAF's intake track. Any bends or sharp edges near the MAF will affect how even the flow will be through the MAF. I know the streetable Trick Flow Twisted Wedge head. And the more strip-oriented TF Track Heat version of those heads? But I'm not familiar with the TF TEA heads. Are those a "race" head that complements the Box R intake? So that being said, what cam and injectors are you planning on? I have no feel for how much HP this combination can make. But being a 408w, you'll have a lot of HP potential but you'll have to blueprint and balance the heck out of the engine to get into the 6000+RPM range a "race" intake and cam is going to want to run the engine. Most big displacement engines don't handle going much above 5000RPMs without very specialize parts like all-forged bottom end, high RPM flywheel & balancer, and an excellent balancing job by an experienced machine shop. That being said, if all your parts are "race" oriented, putting a mild torque cam in there is going to be a bad mis-match of parts. But if you "matched" all the parts to be a race application, then low RPM torque is going to be something you just aren't going to have a lot of. The fact that it's a 408w will help, but a high RPM cam will generally have a lot of reverberation (i.e. intake air being blown back into the intake) at lower RPMs. The higher the CID of the engine, the more reverb there'll be with the same H/C/I combo. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Hi injector pw and low duty cycle Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jul 15, 2008 7:34 pm Hitting 20ms@3500RPMs doesn't mean you are maxing out your injectors. That's far from maxed out. Hitting 20ms@6000RPMs is a bad thing...that's 100% duty cycle. Remember, the PW isn't what's important. What's important is the duty cycle value and as long as you are below 90ish, you are still safe. Ideally, you won't be above 80s. But as long as you aren't peaking 100%, you are ok. More about InjPW...the InjPW will track with your torque curve. Thus your PW will increase as your torque curve increases. However once your torque curve peaks (generally in the 3800-4000RPMs for a stock motor), the PW will begin to decrease as RPMs continue above the torque peak. So by the time you hit 6000RPMs, the PWs should be well below 20ms on a stock motor with 19lb injectors. But most stock motors don't do well past about 5000RPMs and as long as the PW is not much above 20ms@5000RPMs, you should be fine. Again, the Duty Cycle will tell you everything you need to know. When sizing injectors, you aim to produce a max Duty Cycle of 80%. However as long as you are below 90ish%, all is still OK. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Hi injector pw and low duty cycle Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jul 15, 2008 7:54 pm Now that's something completely different. All that means is that the RPM/Load is too large to guarantee the injector fires when you say you want the Injector Fire to start and that's normal. In fact, even with very large Injectors, it's fairly impossible to squirt all the fuel needed in the time between when the Intake Valve Opens to when it Closes. Once the RPM/Load gets up to that point, you have to accept that you will need to allow the injector to fire earlier than your setting. You do that by simply clipping all the values in the list to some max. Typical clip value is around 550...so anywhere EA calculates a value higher, enter 550 instead. The effect is the injector will simply fire sooner...but that's what you want. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Hi injector pw and low duty cycle Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jul 15, 2008 8:09 pm What is your cam? 597° seems a little late to stop the injectors. Even with a fairly aggressive cam, the intake valve is closed pretty far by then and thus any additional fuel that's still spraying at that point may not get into the cylinder. Most cams do well with a value of 540-560°, but I'm curious what your cam is. 327° sounds like when an intake valve opens to .050". The injector should've been firing way before that if this is a mild, non-overlap cam to get the smoothest idle. Most mild cams that will allow you to fire the injector early can let you run the injector START time in the 200s. The stop time you enter in the table will be as low as 280s at the lower RPM/Loads. Like I said, once the RPM/Loads get high enough that they hit your 550° limit, the start time will begin backing up. But again, that's inevitable and not a problem. Think about it like this, max duty cycle of 80% is considered very acceptable for an injector. If the injector is firing 80% of the time, that means MOST of the fire is being done while the intake valve is closed...yes closed. Here's how it breaks down, there's 2 rotations of the crank per cycle giving you a total of 720° degrees for a complete cycle. 80% (duty cycle) of 720° is 576°...thus the injector is firing for all those degrees. Most mild cams have the intake valve open for less than 220°@.050". But lets assume this is an E303 which has a duration of 220°@.050". If the intake valve is only open for 220°, then that means 356° of the time, the injector is firing on a closed intake valve. At light to moderate loads, that wouldn't be a good thing. But for WOT, the air flow is so heavy and turbulent that any pooled fuel will atomize into the air without much trouble. posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Wed Apr 23, 2008 11:55 am As a starting point I would set the high slope to 89.95 lb/hr (this is the rated flow adjusted for the difference in base fuel pressure). Then start off with the low slope at 94.5 lb/hr and see how that works out. The breakpoint is used to determine the intersection point of the two injector slopes. At small fuel flows only the low slope is used but both are used as the flow increases with the low slope having a diminishing effect as flow increases. It is a tricky one to get right, I certainly do not know how it is calculated by Ford. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 31, 2008 10:23 am In my case last year, the problem was a bad connection between the MSD box and the TFI module. This was causing the motor to intermittently run and not run. Sometimes it would work and not work a few times a second which felt something similar to a misfire. The computer and TFI module continued to work perfectly during these conditions, but the MSD box was simply not getting the signal from the TFI to fire the coil so it never fired the coil or my tach (stupid spade connectors got corroded). Since I have my tach on the MSD's tach-tap, I could see my Tach dump to 0 when the motor would cut out, but my datalogs continued to run including the RPMs updating (I have a manual tranny). This is how I knew it was NOT an EEC issue. A few months later, the EEC relay went bad. This was causing low-voltage conditions on the EEC. At low-Injector PWs, the motor would crank and run, but the CEL would be dimly lit. As soon as I hit the gas, the motor would cut out due to lean condition BUT I still had spark during the outage. I eventually found it was the EEC relay. It was the original relay from 1989 so it was time to be replaced. What was running the EEC was the small amount of current it could pull from the ignition power line which is NOT intended to be the EEC's main power source. The power coming from the EEC relay is. In your case, the computer is dieing completely. Which means, it's not just getting low-volt conditions (the computer can continue to run and operate down to ~5v). It's getting a no-volt condition OR is being told to turn off because the ignition line from the ignition switch is going dead. Note the power from the ignition switch and the power from the EEC relay are two different voltage sources for the EEC. On my harness, the EEC relay was located down by the EEC. My EEC is in the passenger-side kick panel. The EEC relay is tucked in there with all the other mass of wires coming through the firewall. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: BobCat Professional Tuner/Shop Owner Posts: 447 Joined: Thu Apr 13, 2006 3:19 pm Contact: Contact BobCat Website Yahoo Messenger Quote Post by BobCat » Thu Jan 31, 2008 11:18 pm With methanol you should be able to run 25-27* which will be right around MBT for that combo. The 2.5 pulley on the T is a waste though as you'll never keep if from slipping. Anything smaller than 2.75 is a joke and 90% of the time you will get more boost/less slippage from a 3.0 Renegade than the std 2.75. If more boost is desired a larger crank pulley will really wake things up. The 8.0 crank 3.0 upper is a killer combo and is what i run on almost everything. I wouldn't attempt to run any more than 20* w/ 18psi on 93 Octane w/ 10:1 compression. In fact I wouldn't run that combo at all without Meth or race fuel. Also when I tune w/ Meth I tune it to 12.0 and then add meth till it's 11.0. Normally this is the point at where power will start falling off if you attempt to add more Meth. If the owner is careful you can tune to 12.5 then to 11.5 w/ meth and it will pickup some more power but at the expense of being on the edge. Quote Post by patrickmx2 » Fri Nov 30, 2007 2:22 pm 88beast wrote: Hello all. I have been lurking around for a few weeks and finally registered and have been reading furiously in anticipation of my tweecer. Finally got it, downloaded BE and EA, and started editing the base A9P tune. So I am looking for anyone to look over what I did and just give me a thumbs up or thumbs down. So here is what I did: loaded ProM-30 MAF transfer set Injector High slope 30 set Injector Low slope 36 Changed OL fuel multiplier to 1.1016 to lean out curve for now changed Injector offset vs. batt volt using the ford 30# numbers from EA Forced OL for now because my exhaust is being re-made And that's it. I should be getting my registration codes for BE and EA tomorrow (thanks 86GT) so I'll do some more stuff then. How'd I do?? Setup: A9P, 302, F303 cam, 1.6 hydraulic rollers, Windsor JR heads, Edelbrock performer upper and lower intake ported to match heads, 30# injectos, Pro-M 75mm, 70mm TB with EGR, stock fuel rails, MSD Pro Billet dizzy.... I'm sure everyone has their preferred method but all arrive close to the same place. Some longer/quicker than others but similar tuning in the end. That said it has been my experience to start with your stock tune of course pulled right out of the EEC. Leave the MAF transfer Stock. Since you have direct access to it there is no sense in loading anything from PRO-M. It is going to change anyway when you trim it up using the EA. My preferred method is to tune with a wide band in full time open loop. I have done it with out it but at $200 it was cheaper to install an LC-1 wide band than to account for the time in labor it was to tune without it. I mean if you make a nickel an hour you might save money not buying a wide band. Until I owned one I never really saw a great need for it. Now I own two, one for each car. - The EA can use the wide band data to trim up your MAF. I would leave the OL modifier alone. Else you'll always be tuning around it and it will influence all your decisions. Then when you set it back to stock all your data will suffer for the difference. BUT I do see why you did it short term. I set PRLDSW Air - Load Scaling Switch (Percent Load) =1 Since I'm naturally aspirated I like dealing with load values that are actual. (thanks to Clint that has worked better for me). In fact my E303 motor nearly hits 100% and with scaling it seems the EEC is always on some other part of the table. Scaling is like grading on a curve anyway. Do some searching here for the topic LOAD. We have beat that one to death on here. Now on my E303 motor I started out with 19lb injectors. I wanted to work with those later. Heck my stock Explorer motor in my other car maxed out the 19's but I didn't want to tackle that just yet with the 36's. I allow my CBAZA car to hit CL only at cruise loads. Idle is OL. Even with HEGO Bias the idle isn't as stable as I like with the E303 cam and 1.7 rocker. In OL it idles like a stock Mustang should. The main thing is this last point and I'll use this disclaimer. This is how I do it and most any other way simply seems to take longer. Dial in the MAF transfer FIRST. Just go ahead and set up your CID which is stock, EGR, Thermactor, injector size for what you are running. Leave everything else alone because you'll have plenty of bugs to work out later. Datalog about 10 miles and export your Stock MAF transfer out of the BE and feed (import) it to the EA. Let the EA use your trims or Wideband to shape your MAF and export/import back into the BE. You will have to do this several times. Always give the EA your CURRENT MAF transfer you used while creating the datalog. It will eventually dial in most of the MAF. Do not do any WOT hits during this time. Now for WOT. Typically after the bottom end of the MAF is generated/shaped/trimmed up I just take the upper portion (where WOT would use) and shape it to flow with the lower end - as a starting point. Going too rich here is a plus and safe bet. Then you can try a few WOT passes and feed that to the EA back and forth and let it shape up the top end. So far I have been able to take a hand full of stubborn Mustangs in my area that come in all rickity rick idle, eye burning fumes, surging, popping, you name it and tame them down inside an hour using this method. I then burn them a chip from Moates and send them on their way. Now as far as injector offset and battery voltage. Mustangs are notorious for weak charging systems. I usually start out by running two extra ground wires. One from the engine block to the body. Heck just last weekend a guy came in and the only one he had was loose and his alternator was surging. This is pretty common I have found. The second ground I run is from the Battery negative to the body, you already should have one from the battery to the engine. This will greatly help reduce grounding issues and current problems. Actually on both my cars the offsets and such didnt make a hill of beans either way. I'm running newer style alternators and my voltage with dual fans, A/C, and head lights never dips below 13.5 on either car. If anything when I bottom out the power windows is the only time you could tell any difference in the engine, only then did changing the offset at that logged voltage dip did I see a difference. Meaning it really didnt pull the engine down after that. Sort of like when the A/C compressor kicks on my engine just idles up and the fans kick on and I never see a difference. So these things are for perfectionists, like most of us, I would say. The masses would probably never know the difference or take time to worry with it. Injector breakpoint is important for your idle area. I have mine switch to low slope for better idle control on my e303 car. I'm running like 36/46 with a breakpoint of 1. It cured issues like hot starts, starts where it would die in a few seconds. Surging idles. Starts where it would crank perfectly, idle 20 seconds and just shut off. Unfortunately feeding this to the EA gave me numbers that never worked right for me. The car is so tame and driver friendly my wife loves it and it pretty much has to drive like our family car for her to say that. Hope this helps. Here's what you are looking for. ...the Adaptive Control & Update Rate Table (FN1325). This table indicates all the RPM/Load positions that KAMRF learning is allowed in. You'll notice there are positive and negative values in this table. Positive values indicate time (don't know the units) to be in an RPM/Load before learning and adapting to what the LAMBSEs are indicating. Negative values indicate that these cells aren't allowed to learn and thus they harness from the learning done in another cell. The number indicates what cell they are referencing for the KAMRF value. The first number is the column, the 2nd is the row. Numbering start at 0 and counts up and over. Thus -57 is 2500RPM@50% load. If you are looking at the table, you'll be able to count up from the bottom, starting at 0, up to 5 and you should be on the 50% row at the count of 5. Same thing with the row. The scheme you see by the factory setting works fine for a tuned vehicle, but during the tuning phase, this setup just gets in the way and can slow down your efforts to tune a MAF. What you want is for most all these cells to be allowed to learn individually except for maybe the idle and light load rows. Notice the very top row labelled 0.00 load is a reserved row. This is the idle row. The EEC can learn idle separately from the rest of the tune. This can work for you or against you. There are a number of different ways to setup this table. I personally null the idle row from learning by referencing the idle row to the 20% row of the same column. I do the same thing for the 5% and 10% load rows. This way the KAMRF doesn't jump around as I go from idle to a loaded condition... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

But one thing I have gathered just by listening to others talk, is there are differences in quality between WBs. Most WBs are accurate, but what you don't realize is they aren't all "fast" to respond. Some have a lag or sluggishness to them which isn't very useful if you are trying to diagnose split-second conditions that happened at high RPMs (where you'll very likely be using a WB to tune). Higher quality WBs will be much crisper in their response to changes in exhaust conditions. The more expensive ones also have the ability to emulate a narrow-band so you don't have to cut another hole in your exhaust. The nicer ones also have configuration software that allows you to change the behavior of the WB some. Point is, you get what you pay for just like most anything else in life. So before you skimp on a WB, make sure you know what you need it to do, and get one that does everything you need it to do...not just the cheapest in a list of WBs. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Aug 28, 2007 10:11 pm That's certainly an option, but not necessary. Properly operating motors should burn about the same from left to right, however there will always be a slight difference but not enough to be of any concern on a properly running motor. As long as your LAMBSEs in Closed Loop are averaging within .3 of each other at any given time, then 1 WB should be all you need. I checked my logs and only spark seems to be affected but in searching the internet I found this interesting clip: "We have had great experiences with the MSD Super Conductor wires on many applications, so we elected to use these wire on this project. For this project, these wires would turn out to be the wrong choice. The Electromotive TEC-III engine management system uses a 60-tooth crankshaft magnetic trigger sensor. Due to the high-resolution of this input trigger, we found out that the Electromotive TEC-III engine management system to be very susceptible to EMI. We could have discovered this sooner if we just read the Electromotive manual and used spark plug wires that met their requirements for resistance. Since we didn't listen, we found the MSD wires to not be compatible with the TEC-III engine management. The result was that even the small amount of EMI caused by the MSD Super Conductor wires was enough to cause the TEC-III to misinterpret the crank trigger signals and this caused failures to fire injectors and erratic ignition timing. On the dyno, the result was the engine making far less horsepower than we expected. After trying just about everything else, we finally decided to listen to Electromotive's recommendations and install a set of Magnecor wires that meet Electromotive's requirements for resistance. The result was 200 additional horsepower at the wheels and an engine that was running on all four cylinders. On a side note, we've never seen a problem with the MSD Super Conductor wires on any application except on Electromotive TEC-equipped vehicles. On the contrary, we have seen measurable performance increases on nearly all applications that we have tested. For any application where on-board electronics or engine management is susceptible to EMI (i.e. any Electromotive engine management equipped vehicle), our first choice would be a set of Magnecor ignition wires." My problems aren't anywhere near this significant but it does turn out I jsut bought MSD wires to replace my FRPP ones. I am not sure if it is possibel to shield this sensor. It does have open wires running to it just like the factory. I struggle to justify $300 for another set of wires for a test. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Feb 04, 2007 7:58 am I figured out what the problem is. It's the equation in the definition file. For whatever reason, BE isn't parsing the parenthesis in equations correctly. To correct this, click the EDIT button for the Definition file. Scroll down to the SARCHG scalar and go to the equation. In my GUFB Rev 3.XLS strategy file, the equation looks like: (X *8/.000044256)/4194304 I modified it to look like: X*8/.000044256/4194304 Mathematically, that is the same equation and in this case, the parenthesis had no purpose. I looked at any other equation with parenthesis and those scalars are also misbehaving. After removing the parenthesis, and rewriting the equation to work without parenthesis, they worked as well. In GUFB, the only other one I found was the Accel Minimum Fuel TP Movement (TPDLTA) and TPS Breakpoint Voltage for Part Throttle (DELTA). These two scalars use the same equation. Original equation: (X/64)*(5/1000) I modified it to look like: X*5/64/1000 In the functions, I found Accel Enrichment Multiplier vs TP (FN331B) has parenthesis in its X-axis equation. Original equation: (X / 12800)*256 I modified to be: X*256/12800 I also found the MAF transfer function (FN036) had parenthesis in the Y-axis equation (you have to scroll horizontally to see the Y-axis equations on a smaller monitor). This would explain why you were having troubles with getting your MAF transfer to work. What it doesn't explain is why I wasn't. Hmm...But no matter. I'm sure the same fix will fix you up as well. The MAF Y-axis original equation is: X*(25000000/2147483648)*60/2.2046 I modified it to: X*60*25000000/2147483648/2.2046 If you can, make these modifications to your definition file and save it by another name, then make sure this fixed each of your issues as well. I've already emailed Clint about this and to look into why the parenthesis aren't being handled correctly. But in the meantime, this should take care of it for you to get you back moving. From what I have gathered through research and e-mail discussions the best way to do this is as follows: Jack the TPS WOT point to the moon, this keeps the EEC in closed loop for as much as possible on the MAF curve. As I understand it, the EEC only follows the O2s while in closed loop. Start a log rolling, and then drive the car around while in closed loop. Make certain to record the KAMFR against the MAFV, at the very least. Take the log file and pop it into EA. EA shows the diffs between the KAMFR and the MAFV values. EA even will suggest a MAF transfer for you, I think. Record the new MAF adjustments to the transfer as being used in CalEdit, and then run the same driving route again after clearing KAMFR. Keep going at it, looking for the figure closest to 1 in the KAMFR field, as well as 14.64 in LAMBSE data when under cruise. .... Does this sound like the plan? I appreciate any help you can give me. I will be tuning my own car after the local guy whom uses SCT has given up on me / it. He's just too green, and his SCT doesn't feed back any data nor does it allow any real time observation. posts.content: motorheadcrm Gear Head Posts: 51 Joined: Sun Oct 30, 2005 2:31 pm Location: denver co Quote Post by motorheadcrm » Tue Dec 26, 2006 12:27 am Hey Adam, I used the 90mm lmaf template from caledit to get started. The car would start and run but not very well. Did not bother with the wot point. Started the car in the garage let it go to closed loop and made a 10 min Datalog of idle and off idle no load operation. Plugged that in to EA and started again with a new bin a note in my tuning book and a adjusted maf transfer. As the car started running better I would make datalogs of short drives around the neighborhood at low to med rpm’s but still low loads. Once the car was running fairly well at these rpm’s I adjusted the injector slopes with EA, same process as the maf transfer. I am not sure of the maf you are using but the stock ford maf’s have a higher resolution at the lower end. That’s why I spent so much time adjusting the low end of the maf transfer. Get the bottom right then Start standing on the gas progressively harder for the rest of the maf transfer datalogs and adjustments. I can’t say this is the correct textbook approach to these adjustments but it worked for me. The higher rpm and load ol afr tables should be adjusted with a wideband. It sounds like work but it’s a lot of fun. Chris FFR cobra, sn95 driveline, vortech s trim,t rex,42#injectors, 90mmLMAF, J4J1 cbaza, tweecer rt v1.30a9 378 RWHP 395 RWT Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Sun Oct 01, 2006 5:06 pm Have you compensated your LM-1 for the typical ground-offset issue? There is a quick way to see about how much it is - set the analog output you are logging in Calcon to read exaclty 14.7 AFR while the heater is warming up. Turn the car key on and start logging. The AFR should read very close to 14.7. Once you get it close, do a log in the LM-1 and one with Calcon at idle when warm - average both & compare the averages to see how off you are (electrical noise when engine is running will affect LM-1 output too). Tweak transfer curve. If you already did this - never mind. :D BTW, even the slope is off a bit in my LM-1. I also compared WOT runs and had to adjust the tilt of my transfer curve to get the area near 11:1 AFR accurate (was off by about 0.5 AFR!). 428w now Top

posts.author: Carl
posts.content: Carl Regular Posts: 81 Joined: Wed Mar 05, 2003 10:35 pm Location: Canada Quote Post by Carl » Wed Oct 04, 2006 10:03 pm I think that you and me have similar "problems". You have a cam with a fair amount of duration, and I am ASSuming a fair amount of overlap. I have a smaller cam, 228@ 0.050 in a 302 engine. Long story short, I tried unsuccessfully to achieve closed loop idle control and up until recently closed loop low apeed (under ~2k rpm) driveability. I haven't fully tested the driveability part of my new tune much and it may yet change. Basically,what I have concluded was happening was due to the overlap, my intake charge was "short circuiting" right out the exhaust valve, the sensors would read lean and adding fuel to achieve commanded or"stoich" would result in a very rich mixture ( even though my W/B "read" as commanded) poor driveability and the near conclussion of swapping to a Holley carb! My solution was to command open loop up until ~30% load, which means O/L until ~2k rpm in fourth gear, fifth gear drops C/L much earlier. I then changed my Base O/L Fuel Tables to command from 16.8 to 15.7 in my load regions up to 27%. This has worked well for me, but is still in the development stages. The Scalor, MIN Load for Closed Loop Control is what I changed. posts.author: dsleepy47
posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Mon Dec 20, 2004 3:45 pm The EEC doesn't care how the O2 sensor measures lambda all it is looking for is a voltage above or below 0.45 volts thats why it is called a "switch". If the sensor output is >0.45 volts the EEC dcreases the pulse width to lean the mixture, if the sensor output is <0.45 volts the EEC increases the pulse width to richen the mixture. For example: If the O2 sensor reads exhaust gas from cylinder #1 and the voltage is >0.45 volts the EEC decreases the PW. That O2 sensor will see exhaust gas from 3 other cylinders before the exhaust from the cylinder that that got the decreased PW gets there. If the EEC doesn't know how long to wait for the exhaust with adjusted PW to get to the sensor it could make an adjustment based on the exhaust gas from one of those 3 cylinders. That could set up an oscillation larger than the desired control band. As long as the delay is long enough for the adjusted cylinders exhaust gas to reach the sensor it doen't really make much difference if it is a little longer than actual transport time. Here is a Quote from the documentation I have: System transport lag time; time delay from when a fuel change is made until the EGO sensor indicates this change, units are REVs. X-input = FN039 - Normalized engine speed, RPM Y-input = FN071 - Normalized engine load, LOAD Output = Transport delay, REVs or RPS An EGO switch is defined as either: 1. The EGO sensor reads rich during the current background loop and it reads lean during the previous background loop. 2. The EGO sensor reads lean during the current background loop and it reads rich during the previous background loop. "After an EGO switch, a finite amount of time (equal to the transport lag) should pass before the EGO can switch. Noise in the EGO system could be interpreted by the computer as EGO switches. These phantom switches could occur at a faster rate than dictated by the system transport lag time. Since the jumpback is made from the lambda when the EGO switches, phantom switches could make the jumpback go beyond the average Air/Fuel ratio. A high rate of phantom switches would create a high rate of jumps. A special feature of the closed loop strategy prevents this problem. A full jumpback is done only if the proper transport lag time has elapsed. If not, the jumpback distance is reduced to match the reduction in transport lag time. The actual strategy uses PIP signal counts to control this feature." On the second point a narrow band sensor does not have a pump. A wide band sensor is essentially a narrow band sensor with an O2 pump. Narrow bands do not refernce outside air, that is why they are narrow band. This sends out a voltage greater than 0.45 volts. If the engine is running lean, all fuel is burned, and the extra Oxygen leaves the cylinder and flows into the exhaust. posts.content: WA2FAST Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Wed Sep 29, 2004 1:04 pm Location: MI Contact: Contact WA2FAST Website AOL Yet another LONG post... Quote Post by WA2FAST » Wed Dec 22, 2004 12:41 am Yeah... actually, the papers that I have on this I have been studying for a while today and have a complete grasp on them. The HEGO Bias (FN1353) tells the computer to bias either higher, equal to, or lower than stoich during the switching. If set to a + number... it will switch away from lean faster than the rich side... so it is biased to keep the AFR = or richer than stoich. In the event of a + number, it will swing slowly away from rich and quickly away from lean, keeping it biased to this value. There is no reason in my mind to touch this... this fine tunes things that without a gas analyzer and damn good reason that there is simply no point (I agree with you completely). HEGO Amplitude (FN1352) is the peak-to-peak absolute value in which the "swing" in AFR is aloud to go before correcting... this is designed to avoid long switching cycles. This is why the AFR never regularly (or even at all) goes out of range on what we can see and the EEC can calculate. In other words, it's the floor and ceiling... the EEC puts its foot down when the swing approaches these values. Now... the interesting thing I have found... the VERY interesting thing I have found is that the Exhaust Gas Pulse Delay (FN1351) is extremely crucial. In the documentation (from Ford) that I have, it specifically says that this value must absolutely be correct for the EEC to be able to make a proper decision on how to change itself the next cycle. The values are NOT ms like everyone thinks... they are not time... they are revolutions. So with the stock settings... when the injector fires... 10 revolutions later, the EEC's reading of the O2 IS OF that event to it... so it applies correction to THAT injector the next cycle. Basically, the logic is that the O2 gets a reading and the EEC says, "Okay, what happened 10 revolutions ago?... oh... cyl #8 fired, okay it was a little rich, let's not open that injector for quite so long next time." Now if these numbers are not accurate (which they aren't in most of our cases since we have modded our engines, exhaust, etc.), the EEC will naturally be working on an "average" from that bank as it will simply be making the compensations for the wrong injector over and over and over again, but the adaptive will pick up any significant variations and correct it... as an average. I see this as incredibly crucial to the tune. Will the car work without changing these numbers?... sure it will... they do after all work without changing these numbers... BUT I believe that by nailing these numbers accurately or even very close... the EEC will have a MUCH more precise handle on the AFR and closed loop operation. After all... closed loop is controlled by the O2's in the end anyway... so if they are not told which cycle the reading was from accurately, they are not going to be able to control the AFR accurately. Again, this is from reading the Ford white papers... if you do a search in it for FN1351... you'll see exactly the section I am talking about. It explains all of these functions very clearly. But the fact that they stress with a huge "WARNING" sign that the Exhaust Pulse Delay MUST be correct... that tells me that it is important, and I am determined to figure out how to make the proper corrections here. dsleepy47... I think we are on the same page with all of this. :) -Don- 87' GT, A9L, TwEECer RT, P1SC@12psi Non-Intercooled, AFM PP, 3" Pro-M#42, 70mm TB, GT-40 Intake, GT-40X Heads, B303, 1.6, BBK 1-5/8" Long Tubes, 306 Built Bottom End, Probe Block Girdle, TR3550, 3.55, PLX WB, Jan 07 Modified Mustangs Feature Car Top

FN1351(N,LOAD) = System transport lag time; time delay from when a fuel change is made until the EGO sensor indicates this change, units are REVs. X-input = FN039 - Normalized engine speed, RPM; Y-input = FN071 - Normalized engine load, LOAD; Output = Transport delay, REVs. *********************** ***** WARNING ***** *************** It is imperative that an accurate value for the system transport lag be entered. posts.author: WA2FAST
posts.content: WA2FAST Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Wed Sep 29, 2004 1:04 pm Location: MI Contact: Contact WA2FAST Website AOL Quote Post by WA2FAST » Thu Jan 20, 2005 7:08 am More info that I found it... After an EGO switch, a finite amount of time (equal to the transport lag) should pass before the EGO can switch. Noise in the EGO system could be interpreted by the computer as EGO switches. These phantom switches could occur at a faster rate than dictated by the system transport lag time. Since the jumpback is made from the lambda when the EGO switches, phantom switches could make the jumpback go beyond the average Air/Fuel ratio. A high rate of phantom switches would create a high rate of jumps. A special feature of the closed loop strategy prevents this problem. A full jumpback is done only if the proper transport lag time has elapsed. If not, the jumpback distance is reduced to match the reduction in transport lag time. The actual strategy uses PIP signal counts to control this feature. The transport delay (FN1351) is entered as REVS. The strategy uses units of both seconds and PIPS. The transport delay in PIPS is: TDPIP = FN1351(N,LOAD) * ENGCYL Transport delay in seconds is: TDSEC = FN1351(N,LOAD) * 60/N TDPIP and TDSEC are temporary registers. -Don- 87' GT, A9L, TwEECer RT, P1SC@12psi Non-Intercooled, AFM PP, 3" Pro-M#42, 70mm TB, GT-40 Intake, GT-40X Heads, B303, 1.6, BBK 1-5/8" Long Tubes, 306 Built Bottom End, Probe Block Girdle, TR3550, 3.55, PLX WB, Jan 07 Modified Mustangs Feature Car Top

posts.content: Voss Gear Head Posts: 7 Joined: Wed Jul 12, 2006 9:10 am 347 gradually leaning out Quote Post by Voss » Sat Aug 12, 2006 9:47 am Hi, I have been tuning on a N/A 347 for a couple of years now. :) The car runs very good, and is used at road racing events, however it is still street legal. I have noticed one disturbing issue when logging the actual AFR (with my LM-1 and the EGR EVP signal): The AFR gradually leans out with increasing RPM/load. In order to confirm this, I entered the Pro-M MAF curve according to my calibration sheet, entered 36 on high slope and 40 on low. I also forced the car to run in OL all time, and entered a commanded AFR of 11.8 at loads > 30%, > 2500rpm. The fuel pressure is 39psi with the vacuum hose disconnected. After clearing the KAMRF's and warming up the car, a number of WOT runs are made in 3rd gear with brakes applied, and gradually releasing the brakes so I get a number of data points as the car goes from 2500rpm up to 6000 rpm in let's say 20 seconds. When analyzing the logs, I can see that the EEC commands 11.8 (as entered), but the actual AFR is higher, and is increasing with increasing load/rpm. If I plot this error (using Exel, error=commanded-actual) against MAF kg/hr, it is very easy to see the trend that the AFR is leaning out with increasing kg/hr. My measurements are taken from approx. 300kg/hr up to 1100kg/hr. In this range the logged AFR goes from 12.0 gradually up to 13.3! If using 36 degrees total timing, pinging is easily heard at higher RPMs. I have verified the TwEECer logged AFR against the AFR presented on the LCD on the LM-1 with the aid of a passenger. Earlier this week, I replaced the Pro-M MAF with the stock Cobra MAF and stock air-filter/housing and repeated the test (replaced the MAF transfer curve of course with the stock J4J1). The same trend can be seen with the stock MAF: A gradual leaning of the AFR with increased MAF output, however perhaps slightly less error as compared with the Pro-M. But the maximum AFR was in the 12.8 range at 750kg/hr (I aborted the test earlier to avoid pegging the Cobra MAF at 850kg/hr). (I honestly thought I would see AFR's +/-0.1 from 11. . Does anyone have any suggestions on how to cure this problem? I could tweek the MAF curve in order to compensate for the error, but I get the feeling I then try to fix one error by introducing another error in the system. I would like to see perhaps a maximum deviation of +/- 0.2 in AFR over the entire range. I have a couple of toughts about the cause: 1) Can the stock fuel lines and stock fuel rails be to small? I have 36# injectors, a 190L in tank pump and an adjustable FPR, but the rest of the fuel system is stock. I can not see any strange behaviour on my fuel pressure gauge, but this does not necessarily mean that the fuel flow is enough? 2) I think my injectors are sold through FMS (although I purchased them from Pro-M before they went out of business). At what fuel pressure are they rated? 39? 42? 42.5? 3) I don't think the injectors are flow matched. Problem? Hmm... 4) MAF fine tuning will be needed, but I don't like to see the same trend with the stock MAF, although perhaps not as bad as with the Pro-M. But perhaps the stock MAF is not more accurate than this? (12.8/11.8 means 8.5% too lean) 5) Is is possible to get the AFR in a +/-0.2 range with the OL condition? The ideal case would be to have one WB in each exhaust and run CL conditions at all times. :) It is also worth to note that if adjusting the injector slopes to compensate for the lean condition at high loads (or adjust the fuel pressure), it is possible to use 36 degrees total timing, and see perhaps 12.5 AFR at high loads, and the car runs VERY strong without any pinging. So this behaviour can only be observed with the aid of logging the WB signal. I have earlier been able to adjust the slopes and breakpoints to achieve KAMRF's in the range +/-3%. So without the WB I would be luckily unaware of what's going on. :) Feel free to jump in with ideas! /Martin Sweden Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri Jul 07, 2006 1:32 am 2Shaker wrote: I thought about that, but if it were the lines and/or rails wouldn't I see a drop in pressure as I approach 100% DC? The fuel pressure holds steady the whole time. You can maintain pressure if the pump is the correct size, but if the size of the lines are not large enough the flow will not be enough. This is why the the DC is increasing. The lines can only supply x amount of flow at 39psi even if the line was cut or wide open. This is exactly what the BAP is solving. It just simply raises the Fuel pressure so the flow will increase. With the BAP, it does not kick in untill boost which is most likley WOT. At WOT the adaptive is not learning. This means that if your tables are targeting 12.0 AFR and then the BAP kicks in then the actual AFR might goto 11.0 or even lower with the added pressure. This would mean that you either have to lower the WOT part of the MAF or readjust the fuel tables. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sat May 20, 2006 4:41 am Fuel_Equilib_Intake_Surface isn't the same as Manifold_Volume, it's an adjustment for fuel drop out onto the inside of the manifold surfaces. The A9L has no manifold volume scaler, but there are two other scalers that are used to compensate for manifold filling; FKARCH and FKARC1. These are the slow and fast manifold filling filter constants and the equation for determining their values is; FKARCH or FKARC1 = vol. efficiency * (engine displacement / manifold volume) / (2 * ENGCYL) The volumetric efficiency for slow filling is that at part throttle and the fast filling volumetric efficiency should be the maximum efficiency at WOT. You'll find you can access the filter constants using TunerPro. Top

posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Wed Jun 07, 2006 3:45 pm I think I got a handle on this one - at least it fixed the issue for me. AEFUEL is the accelerator enrichment fuel flow (adder) function. This adds injector duty cycle on top of what is needed for steady state operation during acceleration. Some have suggested adjusting the MAF function to account for these transient conditions, but the MAF is only good for steady state and is not part of the AE fuel subroutine. Here is a description of "Acceleration Enrichment Fuel" In the RUN and UNDERSPEED modes, whenever the rate of change of throttle angle exceeds a minimum value , acceleration enrichment fuel is delivered until the manifold filling effect is completed ( LOAD stops increasing ). The fuel is delivered at a rate determined by AEFUEL . AE fuel is delivered synchronous with the base fuel pulse. AEFUEL is added into the FUELPW calculation (See the FUELPW logic and equations). No separate AE pulses are delivered I have underlined the important points in the paragraph above. AE fuel is active during positive throttle transients while load is increasing and is designed to account for manifold filling. The calculation of AEFUEL is: AEFUEL = (AEM*TAE(FN1303)*FN331B*FN378)/60 lb/min AEM = Global multiplier TAE = FN1303 which is called "Accel Enrichment Fuel" in TwEECer. = An 8x7 table of fuel flow as a function of throttle angle rate of change (TAR) and temperature. The temperature input can be ECT or ACT as defined by the combination [FRCTAE*ACT +(1-FRCTAE)*ECT]. The normalizing function for TAR is FN019B. The normalizing function for the ECT/ACT temperature combination is FN020B. FN331B = "Accel Enrichment Multiplier vs TP" in TwEECer, FN378 = "Accel Enrichment Multiplier vs BP" in TwEECer. AEM is a global multiplier which when made larger causes more transient fuel to be added. I previously changed this from 0.39 (stock A9L) to 1 - which basically increases AE fuel at all TP rates & temperatures, but not by a lot in the big picture. At "1" it can basically be ignored in the calculation, which simplifies things. TAE (FN1303) - this is where I decided the action was. At typical ECT (ACT is factored in too) temperatures (150-200), you see the multiplier can be as high as 29 with a fast throttle rate. Here you can see why when most people adjust AEM they do not see significant results - significant fuel is not added until the multipler is increased significantly. I was thinking about this and it occured to me that the amount of airflow per degree of throttle blade opening is significantly higher with the 85mm TB I am using compared to the stock A9L 60mm unit. I noticed the lean pop came back worse than ever when I switched from the 75mm TB to the 85mm. It's similar to the bog you used to get with an oversized carb - especially for me where I now have a short-runner intake with the KB on there. Anyway, I had done several decel/accel datalogs and the A/F was going to 20:1 on every tip in during the time the TPS was increasing and load was still increasing - this is where this table is used! I noticed the cells at the slow TP rate (TAR) and normal operating temps had a multiplier of only 1.5. The formula shows only a 0.025 lb/min adder. I changed all the cells that were less than 8 to "8". FN331B - this is a function that reduces the AE fuel adder at higher throttle positions. This makes sense as we know that the airflow change from 70-80% throttle is much less than the airflow change from 0 to 10% throttle. Since I was seeing the issue most at 1-2V throttle, I decided to change the 2.2V multiplier from the stock 0.3 to 0.8 (I had previously changed this to 0.65 per posts here). FN378 - this is barometric pressure compensation and probably does not need to be touched. So I had previously increased AEM to 1 from 0.39 & the third point in FN331B to 0.65 from 0.3, but this was having almost no effect. Changing the lowest points in FN1303 from 1.5 to 8 really did the trick though :D (changing point three in FN331B to 0.8 from 0.65 helped too). I am even a little on the rich side now - I see AFRs on tip in from 10.8 to 12 - but I'm not complaining - it's SOOO smooth now when I tip in from a decel. I can now do a few more decel/tip-in datalogs & dial it in exactly. BTW, the AEFUEL addition only continues until the manifold is full, even if the throttle rate of change is above the threshold (AETAR). This describes the AEOFLG: AEOFLG LOGIC The AEOFLG indicates whether the LOAD rate of change indicates the occurrence of the manifold filling effect. The rate of change of LOAD represents the engine response to the driver demand command. There is a short delay between the TP change and the LOAD change. During this delay, the AEOFLG remains at zero. After the LOAD begins to increase, the AEOFLG is set to one to signal the occurrence of the manifold filling effect. After the manifold has filled (LOAD stops increasing), the software turns off the AE fuel regardless of the status of the TAR circuit. TAR > AETAR--------------------| AND ---|S Q-| SET AEOFLG = 1 LOAD - AELOAD > AEACLD ----|---------|-----| (Manifold filling) ----------------------------------------------|-----| OLDTP = TP TAR = 0 ------------------------------------|C---|--- ELSE --- ----------------------------------------------------| ----------------------------------------------------| SET AEOFLG = 0 ----------------------------------------------------| (Manifold not filled) ----------------------------------------------------| OLDTP = TP MORE INFO There is another transient fuel adder called EFTRFF. EFTRFF is the "Equilibrium Fuel Transfer Rate" for transient fuel compensation. This function has to do with fuel wetting of the intake manifold wall. I do not completely understand this function and the parameters for this function are not available within TwEECer so this one will have to be figured out at a later date by some smart person. FKARCH or FKARC1 The filters talked about above in this thread are related to another strategy known as the "Manifold Filling Model" - this is described below: OVERVIEW Because of the delays associated with manifold filling, the airflow through a meter mounted up- stream of the throttle body is not equal to the port airflow on an instantaneous basis. This leads to fueling errors during transients. To compensate for these errors, a filtering algorithm was developed. When the throttle body airflow changes slowly, the filling filter constant is proportional to engine displacement/manifold volume and volumetric efficiency. A close approximation is an air charge filter constant, FKARCH, that is proportional to (VEFF) * (engine displacement/manifold volume)/ (2 * ENGCYL). During a fast tip-in the air charge can be approximated by a different filter constant. The constant, FKARC1 is proportional to 1/2 * (VEFF) * (engine displacement/manifold volume)/ENGCYL, however the volumetric efficiency at wide open throttle is used. I understand this concept, but I have no idea how to modify the filter constants as per the discussion above in this thread. Since these filter constants cannot be modified in TwEECer without using an independant bin editor, it may be a while before anyone experiments with these filter constants. posts.author: Daggar
posts.content: Daggar Gear Head Posts: 58 Joined: Fri Nov 12, 2004 6:33 pm Quote Post by Daggar » Fri Dec 16, 2005 10:04 pm JuiceSC wrote: Now as far as N/A vs S/C calibration, its about a 15% difference. What I don't understand is why the S/C calibration is 15% LESS than the N/A. To me that would lean out the mixture 15% not richen. It is because of the brake specific fuel consumption differences on a N/A motor vs. a force inducted one. When you add boost you're significantly increasing the volume of air that you're asking the motor to process while not changing the actual size of the motor or it's effeciency in cumbusting an air/fuel mixture. In effect, it makes the motor less efficient (boost simulates a larger motor although it's physical size has not changed. Though boosted apps tend to require mixtures richer in fuel than normally aspirated applications, the volum of air being forced into the motor is less than what it would be for a larger more efficient motor making the same power. It's also why N/A applications are able to make more power with smaller injectors than forced applications. Stolen from some website for definition: Brake Specific Fuel Consumption is the ratio of fuel consumed (in lbs. per hour) to horsepower produced. This ratio is a direct indicator of how efficiently the engine converts fuel into power. Most factory gasoline type engines run approximately a .50 to .55 Brake Specific Fuel consumption (BSFC) range while a highly efficient normally aspirated race engine operates at approximately a .40-.45 BSFC. Most common turbocharged or supercharged engine configurations run in the .55 to .60 BSFC range. For Methanol powered applications the BSFC is doubled (i.e. turbo/methanol: 1.10-1.20). These factors should be considered when sizing & selecting injectors for your particular application Top

posts.content: mach1 Gear Head Posts: 17 Joined: Thu Jun 23, 2005 4:25 pm Quote Post by mach1 » Sun Dec 18, 2005 3:18 pm the point of the 1 to 1 on a regulator is to compensate for pressure conditions in the manifold. here is a example. with the engine pulling vaccum the fuel pressure doesnt need to be as high because the vaccum is "pulling" the fuel through the injectors therefore if you ran the same fuel pressure as without vaccum then the car would be rich. on a boosted setup the boost is pushing the fuel through the injector(not exactly pushing it through but putting more resistance on it) so the FPR must increase fuel pressure to keep the same mixture. in the sitation of a fmu it just shoots the fuel pressure sky high which with richen the motor but if you pull fuel pressure under vaccum and add fuel pressure under boost (1:1) it should keep the injector flowing the correct amount the whole time, not make it lean or rich... Top

2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Fri Jun 10, 2005 11:44 pm Cougar 5.0 A couple of months ago several of us had 2 very long threads concerning injector timing. Unfortunately those threads have disappeared with the name change of the board. Nevertheless, here are some of the key points that were made: 1. Injector timing becomes less of a factor at high RPM. Here's why. At 6000RPM it takes only 20 msec for 720 degrees of crank rotation. Also at 6000RPM you will be seeing injector pulse widths (PW) of 16 -18 msec or even higher. When you factor in the injector open and close times it becomes obvious the injector is almost continuously flowing fuel because it is barely closed (if at all!). 2. EA has radio buttons to choose to set the timing to the injector off event or injector on event. But we can't set that logic in our EEC so I'm not sure how this is supposed to work. 3. There was a lot of talk about firing the injector while the exhaust is open and fuel flowing out the ehxaust. In my opinion this will not happen at low/mid RPM's on a street driven car with a full exhaust. I do not believe any cylinder scaveging occurs and indeed there is likely to be pressure in the ehxaust system, not vacuum. This pressure is causing a reverse flow momentarily when the intake valve opens. 4. Related to #2 above, I'm not sure that we really know what these values are in the table. Yes we know they represent crank degrees, but relative to what? Trailing edge of the PW. Leading edge? TDC? 5. Some have said they see a marked difference in the way their cars run when they change these values. I have not found any discernable difference after trying standard and really radical values. I also looked at the CBAZA J4J1 file a few days ago and was surprised to see that Ford has every cell in the table set to the same value (as I recall it is 300). posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue Nov 01, 2005 10:33 am I like the TDC method because no matter if the exhaust is open or not after TDC the fuel is going to be pulled into the cylinder. Since the pistion is on its way down it is causing the vacuum. This will pull in the fuel and hot exhaust if the exhaust port is open. The hot exhaust will help with the atomization (Vaporize) of the fuel. If you use the Exhaust close event then you dont allow for any atomization and it also gives less time to inject the fuel. If you have big enough injectors then thiss would most likley be ok. Most of us will max out the inkake event pretty quick if we use the exhaust close event. In the end it is a personal preference. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sat Sep 10, 2005 5:54 pm JuiceSC wrote: As a side note, I've found that LOWERING this value seems to hold high idle longer, and RAISING it can cause stalling when nothing else is changed. Me too- For those curious about the specifics, the TB airflow scalar value is subtracted from what the EEC calculates the amount of airflow needed to hit the desired idle. Then that resultant value is the amount of air commanded from the ISC. Thus if the TB airflow is made larger, more air is subtracted, and a smaller ISCDC is generated, leading to RPMs dropping too low and perhaps a stall. Conversly, if the TB airflow is made smaller, less air is subtracted and the resultant ISCDC is larger, hanging the idle RPMs too high, until adaptive corrects. Say the ideal TB airflow is 0.7, and the amount necessary for idle is 1.0. That leaves 0.3 air for the ISC. If you change the TB airflow lower to say 0.5, then the ISC would get 0.5 air. If you go the other way, TB airflow = 0.9, then the ISC would only get 0.1 air, and could stall the engine. Changing the ISC neutral idle airflow may help counteract this, but setting BOTH correctly is what is really needed. posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Wed Jun 01, 2005 3:54 pm EFIpunk wrote: I write the TwEECer all the time with the car running....car runs alittle ruff for a few, but has never gave me a problem. As stated, you can write to TwEECer with the engine running. TwEECer essentially runs off of position five (off) during the write operation. This will have your car running from the stock calibration for those few seconds. It then returns to your custom tune after the write is complete. If your car will not run at all during this and you're tempted to use the throttle, note that using the throttle to keep it running can have the effect of changing the closed-throttle voltage (this my be limited to SN-95s). Also, I've noticed after TwEECer returns to the custom tune, the car acts like it is in a warm start cycle, therefore it will take a few more seconds to idle down. I almost always write tunes with the engine running. Daren 94GT, AFR165, E303, 1.72 RR, GT-40 Intake, 70mm TB, 24lb inj, ProM 75, BBK LT, J4J1, PLX M-300 WB Top

posts.author: Frit
posts.content: Frit BIN Hacker Posts: 376 Joined: Fri Apr 20, 2007 10:48 pm Quote Post by Frit » Fri Jan 04, 2008 1:00 am If you have an opcode in the dissassembled file that says SHL REG_80 then that means take the word value stored in register 80 which is memory address 0x80 and shift all the bits of that word left one, which is like multiplying by 2. A word takes two bytes of memory. The eectch98 document lists all the opcodes and what they are. You should also look for documents that cover the Intel 8061 processor for more information. The REG_## is a register or memory location that exists within the 8061 processor that is faster for it to use than the rest of the memory it has access to. For the memory offsets from 0xF0, if you see a command like ld REG_42, 0x50[REG_F0] that means to load the number that is a word located at the address stored in register 0xF0 plus 0x50 into register 42 which is address 0x42. In the GUFB strategy, 0xF0 will have 0x8C00 in it, so the above number that will go into REG_42 will come from the address 0x8C00+0x50=0x8C50 If your looking at a bin file directly with a hex editor, then you will need to look at 0x6C50 for the value, because most bin files you see actually start at 0x2000 and don't include the lower addresses. Hopefully I just made things as clear as mud :( . Its not a simple thing to understand low level coding like this and has taken years for me to learn so its not elementary to me ;). posts.author: Frit
posts.content: Frit BIN Hacker Posts: 376 Joined: Fri Apr 20, 2007 10:48 pm Quote Post by Frit » Fri Jan 04, 2008 1:08 am To get the memory offsets that get stored in 0xF0 etc, look at the disassembled code starting at address 0x2022 and you'll see the addresses that get loaded into 0xF0. Here's what the GUFB code has. 2022 008C word $8C00 2024 5A8E word $8E5A 2026 D68F word $8FD6 2028 A893 word $93A8 202A 3094 word $9430 202C A897 word $97A8 202E 7E9A word $9A7E 2030 5A9E word $9E5A so 0xF0 will contain the numbers of the address $8C00 and 0xF2 will contain the numbers for address $8E5A and so on. Now keep in mind that the numbers are stored in low byte/high byte order. If you look at the line 2022 you'll see the numbers 008C... That is how it is stored in memory directly. so 0x2022 will hold 0x00 and 0x2023 will hold 0x8C. To get the number you want, flip them so you get 0x8C00, and ironically this is a word ;). posts.author: Frit
posts.content: Frit BIN Hacker Posts: 376 Joined: Fri Apr 20, 2007 10:48 pm Quote Post by Frit » Sat Jan 05, 2008 3:10 pm All computers run on bits, and 1 bit will only be a 0 or 1. A byte is eight bits together, and if unsigned will hold 0 to 255 or if signed will be a number from -128 to 127. A word is 2 bytes long or 16 bits. An unsigned word will go from 0 to 65535 (0x0000 to 0xFFFF) and a signed word will hold -32768 to 32767. A double word is 2 words long, 4 bytes long 32 bits. An unsigned dword will go from 0 to 4294967295 (0x00000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF) and a signed dword will hold -2147483648 to 2147483647. Typically the most left bit will be used to indicate if a number is negative( 1) or positive(0) if its a signed number. So far I haven't seen the use of any dwords in the EEC code but I have only looked at the A9L and the A9U2 code. posts.author: Ziggy
posts.content: Ziggy Gear Head Posts: 52 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 2:23 pm Contact: Contact Ziggy Website AOL What do I need to change to make my car faster/run better? Quote Post by Ziggy » Mon Nov 18, 2002 10:57 am There are no magic settings you can change in the computer to make more power. What the TwEECer allows you to do is change settings in the PCM. That’s it. If the stock settings don’t fit your engine because it is modified significantly which causes it to run sub-optimally. Then, changing those settings in a way that makes the engine run more efficiently may increase the power output of your engine. Rather than ask, "What do I need to change to make my car faster?” You need to discover what about your current tune is making your car run less than perfect. The ways you can discover what is wrong with your current tune: 1: Data logging 2: Reading spark plugs 3: Using a Wide band O2 4: Running your car on a chassis dynometer and comparing HP/TQ from run to run. 5: Using your quarter mile ET's/MPH I’m sure I forgot/don’t know some but it's a start. title: How do I datalog with the TwEECer? - EECTuning.org

posts.content: Jon 94GT Site Owner Posts: 370 Joined: Thu Sep 12, 2002 3:16 pm Location: Houston, TX Contact: Contact Jon 94GT Website AOL How do I datalog with the TwEECer? Quote Post by Jon 94GT » Fri Mar 14, 2003 12:54 pm Note: This FAQ assumes that you have a working and installed TwEECer on your car and that you are using CalCon/CalEdit v1.20b or newer. 1) Connect the USB cable from the TwEECer to your computer. 2) Startup CalEdit. 3) Click the tab labeled "Utilities" at the top 4) The top right of the screen contains the various variables you may datalog (you may select up to 16). Select the items you would like to datalog. 5) Click "Payload". 6) Click the tab at the top labeled "Input / Output". 7) Check the box labeled "Data Logging" which is right below the button called "Read EEC". 8) Turn the key in the ignition to the ON position and wait 5 seconds (so windows can have time to load the USB driver to talk to the TwEECer). 9) Click "Write TwEECer". * wait for CalEdit to write the binary and payload to the TwEECer * 10) Close CalEdit and Startup CalCon (CalEdit cannot write to the TwEECer while CalCon is open). 11) Click the tab at the top called "Dashboard" or "Digital" (doesn't matter which, just pick whichever display is preferable to you). 12) Select the correct RT Method (pick from list under "Log to File" checkbox) 13) Check the box labeled "Log to file" in the top right hand corner. 14) Start the car. 15) Click the button labeled "Start Logging". The guages in the display should now spring to life showing you the various items you selected in your custom payload. If it does not, or very strange values show up, please make sure the connection with the J3 port on the EEC is clean, and that you followed the steps above correctly. Last Updated: 5/6/2003 :: Owner and operator of EECTuning.org :: Top
