title: Setting idle on A9L - EECTuning.org

posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Setting idle on A9L Quote Post by boss96 » Fri Jul 25, 2003 1:31 pm Got this from another bbs, it should get you in the ballpark at least :) 1. Adjust all the parameters for you modifications, Injectors, MAF, engine size ect. 2. Set your idle speed, if it won’t idle at your desired speed set the idle speed high enough so the car will be able to idle for several minutes at a time. 3. Turn off adaptive tuning by setting the following tags to values that will never be reached. MIN_ACT_FOR_ADAPTIVE_CONTROL MAX_ACT_FOR_ADAPTIVE_ CONTROL 4. Clear the KAM by removing the battery cable. 5. If the engine isn’t warmed up do that now. 6. Start the engine and let it idle for two minutes, one minute to allow the ECM to get into closed loop and another to get data to look at. 7. Retrieve the datalog. 8. Look at the airflow when the engine is idling. Set the DESIRED_IDLE_AIRFLOW_IN_NEUTRAL tag value to the idle RPM and the actual observed airflow at idle. 9. Download the changes to the ECM. 10. Start the engine and let it idle for two minutes, one minute to allow the ECM to get into closed loop and another to get data to look at. 11. Retrieve the datalog. 12. Look at lambse1 when the engine is in closed loop. If it is above one you are too rich, below one you are too lean. Adjust the MAF_FUNCTION tag at the airflow value that the engine is idling at from the datalog to richen or lean out the idle. 13. Repeat steps 9 thru 12 until lambse1 stays at one +/- .01, or as close as you can get it. 14. Increase the idle speed 500 rpms and repeat steps 9 thru 12 until you reach the maximum that ISC can provide, about 2000rpm. 15. Now set the idle speed 100 rpms lower than your desired final idle speed and repeat steps 9 thru 12 until your reach the lowest speed your engine will idle at. 16. Set your idle to the final desired idle speed and repeat steps 6 thru 8 17. Turn adaptive control back on by resetting the following tags to their original value. MIN_ACT_FOR_ADAPTIVE_CONTROL MAX_ACT_FOR_ADAPTIVE_ CONTROL Miscellaneous tips for Idle If the idle surges you most likely are too rich. Zero out the last three columns of the STARTUP_FUEL_TABLE to lean out the engine and stop the surge that lasts for a few seconds on hot starts. If the idle won’t come down to the value you have set, then the DESIRED_IDLE_AIRFLOW_IN_NEUTRAL tag is set too high. 96 GT, Vortech Si trim,Procharger 3 core intercooler, forged bottom end, MAC longtubes, ported PI heads , Edelbrock intake, Crower cams-.580lift/234dur@.050, 80lb injectors, CDAN4/GGL4 processor. Top

title: More info on setting idle on A9L - EECTuning.org

posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL More info on setting idle on A9L Quote Post by boss96 » Fri Jul 25, 2003 1:50 pm Many thanks to 86GT for posting this info! It's a little long...:) I was having problems with my idle quality, until I read all of the post on the EEC Tuner and Tweecer forums. I would like to give credit where credit is due, but I read so many different posts that the list would go on forever. So basically, I would like to give credit to all members of the forums that have posted any thing about idle quality. What I have done here is consolidate the efforts of many individuals and threw in my two cents along the way. This procedure is written around an A9L processor. · Adjust the idle screw on the Throttle Body (TB) all the way out allowing the throttle plate to fully close. Now turn the idle screw in just until it touches the mechanical linkage. Finally, turn the idle screw in one full turn. This will place the TB plate at the correct location. · Adjust the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) to .98Vdc using CalCon. You may have to ream out the mounting slots on the TPS in order to achieve .98Vdc. There has been a lot of discussion about what the correct TPS setting should be, but I have found that .98Vdc works fine for me. Note: the voltage reading at the sensor may be different from CalCon’s reading due to line resistance. If the TPS wiring is in good shape, then the voltage difference should be minimal. If there is a significant difference find the bad connector or wiring and fix it before continuing. · Unplug the Idle Speed Controller (ISC) so that you can datalog the base idle. Now start the car and datalog the idle RPM and Mass Air Flow (MAF) voltage at normal operating temperatures. After achieving the datalog, calculate an average MAF voltage vrs RPM. For example: MAF RPM .8 675 Plug the ISC back in. · Now its time to start entering parameters into CalEdit, but first let me describe how the functions and scalars work that pertain to the ISC. The scalar “Throttle Body Air” is used to tell the EEC how much air in pounds per minute enters the engine through the TB at an idle. The factory uses a 60mm TB and a 55mm MAF with a base idle of 550. The stock combination will produce a MAF voltage of .615 Vdc at 550 RPM. Using the formula (MAF * 2.2046226 / 60 = TB Air Flow) you will see how the factory came up with the numbers they did. For example ( [.615Vdc = 14.969kg/hr] *2.2046226 / 60 = .55005 pounds/minute) will result in the factory setting of .55005. With that in mind, I’m using a 70mm BBK TB and a 73mm C&L meter with a 93 Cobra intake, which produces a MAF voltage of .8 at 650 RPM. Using the formula above and the MAF curve I calculated the new TB airflow. Keep in mind the MAF curve needs to be tuned properly, or this calculation will be wrong. My new TB airflow is ([.8Vdc = 25.357kg/hr] * 2.2046226 /60 = .93). Also keep in mind that every time you adjust the idle that the TB airflow needs to be recalculated. · Now the function “ISC Neutral Idle Air Flow” can be adjust to accommodate the new TB airflow. The factory uses .75 air for 672 RPM, thus by subtracting the TB Air Flow you get .2 air at 672 RPM. Here is where I believe people get confused. I have read in many of the forums that the ISC should be about 20 % duty cycle at an idle, but I believe this to be miss leading. If the stock application has .2 air at an idle, as proven above, then by looking at the function “ISC Transfer” you will see that .2 air dictates that .34 or 34% duty cycle is applied. Maybe I’m wrong, but if you now adjust the idle up a little by using the TB set screw then the ISC duty cycle will go down in order to maintain the desired RPM. This is how I believe the 20% duty cycle is possible. The factory Idle is set to 672 with a base of 550, which is a difference of 122 RPM. This difference is what allows the ISC duty cycle to be at 34%. So if you take the desired RPM and lower it, you should see that the duty cycle should also decrease and vise versa. For my set up I entered values into the function “ISC Neutral Idle Air Flow” that corresponded to my new MAF curve. · The purpose of the function “ISC Dashpot Pre Position” is to tell the EEC where to maintain the idle during release of the throttle. In my case the desired RPM is 750, which tells me that the preposition of the ISC is .36 air or .42 duty cycle. In my case this held my RPM’s at 1000. The time that the RPM’s are held is dependent on a couple of thing, one the Vehicle Speed Sensor (VSS) and some constant, which I cannot find. As long as the vehicle is moving above (7 MPH I think) the Dashpot Preposition is active. Once the vehicle drops below 7MPH then the RPM’s will drop to the desired RPM. If the car is at a stop and the engine is reved then I believe some time constant is used for the Dashpot Pre Position. On my set up, the RPM’s will drop to 1000 and hold there for about 2 seconds. I can’t seem to find this setting anywhere. · The purpose of the function “ISC Decay Rate” is to tell the EEC how fast to drop the RPM’s to the Dashpot Pre Position. I believe the units are in seconds. This means that the stock application will drop the RPM’s over 750ms or ¾ of a second. For my set up, I did not have to touch this function. I found another discovery that may help people. I had a stable idle with the procedure above, but my timing was swinging all over the place. It was swinging from 15 to 31 degrees. After looking at the "Idle Spark vs. RPM" function, this is what it is suppose to do if the RPM error exceeds 175. This meant that the "ISC Neutral Idle Air Flow" was not set correctly. I verified this by zeroing out the "ISC Neutral Idle Air Flow" function and watching the idle. It was about 200 RPM's below desired. This explained the timing adder. WOW, I'm finally starting to get a hold on this idle thing. I also had a Ford mechanic (mustang guru like us) look at it, and he told me that Ford had issued a Tech Bulletin that stated the idle should be set by monitoring the timing if any after market air componets have been installed. They are suppose to adjust the Idle set screw in (higher RPM) until they achieve a time of around 12 degrees, but they are not to exceed 750 on the idle. He said this was to get rid of the RPM error. He also stated that the EEC was designed to control the idle with the ISC and that the timing is supposed to be used as a secondary idle control. Ford states this is a common problem with larger TB and air meters. With that in mind, I created an excel sheet that calculates a new TB airflow scalar and the "ISC Neutral Idle Air Flow" function. These calculations are based off of a good known MAF transfer function and a datalog with the ISC disconnected. The datalog must contain an RPM range up to 2000. If anyone is interested, I will send it to you via E-mail. I now have a rock solid idle. posts.content: wkstill Regular Posts: 125 Joined: Wed Apr 02, 2003 8:02 pm Location: New Port Richey, FL Contact: Contact wkstill Website Quote Post by wkstill » Fri Jan 09, 2004 5:55 pm oh, and "here" is a post from LaSota Racing.. You HAVE to setup WOT A/F with the MAF transfer function or else temperature variations, barometric pressure and season differences will change the A/F ratio. Also if you tune via adders, you'll have to retune for every airflow improvement you ever make, from air filters to more boost. Here's an example, my car was tuned via the MAF transfer function at WOT, since the original tune, I have: added a bigger blower; added more boost; added a bigger inlet manifold; added a bigger TB; added a fairly radical cam; added a powerpipe and CAI and did some general airflow improvements. All without a retune. The A/F is exactly the same at WOT as it was when the tune was done. posts.author: Brian-Mc
posts.content: Brian-Mc Regular Posts: 244 Joined: Sun Nov 30, 2003 12:43 am Location: Georgetown Ky Contact: Contact Brian-Mc Website Yahoo Messenger comment about a FAQ... Quote Post by Brian-Mc » Fri Apr 09, 2004 12:00 am I was doing some searching and found a thread in the FAQ forum that I wanted to add a bit of electronics info... here is the contents of the post.. (had to copy them..) I copied this from the faq submission forum. Many thanks to those who contributed. Normal procedure is to disconnect the battery positive terminal for 30 minutes, and this flushes the KAM. However, there is a quicker way. Someone else suggested this, so I'm not going to take credit for it. Sorry, I can't remember who said it though. Anyways, disconnect the battery positive terminal, and then press and hold the brake pedal for a minute. Reconnect the battery and you're all set. Holding the brake pedal drains any residual energy out of the capacitors and stuff quicker then letting them decay by themselves. It works! I just tried it on my car. Started it up and datalogged right away... KAMRF values were 1.000 Thanks to "Twinturbostang", Brian Kam switch: installation/operation [Mustang] Kam requires a constant 12V supply to retain it’s memory,it receives the supply from “keep alive power”on pin #1 [86’-95’] or pin # 55 [96’-?] . On pre-94’you can access the feed for pin #1 at the EEC power relay[behind the R.H. kick panel]. Once you locate the feed wire for pin #1 [color of wire depends on year of car],cut the wire & install a male-female connector to join the wire back together[make the wire’s long enough so the connector can be accessed after the kick panel is installed]. Install the female end of the connector on the feed side of the wire[12V] , install the male end of the connector on the pin #1 side of the wire [0V] & plug the connector together. To clear KAM all you need to do is turn the key “off” unplug the newly installed connector & momentarily ground the male side of the connector[this will erease the KAM ], plug the connector back together & you are good to go. You could install a remote switch as I did but it requires more wiring to be done.[k.i.s.s.] Now being the guru that I am and always out for a big prank, we use to take capacitors and charge them up with some unknown value an bend the leads together but not touching... and toss them at an unknowning workmate and BBOOOMMM the cap pops real loud and makes them about piss their pants. And give them a little shock.. depending how much it was charged. Well one day this got very nasty... someone charged up a ideal cap that is similar in size to those that are in the EEC... well as he tossed it, the guy reached up in the air to catch it and as he caught it, the cap ended up blowing up. It was not just the pop of the cap discharging, it actually blew up, ended up burning the piss out of his hand and a little bit of the metal casing went into his hand.. needless to say, we don't do that anymore... this could actually happen if you do as indicated above by touching the KAM wire directly to ground. This creates a very quick discharge rate. most of the time it maybe fine and never have any issues, but it would be best to discharge the wire through a resister. just get a standard 1kohm resister from Radioshack or other electronics store and discharge the wire through that... that give it some type of a RC timeconstant to follow and is not as violant. Like I said.. it may not ever have any issues... but it COULD happen... 306 (stock block),TFS Track Heat Heads, E303 Cam, TFS track heat intake, 70 mm TB, 75mm Pro-M,42 lb injectors,Aeromotive AFPR, 255 lph intank, Crane Hi-6/LX-92. posts.author: thunderstang
posts.content: thunderstang Regular Posts: 204 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 3:30 pm Location: Toronto Canada Quote Post by thunderstang » Sun Jun 15, 2003 4:01 pm Kam switch: installation/operation [Mustang] Kam requires a constant 12V supply to retain it’s memory,it receives the supply from “keep alive power”on pin #1 [86’-95’] or pin # 55 [96’-?] . On pre-94’you can access the feed for pin #1 at the EEC power relay[behind the R.H. kick panel]. Once you locate the feed wire for pin #1 [color of wire depends on year of car],cut the wire & install a male-female connector to join the wire back together[make the wire’s long enough so the connector can be accessed after the kick panel is installed]. Install the female end of the connector on the feed side of the wire[12V] , install the male end of the connector on the pin #1 side of the wire [0V] & plug the connector together. To clear KAM all you need to do is turn the key “off” unplug the newly installed connector & momentarily ground the male side of the connector[this will erease the KAM ], plug the connector back together & you are good to go. You could install a remote switch as I did but it requires more wiring to be done.[k.i.s.s.] Happy tuning, Brian Top

title: EECV timing tables - EECTuning.org

posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL EECV timing tables Quote Post by boss96 » Wed Feb 23, 2005 8:59 am This is a general explanation of how timing is done on a eecv. Not comprehensive but it should get you going. There are 4 main spark tables used. MBT spark--Maximum brake tq Alt spark--spark used at high altitudes Bdln spark--Borderline spark, also known as max allowable spark Base spark--just as the name suggests There are also modifiers to the spark tables based an iat (inlet air temp), ect (engine coolant temp), imrc (used on a 4v motor, a spark adder when the imrc plates open) base and bdln adders for a/f ratio(an adder for more spark as a/f goes richer). The main thing to remember is the eec will look at all the spark tables and use the lowest spark value . Most timing values used in normal driving come from the bdln tables. The bdln table values are the spark settings that will keep the motor from detonating (pinging) when running in CL (closed loop fuel control) and an iat temp of 70 degrees. The bdln spark values are therefore lower than the values found in the base and mbt tables. Spark is added to the bdln values under high load and lower a/f ratios which can be seen by looking at the "spk bdln add a/f" table. The motor can usually tolerate more spark advance when running a richer a/f ratio. "Spk bldn retard for iat" is a table or function that retards timing as iat temps go up. On most eec's the timing retard/advance is zero at 100 degrees iat. Below 100 degrees iat the spark is advanced to some extent. Above 100 degrees timing starts to get retarded. The values in the table are big, for instance, at 140 degrees iat the value is -46. This does not mean that timing is retarded by 46 degrees. The number is multiplied by the values in a table/function called "spk bdln retard act multiplier" which contains values that are low, in this case around .1 for the higher load/rpm values. Multiplying -4.6x.1 gives you a spark retard value of -4.6, so you have 4.6 degrees of timing retard being applied to the spark values in the bdln table at those particular rpm/load values. Same logic goes for the "spk retard for ect" tables but the values in this table are not so aggressive as changes in ect do not effect the tendency for detonation as much as iat temps. So, in the above example you could determine how much spark the motor will see at a particular rpm/load by looking at the adders and bdln tables for that engine range taking into account the ect and iat temps and the a/f ratio you are commanding at that time. If you have a 4v (cobra) then you would also look at the amount of spark that is added for when the imrc plates open. Now for the other tables. Not to be taken as gospel but this is how it was explained to me and it does seem to work this way in real life. MBT spark-Like said above, this is the spark values that Ford determined will make the most power for that particular motor. On a STOCK motor, advancing the timing beyond these values will not increase hp. This table is used more or less as a "reference" table of values, not really used in normal operation. Base spark-Similar to MBT in that it is used as a reference table for the eec to compare the other spark tables to and then choose the lowest values. If for instance at a certain rpm/load value the spark commanded from the total spark values from the bdln table plus any adders is higher than the spark commanded in the base table at that rpm/load then the eec would allow that spark to be used, it would look at the base tables lower value. However, you would also need to look at "spk base add a/f ratio" to see if any spark is added to the base values during richer a/f ratios also. Altitude spark- I'm sorry to say I'm not clear when this table is used by the eec, presumably when higher altitudes are seen by the maf then they are used. Since I don't live in a high altitude area I have not noticed it being used that I can tell. As far as how to use this info to set your spark...it's up to you. Many people will simply datalog their spark values and add/retard spark through the bdln tables to arrive at the spark that they want and leave the other tables alone. If you want to simplify things you can disable some of the tables so you are only using one spark table. The way to do this is to input "55" for all rows/columns in the tables you don't want to use. Remember, the eec will choose the lowest spark values from all the tables so having 55 in the base table for instance means that those values will never be used. I can use my car as an example. It has a supercharger and I want to set the spark relatively low for safe operation. In my case I want to use the bdln table for spark control so I can also relocate the iat sensor in the discharge side of the supercharger. By doing this I can retard timing by using the "spk act retard" table so as discharge temps go up from the blower my timing will go down. I disable the ALT, MBT tables by setting them to 55. I also remove any spark adder values from the "base/bdln add a/f" tables by setting them to 0. The base table is set to the same values as I have in the bdln table. Now I can set my spark to whatever I want and that is what they will be. I also have spark retard for iat/act temps so if the weather is cooler then I will have a little more spark advance and more power. Hotter weather means the spark will be retarded and therefore "safer", compared to using a fixed spark value. Another benefit is if you were to use water injection you could see increased power from the lower iat's but if the water inj. fails you would simply see less timing and not damage anything. posts.content: shonut Tuning Addict Posts: 462 Joined: Mon Sep 15, 2003 7:11 pm Location: Ingleside, Ontario, Canada Contact: Contact shonut Website Re: HANGING IDLE Quote Post by shonut » Wed Apr 28, 2004 8:20 am richard wrote: MY CAR IDLES HIGH AFTER PEDAL IS RELEASED. CAN ANYBODY HELP Check for a sticky TPS. That's a classic symptom of a sticking TPS that tells the EEC that the throttle is depressed after you have released it, so it commands more timing etc., giving a higher idle. Look for a TPS voltage > 1V or > 0V with CalCon, depending on the car and what the TPS strategy is. Or it could be a good old fashioned sticky throttle cable (who thinks of that in this modern day and age of electronics?) posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Mon Apr 25, 2005 6:31 am For the 347, all you need to do is change the CID scalar with the tweecer (along with changes to compensate for your mods). That said, if you did nothing to compensate for the stroker motor, the result would be skewed load% calculations. (much like adding a supercharger or turbo as far as the eec is concerned) You don't NEED a new computer. The tweecer has a steep learning curve. You need to have good tuning skills and be computer 'friendly' to pick it up effectively. The tweecer was one of the best investments I made. If your drag racing only, then maybe you don't need a tuning device/chip. posts.author: qikgts
posts.content: qikgts Regular Posts: 295 Joined: Tue Jul 08, 2003 9:18 am Location: Rockledge, FL Quote Post by qikgts » Thu Feb 17, 2005 8:32 pm The ISC screw on the SN95's is just an air bleed. Running it in and out changes the amout of air being fed to the idle control motor... Essentially it is the same thing as the idle air bypass deal that people installed on the Fox throttle bodies to correct idle problems back in the dark ages. It does nothing electronicly speaking, it just changes the effect of the duty cycle of the ISC motor. Adaptive must look at the duty cycles and determine the legnth and amount pulses needed to maintain a target RPM and then make changes to the pulses based on what it wants it to be. On my car, an extreme adjustment just makes the idle hang and or surge. Turning screws on a Holley 4180c these days... My Hooptie: '85 GT. Just about bone stock and knocks down 24 on the highway... This stops the EEC from trying to bring the idle back up while trying to get a base idle logged. If the spout was plugged in, the EEC would increase spark trying to stablize the RPM around the desired RPM. The same goes for the ISC. You can leave them disconnected and increase the RPM at 100 RPM intervals until you get to 2000rpm. In order for the O2 sensors to operate properly, they must be at, and stay at, a minimum temperature. If you place the HEGO O2 sensors farther away from the head than the stock location, you may have the sensor too far away to keep it hot enough to read correctly due to the cooled exhaust gases. I have an 80mm MAF, Novi2k, 75mm TB and TFS intake and heads (on a 351w) in case this is necessary info. Any help is appreciated. Disconnect the ISC and let the car idle. Set the throttle body screw so that the car will just barely idle. Set the TPS to ~0.99. Now datalog the car for about 30 seconds after it is fully warmed up. Average the airflow and convert it to the correct units for the throttle body airflow, sorry don't remember off hand. Set the throttle body airflow. Now reconnect the ISC and datalog the car at several different RPM points for at least 30 seconds. Set the idle RPM to do this. Average the numbers for RPM and airflow and set the X & Y values in the ISC nuetral airflow function. You will probably have to change the X values to match the RPM values you average from the datalog as it will not match what you set the idle to. Compare the new ISC settings to the old settings and figure out what percentage increase you have. For me this was the exact same percentage for all Y values in the function. Increase the dashpot pre-postion by the same percentage. air flow conversion factor is: MAF * 2.2046226 / 60 Randy Cobra Intake / AFR 165 Heads CompCams 270H Camshaft 1989 Saleen Coupe # 653 ***** Top

posts.author: R&D
posts.content: R&D Regular Posts: 79 Joined: Thu Apr 14, 2005 11:27 am Location: CALEDONIA, MI Quote Post by R&D » Fri Apr 22, 2005 9:35 pm How new is the motor? If you just rebuilt it you have to make sure that the two main lifter gallies right above the pcv inlet is properly plugged. You can go to Napa and get the correct size.....I think it was 3/4's of an inch or so. I had a similar incedent with my 347 just after rebuilding it. We didn't have the right galley plug so we made a plug out of steel. This has worked very well in the past with other engines when we didn't have the correct size on hand but for some reason the preassure was too much and the plug popped right off. Once the plug popped off oil would start dumping in my motor and huge clouds of smoke developed. After further inspection I found that on throttle conditions, the oil would shoot up past the pcv, into the breather tube, and finally ending up in the plenum. It wouldn't take long and the oil would start puddeling up. To fix the problem I obviously had to pull the upper and lower intake off and get the correct size plug with some good sealer and pop it into place. luckely I had a high volume oil pump. I was amazed that the pump could keep up with the demands though. When you actually look at the gallies you'll see that there are (2-3....can't remember right off hand) that come together in one spot. The two that come in on angles feed the lifters. THAT'S LIKE CUTTING ONE OF YOUR MAIN ARTERIES IN YOUR BODY AND ASKING YOUR HEART TO STILL KEEP PRESSURE AT NORMAL LEVELS! Starting around 2k rpm the load should be closer to 100% and at higher rpms probably around 130%. After that you will want to change your "open loop load" function to go OL at lower rpms, again probably around 2k rpm and at around .5 load and lower as rpms increase. Timing will have to be reduced starting at lower rpms and lower loads, set it relatively low at first for testing and see how much timing you can use without detonation. posts.author: lcpldontkno
posts.content: lcpldontkno Gear Head Posts: 3 Joined: Mon Apr 25, 2005 3:24 am Location: Iraq Done my research, gurus please verify... Quote Post by lcpldontkno » Mon Apr 25, 2005 3:34 am After days of searching for info, this is the list ive compiled of values i need to modify for my single turbo 5.0 @ 8psi. I wont have hands on until i get back to the states, but im trying to get a very good idea of what i need to do when i get back. The turbo setup will be installed when i get back so i wanted to get it tuned asap. Am i missing anything from this this? Please add or make corrections to the list as you see fit. Also, specific or approximate values would be appriciated. Thanks in advance. Timing 3 spark tables (altitude, limp, and sea level) Control your timing everywhere, but WOT Base OL spark – should be set at 10, push the limit without detonation WOT spark advance vs RPM – take degrees out to prevent detonation at boost levels. Air/Fuel Ratio Disable adaptive mode - ACT maximum = 1; ACT minimum = 250. Adaptive will only function if the air charge is less than the maximum and more than the minimum. So setting the two values like this keeps adaptive from ever kicking in. Once tuned, re-enable and set fuel table adaptive update rate to all 10s except the top row. This will help the engine learn better at all levels. Also change adaptive min and max to 30 and 200. This will help the engine learn at all temps. Base OL fuel Table- controls all your fuel except WOT and startup. Use the Base OL table, plug in 11.5, then data log, and make corrections on the MAF transfer to get it to a 11.5 at the exhaust end. Fuel table startup OL – change fuel delivery for ECT, last two columns for hot start Fuel table stabilized – switches to this table once ect is stable. Set you a/f ratio according to load WOT fuel multiplier- Set to all 1's initially. Controls your fuel at WOT, BUT this is a multiplier (i.e. 1=stoich, .9 = 10% rich, 1.1 = 10% lean) it gets its final value from the base OL table. The WOT Fuel multiplier is almost last resort to get the A/F nice and stable throughout the RPM range. Accel enrichment vs. TP – add or remove fuel. 3rd y value, boosted should be around .450-.650 Cranking fuel PW vs. time – lower this if necessary to help with startup. 0.6 or so PW vs. ECT – lower this as well to ease hot start. MAF/Injector compensation MAF Curve – increase or decrease values (kg/hr) to correct a/f ratio if needed. Should be close to stated values. Multiply stock number by less than one to enrichen, more than 1 to lean out. Injectors – Change high slope to 42.00, low slope to 42.00*1.2=50.4. This lets the low slope make low rpms smoother. May have to set low slope to 42.00 after installing 255 lph pump. Injector offset vs. battery voltage – for 42 lb injectors, .45*Y. Y=stock scalar values Misc Scalars WOT breakpoint – lower to 2.0 to engage WOT tables sooner Speed limiter A&B – set both to 127.5 to disable Rev limiter half fuel on/off – set on higher than off, set both to 7000 to disable Time at high load to force open loop – set to 0 Top

posts.content: pthornton Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Sat Nov 01, 2003 5:11 pm Location: Tupelo, MS Quote Post by pthornton » Wed Apr 27, 2005 11:02 pm Antonymooreus wrote: Have you checked your TDC with your balancer? Yep, dead on. This is pretty standard timing for AFR heads on a 302. This timing is with AFR of 12.8/36 degrees(peak tq) - 13.0/38 degrees(peak hp). More cubic inches generally needs less timing which would apply to your 428. In general, you want to increase timing until the engine doesn't increase horsepower. So you really do want to run as much timing as you can. Most engines will ping at this point which is why they won't make any more power, but that is not cast in stone. Of course, supercharging is another issue entirely. But then again, not much different. I set the AFR to 11.8. I then bump the timing until it pinged and backed off 2 degrees. This resulted in 16 degrees timing on my modular 2V. The total timing is VERY dependent on the AFR for supercharging. I could run much more timing with a much richer mixture, but probably not make any more power according to the article by innovative. The EEC expects to see a difference between the front and the rear, and if they report the same, then the thermactor system is not working correctly. This is why you need MIL eliminators if you go catless. This is mandated with OBD-II. You will not benefit from replacing any of them with a WB. A WB is best used in addition to the factory NB O2s. It is mainly for instrumentation, not computer control (with our EECs). The book costs $75 as far as I know. I had heard the book basically tells us stuff we already know, however, after reading the tuning section I am very impressed! I can see they would have tuned my vehicle quite differently than I did. Some stuff of interest, they use the stock maf curve as a starter then (if using a ProM cal'ed for bigger injectors) they just multiply the difference in max flow rates and derive a new curve from that instead of using a 10-30 pt conversion table. Of course they point out that further tuning will have to be done. They seem to move engine CID around to get load values where they want them to be. They provide inj breakpoints for injectors up to 60lbs. An interesting one to me was using "manifold volume" to increase tip in fuel (accelerator pump). I was surprised at how high to set the value. On my car the stock setting (bullitt intake) is "9", they said going as high as "17" was not out of the question. No wonder my changing it to "11" did not seem to make a big difference. They talk about how 03 cobras won't accept maf values higher than stock (about 1800 kg/hr if I remember right) and how to get around it with a "bigger" meter. Info on "batt inj comp" tables for various injector sizes, adaptive update table info and how it works, what the numbers mean, etc. Lots of good stuff relating to ISC settings. There is more and I have not really read it all yet but I think this book is very worthwhile even at $75.00. Some of us may not need the info but I will be trying some of their ideas on my car soon. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Sat Apr 30, 2005 9:58 am Read some more, think I found some mistakes. They give a table of recommended "batt inj comp volt" values for various injectors sizes and they seem to be mixed up. Usually the values go lower as injector size goes up but the numbers are not following that pattern. An interesting thing I learned is for some newer cars, 02 and up GT's and the 03-04 cobras. You cannot enter in a higher maf flow value beyond what the stock setting is. Therefore if you try to put the flow values for a cal'ed meter it won't accept them. The work around (probably some of you already know this but I did'nt) is to leave the maf curve alone as well as the inj slopes. Find the difference in inj sizes that the new meter is calibrated for (lets say you have 50lb inj. and a meter to match) divide 50 by 19 to get .38. Multiply .38 times the engine cid value, 281*.38=106.78 and enter that value in. This makes sense as the new meter will output a lower maf voltage compared to stock and cause the eec to think the load is much lower. By reducing the cid size the load is brought back up and you can tune from there. From what I have read I suspect that most of the time this is how they compensate for ProM's, etc, instead of getting a flow sheet and entering the values. Also, the numbers in the "fuel adaptive update" table are in seconds, the number means how long learning is allowed before a change is made. For supercharged guys like me, the bigger the bypass valve the better, but more important is the location of the bypass tube on the supercharger inlet side, too close to the maf and it causes erratic maf voltages. Mounting the bypass tube in the power pipe angled towards the blower inlet is best. Of course all the power pipes I have seen do not angle the tube . I will be working on that one this weekend as I have seen the maf voltage jumping at certain throttle positions. posts.author: dsleepy47
posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Sun May 01, 2005 11:26 pm There are a number of things that can induce voltages on the LM-1 ground causing the output to vary. And the analog out is unfiltered while the LM-1 display is filtered so the numbers don't jump around so fast that they are unreadable. You can put an RC filter on the analog out, use a 10k resistor and a 1.0 - 1.6 uf cap. After that offset your LM-1 output voltages to compensate for the difference in voltage between the LM-1 and Calcon. I also set my analog out for 0 - 5v and wrote my own innovate file. Increasing the voltage range decreases the effect of fluctuations. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Tue May 03, 2005 12:49 pm To get the best economy you need: the most timing you can run and a lean mixture (14.7:1). To achive this, you need to get your load% in the 40-50% range at your desired cruising speed. Load% was the key for me. If your load is higher the eec will pull timing and add fuel for the higher load, and that kills your fuel economy. Look at the base fuel table and see what load range has 14.x as target AFR. Thats what your trying to hit to get the best milage. This has worked for me, YRMW. My last tank got me about 18 mpg city roughly. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Wed May 04, 2005 11:46 am The way I think about it is: ALL EEC's have both a strategy and a calibration. The strategy is the combination of both the hardware and the (unchangable) firmware code in the EEC. The firmware is the program that the EEC actually runs. The calibration is a set of values that the firmware uses in it's workings (sorta like RAM). A calibration is not a program, just data. For example, the strategy (firmware) might say "to calculate fuel in this particular instance, I'm going to look to the calibration for the value to use in location 3459 (say fuel_base_table_OL) THEN multiply that by location 4865 (say OL fuel multiplier) etc. You can't change how the strategy decides how to calculate fuel (like multiplying location 3459 by location 4865), but you can change the values in locations 3459 and 4865 to alter it's outcome. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sun Apr 10, 2005 7:52 pm The best way to adjust this is to log LAMBSE and note what the swing is. What I mean by this is, the EEC cycles the AFR around 14.64 in CL. So if you let the car idle and watch the LAMBSE it will go to around 14.9 and then swing to 14.1. It will continue to do this until OL is activated. What I did was adjust the exhaust pulse delay until the swing from rich to lean was at its minimum. When adjusting, start low and work your way up just to the poit where the swing get larger. You will have to repeat this for each RPM and Load range. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

title: Kamrf's were stuck at 1.000 - EECTuning.org

posts.author: 7000rpm
posts.content: 7000rpm Gear Head Posts: 12 Joined: Thu Mar 31, 2005 9:18 am Kamrf's were stuck at 1.000 Quote Post by 7000rpm » Tue Apr 19, 2005 12:47 pm I wanted to contribute to the forum by telling of my latest success with the tweecer. I was having problems some others have had with the adaptive not working. Injector slopes and MAF transfer were good enough to give me good drivability and startup but the adaptive wasn't working. I tried reloading the tune in the tweecer. I tried removing everything and cleaning again. I had an exhaust leak at the headers and fixed it. I even replace the old 02 sensors. The car ran really well but the adaptive wasn't working. I noticed the check engine light and have come to find out it was my problem. I was getting a code 15 and a code 31. The code 15 was for ROM failure. I changed the checksum base address to 0 and the code 15 went away but the adaptive still didn't work. Today I went out after doing some reading on the forums and disabled the EGR system altogether and zeroed out the EGR spark tables and various adders and multipliers. I cleared the codes and then turn it on and pull them again and get codes 11 and 11. I take it for a drive and the check engine light is off and kamrf's are fluctiating like they should be. Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Mon May 09, 2005 7:42 pm Welcome fellow CBAZAer, There are 5 positions on the switch box. Farthest Counter Clock Wise (the dot) is #1, and farthest CW (AKA farthest from the dot) is #5. #5 is tweecer disabled, eec running off of the calibration in the eec. You cannot write to #5. If you try, I believe that it ends up in #1 (not certain, just don't do it). To get a tune from caledit into the tweecer, you put the switch in the position that you want the tune to go into, turn on IGN, wait for USB driver to load on PC, then click write tweecer. You have to do that for each switch position. As for it not running well on other tunes, it could be that the tune is not set up right/untuned. It could be that you don't have a good J3 connection. To test this, connect CPU with tweecer on EEC, and do a read eec. Then look at the read values. They should make sense, if you have a bad J3 connection, then the values would be all screwey, like idle speed 32423, engine displacement = 1832.33, etc. Rick I no longer have (but what all my posts refer to): 94GT, 302NA, AFR165, FTI hyd cam, Performer, 24lb-hr @39PSI, 65TB, Pro-M 80 w/ NA 94-95 GT cal, long tubes, egr & smog delete, T-5 TwEECer RT v1.20b3, J4J1 base, PLX M-300 WB, EEC Analyzer Top

After getting my idle a/f's inline with LambSe1&2 (or commanded a/f), I tried smoothing the maf curve for the volt values below the .8-.9 . Once that was done I didn't even touch the kg/hr values that corresponded to voltage values lower than idle. Then, after a bit I had the maf curve right were I wanted it and my KAM's fluctuating really really close to 1. No matter how hard you try you'll always will have some correction. I shoot for below 5%. Since my O2s are pretty much dead, I had to compare the commanded a/f's with my wideband. At times the KAM will show correction but my wideband will show that it's right in line. Tommorrow I'll put those old O2's to rest. Hope this helps. It will calculate the best fit of a line for the injector slope. It will use the KAMRF's percentages or AFR error to correct the MAF curve. Cam calculation are based off of the PW logged in the datalog and the cam profile build sheet. posts.author: pthornton
posts.content: pthornton Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Sat Nov 01, 2003 5:11 pm Location: Tupelo, MS Quote Post by pthornton » Sat Apr 30, 2005 11:50 am Do you have an RT? If no then upgrade to an RT. If yes, then buy EEC Analyzer. Best investment of your time you can make. You need to dial in the injector slopes and the bottom part of the MAF curve up to say 3.0 volts. Download EEC Analyzer and read the help files on the techniques involved. You can download it and review the help for free. Next step is to go to a dyno or get access to a wideband. Set the WOT fuel mutliplier to 1.0. Go into base fuel OL table and set the AFR to something fairly rich like 12.6 and make a WOT blast on the dyno. Compare the AFR. If it is 12.6 your MAF curve is on, if it is lean then richen the MAF curve or vice-versa. When it matches, start making some runs for power. Try AFR around 12.8 to 13.2 to see what the car likes. Now use the global WOT global spark adder to add timing to see what power you can get from that. You're done. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sat May 14, 2005 12:10 am I posted this a while back. I must say that every combination is different therefore tuning will be different. Below is a kist of steps that I would start with. 1) Enter the MAF and injector slopes and offsets that will get the car running. This is usually a first guess of what the slopes and MAF curve should be. They do not need to be perfect at this point. 2) Enter cam specs and calculate the base injector timing. I would not recommend doing a WOT or heavy load pull at this point. This is just to get a base. What ever cells in the calculation are empty (N/A), I would fill in with logical numbers from surrounding cells. Again this is just to get a base injector timing table. 3) At this point the MAF and or slopes need to be dialed in. There are several approaches to do this. 3a) If you have the MAF curve from the manufacture, I would start with that, and then I would calculate the slopes using the EEC Analyzer. This is done on the "Injector Slope" dialog and not the PW vs KAMRF tab. This will get the slopes very close. After that I would fine tune the MAF with either a WB or KAMRF's. The object is to get the KAMRF's as close to 1.0 as possible if you are using a KAMRF method. If you are using a WB, the object is to get the LAMBSE's and WB readings as close as possible. 3b) If the MAF curve is unknown and the slopes are known, then you should leave the slopes alone and adjust the MAF to match the slopes. You can use either the KAMRF or WB method to do this. 3c) If the slopes and MAF are unknown then you can either adjust the MAF to match the slopes or the slopes to match the MAF. In most cases I would match the MAF to the slopes. It is easier to guess at the slopes than it is the MAF. This means that you should leave the slopes at some known value and adjust the MAF to match. 4) Now calculate the Throttle Body air flow and ISC Neutral air flow numbers. 5) Now you can do a few WOT pulls and fine tune the Injector timing. 6) I would now tackle the sea level load scaling. Run a data log through the EEC Analyzer and adjust the blue line up or down to match the red line. The above six steps (overly simplified) have worked for me. Each car reacts differently and will require different adjustments. This is the main reason why I have not tried to publish a sequence of calculations. It is solely up to you. If I am missing some step here please jump in and add it. After the above steps are done to your satisfaction, you can then adjust the spark and fuel tables for performance gains. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue May 17, 2005 9:40 am In my opinion the fuel tables and spark should be left to last. The LAMBSE is the target AFR. If the tuning seps go well then the actual AFR and commanded should match. The fuel tables should only be adjust for performance and not drivability. Again in my opinion, the WOT multiplier should be set to 1.0, this would allow the user to concentrate on the fuel table. This would mean that whatever you put in the table is what you are targeting at WOT. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: gt90stang
posts.content: gt90stang Tuning Addict Posts: 531 Joined: Wed Apr 16, 2003 2:11 pm Location: CA Quote Post by gt90stang » Fri Apr 29, 2005 3:18 pm Whitehorse, I had to redo my MAF curve due to my MAC cold air kit with a 90* bend in front of the MAF. Since you have it running start by changing the values in the tables to the AFR you want at higher loads. Then get your lower and upper injector slopes correct. Then tune the lower part of the MAF curve based on your Kamrf's running closed loop. You can take the % increase or decrease for the three highest CL MAF changes and extrapolate that on up the curve. Next comes the upper part of the MAF curve, you have to be careful here not to detonate, also it is best done on a dyno. Just look at your logged AFR and it should be equal to Lambse. I had good luck using: (((1-(AFR/Lambse)) x 0.5) + (AFR/Lambse)) x MAF Kg/hr = new MAF Kg/hr ***ok double checked this and now it is correct. The intent is to increase or decrease 50% of the difference between AFR and Lambse. This worked well for me and gave right on adjustments, YMMV. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Tue May 17, 2005 9:05 pm You are right, you can't change the amount of air the turbo is blowing through. What I am trying to say is that the MAF needs to be recalibrated to measure more air because it is hitting 5 volts too soon. The way it is recalibrated is to set it to a larger injector size than it is currently set for. Think of it another way. Because of your mods the engine is capable of ingesting way more air than the hot wire sensor can account for. The sensor reaches 5 volts too soon because it is set for smaller injectors on the assumption the engine would never ingest this much air. The amount of air possible to shove into the motor needs to be matched with injectors big enough to achieve an 11.0:1 (or richer) mix at max air volume possible with your particular combination. posts.content: R&D Regular Posts: 79 Joined: Thu Apr 14, 2005 11:27 am Location: CALEDONIA, MI Quote Post by R&D » Thu May 19, 2005 4:46 am O2's generally have a hollow tube down the center of the sensor that allows small amounts of outside air to reach the inside. From here, the o2's are able to generate voltage output based on oxygen diff. greater difference from outside air to exhaust.....more voltage. Do you have a wideband? If you do, try clearing your KAM.....re-writing a clean file......and throwing it into open loop. Then compare your wideband reading with your comanded A/F using the dataloger. While dataloging, also make sure that your % duty cycle is the same for each bank. This should then give you a good idea of how accurate the o2's are. Another quick thing.......have you dataloged with the o2's payloaded? If you have........do the voltages appear slugish in changing? If you've started messing around with the wiring for the 02's, I'll bet that's a big contributor to your problem. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Tue May 17, 2005 9:18 pm I hope it isn't nitpicking but when ProM sends you a "supercharged" maf meter it is intended to be used in the "cheat" mode. In other words, a guy who wants to compensate for different size injectors and is not using a tweecer, etc. The output of the meter deliberately increases fuel more than normal at the top end for a blower car. It also has the effect of limiting the max airflow the meter can read compared to a straight n/a calibration. Changing the curve in the tweecer can indeed negate this effect but the meter still responds electrically the way stated above. I had my meter recaled by them awhile ago and specified a 50lb cal n/a so it would have as much "room" as possible. It worked out well as on my combo I only have hit 4.2 volts max. As long as the timing light is showing your timing to be -10 (as long as the damper has not slipped) then the distributor is in time with the cam. posts.author: Chris Mureen
posts.content: Chris Mureen Tuning Addict Posts: 443 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 6:44 pm Location: Austin, TX Quote Post by Chris Mureen » Thu Nov 25, 2004 9:31 am The EEC makes the decision based on timers that are programed into the PCM. I know on my strategy these are scalars but the Tweecer doesn't have them. I think yours is based on ECT and number of O2 switchs. The engineers built logic to account for normal warm up time with heated O2s. Once that time has past, the O2s start sending a swinging voltage to the EEC from the measurement of a/f. If the exhaust getting to the O2s is cooled too much then the reading returned may be incorrect. Old O2s lose their ability to swing as much or swing too slowly which results in incorrect a/f measurements around stoich. Keep in mind that narrow band O2s are very inaccurate as you move away from stoich so once they start being off they may be way off. So the answer to your question is that the heater in the O2 is what gets it hot and if broken then your tune would be all screwed up. If the O2 is fine and the distance is too far so the exhaust is too cool then the reading would be off. Frankly, I have never run into this myself. Most dynos even stick their wideband sensor into the exhaust pipe, which is many feet away and much cooler exhaust. If the sensor is in good shape, it is generally pretty accurate when compared to my wideband welded into a bung on the headers, as long as there aren't cats in between. I have seen a corrupted binary cause this type of issue. Have you tried starting over? Disconnect the PCM and let it discharge and then reload a totally fresh binary. A corrupted adaptive table does odd things. posts.content: WA2FAST Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Wed Sep 29, 2004 1:04 pm Location: MI Contact: Contact WA2FAST Website AOL Quote Post by WA2FAST » Thu Nov 25, 2004 1:18 pm Chris Mureen wrote: Once that time has past, the EEC starts sending a swinging voltage to them to use in the measurement of a/f. I agree with what you said with the exception of what you wrote here... the EEC does not send any swinging voltage to the O2's. The O2's generate voltage based on the oxygen content differential between the exhaust gas and the atmosphere... they are swinging because of the corrections the EEC is making on injector pulsewidth while the engine is running. The only voltage sent by the vehicle to the O2's is for the heating element... this is only to aid in the O2's heating up faster so that the car can control emissions sooner. Yes, it is all based off of timers though and I still beleive that there are plenty of usefull items that we still do not have access to with the TwEECer. -Don- 87' GT, A9L, TwEECer RT, P1SC@12psi Non-Intercooled, AFM PP, 3" Pro-M#42, 70mm TB, GT-40 Intake, GT-40X Heads, B303, 1.6, BBK 1-5/8" Long Tubes, 306 Built Bottom End, Probe Block Girdle, TR3550, 3.55, PLX WB, Jan 07 Modified Mustangs Feature Car Top

posts.content: SHaFT7 Tuning Addict Posts: 348 Joined: Sun Jul 25, 2004 3:17 pm Quote Post by SHaFT7 » Fri May 20, 2005 12:45 pm technically, as long as you have the proper transfer function for that maf, you can put whatever injector you want in the combo, as long as you also adjust the slopes to match. the only time you MUST match the injector size to the maf cal is if you aren't running a tweecer/chip, since the cal of the maf 'fakes' out the computer. now, if you're going to peg that 24lb prom maf, then by all means have it recal'ed higher, and i agree that getting it cal'd higher than your current injector is a good idea, as it lets you grow into it. pegging meters is bad for your engine's longevity, so make sure you're within the airflow max of the meter, and you're good to go 91GT, TwEECER R/T, A9L mods back to NA H/C/I for now, turbo combo coming this fall! 02 ZX-6 - stock Top

posts.author: Daggar
posts.content: Daggar Gear Head Posts: 58 Joined: Fri Nov 12, 2004 6:33 pm Quote Post by Daggar » Sat May 07, 2005 8:31 am To my knowledge, none of the Ford OEM SD setups were BAR/MAP and therefore do not read boost pressures. I would be suprised to find out there was something different from that, even in a Lightning. I'm going to assume that your SD setup is the same as or similar to the 86-88 Mustang. There should be a line running from the unboosted manifold to the boosted manifold, then to a one way check valve (isolating boost from the MAP), then to the MAP sensor. There should be a .070" orifice installed in the line running from the boosted manifold (it slows the equalization of the boosted and non-boosted manifolds within the vac line). posts.author: kickerscrt
posts.content: kickerscrt Regular Posts: 122 Joined: Wed Feb 02, 2005 4:41 am Quote Post by kickerscrt » Thu May 26, 2005 1:29 pm From what I understand, LAMBSE is the commanded a/f ratio. In closed loop, the eec is trying to get the a/f ratio to 14.64 as shown in the stabilized closed loop fuel table. Once warmed up, the car should remain in closed loop until a certain load percentage is reached, and a certain voltage from the TPS. As far as open loop, from how I understand that is the eec reads the voltage from the maf sensor, goes to the MAF transfer function to see how much air that equals, and then goes the the open loop fuel table. You said it seemed lean at higher rpms, so I'd have to think you'd be in open loop, so all I can suggest is to take a look at your fuel table-base ol and see what values are under the 180* ECT at higher loads. What kind of LAMBSE numbers are you seeing at the higher rpms? Also, if you're not sure of the age of your o2's, it really can't hurt to change them out (well, besides your wallet). My car was showing real lean on cruise, but once I swapped in a fresh set of o2's, everything came back to normal again. 91 LX Coupe, A9P/A9M, Intercooled ProCharger P1SC (9 Psi), FMS 42lb, PMAS 3" ProTube (42lb N/A Curve), AFR 165 heads, E303, FRPP Cobra Intake, Bassani exhaust, 3.73, aod-t-5 conversion Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Thu May 26, 2005 5:20 pm Check your signal return (EEC's sensor ground) wire. Sounds like you either have a ground issue or a wet connector shorting out. I had a similar thing happen to me. The connector that connects the main engine harness to the lower engine harness (near the waterpump and ground stud) got wet. What happened was I had that connector unplugged and had the lower rad hose off, then I jacked up the rear of the engine and the waterpump dumped coolant into the connector. I tried to get it all out, but didn't get it all. My HEGO2 was reading higher voltages than normal, and the car wanted to go into self test mode on it's own. Signal return was in that connector. posts.content: scott88 Tuning Addict Posts: 318 Joined: Thu Dec 09, 2004 6:00 pm Location: Albany, NY Quote Post by scott88 » Mon May 30, 2005 12:31 pm Ok, I have been busy with the car for a couple days, trying to figure out why it won't even run at all now. No matter what tune I run, even a stock read, the car wouldn't run right. Sputtering, coughing, etc.- so, I replaced the "fixed" (soldered) switch cable I had been using, after I accidentally cut it- the solder was perfect, but just to be sure, I replaced the cable anyway with a brand new one that is about 50 feet long (looks great wadded up inside the dash!). I did a read of the stock eec, and copied my changes from my most recent tune (thanks Juice). Last night I'm fiddling around and the car still runs like crap. on every switch position, and won't even run at all on the tweecer tune. Last night, it even went dead a couple times- I would try to start it, and nothing (like the starter went, but it had battery power). So, this morning I get an idea- the car sounds like it is missing when it runs on the tune, so I unhooked my brand new MSD 6-AL box (which is never hot because it sits next to the front seat), rewired the tach to the stock coil wire, and fired the car up on the tweecer tune. It ran perfect, like nothing had ever been wrong, except for some surging because I'd had the negative unhooked. This surging lasted for about 30 seconds, then the idle smoothed right out. Took the car down the street, and smoked the hell out of the tires in 2nd, 3rd, and 4th. I know it's early, but it seems to have fixed the problems I was having- no more wacky noises coming from the filter, and the car runs great so far. Do any of these symptoms sound like they could have been caused by the MSD box? I can't believe this thing is bad, I just got it brand new. I used the quick disconnect harness from MSD, for these very times whem I would need to revert to the stock ignityion in case of failure. Has anyone heard of the MSD screwing up the tweecer? I triple checked all the wiring, grounds, etc. and they were all solid on the MSD. But, it now runs better without it hooked up. It seems now like all my tweecer problems were not in fact problems with the tweecer at all. Any takers? posts.author: Carl
posts.content: Carl Regular Posts: 81 Joined: Wed Mar 05, 2003 10:35 pm Location: Canada Quote Post by Carl » Mon May 23, 2005 11:12 am WOW! What an interesting problem. If you have any problems with a stuck/bent or burned valve,you will pick it up with either a compression test or better still a leak down test.With a leak down test you will be able to determine if your compression loss is through either the intake or exhaust valves or through the rings.Broken valve springs,relating to my own experiences with them,always produced an unstable idle,the engine also would not be able to rev out cleanly,there was a lot of stumbling.If you are using double or triple springs,my guess would be with a B303 cam your running double springs a compression or leak down test will not show anything abnormal.Pulling the valve cover from that side is one sure fire way of checking your springs,they are usually quite easy to spot,especially if it is an outer spring. Did you pull any of the plugs? The plugs on that bank should have been able to give you some clue as to where your A/F mixture was at. Next I would check that cylinder's plug wire,check for resistance,general rule is approximately 5000 Ohm's per foot.Also pay close attention to the plug boot,has it been damaged (dry,splintering,cracking) by the extreme heat.That will give you a miss and will send raw fuel into the exhaust. Last but not least check the plug.Is there any carbon tracking on the outside where the porcilan meets the steel hex.If your are in doubt,swap the wire and plug one at a time with a different cylinder,one that had no problems. Good luck, Carl 89 LX.302,A9L,BXR intake,Brodix heads,Z303,Hooker L/T headers,EDIS equipped. 85mm Accufab T.B, 85mm C&L Tuner MAF 36lb Bosch Injectors. Top

posts.author: Carl
posts.content: Carl Regular Posts: 81 Joined: Wed Mar 05, 2003 10:35 pm Location: Canada Quote Post by Carl » Mon May 23, 2005 12:21 pm On my roller lifters,I am using one full turn of preload.The way I adjust them,tighten the down until you can feel drag on the pushrod,(spin it between your fingers) I then add one full turn and then tighten the lock nut.Your's will be similar except you should start to feel torque.I know many will say that one turn is to much preload,and I would normally agree,but I have found my valve train way too noisey for a hydraulic lifter using anything less.Ford's roller lifters have an aweful lot of plunger travel,general rule used to be adjust to two thirds of the total lifter travel,which I believe is around two full turns.At any rate,I don't think your problem is lifter preload related.Check the conector on the injector,make sure its snug.I am sure you have checked the o-ring on the manifold side right. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Wed Jun 01, 2005 6:54 am WOT breakpoint and OL TP breakpoints You don't have these scalars on your eec. "load limit open loop vs rpm" is what determines when you go OL on your car. It is under functions. Look at the values, you will see it takes high load ( .8 ) at 2krpm to enter OL, as the rpms go higher the amount of load needed to go OL decreases. You can reduce the load values if you want to enter OL sooner. Under scalars I see "fuel OL mult delay" of 38 seconds. since the OL multiplier is not used in your strat it does not matter. Manifold volume can be used to help with "accerator" pump function on tip in, on my car (but maybe not on yours) reducing the number increases fuel. You may have to increase the number to get the same effect. It sounds like the maf curve needs to be adjusted for the stutter more than anything else. Decay rate does not seem to do anything except when the car is revved while not moving. Dashpot clip seems to be the one that is active all the time in that air is present all the time and when you let off the gas it keeps a certain minimum of air through the TB. Too much air and the car "shuffles" too little and it decelerates quicker. About the fuel cutoff, are you sure it is actually shutting off? Do the inj pw on your datalog show 0 pw when it happens? The shuffling I mentioned feels similar to the fuel shutoff. posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Thu Jun 02, 2005 9:18 am Ok, here is the deal. Brian wanted to lean out the closed loop afr to get better milage. The problem with this is it does not address timing. If the eec is commanding a richer mixture due to load% being off, then I guarantee that it also is commanding LESS than optimal timing advance. (due to load being skewed). So kickerscrt, now you stated that you adjusted afr and timing tables to get fuel economy. Where I just fixed my load% and let the eec use the factory afr (14.7) AND advance the timing. Both of these are a MUST to get fuel economy and to burn a lean mixture without drivability problems. To me its just easier to get the load right and use the factory settings. If load% isn't right, then the eec is most likely going in and out of open loop while cruising. And that does nothing for gasmilage. Probably great for passing cars though. :D Look at the base OPEN loop table and see what load% and temps the eec would command 14.x afr. <<< This is where you want to be while cruising. So even if you do go into open loop occasionally, its still not going "full rich". This also happens to give you a smoother transition from part throttle to WOT. 180* & 40% seems to be where you want to be. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Sun May 29, 2005 4:37 pm First off you said you have a "blow off" valve, does that mean you are using the maf in a blow through config? If not then you need to use a "bypass" style valve so it is always bypassing air back to the blower until you go into boost. If you are running a lot of boost you may also need a bigger bypass valve and tubing. Angle the tube going into the inlet pipe towards the blower inlet if possible too so the recirculated air won't go towards the maf. You'll need some welding done to do this. As far as the "shuffling" during decel, your isc settings will effect that so some extent. Dashpot clips control the amount of air being sent through the isc valve during decel and too much air causes shuffling and slow decel. My car pops out the exhaust to some extent no matter what, I find that if you are in CL the effect is lessened as the eec tries to compensate for a/f during decel but not completely. When I run the car in fulltime OL it pops more often. Hope I did'nt make it too confusing :D Bob Back to the decel problem, if you maf curve is accurate you can try disabling the dashpot pre-position by setting it to all zeros. This will make the engine come down to idle much faster. It will still "hang" at around 1000 rpm with the clutch in until you come to a complete stop which is not a bad thing as it avoids stalling. 96 GT, Vortech Si trim,Procharger 3 core intercooler, forged bottom end, MAC longtubes, ported PI heads , Edelbrock intake, Crower cams-.580lift/234dur@.050, 80lb injectors, CDAN4/GGL4 processor. posts.author: pthornton
posts.content: pthornton Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Sat Nov 01, 2003 5:11 pm Location: Tupelo, MS Quote Post by pthornton » Wed May 11, 2005 7:04 am Disconnect the ISC and let the car idle. Set the throttle body screw so that the car will just barely idle. Set the TPS to ~0.99. Now datalog the car for about 30 seconds after it is fully warmed up. Average the airflow and convert it to the correct units for the throttle body airflow: MAF * 2.2046226 / 60 Now reconnect the ISC and datalog the car at several different RPM points for at least 30 seconds. Set the idle RPM to do this. Average the numbers for RPM and airflow and set the X & Y values in the ISC nuetral airflow function. You will probably have to change the X values to match the RPM values you average from the datalog as it will not match what you set the idle to. You have to set throttle body airflow and ISC at the same time. TB tells the car how much air flows without ISC and the ISC table tells it how much air is needed to maintain certain RPM. You MAF curve has to be accurate for this to work. Cobra Intake / AFR 165 Heads CompCams 270H Camshaft 1989 Saleen Coupe # 653 ***** Top

posts.author: Daren Woodall
posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Tue Apr 26, 2005 9:26 am Whitehorse wrote: If I put one NB by the turbo and the other down further, is that going to cause problems? First off, am I correct to assume you are a single turbo setup, with both cylinder banks feeding the turbo? You have a tricky setup and I am hesitant now to offer any recommendations. The concern I currently have is that if both NB sensors are located at different points in the down tube and the return signals differ any, the EEC will adjust the fuel trim at the cylinder bank level. It seems to me the ideal location for the stock NB O2 sensors is on in each exhaust side leading to the turbo. This way, the adaptive logic is receiving O2 readings for each bank properly. This is further complicated by your proposed scenario of having one NB on the down pipe and a WB further down the pipe emulated the second NB. You risk throwing off the AFR for a single bank which could be particularily bad for your combo. posts.author: final5-0
posts.content: final5-0 Regular Posts: 269 Joined: Tue Dec 17, 2002 10:02 pm Location: DFW Texas Quote Post by final5-0 » Sun Jun 05, 2005 10:40 am Here is how I view CBAZA fuel ratios ...... just the basics When in CL or cruise around town conditions, the pcm will use O2's & adaptive to try and maintain 14.7. You can use the KAMRF data to adjust inj values and maf curve to get your CL conditions very close to the point that adaptive is not changing things very much. When in OL or more specifically WOT conditions, the O2's are not used so the pcm uses the OL table. You must have a WB for accurate data. You use the data from the wb, fuel table, & maf curve to set your final ratio. As for the t4m0/j4j1 file thing.................... I would think the j4j1 would work better for you but if things were corrupted, then you would have to start over with a clean file. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Jun 05, 2005 10:56 am Hey, why don't you guys that can use v1.20b3 use that? I believe, that for CBAZA at least, v1.20b3 is a better choice. I have no interest in 'downgrading' to v1.30a9. With v1.20b3: CL logs and displays correctly, plus it logs extra data that v1.30 doesn't (stabilized or not). This makes it easy to filter out OL operation for calculations in EA. Especially important if you are forcing OL at idle. You get lots of 'erronous' KAM=1.0000 at idle PWs. You can then also, at the same time, filter out all records that are before the car is stabilized. ACT is also logged correctly. EA uses the ACT to calculate load scaling. Without (correctly) logged ACT, your calcs are going to not be as accurate. There are no data spikes or dropouts. The spikes are very annoying to deal with in LogAnalyst. They can be filtered in EA, but that ends up just taking longer. There is also a workaround for WBs that are not listed in calcon v1.20 (namely PLX). I use my PLX with v1.20b3 with no problems. The only downsides are that ECT doesn't log right, and the screen is a bit smaller. Newer isn't always better... The alpha status of the 1.30a9 along with the "not fit for human consumption" discouraged me... posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Jun 05, 2005 11:31 am What I think that is commonly misunderstood (I know I didn't for a long time) is that the vacuum to the FPR changes the rail pressure (and the pressure that is read on a gauge), but that doesn't change the injected pressure (pressure at the tip). The vacuum is designed to adjust the pressure so the injector is always spraying at a constant PSI. If you don't run vacuum to it, then the injected pressure will change with changing vacuum. I imagine that this condition would be difficult for the EEC to compensate for. Is the intended operation that you want? posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Jun 05, 2005 10:48 pm Yep. When there is vac in the manifold, the FPR lowers the FP at the rail, but at the same time that manifold vac 'pulls' an equal amount extra through the injector to effectively achieve 39PSI. As manifold vac decreases, rail side pressure increases JUST AS the extra 'pull' through the injector decreases. The injector is always, effectively, spraying 39PSI. Without (correctly) logged ACT, your calcs are going to not be as accurate. There are no data spikes or dropouts. The spikes are very annoying to deal with in LogAnalyst. They can be filtered in EA, but that ends up just taking longer. There is also a workaround for WBs that are not listed in calcon v1.20 (namely PLX). I use my PLX with v1.20b3 with no problems. The only downsides are that ECT doesn't log right, and the screen is a bit smaller. Newer isn't always better... The alpha status of the 1.30a9 along with the "not fit for human consumption" discouraged me... I know that several CBAZA users feel the same way, including Grady. posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Tue Jun 07, 2005 11:28 am I thought I would chime in with some information to consider when tuning idle. If your idle seems intermittently unstable and you can't figure out what's going on, take into consideration the changing loads caused by the engine accessories. If you are sitting at a stop light and suddenly your idle takes a nosedive, it is probably because your electric fan just kicked on and created a drain on the alternator. In other circumstances it could be cause by your power windows. My idle is nortoriously worse at night with my headlights are on. Sudden turns of the steering will create load from the P/S pump, or engagement of the A/C clutch. Factor these things into your troubleshooting. The solution can be either A/F problems or poorly calibrated TB Airflow or as stated "isc neutral idle air". Just thought I would throw that out there. I don't think that reverse engineering would describe the difference bewteen the W4H0 and J4J1. The way I think it works is that the CBAZA strategy has the same address map for all processors within the family. The address location for the rev limiters should be the same for W4H0 and J4J1. There have been recent posts concerning the accuracy of the J4J1 file that is posted compared to a "real" J4J1, so that could be a source of error. posts.author: Toy 94 GT
posts.content: Toy 94 GT Regular Posts: 180 Joined: Thu Apr 21, 2005 6:39 pm Quote Post by Toy 94 GT » Fri Jun 10, 2005 5:29 pm It took me a while to understand this concept. Somebody out there correct me if I explain this wrong. When they recalibrate the meter they are changing the amount of voltage output based on air flow. For example a Pro-M calibrated for 19# injectors puts out 2.1 volts for air flow of 118.5 KG/Hr. A Pro-M calibrated for 30# sends the same 2.1 volts for air flows of 187 KG/Hr. Thats a 58% increase. 30# injectors flow 58% more then 19# injectors. The computer will command an injector pulse width of say 3.5 ms for a MAF reading of 2.1 volts. With 19# injectors that will support and air flow rate of 118.5 KG/Hr but with 30# injectors that will support an air flow rate of 187 KG/Hr. Another way to look at is the Pro-M calibrated for 30# injectors puts out 1.65 volts for the same 118.5 KG/Hr of air flow. This reduced voltage output will cause the computer to reduce the injector pulse width so the 30# injectors will only spary enough fuel to support the 118.5 KG/hr of air. This is a long explination I hope I cleared things up instead of making you more confused. The real easy part is you have a Tweecer and all you need to do is input the MAF transfer numbers you get with the meter. Set the injector slopes for the size injectors you have. (in your case a good starting point would be #30 for the high slope and 39# for the low slope) This will work as long as your engine does not flow more air then your MAF can measure (also known as pegging your meter). That should be the only time you need to have your meter re-calibrated when you have a Tweecer. The real easy part is you have a Tweecer and all you need to do is input the MAF transfer numbers you get with the meter. Set the injector slopes for the size injectors you have. (in your case a good starting point would be #30 for the high slope and 39# for the low slope) This will work as long as your engine does not flow more air then your MAF can measure (also known as pegging your meter). That should be the only time you need to have your meter re-calibrated when you have a Tweecer. Hope this helps Bruce Looks pretty good to me. If you focus on the fact that the pcm can only deal with 0.0 to 5.0 volts from the maf and whether you got a combo with airflow that 19's can support or your combo has the airflow requirements of 42's......The amount of airflow has to be delt with by that same voltage range. posts.author: gearhead143
posts.content: gearhead143 Gear Head Posts: 27 Joined: Thu May 19, 2005 11:35 pm Quote Post by gearhead143 » Sun Jun 12, 2005 12:35 am The baro is a inferred value in almost all MAF vehilces except 3.8 SC cars. When KAM is cleared it go's to a defualt value which is in most cases 166Hz. At this value the PCM thinks the car is at about 3000 feet below sea level. Ford says to make 3 or 4 heavy sustianed accelelerations at greater than half thottle to allow baro to update. We have found this to take quite a few more times to get the value to 159Hz. Yes it will relearn on the fly but only with the heavy accel, other wise it will remain at or close to its default value. Baro can also aid in diagnosing a bad MAF sensor.
