posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Jun 01, 2005 4:23 pm The PW vs KAMRF is more or less a good visualization of the overall KAMRF's. What I use it for is to determine if the slope need to be adjusted. If the rolling average line is generally sloping upward or downward then the slopes need to be adjusted. If there are spikes or hills and valleys then the MAF and or breakpoint need to be adjusted. If the slopes need to be adjusted then use the Required fuel vs PW calculation. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: Carl
posts.content: Carl Regular Posts: 81 Joined: Wed Mar 05, 2003 10:35 pm Location: Canada Quote Post by Carl » Thu Jun 16, 2005 9:58 pm On the TFI module connector,you should have one wire that is powered (+ battery voltage) with the key in the run position.On my car this is yellow with a light green tracer.You should also find another wire (red with a light blue tracer) that has power to it only when you hold the key in the start position.I usually disable the starter solenoid by removing the same coloured (red with a light blue tracer) wire off of it.I then have someone hold the key in the start position and look for battery voltage.Power at the OTHER wire (hot in run position) will have NO power while in the start position.If both wires have power in their respective positions I would say a module is a sure thing to replace. posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Thu Jun 16, 2005 1:19 pm Idle strategy (what your calling logic) should only take 6 min to teach the eec after a battery disconnect. To teach the eec idle strategy after you reconnected the battery: Let the car idle for 2 min in neutral. After 2 min are up, turn the wheel back and forth, turn the a/c on, turn on lights, wipers, etc. If your standard shift, your finished. If automatic, you need to repeat the above steps in drive. You really should "teach the eec idle" after every battery disconnect. If that doesn't get your idle stable your tune is not close enough. That takes care of idle. You need to clear KAMs anytime you changed the maf transfer, injector slopes, or injector offset since those have the greatest impact on adaptive. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. title: Fuel table tip for CBAZA, WB users - EECTuning.org

posts.author: Daren Woodall
posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Fuel table tip for CBAZA, WB users Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Wed Jun 15, 2005 10:03 am For others using the approach I am, which is running full-time OL with a WB O2, I have a tip for setting up your fuel_stabilized_Ol table. Using the load limit open loop vs RPM function from the J4J1 calibration as a guide. Set all cells in the fuel_stabilized_OL table to 14.7 (14.64 corrected) below the load/RPM indicated by the function. For example, 2000 rpm column, set all cells from 85% load and below to 14.7. In the 3000 rpm column, set all cells from 70% and below to 14.7, and so on. You will need to give cells below your idle load (occurs during decelleration) special consideration. Use the stock values as a guide. Combined with an EA corrected MAF Transfer and properly scaled load, this should provide the best mileage/emissions during everyday driving conditions. Tune the cells outside of this area for power. Daren 94GT, AFR165, E303, 1.72 RR, GT-40 Intake, 70mm TB, 24lb inj, ProM 75, BBK LT, J4J1, PLX M-300 WB Top

posts.author: Daren Woodall
posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Mon Jun 20, 2005 12:22 pm I started doing this way back, in fact I may have even been the first to try this in the CBAZA strategry. The motivating factor was persistant lean readings from my O2 sensors at idle. This in turn cause the adaptive to enrichen up to the adaptive limit. The rich idle caused surging, stalling and hot start-up problems. I attributed the faulty O2 reading to a cooling effect caused by the long-tube headers during times of low flow. At this point I should clear the record and say that I am not convinced this is still the case. There are many problems that can cause this same symptom including, exhaust leak, unburned charge as a result of the cam, incorrect MAF Transfer. The reason I doubt this assertion now is that my WBO2 also shows lean at times, and it has a much lower operating temperature range. 86GT (Clint) posted a test he did with a thermal gun that supports the long-tube theory. I also have reason to think that it is this interferance with the proper function of OEM O2 sensors that keeps long-tubes from being street legal. That being said... Running full-time OL gives a level of control not otherwise possible which is to control the AFR during idle and cruise. If your car idles best at, say 13.8:1 because of a cam, the EEC will not allow this with CL enabled. As you probably know, the EEC only targets 14.64:1 during CL. Additionally, the OEM O2 sensors are designed to only validate stoich. In short, disabling CL is NOT recommended unless you have compelling reasons to do so. If I dedicated the time I could confirm the above issue by combining the readings of both the OEM O2 and the WB O2, but I must first confirm there are not other issues that could skew the results. I also need to have a bung welded into my h-pipe and reinstall by OEM O2s and I've not felt compelled to do this yet. If you just do lets say a 15 minute drive and then use the info in EA you will find the recommended maf curve is jagged which reflects the changes in a/f during decel being averaged into the maf curve calculation. This is the reason Clint added the filters. If you use filters for max and min AFR, TP, etc. You can filter the records down to only those you wish for consideration. Very slick. Another trick you can do is set your entire fuel table to 13 (depending on your case) and datalog your car's ability to achieve this AFR. Once your MAF is dialed, go back to your standard tables. This helps the accuracy because the LAMBSE is only one value throughout the load range. I believe on a cold start the thermactor is using the diverter valve to dump the air into the atmosphere as the o2's need to heat up as quickly as possible. Then once the vehicle reaches operating temperatures it will close the diverter valve and send it to the bypass valve which will either dump to the cats or to the cylinder heads. I was pulling code 44 and 94 for the longest time so it gave me the opportunity to learn quite a bit about this system. As far as the resonant buzzing sound, to me that definitely sounds like the diverter valve dumping into the atmosphere. I can't say for sure, though, without actually being there and hearing the noise for myself. There is one scalar that might work for you called "Fuel shutoff time to enable". It has been a long time, but if memory serves, this scalar controls the amount of time before the injectors shut off during decelleration. The default value is 1. You can try setting it to 0 and see what happens. You can also look at the fuel_stabilized_OL table for mid to upper RPM and for loads below your idle load. When you come off the gas to shift, datalog the load during the shift. You may be able to set those RPM/Load values to very lean effectively pulling fuel out during decel. posts.author: 95BlackTan50
posts.content: 95BlackTan50 Regular Posts: 173 Joined: Tue Dec 02, 2003 5:53 pm Location: Johnson City Tennessee Quote Post by 95BlackTan50 » Wed Jun 22, 2005 7:52 am Sealevel_Load_Scaling_vs_RPM is the function that converts Load into LoadX. For example, on the A9L, the stock load scaling value is 0.725 at 2000 RPM. If you have a Load of 0.6 at 2000 RPM, divide that by 0.725 and you get a LoadX value of 0.828. I think that the goal of this function is to have your max LoadX to be close to 1 across the RPM range. Now, depending on the state of your scalar Load_Scaling_Switch, the EEC will either use Load or LoadX to select a table value. If you are using LoadX, then you should be able to modify the Sealevel_Load_Scaling_vs_RPM function to adjust the LoadX values to give you the right spark at the right load. The possible downside to this is that you will be adjusting LoadX for all of the tables, not just spark. You could always just adjust the spark tables in the areas that you are having troubles. If your Load_Scaling_Switch is set to use Load, then this is how you will need to adjust your timing for load. You may need to search for what to set the Load_Scaling_Switch to since I don't know what it is for your EEC. That's the beauty of tuning, there is more than one right answer. Good luck. 95 GT Vert, 76 mm C&L, 24 lb Injectors, Performer 50 Intake, 65 mm FRP TB, Ceramic Coated FRP Shortie Headers, TwEECer RT 1.30A9, W4H0, Adj. Load Scaling Switch Switch to select definition of perload, unitless. ** FN035 is the Sealevel Load Scaling Function and n = RPM This definition is MAF-based, but is corrected for changes in ambient pressure. PRLDSW = 0 perload = (load / fox(&FN035, n)) * (29.9 / bp) This definition is not a percent LOAD, but just a normalized air charge, it is NOT corrected for changes in ambient pressure. PRLDSW = 1 perload = load This definition is not MAF-based PRLDSW = 2 perload = pct_load This is in the notes when you click on the Load Scaling Switch under the Scalars Tab in CalEdit. posts.author: kickerscrt
posts.content: kickerscrt Regular Posts: 122 Joined: Wed Feb 02, 2005 4:41 am Quote Post by kickerscrt » Sat Jun 18, 2005 3:42 am I'm not exactly sure how to totally disable adaptive, but I do know that disconnecting the two narrowbands will lead to serious problems as the eec will no longer be recieving any type of input as to what the approximate AFR is. If running a piggyback system like tweecer, eec tuner, or pms, the three most important sensors are MAF, O2, and TPS. I could be totally wrong here, but the only way for something like that to work would be to go with a standalone system like accel dfi or F.A.S.T. where the standalone ecm is reading the value off of your wideband o2 sensor. That being said, try raising the minimum for adaptive to 254* which is supposedly supposed to disable adaptive fuel control. But here again, I'm not sure because from what you say "Very shortly I saw the AFR settle into 14.7 and KAMRF data continued to post." it leads me to believe you're coing into closed loop and from what I have read adaptive is always active during closed loop. You may need to find the scalars so that you can force open loop at all times, thereby totally disabling adaptive fuel control. But please, don't take what I say as the way it is because I am not 100% sure. Hopefully someone else with more knowledge than me will chime in and clear things up. posts.author: Daren Woodall
posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Thu Jun 23, 2005 12:17 pm The TPS voltage isn't really that important in the schema of things. For CBAZA Strategies, the throttle_WOT_breakpoint function determines the voltage above which is considered wide open throttle. As long as your TPS works within some reasonable range from .9 and 4.5, everything will be fine. My experience has shown that the CBAZA strategy remembers the lowest voltage and treats that as closed throttle. It also uses the value 2.832 volts and above as WOT. The only other function of the TPS that is monitored are sudden changes up or down. Your max voltage appears completely normal to me. I think mine is 4.73. I had a Baumann, which is very similar to the TransGo, and realized it was doing more harm than good. I'd recommend upgrading to a newer VB ('96+, '01+ preferred) and working with that. Go over to TCCoA and check their Technical Articles section. Read up on the Jerry's Thesis and use what he's provided. It'll be about the same price as a "good" (expensive doesn't mean good) shift kit, but it's designed to be something that works better. It's not a difficult thing to do, but if you're not mechanically inclined then have a trusted mechanic do it for you. Doing this mechanically OR electrically will net you results, period. However, stacking them together just completes the system. The timers and such that the EEC controls are a bit of a gold mine when it comes to really tweecing the AOD-E's and 4R70W's. Playing with shift points and convert un/lock schedules are just the tip of the ice berg. Depending on your processor code, you probably don't see half of what's REALLY in there. 3-4's will always be soft - you gotta watch out for the OD band. posts.author: lazybird4pt6
posts.content: lazybird4pt6 Regular Posts: 179 Joined: Thu Jul 10, 2003 9:41 pm Location: Toronto, Ontario, CANA-DUH Quote Post by lazybird4pt6 » Fri Jun 24, 2005 3:49 pm Barney - yes, the Devil IS inside the details. While the basic theory of re-calibrating a trans VB is the same, what you change to what, how and by how much are indeed what makes the difference between "it's been awesome for the past 2 years" and "it ran for a while and now it's shot". To sum it up briefly; TransGo makes you drill an extra hole in the VB casing itself - VERY bad, despite it's claim of being "better"; Baumann changes specific springs and it actually DOES create a hydro-planning situation on the clutches (I found out about this personally on my Bird). One more warning - stay the hell away from the B&M electronic Shift + thingy!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Gauranteed destruction with prolonged use (again, personally experienced, but it was removed before harm was done) 2Shaker - don't touch anything on your trans electrically. When companies like ArtCarr and Lentech do "their thing" they do so with the intent that THEY are "in control" (ie, their tranny) WITH the stock EEC programming. Altering the electrical side of things should be consulted with the builder before anything is touched. They can void your warranty for this. That would suck. Keep in mind, guys - the 4R70W is stronger than the AOD-E for several reasons. Don't go nuts with changes. posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Fri Jun 24, 2005 4:29 pm What is your lowest MAF transfer point at? What is your lowest logged MAFV? I had an issue with my car stalling on the highway during compression braking because the MAFV dropped below my lowest MAF transfer point. I had it happen before on off ramps. It would start right back up, though. One you can convert 9pt flow sheets to predetermined voltages or flows or even create a new linear curve. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue Jun 28, 2005 7:42 pm For the 95+ cars the slopes are calculated on the Required fuel tab. The calculation on the KAMRF tab only gives you a correct slope based on where you put the breakpoint. The new slope suggestions on the KAMRF graph are not slopes that need to be placed into the tweecer. they merely tell you the average correction would be based on where you place the breakpoint. The calculation you are after is on the same tab but use the "Required Fuel" graph and use the settings button to set up the calculation parameters. Then use the auto calculations. posts.author: Daren Woodall
posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Wed Jun 29, 2005 2:13 pm The processors are organized at several levels: - Generation (Hardware) - Strategy (software logic) - Calibration (the configuration data) - This part is editable using TwEECer. For 1994 - 1995 Mustangs, the processors are: Generation: EEC-IV Strategy: CBAZA Calibrations: T4MO, U4PO, J4J1, etc. The J4J1 is the OEM calibration for the 1994-1995 Mustang Cobra. It is popular because its OEM calibration is for 24lb injectors. It also has different load scaling calibration and just seems simpler to work with for modified cars with up-sized injectors. Also, you can completely interchange calibrations for a given strategy. For example, my processor has a label "T4MO" yet I use the J4J1 calibration data as my base tune. This is a common practice. Many are using the 1993 Cobra as a base tune for their modified A9L Foxes. It is a good approach to choose an OEM calibration that best matches your car as a starting point. In my case, heads, intake, cam, 24lb injectors, etc. most closely match the Cobra so I used the Cobra tune to start from. It occours to me that ideally you want the eec to go "wot" on a blower car right about at 0 inches of vacuum or just before. When there is manifold vacuum, the car should be in "closed loop" for fuel economy. But as soon as vacuum drops off near zero, it needs to go "full rich" or "wot". The more seperate corrections you have the more confusing it gets, and the easier it is to run into problems (DETONATION ) I would recomend just leaving your base at 10 degrees, input 55's in your spark MBT and spark bndl tabels, and then you'll only have to worry about the values that are in your spark base and spark alltitude. The reason why I say put 55's in those two tables is because the EEC looks at all three different tables. Whichever has the lower value for spark advance...........is the one the EEC uses. This way, since the 55's make the final timing much more than your base table, your base table will always be used and you know exactly what the comanded timing will be. Also, be sure to mimic your base table in your altitude table. Then you know everthing will be running of your base settings. According to the posts by Chris Mureen I have extracted the reasoning that there are adders for each table: base, borderline, and max brake torque (MBT). Now each of these tables has its own adders and multipliers. What the EEC does is compare the tables with their adders/multipliers in effect and then it takes the lowest value of the three. So with that reasoning then yes the total spark can exceed that of what your base table reads. http://66.102.7.104/search?q=cache:7KM9 ... 220+&hl=en Justin 93 A3M (A9L), 331, 30lbs inj., '02GT MAF, Trick Flow 'R' intake, Tremec TKO, 3.55's 2001 GT automatic with NUX1 stock. Your 30# are not enough to feed the engine without an FMU. So, a maf calibrated for 30# won't be able to measure any more air than your 30#'s can support WITHOUT an FMU. You are creating yourself on headache of a tuning problem IMO. You WILL Be pegging the maf cal'd for 30's and bumping fuel pressure under boost. The eec has no idea about the fuel pressure change. posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Mon Jun 27, 2005 4:04 pm I've followed the thread and I have to concer with the prior advice. I've been at this for a number of years now and thought I would bullet point a combo for ya: - Ditch the FMU or set it to stock ~39lbs. FMUs make global fuel adjustments that can muck with the EEC's adaptive strategy giving unpredictable results. - Get injectors large enough to flow for your HP level at stock fuel pressure. 42lb is good and gives some headroom. - MAF cal'd for 42lb SC. Important: If possible, get a flowsheet . - Get a custom dyno tune from an experienced tuner OR buy TwEECer RT and commit to becoming your own expert tuner. There are distinct advantages getting a product like TwEECer: - You can address drivability issues not practical from a dyno tune - You can continue to update the tune as you learn more and your car continues to evolve (and it will). - TwEECer RT is a powerful diagnostic tool. It's like a window into the EEC. - Addtional tools such as EEC Analizer are available that can "crunch" datalog files and can recommend significant tune improvements, or LogAnalyst that can graphically chart datalog data. Hope this helps, Daren 94GT, AFR165, E303, 1.72 RR, GT-40 Intake, 70mm TB, 24lb inj, ProM 75, BBK LT, J4J1, PLX M-300 WB Top

It did what I needed and little else. being able to integrate into TwEECer was most important to me. If a nice guage is important, you may want to consider another model. Speaking as a fellow software developer, I think you will find learning TwEECer/EEC-IV fun. The EEC-IV is a surprisingly elegant device. posts.author: Dale McPeters
posts.content: Dale McPeters Professional Tuner/Shop Owner Posts: 1772 Joined: Sat Nov 02, 2002 6:08 pm Location: In the dog house Quote Post by Dale McPeters » Mon Jul 04, 2005 1:12 pm Daren, The A9M EEC data locations are a little different than the A9L EEC. If it is a true A9M pcm and not the replacement A3M/A3M1 then you need to use the A9M strategy. If it is a replacement pcm it is more than likely an A3M/A3M1. I ran into this on my '93gt as it had a A9M from the factory and the door jam tag stated A9M, but the pcm was actually an A3M1 which uses the A9L strategy. Of course there were other problems in my instance as whom ever had reconditioned the EEC had left some pins un-soldered where it plugs into the main harness and I had a hard time finding it. Also note that the A9M is still a GUFB based strategy to a certain extent but the addressing etc. is a little different. One more thing you may have problems if you use the copy function under the utilities tab as I had issues with this when copying from A9L to A9M. Just an FYI. posts.author: fireguy50
posts.content: fireguy50 Regular Posts: 172 Joined: Sun Jun 29, 2003 3:19 pm Location: Michigan Contact: Contact fireguy50 Website GUFB (A9*) part throttle spark (hows it work?) Quote Post by fireguy50 » Sun Jul 03, 2005 6:07 pm I've read Richard Whites "Tweecer Defs" excel file. Which states TwEECer has the wrong names listed for the timing tables. So I read the GUFB PDF document, and looked into the stock A9L.bin - FN125 = LOM Load function used to activate LOM spark strategy. Input: RPM and Output: load. This determines the change from table FN901 vs. FN904A / FN905A If you read FN125 the LOAD / RPM points are very low: 35% LOAD / 1500RPM This leads me to believe the “Base sea level table” has a very small window to operate in. - FN901 (SPKSEA) = Base sea level table. X-input = FN070 - Normalized Engine speed, RPM Y-input = FN071 - Normalized load - FN904A (LOMSEA) = Sea level LOM table. X-input = FN070 - Normalized engine speed, RPM Y-input = FN071 - Normalized load - FN905A (LOMALT) = Altitude LOM table. X-input = FN070 - Normalized engine speed, RPM Y-input = FN071 - Normalized load - FN901 = Spark Table - SeaLevel in TwEECer - FN904A = Spark Table - Altitude in TwEECer - FN905A = Spark Table - Limp in TwEECer 3. PART THROTTLE MODE SPARK: Normal Part throttle is (FN904A * FN212A + FN905A * FN129A). During normal part throttle operation, the logic "interpolates" between sea level table (FN904A) and altitude table (FN905A) to calculate base spark. Richard Whites "Tweecer Defs" excel file states the change between FN904A to FN905A is ~26in/hg Baro. After looking at FN129A and FN212A, I’d say that is correct. Tip-in Spark (LOM) is (1 - LUGTMR/LUGTIM) * FN901 On accelerating from a standstill, the strategy uses a more aggressive spark table (FN901) for improved performance. Over a period of time (LUGTIM), the spark shifts from LOM spark to normal part throttle spark. The LUGTMR logic is described in the Timer Chapter. So FN901 is for “improved performance” but only under 35% LOAD / 1500RPM. Those settings don’t make any sense to me Should I tune with FN904A as a “base spark table?” Should I increase the settings in FN125 so FN901 is more of a “base spark table?” Am I confused or starting to understand this more than these documents? But haven't investigated it's purpose or activation window. GUFB.pdf - TORQUE TRUNCATION SPARK - 'C' LOGIC (FN1119) If the AXOD (or AOD) transmission is in 1st gear or reverse, the torque of the engine may exceed the capacity of the transmission. Therefore, the torque truncation strategy is designed to reduce the engine torque by retarding the spark. FN1119 should be calibrated to achieve this torque reduction for all speed-load points. Because the strategy is unable to directly distinguish between first and second gear, first gear is inferred from N/V, TTNOV. TTNOV should correspond to the RPM-Speed ratio for first gear. TTNOV = RPM - Vehicle Speed (N/V) ratio corresponding to first gear. title: Increased Time to Closed Loop for CBAZA - EECTuning.org

posts.author: 95BlackTan50
posts.content: 95BlackTan50 Regular Posts: 173 Joined: Tue Dec 02, 2003 5:53 pm Location: Johnson City Tennessee Increased Time to Closed Loop for CBAZA Quote Post by 95BlackTan50 » Wed May 25, 2005 8:21 pm I just uploaded a file to the Modified BIN files section called J4J1_255.BIN. http://autos.groups.yahoo.com/group/twe ... s/Mod-BIN/ I found 2 scalars in the CBAZA strategy that are not defined by the TwEECer. They appear to control the time it takes for the EEC to switch from Open Loop control to Closed Loop after startup. One scalar determines the time after a cold start and the other determines the time after a hot start. The scalars are as follows: BCFFh - Time to CL warm - Stock J4J1 value 60 seconds (3Ch) BD00h - Time to CL cold - Stock J4J1 value 100 seconds (64h) The range for both scalars is 0-255. The lowest practical value is about 30 since there is some other logic in the startup routine that overrides this scalar. I've confirmed this on two separate cars with some help from rockin_rick and it seems to work consistently. The file that I posted sets both scalars to the maximum value. This file should help out those of you who force open loop at idle. The problem that has been observed is that even though OL is forced, CL is still entered at 100 sec (J4J1) and stays CL until about 400 sec. Changing this scalar will minimize the time that the engine is running in CL. Thanks to rockin_rick and Turbo94Cobra for providing data to help me find and verify these scalars. I've sent a note to Mike G. to see if he can add it to the CBAZA definition file so that you can change the value with the TwEECer. posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sat Jul 02, 2005 1:53 pm After using these changes and observing the data from the car, I think that these scalars are probably more likely to be: "time for startup routine - not stabilized" "time for startup routine - stabilized" It seems to pull A/F ratios from the startup tables/modifiers rather than the base/stabilized tables during this time. I bet the OL operation is just a side effect of this, because the startup routine doesn't use CL. IOW - I don't think that these scalars are ONLY specifically for CL vs OL operation at startup. I suspect that spark values for startup are also getting applied during this entire time, also. (if these are different for startup vs normal) My previously acquired KAMs do get applied during this time (at least calcon shows the KAMs changing). Since OL is getting used, I doubt the KAMs are updating... FWIW - I think that the "load limit vs RPM" function that us CBAZA guys use to force OL at idle only applies when the car is "stabilized". So if you leave the startup routine (the time dictated by these scalars), and the car has not yet gone stabilized, then the "load limit vs RPM" OL at idle force doesn't get applied. This is where these scalars can help out to minimize this time. -------------------------- I've been using this for several weeks now and it seems to be working out good. I have since reverted the "time for startup routine - stabilized" back to stock values, since the forced OL is not needed from this scalar since the "load limit vs RPM" function will acomplish this immediately after startup when hot. IOW - when the car is hot, I don't need this scalar change to acomplish the forcing of OL at idle. I'd just as soon get out of that startup routine (and thus it's different values) ASAP, if the car is ready for it. I also wonder how changing the "time for startup routine - stabilized" to 255 would effect a car on the dragstrip. Unless you let the car run long enough in the starting lanes to exit this 255 sec. startup routine, your run down the strip would be running off of startup routine values.... posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am TB airflow and ISC neutral idle airflow VS ambient temps Quote Post by rockin_rick » Fri Jun 24, 2005 4:22 pm When using EA to calculate your TB airflow and ISC neutral idle airflow, you are supposed to datalog MAF flow to determine what values you need for these settings. How does the ambient air temperature at the time of the datalog effect the outcome? As ambient air temp rises, then the MAF would read less flow, and vise-versa. So it seems that your values for these settings would be optimized for a certain temperature, right? When it's 30°F outside, there will be more logged MAF flow through the TB when closed than if it's 90° outside, no? If that's the case, the EEC calibration designers must have accounted for this somehow. Perhaps the values in those settings are at a specific temperature, and there is a undiscovered adjustment/normalizer function that modifies them a bit per given ACT? :shrug OR maybe, these settings don't have adjustments, and are set to a flow of average temperature, and the change in temp doesn't make that big of a difference, since the swing is not extreme. Wouldn't basing these settings off of logged MAF data that was taken at 90°, then screw up your idle when it gets colder? What is the best temperature to datalog maf flow to set these settings to? 70°F? 50°? An average temp of your climate that you drive in? posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 pm The ISC curve is already temp compensated by the MAF. The TB airflow is also covered by the MAF. It is a number Ford used to cover all static incoming air. Things like the PCV and closed TB plate and so on. If you set this (TB air flow) to high or low the adaptive strategy will learn this and save it to the 9 row in the adaptive update table. The amount that it can correct is unknown to me. It maybe the same as the MAF which is +-12% The key to the decel stalling is the pre position and the decay rate. It can also be caused by setting the base idle to low. Setting it to low causes the EEC to have to try and compensate. It uses a typical PID loop to control this. One of the parameters in a PID loop is gain. This is the speed in which the EEC will react. In other words it is the value the multiplied by the RPM error. We are able to adjust the gain but at a cost. If we go to high on the gain then you will see oscillations and if you set it to low then it will not react fast enough and stall. There are a couple of other parameters in a typical PID loop but they are not available to us. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Fri Jul 08, 2005 12:53 am Given decreasing temps, does the MAF correct for the temperature drop caused by the cooler temp of air, but not for the reduction in density of that same sample? It seems that decreasing temps would be like a double whammy, where the density would increase, while at the same time the lower temps would provide 'extra' cooling. So it would read double (sorta). Is this temp 'doubling' error eliminated by the MAF? Perhaps this is due to the hot wire being heated to a set amount above ambeint? Then as temp changes, so would the heated wire, and the cooling of the wire is strictly from the reduced mass..... So technically, the MAF does both correct for temp, and not correct for temp (in a way). Does this sound right? --------------------- How about "TB airflow and ISC neutral idle airflow vs BP"? I believe that changing pressure/altitude would also change the MAFV. There is a correction for BP in the ISC calculation listed in the GFUB strategy doc: GFUB strategy doc, p. 9-39 wrote: Enter DEBYMA calculation ---| Set DEBYMA = ((DESMAF - ITHBMA) + | (calculate corrected, | FN810) * (29.92/BP) | actual airflow) | DEBYMA_FM = (DESMAF - ITHBMA) + FN810 | (calculate airflow through | the bypass solenoid) | Clip DEBYMA and DEBYMA_FM | at DEBYCP as a minimum | | Set ISCDTY = "A" * FN800 | | (calculate ISC duty cycle) | Clip ISCDTY at 1.0 as a | maximum [this doesn't want to format well... goto page 9-39 (pdf page 264)] Set DEBYMA = ((DESMAF - ITHBMA) + FN810) * (29.92/BP) DEBYMA = actual flow required from the ISC actuator DESMAF = The desired airflow necessary to operate at a specified idle condition. ITHBMA = Throttle body idle mass air flow with throttle plate at idle screw stop and 0% ISC duty cycle. FN810 = Adder to DEBYMA vs. RPM. This shows that the calculation adjusts for BP, and that the 'reference' BP value is 29.92 (the "standard temperature and pressure" standard for air pressure). I believe that it makes sense that when taking a datalog for measuring base idle MAF flow, you should adjust the result based on the ratio of standard pressure/current pressure. Does this sound right? The chemistry term "standard temperature and pressure" says that the standard temp is 32°F (0°C). I think that makes sense that you should also correct temperature. I suppose that while we may not know exactly what temperature to base this on, you have to use your best educated guess to choose a likely amount. To not adjust, is the same as choosing the temp of the datalog samples to be the correct 'standard' temperature. Might as well choose a best educated guess, which I believe is 32°F. Does this make sense? Very frustrating as it didn't do it every time. Here is my latest approach and I'm making great progress so far. 1. Set TB idle adjust screw so in neutral idle with all accessories off you run 18-20% ISC duty cycle in Calcon. 2. Adjust TPS between 0.98-0.985V by reading Calcon TPS voltage, engine can be off with key on for this step. 3. Set the fuel shutoff decel time extended (stock 1 sec to 3 sec) scalar to more than the fuel shutoff time to enable (stock 2sec) scalar. 4. Then adjust accel pump multiplier - global scalar to eliminate bucking or hesitation. It turns out my A9P PCM uses a fixed 1v breakpoint for part throttle. The decel strategy uses this to determine when to turn on transient fuel, so the time between closed throttle and 1v you won't get the right mixture after a decel. posts.author: Paul
posts.content: Paul Regular Posts: 236 Joined: Sat May 28, 2005 11:10 pm Location: AJ, AZ Contact: Contact Paul Website Quote Post by Paul » Mon Jul 04, 2005 11:20 am On the A9* EEC's the injector breakpoint is a fuel adder with deminishing effect from idle to 1500RPM. Meaning the closer you get to 1500RPM the less effect it has. Anyway, to answer your question 1. Here's the formula: (INJECTOR_VALUE/(1000*60*60))*ms 2. In your case that is (24/(1000*60*60))*2.5 = 1.667-E5 I used 2.5 in the above example because that is the stock setting. I think it's hardcoded in the A9* EEC. If it's not them you could feasibly play with that to further fine tune your low RPM fuel delivery. Top

What are your injector slopes set to (high and low)? Basically, the EEC is reading your injector slopes and where you are in your maf curve, using your commanded A/F in your fuel tables, and calculating how long it needs to hold the injectors open to obtain the desired A/F. If your maf curve is off then you'll either be running rich (to much duty cycle) or lean (not enough duty cycle). Just because you hit 5 volts doesn't mean the computer will command 100% duty cycle. at your 80%, what is your A/F? Paul, If it is a heavily modified 347 like the one I had was you will have to "adjust" the sealevel load scaling to so that the EEC will see (or extrapolate) the correct rows in the tables for fuel spark etc. as the VE will be higher than a stock 5.0 engine. On mine instead of the .79 (for stock A9L) I had to change it to .90 and adjust as required for load, spark, fuel etc. You will have to datalog to see where the min. needs to be set to for your application. Also the bucking is more than likely from the MAF curve being off or the EEC reading the wrong row in the tables. I had this problem once as I was trying to run the car to lean. More than likely this is at 1/3-1/2 throttle or light cruising conditions. I had to richen around the first 10 points of the curve and adjust the injector "stuff". A heavily modified 347 engine will require a good amount of fuel "IF" it is setup to make quite a bit of HP. At least more than what one would at first think. posts.content: Dale McPeters Professional Tuner/Shop Owner Posts: 1772 Joined: Sat Nov 02, 2002 6:08 pm Location: In the dog house Quote Post by Dale McPeters » Wed Jul 06, 2005 11:06 am SHaFT7 wrote: well right now i'm getting 13mpg, which is just stupid...i got 20 before all these mods, and if i keep my foot out of it (which i try to) then, since the motor is technically more efficient now, i should get the same or better.... plus, 13mpg of 91 octane with these gas prices would prevent me from driving this car all the time, which i really want to do! If you are only getting 13 mpg with the mods that you have then your tune is way off......You should be able to to get at least 20 mpg min. on the interstate by keeping your foot out of it. I also disagree with Juice's comments about the load scaling issue. If it is done properly it works just fine as the EEC's 4 pt interpolations are closer to being correct. Now note this is based on a car that has been modified with HCI or some kind of power adder like SC/Turbo etc. and when and how much boost etc. is applied to the engine. Normally centrfugal SC cars will be scaled up to 1.5-1.6, unless you are in Chris M.'s predicament... . While turbo & KB cars will be adjusted differently as they build boost a "LOT" sooner than an rpm based blower car will. If it is a stock 5.0 with headers etc. then I would not even fool with any scaling at all.... If any of you will datalog a stock 5.0/4.6 car and check the load or load% whichever one that you use and then datalog a 5.0/4.6 mustang that has been stroked with an after market HCI & header combo, blower/turbo etc. to see the difference in the VE and load/load% you will see what I am talking about. There is a lot of difference between them which in turn "WILL" change the load scaling and effect which row of the tables etc. that the EEC will look to make its calculations. Also note that this same princable can be accomplished by scaling the cu/in and in some cases the injector "stuff" as there is always more than one way to skin a cat...... Just my 2 cents, now back to work I go...... '88GT, T-Top (Being rebuilt)-Moates Hardware waiting.... BE & EEC Analyzer '93 Teal Cobra-Moates Hardware Paul's EEC-Editor Top

posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Fri Jul 08, 2005 8:25 pm When lambse (commanded afr) is lean like that it means your actually too rich. THe eec commands lambse so the actual afr is what its supposed to be. So if the car is rich, lambse will command lean and vice versa. On decel, its not unusual to see lambse really lean. Don't worry about decel right now. If your cruising with a steady throttle and lambse is 16 or more, your tune is too rich. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Sat Jul 16, 2005 9:50 pm Well, since you are getting different injectors soon you may find you have to re-do your maf curve when they are installed. For now, if you have a wideband in the car, force OL using the "Load for OL" function and then datalog watching your "commanded lambse" values vs the reading you get on the wideband. Easiest way to do it is to start at low rpms and gradually accerate up to as high a maf voltage as you reasonably can. Don't let off the gas while datalogging this, just stop the log, then let off the gas. You can then play back the log and see how accurate your maf curve is and make whatever changes necessary. Only pay attention to the a/f while accelerating, if you let off the gas your a/f will change quite a bit and may mislead you. As far as timing goes, retard the timing at high load/rpm in the borderline table, start at maybe 5 degrees less than stock from .6-.9 loads and you should be very safe but listen carefully anyway. On the datalog, check off maf voltage, maf kg/hr, spark timing, lambse, rpm and throttle position. Another way to deal with the timing is to relocate the iat sensor like in the article, you would then datalog iat temp also. I suspect just doing that would reduce timing enough to be safe, probably too much in fact. title: Load VE Calculations - EECTuning.org

posts.author: Dale McPeters
posts.content: Dale McPeters Professional Tuner/Shop Owner Posts: 1772 Joined: Sat Nov 02, 2002 6:08 pm Location: In the dog house Load VE Calculations Quote Post by Dale McPeters » Mon Jul 18, 2005 1:34 pm Bob, Can you add this to the FAQ Section as I have had a lot of people that have been asking for it. Thanks, Dale OK, after a constructive debate I've slightly revised this post to use standard air mass and remove ACT considerations from the formula. ********************************** Load or Volumetric Efficiency (VE) is a critical value used in the scaling of many of the key EEC tables and functions. Generally speaking load is the ratio of real airflow aspirated under a given RPM versus the maximum volumetric capacity of an engine. Normally aspirated engines will peak at a load value near 1.0 (although can slightly exceed 1.0 in special cases) where forced induction engines may approach peak load values of 2.0. Load is calculated in the following manner: Load = MAF/[PI*(Bore/2)^2*Stroke*RPM*0.5*60*8*(STP air density)] (STP means Standard Temperature and Pressure = 1.188 kg/m3) If units used in this equation are meters for stroke and bore, and kg/m3 for air density then the kg/hr value from the MAF transfer can be plugged in directly. I found an old post with a spreadsheet attached (Jack Hindley's I believe) for calculating this. I've uploaded the spreadsheet into the tools directory of the files section ( http://groups.yahoo.com/group/EECTuner/ ... s/load.xls ). It is currently populated with the ProM 19# MAF data and a 5.0 displacement but any transfer function can be cut and pasted in and bore and stroke (in meters) for other engine sizes loaded. posts.author: Dale McPeters
posts.content: Dale McPeters Professional Tuner/Shop Owner Posts: 1772 Joined: Sat Nov 02, 2002 6:08 pm Location: In the dog house Topic: fuel_startup_a/f_ratio_**** - 94+ Quote Post by Dale McPeters » Mon Jul 18, 2005 2:06 pm Bob, And another.........for PCMX, GUI-Pro EEC-Editor etc. software.... Author eecgeek posted 03-12-2001 12:44 PM -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- EEC-Tuner s/w:not sure GUI:fuel_startup_a/f_ratio_time, table of lambda values accessed by time in seconds and ECT in degree F. fuel_startup_a/f_ratio_load, table of lambda values accessed by load % and ECT in degrees F. Parameter: Table Processor: ALL to convert lambda to A/F ratio multiply by 14.7. (It really 14.64, Dale McPeters 7/18/05) These two tables control open loop fuel until the ECT (engine coolant temp) stabilizes, which means the car is warmed up. All sensors are active at this point except the O2 sensors. The time based tables value is SUBTRACTED from the load based tables value, thus richening the A/F ratio during warm-up. As the time increase, the amount of richening decreases, until it reaches 0 at 100-120 seconds after start-up. This also applies to a warm engine, even though very little richening is done due to the higher ECT. Look at the right hand side of the table to see this. Once the ECT stabilizes the EEC switches to the fuel_stabilized_OL_table, which is based on LOAD and RPM instead of ECT. These are the tables that need updating if you switch to large injectors, then run extremely rich during cold starts. Edit- 94 and up should be similar to eecv stuff since they use load vs rpm more than the older stuff. The start up fuel is only used for about 45 seconds depending on ect and then goes CL all the way up to "ect stab temp". The idea that larger injectors making it start up very rich seems to not be true either, most of the cars I have put injectors in don't need any changes besides inj slopes and maf curve. The description of how the subtractors, etc, works is correct though. (Edit -7/26/05 I should have stated that the above came from boss96's comments.) posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Mon Jul 18, 2005 9:48 am Hi jruppert, What sort of tires are you running? Your 60' times should be under 2 seconds if you are hooking up hard, so that would be three tenths right there. The big thing is your MPH is only 99 -- that means about 220 hp at the wheels for a 3200 pound car. Warren is correct, your combination should make for a solid mid 12 second car at well over 100 (like 105-110 or so) at least. If you haven't already done so, you might want to consider a quick compression test to see if something isn't mechanically fubar'd. You also might want to make sure you have the throttle body opening up all the way when you (or a friend) put your foot to the floor. Sometimes the simple things are the easiest to overlook (at least for me!). Have you been to a chassis dyno? That is the best way to dial things in, and it will tell you quickly where things are not right with your setup. On my last trip, I managed to pick up about 15 hp by putting in more spark after 3500 in the WOT tables. Are you running an a9l based processor? If so, I could send you the tune I have come up with if it would help. That maybe why some of the tuners are now offering as many as 2-3 free updates with the initial tune... Depending on who is doing the tuning there are different ways to look at it. I'm close friends with the partner of a HP shop that does a lot of tuning and know the economics of it fairly well. Lets say I brought my car for dynotuning there, with all the mods it has. They would have to work with the maf curve by either using the flow sheet or the generic way by changing the stock curve by percentage just to start, then check fuel trims and hope they can get the entire curve close. They would use "suggested" or generic inj slopes supplied by Diablo in their case as well as "batt inj comp" and "min pw". From there they would have to decide how to get the fuel trims in line using the above functions. Hopefully they will be able to get the car to idle smoothly. Then they can go with the wot tuning, deciding on how much/little timing they can run, etc. Time between runs to let the car cool down to some extent so they can get a fairly good hp number for you between changes, time to reburn the chip, etc. This would probably take 2 hrs if they are pretty good tuners. Depending on whether or not you get a chip or a handheld like the Predator would determine your cost. A chip costs them about $125 each, they would mark it up to around $300 or a little less, the Predator cost's more, don't know what they pay for it but you end up paying around $400 for it. Then they charge you for dyno time, lets say about $100/hr (maybe a little less) and there you go. In the case of the chip they made $175 plus $200 for dyno time, so $375+tx for 2 hrs of work. That is not bad for you and me but when you have to pay employees, rent, etc, it is not much, plus they could be working on more profitable repairs, etc, and make more. Not to mention how I would be coming back for more tuning because the car will still stall out occasionally and does not run well when cold. Either they are good guys and reburn the chip for free or they try to make something for the additional work. This is why "canned" tunes are so valuable to most tuners as hopefully many of the problems have already been worked out by others and they can get the job done faster. Of course all this points out how most of us prefer to do the tuning ourselves since we have more time to work out the little things and get some satisfaction in doing it ourselves. 96 GT, Vortech Si trim,Procharger 3 core intercooler, forged bottom end, MAC longtubes, ported PI heads , Edelbrock intake, Crower cams-.580lift/234dur@.050, 80lb injectors, CDAN4/GGL4 processor. SO - Perhaps you need to tweak LS, HS, BP, and inj offset. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Thu Jul 21, 2005 8:19 am Do a datalog at wot watching your wideband a/f vs commanded lambse, maf volts and kg/hr vs rpm. You want to adjust the maf values where the a/f differs between commanded lambse and actual a/f from your wideband. You would increase the kg/hr values where you find the a/f you are getting is leaner than what is being commanded, etc. Commanded lambse is the actual a/f ratios you are commanding from the "stab OL fuel table" but you have to get the maf curve accurate to actually reach those a/f values. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Mon Jul 04, 2005 7:42 am I think you said this but just to cover all the bases..the inj slopes you entered are fine, make sure you used the flow sheet from the ProM meter and converted them to 30pts and enter that in your maf curve. If the car is too rich at idle do a datalog and observe your fuel trims (KAMRF) values and take note of what percentage they differ from a value of "1". For example, lets say the fuel trim is .8 at idle, that means 20% fuel is being removed to get the a/f to 14.7 which is what the car is supposed to be idling at. Note how much kg/hr is being read during that time, this corresponds to the kg/hr value on your maf curve. You would want to also drive the car a little to see if the 20% fuel trim is happening all along the maf curve values too. You can then reduce the maf values by 20% in the maf function, write that to the tweecer and re-check your fuel trims. You should disconnect the battery and clear your eec's memory so you will be starting from scratch as far as fuel trims go. See how close you get to 1 on the fuel trims and you should be on your way. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Sat Jul 09, 2005 7:57 am Any thoughts on how I can get the thing to idle? The KARMF seems to go to about 1.24 right about when the car dies. I'm guessing that's because it's gone pig rich, and the ECU can only really tweak it about 24%. Does that make sense? When KAMRF goes positive, like above, that means the eec is ADDING fuel to try and reach a CL (closed loop) a/f ratio of 14.7-1. 1.24 means it is adding 24% fuel, therefore your maf curve is lean in that area. You can richen the maf curve by noting what maf voltage or kg/hr value you are idling at and then going to the corresponding part of the mar curve and adjusting the kg/hr values higher to try and get the KAM (fuel trim) value closer to 1. Chances are the entire maf curve will be off by the same amount so I would just richen the entire curve first and then drive the car while datalogging the fuel trims to see if there is a trend of adding the same amount of fuel overall. I would not go wot with the car until you get a wideband 02 meter to verify your a/f under boost. Nowadays you can buy them pretty cheap, I just got a PLX wideband for $350. posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Thu Jul 21, 2005 10:03 pm Lambse values at WOT are accurate IF YOUR MAF TRANSFER is accurate. By no means do they represent actual afr. Now ideally, they would (and eventually should) represent actual afr if everything else in your tune is accurate to your combo. Now this is where it gets interesting. Is adaptive being applied at WOT? I haven't seen this subject discussed in a while. Now there are a couple of very sharp guys on here that know the inner workings of the eec much better than me. But from personal experience, I belive that the eec does apply adapive at WOT The lambse display on calcon is simply the a/f ratio you are commanding at a given rpm/load that you have commanded in your "stab OL fuel" table. If you have 12-1 a/f @ 5000rpm and .9 load in the fuel table and you reach that point during a wot run then that is the number you will see in Calcon. Like was said in the quote above, it has nothing to do with the a/f you are actually getting because it depends on how accurate your maf curve is. You need a wideband to veryify and correct this. Is adaptive being applied to wot? Yes it is, looking at the "fuel update rate" table you will see that higher loads and rpms look at lower columns/rows for fuel trim information. If you change all the values in that table to positive numbers then you will prevent fuel trims from being applied to wot. At wot you are not in CL (at least normally ) and therefore the eec would not learn fuel trims at those high load/rpm ranges even though the numbers are positive and therefore allow learning. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Thu Jul 21, 2005 9:55 pm Well, here is my not so informed explanation. :) Your load tables for fuel and spark are usually based on .1-.9 load range, lets say from 0-100% for simplicity. Load is another way of saying VE (volumetric effiency). A n/a motor will not reach 100% VE normally unless it is exceptional. You will reach maximum VE around lets say 5000 rpm on your motor, lets say it is .9. On the sea level load scaling table you would make the load value .9 at 5000 rpm, above that rpm it would probably be less, maybe .8, at idle .5, etc. If you look at the stock values in the table you will see something close to this. By setting expected load values to rpms the eec will know where to look in the fuel/spark tables for fuel/spark based on that table. If you car is supercharged you want to "fit" the higher loads obtained along the rpm scale by telling the eec how much load to expect. Usually 140% load is seen or higher. By resetting the values to 140% at the correct rpms you will go to the correct area of the fuel/spark load tables where you want to be. If you datalog load and loadX you will notice on a supercharged car that loadX (%) will not go past 100% but "load" will go to 140%. If you command 10 degrees of timing at 100% load then when the motor reaches 140% it will look at the 10 degrees timing at 100% load. In other words you have "fit" the 140% range into the 0-100% table. Someone please correct me if I have it wrong but this is the way it seems to work on my datalogs. The only thing I would check would be during a datalog I would check to see if the timing/fuel that you are commanding at a certain load and rpm are actually happening like you want. If not, then change the load value in that rpm range to get the eec to give the correct spark/fuel you want. I had a friends car recently that I datalogged and noticed that at idle his load was 40%. What happened because of this was as I accelerated normally, not aggressively, the car would enter OL way too soon and was using spark/fuel values from the higher parts of the load tables. Since I was nowhere near hitting actual high load on his engine I increased the load value in the sea level load scaling table to 1 at low rpms and increased it as it got higher rpms. His car was supercharged btw. This immediately brought idle load down to 20% and the car ran better due to going to the correct load values. Another thing that will directly effect load calculations are the maf values themselves, if you were to reduce all the maf kg/hr values by 20% you would see the load go down when looking at it on calcon. I guess you just have to use common sense when getting your load values to be acceptable. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri Jul 22, 2005 1:24 pm Here is how Calculated Load is figured out: Load = (load/load scaling) x (29.9/BP) Take the absolute engine load which is deived from the MAF and divide it by the Sea Level Load Scaling and then multiply it by the Barometic Pressure correction. The EA shows the actual Datalog 'LoadX' aslo known as calculated load. It also shows VE which is calculated based off of the MAF and air temperature and so on. The idea is to raise the black line (factory) up to the red line (datalog). Then enter in the numbers for the black line into the tuner. You could also smooth out the red line manually and then pick out a select few point to enter into the tuner. Either way the result will be the same. Once you raise the values in the tuner you will notice on the next datalog that the calculated load values will come down. If you look close the red curve should represent the torque curve for your cam. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sat Jul 23, 2005 6:39 pm I checked into this more with the GFUB strategy doc. While this is not exactly the same strategy, there's a good chance that it works the same. It says that this function 'fuel enrichment for high speed' ONLY gets applied when the conditions for stage 1 speed limiting is in effect. The function 'spark retard for high speed' also gets applied then. It also specifically says that if 'spark retard for high speed' is set to 1, then 'fuel enrichment for high speed' should be set to 0.996. Given this, I don't suggest changing this function to 1. The conditions for stage 1 speed limiting are determined by the 'speed limiter A' and 'speed limiter B' (terms for GFUB). I'd equate those to CBAZA's 'speed_limit_stage1' and 'speed_limit_stage2'. Also, FWIW, speed limiter B (aka stage 2), DOESN'T use these functions, but rather uses normal fuel strategy, but fires every other injector as it's means of speed limiting. (keep in mind this is how GFUB works, and most likely (but not confirmed) this is also how CBAZA works) SO, most likely , CBAZA works the same and if you've disabled the scalar(s) 'speed_limit_stage1' (by setting it to 16383), then the fuel enrichment for high speed NEVER gets applied. That said, I probably will still change that function to all .992, just in case something has changed from GFUB to CBAZA.... certainly won't hurt! posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Jul 24, 2005 4:39 pm According to the GUFB strategy doc, the "fuel shutoff time delay" is the amount of time that must pass from vehicle start before allowing fuel shutoff (FS). So FS is enabled after 255 seconds since vehicle start. I've just studied this pretty thouroughly, and feel I have a good understanding of GFUB fuel shutoff operation. (In my terminology, FS is a bit different than fuel shutoff on decel (FSD). FS includes both FSD and FS shifting. FSD only means 'on decel' and doesn't account for FS shifting) Perhaps FSD is disabled in your calibration effectively through FS time to enable. This is the amount of time that must pass after the throttle goes closed before FSD is enabled. Since the stock value is 31, this requires 31 sec before enabling FSD. This is probably what you should lower to enable FSD. BUT, this doesn't completely disable FS, as FS during manual trans shift doesn't use that scalar. If you only changed "FS time delay" (and left FS time to enable = 31) and was thinking that FSD was enabled and felt a surge (with less than 31 sec passing since going to closed throttle), perhaps it was placebo. What did your logs (of PW) say when you feel this 'surge'? FWIW- Based on the logic explained, to completely disable FS (both FSD and FS shifting), you need to either set the FS min RPM's really high, or set function 'open loop fuel mult., RPM' to all '1'. That function is the final and ultimate 'shutoff mechanism' used by the FS strategy. IOW - if all conditions are met to shutoff the injectors, then this function get's applied. The multiplier value of '0' is what actually does the shutting off. The shutoff is not hard coded into the EEC. It seems that FS is the only use of that function. Given the logic outlined, the FS min RPM scalar, IMO, is the best bet to completely disable FSD and FS shifting. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Jul 27, 2005 12:42 pm wa_4x4builder wrote: When you wired the A9x to the CCRM, did you trigger both the low and high speed fan relays or just the high speed? The CCRM that I have has a fail safe Low Speed fan setup. What I mean by this is, the low speed fan requires an open ciricut or 12vdc signal to turn ON the fan. This is considered fail safe because if something happens to the EEC wiring or so on the fan will turn on automatically to prevent an engine overheat. The high speed fan is just the opposite. It requires a ground to turn it on. In my case I gounded the low speed fan to turn it off. I only used the high speed fan signal. You can wire the low speed fan upto the ignition and have it on with the key on. This is something that I did not opt to do. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Thu Jul 28, 2005 9:22 am I don't know what exactly the numbers represent but they are airflow numbers that correspond to the rpm values. If you have an rpm of 1500 lets say, you need an airflow value that will make the car hit 1500rpm. If you put the wrong value in it, too low for instance, then the car will try to hit 1500, will undershoot it and the the eec will try to compensate which will end up being a surging around that rpm. On my car I put all zeros in the pre-position table, this makes the motor come down to idle faster but does not eliminate the "hang" at around 1000rpm that happens until the car completely stops. This "hang" at 1000rpm keeps the car from stalling. As for your stalling problems, you probably need to get the "isc neutral" air flow values closer, again, the values are target airflows that the isc motor uses to achieve a certain rpm, if it is too high or too low then the eec overshoots trying to compensate and the idle is unstable. The easy way to set "isc neutral air" is to set an idle speed, then adjust the airflow value to achieve that rpm. You must also look at your timing at idle through Calcon to see if timing is "hunting" which would indicate that the airflow value is too high/low and the eec is compensating for this by adjusting timing to get the idle rpm correct. This assumes you have your TB opening (manually) correct and not too little or too much. posts.content: stangfreek94 Regular Posts: 210 Joined: Fri Jul 16, 2004 1:41 am Location: Eastern shore Maryland Quote Post by stangfreek94 » Sun May 22, 2005 6:18 am Hard to tell but, it looks lean. Doesn't look like the plugs are bad enough to be causing problems though. Recheck all vac. lines, and the cap and rotor. Vac. leaks will play havoc with everything. What have you changed in your tune? Your loadscale may be of a little. Try lowering the values over 2000 rpm in your sealevel load scale by 0.2-0.3, see if that'll send you into OL a lil' quicker. You prolly have it scaled so you barely go over 100% load in the upper rpms, in which case you would have to rescale you OL fuel and timing tables to reflect that. You want to try to get the load scale in line up to @ 2500 rpm, then anything over that, scale down a lil' so you know you're very close (90%) or just over 100%, for being in boosted situations. This method is easier than trying to completely redo the OL fuel and timing tables. 94 GT, New PTK turbo, TW heads, TFS stage 1 cam, 75mm TB, 60#inj., full aeromotive fuel system, Snow stage 2 meth injection, forged 306, PLX wideband, PMAS pro tube Blowthru Vortech Times 10.80 @ 126.44 mph, with a 1.57 60ft. 3600#s Top

posts.author: dsleepy47
posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Fri May 27, 2005 10:37 am I have seen this symptom a number of times. Every time I have seen it it has been the result of a lean misfire. The root cause can be a number of parameters. The thing that seems to make the problem so bad is that when you get the misfire you lose the acceleration enrichment because your rpm quits increasing and the maf flow fluctuates because of the misfires. The popping is lean mixtures that are burning in the exhaust. The last time I saw this problem the tune had the injector breakpoint set too high and it was causing a lean spot in the 1000 - 1500 rpm range. Richen things up in the affected rpm range using the maf curve or injector scalars. The idea here is to richen things up enough to get rid of the miss and popping so you can get some useful tuning data so don't be shy about adding fuel. posts.author: stangfreek94
posts.content: stangfreek94 Regular Posts: 210 Joined: Fri Jul 16, 2004 1:41 am Location: Eastern shore Maryland Quote Post by stangfreek94 » Mon Jun 06, 2005 10:57 pm You have to log a run, I use 4th gear, from as low an rpm as I can get. I have calcon running, click the log button, mash the throttle, hold it to the floor until redline (@6000). Try to keep from spinning or letting up on the throttle, as this will scew your log. Then go to EEC analyzer, make sure you have the correct maf curve entered. Open the log, I filter out all CL, and anything that looks fishy manually, as the log isn't that long. Then run it through the load scale calculator. It will scale your load. Sometimes it will have spikes, so I take a scrap of paper, or cd case, something straight. Place it on the screen, to smooth out the curve. Use the mouse pointer to highlight the rpm that is in the load scale function in the tweecer, fill in the corresponding load cell for the rpm in the tweecer that is displayed in the analyzer. I just scale it down to 650 rpm, or whatever the lowest value is in the function without moving my straight edge. The scale below is close to what I'm using now. It has been changed, but not much. 0.7, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0, 1.2, 1.3, 1.3. I was seeing over 200% load, before using this method. Now, the analyzer is assuming that you are NA, so if you are blown, you will have to rescale the fuel and timing tables, to achieve the desired results. Or, what I do is, scale back the cells in the load scale a few tenths for rpms over 2500. This allows me to use the stock fuel and timing tables, with only the top row with the highest loads needing adjustment. I set them to the desired afr and timing for the corresponding rpm. Then I run another log to make sure that once I'm in boost, I'm over the max load in the fuel and timing tables. With this method, if you are cruising, or lightly into the throttle, you should be under 100% load, but if you go WOT you should be just over 100% load. This will target the highest cells in the fuel and timing tables. I generally see about 110% load at @ 2000 rpm, gradually increasing to @ 160% load at the top of the tach when I pull another 4th gear run. And I get the desired load at cruise, and all other conditions. My idle is in the high 20s to low 30s, and I think my cruise is in the low to mid 30% load range. Hope all this isn't too confusing. 94 GT, New PTK turbo, TW heads, TFS stage 1 cam, 75mm TB, 60#inj., full aeromotive fuel system, Snow stage 2 meth injection, forged 306, PLX wideband, PMAS pro tube Blowthru Vortech Times 10.80 @ 126.44 mph, with a 1.57 60ft. 3600#s Top

What your seeing seems to be a KB behavior, thats pretty much what stangfreek was fighting with his KB. Your load% is pretty much calculated from the amount of air registered by the MAF. (i know, its an overly simplified statement) But, I don't belive your KAMFRS actually reflect what is going on. Since your soo far off that its popping, so I'm looking at lambse as the indicator since lambse and KAMFRS don't agree. I think your maf transfer is off somehow. Seems to me that in some places its RICH and thats where KAMFRS are built up with the less than 1 values, the eec is pulling fuel. So now, your running in closed loop, the eec thinks your rich (based on KAMFRS) and it commands a LEANER mixture as seen by lambse and wideband. The moment you go to open loop, you said it runs ok. Whenever there is such a drastic difference between closed and open loop, that tells me the maf transfer is off. The KB presents quite a tuning challange since you get boost instantly, so any inaccuracies in the tune will be mangnified. If I tell EA to use the WB info for input, it will adjust the curve upward - thus indicating more airflow for a given voltage and extending the duty cycle (richening). How is this possible? I need direction here - this is driving me insane. Every other time I adjust it it tells me to adjust the opposite direction - after one "recommended" curve, the car started up with 20:1 AFR's - I'm glad I was paying attention and noticed before the ECU compensated - it should NEVER be so far off when KAM's are cleared. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Wed Aug 03, 2005 10:07 am Frustrating, isn't it? This is how to do it. If you use KAMRF in EA it will work out pretty well. If you ask it to use wideband info it will be wrong and here is why. When you are accerating you can use the wideband info to see the difference between commanded a/f and actual. BTW, you need to be in OL to make this work reasonably accurately. Once you let off the gas your a/f's will go lean or at least bounce around a lot and if you include this info in the datalog then EA will take that into account and try to compensate. But this is "false" info and you don't want to tune based an a/f's during decel. The best way to use EA for wideband tuning is to get on a dyno and datalog a run going from very low rpm to redline. You will have to stop the log before letting off the gas or delete that decel info from the log before using it in EA. Note that CalEdit has X & Y axis labels backwards - "X" axis is "TP rate" & "Y" axis is "ECT". posts.author: J_P
posts.content: J_P Regular Posts: 186 Joined: Wed May 04, 2005 2:06 am Location: Ashburn, VA Contact: Contact J_P Yahoo Messenger Quote Post by J_P » Sat Jul 30, 2005 8:21 am Something else that hasn't been mentioned is that fooling the computer with meters cal'd for larger than stock injectors also changes what parts of the fuel table the EEC uses based on load. If the EEC thinks it's only getting 500kg/hr of airflow but is really getting 800kg/hr it applies a different load value than what you're engine is actually seeing. I think this can really make things difficult when increasing cubic inches from stock and when using power adders. My suggestion would be to datalog a WOT run with the computer fooled and note what load, A/f, and spark it is seeing/commanding. Then you can determine what parts of the spark/fuel tables the EEC is using. If it runs well like that then you can input the MAF transfer and injector slopes and datalog again. See what loads your EEC is seeing and adjust the spark/fuel to match where your car was running well at before with the EEC being fooled. Then you could fine tune for most power. Does this make since? It is not the best way to tune but just an idea I came up with while reading this thread. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Aug 03, 2005 11:36 am COBRAQUICK: The best thing for you to do is re-install the factory meter and then adjust the injector slope and battery offset to achieve a base tune. This will take the MAF out of the equation. Once you have the slopes and offsets dialed in then you can install the C&L meter. You will then know what affect the meter has on the combination rather than guessing if it is the slopes, offsets, breakpoint or MAF. jruppert: As for the C&L meters in general, the calibration tube only changes the sample area. It does not change the flow characteristics. It only changes the 0-5 volt signal range. Lee at C&L is correct is stating that you will lose HP and TQ if you simply plug in the flow number and here is why. The factory curve was tuned off of the car and on a flow bench. When the EEC was calibrated the flow data from the bench was used. Then Ford could base all of the fuel and spark off of that. C&L also cal's there meters on a bench, but there meters are designed to be richer at the top end of the curve. For example the C&L 73 with the clear tube will have almost the same curve as the factory curve, but if you look close at the upper end of the C&L curve it will be Richer. Here's the trick. Ford designed the EEC to have a certain window that it can learn. This window is load and RPM dependent. At the lower loads and RPM the EEC can correct for any problems in the C&L meter, but if the load and RPM are outside this window then all learning stops and the flow numbers are used regardless if they are accurate or not. Lets say you have the C&L installed with the factory curve in the EEC. Now let’s say you are at an RPM that is above the learning window. The C&L flows a tad bit more than the factory therefore more air is coming into the engine than what the EEC sees. Let’s say the MAF is reading 4.3 volts. The factory curve is reporting 655kg/hr to the EEC but the actual flow from the C&L is 745kg/hr. This means that the Car is seeing the 745 but the EEC is commanding a injector PW based off of the 655. This will result in a leaner mixture causing more HP and TQ By placing the actual air flow curve in the EEC from the C&L cal sheet you essentially take out the error mentioned above. This error is what makes the HP and TQ difference. This is the whole trick behind any aftermarket MAF. They are solely basing there HP and TQ gains off of the area the EEC can not learn. I hope all that makes sense. I recommend putting in the actual flow numbers and then adjusting the fuel tables to accomplish the same thing C&L did. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top
