posts.content: Jon 94GT Site Owner Posts: 370 Joined: Thu Sep 12, 2002 3:16 pm Location: Houston, TX Contact: Contact Jon 94GT Website AOL ANNOUNCEMENT - YOUR feedback appreciated! Quote Post by Jon 94GT » Tue May 17, 2005 2:56 pm Ok guys, I've decided to expand the site. As some of you know, I am the administrator of the site here, and have been managing and keeping this place running for the past 3 or so years. There is a great wealth of information on here, and the site can be so much more than just a plain jane message forum. So here are a few ideas I have been shooting around in my head, and some things I already have coming: 1) I registered a new domain name, which should be active within the next 24 hours. The new URL will be http://eectuning.org (the old one will still work also to avoid losing anyone). 2) This site will no longer be TwEECer oriented only. I will add sections comparing all of the various known tuning devices. Pros, Cons, etc (this is one of the areas I will be needing other peoples experiences and opinions on). 3) I am a software developer by day, and will 'flesh' out this site with a tuning/log file management and posting section, details on the ideas I currently have are below. SOFTWARE NOTES 1) Online real-time calibration/log file submission which is integrated with the web boards user database. This enables users to submit their logs and calibrations without the need for an additional username/password. 2) CCF calibration files are tagged with several variables, which include, but are not limited to: Year of car, EEC processor (J4J1/A9L/etc), modifications, and misc notes. 3) Log files are tagged with several variables, which include, but are not limited to: Year of car, EEC processor, EEC processor calibration base (ex: J4J1 on a WH40, etc), modifications at time of log, and misc notes. Another item of note is that log files submitted will be automatically compressed, parsed (to attain version of calcon the datalog was generated in), and the number of records and approximate length (in time) will also be recorded/displayed along with it. I may add the ability to graph sections of the log(s) to compare them online (just another idea I thought of right now). 4) Users will be able to search and sort based on EEC processor/strategy, year of car, description, and notes. 5) All users will be allowed to compose FAQ’s/Howto’s/technical documents which may be submitted and approved by certain defined moderators/users. The users allowed to approve such documents for listing will be configurable. Approved documents will be displayed to all users for viewing. 6) An administration panel which controls many different features such as: users allowed to approve technical documents such as FAQ’s/Howto’s, limits on number of log/CCF files each user may post, limits on the size of log files submitted (based on size or length), the ability to ‘prune’ the submitted items and remove/modify any undesirable/wasteful data. 7) A rating system in which all registered users may rate a technical document as to the amount of information/help it provides (basically a ‘how helpful was this to you?’ poll). 8 ) A function/scalar/table definition section. This would include the name of the item, the tuning device that it covers (tweecer, eec tuner, etc), the processor/strategy it is for, the units of the/each value, and how the value affects the vehicle. Users are allowed to submit updates/changes which are then approved by the ‘moderators’ of that section (configurable from within the management interface). ---- I am currently without a mustang, so this is my way of staying in the hobby while I am in-between cars. I feel that a general Ford EEC tuning site with the ability to post tunes, track logs, etc would be of great benefit to everyone, so thats why I am doing this. Now as most of you know I have been running/managing this site absolutely free of charge to all, with no ads whatsoever. I plan on keeping it this way...only that I will provide a method by which those that wish to support my work via donation to do so. There will be no min or max donation, nor a requirement to actually donate...I will just ask that if you enjoy and benefit from what you recieve here, to please support the system that brought it to you. Right now I am mostly still in the planning stages, and would appreciate any feedback and ideas any of you have. The tune/log/etc management probably will be available in a few months. Last edited by Jon 94GT on Thu Jun 01, 2006 6:10 pm, edited 2 times in total. Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Aug 07, 2005 3:26 pm If you disconned the switch box, it will use (default to) position 1. So, without the box connected it is just like it is connected and in position 1. You can put a "anti-theft" calibration in position 1 and your actual calibrations in 2-4. Then you can disconnect the switch box, and your car will not run. You could instead put a "KAM clearing" tune in position 1, which will also act as a "anti-theft" tune. I use CBAZA strategy, and have A9L in position 1. If I disconnect the switch box, the car will not run AND if I turn it on (in pos 1 or disconnected) it will clear my KAM memory. You can't change strategys ever. A strategy is defined by the EEC hardware and the unchangeable firmware in it. This is not the same as a calibration. Perhaps you have your terminology mixed up. There is no reason that you need to use more than 1 position ever, but sometimes it can be helpful. I only use 1 position at a time... but will cycle through them with my latest tune. That way I still have my last 2 in there, but really hardly ever revert back... sometimes though. It wouldn't be really all that hard to just re-write the tweecer, though. Honestly, other than the anti-theft tune, I don't really see much need for more than 1 calibration.... If you tune it right, it should run like you want in all situations. Perhaps with a power adder more than 1 would be useful?? posts.content: Toy 94 GT Regular Posts: 180 Joined: Thu Apr 21, 2005 6:39 pm Quote Post by Toy 94 GT » Sat Aug 06, 2005 11:50 am To tune the idle I sit in the driveway with the car idleing and calcon up and tune the MAF curve in the idle volt range (my voltage is .85 in netural and .9 in gear) until I get real close to a KAMRF of 1. As you may have noticed if you have an auto you will need to do this both in netural and in gear. My netural KAMRF's are around 1.02 and my in gear are aroung .98. I might be able to get them closer but they overlap each other in the MAF curve and that is pretty accurate. Once you dial these in and you use EA to adjust the rest of the MAF curve just ignore any changes in that voltage range. Now if you change slopes, break point, TB air flow or ISC airflow you may have to do this again. posts.content: 2fast4u Regular Posts: 166 Joined: Mon May 16, 2005 1:45 pm Location: Fredericton, New Brunswick steps to find out the TB Air Flow Settings and Idel RPM Quote Post by 2fast4u » Mon Aug 08, 2005 12:39 pm The stock number should be your starting point.... or number Steps.... 1. Get the car warm to operating temps 2. un-hook the Idel Air ByPass 3. Start the car up and Data log the rough idel.... get the car to just idel with the IAB unhooked.. play with the idel screw on the Throttle body if you need to get the idel lower or higher... 4. Take a estimate of what the idel is and take an estimate of the MAF flow in Kg/hr 5.With the MAF number u get... (MAF Value) X 2.205 then divide By 60 this will give you the TB Airflow Scalar to enter in. 6 With the estimate of the Rough RPM that you data log with the IAB unhooked u take the RPM value and divide it with the TB Airflow Scalar that you figured out from the last step ... this will give you the RPM value that you will put in the "Idel In Gear" and "Idel In Neutral" scalars This should work for ya, good luck.. 88 GT - D.S.S 331 - Holley SysteMAX II upper & lower - 05+ Slot Style MAF - Underdrives - 70mm Throttle Body - Comp Cam XE274HR - MAC LongTubes - 30lbs Injectors - 255lph Fuel Pump - MSD 6AL - 4:10's - 31 Spline -Tremec T-5 -TwEECer RT- BE & ECC Analyzer - A9S Top

posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Thu Jul 28, 2005 7:48 am Hi, I think the reason running too lean results in high HC is that the engine begins to misfire. If you miss one or two combustion events, a lot of unburned fuel gets into the exhaust. The catalysts also work in a very narrow range, like between 14.5 and 14.6 for maximum efficiency, and beyond that the drop off is pretty rapid. If you're running rich by half a point or more, both the CO and HC will be high because you've used up all the oxygen and the CO is the last thing to go. That, and the catalyst efficiency drops off by about 40% if you're running at 14.0:1. If you lean out too much, the HC will hook up but the CO should stay low. For across the board leaning out, you might change the injector slopes, but it looks like you may have been running a little lean. The NOx looks fine, probably because you have low compression and you weren't under boost :-). If you make it just slightly richer at idle, the results may improve. posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Fri Jul 29, 2005 8:28 am Hi, I agree with 2shaker here, you don't need to change them much for what you want to do and making the injectors smaller should richen the mixture, larger should lean it out. You may only need 2%. The big injectors you've got can be tougher to control at low pulse widths, so they may need a little more refinement on the injector slopes than 30# or 24# injectors. You should be able to tweak them enough to get your plates, though. What sort of cam do you have? If you're running too much duration, that can make the idle stability poor (i.e. sounds cool but cannot pass emissions). I think overlap is the killer, where both valves are open at the same time and the fresh mixture can get contaminated at low speeds. Usually turbo guys run wide lobe centers which minimizes overlap -- is that what you're doing? Not much you can do about that, except maybe move your injector timing at low speed back to where the intake valve is closed (in the injector timing table) so that you don't spray raw fuel into the combustion chambers. That might help... Good luck, Fritz Coast 342, AFR185's, TFS stage II cam,30# inj, 76mm C&L, 1 3/4 hooker long tubes, 3.70 gears, Spec stage II clutch, an A9L and a TwEECer RT, 11.84 @120.4 w/100hp shot Top

posts.author: DrDirt
posts.content: DrDirt Tuning Addict Posts: 512 Joined: Wed Jun 30, 2004 7:45 am Location: Largo, Fl Quote Post by DrDirt » Fri Aug 05, 2005 9:24 am Oops! I had a brain fart up there. To get stock bin from your ECU, click on the Ford logo at the top of Caledit like I said but that is "Read ECU" not "Read Tweecer". As for clearing the KAM, that should do it (if by disconnecting the module you mean you disconnected the battery...simply pulling Tweecer off the ECU will not do it as the KAM is stored in the ECU). You might want to hold the brake pedle down for a minute or so before you hook the battery back up to make sure the capacitor is drained. The quick and easy way though is to write a bin file for another strategy to one of the positions on Tweecer. Then you can just turn the switch to that position, turn the key on for a second, turn it back off and then turn the switch back to your tune you will be running. KAM is instantly cleared. Some people have had a problem with this method but it has worked for me every time. I am running an A9P also and I use the J4J1 bin to cleam KAM. It is loaded onto Tweecer right next to the stock position. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Aug 10, 2005 6:42 pm Not sure about your smog requirments but in California a B303 cam will not pass, also if the EGR has been deleted it would not pass the visual. Did you disable the EGR in the tune. On the A9L the idle has a strategy that will open the EGR if at an idle for extended period of time. This is to lean out the mixture for better emissions. It sounds as if you have other problems, if you are able to smell it. Are you sure the MAF curve and injectors are tuned correctly? If you are out by say more than the allotted +-12% then the EEC will think something else is wrong and NOT adjust the KAMRF. This can be very misleading. Especially if you have reset the KAMRF and they never move. This would make you believe that you have a perfect tune. We both know that having KAMRFs dead on at 1.0 is impossible. I would make sure that if you adjust the MAF that the KAMRF do react. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Tue Aug 09, 2005 8:26 am Chances are that the change you made is an attempt to get the KAMs to be = 1, and before they were not, so without a 'reset' you have to wait for them to react and readapt to the new settings. Clearing the KAMs makes them = 1, so if your KAMs were at 0.928 before the changes, and the new calibration will eventually get them to 0.980 (which you don't know ahead of time, but just assume this), then starting off at 1.000 will get them to 0.980 faster than starting at 0.928. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Tue Aug 09, 2005 8:34 am Something else that I recently discovered (in the GFUB startegy doc) and have never seen discussed before, is that when the KAM's are cleared, a 'number of warm-ups' counter also gets reset to 0. This counter is part of the KAMs and increments each time the car cycles from cold to warm (stabilized). Then during adaptive, if the 'number of warm-ups' is less than [a tweecer unaccessable scalar] (suggested to be set to 3-5), it enables 'fast learning'. This is a mode that allows adaptive to react and learn faster than normal. So if you don't clear your KAMs with each change, then you could be out of the fast learning mode, and thus take even longer yet to get the KAMs fully readjusted. posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Thu Aug 04, 2005 9:34 am Sorry, I just saw your post today I'm not sure of all the different names for spark in your app., what year car, etc, is it used in? MBT spark table - same as in desc. on eecv timing BDLN knock table - same as above Max allowed spark table -not sure, sounds like the "base" spark table Max allowed spark table cold start -just as it says, spark when cold, probably can leave it alone. Spark adder after load increase -you have to experiment with this one, is it a temporary spark adder or does it add spark all the time? Spark adder for a/f when open loop -sounds like "spk adder for OL" mentioned in the doc. Spark adder to max for a/f when open loop -probably a limiter to how much spark you can actually use Spark altitude table -same spark retard act multiplier -same Spark retard ect multiplier -same If you have a blown car chances are you can simply log spark during wot and reduce it by reducing the spark values in the BDLN table as that will tend to be the lowest spark value. Keep in mind the spk adders will be used also. posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Sat Aug 13, 2005 8:27 am When you enter maf values manually you have to enter the first new number in the box, then hit "enter" on your keyboard. This "enters" the new value. Then hit "shift" right or left to the next box you want to change, hit enter for the new value, etc. If you don't do that, just keep entering new numbers for each box only the last value you entered will be kept. If you like the new values then hit "save" or rename the tune if you don't want to change the current tune, then you can write it. DON'T write to the tweecer using the "update" feature, it will cause many problems. Too bad too because I could have picked up the motor (2K miles), tranny, wiring harness and computer for cheap ($1500.00). You are (more than likely) running into the anti-theft (WALL) . If you go to the Motorcraft website ( http://www.motorcraftservice.com/vdirs/ ... efault.asp ), you can, for a reasonable fee, sign up for a certain vehicle access. Then once signed in, you can get into the schematics of the car and you will see what kinds of walls you are facing. One other website I just found ( WWW.FORDFUELINJECTION.COM ) is overrun with information. Go the harness tab and look at harnesses for 4.6L & 5.4L harnesses and it will redirect you to another website that deals with nothing but harness changes and computer changes to rid the evil spirits from both. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Thu Aug 11, 2005 9:34 pm OK, I think I figured it out after looking at a bunch of cranking logs. The formula is (Function: fuel_crank_multiply_ECT) X (Function fuel_crank_multiply_BP) X (Table: fuel_crank_pulsewidth) = cranking PW. The values in the table and the fuel_crank_multiply_ECT are seconds. And fuel_crank_multiply_BP is compensation for barometric pressure. Because we have larger injectors we need to reduce the PW and I have decided I will try changing the Function fuel_crank_multiply_ECT values by 19/42. (19# stock injectors replaced with 42#'s). Black70Fastback, I think you are right about Ford wanting to get the oil moving when it is extremely cold before firing the injectors. I also thought about the fact that at first the engine turns very slowly when it is real cold so no need to feed it fuel at the outset. And of couse it might only turn 3 or 4 PIP's and die when it is this cold so 0's in the table now make sense. 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. Such as the wideband saying 14.7 but Calcon saying 14.0-1 or something like that? If that is the case one problem can be the DATAQ box, it sometimes shifts the output signal by some amount causing the problem. Or, the transfer file in tweecer is wrong and needs to be corrected. If you go to the "explore" menu and open the tweecer file, under "data" files you will see your wideband file (UEGO, etc). You can open that file with Excel and see the transfer function that shows what the voltage output from your wideband sensor corresponds to in a/f ratios. You can make corrections there by changing the values, usually it is off a fixed amount such as .2 or something and you just change all the a/f values by that amount and then you are good to go. posts.author: a50sn95
posts.content: a50sn95 Gear Head Posts: 20 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 8:31 am Location: Elk Grove, CA Quote Post by a50sn95 » Fri Aug 19, 2005 5:45 pm It is a special O2 sensor, and a controller. A W/B sensor requires a heater circuit, which our cars don't have, and output in a much wide range than our computer can use. The controller will interface with the Tweecer through various methods, and some can even output a Narrowband signal so you can replace one of your existing sensors and not have to weld on a new bung. I would recommend getting one that is known to work with the Tweecer. All of them are fine, any of them are better than nothing..... Reading plugs is fine, but remember that the reading the plugs is only accurate for the LAST operating condition of the engine. So if you go out and do a WOT pull and then drive back home, your plugs will only indicate what your engine was doing right before you shutoff the engine. (idleing in the driveway.) Nascar drivers do a WOT pull down the backstretch, shutoff the engine and coast back to the pits to do a plug check. Starting the engine or idling will remove the evidence you were looking for. .020 over 302, 8.5-1, TFSTW's, Crane 2031, TFS 1.7's, TFS Street Heat, PP 75mm, Pro-M 80mm, FMS 42's, BBK Shorty's, Vortech at 8 lbs, J4J1 on T4M0 Startup and Idle Sounds Top

posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Aug 21, 2005 1:00 am There is also a 'fast learning mode' that the EEC uses for the first few warm cycles of the engine since last KAM reset. Number of warm cycles of the engine is also stored in the KAM. So if you haven't reset the KAMs and just turned on adaptive, you may be out of this 'fast learning mode' (number of warm cycles in KAM > [calibration constant 'number of warm cycles to enable fast learning']), and updates may take longer (the speed set by the table). I DO NOT know the speed relationship of 'fast' to normal modes, (GUESSES - it is fixed to a fast speed (maybe the equilivant of a '1' in the table), or maybe it is say 1/2 of the value in the table, or what...) I suggest always clearing your KAMs (to erase that number of warm cycles counter and enable fast learning) when trying to get the adaptive KAMRF values acquired. Also like Clint said, change the values to a low number, too. Some strategys do not have that scalar option available for modification, or even viewing/confirmation (some calibrations are a mystery). It is believed that all calibrations of CBAZA and A9L are trailing edge, so you should set it to trailing and NEVER change it (unless you change that scalar somehow...) posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Aug 14, 2005 9:45 pm Toy 94 GT wrote: I have a question on this. At load of 75% and above 4000 RPM EA says that I have exceded the injector fireing event and says to set it at 570 degrees. Toy 94 GT wrote: The max PW above 4000 RPM and high load is less then 17ms. Is this correct? Do I need bigger injectors? My fuel pressure is set about 39 lbs. Thanks EA is telling you that you can't fit in all of the PW firing into the time that the intake valve is open, NOT that you can't fit it all into a complete cycle. All that this really means is that you are going to have to start the PW before the int opens, thus during overlap. Unless your injectors are grossly oversized, this is unavoidable. At 4000 RPMs, 1 cycle takes 30ms from intake open to the next intake open. The time that your intake is open is not even half of a entire cycle (<15ms @ 4000 RPMs). At 6000 RPMs, an entire cycle is only 20ms. To spray the injector only while the intake is open would require a max PW of say ~7-8ms, and would require you to have 42lb-ers or something! That would then kill your idle quality, as the PW would be super low, like 1ms... EA's suggestion of 570 is about when your intake valve is closing. Remember, the value in the table are when the PW ends. So when the PW is too large to fit into the int open event, the EA will start the PW sooner. Again, you can't avoid this. EA clips the PW ending to the int close event, as you don't want to be spraying your fuel after the intake valve closes. It has to start the PW sooner. Really, the red values aren't really bad, just so you know that the PW is starting before your chosen 'PW start' event (say TDC). Now, this clip value (570) is also something that you may consider adjusting, and is a matter of user methodolgy. IMO, I don't want to spray fuel right up to the int close event, as for the last, say 50° of it, lift (and thus airflow velocity) is super low. I can't imagine that fuel atomizes or mixes with air very well at such low flow velocity. I would then choose to clip the max value to something less, say 540 (or 500???). This allows more time and airflow for the air and fuel to mix and atomize. This also then has the effect of causing more conditions of starting the PW before the int open event, and thus spraying during overlap. What's better? Spraying during overlap and risking it going out the exhaust, or not atomizing well in the cylinder and it going out the exhaust that way (due to poor atomization and vaporization)? Clipping the timing value to 540 or 500 is something that you are just going to have to do in your head, as EA does not have a way to do this (other than fudging your cam specs). BUT it's easy. Anytime that the number shown by EA is >540 (or 500), type 540 (or 500) into caledit. The HP that you are making doesn't really determine your injector size. It may provide sort of a guesstimate, but what really matters is your max duty cycle (DC). Under 80% DC max is desirable, but you may push it to 85-90% intermittently, if necessary. The logged PW value is NOT the total commanded PW. The PW adder from the injector offset for batv function is not logged, and get's applied to the logged value. So with (for example) J4J1, it's usually about 0.5ms more than logged PW at 13V. Since you are using EA, it will calculate your DC (and max) for you. You need to have your injector offset values entered into the inj offset tab, and choose 'calc inj DC on datalog load' (something like that!) on the settings tab. Then EA will add a column to the loaded datalog with the inj DC for that row. You can click on the INJDC column header to resort the table so that the max DC in the datalog is on the top. ALSO, when you enter your inj offset into the inj offset tab, the inj timing calculation will take that time into account and provide more accurate calculations. This means that your injectors are borderline too small. Your A/F ratio will also effect this... If your commanding 11.9 (like stock J4J1), going to 13.0 will shorten your PWs, and thus your DC. posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Mon Aug 15, 2005 5:51 pm jetuomi wrote: I have never really messed around with injector timing (and have a post outstanding about my turbo 331) but I have greatly mis-understood this topic, thanks for clarifying... Well, it wasn't until about a year ago (maybe a little less?) that the belief changed from the values being leading edge to trailing edge. jetuomi wrote: I have values of 300 in the table "stock" J4J1 table. This means that the pulse ends at 300* ?? that means they really put a lot of fuel on the intake valve while it is closed don't they?? Yep, all of it. Not certain why, but I discussed it before, you were there... viewtopic.php?t=4946 I was wondering then if you wern't up to date on the leading to trailing belief switch... jetuomi wrote: So if I make sense of this, EA program takes cam specs, figures out intake valve close event.. so when you're getting near max duty cycle, I would assume that your injector timing #'s should be closer to the intake-close event (minus some time where you said the airflow is bad).. Yep. EA's goal with trailing edge and exh close (or TDC or int open) settings is to have every PW start as close as possible to the exh close (or TDC or int open) as possible. Since the EEC is expecting PW end values, it takes some calculations to determine this. For example, if it finds that at say 2000 RPMs and .3 load that PWs are about 5ms long, then it calculates how many degrees of engine cycle those 5ms will take up. This is when the PW ends, and the value in the table. Thus the PW will start at the exh close (or TDC or int open) event. It kinda 'works around' the trailing edge configuration to essentially allow you to set your inj timing to a (pseudo) PW start configuration. You could just change the injector reference scalar to make the EEC leading edge, but that is only beneficial at those times when the PW will fit into the intake open event. Once you exceed that, then you need to do calculations to determine the PW start to avoid spraying into the next cycle. IMO, EA's calcs with a trailing edge calibration give you the best of both worlds. Besides, that scalar is unknown (and thus unchangeable) with CBAZA... Thanks If you have the TDC option selected, the EA will start the PW at TDC and calculate the end point. If the PW is greater than the allotted time (TDC to Intake Close) then the EA will calculate the PW end point at the intake close and then calculate the PW start degree. Or is it because it is higher then 540* BDC on the intake stroke? Thanks The reason for 576 is because you have an initial distributor setting and maybe lifter compensation and so forth. IOW - if you use that 576° value, then the PW will end at 603°. That table references the PIP signal and the initial distro setting effects this. The inj delay also has a play in this. When the EEC turns on the injector, it takes ~.5ms for the injector to actually start spraying. This then actually delays the PW some, and that delay (in degrees) varys with RPM. If you choose trailing/int close, EA will tell you these 'corrected' values per RPM. (The estimated my be a bit off, each column will always be the same) If you choose leading/int open, it will tell you the 'corrected' intake open values. If you adjust the inj delay, you can see the effects that it causes. 86GT wrote: Toy 94 GT wrote: I would think at low speeds and low load centering it would be more effecient. If EA does not center it do you think it would be more benificial to set the lower loads to TDC and the higher loads to intake opening? Thanks This is one of the theories that are out there. Some people believe that the max flow is when the valve is at max lift. There is an option for this too. To counter that some believe that at max lift and with max flow that the temps are less and the atomization will be less. This would mean less efficient. I personally believe Ford sprayed the back of a closed valve because it was hot which caused atomization. It also was used as a engine cooling method. Keep in mind that most of the stock cams had very little cam overlap therefore they did not have the problem of fuel scavenging (fuel going out the exhaust). This is the reason Why I choose the TDC and or Exhaust Close option. You may not get the atomization that the factory gets by spraying the back of a hot valve, but at least it does not have the chance to go out the exhaust. I don't know what's worse, a bit of fuel going out the exhaust before the combustion, or a bit going out after (due to poor atomization). I don't know just how much overlap is "needed" for fuel scavenging. These are the types of issues that engineers with lots of calculations and testing figure out. On that note, I emailed Ed Curtis (of FTI, who designed my cam profile) recently (mid July) about this: rockin_rick (in an email to Ed Curtis) wrote: Mr. Curtis, I purchased a custom cam from you a while ago, and am very pleased with it. ...(attached is the spec card you sent me). For your reference, specific engine specs are below. I am wondering about the flow characteristics of my specific cam during overlap. I would like to know wether or not the unburned intake charge ever gets sent out the exhaust, and at what RPM range this occurs in. I've read before that during overlap with a larger than "stock sized" overlap, it can cause intake charge dilution due to reversion at low RPMs - flow into intake port during overlap, thus leaning out the mixture and contributing to "8-stroking" or lope. And with the same "large" overlap cam, at higher RPMs, it can "leak" the intake charge into the exhaust before it gets ignited. Would you believe that my specific cam exhibits either or both of these traits, and to what degree? Specifically, I am trying (via EEC calibration mods via tweecer) to calculate/asertain when to fire my injectors in relation to my cam events, and flow during overlap is a factor. (Do you have any insight into injector timing?) Thank you for any help, it is appreciated! and he replied: Ed Curtis (in an email to rockin_rick) wrote: As for the overlap issue, at the timing events shown on the card, you actually have "zero" overlap at .050" tappet lift. You should have no issues at all with any type of reversion unless the exhaust is very clogged and/or restrictive. Ed (I'd imagine that this only applies to NA.) Given this, I'm going to assume that fuel is not going to go out the exhaust during overlap, and I'll benefit from the hot intake valve vaporization (atomization) with J4J1 style settings (spraying the back of the valve before int open event). My exh close (@ 0.050") is at 4° BTDC, and my int open (@ 0.050") is also at 4°BTDC. I've been using '292' in all cells for a while now. This is 40° less than my intake open event, just as J4J1's '300' values are 40° before it's intake open event. BARO is updated only when the vehicle is at high throttle openings. Barometric pressure (in. hg.)-------- Altitude above sea level ft. 15 ---------------------------- 14000 20 ---------------------------- 10000 21 ---------------------------- 9000 22 ---------------------------- 8000 23 ----------------------------- 7000 24 ----------------------------- 6000 25 ----------------------------- 5000 26 ----------------------------- 4000 27 ----------------------------- 3000 28 ----------------------------- 2000 29 ----------------------------- 1000 30 ----------------------------- 0 sea level All of this is from Ford TSB 98-23-10. Shelby Top

posts.author: Chris Mureen
posts.content: Chris Mureen Tuning Addict Posts: 443 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 6:44 pm Location: Austin, TX Quote Post by Chris Mureen » Wed Aug 17, 2005 3:50 pm Very interesting info. Thanks for posting it. I've never seen that table, but can only comment about how I've seen the EECV in Mustangs use the data. I have seen functions and tables in the PCM and none handled 27hg any differently than 30hg. However, they did start managing data differently when it dropped much lower. I actually locked mine to 30hg and then changed it to 27hg and logged no difference in fuel or timing. One other point, the strategy doc defines that if an error ocurrs then to use the default BAPFFM which is set to 27hg stock. If you set Max and Min to 30hg, it defaults to 27hg unless that value is also changed. Interestingly enough, I pretty sure that still only the CRAJ0 startegy has that scalar revealed because I found it and added it. SCT doesn't reveal that scalar for tuning so I am pretty sure that is why they feel comfortable recommending 27hg as the default for max and min. I don't doubt the validity of your data, I am only questioning as to what the EEC does different at each altitude. Based on my experience, 27hg=30hg. One other point. I once tuned a car with a Pro-m Univ meter (I said Lightning above and I remembered wrong). At startup it would default to 27hg, but as soon as it went into closed loop it would start diving downward to where it pegged at 18hg. There it would hang until the engine was killed. I never tried WOT to see if it changed but it was a real mess until I figured out the tag to turn it off and added it to my binary. Chris 1998 Cobra - CRAJ0/AOL3 http://eecanalyzer.net http://beast.freehompage.com Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Aug 17, 2005 6:33 pm On the older speed density the EEC would take a snapshot of the MAP sensor at startup. This would be the barometric pressure used for the remaining of the drive cycle. Since the MAP and BAP are one in the same when the vehicle is not running this is the way Ford did it. When the vhecile was started the sensor read manifold pressure. When Mass Air came out the MAP was not needed, so they converted it to a BAP by removing the vacuum hose. I'm not sure when they removed the sensor but I know it is there on the 86-93 Mustang 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

And trust me, if it has a guage I'm watching it closely. First thing I would do is run it with the cap off and looking into the radiator to see what kind of flow your seeing. A good cooling system flows quite a bit of water if you rev it a little above idle. This is somewhat obvious, especially if your watching it as it heats up. The moment the tstat opens, you can really see the water flow. And I've seen cars that run hot 'fail' this simple test. I would make sure that there is good airflow through the radiator. posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Sat Aug 13, 2005 8:21 am It is normal for there to be a bank to bank difference in fuel trims, this reflects differences between the banks of the engine, ring seal, valve seal, etc. The differences are most noticable at idle for some reason and they get closer as rpms go up. It should be relatively small, 5% or so. FWIW, if you have a mechanical problem, particuallarly if you have had a valve job done recently, you may have some valves that are not sealing properly, on mod motors you have to watch out for that as they are alum. heads. The valve seats need to be lapped in by hand no matter what the head guy says as they tend to change sealing once the car is run. Happened to me, had a difference of 10 percent at idle and some fuel smoke out the tailpipe. Not good for your rings. posts.author: J_P
posts.content: J_P Regular Posts: 186 Joined: Wed May 04, 2005 2:06 am Location: Ashburn, VA Contact: Contact J_P Yahoo Messenger Quote Post by J_P » Tue Aug 16, 2005 1:00 pm One place to correct this problem would be the portion of the MAF transfer that is affected. You could lower the airflow numbers at the points that your car is getting to rich. Go slowly as you don't want to lean too far. However, the best route to go is, to completely adjust the entire MAF transfer until your wideband is reading what the computer is commanding. At that point you can adjust the fuel tables to whatever you want the A/F to be. posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Tue Aug 23, 2005 9:18 pm The adaptive switch I mentioned may be just an eecv thing but I doubt it, it does what I said on my car. To force OL there should be a function called "open loop load" which has rpm vs load. You will see high load numbers at low rpms, .9 or so which means that at low rpms it will stay in CL until it hits .9 load. As rpms increase the load value to go into OL is set lower and lower. So..make all the load values "0" for all rpms and you will be in OL all the time except during warmup. The car will initially go OL at first start-up, then go to CL after about 45 seconds and stay in CL until you reach the temp for "ect for stab OL" which is in scalars. Most of the time it is set to 180 degrees ect, after that you will go full time OL with the settings I recommend above. Of course if you want to run OL even when the motor is cold you could reduce the scalar to a low ect temp to force that too. Then I added an offset that I calculated by taking simultaneous data logs using Calcon & the LM-1. Then I averaged the hundreds of points in Excel for each (Calcon & LM-1 data) and came up with a correction factor. I changed the first couple of points in the new Excel file created using the Horriba file - e.g. I turned 2.5V to 2.42V for 10 AFR etc and did an auto-fill-drag. I saved the new WB file under a new name (same extension). I then edited the Calcon.ini file in the windows directory and replaced the file name of the WB file to the new file in I had just created. Works good and consistantly now. 428w now Top

Don The ground offset is within the LM-1. The display and data recording are good because they are referenced to the offset ground within the meter. Any output from the meter that is acquired using an external data collection device referenced to true ground will have an issue. Now if the DataQ has floating inputs such that it is referencing the LM-1 signal WRT it's (LM-1's) own signal ground, then the offset should not be a problem. It sounds like you have the latter situation which, as you said, is not a problem... 428w now Top

posts.content: Daren Woodall Tuning Addict Posts: 833 Joined: Thu Oct 31, 2002 3:48 pm Location: Austin, TX Contact: Contact Daren Woodall Website CBAZA Strategy observations... Quote Post by Daren Woodall » Thu Aug 18, 2005 3:12 pm I'm sure several of you have taken the time to compare the T4MO to the J4J1. One thing curious is the big differences in the fuel stabilize OL table. The J4J1's entries are considerably richer then that of the T4MO. In fact, the J4J1's stabilized AFR numbers appear too rich to be appropriate for any production N/A motor. The T4MO seem more inline with expected AFR values. In addition to this, the MAF Transfer functions for these two tunes are different. I assumed this to mean the J4J1 (Cobra) had a different MAF sensor from the GT. I have since learned the MAF part numbers are identical for both models. :? So the question... will the true MAF Transfer please stand. I have a Pro-M 24 MAF and no original flow-sheet. I use the TwEECer provided PROM-24 transfer and EA to optimize it using a WBO2. The mystery is the dramic correction EA suggested made no since to me. Why would the transfer be wrong by this much? Something else must be up. This problem is most evident at idle. My idle AFR from the WB is between 17 - 20, way lean. I was convinced I was getting unburned O2 in to the exhaust. But, I have an E-cam. It doesn't have the overlap to cause this nor is the idle choppy enough to be putting unburned O2 in the exhaust. This doesn't appear to be a leak. In my frustration I decided to remove one significant variable from my mystery. I purchase an OEM MAF ($60 eBay), installed it and placed the OEM MAF Transfer in the tune. What I observe is the idle AFR and cruise (light load) AFR falls right in line with my expectations re-enforcing my suspicious that there is no unburned O2 in my exhaust. I've concluded that the MAF Transfer for my Pro-M was way off at idle but... The AFR using the OEM MAF in the upper loads were much leaner then the commanded LAMBSE. While the commanded might range from 12.5-11.5, the actual was 14.1 - 13.1. This suggests even the OEM MAF Transfer is not close to accurate in the upper loads. :? So what does this mean? I'm beginning to think that the J4J1 is a "hack" tune. It was not created by Ford using the AFR tuning principals by which we use, nor would you want to use EA/WBO2 to optimize your MAF Transfer to utilize the J4J1 stabilized fuel tables as they are. Anyway. I haven't fully reached a conclusion to this. I did resolve the mystery of exhaust O2. I can now trust the AFR and perform the ISC and TB Airflow task in EA. My cold start problems stemmed specifically from an incorrect MAF transfer (much too lean at idle). It appears that I will still need to use EA to suggest a MAF Transfer then fully re-enter the fuel tables to my liking. I thought I would pass this bit along and hear any other thoughts on this stuff. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Thu Aug 18, 2005 3:32 pm I wanted to add a tid bit of info that I found on my experimenting. If you leave the "Adaptive update rate" to its factory settings and install a MAF that is not accurate then you will be fighting a vicious circle. What I mean by this, For example say at 2000 RPM the MAF is off by -3% and then at an idle the MAF is off by say +3%. The EEC uses a four point interpolation therefore the four surrounding points are also used. This caused updates of the surrounding idle cells with data from the 2000 RPM range. So the end result means that some cells maybe out by as much as 6%. This is just an example. What I did to resolve this was to set the adaptive update table to something like '2', which allowed for a quick update. I only did this during the tuning process. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Wed Aug 24, 2005 4:46 pm 2Shaker wrote: Thanks Bob. Someone else suggest that this table contained the values at which it would go to OL which jives with your comments. Let's see if anyone else jumps in here. It doesn't do this. The sealevel load scaling function is the multiplier for load to generate loadx. There is a load scaling switch in the calibration that essentially allows you to choose wether the EEC uses load for the tables or loadx. You can consider sealevel load scaling as a global load modifier. IIRC, J4J1 uses loadx (load scaling switch = 0) for the tables, while T4M0 uses load (load scaling switch = 2). The OL operation that the sealevel load scaling function can 'control' is much more indirect due to the EEC using different table rows and such after the load gets adjusted. Say the OL load trigger is 70%, since the loadx has gone from 50% to 20%, there is more "time" (range of load) before the loadx gets large enough to trigger OL mode. Make sense? posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Tue Jul 05, 2005 1:18 pm NO! The 4.8V voltage you are seeing is normal - it is a fairly high impedance source and will have some droop - this is perfectly normal. Also, when hot the voltage goes down and can get pretty low at a higher temperature. Also, the 5V reference used for the sensors is used throughout the ECU - and it is protected by a ~10-100k resistor so you can't pull down the internal reference. In fact, when hot the ECT & ACT are practically shorts. BTW, 0.97 V = 163 deg F The 0.18V is probably just a ground offset. Read this : http://www.fordfans.cz/download/manual/eectch98.pdf 428w now Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Tue Jul 05, 2005 6:36 pm There are two pins on the sensor and one is connected to signal return (along with all the other sensors). That means that the voltage on the high side IS the sensed voltage that you use the lookup table to determine the temperature. Think of it like this - Vref is about 5V, it feeds a resistor going to the sensor, the sensor is a resistor. The ECU reads the voltage between the resistors. The signal return side of the sensor often has an offset on it because it is grounded at the ECU, not the engine block (to minimize noise). 428w now Top

Don It is, but it is INCORRECTLY calculated by CalCon, nor can be logged. The logged PW value is NOT the total commanded PW value, and that is what is needed to accurately determine INJ DC. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Mon Aug 29, 2005 10:37 am Without the volt meter is a craps game. If you are certain the TPS is good then the only two possible things it can be is: 1) the connector or wiring is bad. Take a close look at the pins on the connector and make sure they do not get pushed in when you plug the TPS in. Also check pin 60 on the EEC and make sure there is no corrosion. 2) This is the one that you do not want to be true. The EEC internal voltage sensing ciricut could be bad. If some how a 12 volt source was applied to this ciricut then it is possible that it has been fried. I would check all other possibilities first. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: dsleepy47
posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Wed Aug 31, 2005 11:40 am Look at the base open loop fuel table and what Lambse is running on the highway. If open loop is commanding the same thing as closed loop mileage won't change. If it commands more fuel than closed loop the mileage will be worse. Kamrf's are still in effect in open loop so if you force open loop you need to clear the memory or the stored values will be used. Before I used my WBs to control closed loop I had a mileage tune that ran open loop all the time that gave me 2mpg better than closed loop because I could highway cruise at 15.5:1. The 14.64 afr box for the stock A9L OL fuel table is only 180-210 degF ECT and 40%-55% load so any time you are outside of those values it will run richer than closed loop. The open loop fuel vs ACT function will also richen things up below 76 degF, if you run EGR blocked off in Minnesota like I do the ACT function will definitely affect things. Check the %load and ECT under the conditions you want mileage in open loop and change the OL fuel table to give you the AFR you want in those conditions. ALL this assumes you MAF and injector parameters are correct first.!! posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri Sep 02, 2005 9:38 am Don't think of it as a table. Since all the values in the table are the same, then it is really like a scalar. This one point such as 3.045 is actually .00003045 lbs of fuel removed from the final calculated PW. It is there to account for the in-accuracy of the low PW on the injectors. Since most injectors are sloppy at low PW this is the way to try and correct. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Fri Sep 02, 2005 2:03 am VREF is +5V SIG RTN is ground (sensor ground reference) If you connected the ground of the LM-1 to the +5V reference of the EEC, you are lucky you didn't f something up. Most likely what happened is that you pulled down your VREF to lower than +5V, and that messed up all the sensor readings. I don't know what your wire color codes are. Um, check your instructions. (or online) If that other one is simply analog ground (and there is another ground, (perhaps power ground)), then connecting to SIG RTN probably is a good idea. If it is an overall ground (the only one), then don't connect it to SIG RTN, as it can't handle the power. There must be more than 3 wires coming out of that thing if 2 of them are analog outs. You gotta have power, gnd, out1, out2, at least. The EEC and the LM-1 need to see the same ground potential so that the EEC will 'see' the same voltage that the LM-1 is putting out. So if you only have 1 ground wire, then connect it as close to the EEC's ground spot as possible. Technically, the LM-1 (or anything) doesn't put out 5V, but rather a 5V difference over ground reference. It just so happens that most of the time ground reference = 0. So if the LM-1 is putting out 5V over reference, and the EEC's ground reference has a 1 volt differential than LM-1 reference, than the EEC will read 1V off. Of course, 1V is A LOT, and would most likely never happen. But 0.1V could, and that WILL mess up your A/F reading. posts.author: ttlx
posts.content: ttlx Regular Posts: 93 Joined: Thu Jul 07, 2005 2:11 pm Location: Magnolia, Texas Contact: Contact ttlx Website Quote Post by ttlx » Fri Sep 02, 2005 10:56 pm Here's what I did with my Bailey AFM-1... Open any .DBF in Excel. I used HORIBA.DBF and what you should see is two columns of data and a label at the beginning of each column: 'VOLTS' & 'AF'. Take your wb.xls 0-5v spreadsheet and delete the blank column F. Select and Copy just the numbers in column E & F. Note that the "Save as Type" should be "dBASE4 .DBF". posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sat Sep 03, 2005 12:12 am I believe that any 'normal' NB oriented A/F meter (with a 0-1V) input can be used with the LC-1. I think that you can use one of the LC-1's outputs as 0-5V for the EEC and tweecer, and you can set up the other analog output for 0-1V output for the meter. This 0-1V output should be more of a linear curve (straight line) of 10-20 A/F rather than the 'default' 0-1V 'NB' emulation curve. BTW- I believe that the XD-1 gauge uses the digital serial output of the LC-1, which is then essentially error free communication to the gauge. This eliminates any possible ground offset or voltage drop errors due to wiring. So the gauge displays EXACTLY what the LC-1 is computing. That's kinda nice. This also frees up the 2nd analog output for NB emulation to the EEC. I think that gauge also shows a direct readout of the A/F (in digits) rather than a sweeping 'needle' that has low resolution. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Idle air valve (ISC) tuning Quote Post by boss96 » Sat Sep 03, 2005 12:45 pm Setting idle air (isc). Datalog the isc duty cycle, should be 30%. If higher, first verify that car will idle with the isc motor disconnected. It should be adjusted mechanically to idle about 100 rpm lower than the desired idle speed. Re-connect isc motor, check duty cycle, if still too high, set the "isc neutral air flow" values to stock, adjust the air values around the desired idle rpm to obtain 30% isc duty cycle. If you can't datalog isc duty cycle then observe the timing at idle, it should be steady. If the timing values are hunting at idle, then that indicates you have too much or too little idle air through the isc valve and the EEC is trying to compensate by adjusting timing to control idle. This will make idle unstable though. If you have aftermarket cams in the car you will probably need to increase the isc air values somewhat in the idle region. If the idle hangs you can reduce or zero out the air values in the "dashpot pre-position" function to make the idle come down faster. If you zero it out it should drop right away with the exception of hanging around 1000 rpm when off throttle and car is still moving. Once it gets below 3mph it should go to idle speed Bob 96 GT, Vortech Si trim,Procharger 3 core intercooler, forged bottom end, MAC longtubes, ported PI heads , Edelbrock intake, Crower cams-.580lift/234dur@.050, 80lb injectors, CDAN4/GGL4 processor. title: injector timing theory - J4J1 style best for NA? - EECTuning.org

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am injector timing theory - J4J1 style best for NA? Quote Post by rockin_rick » Fri Jun 24, 2005 4:10 pm I have been pondering the injector timing for a while now. With a NA application, I am now leaning more to towards a J4J1 style of injector timing. I am unsure if this is the best method for boosted, and perhaps starting the pulse after the cam overlap is the best method there (in which case EA does a great job of calculating). Everything I'm describing past here is considering a NA application. It seems that the common belief (myth?) is that intake charge is pushed out the exhaust during overlap if you fire the injector before the exhaust is closed. I, while uncertain (this is why it's a theory), don't believe this to be true. I think that the pressures and flows in the combustion chamber are such that intake doesn't flow into the combustion chamber until after the exhaust valve is closed. If anything, air flows from the chamber into the intake, causing intake charge pollution. (BTW - this is why boosted may be different) So with the J4J1 and trailing edge firing, the methodolgy that I believed Ford used was to fire all of the fuel on the back of the intake valve. I believe that this causes the fuel to vaporize better. The extremely hot intake valve will boil the fuel and vaporize it. This also cause the intake valve to cool. Background: First what is needed is an explanation of how fuel burns. Fuel vapor is the only componant of gasoline that can burn, liquid fuel can't. The liquid fuel needs a way to vaporize to burn. In every combustion event, not all of the liquid fuel is vaporized. If you can increase the % vaporized, you increase MPG (as you can inject less fuel) as well as power (more burn per cycle). There are a few ways to vaporize fuel. One is evaporitazation. Atomization is done to break down the liquid fuel to tiny droplets to increase the surface area of the liquid fuel so that it may (on it's own) evaporate and turn to fuel vapor. Another method is heating. This can be acomplished by either direct heating (like spraying on a hot intake valve) or from heating due to the friction from the shearing action of the droplets moving through the air. So, if you spray on the back of the intake valve, you not only get immediate vaporitazion from the heating, but the fuel will get hotter, and then need less heating from the friction of the shearing action of flowing into the cylinder once the valve is opened, which ultimately will result in even more of the liquid fuel getting vaporized. Why 300°? J4J1 ends the PW ~40° before the intake open event. I think that the methodology of J4J1's inj. timing values of 300 are either: To have the pulse end ~40° before the intake valve opens to have that amount of time pass to heat the fuel. If it ended 5° before the intake opens, then there would be less time to absorb heat and vaporize. OR - that value is determined by the PW length at max DC as to start the PW right after the intake valve closes (on the previous cycle) and, with the stock engine combination, the max PW/DC time with the PW starting right after the intake valve closed, resulted in it ending at ~300°. And then they just set all values to that number. Perhaps with the engine in the 94-95 cobra and 24lb injectors, the DC probably didn't exceed 70%. I'm guessing that with my combo, I've got a good 75+ HP on those, and my 24lb injectors max at ~90%. Perhaps it is a combination of these.... Well, this is a theory, and I welcome any comments or thoughts regarding this, if they back up my statements or not. I am not a fluid dynamics engineer, thermodynamics engineer, or even an automotive engineer. While I believe what I said to be true, it is possible that I've been misinformed. IOW- don't take this as gospel! In the end, I don't want to be right, I want to figure out what is best. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri Jun 24, 2005 6:17 pm I agree with most of what you have stated. The only thing that I can add is the 93-95 cobras use a cam that has a lot less overlap. This would indeed allow for earlier injector firing. The only part that I would say that I may differ on is the fuel pushing out the exhaust. If the piston is on its way up (BTDC) during the valve overlap then fuel has two ways it can go. One, if the venturi effect caused by the exhaust is greater than the vacuum in the intake then it will go out the exhaust. Second, If it is less then venturi caused by the exhaust then it will go up the intake runner. Now if the piston is on the way down (ATDC) during the overlap then it will draw the least restrictive. What I mean by this is that if the exhaust has 15 in of vacuum caused by the venturi and the intake has a 10 in vacuum then the fuel will be drawn in. I would like to know wether or not the unburned intake charge ever gets sent out the exhaust, and at what RPM range this occurs in. I've read before that during overlap with a larger than "stock sized" overlap, it can cause intake charge dilution due to reversion at low RPMs - flow into intake port during overlap, thus leaning out the mixture and contributing to "8-stroking" or lope. And with the same "large" overlap cam, at higher RPMs, it can "leak" the intake charge into the exhaust before it gets ignited. Would you believe that my specific cam exhibits either or both of these traits, and to what degree? Specifically, I am trying (via EEC calibration mods via tweecer) to calculate/asertain when to fire my injectors in relation to my cam events, and flow during overlap is a factor. (Do you have any insight into injector timing?) Thank you for any help, it is appreciated! and he replied: Ed Curtis (in an email to rockin_rick) wrote: As for the overlap issue, at the timing events shown on the card, you actually have "zero" overlap at .050" tappet lift. You should have no issues at all with any type of reversion unless the exhaust is very clogged and/or restrictive. Ed (I'd imagine that this only applies to NA.) Given this, I'm going to assume that fuel is not going to go out the exhaust during overlap, and I'll benefit from the hot intake valve vaporization (atomization) with J4J1 style settings (spraying the back of the valve before int open event). My exh close (@ 0.050") is at 4° BTDC, and my int open (@ 0.050") is also at 4°BTDC. I've been using '292' in all cells for a while now (since about the time I first started this thread). Seems fine. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Tue Aug 16, 2005 10:38 pm Oh I just can't resist anything with "...injector timing..." in the title :-) I questioned the validity of the J4J1 cells at 300 in another thread a while back. A guy sent me a direct read of the EEC from his 95 Cobra. Indeed, the cells were all 300. As for intake charge going out the exhaust, I don't think this happens at low and mid RPM on an NA car with street legal emissions compliant exhaust. Even with the piston coming up the cylinder the column of air coming in from the intake would negate the effect of the rising piston. Casual observation of the intake when removed will show exhaust has been in the intake and well beyond what the EGR would supply. Blown cars would only have a potential for blowing part of the unburned charge out the exhaust when under boost. And I do accept that at WOT with a good flowing exhaust on an NA car you may actually scavenge the cylinder and an incoming charge. As for the values in the cells, I like the lower numbers and spraying the back of the intake for the reasons Rick explained. Besides the PW's are likely less than 10Mms so not much risk of spraying raw fuel on the cylinder walls. But at high RPM and 90% duty cycle I focus on the intake close event. I want the injector to finish just before the intake valve closes even at 90%+ DC's. I have fooled around with different settings and so far I've not been able to detect any significant change in the way it runs. Ford knows a whole bunch more than me so I stick pretty close to J4J1 at low and mid RPM, then switch to 570 degrees at 4K RPM and above. We can't seem to get under 12:40's so as the frustration increases I might try fooling with these some more. posts.author: juskevhere
posts.content: juskevhere Gear Head Posts: 1 Joined: Fri Aug 12, 2005 9:18 pm Contact: Contact juskevhere Yahoo Messenger injector timing (hope this helps) helped me Quote Post by juskevhere » Mon Sep 05, 2005 8:11 pm Tuning Injector_Timing 1.1.3 (7/14/03) By David Crow, with input of many Injector timing is the delay before each injector output is fired. The delay is taken from TDC of the reference PIP signal for each injector output [for each cylinder]. The units for injector timing are absolute engine crank degrees. The range is 0 degrees TDC to 720 degrees ATDC with 4 degree resolution. Either edge (on or off) of the injector pulse can be timed. The calibration switch INJREF defines the reference edge for injector timing. INJREF = 0, Use start of fuel pulse. INJREF = 1, Use end of fuel pulse. Most strategies use End pulse Timing. If the stock injector-timing table has values around 300-400, the strategy uses End pulse timing. If the stock injector-timing table has values around 100-200, the strategy is using Start pulse timing Regardless of which edge is used; the injector delay is used only to start a fuel pulse. Once started, pulsewidth accuracy has top priority. When the system is not in sync (SYNFLG = 0), the injector timing is coincident with the relevant PIP signal. The injector outputs are fired in sequence after receiving the rising edge of the reference PIP signals. Actual timing will be the result of the random link between signature PIP (cylinder #1) and #1 injector output. The delay to output is related to your camshaft profile, particularly the intake lobe profile. A cam spec card list degrees as xATC or xBTC, xABC or xBBC, these are After/Before TopCenter/BottomCenter. Some cam spec cards list “-“ negative degrees, this really just flips your value from After to Before or Before to After. ( -9ATC = 9BTC). Also most cards list open/close events @ .050, but some also list @.002. If your spec card lists degrees @.002 lift, you can forgo the corrections in the examples to get the start of valve opening. Some cam manufacturers list degrees as (A,B)BDC and (A,B)TDC, this can cause confusion as “Dead” centers typically refer to the crank, but these do not seem to refer to crank degrees. The 4-stroke cycle can be mapped to abs crank degrees as follows: 0-90 (+/- 30) Power stroke 90-360 (+/-30) Exhaust 360-630(+/-30) Intake 630-720(+/-30) Compression The intake stroke 0TC=360abs engine crank degrees. Intake stroke 0BC=540abs. 1 degree cam move = 2 degrees abs crank move (ie: advancing your cam 4* = -8*abs) Lets take the stock 302HO cam from a 90’s GT (A9L, End pulse timing): 302HO: Int Open: 11ATC Int Close: 41ABC Int Duration: 210@.050/266Adv This puts our valve timing at: IO (@.050):382 IC (@.050):622 But this must be corrected for raw lobe start. To get our raw start position we must use both the Advertised duration and duration @.050 lift. (382-( (266-210) /2))= 354 raw start position Note: Ford ended the injection pulse 2 crank degrees early. Now to the HIGH LOAD/HIGH RPM (HIGH oil pressure). At high pressure the hydraulic lifter is nearly a solid lifter. ((622-382)/2)=120 382+120=502 Halfway through the lobe. Now you say… 502 does NOT equal 464 from the stock table. Well there is still the matter of just how much lobe you can use. At 502 the valve is as high as it is going to get. Ford decided to set the max to 464. This could have been for a number of reasons. Perhaps the 19LB injectors required this much extra time to inject enough volume at these high loads. It seems that you could move this either direction. Keep in mind that the Exhaust valve on this cam will begin opening at 72, and the intake is closed at 650. Larger injector should not be a major consideration in low-mid load/rpm End pulse timing, unless you would like more fuel on valve time. But on the same note, larger injectors could reduce the required high-load/rpm time, as they require less lead-time per given volume. It has been recommended to fire earlier rather then later. Firing the injectors too late can cause the fuel to wash down the cylinder wall causing excessive wear and oil contamination. While firing the injector early will puddle fuel on the top of the valve, this does allow the fuel to absorb heat from the intake track and valve. This heat will help keep the fuel close to vaporization. The longer it sits on top of the valve the more heat it can absorb. But this could also be very hazardous under boost, were you want the coolest charge possible. It has been stated that fuel on the valve could cause carbon buildup. I don’t believe this to be the case. Carbon buildup is most likely caused at the point where the exhaust valve is closing, the intake is opening and there is residual pressure in the chamber is higher then intake pressure (nearing TDC, just as the intake stroke starts). This pressure zone occurs for approximately 31* with an E303 between the exhaust to intake overlap. With these methods in-place, lets look at the E303 (A9L, End pulse timing): E303:: IO:0BTC IC:40ABC EO:40BBC EC:0BTC INT 220/282 EXH 220/282 LC INT 110 LobeLift:.311/.311 IO:360 IC:620 360-((282-220)/2)=329 (IO start) 329-2(fords example)=327 setting for low-med load/rpm ((620-360)/2)=130 360+130=490 (top of intake lobe) 490-32(fords example)=458 (high-load/rpm setting, obviously a very flexible) Exhaust valve begins opening (under high pressure) at (100-((282-220)/2)=69 The intake valve closes completely at 651, 620 @ .050 So at high load/rpm we are finishing our injection roughly 331abs deg before the exhaust valve opens. This allows about 200abs for the compression and power strokes from int@.050 <mailto:int@.050> to exh@.050 <mailto:exh@.050>. This leaves the between values. They should be “feathered”, using the difference between stock values applied to your new values. (this has worked well for me) E303 Example w/ 3-14extra advance for more heat soak: Injector timing is about the accurate, delivery of fuel volume at the correct time, and there are many functions that could affect this. Injector Offset VS. Battery Voltage changes pulse width accuracy. This in turn affects your injector timing. Getting the injector timing right does affect you’re A/F Ratio’s. You will need to re-tune your MAF_Transfer function. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Tue Sep 06, 2005 11:31 pm What strategy are you running? Please add your engine specs to your signature, as stuff like this matters with the tweecer. Please add at least year, cid, induction (S/C, T/C, NA, etc), inj size, calibration code, tranny, etc. I doubt that there is controls in the eec to 'enable' secondary injectors. It would sure make your job easier, though. IMO, I think that your easiest method would to have a secondary injector controller that both sets of injectors were ran off of. The EEC's inj outputs would be inputs to the controller (not driving any injectors), and the controller would determine when to spray both sets, and how much PW each gets. I'm imagining setting up the EEC to see the total inj size of both sets. Say you are running 2 sets of 24's, then the inj slopes would be setup for 48lb-ers. Then at low PWs, the controller takes the outputted PW, and converts it into a PW for just one set, while the secondary are off. With the two 24 sets example, the controller would double the PW output to the primary set, for the given EEC PW output. Once that set gets to 80%DC (or whatever) (while the EEC is outputting say 40%), then clip that set to 80% and start sending PW to the secondary. Then the secondary set will build PW. Of course, you could add more complex logic so that when the primary set hits 80%, then on the next cycle, back the primary down to like 60%, so that you can hit the secondary with like 20%, to avoid small PW on the secondary. I've never heard of such a device existing.... posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Load scaling switch (scalars) Quote Post by boss96 » Wed Sep 07, 2005 11:59 am Many thanks to "RockinRick" from the forums! Bob This is my interpetation of the load scaling switch taken from the CRAI8 strategy document. Most likely this applies to all EEC-V, along with CBAZA. According to the GFUB strategy document, A9L (and such) use only switch values of 0 and 1.] LOADX (aka. perload "percent load") is a variable used to control air/fuel ratio and upstream air. The air/fuel ratio control includes: 1) stabilized open loop enrichment 2) MPG mode cruise enable and desired air/fuel 3) cold start enrichment. The calculation method of perload (LOADX) is determined by the scalar "Load Scaling Switch". The load scaling switch can be 1 of 3 values: 0) LOADX = (LOAD/'Sea Level Load scaling function') x (29.9/BP) LOADX is MAF-based, and is corrected for changes in ambient pressure. 1) LOADX = LOAD LOADX is MAF-based, is not a percent LOAD, but just a normalized air charge, and it is NOT corrected for changes in ambient pressure. 2) LOADX = pct_load (Percent inferred load) LOADX is NOT MAF-based, and is an ESTIMATE of load independent of the air meter. pct_load is determined from non-MAF based tables of load, generally produced from engine dynamometer tests. pct_load does not use bp in its calculation and is therefore immune to any inaccuracy in bp. pct_load has the characteristic of going to 1.0 at any altitude and any engine speed when maximum air flow is reached, thus indicating that the driver is demanding maximum torque. (This only happens when those tables are setup to match the engine. Stock tables will not work well with your modified engine!) MY TUNING SUGGESTIONS: Use Load Scaling Switch = 0 Why? You have the ability to 'scale' your LOADX (and thus tables) to the range given in the tables. Most likely, your combo will make more load than stock, and can benefit from scaling load to fit the given ranges. This is especially important for those that are using forced induction. For example, a stock engine may idle at about 20% load, but with your supercharger, your idle load may change. That will cause the EEC to use A/F values from incorrect locations in tables, and cause havoc. Scaling the load back down to 'stock' levels will improve your performance and driveability. With 'Load Scaling Switch = 1', you don't have that ability to 'scale' your LOADX (and thus tables) to the range given in the tables. Although it is possible to scale all the tables and such to fit LOAD, there are other items in the calibration that LOADX calculates, and they will then be off. And, since the 'Load scaling switch=2' method uses dyno produced tables to calculate load BASED ON THE STOCK ENGINE, your combo will have different load values than what the EEC is looking up. This is unless you reproduce those tables with your engine combo on a dyno. That may be difficult as those tables are not accessable in some strategys, like CBAZA. That nearly rules out this method. I also believe that this is the root cause of "problems" that T4M0 users have. posts.author: Whitehorse
posts.content: Whitehorse Regular Posts: 87 Joined: Fri Jan 14, 2005 9:30 pm Location: Maine Contact: Contact Whitehorse Website Quote Post by Whitehorse » Sun Sep 04, 2005 9:29 pm You are correct in your statement about the Cranking fuel vs time multiplier and the Accel pump multiplier global. Now, on the WOT fuel vs rpm multiplier, you want to use a # lower than 1 to increase fuel and higher than 1 to decrease fuel. Most guys use the MAF #'s to increase fuel, but if your pegging the MAF you can use this multiplier to get the extra fuel you need as long as you don't max the injectors. I used this method and it worked well for me. I've since used the MAF #'s to get the A/F I want. If you want to be 5% richer just put in .95 at the desired rpm and so on. What you can do as long as you run the stock FP, is multiply 12.35(which is the A/F in the Base OL table, at max load) by the multiplier. For example, 12.35x.95=11.7 A/F. You'll be suprised how well it works as long as the computer knows what you have for hardware. posts.content: 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Finally - 11.99!! Quote Post by 2Shaker » Thu Sep 08, 2005 10:36 pm We did it. The car ran a 11.99 and a 11.95 tonight along with a 12.03 and a 12.04. Our objective 3 years ago was to build a car that would look like an ordinary Mustang but run in the 11's, meet emissions, have all the creature comfort with a fairly quiet exhaust, and get reasonable gas mileage. We have now acheived it and it would not have been possible without TwEECer (or some chip) and EA. I love it when the ricers look at my car assuming it is just another Mustang that they will dust off with their little fart pipe equipped Japtalian special. Oh are they ever surprised :-) The first time we ran the car it went 16.19 at 83MPH. The AODE was in terrible shape and the motor had a ton of blowby. That was 3 years ago this month. It was a dog. But after a lot of money and fun, we have hit our objective. Probably one of the biggest discoveries I made this year is the OL Fuel Multiplier vs ACT. I have been fighting AFR's or 8:1 to 9:1 at the track all season. The stabilized fuel table has 11:44 in the high cells. Then last week I discovered that in T4M0 there is this function which begins to richen the AFR if the ACT is at 126* or higher. We have been logging ACT's well into the 150*-170* range. The simple answer was to ice the intercooler and we put a slightly smaller pulley on the blower because I now know my problem was not due to a bad MAF curve. We were rewarded with an 11.99 right off the bat. It is interesting to note that the J4J1 has this function set to 1. The T4M0 values seem logical as you would want to spray lots of fuel to cool the combustion chamber if the ACT were getting out of hand. Wonder why J4J1 is the way it is? 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. posts.content: 95BlackTan50 Regular Posts: 173 Joined: Tue Dec 02, 2003 5:53 pm Location: Johnson City Tennessee Quote Post by 95BlackTan50 » Tue Aug 30, 2005 9:27 am A couple of comments and questions. I noticed that you have a "built AOD" and you are using a modified J4J1 tune which is for a manual tranny. If the electronics of your AOD is like the AODE for the 94/95 Mustang then you may want to start with the W4H0 or U4P0 for a base tune and make the changes that you discussed. It's hard to say if the tranny parts of the tune would have any impact on your idle spike. You can always copy J4J1 tables and functions later. If your wideband is reading 16-17 and your KAMRF values are around 1 and your lambse values are cycling around 14.65 then you could have old O2 sensors giving you false readings. That's just a guess. Under what conditions do you see KAMRF values around 1.2? Is that still at idle? Are the two banks normally about the same? When the one bank is at 1.2, what is the other one at? I had some areas where I had a lean spike in my KAMRF vs PW plot. It turned out that my MAF curve was lean down at the lower voltage range that corresponded with idle MAF readings. I read my MAF voltage at idle and richened the MAF curve in that area and it pushed down the lean spike. If you have a big difference between the banks then changing the MAF will not make them any closer to each other. Just a general comment. Make small changes and don't change too many things at a time.
