posts.content: WA2FAST Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Wed Sep 29, 2004 1:04 pm Location: MI Contact: Contact WA2FAST Website AOL Quote Post by WA2FAST » Thu Nov 10, 2005 12:42 pm The startup table is simply a timer based on time vs ECT. Depending on what the ECT is (X axis), it will richen the mixture that ammount for that much time (Y axis). If you leave it alone with 42's, yeah it'll work, but you are dumping fuel for 45 seconds as opposed to metering the fuel properly. With an engine that has been sitting and no oil circulating, the last thing I want is cold startup with cylinder wash for 45 seconds. That table simply richens the fuel mixture to keep the engine running in OL while it warms up before it even thinks about going into CL. You can do what you want with it, but remember, that table is there regardless... your car doesn't just immediately start calculating A/F right off the bat even if it is warm... ever notice how the commanded a/f changes uniform durring it's startup cycle? That's what you are changing. If you don't lower that table, it is richening the fuel mixture based on a 19lb injector, not a 42. It'll run just fine, but when I changed mine, my car started right up and the warmup cycle for the first 45 seconds is now flawless... no idle hunting, no puking fuel out of the dumps, no chugging idle, no nothing... it's as smooth as can be. The car can not determine proper A/F when it's cold, so it doesn't try, it goes off of the crank functions as mentioned above to get it started, then goes off of base OL modified by many things, including this startup timer for the first 45 seconds. If that table is setup for 19's which it is from the factory obviously, you are dumping a TON of fuel at that point... when there is no oil anywhere and any and all oil that does get on the cyl wall is going to be washed off by the excess fuel... while the engine is cold... ouch! -Don- 87' GT, A9L, TwEECer RT, P1SC@12psi Non-Intercooled, AFM PP, 3" Pro-M#42, 70mm TB, GT-40 Intake, GT-40X Heads, B303, 1.6, BBK 1-5/8" Long Tubes, 306 Built Bottom End, Probe Block Girdle, TR3550, 3.55, PLX WB, Jan 07 Modified Mustangs Feature Car Top

If the EEC thinks the injector is bigger at low pulsewidths, it should cut back on calculated PW and minimize the excess fuel issue after startup. The Injector Offset vs Battery Voltage also comes into play here. The offset if a fixed abount of time (in mS) that the EEC adds to the pulsewidth to compensate for delays in the injector. This delay changes based on battery voltage (may be related to the solenoid reaction time). So the typical offset of about 1 at 12.5 volts adds 1 millisecond to the calculated pulsewidth - no matter what. You can see where this would affect fuel ratio if it was off significantly. At 5V battery, the offset function would add 7 mS to the pulsewidth! Anyway, I sure wish there were some fixed numbers for Cranking pulse multiplier, Injector Offset, Low Slope and breakpoint we could use for the extremely common FMS 42lb injectors so that we could then simply focus on tweaking the MAF function. :D Top

posts.content: ponyboy4737 Regular Posts: 86 Joined: Thu Apr 10, 2003 8:58 am Location: Chgo nw burbs Quote Post by ponyboy4737 » Mon Nov 28, 2005 10:57 pm I fixed y hot start problem. Here's my step by step approach and a log to back it up. To help others, I'll summarize what I did to fix it I learned some things about eec while doing this. Listen up. First, set payload to log batt volts ect act pw rpm mafv. Note your current baseline crank pw for both cold start and hot start. For first start in the morning after cooling all night, log startup. Note ect act and pw. When you review log, you'll notice crank pw is held constant until it fires. Let her warm up good and hot and note what your hot idle pw is. You will need this number. My hot idle pw was 2.2ms. That's the number you will be targeting when cranking hot. My theory is: if it idles at 2.2ms, it should start hot with a 2.2ms pw. Lot's of folks said change function crank_pw_mulitply_ect by factor of old inj/new inj for ect>150, 180, and 65534. I did that, however, the j4j1 resolution for over 150 and over ect would only allow 3 decimal places. It helped some, but did not fix it. My hot crank pw was 2.7434, still too rich. I then changed table crank pw vs act for temps 100 and 140 (top 2 rows of table). I multiplied stock values by 2.7/2.2. Presto. Hot crank pw went to 2.2 and she starts right up. Here's a hot start log. battv pw1 lambse1 rpm mafv ect act 12 0 14.64 0 0 188 120 9.5 2.2255 14.64 87 0.4448 188 120 9.875 2.2255 14.64 137 0.5181 188 120 10.5 2.2255 14.64 603.5 0.914 188 120 10.8125 2.4892 13.0944 1115.5 1.0606 188 120 <-pow. she fired. 11.25 2.2686 13.0944 1451.75 1.0704 188 120 12 2.0576 13.0944 1398.75 1.0802 188 120 12.625 1.9329 13.0944 1380.25 1.085 188 120 So, there's the proof. In logging many crank sequences I learned that the eec uses a constant crank pw until rpm > idle rpm. So all you need to do is tweec the function, or table, (or maf) or maybe inj offset vs batt until you get crank pw = idle pw. It worked magic for me. -ponyboy '95 Cobra, 331, J4J1, built AOD, Stallion 3000 stall, Kenne Bell Blowzilla Flowzilla, 42#, Aeromotive pump and rails, Edelbrock Performers, Comp Cams, 3.73, Cervini R hood, HPM control arms, Centerline wheels, Kicker, Alpine, MBQuart. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Wed Nov 30, 2005 4:56 pm DON'T set cid scalar to that value! Your combo does not warrant a change in the cid scalar. Setting it that high would basically prevent the eec from ever going to WOT and most likely its just a matter of time before you would melt pistons. I would make the changes to go with what your changing in the fuel system. MAF & injectors, so I would enter the maf transfer and injector scalars. Don't use caledit to convert your flow sheet. Use an excel sheet, the supplied Prom maf files or Eec Analizer to do the 10 to 30 pt conversion. Back to the cid scalar. By raising the value you reduce the load caculated by the eec and vice versa. For forced induction applications the CID scalar can be used to bring load down. posts.content: pthornton Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Sat Nov 01, 2003 5:11 pm Location: Tupelo, MS Quote Post by pthornton » Wed Nov 30, 2005 10:02 pm 19/30 * actual displacement The calibrated MAF is telling the computer lower air flow values than actual so the computer calculates a load value that is too low. Reducing the CID will up the load values calculated. Really a combination of two hacks. It is best to input the actual MAF, injector and cid scalar before making any serious changes as this hack will throw off any other changes you make. I'm not 100% familiar with the tweecer yet, but I understand the concept and am good with computers and math, so I should pick it up quickly. I will briefly describe the problem I am having, and what I want to get out of this is, is this a common problem that can be fixed by using the tweecer.. I want to avoid having a chip burned that has to be reflashed should I ever make a change and need a new tune. Ok, combo: 93 LX, 5 speed, stock computer that has never had a tune, 347, 10.9:1 TFS TW heads, unported TFS Track Heat intake, unported TFS Stage 2 cam, 1.6 RR, 70mm TB 75MM MAF, cal'd for 30lbers 30lb injectors 1 5/8 headers, 2.5 inch exh 3.73 gear Base timing is down to 12 degrees BTDC while I am having this problem, but TFS reccomends around 18deg BTDC.. The problem I am having is a little bit of detonation. It happens after the car is warm, and while I am lightly or even somewhat heavily rolling into the throttle below 2k RPM. Even just normally accelerating in say 4th gear at 40mph gives me some detonation. It gets "past" the detonation above 3k RPM and from there on out it seems fine. During normal driving, however, I am rarely above 3k RPM so you can see my dilemma. At WOT I do not hear any detonation, and I can give it a good amount of throttle at a fairly low RPM even in 3rd and 4th when the car is cold, and no detonation there either. I wasn't sure if this is because the parts hadn't heated up yet, or because it's still running a richer fuel curve at that point... When I go WOT it doesn't detonate, but the engine seems to "break up" around 4500+.. I don't really know exactly where to start with that part.. I don't want to throw ignition parts at it to try to fix that because I'm guessing it's the tune and not the ignition. I haven't been to a dyno yet. I want to get the tweecer before I do go to the dyno so I can make some adjustments there with the help of some friends who know more about it than I do. Based on what I've said, is this something that is commonly tuned out with a tweecer? I realize the compression ratio is high at almost 11:1, but plenty of people run that kind of compression ratio in Mustangs with no problem. From what little I've read so far, this may be because my tip-in settings are either too lean or there is too much timing there.. Thanks for any help! Please let me know if you need anymore information. Thanks, Chris www.lxcoupe.com Top

posts.author: Jack Hidley
posts.content: Jack Hidley Regular Posts: 64 Joined: Mon May 12, 2003 1:13 am Location: Danville CA USA Quote Post by Jack Hidley » Fri Dec 02, 2005 2:12 am Chris, This will be easy to fix with the Tweecer. Basically you have one main problem. The EEC is coming up with the incorrect engine load because there are things about the sensors and engine displacement it doesn't know about. Specifically the use of an MAF "calibrated" for 30lbs/hr injectors means that the EEC thinks the engine load is 19/30=63% of what it really is. At lower loads, the EEC is going to command more spark advance. This is why you are not getting detonation at WOT. Under WOT, the A9L goes to a nonload based function to determine timing. I don't know the specs on your camshaft, but the duration of it may be narrow enough that the 10.9:1 compression ratio is simply building too much cylinder pressure at low rpms. This is easy to compensate for in the various timing tables. If you do a search, you can find tons of information on the subject of inaccuarte load calculations from the EEC not having the correct MAF transfer function. Jack Hidley Maximum Motorsports Tech Support Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue Nov 22, 2005 6:14 pm You definitely need to go to one HEGO and not two. The two are fighting one another in the EEC. If bank one is rich and the EEC commands a leaner mixture then bank two will try to richen the mixture to compensate. You will end up going in circles. You have to eliminate the drivers side HEGO and set the port to 1 on all the injectors. You also need to make sure the HEGO is within 650 to 800 degrees F. Either side of these temp ranges will skew the EEC readings. Also make sure the HEGO is not mounted at the six o' clock range. It will get contaminated by moisture if it is. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: 88mustang
posts.content: 88mustang Gear Head Posts: 47 Joined: Mon Jun 21, 2004 4:25 pm Re: one more thing Quote Post by 88mustang » Tue Dec 06, 2005 12:10 pm Lethalride wrote: also could somebody explain injector offsets Vs Battery voltage?? At different battery voltages injectors open and close at different speeds. Because of this the amount of fuel delivered when your battery is putting out 10 volts will be less than the amount delivered when your battery is putting out 13 volts. This function tries to correct that by increacing/decreacing the pulse width accrodingly. Of course this change is not going to be very large but it is enough to make a difference. I also use 60lb injectors so I multiply each y value by 19/60 (or .316666). Some people think this works great others will say you don't need to change it. Dan I've done some research into these scalars and here is what I have determined (all this is based on the A9L and GUFB strategy. However, I took a quick peek and the CBAZA strategy has the same default values, so I will assume the meaning is the same for either strategy): Max High Speed Dwell (MINDLB) DWLTOT is clipped to this scalar value % of PIP period at low RPMs to prevent excess coil charge time. This value is a percent of dwell, not a millisecond value as CalEdit suggests. Used by the ignition timing strategy, page 7-25. Default value of 0.199997 (20 %) Definition of DWLTOT: (dwell turn-on time) is the time when the coil should start charging to allow sufficient charging time (DWLBSE) as well as time for maximum engine acceleration movement of PIP (PIPACL) and maximum change of requested spark advance allowed (6% of PIP) (SPTADV). Max Low Speed Dwell (MINDLA) DWLTOT is clipped to this scalar value % of PIP period at all times other than low RPM, to prevent excess coil charge time. This value is a percent of dwell, not a millisecond value as CalEdit suggests. Used by the ignition timing strategy, page 7-25. Default value of 0.5 (50 %) That is a bunch of mumbo-jumbo for saying that the percent of dwell time will never go outside the range between 20% and 50%. I really can not see any reason to change these values. The capitalized names are scalars which may or may not be available via CalEdit. Since these are percent values, I'd assume the range is 0 to 100. But, I've never changed them. Chris '93 EDIS 5.0L with A9L installed into a '77 Bronco. Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Aug 21, 2005 11:12 pm ADDED I believe that the purpose of this table is to account for the delay in the opening of the injector. When the injector driver turns on (grounds the injector) it takes a bit before the injector reacts. This has to do with electrical delays in the EEC, and mostly the resistance of the injector. It takes a bit of current to build in the windings of the coil in the injector before it can overcome the resistance of the spring in the injector that holds it closed. The lower the voltage is, the more time it takes before that injector will open. Thus, more adder is needed. I believe that this has been verified on an EEC-IV by someone with an oscilloscope in the past. The magnetic field needs to build in the windings, and that will always take some time, and that time has to be accounted for somewhere . If you set up the 'delay function' (this inj offset function) so that at normal voltages, the adder is = 0, then you MUST be adding in a delay factor somewhere else. Then the function could act as you describe, but yet the 'nominal voltage adder' is still there in either another calibration value, or hardcoded. I think that they just used this 1 function to allow ultimate flexibility. The PW adder from the 'inj offset vs vbat' function is not logged in the PW value, and is part of the total PW needed for the inj duty cycle calc. Calcon does not know what that function is or the PW value that gets added. IOW - logged PW is not total commanded PW. posts.content: wa_4x4builder Regular Posts: 106 Joined: Wed Mar 30, 2005 12:37 pm Location: Seattle, Washington Re: J4J1 rev limiter Quote Post by wa_4x4builder » Wed Nov 30, 2005 11:59 pm ninjzx998 wrote: I also read somewhere that there was another way to limit the revs using PIP count. Of course I can't find it now. I really want to set up a limiter without risking going lean. any suggestions or a link to the PIP method? GUFB.PDF wrote: The PIP filter ignores PIP transitions which occur at a higher rate than the maximum possible engine RPM. The maximum possible engine RPM is generally assumed to be the RPM at which the valves begin to "float". MNPIPn = 60 / (ENGCYL * "MAXRPM") * "Clock Freq" / 36 n = 4 for a 4-cylinder engine MNPIP4 = 1923 at 15 MHz n = 6 for a 6-cylinder engine MNPIP6 = 1282 at 15 MHz n = 8 for a 8-cylinder engine MNPIP8 = 961 at 15 MHz Note: MNPIP should correspond to an RPM which is greater than the speed at which the strategy turns off the fuel (speed limiter). The base values are equivalent to 6500 RPM. It is saying that any PIP transistion recognized sooner than 961 processor clock ticks will be ignored. Thus, it behaves like a rev-limiter. But, it clearly states you should allow the rev-limiter to do it's job. Like Rick, I would suggest studying the rev-limiter scalars (they can be a bit confusing) and use them instead. posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Sun Oct 09, 2005 4:36 pm I use a C&L 80mm w/36's & now 42's. Car runs like stock. All meters run differently depending on what is upstream from it (not just C&L) - stock airbox vs. cone filter, bend or no bend. People who don't understand how the meters work or use the wrong electronics bash C&L, but it's because they probably never called C&L for help. You have to be prepared to tweak the MAF transfer curve to make it work correctly. The curves you found on the EA homepage are for a MAF using the sensor from a 55mm meter. If you are using the sensor from a 70mm meter ('94-'95), you will need a different transfer function. Call C&L and tell them what you have, they will fax or email you the correct transfer function. EA has many curves in the software program (you can download it and install it to see the curves), but I didn't see one for a 73mm meter using the 70mm sensor ('94-'95 meter). On Edit, wouldn't you want to multiply by the ratio of meter diameters? I'd suggest using that logic to get to a decent starting point and then carefully take some datalogs & dial it in. The basic shape of the curve using the 70mm sensor will be similar from sample tube to sample tube. My only concern is that I was using the blue tube and I pegged my meter @ 5V when I added a Flowzilla & had 36# injectors. No matter how you slice it, the meter will still peg with a given tube and flow rate - so I switched to a red tube from a blue tube when I went to 42# injectors - the main reason being that my motor is now making more HP than the blue tube can support. Make sure your meter is not pegging. The main variable for me is that I'm using a cone filter in front of my C&L which forces a more air across the element (compared to bypass air) making it peg sooner - I have to use a curve 2-3 tubes leaner than the tube I'm using due to the cone filter - otherwise I was running WAY to rich after the adding the cone filter. I'm sure this reads a little confusing to you - think about it. Bottom line, I'm using very close to the basic "blue" sample tube MAF curve for my 80mm & 42's even though the meter actually has a red tube in in (three tubes bigger/leaner). This is due to the cone filter making the flow more uniform through the meter (I think). Anyway, you're approach will work fine - just get a curve in there that's somewhat close and run it until the EEC compensates for it (if it can) then adjust it 'till it's within 5% KAM's. The EEC on the other hand has a 5 volt limiting ciricut. The 5 volt ciricut has a few tenths of tollerance. If you have a MAF curve that only goes up to 5 volts and the EEC is reading 5.1 then it would be off the edge of the curve. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Mon Dec 12, 2005 7:00 pm In my investigations with my strategy, ALL functions as calibrated from Ford, have MIN possible as the lowest point, and MAX possible as the highest REGARDLESS of "typical" min and max values. Getting technical, the functions are stored in the eec in binary. The EEC and caledit converts the binary into a decimal range. Basically, if the function is 8 bit and positive values only, then the 'binary' range is 0-255. That function will have 0 as it's lowest point, and 255 as it's max. If the function is 16 bit and positive values only (like the MAF transfer), then the lowest value is 0 and the max is 65535. In the case of the MAF transfer, 65535 converts into 15.9998V. (FWIW - 65536 would = 16.0V, but 65536 is unattainable (it rolls over to 0), and thus the max can't be exactly 16V) I had an issue with not having my min set to 0. My min was set to 0.6V, and my maf would occasionally dip below that and it caused the car to stall as the function conversion routine got messed up. Perhaps there is an upper 'overflow' catch, but there isn't a lower (on my strategy anyway). Perhaps (with my strategy anyway) there isn't any coded 'catch' to detect these overflows, and the way to avoid the issue is to require all functions to have min and max set to min and max (as shown in my strategy).... I suggest always setting the min and max to min and max and avoid the potential problem. posts.author: Chris Mureen
posts.content: Chris Mureen Tuning Addict Posts: 443 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 6:44 pm Location: Austin, TX Quote Post by Chris Mureen » Fri Dec 09, 2005 5:54 pm If you have a 98 4v then none of the above advice applies unless you have a A9L. The first questions is correct, however: Where are you trying to advance timing? Are you looking to adjust the timing for regular driving, or WOT? If you have a OBDII computer then: There is a global scalar adder for adding timing across the board in all conditions. However, there is no WOT timing table. There are 3 table categories, Boarderline, Base, and MBT. Multiple table roll into these categories and the EEC picks the lowest net timing to use. If you add timing to any one table it won't likely be used becuase the net timing will be higher. You need to make any timing increases to all tables to make sure they take. This can obviously be fairly complex for the new user. With my 4v I sometimes make my changes uniformally to the 3 IMRC tables to simplify things. posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Sun Dec 18, 2005 4:13 pm "Can you guys give me link to a good write up on how to tune the maf transfer curve?" I like to use lambse to help dial in the maf. Lambse with no KAMRF build up is a pretty good indicator of whats going on. It should be between 12~15 depending on driving conditions. If you see lambse over 15 mostly, your tune is RICH and its LEAN if your under 12. But this is just a general guideline. As KAMRFs build up, lambse (commanded afr) stabilizes. Ideally, you should have lambse equal the wideband reading or very close to it. By looking at lambse, I don't have to wait for KAMRFs to build to get the maf close. Just a min clamp value - so if calculated PW is > min PW scalar, then commanded PW = calculated PW, but if calculated PW < min PW scalar, then commanded PW = min PW scalar. However, fuel shutoff on decel mode doesn't use this, and in that condition PW = 0 (less than the min). posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Fri Dec 16, 2005 8:05 pm Ah right, I understand it now. KAMRF isn't your MAF curve, it's the adaptive fuel trim correction stored in the KAM. By lowering your MIN_INJECTOR_PULSEWIDTH the calculated pw is less than is required for a stoichiometric AF ratio at idle and therefore the hego feedback is signalling that the AF ratio is lean and this results in your KAMRF value being increased to compensate. Top

posts.author: craig429
posts.content: craig429 Regular Posts: 113 Joined: Thu Aug 14, 2003 9:58 am Location: Oregon Contact: Contact craig429 Website Quote Post by craig429 » Mon Dec 19, 2005 2:21 pm You don't want the Minimum injector pulsewidth to be used and therefore effect KAMRF's, It was more for a safe guard. I selected .0003 Seconds for use with 42# injectors. During deceleration, the EEC would command the lowest injector pulse widths. The problem you had was that the Mininum injector pulsewidth clamp value was reached even though the EEC calculated a lower PW using the current MAF curve so it had to command the higher Mininum pulsewidth value to the injector. Therefore the lower part of the curve was not really being used. Now when you lowered the Mininum injector pulse width, the EEC is now able to command a lower injector pulse width as determined by the MAF curve but the current MAF curve was lean in the lower values so the KAMRF have to compensate by being larger to keep the AFR at 14.7. The MAF curve was actually being used. 1994 Yellow Mustang GT. Griggs GR40. Tweecer RT, LC-1, T4M0 w/J4J1 tune. Cartech Outlaw Turbo. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Wed Nov 30, 2005 12:40 pm Or do what I did - burn 3 pistons (see my "good news..." post in Lounge area of this board). We have a Procharger and I thought we would hear the detonation because we run with closed exhaust. Wrong. We also have a wideband and it was indicating an AFR of 10.5-11.0:1 in the lights so it seemed rich enough. Our problem is probably due to too much timing at 32* at 12# boost. I thought we were getting away with that. Also wrong! I see you are running J4J1. Watch out for the function "open_loop_fuel_multiplier vs ACT" because in J4J1 this is set to = 1 (doesn't do anything). In the W4H0 calibration that I have it deliberately richens the mixture at fairly low ACT's (starting at 116 degrees) to cool the incoming charge with more fuel. I had also changed this to be like J4J1 and although the wideband said we were quite rich I am going to restore this function to its original values. I think J4J1 is wrong. By the way, we were seeing ACT's at 85* on launch (ambient) and 175*+ in the lights! Get a wideband and keep your maximum advance to something like 20* - 24*, add an intercooler if you don't have one, consider water injection, and make sure your MAF curve is right and the injectors are big enough. 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Sat Dec 24, 2005 9:44 am 50mikey, Welcome. You have a pretty steep learning curve but in the end I think you will discover you made the right decision. Getting started is tough, but there is a tremendous amount of help on this site, especially for the A9* series that you have. Look for some of the other posts on this board that have "New" (or "newbie") in the title and you will find others who came before you who got good advice for begginers. BE SURE you are looking at advice for your EEC strategy and calibration!!! Start with your scalars. The very first thing I did was set the idle. Doing this will give you a feel for using the TwEECer as well. Set your injector slopes and CID. You will probably then want to input your MAF curve and perhaps change the crank and startup fuel tables/functions. Keep in mind the TwEECer software has its share of quirks (bugs? :-)) and you will need to learn these too. Perhaps the most annoying is when you want to change values in a cell, say for the MAF curve. You need to step into the cell with your keyboard arrows, make the change, and step out of the cell with the arrow to make it really changed. And do a few changes then, save with a new file name, then exit TwEECer and reenter. Make sure when you reenter TwEECer that you open the new file name as TwEECer reverts to the last file name it opened. It took me a while to catch this. Hope this helped some. 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. posts.author: 88mustang
posts.content: 88mustang Gear Head Posts: 47 Joined: Mon Jun 21, 2004 4:25 pm Quote Post by 88mustang » Mon Dec 05, 2005 8:07 pm There are a few ways to do this, this is what worked well for me using an A9L computer. 1. Dial in your Maf curve. (You must be able to datalog with a wide band O2 sensor to use this method.) Turn off closed loop and adaptive then clear your KAM's. Drive around datalogging Lambse and AFR at various loads and RPM's. Put these two logged values on a chart and make changes to the MAF curve until these two values are the same or at least close(EEC Analyzer helps out greatly doing this). Here is an example 2. Depending on how modified our car is you may need to rescale you load values using the Sealevel load scaling vs.RPM function. This keeps your cars load levels within the the Fuel Table - Base OL. 3. Using the Fuel Table - Base OL set the AFR you want to achieve at the different load levels. 4. You can now turn closed loop and adaptive back on if you want but know if you do this the computer will switch to the closed loop table during closed loop operation. I run open loop all the time because of my turbo setup (I want to keep it kind of rich) and it works great for me. 88 Mustang GT, AOD, A9L, 427 stroker (8:1), HP 66mm Turbo Kit, PMAS Pro Tube, 75mm Throttle Body, TrickFlow 90mm Intake, Ported TrickFlow Twisted Wedge Heads, 60lb Injectors, 3" Exhaust, 3.27 Gears, 31 Spline Axels Top

posts.author: 88mustang
posts.content: 88mustang Gear Head Posts: 47 Joined: Mon Jun 21, 2004 4:25 pm Quote Post by 88mustang » Tue Dec 06, 2005 11:43 am Sorry I can't help you with the Zeitronix wideband. Until you can datalog your wideband I would suggest dialing in your MAF using Kamrf's (you can still use EA). I have not used this method so I will not try to tell you how to do it. Read the help file under the MAF tab in EA. You can also search this site for setting idle help, there is plenty of information on this subject. Now to answer your question. You said it runs fine at higher RPMs so deal with the lower part of the curve first so you can drive your car without getting frustrated. You are more likely to do damage when going lean at high RPM's than at idle, so you want to tune the upper portion of your MAF curve with your wideband. Every time you change your MAF curve remember to clear your KAM's. Still keep an eye on the wideband. I am still working on my idle so I am by no means an expert. I hope this helps. posts.author: runner
posts.content: runner Gear Head Posts: 7 Joined: Mon May 03, 2004 9:19 pm Quote Post by runner » Sun Dec 25, 2005 12:19 am To expand more about setting the TPS: All 5.0 EEC-IV's use the "turn-on" voltage of the TPS as a base voltage - consider this voltage "Relative Zero". The EEC-IV's+ have diagnostics to make sure that the sensors "make sense". For the TPS, those voltages are roughly 0.6v and 1.1v at start-up, and ~4.9v max. But, you can not just set the TPS voltage near a limit and expect everything to be okay. The EEC supplies the +5V to the sensors. That voltage can vary by ~2.5%. Also, all resisters have some sort of temperature coefficient. That means that the resistance changes with temperature. Also, you have the contraction/expansion of the TB-tab going into the TPS. Also, you have expansion/contraction of the TPS body. Also, you have the uncertainty of the EEC A/D convertor (Approx equal to a few counts). Also... well, you get the point. :) Those are just some of the factors that go into a proper analysis of a sensor and it's "meaning". For stock OEM TB and TPS, it "should be" plug-and-play. But, change the idle setting, use a non-Ford TB , and you must to check the TPS idle voltage and you may have to elongate the TPS mounting holes. Thankfully, the TPS is not a "super" critical sensor (like the MAF and the O2's are). The "main" use, IMHO, of the TPS is rate of change to "estimate" the proper injector pulse width for the desired A/F. The O2 sensors and MAF are "very slow". Probst gives a basic explanation and insight into the how the EEC-IV uses those sensors. So... what about the urban legend of setting the TPS to ~0.95V?? That's easy. :) Many people adjust the idle screw and/or change the TB. Many aftermarket TB's "may" not allow a plug-and-play with the TPS. There are a "few" low-quality 5.0 parts suppliers that supply, IMHO, junk with very low quality and very loose "specs". So, once again, if you use a non-Ford TB, or adjust the idle screw, you must check the TPS idle voltage. But, for a "100% stock" parts that meet all of the Ford Specs, the (Ford) TPS "should be" plug-and-play. Top

posts.author: Ryan Bailey
posts.content: Ryan Bailey Regular Posts: 174 Joined: Sat Oct 19, 2002 10:59 am Location: OH Quote Post by Ryan Bailey » Sun Dec 25, 2005 8:28 pm 2.02 valves in a stock angle head wont clear with most cams. They will clear with NON "inline" heads such as trick flow. The valves in trick flow heads are angled differently to allow it to work with stock pistons. The problem is with the valve diameter. You have a 2.02 valve trying to go into a smaller stock "eyebrow" relief in the stock piston. What you need to do is just call Isky racing cams and order the piston notching tool. I used this tool when switching to AFR 185 heads. You can rent the tool for around $65.00. You will also need a valve spring compressor or a bare head to use the tool in. The tool is basically a big valve that fits into a head with a cutting bottom on it. You install it in the head and set the head on the block. Then just get a ratchet and start turning until it stops cutting. The tool is designed so that it will only cut a larger diameter eyebrow, but wont cut any deeper than the original relief. title: ISC tuning tip - EECTuning.org

posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL ISC tuning tip Quote Post by boss96 » Wed Dec 28, 2005 9:07 pm Thanks to Randy (PThornton) for the following . Disconnect the ISC and let the car idle. Set the throttle body screw so that the car will just barely idle. Set the TPS to ~0.99. Now datalog the car for about 30 seconds after it is fully warmed up. Average the airflow and convert it to the correct units for the throttle body airflow. Set the throttle body airflow. Now reconnect the ISC and datalog the car at several different RPM points for at least 30 seconds. Set the idle RPM to do this. Average the numbers for RPM and airflow and set the X & Y values in the ISC nuetral airflow function. You will probably have to change the X values to match the RPM values you average from the datalog as it will not match what you set the idle to. This step is if you have problems with stalls on pushing in the clutch on coast down. Compare the new ISC settings to the old settings and figure out what percentage increase you have. For me this was the exact same percentage for all Y values in the function. Increase the dashpot pre-postion by the same percentage. air flow conversion factor is: MAF * 2.2046226 / 60 _________________ 96 GT, Vortech Si trim,Procharger 3 core intercooler, forged bottom end, MAC longtubes, ported PI heads , Edelbrock intake, Crower cams-.580lift/234dur@.050, 80lb injectors, CDAN4/GGL4 processor. title: tuning idle air settings - EECTuning.org

posts.author: pthornton
posts.content: pthornton Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Sat Nov 01, 2003 5:11 pm Location: Tupelo, MS tuning idle air settings Quote Post by pthornton » Wed Dec 28, 2005 5:42 pm Disconnect the ISC and let the car idle. Set the throttle body screw so that the car will just barely idle. Set the TPS to ~0.99. Now datalog the car for about 30 seconds after it is fully warmed up. Average the airflow and convert it to the correct units for the throttle body airflow. Set the throttle body airflow. Now reconnect the ISC and datalog the car at several different RPM points for at least 30 seconds. Set the idle RPM to do this. Average the numbers for RPM and airflow and set the X & Y values in the ISC nuetral airflow function. You will probably have to change the X values to match the RPM values you average from the datalog as it will not match what you set the idle to. This step is if you have problems with stalls on pushing in the clutch on coast down. Compare the new ISC settings to the old settings and figure out what percentage increase you have. For me this was the exact same percentage for all Y values in the function. Increase the dashpot pre-postion by the same percentage. air flow conversion factor is: MAF * 2.2046226 / 60 Cobra Intake / AFR 165 Heads CompCams 270H Camshaft 1989 Saleen Coupe # 653 ***** Top

posts.author: sstock1
posts.content: sstock1 Gear Head Posts: 47 Joined: Thu Mar 11, 2004 10:34 pm Location: gig harbor,Wa Quote Post by sstock1 » Mon Jan 02, 2006 2:11 pm There are quite a few of us that run tweecers with SD EEC's. It was once said that SD was useless when making power upgrades. I think time has told that this story was incorrect. There are many of us running deep into the 11's with 4500 lb trucks with decent size power adders. Visit the nloc.net there is some stuff on tweecer tuning. Your right cam choice is huge. Many of us run the mustang HO cam. The cam you are wanting to use is still too much overlap to be properly tuned with SD, IMHO. Stick with 114 lobe separation angles or greater, and definately stay in the 215 degree intake duration or smaller. It is the overlap that kills the idle vacuum that is the concern, you really want 15-16" minimum or the MAP will start to drop fuel causing rich idle/part throttle and drivability issues that will wear you out. Steve Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Wed Jan 04, 2006 8:16 pm OK people, class is in session FN389 CALIBRATION 1. Plot fuel flow per pulsewidth as a function of Pulsewidth at various battery voltage. (see Fuel Mass versus Fuel Pulsewidth figure on next page) 2. Make a table of fuel flow breakpoints, at which the injector slope changes. NOTE: The breakpoint is the FUELFLOW -- not the pulsewidth. 3. Convert the breakpoints into FN389-y parameters. FN389 y-value = BREAKPOINT * NUMOUT*INJOUT/PIPOUT * ENGCYL The BREAKPOINT is equal to the fuel flow at which the injector slope changes for the corresponding battery voltage, lb/pulsewidth. For example, the injectors used on a 5.0L engine have two slopes. These slopes intercept at 3.0 mg/pw at VBAT = 13.5V. Thus, FN389 = 3.0/1000*lb/454g*(8*1/8 )*4 = 2.64*10E-5 lb/rev. NOTE: FN367 breakpoints may require recalibration. Calibration Constants: - AHISL = High fuel flow injector slope (lb/sec). - ALOSL = Low fuel flow injector slope (lb/sec). - ENGCYL = Number of cylinders per engine revolution. - FN306(CRKTMR) = Cranking fuel pulsewidth as a function of time in crank. - FN348(ECT) = Crank fuel pulsewidth as a function of ECT. - FN367(VBAT) = Injector offset as a function of VBAT. - FN387(ECT) = Fuel pulsewidth muliplier as a function of ECT. - FN389(VBAT) = Dual slope injector breakpoint. Input = VBAT, volts and Output = lb/rev. - INJOUT = Number of injectors fired by each output port. - MTCF = Milliseconds to clock ticks conversion factor. - NLMT = Overspeed RPM. - NLMTH = Hysteresis for overspeed RPM. - NUMOUT = Number of injector output ports. - PIPOUT = Number of PIP's between injector outputs on each injector port. 428w now Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri Jan 06, 2006 1:58 am It is not as bad as it looks. Use it as a fine tuning tool for the lower end of the MAF. This value is really going to depend on the MAF that you are using. For example the 03 Cobra MAF and the 02+ Lightning MAF are supposed to be the same. They are when it comes to physical size. They are even the same part number, but if you look at the curves for both they are different. The 02 lightning is richer all the way threw. Since I have one of these MAFs, I decided to do a little test the other day. By only changing the MAF curve, my KAMRFs started to swing a small amount at an idle. The breakpoint allowed me to bring the KAMRF's back in. On the 03 Cobra MAF curve I had my breakpoint set to 2.0 On the 02 Lightning MAF curve I had my breakpoint set to 0.5 In cal edit these values are entered in as floating point number but what it does not tell you is that Cal Edit converts that number into engineering notation. Cal Edit will tack on a e-5. So if you enter in a 2.0, this will be converted to 0.000020 when it gets downloaded to the EEC. With the 03 Cobra MAF my car ran real lean at the upper end. The only way to fix that was either offsets or slope adjustments. I'm not sure why Ford has teo different curves for the same meter. It could have something to do with the TB and Supper chargers on these vehicles. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: igotbit
posts.content: igotbit Regular Posts: 79 Joined: Sat Jun 21, 2003 9:44 pm Quote Post by igotbit » Sun Jan 01, 2006 11:33 pm I hate to say this but yes I had too much HP with the SC in a light weight car. It was dangerous when the tires got wet.. You should be fine with 42 lb injectors with a stock engine. I would ditch the FMU if you can. It is very hard to tune, lean one second then rich another. I actually ran 60 lb injectors no FMU but I have more cubes. LMAF should work with your ECM. Was it difficult to smog your FFR in CO? I am from Arvada and may move back someday.. edit - I used the 90mm LMAF maf curve and tuned the curve from there.. still using the 60 lb injectors.. you might not need to adjust the curve since you have 42s and the LMAF was designed for 42s. T76coupe- The extender works good with a9l. The a9l can only read 0-5 volts. The maf can actually put out 0-7 volts. (7 being on the high side) The extender rescales the maf output for 0-5 volts even though it recieves a 0-7 volt input. There are four different settings that reduce the low end output to the a9l. Each setting is used for more airflow. I had mine set on the second dip-switch setting which gave me plenty of room for an LMAF curve with ~550 rwhp.. the last two settings make it hard to tune on the low end/idle side of the maf curve. In short, you wire in the extender, pick the switch that closest to the airflow you think you have (carefully, slowly so you don't blow your engine) tune your maf curve like you would normally do. Then adjust all of the other things maf curve dependent.. WOT fuel mult. vs. rpm etc... makesure to wire it in by the ecm.. it doesn't like the engine bay heat.. I have a mafxtender that I am not using anymore... $50 and it yours.. DB Last edited by igotbit on Mon Jan 02, 2006 12:18 am, edited 1 time in total. 351W, A9L, TF intake, AFR 185s, 75mm TB, NA. Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sat Jan 07, 2006 4:50 pm Oops, forgot there's no MIN_INJECTOR_PULSEWIDTH on A9L. If your ProM calibration sheet is a true air flow sheet then you need to set the injector high slope to the actual size of the injectors to get the fuel calculations right. Any WOT A/F ratios will then be out because you are going off the top of the tables due to your setup producing more than 100% load now, you will need to rescale the tables to match your peak load (spark tables will also be off). If you don't want all the work this entails then you will need a different MAF transfer table to 'fool' the ecu (not my preference for tuning). At the rpm range you are looking at I think you can ignore the breakpoint for now. Top

posts.author: 88mustang
posts.content: 88mustang Gear Head Posts: 47 Joined: Mon Jun 21, 2004 4:25 pm Quote Post by 88mustang » Sun Jan 08, 2006 1:18 am You can change all the variables in the computer. The problem with the MAF is all the computer sees is a voltage between 0 - 5 volts. The electronics in the meter itself are calibrated to send out a certian voltage for a given amount of air. Once you go over that amount of air the meter will continue to output 5 volts no matter how much air passes through it. That is why it is ok to have a meter that is too large for your combo but not to small. There are some programs that help you choose the correct injectors for your application. These are not exact just guide lines. I am sure someone here will say they made more horsepower than I say with a certian injector, but this is what I found. These numbers are NA. Boosted applications require more injector. 24lbs injectors 300 - 325 hp 36lbs injectors 400 - 450 hp 42lbs injectors 500 - 550 hp So decide how much hp you plan on making and go from there If you already have the 24lbs injectors and the MAF cal'ed for 36lb'ers try them out before you buy anything else. With the TwEECer you can make this work (remember more meter than injector is ok). 88 Mustang GT, AOD, A9L, 427 stroker (8:1), HP 66mm Turbo Kit, PMAS Pro Tube, 75mm Throttle Body, TrickFlow 90mm Intake, Ported TrickFlow Twisted Wedge Heads, 60lb Injectors, 3" Exhaust, 3.27 Gears, 31 Spline Axels Top

posts.author: nate
posts.content: nate Gear Head Posts: 17 Joined: Thu Aug 11, 2005 8:19 am Location: so-cal Possible twEECer glitch with Kodak camera software Quote Post by nate » Sun Jan 08, 2006 3:02 pm Since my last write to the tweecer approx a week ago, my car has been pining like crazy. I finally did a data log and found the ign timing fixed at 47* except when at idle. This only happened on my latest tune. I saved a previous good tune in a different position of the tweecer. Now I have two positions with the timing fixed at 47*. Approx 2 weeks ago I installed Kodaks easy share camera software on my computer. Thinking maybe this was causing a problem I exited the kodak software, saved my latest tune, and it now works correctly. My guess is that the kodak software keeps looking on the USB port to see if the camera is plugged in and this somehow is causing a conflict with the tweecer during tweeker writing. I'm afraid to try to verify this by saving again while the kodak software is running in the background... I dont want to somehow corrupt the tweecker. Just thought I'd pass this info on in case anyone else is having similar issues. posts.author: runner
posts.content: runner Gear Head Posts: 7 Joined: Mon May 03, 2004 9:19 pm Re: Possible twEECer glitch with Kodak camera software Quote Post by runner » Tue Jan 10, 2006 4:01 am nate wrote: My guess is that the kodak software keeps looking on the USB port to see if the camera is plugged in and this somehow is causing a conflict with the tweecer during tweeker writing. I've heard other say bad thing about the Kodak software. I don't have Kodak camera, so I can't say first hand. To simplify things a lot , the way USB is "suppose" to work is that when you plug in a USB device, the OS (windows) scans the device, gets an ID/type, and then sees if there is a driver for that ID/type. But, if the Kodak driver starts up with the boot-up, it may scan USB ports because of the way the software is written. Who cares if it violates the "USB spec". :) Wouldn't be the first or last time that a driver violates standards. The Kodak software may be installing a version of a Windows file (DLL) that isn't compatible with a some software. Regardless, I would leave the Kodak software off. :) Top

This means that you need to scale your load based tables to suit your maximum load. If Ford saw fit to do it this way it might be the best way to tune a forced induction car as some tables use only LOAD and adjusting the LOAD_SCALING_SEALEVEL_TABLE will mean that these tables are way off if left untouched. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Mon Jan 09, 2006 7:24 pm RPM and LOAD are correct for the axes of the ECT & ECT retard tables. The scaling for the axes is done using the hi byte only of the two. For example, in my ecu you get the following for the caculation of the borderline spark: BORDERLINE_SPARK = (SPARK_BORDERLINE_TABLE * 64) + (SPARK_BDLN_TEMP_LOAD_INCREASE * SPARK_BDLN_LUGGING_TIMER / 2) + (SPARK_BDLN_ADD_AF_RATIO * 32) + (SPARK_BDLN_ADDER_EGR * EGR_PERCENTAGE) + (SPARK_BDLN_RETARD_ECT_TABLE * SPARK_RETARD_ECT_MULTIPLIER / 2) + (SPARK_BDLN_RETARD_ACT_TABLE * SPARK_RETARD_ACT_MULTIPLIER / 2) + (SPARK_BDLN_ADDER_MAP * 32) + SPARK_BDLN_ADDER_OCTANE_JUMPER The T4M0 code is identical except for the octane jumper spark adder, in mine this varies according to rpm, in T4M0 it's fixed regardless of rpm. Hope this helps. Edit: changed this slightly, first value is * by 64 and not 6 as originally posted, the tables are the retard tables and the function the multiplier Last edited by sailorbob on Sat Jan 14, 2006 4:23 pm, edited 3 times in total. Top

posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Tue Jan 10, 2006 8:19 am Under functions in my strategy there are tables for "spark for act" and "ect" which show how much spark to reduce according to rising temps. The multiplier tables you talked about are just that-multipliers against the function tables to arrive at particular spark reduction according to rpm/load. For example, if you are asking for 6 degrees of spark retard at an act temp of 150 you would look to see what the multiplier is at a certain rpm/load value. Lets say the multiplier is .5 at 4k rpm and .8 load. Then your total spark retard would be 3 degrees. A multiplier of "1" would be 6 degrees, etc. Bob 96 GT, Vortech Si trim,Procharger 3 core intercooler, forged bottom end, MAC longtubes, ported PI heads , Edelbrock intake, Crower cams-.580lift/234dur@.050, 80lb injectors, CDAN4/GGL4 processor. posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Mon Oct 10, 2005 10:32 am You generally want your load at idle to be around 20%, etc. Why? Because all of the fuel and spark tables use load to determine what amount of spark/fuel to use. It is possible to have a recalibrated maf and then see your load at idle too high, like 50% or what ever. Once you start accerating you will find yourself seeing even higher load values and therefore the wrong fuel/spark values being applied during part throttle. You can adjust this with a function called "sea level load scaling" where you input a load value"range" for various rpms. At idle you may put a value of .8, at higher rpms (since you have a supercharger) you will , as rpms increase, input values like 1.2 and higher. This will allow the eec to target the correct fuel/spark values for the loads your engine will actually see during operation. posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Mon Oct 10, 2005 10:09 pm 86GT wrote: The tables alway use LOADX not mater what the load scalar is set to. Yes. For clairity, the tables ALWAYS use LOADX, but if load scaling switch = 0, then when the EEC calcs LOAD and LOADX, it takes LOAD and processes it through the sea level load scaling function to determine LOADX. Then this value ends up getting used in the tables. If load scaling switch = 1, then when the eec calcs LOAD and LOADX, it sets LOADX = LOAD. Then when the tables use LOADX in their calcs, it really is, in effect, LOAD. FWIW - For the most part (mainly the important ones), this can be the assumed operation. However, some calcs (and tables) are based on LOAD regardless of the load scaling switch. Some use LOADX (and then can be modified by the sea level load scaling swtich, if set to '0'), some use LOAD, and thus the sea level load scaling function doesn't get a chance to be applied. I have not taken the time to catalog these, and I'm sure there are some variances between strategys as to what uses what. 86GT wrote: The load scalar sets LOADX= LOAD if the scalar is set to 2. I don't believe this to be true. This is how load scaling switch = 1 works, but load scaling switch = 2 sets LOADX = pct_load (Percent inferred load) (according to CRAI8 strat doc). I don't believe that load scaling switch = 2 is an option with GFUB (A9L). GFUB strategy doc only lists 0 and 1 as options. pct_load is NOT MAF-based, and is an ESTIMATE of load independent of the air meter. pct_load is determined from non-MAF based tables of load, generally produced from engine dynamometer tests. pct_load does not use bp in its calculation and is therefore immune to any inaccuracy in bp. pct_load has the characteristic of going to 1.0 at any altitude and any engine speed when maximum air flow is reached, thus indicating that the driver is demanding maximum torque. (This only happens when those tables are setup to match the engine. Stock tables will not work well with your modified engine!) (IMO, I also believe that this is why T4M0 (with it's load scaling switch = 2) is "unfriendly". LOADX is always being calculated from mapped load data, while your modded engine produces different load.) I did a little FAQ about this.... viewtopic.php?t=5400 Also, FWIW - (according to CRAI8 strat doc) even with load scaling switch = 1 or 2, the sea level load scaling function is used for some ISC calcs. Perload_isc is another load variable that gets calculated like load scaling switch = 0 causes LOADX to get calculated, regardless of load scaling switch. For instance, the ISC transfer table uses perload_isc, not LOADX or LOAD in it's table. There are also a few other ISC functions that use perload_isc, but are really not that essential. Again, FWIW.... 2Shaker wrote: 6. Setting the Load SW scalar to 0 causes the EEC to use LoadX with the tables, while a setting of 2 causes the EEC to ignore the "sea level load scaling" function and use the basic load values computed by the EEC at any given instance. It ignores the sea level load scaling function (except for the above mentioned ISC stuff) and uses mapped (pre calibrated) load data. It determines LOADX from pct_load which is from a table based on RPM vs throttle position. This table's load values are what the stock engine produced when the calibration was made on a dyno. It does not use the MAF to determine LOAD. IMO, I don't think the load scaling switch should be set = 2, unless you remapped those tables. I don't believe that those tables are tweecer avaliable... posts.author: 95BlackTan50
posts.content: 95BlackTan50 Regular Posts: 173 Joined: Tue Dec 02, 2003 5:53 pm Location: Johnson City Tennessee Quote Post by 95BlackTan50 » Mon Jan 30, 2006 4:38 pm There are three switches on the clutch pedals for the 94/95. Two of them are closed when the pedal is depressed and one of them is closed then the clutch pedal is not depressed. This third one is separate from the other two and has it's own short wire harness while the other two are hard mounted to the pedal. The single one is for the cruise control. If you are cruising, the switch is closed. when you step on the clutch, the cruise control will be disabled. There are two connectors under the dash that have jumper plugs in them. One of these plugs shorts out the cruise control switch and the other shorts out the other two switches ("crank safety" and "neutral detent"). For the one that goes to the cruise control, remove the jumper plug and plug the connector into the pedal connector. The other jumper that shorts out the two switches gets pulled out but there are two other empty connectors that get plugged into the pedal assembly. I haven't looked at the spark since I've converted over to the 5 speed, but from what I understand, the timing is retarded for the manual as well as the automatic. 95 GT Vert, 76 mm C&L, 24 lb Injectors, Performer 50 Intake, 65 mm FRP TB, Ceramic Coated FRP Shortie Headers, TwEECer RT 1.30A9, W4H0, Adj. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sun Jan 29, 2006 4:22 am The Stabilised Fuel table is used during open loop after ECT is up to temp and the WARM_HEGO_FLAG = 1. The Base Fuel table is used during open loop when ECT is low and the WARM_HEGO_FLAG = 0 The Startup Fuel table is subtracted from Base Fuel table for start up enrichment (stock setting is for up to the first 45 seconds of running). Hope this makes sense. Top

I adjusted my MAF every way possible, all it did was mess up my KAMRF's big time under normal conditions. I think maybe the issue has to do with the breakpoint of these injectors not being well understood by anyone. One thing's for sure, if I compensated for the lugging in my MAF, the tune would otherwise get all f'ed up. I decided to treat this is a special case and just have the loop go open just a bit sooner than the stock settings - made all the sense in the world after I did it as the car runs perfectly now. I've found that the trick is knowing when to pay attention to lambse and KAMRF and what is normal behavior for them. As for the injector breakpoint, i'm using the stock values in the A9P processor and have a very well working and drivable tune now. The calculated load also has a big impact on drivability. Even if your maf transfer is dead on (along with injector slopes, etc), if load% is not right then you wont' have good drivability or fuel milage. All of the above must work together. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Thu Feb 02, 2006 3:59 pm The manifold_volume value is for the volume of air between the MAF and the intake valve. It's to allow the ecu to compensate for unmeasured (at the time) air, two conditions cause this; Firstly closing throttle, i.e. when you come off the throttle from WOT, the air passing through the MAF becomes virtually nil but there is still a large amount of air behind the MAF that has yet to be drawn into the engine. If the ecu fuelled for the measured air you would end up with a very lean mix for a few revolutions so it uses this figure to compensate. Secondly opening throttle, i.e. going from a light cruise to WOT, the amount of air behind the MAF is very small (high vacuum) but the MAF measures a lot of air starting to rush in. The opposite of the first condition applies and you would get a very rich mixture for a few revolutions until the things stabilise. I've used extreme throttle changes as examples but it still occurs at lesser degrees of throttle change. Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Mon Feb 06, 2006 11:50 pm You need to start with a MAF curve that you think is close. Enter that into both the EA and the Tweecer. Then go run a datalog. Then run the EA on that datalog and find out which way you need to move the flow curve. You may have to start with richining or leaning the entire curve to get it close. After the adjustment you will need to reset the KAMRF's by disconnecting the battery or downloading an invlaid bin. it is up to you. Then what ever changes you made to the maf will need to be updated to the tweecer and EA for the next calculation. Just keep repeating the above until the MAF is close. You can then fine tune individule points. The light would go off while cruising and come back on at idle. Great. :mad: So I hooked up the notebook to the TwEECer and kicked off CalCon. It didn't take too long to notice that the Throttle Status (TS) was "part", even though the Throttle Position (TP) voltage was .880 and I had my foot off the gas. The TS should be "closed" under those conditions, not "part". So I pulled over, popped the hood and checked the throttle. Sure enough, it wouldn't close all the way, because the cruise control (CC) cable was (is) either too short or the CC motor is not disengaging completely or something. After disconnecting the cruise control cable, the CEL went away and now the idle is actually where I have been trying to get it all along, about 750. The TP voltage is now .822 at closed throttle and the TS is "closed". Looks like this may have been the cause of my idle problems all along. posts.author: po-po 5.0
posts.content: po-po 5.0 Regular Posts: 207 Joined: Thu Jul 29, 2004 12:51 pm Location: Oklahoma City, OK Contact: Contact po-po 5.0 ICQ Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by po-po 5.0 » Thu Feb 09, 2006 9:15 am mipfish wrote: So your MAF DOES NOT have to be cal'd for the size injectors your running? Thats where editing the MAF curve comes in? If its a stock MAF, the computer already "knows" the MAF curve for it. However, by default a GT's comptuer calculates injector pulse width assuming that the motor has 19# injectors. When you install a different size injector the assumption fails, and the computer calculates and innacurate pulse width. So what you gotta do is tell the computer what the real injector size is, and it should control the injectors better. posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Thu Feb 09, 2006 12:59 pm You want to watch:maf, lambse, KAMRF, mostly, along with them I like to see O2 sensors, tps, rpms, timing, load, and engine temp. What you want to see is lambse in the 11.5-15.0 range most of the time. Lambse is target AFR as calculated by the eec. If lambse is outside of this range, that means the eec's base fuel calculations are off for whatever reason, and the eec is using O2 readings to try to achieve true afr in the 12-15 range. KAMRF is your adaptive memory where 1 equals to "no correction needed" below 1 the eec is taking fuel out and above 1 is adding fuel as based on O2 sensors. Thats basically it. WOT/open loop is another story where you need to determine afr by other means. Stock O2 sensors are not accurate enough. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Thu Feb 09, 2006 3:42 pm It depends on the selected setting on the req fuel calculation. Are you using the option where the slopes are equal or where the breakpoint is set as a function? Remeber the the KAMRF calculation is based off of averaging and is also based off of where you set the breapoint. The breakpoint is not calculated if you use the KAMRF calculation. In my opinion the required fuel calculation is more accurate when trying to get a base tune. Then it would be upto the MAF calculations to dial it in. The kamrf calculation is more for observation to see where the MAF is out. You could use it to dial in the slopes too, but I think the req fuel is a better choice. It maybe not what you wanted to hear since it is working oppsite for you, but make sure you have the right settings. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.content: wa_4x4builder Regular Posts: 106 Joined: Wed Mar 30, 2005 12:37 pm Location: Seattle, Washington Re: Please give me a quick rundown on these functions... Quote Post by wa_4x4builder » Thu Feb 16, 2006 8:40 pm WA2FAST wrote: I need help on the following groups and/or speciffic fucntions: Dashpot Minimum Clip Dashpot Maximum Clip Dashpot Preposition Dashpot Preposition Offset ISC Dashpot Decay Rate ISC Drive Idle Airflow ISC Neutral Idle Airflow ISC Neutral RPM Adder Don Hey Don, Here's what I've got based on the research I've done. Maybe it will help, maybe not... (BTW- you've got me on these three: Dashpot Minimum Clip Dashpot Maximum Clip Dashpot Preposition Offset What function numbers are they?) ISC Drive Idle Air Flow Airflow required for closed throttle operation in drive FN875D (DSDRPM) Input = absolute DSDRPM Output = base desired airflow for the requested RPM measured in lbs/min Desired engine speed (DSDRPM) = [base desired speed (NUBASE for neutral or DRBASE for drive) + RPM adder (DNAC) if A/C is on + RPM adder (DNPOWS) if a power steering pressure switch is used and power steering load is high + ECT and ACT and start-up modulator functions (FN825A, FN825B & FN826)]. Desired idle airflow (DESMAF) = [base desired airflow (FN875N for neutral; FN875D for drive)) * FN1861] + discrete airflow increments for A/C (ACPPM) and power steering (PSPPM) if either load is present. ACPPM = Airflow increment required with A/C on. Value is used to increment both the desired flow through the ISC actuator (account for increased load) and the filtered air mass (FAM). Typical value - 0.15 lbs/min. PSPPM = Airflow increment required when power steering load is sensed. Value increments both the desired flow through the ISC actuator (account for increased speed/load) and the filtered air mass (FAM). Typical value -0.10 lbs/min ISC Neutral Idle Air Flow Airflow required for closed throttle operation in neutral FN875N (DSDRPM)Input = absolute DSDRPM Output = base desired airflow for the requested RPM measured in lbs/min See FN875D for additional details. ISC Dashpot Decay Rate FN879(DASPOT) A background driven decrement to the dashpot pre-position airflow register (DASPOT) as a function of DASPOT. Input = DASPOT Output = an airflow value to be subtracted from DASPOT FN879 can be calibrated to achieve an exponentially decaying dashpot which is useful in decaying the large DASPOT values used to control over-rich tip-out conditions. DASPOT = DASPOT - FN879 (DASPOT clipped to zero, if necessary) ISC Neutral RPM Adder DSDRPM adder vs. time at idle and in neutral FN880 (CTNTMR)Input = CTNTMR measured in seconds Output = RPM to add to DSDRPM only during “Hi-cam” RPM calculations, otherwise used as a hysteresis term to determine if idle RPM value is “close enough” to the desired idle RPM CTNTMR = Closed throttle neutral timer. See FN875D for details on DSDRPM. ISC Dashpot Pre-Position Maximum allowed dashpot pre-position airflow FN882(N) DASPOT calculation clipped at this value. Input = N Output = pre-position airflow measured in lbs/min The calculated pre-position airflow increment is added to an adaptively-corrected idle flow requirement (DESMAF) prior to output of the ISC duty cycle. Pre-position airflow (DASPOT) is a function of the difference between a filtered throttle position (DSTPBR) and a throttle position equal to the closed throttle breakpoint (RATCH + DELHYS). This value is clipped to zero, as a minimum, if the difference becomes a negative value. DELHYS should be set equal to DELTA + HYSTS (the closed throttle breakpoint). DASPOT can be clipped to DASMIN as a minimum if vehicle speed is high enough to prepare for declutch. During closed throttle mode, the DASPOT airflow is "bled off" by decrementing it. This action smoothes the transition into RPM control by gradually eliminating the DASPOT contribution to the idle airflow, DESMAF. The bleed rate is determined by FN879, unless clipped to DASMIN. When vehicle speed falls below DASMPH, normal bleed off will resume. DESMAF = FN875N/D * FN1861 DASMIN = Minimum DASPOT clip for declutch, lbs/min (i.e. keep at this amount of airflow, then resume normal bleed off when vehicle speed falls below DASMPH) DASMPH = Minimum VSBAR for declutch DASPOT clip in MPH. VSBAR = Vehicle speed in MPH. ISC Dashpot Pre-Position Maximum allowed dashpot pre-position airflow FN882(N) DASPOT calculation clipped at this value. Input = N Output = pre-position airflow measured in lbs/min The calculated pre-position airflow increment is added to an adaptively-corrected idle flow requirement (DESMAF) prior to output of the ISC duty cycle. Pre-position airflow (DASPOT) is a function of the difference between a filtered throttle position (DSTPBR) and a throttle position equal to the closed throttle breakpoint (RATCH + DELHYS). This value is clipped to zero, as a minimum, if the difference becomes a negative value. DELHYS should be set equal to DELTA + HYSTS (the closed throttle breakpoint). DASPOT can be clipped to DASMIN as a minimum if vehicle speed is high enough to prepare for declutch. During closed throttle mode, the DASPOT airflow is "bled off" by decrementing it. This action smoothes the transition into RPM control by gradually eliminating the DASPOT contribution to the idle airflow, DESMAF. The bleed rate is determined by FN879, unless clipped to DASMIN. When vehicle speed falls below DASMPH, normal bleed off will resume. DESMAF = FN875N/D * FN1861 DASMIN = Minimum DASPOT clip for declutch, lbs/min (i.e. keep at this amount of airflow, then resume normal bleed off when vehicle speed falls below DASMPH) DASMPH = Minimum VSBAR for declutch DASPOT clip in MPH. VSBAR = Vehicle speed in MPH. Chris '93 EDIS 5.0L with A9L installed into a '77 Bronco. Top

posts.author: wa_4x4builder
posts.content: wa_4x4builder Regular Posts: 106 Joined: Wed Mar 30, 2005 12:37 pm Location: Seattle, Washington Quote Post by wa_4x4builder » Fri Feb 17, 2006 7:38 pm WA2FAST wrote: So tell me something... if the Dashpot Pre-Position is "clipped" to dashpot minimum, there will be no slow RPM drop... am I reading that right? Also, am I understanding DeClutch correctly... when it declutches something, it applies that modifier till that point, when it declutches, it no longer uses that modifier? It almost seems like I could either decay the hell out of daspot (dashpot pre-position) with the decay rate... (does that mean I set that to high values or low values), OR... I could just set daspot (dashpot pre-position) to dasmin to eliminate the adder (daspot) of air as long as dasmin won't stall the car out bassicaly...? Here's my take on this stuff- there will be varying opinions, I'm sure! The term "clipped" means that the value of the variable in question (in this case dashpot) will not be allowed to exceed or fall below a certain value. "Clipping" is an engineering term. So, in this case, they are saying that the dashpot value will not be allowed to fall below DASMIN (a scalar which is unavailable in CalEdit in the A9L strategy and, apparently a function in other strategies). Declutch in this context means the driver presses the clutch pedal. So, that's to say the dashpot value will be "held" at a constant when the vehicle is traveling fast enough in preparation for the driver pressing the clutch. Once that happens, the dashpot logic will be activated and the dashpot will be bled off as expected (assuming you are below the DASMPH scalar value). The answer to your question about which of the two functions to fiddle with is difficult to answer. I think the "two ways to skin a cat" saying applies here. You could try tackling it either way. I recall you said you were trying to cure a hanging idle. My best suggestion would be to determine exactly what conditions exist during the hanging idle and then come back to these variables to determine if your changes solve the problem. Idle is one of those really common problems which is also like applied rocket science to get fixed! Chris '93 EDIS 5.0L with A9L installed into a '77 Bronco. Top

The BA2800 i have heard may peg in the 550-600 rwhp range in blowthru but you can use an extender but that is additional tuning that is going to be required in the maf curve. I have a B@G kit with a T-76 and i'm running a blowthrough 75mm bullet caled for 50s. I sent PMAS my entire intercooler pipe containing the maf and they recaled it and sent me a flowsheet. I've been messing with getting the 30 point conversion done but i have been seeing different values as far as the max kg/hr at 5 volts...the caledit one goes all the way to 3250 kg/hr while the EA version goes to 2500 kg/hr but starts at .6 volts. posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Sat Feb 25, 2006 1:12 pm I've had some luck doing the conversion in excel. I would suggest plotting each time you calculate the curve fit to make sure the curve doesn't go wild above where you have data. A lot of times, a third or fourth order fit will give you a better extrapolation than a higher order one. After you are satisfied that the curve fit is accurate enough, you can get the values out of it at the stock voltage points and put it in using the tweecer. This is where the fun starts, looking at KAMRF and bumping the values up and down to get the MAF to where what the computer commands is actually what comes out of the exhaust pipe. If you have a wide band, this makes tuning the top (above 2.5v) of the MAF curve much, much easier. Then you can go after idle, cold start and all the other drivability things which drive everybody nuts. You should be able to disable EGR in your strategy without any problem, other than occasionally knocking under part throttle. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sun Jan 15, 2006 5:53 am FN703A is a combined transfer table for both ACT and ECT sensors so any change for one could be detrimental the output for the other sensor. It is located at 0x8DB0 in the A9L as a byte sized XY pairing, X being the input and Y the output (resolution 0.5 and signed). Top

posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Sun Jan 15, 2006 11:04 am sailorbob wrote: FN703A is a combined transfer table for both ACT and ECT sensors so any change for one could be detrimental the output for the other sensor. It is located at 0x8DB0 in the A9L as a byte sized XY pairing, X being the input and Y the output (resolution 0.5 and signed). Yeah, I noticed that in one section of the GUFB document it mentioned that it was for both ECT & ACT, in another it only mentioned ACT (though that's all they were talking about there). The two sensors have the same resistive response to temperature, so it makes sense that they are handled by one function. If a resistor was added to one sensor to extend it's range, then the other sensor would also need to have that resistor changed. You would lose some resolution but maybe you could calibrate the sensors and make them even more accurate in the end. 428w now Top

posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Sun Jan 15, 2006 11:13 am TripleBlackVert wrote: Cougar5.0 wrote: Fuel pump will sieze up with water. I inject before the blower - some inject after the blower - the jury is still out on which is the better location. ok, no fuel pump :( do you have any pics of the setup and where in the intake you put the nozzle? I don't really have any pictures - the pump is mounted inside the inner fender near the washer fluid bottle (drivers side inner fender on a Cougar) that I converted for this use. I ran the line to the solenoid valve mounted on the engine compartment side of the shock tower near the pump/washer fluid bottle. From there I ran a line to the nozzle which I tapped into one of the vacuum ports on the inlet manifold (opened up to 1/2 NPT). This sprays the water into the inlet just after the TB and down toward the blower inlet. A few folks have had good success doing it this way. Certainly nice not to have to worry about detonation any more and it cools the air charge by 10-15 degrees to boot! I'm able to run up to 23 degrees of timing depending on how hot the air charge is (WOT spark advance vs ACT will pull timing if too hot). 428w now Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sun Dec 11, 2005 10:40 am I decided to search this out in CRAI8 to see what's up with this... This scalar is a multiplier to BOTH the decel and accel transient fuel compensation. The calc is: decel = Fuel_Decel_Time_Const [table] * Fuel_Time_Constant_Multiplier [scalar] * Fuel_Surface_Mult_vs_RPM [function] accel = Fuel_Accel_Time_Const [table] * Fuel_Time_Constant_Multiplier [scalar] * Fuel_Surface_Mult_vs_RPM [function] The transient fuel compensation is used to account for varying amounts of fuel that is on the manifold walls during varying engine conditions. Search CRAI8 strategy doc for section Code: Select all 9.6.1 BACKGROUND TRANSIENT FUEL LOGIC (cut and paste that) CRAI8 strategy doc - section 9.6.1 wrote: A liquid fuel film resides on the walls of the intake manifold. The film mass varies primarily with manifold absolute pressure and manifold wall temperature. During steady state conditions, the film mass is constant. The rates of condensation and evaporation on the manifold walls are equal. During transients, the film mass changes creating air/fuel ratio errors. . During accelerations, the film mass increases. Fuel will condense faster on the manifold walls until equilibrium is reached. In an uncompensated system at stoichiometry, fuel is diverted from the cylinders, resulting in a momentary lean condition. . During decelerations, the film mass decreases. Fuel will evaporate faster from the manifold walls until equilibrium is reached. In an uncompensated system at stoichiometry, fuel is added to the cylinders, resulting in a momentary rich condition. The problem is magnified in closed loop fuel systems because the fuel control will incorrectly chase the transient air/fuel excursions. Intent: The Transient Fuel Compensation Strategy (TFC) augments the closed/open loop fuel control to keep cylinder events at the desired air/fuel ratio during all engine transients. The goals are: . To eliminate lean air/fuel excursions during accelerations. . To eliminate rich air/fuel excursions during decelerations. posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Wed Mar 01, 2006 10:04 pm Hi, It sounds like you could be rich. Or not. It is tough to tell unless you start reading plugs. The tweecer (the R/T version) lets you look at what the computer is thinking is going on and lets you diagnose. The problem is that between a tweecer and a wide band air/fuel meter, you are nearly out $800. You've got to balance the frustration of having a car that runs like crap with spending the money and time to figure it out. You could also go to somebody to burn a chip for you, but that will depend on how good that person is at tuning. The tweecer takes a while to learn and can be frustrating, but eventually you can have a car that works pretty well. Personally, I don't know if having all this electronic stuff is better or not for performance. You would probably get the same N/A peak power (or more) with a carburetor and be up and running a lot faster for less money. If you go with a boosted application, though, EFI is the only way to go. My two cents...
