I need 60's... 62's would give me the headroom I would feel comfortable with, but that's a whole different storry. As far as your meter is concerned, not going to work. You need to get a meter calibrated for your injectors. The reason why is if your meter is calibrated for 19's and you have 42's... that's not a problem, where the problem comes in, is voltage output of the meter vs. mass of air. Your #19 meter is electronicaly calibrated to send a 5v signal at ~835 kg/hr. When you throw a blower on your car and exceed that, no matter what you do with the EEC and tuning, it's going to peg the meter at 5v long before you hit your shift point. I have a Pro-M Pro-Tube meter callibrated for #42... my injectors hit max duity cycle at 4300rpm and my meter pegs at 5v at 5300rpm... that is something that tuning doesn't cure, I need to send it back to have recalibrated so that it doesn't peg... and mind you... a #42 meter is pegging at ~1700 kg/hr. That means that no matter how you tune your engine, when that much air is flowing through your meter, it will hit 5v. If you stick with your #19 calibrated meter, you are going to hit 5v long before your shift point due to the new air flow because of the blower... so no, it's not going to work. If your meters calibration wouldn't peg, then yes it is possible. -Don- 87' GT, A9L, TwEECer RT, P1SC@12psi Non-Intercooled, AFM PP, 3" Pro-M#42, 70mm TB, GT-40 Intake, GT-40X Heads, B303, 1.6, BBK 1-5/8" Long Tubes, 306 Built Bottom End, Probe Block Girdle, TR3550, 3.55, PLX WB, Jan 07 Modified Mustangs Feature Car Top

posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Mon Mar 06, 2006 9:44 pm Hi, If your tune is OK (your MAF is calibrated) and you have your air/fuel ratio flat across the whole RPM range at WOT, you should be in pretty good shape. For NA pulls, I was able to add fuel and spark until I hit a peak. For fuel, I just used the WOT fuel multiplier scalar but for spark I adjusted the WOT spark vs rpm function. For supercharged applications, keep the timing conservative until your fuel is straightened out (i.e. 11:1 or richer) before you add timing. It looks like most people run less than 20 degrees, but this depends on boost level. The amount of spark you pull out per pound of boost varies with head a little, but I think it is around one degree per pound. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Mon Jan 16, 2006 6:18 am Mangus, sorry for confusing you, again my (very) poor explanation. To keep things simple (or more likely to speed up calculations) Ford keep seem to keep everything scalable by 2 (i.e. rpm in the code is actually true rpm * 4). By resolution I meant that if you say right shifted rpm by 1 you'd get true rpm * 2 but if Ford hadn't used binary point scaling and lets say code rpm was true rpm * 3.25, right shifting this by 1 would result in true rpm * 1.62 thus losing 0.005 of the multiplier. Does that make anymore sense? Cougar5.0, the input value of the ECT/ACT Transfer function is 8 bit because it only uses the high byte of the A-D value. Ford obviously deem the lower 8 bits of the value too precise for ECT and ACT values. It wouldn't be very difficult to add another transfer table so that the ECT and ACT tables could be used for different range sensors but this is not where the problem lies with the code. Because the eec uses an 8 bit signed value with a resolution of 2 for ECT and ACT the max and min temperatures they can only be are +254 degrees F and - 256 degrees F. If your forced induction engines exceed these values then there is no way for the ecu to know this. It would take a lot of hard work to alter the code to enable it to work with a larger temperature range. The only way I can think of that MIGHT possibly work is to split the transfer function and use a different sensor (or one with a resistor added in series) and rescale any constant/table/function that uses ACT with an offset. eg the eec might be seeing an ECT value that would normally equal 180 degrees but the real temperature would be say 230 degrees. Afterall you are never going to see -256 degrees so why not 'pinch' some of that to use at the upper end. Still a fair bit of work to do but feasible on something like the A9L where most of the code is well documented, a lot harder on a later ecu. Top

posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Fri Mar 10, 2006 10:35 am Hi, I'm running an a9l and I don't know about the x3z strategy. Our combinations are almost the same, I'm running the same cam and same size injectors. I can tell you the things which made a difference on my car. First, any exhaust leaks will mess up your oxygen sensor readings. That will make the computer think there is oxygen in the exhaust stream and you'll run rich. I'd suggest replacing your exhaust manifold gaskets. If you still get differences across banks, do a leak down test to make sure something mechanical is not going on like a leaky valve or something like that. My o2 sensors measure some differences at low load, but are nearly identical at higher loads so I don't worry too much about that. A KAMRF difference of 10% is probably fine at idle, but others probably have other opinions. Also, I think the stock setting on fuel pressure is 38 psi (without the vacuum) which may help you a little. The big thing is the MAF transfer function. If you tell it that more air is getting in, it will put in more fuel. There are a bunch of really good things in the FAQ section, but putting in your flow sheet from pro-m is the first thing you should do. Then, put in the right injector slopes, or an initial guess at them. After that, you can tweak the MAF function so that it is as close as you can get for your intake tract, etc. That will help a lot. It sounds like you're lean in the upper ranges of your MAF curve which may be causing the backfiring. Good luck, Fritz Coast 342, AFR185's, TFS stage II cam,30# inj, 76mm C&L, 1 3/4 hooker long tubes, 3.70 gears, Spec stage II clutch, an A9L and a TwEECer RT, 11.84 @120.4 w/100hp shot Top

posts.author: dsleepy47
posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Fri Jul 01, 2005 2:36 pm Go here: http://www.dataq.com/ to see dataQ. Get the DI-194RS starter kit for $25. It plugs into the laptop serial port. You connect the analog 2 channels to the dataQ and on the setup page of calcon enable the dataQ channels to the AFR and boost gage and select the data file to use. I made a custom dbf file called "LC-1" . Calcon gets the channel inputs from the DataQ directly from the serial port and displays them in the AFR and PSI boxes and the AFR and boost columns of the logs. posts.author: dsleepy47
posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Tue Aug 23, 2005 12:40 pm I'm running the lc-1 on the innovate file with the output of the lc-1 set to 1v=10 2v=20. Is tthis wrong? There is nothing wrong with that, If you have checked for and corrected if needed for voltage offset. I just like the idea of having as small an AFR/Volt ratio as possible to increase the resolution and as large a voltage range as possible to minimize the effects of any electrical noise in the system. My LC-1 file uses 0v-5.0v = 10-20AFR so a 0.1v change is only a 0.2afr change. I have a -0.2v offset (calcon reads 0.2v lower than LC-1 output) so my LC-1s analog out are set for 0.2v-5.0v = 10afr-19.6afr so in reality calcon will never read above 19.6 because the LC-1 won't put out more than 5.0v. Another note is that I use the analog out 1s from my LC-1s for narrow band simulation and I have the voltage set so that closed loop controls at 15.3 instead of 14.64 for fuel mileage. posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Tue Aug 23, 2005 3:08 pm The thing that makes a difference most often about NB simulation is that here in Minnesota I have issues with NB's screwing up at closed loop idle and getting idle KAMRfs all out of wack. With the LC-1 outputs closed loop idle works great. My truck is street vehicle and I do use it to haul other vehicles on a trailer some times so I like being able to set my closed loop to 15.3 for flat empty highway cruising and to 13.5 if I am pulling heavy loads in mountain country. On a 3000 mile round trip to Mooresville, NC and back this summer I averaged 17.8 mpg on the way there and 12.2 mpg on the way back hauling a bed full of engine parts and a car on a trailer both of which are about 2 mpg better than I did the last time I did a trip like that before installing the LC-1s. You could get those results by tuning whithout NB simulation but the more I use it the more I like it. I never really found an AFR display useful, more of a distraction than anything but if you want a display you have several options. The XD-1 gauge from Innovate uses the serial output so it leaves the analog outputs available and can acurrately display the entire AFR range of the LC-1 plus it can log afr for download later. The drawback is the price. The other opton is to hook up the EEC and and the autometer gage to output one. as long as the total amp draw doesn't exceed the capacity of the output you should be fine. I don't think that should be a problem but I would bounce the idea off Klaus at http://www.innovatemotorsports.com/forums/index.php? just to be safe. If you do hook up to the EEC make sure you ground the analog ground to the sensor signal return circuit for the EEC and check for voltage offset. I set the analog 1 outputs to a constant 0.5 volts and logged O2 voltage and I found that my EEC read 0.462v on the drivers side and 0.493v on the passengers side. That doesn't sound like a lot of difference but it is quite a bit with the steep slope of the ND curve. Last because of the drastic difference in how well the WB behaves at idle and low loads I would not recommend using NB simulation on one side and a NB sensor on the other. either use 2 LC-1s or set your EEC for mono O2 correction. posts.content: dsleepy47 Regular Posts: 176 Joined: Fri Aug 01, 2003 12:47 pm Location: Baudette, MN Quote Post by dsleepy47 » Wed Aug 24, 2005 7:18 am Did you need to make any other changes to your calibration to support this? The only thing I do may be different than some is that since I always have WB numbers from both banks available I run all my tunes with adaptive disabled and use lambSe 1 & 2 vs WB 1 & 2 to evaluate what is happening. The EEC seems quite happy to control at whatever AFR I have the switchpoint set at and open loop AFRs are within a couple of 0.1s of commanded. Have you tried logging both a WB in NB sim mode along with a stock NB at the same time to compare? Did you change the ramp rates to more match our NBO2's, or did you find that they were close enough? Yes, I have an LM-1 and a techedge WB as well as LC-1s on on this vehicle and 2 others I have compared WB and NB responses and WB to WB in quite a few different conditions and what I have seen in general is that from cold conditions WBs will read accurately much quicker and NB accuracy is very exhaust temperature dependent even for heated sensors when compared to WB's. It is this last charactaristic that seems to be why mixing NB and simulated NB inputs doesn't work that well. It isn't something you can't do but if you have ever been concerned about how much kamrfs vary from side to side a NB - WB pair will probably drive you crazy. posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Thu Mar 16, 2006 8:52 pm Hi, Swapping pieces of another tuneup over to a new tuneup should be straightforward. For example, if you've got a tune set up for 42 #/hr injectors and you actually have 38 #/hr injectors with a different MAF curve, take the MAF curve from the 38 #/hr tune up and put it into the 42 #/hr tuneup, then set the fuel injector size to 38 #/hr in the scalars. Leave everything else alone and see what happens. You may want to write the new tuneup to disk (back up changes!) and save the old ones in case you need to go back. I think the idea here is that you want to keep the calibrated meter and injector combination consistent between the two tuneups you are using. posts.author: DrDirt
posts.content: DrDirt Tuning Addict Posts: 512 Joined: Wed Jun 30, 2004 7:45 am Location: Largo, Fl Quote Post by DrDirt » Sat Mar 18, 2006 5:50 am Do NOT check the Update Only box...ever. It tends to corrupt the tune and give unpredictible results. Pick the parameters to log, click the PAYLOAD button, check the Data Logging box, laptop hooked up to Tweecer, ignition on, click write to Tweecer. The status bar should say "Complete" when the write is finished. Turn off ignition. Next, to actually datalog, Run CalCon, select setup, I usually change "Samples" to 25000 from 250 so it will datalog longer. In the EVP Signal Transfer box, I select PLX for my Wideband and AFR, check the Log to File box to save the log to disc, click Apply Changes, Choose either Digital or Dashboard, click the red Start Logging Button, start the car and you should be datalogging like a pro. When you are finished, you can either click the red button to Stop Datalogging or simply turn the car off and the file will be saved. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Wed Mar 15, 2006 12:52 pm I thought about this some more since last night. I don't think the load reading on crank is meaningful, nor is it used by the crank program. MAF values are not used in crank either. Crank has a single objective, get the motor going so the EEC can switch over to the start-up program. There are few tunable items relative to the crank program. The most significant item in the TwECer list of things we can play with is the fuel_crank_PW_multiply_ECT function and its associated table fuel_crank_pulsewidth. This is what Dr Dirt was talking about above and I have modified my tune in this area to solve an over rich condition on crank which prevented my car from starting unless I held the throttle plate open. Injector Offset vs Battery Voltage is another. In my tune I have made no changes to this. So if you are saying that with my tune your car will not start (stays in crank mode) there has to be a simple issue of too much fuel (by a lot) or not enough fuel. You say with my tune your plugs have become fouled and so it is obviously rich. So why would it be rich on crank? Lets solve this first before you try to solve the hunting idle etc. The crank proogram has few variables to mess with. Is an injector stuck open? ISC stuck closed? Its not likely to be a vacuum leak. Are all the plugs fouled, or just some of them? And remember, a weak spark would let the plugs get fouled on crank. 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Sun Mar 19, 2006 12:29 pm Do this fully warmed up: Datalog lambse at startup. You will see it gradually climb to around 14.xxx and then start to respond to O2 sensors once it reaches 14.xxx. Now, lambse will either stay around 13.xxx or go higher or lower depending on which way your tune is off. I'm guessing in your case it will peg high or low (10.980 or 18.xxx) 10.xx your LEAN eec is trying to command the richest mixture it can. 18.xx your RICH eec is trying to command the leanest mixture it can. Lambse stays in the 12-15 range, mixture is not your startup problem. Note: crank pw vs ect function, I'm using stock values with 42# and the car starts great hot or cold. posts.author: DrDirt
posts.content: DrDirt Tuning Addict Posts: 512 Joined: Wed Jun 30, 2004 7:45 am Location: Largo, Fl Quote Post by DrDirt » Thu Feb 16, 2006 5:24 pm It will use the stored values and then start to "learn" the new tune and will adjust accordingly. After a time, it will arrive back at the same place as the values in your B tune...assuming that the values are fully matured. The purpose of clearing the KAMRF when you switch to a new tune is so you can see the results quicker. The EEC doesn't have to unlearn the old values before it can settle on the new ones. I'm just trying to determine if it is a luxury or a necessity to be effective at analyzing my data and making decisions. The general consensus is that EA is worth the 50 bucks. You can try to solve some of the same math problems yourself (via Excel, for example), but by the time you dink with it for a few days, you've already spent more $$$'s in time than if you popped for the 50 bucks in the first place. To answer about the KAMRF's, while you are data logging, the variables you selected are saved into records. Each of those records is taken as a complete unit (i.e. all the variables you requested are read at the same time) and a time stamp is placed on the record. This happens over and over and over until you stop data logging. If you forgot to save to a file, each record was tossed out the instant the next record was available. If you saved to a file, when you stop, there will be a data file on disc containing those records. As an example, say you selected the left and right KAMRF, ECT, ACT and the left and right lambse variables. Furthermore, you data logged just long enough to get 100 records. Each one of those records will have all the above variables and their values at the time the record was read from the tweecer (they are read from the PCM really) You can replay those 100 records in CalCon if you wish. You can also replay them in EA and then do analysis on them. If you use EA to make small changes, you would edit those changes in CalEdit, load them into the tweecer via CalEdit and then data log with CalCon again to see the fruits of your labor. This sequence is repeated until you can't take it anymore or you have your set-up tuned to your desires. Under either of those conditions, a guy is likely to stop the vicious cycle '93 EDIS 5.0L with A9L installed into a '77 Bronco. Top

posts.content: DrDirt Tuning Addict Posts: 512 Joined: Wed Jun 30, 2004 7:45 am Location: Largo, Fl Quote Post by DrDirt » Wed Mar 22, 2006 2:58 pm If you are using Tweecer to do the tuning on the dyno, after you make changes, simply click on the Save Calibration to Disk icon in the top left corner of Caledit and give it a name. I'd save it under a new name each time you make a change in case the change didn't work out. Then you could just reload the last named tune and try again. When you get the final tune worked, click the Icon again and give it the final name for your tune and you're all set. One word of warning though. When you write your tune to Tweecer each time and even when you are saving it to disc, make sure the Update ONLY checkbox is not checked. That tends to corrupt the tunes sometimes. If your tuner is tuning with a chip instead of the Tweecer, you will have to send the chip to Mike Glover at Tweecer and he can read the chip and save or email you the tune in Tweecer format. posts.author: DrDirt
posts.content: DrDirt Tuning Addict Posts: 512 Joined: Wed Jun 30, 2004 7:45 am Location: Largo, Fl Quote Post by DrDirt » Wed Mar 22, 2006 6:01 pm Well, anytime you make some changes in Caledit, the first thing you should do is to list the changes you did either in the space provided in the About tab or a notebook and then save the tune to disk. Then you chose a position on the knob selector, choose the parameters you will want to datalog on the Uitlities tab, if any, and turn your ignition to Key On Engine Off and click on the Write to Tweecer icon. When it says "Complete" the tune is now written to Tweecer in that position. If you need to pull a tune off of Tweecer, say your copy on disk got corrupted or you overwrote it accidentally, plug in your laptop and set the knob to the position you want to retrieve from Tweecer. Again, Key On Engine Off and click on the Read Tweecer icon which is the Blue Ford logo. Once Caledit says "Complete", turn off the ignition and you can save that tune you just read to disk by clicking the blue floppy disk icon and giving it a name. Saving to disk does not put the tune into Tweecer. Only clicking Write to Tweecer will do that. If you want it in both places, that is 2 separate operations you have to perform. posts.content: Shaker666 Tuning Addict Posts: 638 Joined: Sun Dec 19, 2004 3:57 am Location: Tucson, AZ Contact: Contact Shaker666 AOL Quote Post by Shaker666 » Mon Feb 06, 2006 5:27 pm Guys, don't forget that you simply don't need that much timing to maximize power output in a blown application. Spark advance in an N/A setup is there to give the combustion enough time to burn properly to make good power; in a blown car, the combustion and flamefront propogation occurs much faster due to boost. Therefore, the more boost you run, the less timing you need to properly synchronize the combustion events. Even after tweaking the MAF after this datalog and changing the "Time at heavy load for open loop" to "0", it still leaned out. I then got the beast to lug perfectly - even with an expanded load scaling! Here is the load scaling I'm using: 0 1000 1350 2000 3500 5000 16384 0.8 0.8 0.85 1 1.2 1.2 0.5 I looked at the load scaling at 1350 because it's between 1350 & 2000 that I saw most of the problems. The scale difference from stock is .85/.715 = 1.19 or 19% larger. I figured I'd lower the FN320A "Open Loop Load Limit vs ECT" proportionally to match the new scale. .78 * .19 = .148 or about .15. My new maximum value is 0.63 instead of 0.78. Now I noticed that the problem was worse when the supercharger was cold - denser air after the charger I figure. Anyway, I added a point at 0 deg F set at 0.5. My new FN320A is: FN320A - upper load limit for CLOSED LOOP control: -65536_|__0__|_200_|_210_|_65534 __0.5__|_0.5_|_0.63_|0.60_|_0.60__ I lowered the 210 & above to 0.6 so it would go OL faster there - same as the stock function except .1 lower. I took it for a ride and did the same lugging experiment as before - here is a datalog with the changes implemented: This is in 5th gear. See how when I get to the ~1.5 TPS point the loop quickly goes open and I can keep pushing into it instead of backing off due to the bog/buck/pop. The loop goes open just as the accelerator function is backing off. The handoff feels great and I even lugged it in 5th going uphill at 1100 RPM! No more of that bucking supposedly due to the cam. Just made that nice hard piston smack sound that you'd expect under heavy lugging. Man, it's a thing of beauty. The kick at light-mid throttle transition is nice and makes the car feel torquier sooner. 428w now Top

You'll know it is working right when your in CL idle and it reads close to 14.7:1 AFR or 1.000 Lambda. I had to adjust my DataQ so that it's full scale and offset are correct. posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Tue Mar 28, 2006 7:35 pm Hi stang88tn, It looks like you are down about 100 hp which could be a number of things, but I'd start by checking the mechanical stuff first. If you're down a cylinder, not only do you have one cylinder not contributing, but it is just causing drag, so you can be more than 7/8 down on power. I'd suggest pulling plugs out to see if everything is firing OK. I'd also suggest a leakdown test which could pinpoint if you have any valve seating issues or ring problems. Tuning devices might help you diagnose, but if there is something mechanically fubar'd, you can't tune around it. You can change your air/fuel ratio and spark curves with the Tweecer, it is also pretty cheap as far as data acquisition is concerned in that you can see what the computer is doing. The problem is that you've got to figure out why the computer is doing what it is doing which is sometimes not at all obvious. First off, though, get any mechanical issues straightened around before you add additional complexity. posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Tue Mar 28, 2006 7:51 pm Hi, Lots of info there! I'm not sure I can help out much, but it looks like your MAF may be a little off. If you're lean at idle, the engine can misfire which will dump fuel into the exhaust and you'll smell gasoline. If you've got long tube headers, you might need to wait a while longer until you go into closed loop so that the o2 sensors can warm up. If you go to a dyno at some point, you can get information about air/fuel as a function of RPM and you should be able to tune the high portion of the MAF accordingly. If the low end of the MAF curve is lean, it could act like you describe and also explain a little about the idle. Another possiblility is the scalar time at high load to force OL could be set to 2 seconds (stock!). I have mine set for 0.25 seconds and other people set this to 0. Setting this to 0 forced my car into open loop all the time, so I set mine to a quarter of a second. For the WOT fuel multiplier, I have everything set at 1.0 across the whole range. If the MAF is accurate, the air/fuel will be flat (or whatever you set the top row in the open loop table to). One straight air/fuel ratio seemed to work best for my combination -- it liked a flat 12.7:1 across the board and about 36 degrees total timing to make best power. Quote Post by 66 injectedcobra » Wed Mar 29, 2006 1:13 pm OK follow me here guys.... I'm currently running a Pro-M 80mm Meter which works PERFECTLY and the Maf transfer which has been in my tune for years is right on for this meter. My old tuner had a program he used for these meters to get the 30pt conversion, once he loaded it to my tune w/ my old (Autologic chip) the car ran great. It has no driveability issues what so ever! Here is my big question that I have not been able to get answers for in detale as of yet. I'm running 50lb injectors and 80mm Pro-M. The tune knows what my maf REALLY flows and injectors set at 50 high and 60 low. Cars runs great! Now what happens when I want to ditch the 50's and go to lets say 60's or ever bigger? I'm obviously going to tell the tune I have 60's for high slope whatever for low.. Do I have to change my meter? Get is so called calibrated for 60's? I just don't get how the calibration thing works for meters? The fact is they flow X amount of air at X amount of volts thats it!! If I already know how and what my meter flows down to a T and my MAF transfer has the information, would I still have to change my meter? ...Mike Lets Race! Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Mar 29, 2006 1:28 pm No the only thing you will have to change is the injector slopes and maybe the injector offset vs battery. I would leave the MAF curve alone if there is no issues with it. Changing the injector size has nothing to do with the flow of a meter. If your meter is cal'd for the 50's all this means is that theoretically you can run the car without the tuner. I would not recommend that anyways. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Fri Jan 20, 2006 12:02 pm Got a look at your datalog, first thing I see is your load is too high everywhere, at idle and under boost. You should see around 20% load at idle but have 43%. Under boost you hit 200% which is probably why your timing is going strange although I did not see you get to 9 degrees, instead you hit 14.75 degrees under boost which is probably safe but not what you were commanding in the timing tables. As far as load goes, I can think of 2 ways to correct that. The first is to put your "batt inj comp" values back to stock, then reduce your maf values until you get close to stockish values at least in the lower ranges. Once you do that you can adjust the "batt inj comp" values to get your fuel trims in line. Reducing the maf values will cause the eec to compute lower load values. Or..you can try increasing the "sea level load scaling" values higher until you get the correct load values at idle, etc. You don't want to hit 200% load under boost. 140% would more normal unless you are running a lot of boost. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Mar 28, 2006 2:54 pm On a V8 Ranger conversion, that's easier said than done. Getting to the back vaccum hoses is not easy. They are slammed against the back firewall with little to no room to see anything. You kinda just have to feel your way around back there to disconnect and reconnect lines. The two X-factors in my setup are the EGR valve and the Canister Purge system. Since I need this truck to be able to pass Georgia Emissions, I maintained all that I could. The factory 89 Ranger canister purge system was nothing more than a vaccum tube that ran up to the front of the TB butterfly. Since the system was Speed Density, not MAF, this didn't create any problems not having a real valve in the line. Since the Mustang, however is MAF controlled, the ECM kinda likes to know when extra "unmetered" air is entering the system, and thus Mustangs had canister purge valves. To maintain this, I put a canister purge valve from a late 90s Ranger (that does run MAF) in, and wired it to the ECM's leads for canister purge. The problem is the Explorer TB doesn't have a canister pruge tube to land on like Mustangs do. The Explorer setup has the canister pruge line on a high-vaccum tap from the upper intake. The canister purge valve is very tiny and doesn't let a whole lot past, but it is possible that the system is getting more air than expected when the ECM energizes the Canister Purge solenoid. Thoughts? As for the EGR, I'm not using the stock 97 Explorer EGR valve and tube. The Explorer setup uses a differential pressure sensor that detects how much exhaust is being taken in and adjusts valve position accordingly. This system is not compatible with an 89-93 ECM so I retrofitted the EGR system back to what A9P used. The catch is, GT40p heads, which are standard on 97.5 and up Explorers don't have intake manifold EGR. They rely on a tube from the exhaust manifolds to deliver the gas up to the EGR valve. Using an EGR from an F-150, which looks similar to a stock Mustang and uses the same exact EGR position sensor as Mustang, this is what I came up with: Is it possible my EGR system flows too much gas as compared to what the A9P's EGR curves are expecting for the same EGR valve positions? Since the EGR position sensor is not detecting flow, just valve position, the actual amount of EGR gas could easily be different...just a thought. And EGR is only active at cruise...when I'm noticing the hesitation. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Mar 28, 2006 9:57 pm Reluctantly, I ran the MAF tune in EA with a 30min datalog including a few WOTs, interstate cruising at 80mph, stop-n-go, and 55-60mph cruising. Without popping the clutch, I can slam the gas at 1500rpm and the tires break loose. The locker keeps'em from lighting up, but they do bark which they didn't do before. Advancing the part-throttle by 4 also restored some of the responsiveness. I guess it is possible I'm suffering from flow differentials in the MAF since I don't have an airbox. My intake consists of a cone filter mounted directly on the MAF, then a modified cold-air pipe from the MAF up to the TB. With the air filter right on the MAF and butted up next to the battery in the engine bay, it is possible turbulance and all sorts of other flow eddies are just causing the MAF curve to be off from factory at low flow conditions. EA calculates my MAF curve dead-on with what it should be at higher flow rates...just skewed at the lower flows. Thoughts? cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Mar 31, 2006 9:34 am I think I found what was causing my cold-start sputters. The low slope injector size value needed tweaking. I have 19lb (orange) injectors on the engine. Like all injectors, they get sloppy when their pulse is very small...as is the case during idle and crank. When injectors get sloppy, they are sloppy on the rich side, delivering more fuel than they rightfully should for their rated size. The ECM expects this and has provisions for this anomaly by having scalars for Injector Slope High (the actual injector size) and Injector Slope Low (some value larger than the injector size). My A9P had a value of 26lb/hr for the low-slope by default. I've read somewhere that this should be about 15-25% larger than your injector's rated value. With 26lb/hr, the ECM was closer to 36% which was way more than the sloppiness of my injectors, creating a lean condition right at crank. Once the engine was running, the ECM would figure out what it needed to do to not stumble, but since the ECM doesn't learn anything during OL, it never learned that it was always off and needed to compensate every time. I adjusted the Injector Slope Low scalar down to 24lb/hr and this morning, the engine cranked normally (cold) for the 1st time since I dropped the engine into the truck. I could probably lower that number down to 22lb/hr since cold-starts are supposed to be a little rich. But as long as it cranks correctly, I'll leave it alone. I also expect my lower KAMRF values to improve. I was enrichening my MAF curve thinking this would fix the problem and it was helping, but never got rid of the problem. With this adjustment in place, I'm betting I'll notice my low load, low RPM KAMRF values will be below 1 instead of 1.12+. I just thought I'd pass that along. If anybody expresses interest, I'll post further findings with regard to this. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Mar 31, 2006 2:45 pm Pro-M is better than C&L so this may not apply. However when looking at a "Stock A9L" which is the factory Mustang 55mm MAF vs the C&L 73mm using the clear tube (calibrating the MAF for 19lb injectors), there IS a difference in the curve. The C&L 73mm w/clear tube is a leaner curve (more air per volt) than the factory 55mm MAF at higher flowrates. There is a crossover point where they are the same. But for low flow conditions, the C&L is actually richer (less airflow per volt) compared to the factory 55mm curve. C&L Performance C&L's website claims their modified curve allows for more power at higher flowrates as compared to the richer factory configuration. Adaptive control will make up the difference when in CL. However at WOT, I always thought you wanted your mix a little rich, but then I'm not claiming to be an expert, selling these things to the public. So what the hell do I know? Point being, in my non-expert opinion, I'd expect a 75mm and 80mm MAF to be a little different, but close enough to get you in the ballpark so you can find out how far you are off and tweak it from there. If it's too far off, you'll get a really bad running engine and an evenutal Check Engine light. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Mar 31, 2006 4:39 pm Being that I'm new with all this myself, I'm in no position to argue with those that know more than I. I'll just make myself look stupid. But I have a loud mou...err...loud fingers, so I wind up just saying whatever I think whether it's right or not. I'll let someone correct me where I'm wrong and I figure being wrong and being corrected are better than always being wrong. :? However my understanding about all this stuff is there are tolerances, and "close" is often good enough for most applications. In this case, the difference between 75mm and 80mm is so small that until you get into the really high flowrates (>1100kg/hr), their curves, if different , will be "close enough." We weren't in disagreement there. If that's the way it sounded, my appologies. Regardless of which MAF size that ProM30 curve represents, it SHOULD be a decent starting point. My point was the curves could still be different, but good for 30# injectors. See, when using larger injectors and a different MAF calibrated for those injectors, the ECM believes the factory MAF and injectors are still there (as you pointed out). What you've done is upped the amount of fuel that gets delivered for any given injector pulse with the larger injector. To "fool" the ECM into compensating and issuing smaller injection pulses to deliver the correct amount of fuel, you install a MAF that lies to the ECM and tells it there is less air coming into the engine than there really is. It's a pretty slick idea actually and for high performance applications where the engine needs those larger injectors, it works ok but is still inferior to a real ECM tweak. The downside to doing this on an engine that doesn't need larger injectors is you throw the load calculations off. The ECM still believes there's less air coming in and every calculation (ignition timing, injector timing, automatic shifting controls if you have any, etc) that's based on the MAF voltage will not be quite right. But again, this is where "close" is often good enough, even if not optimal. However your question was what would I do in this case. I'd have probably tried the ProM curve and if it ran like crap, then used my TwEECer to find out how to tweak the curve to be....less crappy. As well, I'd have gone verifying that my MAF was, indeed, calibrated for 30# injectors. In essence, that's exactly what I did with my C&L 73mm MAF I bought off of eBay a while back. I bought it expecting it to be a 73mm calibrated for 19# injectors as advertised in the auction. I installed it and it ran like T-total crap. Turns out the guy that sold it to me didn't realize it still had a blue sampling tube, the tube used for 24# injectors. I believe it was an honest mistake since the original box did have 19lb written in multiple places. He was probably selling it for someone else and just didn't know. At the time, I suspicioned that the problem was the tube, but didn't know what to look for to determine what type tube I really had. I figured there had to be some kind of identifier somewhere or posted diameter specs that I could compare my tube against. So I began researching how to determine what sampling tube I had inclusing calling C&L. That's when I learned C&L color-codes their tubes and a blue mark on my tube indicated my 73mm MAF was setup for 24# injectors...hence the lean crappy performance. Now that I have a TwEECer, that's an easy fix, but without a TwEECer, the right tube, the right injectors, or some other ECM tuner, my MAF was useless to me. After further investigation, I found that using the blue tube on 19# injectors and tuning the ECM with the blue-tube curve isn't really the best thing to do for resolution reasons which tangents to a different discussion altogether. Now that I've gotten myself way off subject, again, my point was that a C&L 73mm w/clear tube can flow more air than a 55mm will. Because of this, the C&L has a slightly different curve even though both are for use with 19lb injectors. Just like a 75mm & 80mm MAF calibrated for 30# injectors can be slightly different, but still work. But how do they do it? Well, the manufacturers accept the fact that it'll be a little different than factory but still "close enough", and then advertise it as a fine-tuned curve. And who knows, perhaps the factory A9L/A9P tune was a little too rich@WOT and could use some leaning out as C&L claims. posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Fri Mar 31, 2006 7:53 pm Hi, One thing to be careful of when using high order fits. They can wiggle beyond where you have data, sometimes going wild, depending on the points you're trying to fit. High order doesn't always mean high accuracy, especially when you are extrapolating. I would suggest that you plot out each fit over the whole five volt range and take the one which looks the best to you. If it noses over out beyond where you have data points, the curve fit is probably baked. You've got to tune out there anyway, so take the one which is slightly richer and monotonically increasing, just to be safe. My two cents! I made mine run 99% duty cycle Some calculations for determining Injector sizing. Fuel Requirements: Fuel Pressure - 43 psig is industry standard factory set point (except Ford which is 38.9 psig). Increasing the FP at the fuel rails increases the HP potential of the injectors. Injector size - in pounds per hour. Duty cycle - percentage of time operating. To avoid over-heating & damaging injectors, do not exceed 80%. B.S.F.C. - Brake Specific Fuel Consumption - The weight of fuel in pounds required to produce one horsepower for one hour. For supercharged engines = .6 (NA= .55). FWHP - Fly-Wheel Horse Power. RWHP - Rear Wheel Horse Power. ((Fuel Pressure/43)*Injector Size)*((Duty Cycle*BSFC)*Number of Cylinders = FWHP - 17% drive line loss = RWHP or ((43 psig/43)*50 lbs per hour)*((0.80)/0.60)*8 = 533 FWHP - 91 HP (17% drive line loss) = 442 RWHP I hope these help. 1998 Cobra. posts.content: terrorize Gear Head Posts: 3 Joined: Sat Mar 25, 2006 11:47 pm Location: palmdale Quote Post by terrorize » Thu Mar 30, 2006 1:58 pm well first off you need to know what your comp ratio is-----when raising your compression ratio your motor more efficient during the combustion process-----one car running 10psi with a 10:1 cr will make more power than a 9:1 cr car running 10psi--------- general rule of thumb for a hp to injector size is-------set a hp limit(600hp)----next multiply the brake specific fuel comsumption(bsfc)---(were going with a turbofoxbody 5.0 with 9.5:1cr) 600x.57=342 now divide the # of cylinder in the engine 8--------342/8=42.75-----this 42.75 represents the size of the injector in lbs/hr-------this is also @ 100% duty cycle---------now generally the most you wanna run the DC is 80-87%--- 85 ususally best-----this is to keep the injectors from over heating and pthe rreasons im not going into----now divide the 42.75 by .85 for the size injectoor you need to run in order for you to have 42.75lb/hr @85% DC---finally 50.29lb/hr injectors or 50lb/hr-----now BSFC for your car is definately different--that was on a highly modded car already dyno tuned and all figures were methodically calculated Top

posts.content: wa_4x4builder Regular Posts: 106 Joined: Wed Mar 30, 2005 12:37 pm Location: Seattle, Washington Quote Post by wa_4x4builder » Mon Apr 03, 2006 11:47 am cgrey8 wrote: I have an A9P and I set mine from the 100°F default to 35°. I either don't get close enough in my MAF mods or I overshoot and get numbers on the other side of 1. You're trying for perfection and I suggest you will never get it. If you are within +- 3 percent of the ideal 1.000 KAMRF, I'd say you are about as good as anyone could ask for. Remember, that's the job of the KAMRFs- to adjust for variances in the control systems. They are doing their job and there is no sense in tinkering with getting them to stay at 1.000 always. I mean, if you are up for a challenge, I say go for it. But, practically speaking a little variance is just fine. cgrey8 wrote: I'm about to come to the conclusion that my MAF isn't that consistent. However my worst KAMRF values were 1.12 which appears to be as high as the ECM will "learn" to. I've gotten the ECM to learn closer to 1 now, but the numbers are still in the 1.09 range for some area. For the very lowest loads, I found that instead of tweaking the MAF, try adjusting your Injector Low-Slope scalar. My A9P had a default of 26lb/hr which proved too high for my particular 19lb/hr injectors. I've currently adjusted mine down to 22lb/hr and could probably come off of that a tad more to further hone in my numbers closer to 1 on the low end of my KAMRF table. Also making this change fixed a cold-crank stumble I was experiencing. The reason you are specifically seeing 1.121 is because of the scalar named MAXADP. It's default value is 0.621094 which, as stated, limits the maximum value of your adaptive learning cells. The initial value for the adpative tables is 0.5. If you take that 0.5 and add it to MAXADP, you get 1.121094. I'm sure CalCon is rounding this to the 1.121 you see. Raise the MAXADP and see what values you get (you said the max you have now is 1.09, so I wouldn't expect any numbers over 1.121). The maxium value for this scalar is 1.0 resulting in a maximum KAMRF of 1.5. On the other end of the spectrum, you can use MINADP (default of 0.378906) resulting in the lowest stock value for KAMRF of 0.878906. The minimum value for this scalar is 0.0 resulting in the lowest value of KAMRF being 0.5. As you point out, there seems to be multiple ways to solve a problem. While most guys would not change the injector slope values when they use the stock 19lb injectors, you have and seem to have success. Perhaps, it's another option when trying to solve a problem. What exact problem was it that you tried to solve? You state "at the lowest loads"- does that mean idle or are you talking about a decel situation or something else? To answer Pat's question specifically, no, it doesn't seem to have any impact on the control systems after lowering that value. I'm running my min ACT at 40 degrees and have for a long time. I don't see what your setup is, so I can't comment. But, I can say that I'm running all the induction components from a 2000 explorer which has the ACT integrated within the MAF sensor. This produces drastically lower ACT values than a stock Mustang (in my case, I'm using an A9L) which forced me to lower the ACT learning value or I would not have any adaptive take place. I've been running this way for over a year without issue. Lower it and tune away! :) Chris '93 EDIS 5.0L with A9L installed into a '77 Bronco. Top

Think of this as your personal data that you would put into quicken, MS word or excel. The main reasons for the different calibrations is for emmisions. posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Mon Apr 03, 2006 7:33 pm Hi Garsten, You've picked on the right function for timing -- WOT spark advance vs RPM. Have you added timing with one of the scalars (WOT spark adder?) to get to 33.5 degrees total? I'd suggest smoothing out the curve or going to a dyno and getting the thing dialed in so that your whole torque curve is maximized. If you want to change the curve, you can put in anything you like. You can be much more agressive than stock for sure. You could play some games with air/fuel ratio with the scalars (WOT fuel adder in the a9l) if you wanted to tweak for weather conditions. My stock engine liked about 38 degrees total, my 342 likes 36 and doesn't give you any more power if you run more advanced timing. Yours might like something else (YMMV!). Since you're not controlling the transmission with the computer, you can probably set it the load type to 3 (manual) and let the transmission shift when the governor or your shifter tell it to. I think the advantage the tweaker (or EFI) has is that you can max out the whole curve instead of just one point. I will say though that a carb is easier to tune and stays really flat across the whole RPM range once it's dialed in. Best of luck, Fritz Coast 342, AFR185's, TFS stage II cam,30# inj, 76mm C&L, 1 3/4 hooker long tubes, 3.70 gears, Spec stage II clutch, an A9L and a TwEECer RT, 11.84 @120.4 w/100hp shot Top

posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Tue Apr 04, 2006 8:20 pm I think the rule of thumb is to pull out one degree for every 25 hp, so 4 degrees for a 100 hp shot. If you want to add fuel you can use the WOT fuel multiplier or use the open loop fuel multiplier scalar to add it across the board. I tuned mine on a chassis dyno which was very helpful. I pulled enough timing to be safe, then set the jets so that the A/F was 11:1, then added timing back in. I wound up using a 120 hp shot and pulling 5 degrees out. I didn't touch the air/fuel -- I used the same tune as I did without nitrous except pulling the timing out with the scalar. My motor has a 9.25:1 compression which lets me run about 31 degrees total at the 120 hp level. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Mon Feb 06, 2006 11:27 am LOADX is the one you want to look at. This is the calculated load plus minus all other variables. The EEC will use LOADX for all of its calculation. Depending on the setting of the scalar 'Load scaling switch' the EEC will either calculate load from the MAF and engine size which is actual load or from actual load plus or minus other variables. Either way the calculated result ends up in the LOADX parameter. if 'Load Scaling Switch' = 0 then LoadX = (load/load scaling) x (29.9/BP) else LoadX = load end if 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Apr 05, 2006 9:39 am Basically what I did was adjust the curve when the S/C belt was off. I want to dial in the N/A setup to where the motor hit 100 percent at WOT. When the S/C belt is on then the load may see 145 in my case. I then know the efficiency of my S/C. I then scaled all of my load tables to say something around 175. I believe the reason behind this function is so that Ford could use one set of load tables for all models of cars. All they needed to do is adjust this one table. All of the tables referring to load would not have to change there load scale on the X or Y axis. This is not to say that the values for each cell within those tables would not change because they would definitely change. It was simply so they did not have to rescale all of the tables. title: Are there dangers with excessive advance even w/o knock? - EECTuning.org

posts.content: cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Are there dangers with excessive advance even w/o knock? Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Mar 30, 2006 12:03 pm For those following my other issues, I had a hesitation/surge at cruising speeds. Looking at my KAMRF tables, I had values that were up in the 1.12 range for low loads/low RPM. I modified the MAF table to account for this and now my surging appears to be gone. It drove beautifully once I got that sorted out. Next I started tinkering with advance. Since the A9P lets me adjust WOT and partial throttle advance separately, I've been working to find the max amount of advance I can get on either before I get the familiar "ping." Based on a comment someone else made about EGR gas helping to prevent knock, I decided I'd go playing with the EGR tables and functions. I've got a rather aggressive EGR curve now and as a result, I've got some rather high advance multipliers due to that. So far, the truck runs fine, but I'm logging advance in the high 40s and 50s. Occasionally, it jumps into the 60s at cruising loads. But I don't get any valve knock or any unusual behavior due to it. posts.author: Fritz
posts.content: Fritz Regular Posts: 74 Joined: Wed Nov 06, 2002 12:04 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Fritz » Thu Mar 30, 2006 7:30 pm Hi Cgrey, From what I understand, you get more power as you advance until you hit MBT timing. This is the minimum timing needed to produce the maximum torque at a given engine speed. This also corresponds to the most work you can get out of the fuel at those conditions (i.e. a fixed EGR, MAP and RPM). You don't loose as much torque (i.e. work) for too much advance as you do for too little advance, but you loose some. If you start burning too early, you have to do work to compress the burned mixture -- the combustion event is out of phase and you get losses. When you put in EGR or dilution (you dilute the mixture with unburnable gas which happens to have a high specific heat) there are a number of things which occur, some good, some not so good. For fuel economy and emissions, some EGR is good. EGR is not good for making power, so it is shut off at WOT. EGR increases fuel economy because it decreases power -- the burned gasses replace some of the fresh charge and you don't get as much power per cycle. Where you get fuel economy is that you don't have to throttle the engine as much. It is the same idea that they have with cylinder deactivation, you get less power but you don't have the pumping losses that you get when you throttle the engine. Pumping losses are like putting your finger over a syringe and pulling down the plunger. You've got to do work to decrease the density of the air inside (force * distance) which is what you are doing to the engine when you have the throttle shut. You are decreasing the density of the air to reduce the power. EGR improves emissions of NOx because it lowers the temperatures seen during combstion due to the high specific heat. High Cp means that you get less temperature rise for a given amount of energy input. Unfortunately, as 2Shaker mentioned, eventually the mixture doesn't burn (or doesn't burn fast enough) and you can get high hydrocarbon emissions. Good heads can support more EGR than stock, mostly due to better mixing. You could probably increase the EGR a bit, then run a touch more advance. It would be hard to dial this in for best fuel economy, because it might be hard to tell when you stepped over the edge. You shouldn't do much damage with more timing at low loads, but over time if you are knocking, you could eventually hurt something. Good luck with the tuning, you're entering into an area most of us never really touch. Generally winter fuel doesn't get you as good of gas mileage since it is oxygenated, but whether it was the temp or the fuel mix, my advance has had to come way down and I've lost some fuel efficiency. :( I also found that excessive EGR flow was causing some lean conditions during acceleration. What was happening is a slight lean condition was returning way more of the unburned O2 back into the intake which is "unmetered" air that wasn't detected by the MAF. Therefore, the ECM was never able to fully overcome the lean condition until I backed off and allowed the ECM to adjust at a steady load and steady RPM. Eventually it would figure out how much fuel it took to make the O2s go .48v, but as soon as it found it, it was overcompensated. That .48v exhaust runs back into the intake as is far less O2 than the ECM had adjusted for so it then ran rich. Under stable conditions, the ECM would eventually even out and get things under control, but under acceleration, things were happening faster than the ECM would react to. So I had to back off my EGR positions as well. I'm just curious as to why it took warm air to start showing this problem. Cold intake air seemed to work great. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Apr 11, 2006 5:39 am Keep in mind the spark adder based on EGR is accumulative. So if you have .75 in the EGR spark adder table, that's .75 for every % of EGR. Flipping back and forth between the EGR base and EGR Spark adder, you'll notice you've got some pretty high % numbers at places around 2000 RPM and 40%. Thus, you'll get some moderate addition to your base spark while driving in this region. In my version on CalEdit, there are some Notes about EGR Spark Adder that explains what's going on. Check them out to verfiy what I'm saying. You also have some functions that control spark. Some that retard spark based on certain conditions (mostly knock sensor stuff), others that add spark, like the table that adds spark based on RPM or adjusts spark based on ACT & ECT. You may be getting some multiplication or addition in your final spark value from them. It's something else to look at... Also keep in mind these are things I have in my A9P, I don't know what all is in the CBAZA. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: igotbit
posts.content: igotbit Regular Posts: 79 Joined: Sat Jun 21, 2003 9:44 pm Quote Post by igotbit » Thu Apr 13, 2006 12:50 am I'm assuming you have and a9l.. The WOT fuel multiplier vs. RPM is the correct function to modify. This function is used when the WOT Breakpoint voltage Scalar is reached by the TPS. So, if you have the Breakpoint voltage set at 0 or a low number it will activate the function as you described. I had mine set at 2 volts with 12 psi and it worked pretty good... Also set the Open loop throttle breakpoint scalar at the same voltage. Don't set it two high, or you may never activate the function when you need the fuel. This is the only way I know of that creates the problem you are describing with this function. 351W, A9L, TF intake, AFR 185s, 75mm TB, NA. Top

posts.author: pthornton
posts.content: pthornton Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Sat Nov 01, 2003 5:11 pm Location: Tupelo, MS Quote Post by pthornton » Mon Apr 10, 2006 1:49 pm Since you have matching injectors and MAF, you don't absolutely have to enter the correct MAF curve injector settings. You can scale the CID to bring your load values into alignment. This should get the car running well. If you scale the CID down, then you should NOT change the MAF curve, injector settings etc... If you really want to dive into driveability, then you will need to input the correct MAF curve, injector settings etc... You can use the above tune as a fallback until you figure this part out. I would start with MAF, injector settings and use EEC analyzer to dial in the bottom of the MAF. Then dig in to the ISC neutral air flow/ throttle body air flow settings to really dial in the idle. Use a wideband to dial in the upper RPM of the MAF curve. PS. Some say it is heresay to use the CID scalar instead of the correct MAF/injector settings, but to each his own. I say whatever works. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Sun Apr 16, 2006 2:09 pm vristang wrote: JuiceSC wrote: On an N/A engine, you could set timing by vacuum. ) I have never heard of this process. Can you elaborate or direct me to a writeup somewhere? NCFordMan Most of the typical questions you will have on the base setup will be answered in the TwEECer Manual. The manual is a little confusing, but it does have some good info. Don't hesitate to post questions though. thanks jason This techique was passed on to me by a gear head way back in the day. You can set timing by vacuum and listening to the engine. Here are the basics: Start with the engine fully warmed up, pull out spout. Start engine and let it settle into an idle. Now rotate the distributor back and forth to find the "sweet spot". As you retard the timing you will note a drop in rpms and vacuum. Thats your "low limit" now advance the timing until you see the highest vacuum (any more advance won't yield higher manifold vacuum) reading and idle speed should increase. This is your "high limit". Now back start retarding the timing until you start seeing a drop in vacuum. This is where I used to set my carbed cars. This will get you a very close to ideal BASE timing. From here, I like to drive the car and listen for pinging and possibly try a little more timing if its not pinging. This is by NO MEANS AS ACCURATE as a timing light, however, it WILL get you running. Hence, I would not time a boosted car with this method. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. "FIRING ORDERS Another thing to remember when doing an EFI conversion is that there is 2 different firing orders for small block Fords. Early 289's, 302's and some late model 302's run the 15426378 firing order. Late model 302 HO's and 351W run the 13726548 firing order. Installing EFI on the 15426378 firing order is possible, but does not yield the same results as the late model HO firing order. When you mix, match these firing orders you may encounter some driveability problems like poor idle quality. The Mustang EFI system is a sequential fuel injection system, which means that the injectors are fired in a firing order just like the spark plugs. Mixing these firing orders (spark plug & injectors) can cause a rough idle and poor driveability. If you are building an engine for an EFI conversion, make sure that the cam you install has the 13726548 firing order. Some people may tell you that all you have to do is rewire the injectors to change their firing order to match your cam or engine. I can tell you from experience that this does not work, it causes erratic fuel control, back firing thru the inatke manifold (at times), rolling or hunting idle and poor driveability overall. I learned the reason for this once I started reprogramming PCM's for different engine modifications. In the Cal Edit Software there is a table called Exhaust Pulse Delay, what this means is that from the time the #1 injector sprays fuel into the #1 cylinder it knows how many crankshaft revolutions it will take before that exhaust (fuel) passes the bank 1 oxygen sensor and so on for every cylinder of that engine. This also explains why installing long tube headers can cause idle and driveability issue too." 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Sun Apr 16, 2006 10:05 pm The vacuum timing trick works great on a carbureted car but I'm not sure it works on an injected car. Nevertheless, there is a way to figure out mechanically where to time it. It doesn't sound like you have a pointer so you need to put one on. Use a positive stop in cylinder number 1 and gently turn to the motor over unil it hits the stop and put a mark on the damper at the pointer. Now rotate the engine in the opposite direction until you come up against the stop and put another mark on the damper. The point in the middle of these two marks is TDC for #1. Remove the stop and turn the motor to TDC and then mount your permanent pointer and/or install a timing tape if the damper is not marked to work with your pointer. Once you have this figured out then you simply need to make sure the motor is on the compression/fire stroke and install the distributor on number 1. There, do I have you thoroughly confused now? :-) By the way, I think positive stops that screw into the plug hole are available from cam makers. 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. title: Big improvement - switched from W4H0 to J4J1 - EECTuning.org

posts.content: 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Big improvement - switched from W4H0 to J4J1 Quote Post by 2Shaker » Tue Apr 18, 2006 11:52 am I hope you guys don't mind this post here instead of lounge, but I figured it might help others Tweecing. Over the winter we converted the car from AODE to a TKO 600. Built a customized J4J1 based tune to go with the conversion but at first I kept the W4H0 tune I had for the automatic to at least get the car running reliably and any mechanical bugs worked out. This weekend I did the switch to the J4J1 and the difference is amazing, and some things I cannot yet explain. I am using the exact same MAF, injector slopes, injector_offset_vs_battery_voltage, and sealevel_load_scaling in both tunes but the load values being logged are lower with the J4J1 tune. In addition, I changed the fuel crank and startup table and the stabilized fuel table to match the W4H0 tune too. 1. It does not jump out of CL as easiliy as it did with the W4H0 tune. I attribute this to the lower load computations. 2. The bucking has been eliminated 3. The hanging idle is gone 4. It seems to pull harder than with the W4H0 based tune. Could be my imagination too, but it feels incredibly strong. 5. It is much smoother and more responsive just cruising down the road. There is one other thing I did coincident with the switch to the J4J1 tune. I replaced the 42# injectors with a set of Ford "matched" 42# injectors. We did put the old 42#'s on an injector flow tester and found 2 of the 8 flowed almost 10% less than the other 6, but they were still in spec. Interestingly enough, these two injectors were in cylinders 2 and 8 which were two of the cylinders I burned pistons in last year (see the "good news not so good news" post in lounge). I am baffled by the seemingly lower load values being logged with the J4J1 tune. But I am really happy with the way it is acting so I don't think I am going to mess with it much. We are going to the track in the next couple of weeks to see what happens. I do hope that my son quickly gets the hang for stirring the gears at WOT and we go quicker than we did when it was an automatic. :-) And I hope it doesn't break! 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Thu Apr 20, 2006 6:44 am 66 injectedcobra wrote: Juice, thanks for your input. What table exactly would I tweek to get that squared away? Are you refering to open loop like right when I first fire up the car and it has not dropped into closed loop? If it runs alil fat and choppy what table do I go to for slight adjustment? ...Mike I only make adjustments based on logs on a FULLY WARMED UP engine. Logging and making changes based on logs during startup and warmup at first is useless IMO. Get the hot drivability down and it should start fine hot or cold. I like tuning with the maf transfer. I cruise at light loads, maintaining speed and look at KAMRF at specific airflow points. Then depending on the KAMRF, I adjust those specific points only on the maf. When the tune is pretty close, KAMRFs are very active and respond to throttle and airflow changes very quickly. For example, I'm running down the road and I'm seeing 120 Kg/hr flow and my KAMRF is greater than 1. I would adjuts a few points in the maf (to blend the curve) around the 120 Kg flow rate according to what the KAMFRF was on the drive. 1.05 KAMRF, adding 5% should do the trick. But I would add 2% and retest, then 2% more and retest to "sneak up" on it. The bigger the injectors, the harder it will be to get a decent idle and drivability. I've read the analogy somewhere, that its like using a firehose to try to fill a shot glass (idle, low throttle). Injector offset vs batt volts may be one that might need a little adjustment. This function has a pretty noticable impact on the tune at low airflow rates. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. posts.author: DrDirt
posts.content: DrDirt Tuning Addict Posts: 512 Joined: Wed Jun 30, 2004 7:45 am Location: Largo, Fl I think I'll give up on Closed Loop Quote Post by DrDirt » Wed Apr 19, 2006 10:22 am Yup, I'm finally fed up with chasing my tail. I've started over a zillion times and always end up in the same spot, namely a tune that runs pretty good everywhere except I can have my choice of lean idle and good warmup/drive away or a lean warmup/drive away and a good idle. It could be a case of too much information being a bad thing though. When I say lean, I mean in the 16 AFR range at idle or right after startup until the car is fully warmed up on decel and coasting to a light, the AFR will go from 14.6 to 17 or 18 and sometimes even 19 until I take off again. I suppose if I didn't have an AFR gauge or CalEdit to look at, I wouldn't know and I wold think the car was running great. OTOH, I've got a nice Open Loop all the time tune that has everything about where I want it...except for the first 15 seconds of startup is leaner than commanded but it doesn't seem to be a problem for the car. It still sounds good and feels good. I can probably swat that with the Fuel OL Startup multi. But I can't help but think if I could just get that CL tune to click in, I'd be looking at some better mileage. Plus, I'm not really sure how changes in weather will affect the open loop tune. The trouble is, if I stop trying to hit the "perfect tune", I don't know what I will do with all that extra time in the evenings and at work when I'm not eyeball deep in a datalog or some Tweecer definitions. I'm going to need a 12 step program to back down. I have the tune OL set to only one O2, even though I have both in the car. I think I have seen in some posts that the EEC does use the data, it just doesn't store them. I'm not so sure that is the case though simply because my OL tune is so close with the commanded AFR and the logged AFR but if the only change I make going back to Closed Loop is to turn on adaptive and set the min load for closed loop fuel control back up to the stock setting, all of a sudden the AFR is leaner in almost all areas and the KAM is at about .964 at cruise. I could be wrong...and probably am...but I was expecting it would only want to make minor tweeks once in closed loop. Granted, I only drove it as far as it took for adaptive to kick in (about 5 or 6 minutes) and then turned around and drove back home. When I got back, I just cleared the KAM and switched it back to the OL tune because I didn't really want to get back into chasing the MAF transfer around again using $3.00 per gallon gas. As it stands, I've burned enough gas fooling around with the tuning process that I could have probably bought a fully built monster street car and had Chris Johnson fly down and spend a week on a dyno tuning every last little parameter in the EEC...but it wouldn't have been as much fun and I wouldn't have learned anything. Not that there isn't still some tremendous gaps in what I know. That's the only one I know of that has negative numbers. If so, that table is not in the A9P. The A9P has Fuel Table Stabilized CL with all 1's in the cells but it doesn't use that table. If you are running an A9P, I don't think you can just load up a tune for an A9L. I think they use different memory addresses for some of the same things so you will get some strange results. You can manually punch in the values from an A9L into the corresponding A9P but I'm not sure that will get you where you are wanting to go. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Thu Apr 20, 2006 9:48 pm 1) Download the A9M zip file 2) Unzip the A9M.dat file to the 'C:\Program Files\STKR 1.30A\Data' directory 3) It will ask you to overwrite the old file. click yes. 4) Open Cal Edit 5) Open your ccf file 6) Goto the utilities tab and unselect the all payloads except RPM now press the payload. 7) Upload the CCF. Now select all of the payloads that you want and hit the payload button. 9) Now upload the CCF again. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sat Apr 22, 2006 7:59 pm The only code I would be concerned with is the 66. Code 15 is becasue of the base address not being set to 0. The code 95 is indeed the sendary fuel pump circuit. All this is, is a wire that needs to be run from the fuel pump relay back to the EEC. It is a circuit to make sure the fuel pump relay is working. I had to run this wire when I did my Mass air conversion. It will not harm anything if it is not fixed. Code 29 will affect the decel logic in the EEC. On most sticks it will cause stalls on decel. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue Apr 04, 2006 1:07 pm True maf transfer tables are calibrated to measure air mass at the eec STP of air (which Ford have set at 1.1334 kg/m3) and when ever you use a a maf transfer that's calibrated for a particular set of injectors or start major adjustments to your transfer table to bring your adaptive tables to 1.000 it means the eec no longer knows the true mass of air entering. This in turns means that your load calculations will be out as essentially load = VE as far as the eec is concerned. The eec relies on knowing the true characteristics of the engine displacement, air flow injector size etc to function correctly and I sit in the camp of those who think this is the only 'correct' way to tune it. (That said I acknowledge if you have a forced induction engine running lots of boost then it's easily possible to exceed the 200% load limit and then you are into having to fool the eec or if the particular intake system is causing substantial deviations in laminar flow then the maf will be out). My method of rescaling the tables is simple but entails adjusting a lot of tables; if a modified engine produces more load than the last row of the table then I 'shuffle' the values in the table downwards to create a new row that I can populate with figures for the higher load; e.g if my old table had the load in rows 1 to 10 as; 5 10 15 25 35 45 55 65 75 85 and the engine now produces a maximum of 95% load I would rescale the rows as say; 5 11 16 27 38 49 60 71 82 95 and then alter the values to suit. I similarly rescale the tables if the maximum rpm is raised significantly beyond the last table value Top

Right, now looking at your info again, this is what I would do; Set the Load_Scaling_Switch from 2 to 1 (2 means PEAK_LOAD_PERCENTAGE (aka LOADX) = INFERRED_PERCENT_LOAD and 1 means PEAK_LOAD_PERCENTAGE (aka LOADX) = LOAD) this will bring your peak load right down and the LOAD_SCALING_SEALEVEL_TABLE is ignored. I would then adjust the tables for the extra load your engine produces as described before. The alternative is to set the Load_Scaling_Switch to 0 and alter the LOAD_SCALING_SEALEVEL_TABLE to suit the engine and then adjust the values in your tables. My dislike of this is that some tables use LOAD and others use LOADX and I prefer to have the same scaling in both. Top
