posts.author: codedout
posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Hope for newbies Quote Post by codedout » Mon Jul 17, 2006 10:40 am This may be the wrong place to post this so if the moderators feel like moving it go ahead. After well over 200 different tunes and 7 months of work I have the following to offer some of the newer people here. I am not a pro at this by any stretch of the imagination. One thing to keep in mind even thought EA (eecAnalyzer) does a great job there is still things that is cannot compensate for. Specifically it calculates 1 specific thing at a time; it does try to factor in many variables. It will get you 90 percent of the way very quickly. However that last 10 percent could take you 90 percent of your time. Now that being said.... When you start fine tuning, stay in the big picture, all too often I found myself focusing on an issue, only to find I was tuning in the wrong area. Try to make only 1 or 2 gradual changes. EG Don’t just add 6-8 degrees of timing. Add in 2 at a time and remember timing does affect idle, so you may have to go back and re-setup your base idle and ISC transfer. It is a good idea each time you make changes to run through the entire setup each time to make sure that while tuning one thing that it did not affect another thing. Look at it like this imagine water glasses on a table tied together with rubber bands, when you move one, all of them move a little. I am sure many of you will get discouraged as I have been at times. We have all put a lot of money into these cars, and don’t want them to blow up. There were time I made 1 step forward and 3 back. Many times I started over with the original bin file and started from scratch. I save every time I made a change and documented the changes I amde, I also made notes on each change as to its affects on the tune. You can got lost very quickly if you are not organized. One piece of advice I can give, do it right the first time. If not you are wasting your money. Perfect example, 1)I got cheap at the last minute, and re-used the distributor from my old motor, to save $200 bucks. I ended up having to pull the motor and replace the cam, as the distributor seized and tore up my cam. 2)I purchased a LM-1 WB, figuring I could use it on other cars, well the tailpipe piece doesn’t handle vibration while driving very well and vibrates loose, smashing my back window and destroying the O2 sensor and tailpipe piece. Get a good WB and install it in the car if you are tuning on the street. I wish you all the luck in your tuning, and hope you have the success that I have had. I would also like to thank all of the folks on this board for their help and support. BTW it is still not finished, but I feel I am 98 percent there. Love the driveability and the power. The last 2 percent I am going to do on a dyno. I will tell you though that when we ran our car last week I noticed I was only getting 9 degrees advance in the lights but my tables are set to 18 degress at 5000 RPM and above, and .89 load and above. So why was it so low? Because the spark_retard_for_ACT function and the spark_bdln_retard_ACT_multi table were coming into play. We were at 176 degrees ACT at the end of the run (it's supercharged). So I think if you set the max retard scalar to a positive number you will effectively disable this function from occuring. But I wouldn't do that unless you are N/A, and then it wouldn't matter anyway because you will never see an ACT that high. I thought that it might be the bypass valve not operating properly. But I looked at it last night, and it IS functioning at idle at least. It almost looks like it's adjustable (sort of like a fuel pressure regulator), however there's no information on how to adjust it. We re-clocked the MAF though and I think that DID help quite a bit. He said it's still doing the surge but nowhere near as bad as it was. So it could be we need to work on the MAF clocking some more. Unfortunately, Procharger sticks a 90* bend right in front of, and right behind the MAF. Plus it's a C&L, so right there you've got tons of problems. Too bad he doesn't have a Pro-M Universal. That would probably work much better. Hopefully we can get it worked out though. When it's not surging, the thing is an Animal! 14 psi of boost, ported E'brock heads, E'brock intake, F cam, 3.73's, etc. etc. I think it's got 10's in it. www.twinturbostang.com '97 Cobra - VT billet stroker shortblock, LLX4, TwEECer RT v1.30A9 '91 coupe - Incon Twin Turbo (gone, but not forgotten) Top

posts.content: 94Wrangler Regular Posts: 64 Joined: Thu Jun 08, 2006 8:15 am Location: Missouri Sealevel load scaling vs RPM (New Info on topic) Quote Post by 94Wrangler » Tue Jul 11, 2006 11:12 pm I have been using the EEC analyzer and don’t want to step on Clints toes, and I also want to say his program saves me alot of time and is great. But I have come to some different conclusions then anyone has mentioned that I noticed 1. The load scaling graph is identical to your torque curve 2. If you see 110% load at 3500 and the data on your load vs. rpm function shows 85.5 then you take 85.5 x 1.1 = 94.05 that compensates for the 10% over and gives you 100% These are just my thoughts so feel free to throw in your opinions. Also at idle I had 36% load and I feel 25% would be the correct value so I added 10% to my 0rpm and 800rpm value Volume efficiency is tied to the engine combo like the heads, cam, and so on. So there for where the engine can pull the most air it can also make the most power at that same point. In example my peak torque is 4850 and my highest volume efficiency is also at 4850. 94 Jeep Wrangler, Ford 5.0L, A9P, TwEECer RT, .030 over 5.0, Explorer Ported upper and lower, AFR 165's, E303 with 1.6's, 75mm TB, 76mm C&L MAF, 24# squirters, BBK shorty chromes, 2 1/2 w/dumps, AOD with transgo Kit, Explorer 8.8 31spline w/4.88's Top

posts.content: G. Craig Regular Posts: 160 Joined: Fri Oct 31, 2003 9:29 pm Location: Hickory Creek, Texas Quote Post by G. Craig » Sun Jul 16, 2006 4:08 pm TonyF wrote: If something happened to the clearing switch, the car would not start, no power to the computer, there is also the unlikely chance that it could short to ground, thus blowing the fuse. IIRC, the OEM wiring has fusible link in KAPWR. Perhaps what you've indicated applies to an EECIV but, I don't think it applies to an EECV PCM. Because pin #55 labeled "B+ Keep Alive Power (KAPWR)" in the Ford TSP, only serves the (KAM) after the ignition is turned off even though it is hot all the time. Pin #97 labeled "Vehicle Power (VPWR)" is the main source of power for the PCM but switched in conjunction with the ignition. While performing a search I discovered another thread about installing a KAM clearing switch; one of the contributors posted that he has forgotten to turn the KAM switch back on for his car and it started and ran just fine. He also went on to say the PCM began to store information in KAM like normal. So this would seem to indicate that KAM has more than one source of power. 1998 Cobra. CRAJ0/AOL3. Here is what I posted before about the lean-out at tip-in: 1. I lowered the Load Limit for OL vs ECT (FN320A) to .5 @ 0F & .7 @ 200F - this got rid of the stumbling right away until I could figure out why it was happening. Load scaling makes this threshold higher than it used to be anyway, so this change just brings the threshold for OL back to where is was before load scaling. This is not the smoothest transition. 2. I raised the Accel Enrichment Fuel (FN1303) lowest throttle rate (17 deg/sec) from 5 @ 50F to 8 @ 50F , I made it all 6's above that. I blended all the way up to the max throttle rate (122 deg/sec). I was mostly adding more fuel at lower throttle tip-in rates. 3. I changed the minimum TP rate in Accel Enrichment Fuel to 10 deg/sec from 17. (makes it more sensitive to slower tip-ins - with a big TB this is important!) 4. I changed the Accel Pump Multiplier (AEM) to 1 from 0.39 (more fuel here too). 5. I lowered all thresholds for open loop to 0 seconds & OL & WOT thrershold voltages to 2.25 volts (from 2.71) (well, this was done long before the tip-in issues cropped up.) I logged AEFUEL in TwEECer (ver A10 only) and ensured that I was seeing AEFUEL for all tip-ins - even light ones - I was and stopped seeing the lean-outs @ tip-in. 428w now Top

posts.content: JaxMustang50 Regular Posts: 114 Joined: Thu Jul 31, 2003 11:37 pm Quote Post by JaxMustang50 » Thu Jul 27, 2006 11:00 am Sounds like the load scaling is way off. If you are seeing 78% or greater load at only 1.5 on the tps, it will trigger it to go to open loop. There also are two scalars that deal with what tps voltage is considered WOT. They are listed at 2.7xxx or something like that, but this means 3.7xxx roughly. It means that WOT is triggered at 2.7xxx volts above what it is at idle. These scalars are probably not your problem though. I would get the load scaling correct first. Top

posts.author: deron888
posts.content: deron888 Gear Head Posts: 58 Joined: Mon Oct 03, 2005 5:40 pm Quote Post by deron888 » Thu Jul 27, 2006 12:38 pm Your first question, you are going CL to OL because your loadx is high and you need to scale it down. When you are exceeding a certain load value, you go OL. Try this: Under Scalar "Load Scaling Switch", set it to "0". Then under Function "SeaLevel Load Scaling vs RPM", put in from X=0 RPM, Y=1 to X=3K RPM, Y=1.25 to X=6K RPM, Y=1.5. Try that to try to LOWER your load at idle and part-throttle. Your load should be at 18-25 at idle and you need to make sure when you go heavy throttle or WOT you hit the upper load values with loadx=90-110. You will need to adjust "Sealevel Load Scaling vs RPM" so you hit the load values at your fuel/spark Tables. Have you already tuned your MAF function to make sure its close to your MAF meter? You do this by going OL full time and tune with a wideband. Do a search on OL full time on here and just keep on searching and reading. 94 mustang GT, Vortech S-trim 5-lb, stock 5.0 internals, Tweecer R/T v1.30A9, LC-1 O2, extrude-honed intake manifold, shorty headers, after-cat Flowmasters, 70mm MAF, 65mm TB, Crane Cam ignition box w/ timing retard, 24lb injectors. First, your load calculation is off. You dont' want to set "time @ high load to force open loop" to anything but 0 seconds when using a blower. Use the sealevel load scaling function and CID scalar to fix your load problem. Increase CID scalar in 10 cid increments and test. Second, your maf transfer sounds like its too rich. posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Wed Jul 26, 2006 9:28 am There is a way to dial in your WOT MAF nearly perfectly using EA. Check the radio to use WB & hit Calculate. Then, instead of clicking the right hand button to use WB (this will target 14.64 AFR), type in the target AFR (LAMBSE) that you see at WOT in the box on the left & calculate. It will correct the MAF for the difference between your logged AFR & target LAMBSE. It get's it nearly perfect in one try! Note that this is ONLY for points where you are WOT - either filter or ignore the corrections below the voltage where the MAF is at WOT. You can eyeball the datalog to be sure. For closed loop I use KAMRF's to correct MAF as you guys do. 428w now Top

You might be seeing the TwEECer problem with how you enter data in any of these functions/tables etc. However you load your MAF (there are several ways to make it work) is the same method you need to use in this function. Here's how I do it. I put the cursor in the cell I wish to change, use the arrow key to step out of the cell, step back into the cell, and enter the values I want. Then I step back out of the cell and step to the next cell I wish to change. When finished with the entries, I save, then select another function (any) and then return to the function I'm editing to make sure it took. Then I exit CalEdit and then go back in, make sure the file name I just modified it the one displayed, and then go view the function to make sure it is what I wanted, keeping in mind that because of the "binary thing" the value might not be exact, but not off enough to matter either. It's a PITA, but I have been screwed so many times because I didn't go through this stupid process that I have learned to follow it faithfully. You aboslutely can change the values in this function. I do have a granatelli that I´m NOT satisfied with, and no flowsheet either... Peter Get a meter that will flow enough air without getting pegged (reaching 5v) with your long term combination. That way, if you decide to go with larger injectors later on, you will be able to keep the meter without having to replace it as well. There is however a problem with going with a meter that is too large. For example, a Pro-M calibrated for 50# injectors will most likely not flow enough at idle on a small motor to stay above the minimum voltage for the MAF (even after lowering it to something like .001 volts) and you may experience the check engine light with an error 66 Vane Air Flow (VAF) or Mass Air Flow (MAF) signal low. I would probably go with a 42# calibration. posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sat Jul 29, 2006 3:31 pm I use TunerPro RT, it's basically an editor that lets you modify just about anything you want to except the assembler code of an ecu. With it you can build your own ecu definition files (xdf's) or edit someone else's. I'm a big fan of it because I like the user interface and features such as the 'difference tool' that quickly lets you compare two bins for changes. The author, Mark Mansur, is a top man who helps out a lot if you've got a problem with the software and is constantly working to improve it. The only downside is that xdf's for eec's are pretty scarce, there are quite a few people who have developed them for their own ecu's but they aren't listed anywhere. That said, there are people on the TunerPro and Moates forums who do help people get started on their own. I have to develop my own xdf's as the European ecu's I tinker with are not supported by anyone and without TunerPro I never would have been able to get into eec tuning in any meaningful way. Give it a try, the more who use it the better it'll become :D Top

posts.author: 5.0Rick
posts.content: 5.0Rick Regular Posts: 167 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 9:32 am Injector Timing How to -A9L Quote Post by 5.0Rick » Mon Jul 24, 2006 12:24 am Hi Everyone, Just thought I would share how I am using Performance Trends Cam Analyzer to find the appropriate injector timing for a non stock cam. http://www.performancetrends.com/ca20.htm 1st you will need the stock cam specs http://www.carcraft.com/techarticles/11 ... to_12.html Stock Ford HO Cam Specs 276 Advertised duration on Intake 266 Advertised duration on Exhaust LC 115.5 Lift .27823 .444 with 1.6 Rockers Enter these into the CA program and find the lift at the given degrees that are in the stock injector timing table by running a report on Intake Cam Data. Just enter the cam specs in the “test/cam setup” menu and run a “report” on Int cam data. Unfortunately I could not find 0.050 values for the stock cam so used the advertised numbers for the stock cam. Stock degrees lift@cam lobe 352 .0053 380 .0661 400 .1320 420 .1942 464 .2740 Next, enter your cam specs into CA and run the same report. Now lookup the degrees for the same given lifts for the stock cam. For example, where the lift is .0053, the degrees will be your new value to replace 352 on your table. Here is an example using a Crane Cams 449581 http://www.cranecams.com/?show=browsePa ... vl=2&prt=5 Lift at given degrees Stock degrees lift@cam lobe Crane 449581 degrees 352 .0053 320 380 .0661 349 400 .1320 368 420 .1942 384 464 .2740 408 Replace the table stock degree values with the Crane degrees values. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Mon Jul 24, 2006 12:39 pm Rick Firing the injectors is correct if your cam has no overlap. The larger the overlap the more of a chance the fuel will go out the exhaust. The injector timing has two objectives. One to cool down the engine and get better fuel atomization by spraying the back of a hot closed intake valve. The fuel cools the head down and also vaporizes the fuel. Since fuel exnites beter in a gas form then this would be the ideal method for the injector timing. The second objective is to spary the required amount of fuel during the alloted cam intake duration. This is based off of the air intake and RPM. The injector timing can compensate for some of this but when the RPM or air intake is to much then the injection will be saturated. So my point is, if you fire early on a larger duration cam, then pay close attention to the overlap. You will have to balance the cooling/Atomization affect with the fuel loss due to the cam overlap. That cam you gave as an example has a hugh 30 degree overlap. If this is the cam you are using, man that is radical. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue Aug 01, 2006 1:43 pm You got it. you have a total of 720 degrees before your injectors are considered saturated (fully open). This is definitely when bigger injectors are required. In THEORY the best situation would allow the required fuel to be sprayed within the intake valve time. This usually is possible at lower load and RPM ranges. As RPM goes up time will go down. At some point you will need to spray more then the allotted intake valve time allows. This is where you have to decide to spray early or late. Spraying late will cause the fuel to puddle behind a closed intake valve and then be pulled further up the intake runner when other cylinders are creating suction. This caused intake wall wetting and so forth. Then when the intake valve opens the fuel will have to travel back up the intake runner to the cylinder. If you decide to fire the injectors early then it will also puddle behind a closed valve but it will not have a chance to be pushed up the runner before the intake valves opens. This means the fuel has less distance to travel if sprayed early. Cam overlap plays another factor. If you spray early, the fuel has a chance to exit the exhaust during cam overlap. If you spray late then the fuel still has a chance of exiting the exhaust but it has more distance to travel therefore the cam overlap may pass by the time the fuel actually gets to the cylinder. Now for my OPINION, if the cam you have has no overlap then I believe earlier is better. This will allow the fuel to puddle on the intake helping cool down the engine and allow for better atomization of the fuel. If you have a cam with overlap then I would fire no earlier then TDC. Again this is just my opinion. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: vristang
posts.content: vristang Tuning Addict Posts: 919 Joined: Wed Sep 14, 2005 1:40 pm Location: Seattle Wa Contact: Contact vristang Website Quote Post by vristang » Mon Jun 19, 2006 7:33 pm The following is from my website. http://www.freewebs.com/vristang/pcvoil ... issues.htm This will give you some background info on the pcv system and how to trouble shoot your problem. Putting a Stop to Oil Consumption through the PCV Valve Background Info on the PCV System The PCV is an emissions device that allows the pressure and corrosive gasses in the crankcase to vent, without venting these harmful gasses to the environment. The directional valve is in place to prevent a backfire from spreading to the crankcase. In the event of a backfire into the intake manifold, the PCV is supposed to seal shut, preventing the flame front from traveling into the crankcase. Without this directional valve in place (and fully functional) a backfire could also cause a crankcase explosion. All motors will experience some degree of Blowby. Even a freshly rebuilt motor can experience between 5-10% Blowby, as checked with a Leakdown test. (Blowby is not the only source of crankcase pressure however. Due to the reciprocation of the pistons there will be a build up of pressure due to the air not being able to flow as fast as the pistons are moving in the higher RPMs) Blowby of combustion gasses introduces fuel and other combustion by products into the crankcase. Raw fuel, moisture, and various acidic materials will all contaminate the engine oil. Moisture can also enter the crankcase due to condensation overnight. The good news is that most of these contaminants are highly volatile, meaning they will vaporize at relatively low temps; around 200F. Once these contaminants and moisture have volatized though, they must be purged from the crankcase. This is where a crankcase ventilation system comes in. In the old days the crankcase was vented to the atmosphere via a hose that ran under the car or into the exhaust. The downside to this is that these volatile materials were being introduced to the atmosphere, increasing environmental damage. Now a Positive Crankcase Ventilation system is in use. In a positive venting system the crankcase contaminants are purged into the intake manifold so that they can be burned in the normal combustion process. This is very effective at reducing the amount of unburned HCs that are released to the atmosphere. Troubleshooting Your Oil Control Issues The first step is to find out where the oil is coming from. Pull the Throttle Body/Valve Cover hose from the TB. If it is wet with oil then this is an entry point. The normal causes of this are excess Blowby (which needs to be ruled out with a compression test), or the VC baffle has been removed for rocker clearance. Just looking down the oil filler neck should reveal if the baffle is in place. If you see rockers, then it is time to get creative and fabricate a baffle. If there is no baffle but the TB/VC hose is bone dry then you may be able to get away without using a baffle. Next pull the PCV hose. Again if it is wet with oil, this is an entry route. A quick fix for this is a separator from Steeda, Home Depot, or Lowes. For about $25 (The Steeda unit will be more expensive) for the separator and fittings you will be able to remove most of the oil before it gets to the intake. Also, you need to verify that the PCV screen is in place. This often forgotten part is located underneath the PCV in the back of the intake, and helps remove oil mist from the crankcase gasses. Contributed by tmoss... www.tmossporting.com I have seen a BUNCH of intakes (100s) and you can tell the lower intakes that were on cars whose PCV screen had been blocked - they have a very thick coat of grime on the bottom of the lower intake. You know the heads had a nice thick coat below the rockers too as the blow-by had no where to go. When you put the intake in a solvent tank and wash it, it does not cut all the crud off - reason? - the blowby gasses will not come off with safety solvent. why, I don't know. Do your self a BIG favor and install a PCV screen once a year. If a compression test comes back normal, and the above mentioned lines are dry, then the valve guides are suspect. The PCV Problem Many of the Fox Body Mustangs seem to have serious issues with oil consumption through the PCV or Throttle Body/Valve Cover line. There are 3 main causes of this problem. 1. Excessive Blowby 2. Removing the Valve Cover Baffle at the oil filler neck 3. Removing the Baffle and/or the PCV Screen on the lower intake However, in some head/cam/intake (and possibly stroker) combinations the problem can persist. Sometimes a small oil/air separator can be used to help filter out the oil before it gets to the intake manifold. Most who run this setup will remove the small plastic filter, as it tends to plug up and restrict airflow. An oil/air separator is a band-aid solution though, and should not be considered permanent. The goal should be to completely eliminate the flow of oil from the crankcase. Theory The problem seems to be that the stock PCV line does not flow enough volume to allow adequate ventilation in modified motors. The lack of volume flow creates a build up of pressure in the crankcase which forces crankcase gasses through the PCV at higher velocities. With the added velocity the crankcase gasses are able to pick up more oil vapor; carrying it into the intake manifold. Yet another issue is that the stock single PCV system can create rather long flow paths for pressure to vent. For example gasses in the front of the crankcase would have to flow to the back of the block to exit through the stock PCV. The result of a long flow path is that it will take longer to purge the crankcase pressure. Solution The solution is to allow a greater volume of gasses to vent from the crankcase, at lower velocities. This can be done with a larger ID PCV hose and PCV, or by adding a second PCV line. Since larger ID PCV valves can be hard to find the easiest solution should be to add a second PCV line to the drivers side valve cover. The stock drivers’ side valve cover can be replaced with any valve cover that has an oil filler/breather hole. What valve cover is used does not matter, so long as there is a way to mount a PCV valve to the valve cover. A stock passenger side valve cover installed on the drivers’ side would work well, or many of the aftermarket valve covers have holes intended for mounting breather caps. The hose from your new PCV should flow either directly to the intake manifold (parallel to the stock hose), or merge with the stock hose. An air compressor oil/air separator can still be used to filter out any oil that does get out of the crankcase. However, if the system is setup right and the motor is healthy, there should be very little oil accumulation in the separator if any at all. Secondary Benefits The increase in the volume of air that can flow out of the crankcase means lower accumulations of harmful Blowby gasses and moisture. Also, lower crankcase pressures will allow greater efficiency and power (although this affect is probably minimal on a street car). More Notes on Installation 1. It may be better to install the drivers side valve cover PCV toward the front of the motor. This will allow a shorter path for gasses that are trapped in the front of the crankcase. 2. It may not be a good idea to install a third PCV on the aft side of the passenger side valve cover, as this could allow fresh air from the TB/VC hose to vent directly out that PCV. This would result in no fresh air hitting the crankcase, and a greater accumulation of harmful crankcase gasses and moisture. Extra Notes From what I have seen, the oil accumulation in the intake will be greatest when the car is left to idle for some time (stuck in traffic or idling in the driveway), and then with some rpm the oil is picked up and thrown into the combustion chamber. If you live in a humid part of the country, or see a fair amount of condensation on the ground in the morning, then you will most likely notice some moisture in the separator, resulting in the easily recognized brown milkshake appearance of the oil in the separator. This is fairly normal, as overnight condensation will form on the inside of the engine block. Once the oil gets up to temperature, this moisture boils off, and collects in the separator. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Wed Aug 02, 2006 8:19 am It's usually a case of change the MAF transfer or the injector slopes. Changing the MAF transfer when you fit larger injectors is to fool the ecu into thinking there is less air going into the engine (e.g. if you double the injector size you let the ecu think there's half the airflow). The better way IMO is to change the injector sizes and the various other items affected by injector swaps (e.g. Injector Offset vs Battery Voltage). The first way is a bit of a fudge and leaves a lot to be desired, the second way is how Ford intended the eec to be calibrated. What confuses things is that most people change the MAF and injectors at the same time to cope with their other modifications and this is where it starts to go wrong. You tell the MAF supplier that you've got injectors of X size and they supply you with a MAF transfer to suit them rather than a true air flow transfer sheet that represents what the MAF is reading (I accept that the actual installation has an effect on flow but most of the time you cannot buy off the shelf to suit this and this is where your fine tuning comes into play). Top

It turns out my MAF was bad, it eventually died. What I found on datalogging was the during certain random periods the MAF voltage would go to 0V. So the EEC figures no air, no fuel cuts back the fuel and I was going way lean 25-30:1. One thing I found out when I put a new maf in, I did not have a proper bracket for the MAF, and it was bouncing around a little, but when it did it was hitting a nearby brace. I went through 2 MAF's before I found the problem. I put in a proper bracket to hold up the MAF and air filter. Datalog your MAFV, just before it goes lean and see if its dropping to 0V. If this is happening, you need to check all your MAf wiring first, then look at the MAF itself. posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Wed Aug 02, 2006 5:17 pm do'h wrote: Cougar 5.0, Answer me this. Does the Tweecer overide the maf sensor calibration that is within the sensor itself. No, the TwEECer knows nothing about the electronics in the MAF. The MAF output voltage for a given airflow is controlled by the calibration. You need to get a meter that will measure the higher airflow that your engine can take in now. The 19# calibration will hit 5V (max out) at about 300HP! Once you get the new meter (calibrated to 42# injectors), then you will input the new 42# MAF transfer that matches the NEW calibration. The TwEECer is there so you can change the curve in the ECU to the new one (42#). Now when the new meter outputs 2V, the ECU will lookup on the curve and see ~ 240kg/hr airflow and fire the 42# injector long enough to have the correct mixture. With the stock curve it's only looking up 110 kg/hr at 2V. Since you changed the slopes to 42# it knows how long to fire the injector, but when you hit 5V maxed out on the meter you have now, the lookup is only 856 kg/hr or like 300HP. With the new meter & matching curve, 5V is over 2000kg/hr airflow. Do you see how the 19# meter is designed to measure lower airflows & will not be able to measure the airflow your engine can draw? 428w now Top

posts.author: ponyboy4737
posts.content: ponyboy4737 Regular Posts: 86 Joined: Thu Apr 10, 2003 8:58 am Location: Chgo nw burbs Quote Post by ponyboy4737 » Mon Nov 28, 2005 9:53 pm TIPS FOR KB BLOWERS I've run a KB since '96 on my '95 Cobra. . Open up the inlet track. Going to a 75mm made a noticeable improvement above 4K rpm. Before the 75, it would kind of layoff on the top. With the 75mm tb, it pulled more linearly. Next I went with the Flowzilla manifold. That woke it up on top. It gave it a top end charge. It pulls harder and harder as the revs climb whereas before it was pretty much a steady pull. I ditched the stock maf and went with an 80mm (am now thinking about bumping that up. 4 inch from the maf to KB filter box which has 5" duct to cold ram air. I port matched the flowzilla to the egr adapter. It was a huge mismatch, but not anymore. Use 2 plugs colder copper core. Gap narrow .035. Use crane or msd ignition. Keep wires away from headers and egr. With that ignition, you need to do the "look under the hood at night with the garage door shut (hold your breath)" test to make sure you're not arcing. Make sure your blower oil level is right. The following will get you to a safe place from where you can tweec your set up to get your calib right. Then you can starting cutting back fuel and cranking up spark. This is aimed at a KB blower setup. Depending on boost level, cut timing. For 14 psi, I use: dist=10* max timing 18*. I leave spout in. I have alum heads 64chambers at 9.8 cr. I set all fan on/off settings to (stock -8*). 180* tstat. Get a fp gauge. You need to be sure fp climbs with boost. Check the forums to make sure you've got enought pump and injector for your setup. Lean =detonation=new motor= zeroes in the checkbook. Set your hysteresis scalar to 0. With instant boost, you need instant OL. Make sure your fpr vacuum line is plumbed to boost side of blower. If I were you, to start safe (rich and retarded) I would set global spark scalar to -10. I would set global OL fuel global scalar to .92. I would set stablized fuel table values above 50% load and 3000 rpm to 11.5. That should make it fairly safe and plenty wet. Then work on getting your maf dialed, slopes, breakpoint, tb airflow, isc duty cycle. Then restore the spark and fuel global scalars back to 1 (make sure you cut back spark tables before you put the spark scalar back to 1). Boosted motors can't take stock timing. Like I said, I run no more than 18* at 14 psi. Keep it rich and walk the timing in slowly. Get a WBo2. You'll need it to dial in the top end of the maf. I set my stblzd fuel tables for 11.5 over 65% load and 3000 rpm. I use the wb to dial in my maf kg/hr numbers to get the wb to show 11.5. When you got a/f dialed in, you can start putting timing back in, s l o w l y . I forget the exact name of the function, but its OL vs load vs rpm or something like that. For everyday street driving, I set it to go OL over 65% load and 3000 rpm. That pretty much keeps me in CL (higher mpg)unless I push the little pedal harder to force OL. WOT breakpoint set to 2.6. For performance, I twist the tweecer knob to a different position and use the same tune except it goes OL at 2500 rpm and 40% load, and wot breakpoint to 2.2. -ponyboy '95 Cobra, 331, J4J1, built AOD, Stallion 3000 stall, Kenne Bell Blowzilla Flowzilla, 42#, Aeromotive pump and rails, Edelbrock Performers, Comp Cams, 3.73, Cervini R hood, HPM control arms, Centerline wheels, Kicker, Alpine, MBQuart. Here is what it looks like in a datalog: You can see the accelerator pump function richen it up right after I push the pedal, then it just leans out. Look at the LAMSE's commanded. This is heavy load at low RPM bucking that results. Even after tweaking the MAF after this datalog and changing the "Time at heavy load for open loop" to "0", it still does this stupid shit. Even in this datalog it was set at 0.25 sec before open loop but it waited 0.75 sec before going open loop. posts.author: 5.0Rick
posts.content: 5.0Rick Regular Posts: 167 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 9:32 am 42# injectors - tuning for driveability - Findings Quote Post by 5.0Rick » Wed Jun 28, 2006 10:37 pm Hello I am running a turbo with with 42# Bosch injectors and had problems with elevated temperature and part throttle driveability issues. My car now starts, idles, and runs cooler (where it should 180 degrees or so). I believe these problems were caused by incorrect load calculations which lead to retarded timing hence the poor driveability and higher than normal temperatures. My approach to tuning is a bit different to what most are doing. What I wanted to achieve 1st was a stock tune with the correct settings for injector slopes, battery offset, breakpoint, etc. I wanted my changes to be based on factual data rather than trial and error. Since I am running the stock cam, I decided to put the stock MAF back in and work on getting the driveability dialed in. I tried the Lightning battery offset, breakpoints, and injector slopes of 40.6 and the car ran better than ever (from a driveability standpoint) I also divided the values by 1/2 on the Cranking Fuel Width vs ECT function. Once I was pretty sure that these settings were workable, I replaced the MAF with my Pro-M 42# bullet and used the MAF transfer that I generated using the Excel spreadsheet and the data sheet standard numbers. Right away I could tell that something was not right. The car would start bucking at 1800 rpm in 3rd or 4th at light throttle. At 1st I thought it was the accel enrichment multiplier function but after playing around with the fuel, I decided that it had more to do with load calculation rather than fuel since this bucking was not present with the stock MAF meter. I then started looking at the MAF transfer and playing around with the numbers. I figured that Pro-M calibrated their MAFs by scaling the values so I started trying to determine by what quantity. I did a little more research on what numbers to use from the Pro-M data sheet and found a write up indicating that the Calc numbers were what Pro-M shoots for when calibrating a meter. I took the stock MAF transfer and put it in Excel along with the Calc numbers from the Pro-M data sheet and created a graph. I then started multiplying the stock MAF values until the graphs were overlaid (the same). What was interesting was that the multiplier was 2.21. This is the same result as 42/19 or the ratio of injector change. At that point I changed the MAF transfer to the stock values multiplied by 2.21. Unlike the MAF transfer generating Excel spreadsheet results, the lower values were much larger. These larger values are workable with the 40.6 low slope and I have a rock solid stock idle.(BTW, I have both low and high slopes set to this) After these changes the car started and drove better, however the 1800 RPM stumble (bucking at light throttle) was still there (sometimes, not as frequent). I was still dealing with a load calculation issue. That was when I decided to experiment by increasing the Engine Displacement Scalar. I started with 400 and the bucking disappeared. I increased it again to 450 and the throttle response at low rpm improved dramatically. I then decided to use the same ratio multiplier on the Engine Displacement Scalar that I had used for the MAF transfer values (2.21). This change made a HUGE difference. The car drives like stock at part throttle. I believe this brought the load calculation back down to match that of a stock calibration. I did take some safety precautions by lowering the boost (5 psi - waste gate as loose as possible) and altering the fuel and spark tables as well as the WOT fuel and spark functions just in case I was totally off base. I am now fine tuning by altering the fuel & spark tables. Every now and then I will get a slight ping at part throttle while under boost. I believe this is caused by the 14.64 commanded A/F in the Stabilized A/F table. I will need to experiment a bit on how much to enrichen the commanded fuel A/F at a given load. Update: I altered the Stabilized A/F table by adding fuel starting at .3 load and the detonation has disappeared. Misc settings Fuel pressure - 39 psi with no vaccuum 70mm throttle body - all ISC settings and TB settings untouched. Injector breakpoint values - 1.949 base timing 10 degrees Valve cover air inlet connected to intake pipe of turbo after the MAF (very important - this air has to be accounted for or the idle will be too lean. Possible problems starting a cold engine) All emissions equipment present I wish I still had my Tweecer RT so I could datalog :( Tuning via a chip is a PITA Let me know if you find this information useful. Regards, Rick Last edited by 5.0Rick on Tue Jul 04, 2006 5:40 pm, edited 3 times in total. 410WStroker,TW Heads port matched 10.2:1,TrickFlow R intake, 75mm TB, Lunati Voodoo 61013 Cam, Pro-M 80mm (50# cal), 58# injectors, Accufab 1 3/4 mid length headers, A9L EEC-IV with Tweecer RT Top

posts.content: 5.0Rick Regular Posts: 167 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 9:32 am Quote Post by 5.0Rick » Thu Jun 29, 2006 8:23 pm Hi Guys, 1st of all, it is not my intention to flame anyone but this type of discussion is exactly what adds an incredible amount of frustration to someone who is just starting out with the Tweecer. There are lots of opinions and only one right answer. My take is that we should be able to make changes that apply to every engine (with new injectors, MAF, cam) much like the stock A9L code applies to all stock 302s with a stock cam, stock MAF, stock injectors, and stock fuel pressure. At least close enough for the adaptive technology to dial in the rest (25% variance). All settings are relevant, if they were not necessary, Ford would not have included them in the EEC period. I understand that all engines have different fuel & spark requirements, but that is handled by altering the tables. (matching fuel & spark needs to volumetric efficiency) If I had a dollar for all of the opinions that people swear by and all of the tunes that degrade over time, I would be a billionare. With that said, I posted this information to help the new guys that are just starting out. I am tuning via a chip and cannot datalog. I would be most appreciative if someone with a Tweecer RT could test my theory out and post their findings so everyone can benefit. There are 3 parts to my theory and they are as follows: 1. With a change in MAF, the stock MAF values can be multiplied by the injector ratio- in this case 42/19 or 2.21, these numbers closely match the Calc Pro-M datasheet values. 2. Also required to bring the load down to where it should be, you have to multiply the Engine Displacement Scalar by the same ratio - actual CID*2.21 -- for 42# MAF calibration - I have a 317 so mine is set to 700.73 3. The Stabilized fuel table aims for 14.7:1 at all load values. This table needs to be enrichened as load increases. Please keep in mind that safety precautions need to be taken on boosted applications, the stock fuel and spark table values may be too aggressive and will need to be adjusted. Remember, this is not an issue with a car that has matching MAF and injectors because the calculated load is wrong (too high=more fuel and less timing) As stated earlier, the Stabilized A/F table will also need to be adjusted. Regards, Rick Last edited by 5.0Rick on Fri Jul 28, 2006 9:04 pm, edited 1 time in total. 410WStroker,TW Heads port matched 10.2:1,TrickFlow R intake, 75mm TB, Lunati Voodoo 61013 Cam, Pro-M 80mm (50# cal), 58# injectors, Accufab 1 3/4 mid length headers, A9L EEC-IV with Tweecer RT Top

There is no such thing as a meter that is accurate, it is only as accurate as the system you install it in is like the system it was calibrated in. I am not trying to argue with you but I believe they are accurate enough. I mean, there are no absolutes only close enough. How many decimal points are used to determine accuracy? Not only that, but the number rounding that occurs when entering values would not be so drastic. In my opinion, if it was really that important to have it as accurate as possible, Ford would have had values like 13.000001 and not 13.000. Not only that but I believe they would have used different units like g/s instead of Kg/hr to gain more granularity. Just food for thought... Rick I wish it was just a matter of round-off error. The ProM42 cal versus C&L 76mm 42lb cal are close. At 4.8V the ProM is 7.5% higher airflow but at 2.8V the ProM shows 20% more airflow. Two nearly identical diameter meters cal'd for the same injectors are not linearly related. My meter is off by up to 25% at higher flow rates from the manufacturers curves. Air does not flow uniformly through the meter BUT the sample tube is in only one location near the outside diameter of the tube in the case of C&L & the ProM bullet. Anything that effects the uniformity of flow before and after the meter will effect the accuracy of the results. Any bend near the meter effects the results - putting a cone filter where a bend used to be can dramatically effect the uniformity of flow through the meter. If that's not enough food for thought, read the following post: http://forums.corner-carvers.com/showthread.php?t=8535 . Not only is the post rather entertaining, it will REALLY open your eyes WRT to the ProM bullet that you are using. :D 428w now Top

If that point isn't clear after reading that thread, then I don't know what else to say. Would it help any if I told you I was a mechanical engineer and that I do windtunnel testing at work and have helped design windtunnel? We use a "filter" before the area of interest that looks like a pack of straws glued together. This helps to laminarize the flow in the area of interest. We also have to ensure that the area after the measurement area has no changes in cross-section or bends or any obstacles for a significant distance as air "stacks up" and can have an effect on the flow uniformity for some distance before the obstacle in the tunnel. You saw all the grief that guy was causing himself because he had his TB just after his meter - totally bad idea. I can't stop you from believing that a MAF is a precision instrument that is not affected by the system it's in (nevermind variations in calibration accuracy, electronic drift & cleanliness of the measurement elements) & that fuel injectors have no statistical variation to their electronics & they don't vary mechanically (the reason for "matching"). Anyway, have fun - though I really think you should get an "RT" version of TwEECer so you can more easily correct your issues through the datalogs. I can't believe you are trying to tune a turbo "by the numbers". Have you looked at the GUFB document yet? Everything you need to know about the A9X programming is in that document. BTW, your adjusting of the fuel & spark tables to "fix" you issues seems as "trial and error" as any approach I've seen here. 428w now Top

Rick Rick Yes. The ECU thinks the injector is larger when the low slope is set higher, so it will use a lower pulsewidth. The only time the pulsewidth is less than 2ms where it would transition to low slope in my car is when the car is coasting/decelerating, thus when you tip in, the ECU will be transitioning from a larger to a smaller injector (in it's little head) and thus it will dial out the pulsewidth during a transition from low to high. This is the way I am thinking of it today - does it make sense to you? 428w now Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Fri Jun 30, 2006 2:24 pm Started off well this thread, and then lost it's way at bit :D Adding my observations; Larger injectors do require smaller cranking pulsewidths, simulating larger injectors by increasing the pulsewidth shows this. As an aside, my guess is that the MAF signal isn't reliable enough at cranking speeds to calculate a desired A/F ratio and therefore a simple injector pulsewidth based upon ECT is used. I consider that the MAF transfer should always indicate true airflow into the engine, the scaling of it to compensate for different sized injectors is a 'fudge' and because of the complexity of the eec any scaling inevitably causes driveablility problems (I think the sheer number of posts on the various boards about MAF transfer problems bears this out). The eec calibration data should always reflect what's actually fitted to the engine and unless you are developing more than 200% LOAD then the eec will cope with all your modifications. Only if you are exceeding 200% LOAD would I advocate rescaling the displacement to cope. You should rescale your tables to cover the LOAD range your engine produces. Top

posts.author: MaddMartigan
posts.content: MaddMartigan Regular Posts: 126 Joined: Thu Jul 14, 2005 6:21 pm Location: Pickerington, OH Contact: Contact MaddMartigan Website Quote Post by MaddMartigan » Fri Jun 30, 2006 6:39 pm Sorry to interrupt the exchange but I figured I may as well respond to back up my Pro-M remarks. There was a lot of people (here, and other places) that discovered that Pro-M had a bunch of kids doing their flow bench work and that they weren't always doing a good job calibrating the MAFs. Secondly, it has been said already but it seems that it should be mentioned again that calibrating a MAF to "match" a certain size injector is just crap. The whole reason we are all doing our own tuning is so we can do it the right way. A MAF flows what it flows. The transfer table just tells the computer what voltage is being required and the corresponding air flow. There is nothing there that tells the computer what size injectors to use. If you change those numbers to modify the amount of fuel required it is because you are giving the computer erroneous data and making it change the amount of fuel it is sending. If you give the computer wrong numbers then it is going to calculate incorrectly. I don't think any of us are smart enough to calculate all of the variables involved with this. Again, you are going to cause the computer to constantly fight itself. In the end, knowing the actual tranfer function table for the MAF, the appropriate injector slopes and minimum pulsewidth is the first major step towards making this all work. I got my car to idle and cruise just fine by setting the appropriate values in those areas and then "tweaking" the MAF curve ever so slightly to compensate. FWIW, the 90mm LMAF curve that comes with CalEdit does not match what the Lightning ECM has in it. The Lightning ECM apparently also uses injector slopes of 40/46 instead of the 42/50 that I originally started using. I am still experimenting to see if that is the reason I had to modify my MAF transfer. Also, this isn't an argument or fight of any kind. Just an opportunity to learn. 1993 Ford Thunderbird LX, T4M0 EEC-IV, CHP 347, TFS TW's, TFS stage 1 cam,42# inj, 90mm LMAF, 1 5/8 Mac Long Tubes, 3.73 gears, built AOD w/ 9.5" TC, AEM EMS, LC-1 WB O2 and a few other things. posts.author: 5.0Rick
posts.content: 5.0Rick Regular Posts: 167 Joined: Fri Oct 18, 2002 9:32 am Quote Post by 5.0Rick » Fri Jun 30, 2006 7:02 pm Hi MaddMartigan, You are correct the MAF has nothing to do with the injector size. The MAF is used for load calculation. In turn, the load calculation along with the entries in the tables are used to provide the appropriate amount of fuel and spark. Please note, the MAF transfer by itself is not what is adding or removing fuel. If the MAF is off, then the load calcs are off. If the load calcs are off, then the tune degrades over time (changing temp, barometric pressure, humidity, etc). This is why I am focused on getting the load calcs right. So far the changes that I have implemented have had consistent results. The car runs the same (driveability) every time after many on/off cycles and a few weeks elapsed now. If I had an RT I would test (datalog) the following: 1. 19# injectors with stock MAF - datalog to profile the load - what load range while driving (non aggressive driving) 2. 42# injectors with Pro-M MAF with the Calc flow values in the MAF transfer, along with the Lightning injector settings and the scaled engine displacement (engine displacement*(42/19) or 2.21 Then I would compare the datalogs to see how similar or dissimilar the loads are. This would help me determine whether or not my theory is correct. posts.author: TonyF
posts.content: TonyF Regular Posts: 78 Joined: Fri Sep 30, 2005 9:49 am Location: AL Fuel Table - Start up (A9L) Lambda Quote Post by TonyF » Thu Aug 10, 2006 9:45 pm According to GFUB the values in Fuel Table-Start Up are lambda, which means you can multiple them by 14.64 to get the Air Fuel ratio. Agree? Now, say I've upgraded my injectors to 30s from 19. It appears that the multiplier used to correct Fuel Table- Start Up would be 19/30 = .63333. However, the multiplier really should be 30/19 = 1.5789 to lean out the mixture. Here's the math using one of the stock A9L values from the table... 1.7157 * 14.64 = 25.117848 (Stock) (1.7157 * 1.5789) * 14.64 = 39.6 (Leaned) (1.7157 * .63333) * 14.64 = 15.9 (Richen) Does this makes sense so far? Now, what does the time value represent in this table? It think it is ATMR1 (time since start {exit from crank mode}) in seconds. My question is why are the values very lean at time 0, and rich at time 35? Is this to clear the excess fuel left over from the crank mode? And, do I understand this stuff correctly? Or in left field, out of the ball park? Thanks Tony FFR MKIII, 347 10.8:1 comp. AFR 185cc 61 cc heads, CompCams XFI Stroker Cam: Dur. 286/300, Dur @.050 236/248, Lift .579 114 deg sep. posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Re: Fuel Table - Start up (A9L) Lambda Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Thu Aug 10, 2006 9:49 pm TonyF wrote: According to GFUB the values in Fuel Table-Start Up are lambda, which means you can multiple them by 14.64 to get the Air Fuel ratio. Agree? My question is why are the values very lean at time 0, and rich at time 35? Is this to clear the excess fuel left over from the crank mode? And, do I understand this stuff correctly? Or in left field, out of the ball park? Thanks Tony No, actually the values in the table are subtracted from stoic (14.64) to arrive at the new LAMBSE at startup. Just look at the commanded LAMBSE right after startup and you will see that this is true. The values are actually rich at startup and trend toward lean as time goes on. Time is in seconds after exiting crank mode I'm pretty sure. 428w now Top

posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Thu Aug 10, 2006 11:21 pm Hmmm, you are right - the description for FN1306 is deceptive if not just plain wrong. Look at the Open Loop equation though: FUEL CONTROL STRATEGY - OPEN LOOP FUEL - GUE0 PEDD-PTOPE, FoMoCo, PROPRIETARY & CONFIDENTIAL OPEN LOOP FUEL LOGIC During Open Loop fuel Control, the desired equivalence ratios (LAMBSE1 and LAMBSE2) are basically calculated from two tables as modified for various engine conditions. PROCESS Open Loop fuel control ------| Set LAMBSE1 = LAMBSE2 ---------------------------------| = C * [(FN300*FN1307) ---------------------------------| - FN1306] * LAMMUL * OLMCL ... You can see that FN1306 is subtracted from FN300*FN1307 in LAMBSE1/2. This means that I was wrong too - FN1306 (startup fuel) is subtracted from the open loop fuel table (FN1307 - not stoich) assuming that since the engine is open loop at startup that this is the equation used. The FN1306 simply drops out of the equation after 45 seconds, though the engine typically won't always go closed loop until 60 - 80 seconds - though I don't know why this is - I haven't had time to look into this (this is warm engine). 428w now Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sat Aug 12, 2006 6:08 pm You can not adjust one bank. The EEC dose this by adjusting the KAMRF and LAMBSE. I have seen as much as 5-6 % difference in the KAMRFs at an idle. Then as RPM's increase the difference gets smaller. If you are certain that the O2's are good then there are a few areas to be concerned with: Exhaust leak EGR leak Smog pump bypass valve Smog pump divert valve Smog pump cross over pipe PCV If all of these are good then the only thing that could be causing it would be a leak in the intake gasket or something along those lines. There will always be some difference due to imperfections in the intake track and or heads. This small variations will cause different flow for each cylinder. I think mine is right at 4% different at an idle of 760 and it get worse if I lower the idle. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: J_P
posts.content: J_P Regular Posts: 186 Joined: Wed May 04, 2005 2:06 am Location: Ashburn, VA Contact: Contact J_P Yahoo Messenger Quote Post by J_P » Sun Jun 26, 2005 10:08 pm Was the engine warmed up before you took the datalog? Once the hegos are warmed up and the car goes into closed loop the o2 voltages should fluctuate back and forth since they only read rich or lean. If a rich indication is seen then the EEC compensates by pulling out fuel until it reaches a lean indication, then the EEC adds fuel and the process just loops that way. All of the rich lean readings are referencing 14.64 as ideal a/f. Justin Justin 93 A3M (A9L), 331, 30lbs inj., '02GT MAF, Trick Flow 'R' intake, Tremec TKO, 3.55's 2001 GT automatic with NUX1 stock. posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Thu Aug 17, 2006 12:49 am You need to change the PIP FILTER number. MNPIPn - PIP FILTER MNPIPn = 60/(ENGCYL*"MAXRPM") * "Clock Freq"/36 n = 8 for a 8-cylinder engine MNPIP8 = 961 at 15 MHz The base values are equivalent to 6500 RPM. Just plug in the MAXRPM limit you want & you will get the new number to change the PIP Filter to in CalEdit. Clock Freq is 15,000,000 ENGCYL is 4 (number of cylinders/2) 428w now Top

posts.author: codedout
posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Fri Aug 18, 2006 1:59 pm Well from my understang it goes like this: The IAC is basically in a closed loop (phase locked loop). The ISC transfer is merely a guideline for its operating range. Yes I would have to agree that the closer you are on this function, the more accurate you A/F will be, and hte less it will bounce around. However it will basically look at your A/F mixture, and add the appropriate amount of air to match the fuel that is being delivered. The bosch logic of fuel injection as explained by a porsch/bmw speicalist was that they dump in X amount of fuel and modify the airflow to match that. I think this is why some people have degrading tunes over time, I also think that is why Clint recommends that you unhook the IAC valve when you are measuring the airflow to set up the ISC transfer. So the IAC is actually used to accomodate changes in air flow(ie vacuum) changes in fuel density (cold vs hot), and altitude. It can make quick accurate changes where it would be a slower response if you were adjusting fuel delivery. It is also a variable device whereas the injectors are either on or off. This is just my take on it, based on what I have learned over time. Anyone disagreeing chime in. posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Mon Aug 21, 2006 7:30 pm Edit: Note that I had forgotten that I had scaled load so I think the expected load is about 20% for the A9L. Ford seems to be expecting a cruise LOAD of about 20%. You can convert %LOAD to LOAD just by multiplying the %LOAD times the Sealevel Load Scaling vs RPM (FN035) scaling at the RPM you were cruising at. Example: cruising at 2900 RPM - stock A9L Sealevel Load Scaling vs RPM is about 0.80 (80%) at 2900 RPM. Lets say you are datalogging 30% %LOAD. LOAD = 0.30 * 0.80 = 0.24 or 24% LOAD. You can also log actual LOAD if you want to. This example isn't why I think they were expecting a 20% cruising load though - it has to do with the HEGO BIAS table that richens the mixture above 20% load and leans below 20% load. As far as timing - I am close enough to stock loads at cruise so I stick with stock timing. 428w now Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue May 16, 2006 12:06 pm LTMTB 1 & 2 are the two adaptive fuel tables in KAM (8 rows by 10 columns with 6 special cells for idle) FN021 is the LOAD scaling (normalising) function used FN070 is the RPM scaling (normalising) function used FN1325 is the adaptive table learning/use table (again 8 rows by 10 columns with 6 special cells for idle). A value of 0 or a +ve number in this table will allow learning in the corresponding LTMTB cell and a -ve number will disable learning. The higher the +ve value the slower the update rate of the adaptive fuel table. A -ve number forces the eec to use a different cell from the adaptive fuel table instead of the corresponding cell, e.g. a value of -35 in the row 2 column 4 cell of FN1325 will cause the eec to use the adaptive value from row 3 column 5 in the LTMTB tables instead of the row 2 column 4 cell. Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue May 16, 2006 2:25 pm Faster update rates incur the possibility of including transient fuelling deviations to the adaptive fuel tables that shouldn't really be taken any notice of. The downside of this is that the adaptive fuel table constantly is altering and never really settles down as it should. The special idle cells are in the 9th row of the LTMTB and FN1325 tables. The ecu doesn't use RPM vs LOAD to look these up but decides uses them if the REFFLG = 1 (indicating idle air flow) and the ISCFLG = 1 (rpm control for idle). The ISFLAG (indicating the loading at idle) decides which column to use, I think the A9L only uses 4 of the 6 cells. A point I should of mentioned about the adaptive learning process is that the eec doesn't just update one cell at a time, it also updates the 4 adjacent cells with the trend associated with cell update (the special idle cells are an exception to this). Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Thu May 18, 2006 3:54 am I'm afraid you are mistaken about all of the tables using LOADX (are you thinking that all table lookups in the code use LOADX instead of LOAD?). Here's the FN021 loookup routine from the A9L; ad3w R32,Rf0,b2 R32 = FN021 + 0; ldw R34,[R74+de] R34 = [0x025C]; call 360c UWordLu(); ldw Ra8,R38 NRMRLD = R38; ad2w R38,80 R38 += 80; Where the input 0x025C is LOAD and the output NRMRLD is the current row to use in table lookups. LOADX is stored in address 0x0260. I'm also afraid you're wrong about a background loop equalling 3 clock ticks, the backgound loop time is the time taken to run all the background tasks. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri May 19, 2006 1:51 pm Ok I went back and doubled checked. The register you pointed out (0x0350) is the preload register. This register is used in most of all of the tables. This register is set depending on the Load Scale Switch (0x9a80). This switch determines which load value to use. If the switch is set to zero then percent load is used (LOADX) and if it is set to 1 then engine load is used (LOAD). The default switch setting for the A9L is 0 or LOADX. I have further tested this by simply having two tunes loaded in the tweecer and whith the only difference being the load switch setting. While crusing at 2000 RPM on the freeway if I change tunes the KAMRF's will follow suite. This proves that the switch will dertermin which load is used for the adaptive update table. As for the bacground loops you are correct. The clock tick is simply just that. It has no relation to the background loop (Program Pass). Since every operation within the code takes a different amount of clock tick the program scan will very depending on the branches within the logic and so forth. I was hopeing to figure out the time slice per bacground loop, but I dont think it is possible unless there was a watchdog of some sort. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sat May 20, 2006 6:21 am My earlier post had a screw up with the addresses , but carrying on, PRLDSW doesn't decide whether LOAD or LOADX is used by the tables, merely if LOADX is to be calculated or set equal to LOAD. Here's the part of the code that deals with it; Code: Select all cmpb 0,[Rfc+2] [0x9A80]; # PRLDSW - Load Scaling Switch jne 40a8 if (0 == [9A80]); # if 1 goto save PERCENT_LOAD ldw R3e,R3c FLAGS_3e = FLAGS_3c; # FLAGS_3C equals LOAD at this point clrw R3c FLAGS_3c = 0; # clr hi word shrdw R3c,1 (long) FLAGS_3c = FLAGS_3c / 2; # div by 2 divw R3c,R30 (long) FLAGS_3c = FLAGS_3c / R30; # air flow / (RPM * CID) = VE jnv 40a8 if (overflow) { ldsbw R3c,ff FLAGS_3c = (int) ff; } } # clamp max to FFFF ; ;save PERCENT_LOAD ; stw R3c,[R74+e2] [0x0260] = FLAGS_3c; # set PERCENT_LOAD I'd like to look at the datalogs of your test, it would be interesting to see how LOAD compares to LOADX when you got this result. I don't think there's a timer that counts the time taken for all the background routines to run through. It would be fairly easy to add one to the code but I suspect that the calling of the foreground routines would make the value very inconsistent. I suppose if you monitored it for long enough you would get an idea of the longest and shortest times the cycle took. Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sun Aug 20, 2006 4:18 pm Sailorbob is correct, their are alot of tables that use raw load and not LOADX. This means adjust the CID will lower both raw load and LOADX. This will work, but in my opinion, it is not the best way. I perffer to rescale the fuel and load tables to say 0-150% and set the CID to actual CID. This will allow you to have better control over spark and fuel. For example, if you rescale the tables, you can have a different spark for 100%, 120%, 130% and so on. If you simply increase the CID then you only get one point above 75%. For any boosted application the load will incresae fast and you may not want 18 degrees timing for a small acceleration and so forth. You may want 18 degrees more like at 130% load. It basically allows for smoother transitions from acceleration to WOT. This would also apply for the fuel tables. Now there is one more situation. If you car hits 200% with the CID being set at the actual CID then you will want to scale the tables from 0-200 and then scale the CID up to where you never see 200% but rather somthing like 190%. This would give you the most flexability the EEC can provide. Just my opinion. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sun Aug 20, 2006 3:57 pm The best way I have found to do this is to do the following: 1) Let the car idle with ISC plugged in. After the initial startup time of 180 seconds and after the idle has stablized, log the MAV and MAF flow and RPM. 2) Now open the log and average the idle MAF flow points and RPM. 3) Lets just say that idle point is 30kg/hr at 780RPM. Now take that flow number and multiply it by 2.2 and then divide it by 60. This will give you 30*2.2/60 = 1.1lbs/min 4) Now in the ISC Netural function enter the value of 1.1 in the 672 RPM column. 5) Now change the 672 rpm to 780 in the ISC netural function. 6) Now repeat the above for a 1000 RPM and 1500 RPM. I also do this with the ISC unpluged to get a lower RPM such as 600rpm. 7) After the above is done then you can fine tune the idle by adjusting only the TB air flow at an idle to get the ISC to 35%. Just my opinion. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

I suspect it's the latter because I have a suspicion that Ford's own engineering and calibration consoles did something similar. I believe that when you upload a payload to the tweecer that you are telling the tweecer which address to monitor on the bus. The tweecer does not poll for the data but rather monitors the bus. When it sees the value it simple copies it into a holding register. Hince there are only 16 holding registers. Then as Cal Con polls the tweecer it time stamps the data and reads the 16 registers. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Aug 23, 2006 4:36 pm In order to understand the MAF conversion you first have to understand how clock ticks are determined. All of the EEC that I am aware of use three 3 clock ticks per state cycle. The state cycles change depending on the hardware design. Here is what I have in my collection: '12 State Cycles times a 3 clock tick per state = 36 '32 State Cycles times a 3 clock tick per state = 96 ' 28??? = (1/28000000)*96 = .000006480 Years 2002-2004 ' 24mhz = (1/24000000)*96 = .000004000 Years 1999-2001 ' 21mhz = (1/21000000)*96 = .000004570 Years 1998 ' 18mhz = (1/18000000)*96 = .000005333 Years 1996-1997 ' 15mhz = (1/15000000)*36 = .000002400 Years 1987-1995 ' 12mhz = (1/12000000)*36 = .000003000 Years 1986-19xx ' 1 Kilogram = 2.204622622 pounds Now lets take an example from the A9L. The Raw MAF flow value for 15.99 volts is 2637. Here is how I believe the MAF is calculated: This will convert from lbs/min /clk tick to kg/min/clk tick 2637 x 2.204623 = 5813.59 This is to take the clock ticks out of the equation 5813.59 * .0000024 = 0.0139526180424 0.0139526180424 / 1000 = 13.9526180424 This is to convert to kg/hr 13.9526180424 * 60= 837.15 And lastly you can get lbs/min 837.15 * 2.204623 / 60 = 30.76026 This is how I have been doing it. I sure hope it is right. I wish the tuners would keep consistant on the units and only use pounds. I could care less if they are in hours minutes or seconds. those are easy to convert. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

Yep, GUFB verifies that there are indeed 2.4uS/clock tick with the 15Mhz processor. Here's what I came up with for a conversion: FN036 - Yaxis = raw airflow data in lb/2^31 clock ticks To get airflow in lb/min: (raw airflow data/2^31)*25E6 clock ticks/minute For the example where the raw data for the highest flow point = 2637: MAF = 2637*25E6/2^31 = 30.699 lb/min to convert to kg/hr: 30.699lb/min*(60min/hr)*(1kg/2.2046lb) = 835.49 kg/hr Does this make any sense or is there a simpler way to do this? 428w now Top

I recently got going on TunerPro (thanks cougar5.0) and have been inputting my tune from CalEdit A10 into TunerPro. I have had good luck except for one item so far. It is in regards to the Accelerator Enrichment Multiplier vs TP table (FN331B). I have the A9L xdf from the TunerPro website and the 5 cells for volts in this table come up as 0.02 volts (cell 1 comes up as 0.00 volts). So I input the proper volts into the cells as well as the changes to the multiplier cells and save the changes (I have even graphed it properly prior to saving it). When I go back to review the table, it has changed the cells for volts back to the 0.02 v and 0.00 v but properly saved the multiplier changes. Anybody have an idea as to why this is happening and what I can do to fix it? posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue Aug 22, 2006 11:00 am Change the item's X conversion from X/12800 to X/12800*256. The problem is because the table lookup is byte sized instead of the usual word sized lookup. Top

posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Sat Sep 02, 2006 4:37 pm You have it right. High lambse is rich. Low KAMRF is also rich. KAMRF less than 1 means the eec is "pulling" fuel, over 1 it is adding. Ideally, you want to see lambse around 14.xx and KAMRF around 1 while cruising and around 12 WOT. For a blown app, I like 11.5 for WOT. And ignore lambse during "coast down", its pretty much meaningless. A9* processors seem to command a lambse of 10.890 during coastdown. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Fri Sep 01, 2006 2:34 pm Lean misfires will cause high HC. Why? Because each "miss" is a cylinder's worth of unburned fuel out the exhaust. Seems counter intuitive, but richen it up a bit so there are no lean misses and unburned fuel will go down. Right on the EGR, it plays no role at idle. If it still fails you might need to hook the air pump back up. 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. title: Can Secondary Air Controls for A9P be turned off? - EECTuning.org

posts.content: cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Can Secondary Air Controls for A9P be turned off? Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Jun 24, 2005 6:59 am What I have is an 89 Ranger that I'm transplanting a 97 Explorer 5.0L V8 motor into. After investigating options of how to keep the Explorer motor's computer and harness, I found it much more practical to retrofit the motor with 89-93 Mustang 5.0L sensors and wiring harness then control it with an A9L or A9P ECM. So far, every engine sensor the Mustang A9P I have is expecting has been fitted, however the 97 Explorer V8s don't have a smog pump and thus the front accessory brackets don't make provisions for one to be added. This doesn't pose a legal emissions problem for me since the original engine is newer than my truck and didn't require a smog pump in 97. However the Mustang A9P computer is still going to throw codes because it expects the two Secondar Air solenoids to be there. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Thu Sep 07, 2006 11:42 am You will definitely need the 42#'s. I too did not use the FMU and had my MAF recalibrated by Pro-M just before they closed shop. After a lot of TwEECing I find driveability to be quite good and in fact, the car passed emissions. However, I have a lot more to say about the intercooler and timing. Everything I add here will be from the perspective of using the CBAZA strategy. While I don't profess to be an expert on TwEECing CBAZA, I must admit I know less about your A9L strategy. Nevertheless, some of the things I have learned will probably apply. I burned 3 pistons. You can read the saga in the lounge area but you will have to go back a ways. I left the timing stock (mistake #1) and then eliminated a function which richened the mixture based on ACT (mistake #2). This was with the W4H0 calibration. I have since converted to the 95 Cobra calibration J4J1. In J4J1 Ford reduces timing for high ACT instead of richening the mixture. I have decided not to defeat this function. From all of my experience I can tell you that the P1SC intercooler (I have the 2 core) seems to work pretty good. But with a 12 pound pulley, I still see ACT's that are at 80 (same as ambient) at the starting line and upwards of 170 degress at the lights 12 seconds later. I called ProCharger to ask what I should expect and the guy said without the intercooler I would have seen temps 100 degrees higher or more. In any event, my car's performance and engine reliability are highly affected by the steep rise in ACTs. Several here on the forum have suggested I add a water injection system to cool the ACTs under high boost. I think it is a good idea, but haven't gotten serious about doing it. One other thing I have learned. The 42#'s are just about maxed out with the 12 pound pulley. For I while I couldn't understand how that could be given that 42#'s are supposed to be able to support up to 550 HP, and I am only showing 425 on the dyno. Then I realized it is taking 75 or more HP to spin the blower, and that lost HP would not be accounted for in the dyno readings. I think the motor is capable of generating more power but right now its blowing through a pretty restrictive exhaust with cats. So I want to take these off, but I am worried that I would see injector duty cycles at 100% well before red line if I stick with the 42#'s. The EEC constantly adjusts fuel in small amounts just so it knows that the o2 sensors are functioning properly. It will send a little extra fuel and make sure that the sensors report a slightly richer condition and less fuel for a leaner condition. It takes the range of 0 - 5.0 and sets it to 0 - 1.6 on import - at least that was my experience. CalEdit 1.30.v10 is supposed to be rid of this issue, but I haven't had any luck trying it yet. Otherwise, you have to key the values into the MAF cells one by one, and even that can be tricky. Here is how I get it to work. Put your cursor in any cell, then use the arrow keys to step to the cell you want to change. Input the value, hit enter, step out of that cell and step to the next with the arrow key. posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Tue Sep 12, 2006 10:16 pm This is normal. Basically you are running a little rich. the KAMRF is basically a long term fuel trim. Unless you run lean it will never go above 1.000. there are 2 ITEmS that determine fuel trims the LAMBSE which is what the Eec is currently commanding. you will probably finr that yours is reading 14.6 and above. if the reading were say aroudn 15 that would mean you are running rich, and the Eec is commanding a leaner mixture. If say it wass commanding 13 it would mean you were running lean and it is trying to make the mixture richer. If the Eec consitently commands richer IE below 14.6 then eventually it will update the KAMRF's to a higer number above 1.000 hence adding fuel. If it consistently commands leaner IE above 14.6 it will update the KAMRF's to a number rlower then 1.000 hence removing fuel. KAMRFS are stored in a table so as you accelerate or decelerate you will see it change based on where you are in the table and wheter it need to add or remove fuel at that given range.
