posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Fri Sep 15, 2006 10:04 am Well this may not be the correct method. But it worked for me. I basically took as stock datalog, and looked at the flow rates compared them to my new flow rates. figured out the difference in percentage and then multiplied by the difference. Load is deterrmined primarily from airflow, so say at idle you were flowing 35kg of air and now you flow 45 kg of air at the same rpm, you effectively have a 23% increase in load. so multiply the sealevel load scale for that rpm by 1.23. From what i understand of EA's load calc, you are supposed to pull a full run in 3rd, (simulating max load). Unfortunately here in Fort Laud there is no place I can get up to that speeed without going to jail. So I came up with the above thoery. Someday I will get back to the track or the dyno. posts.content: Carl Regular Posts: 81 Joined: Wed Mar 05, 2003 10:35 pm Location: Canada Quote Post by Carl » Thu Sep 14, 2006 6:00 pm Another problem that I found out about earlier this year with Calcon, is doesn't record engine temperature accurately. I am still using 1.3a9, at elevated engine temps ~230+ it will actually start to read ~170. I know this first hand, I might even still have the datalog. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Mon Sep 18, 2006 11:40 am Not quite. Don't use the A9L bin. You want to select "A9M" in caledit. Here is what I did. After the tweecer was installed and verified, I did a "read eec" and saved that file as "myeec.ccf". posts.author: boss96
posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Tue Sep 12, 2006 8:00 am I use it on my car and it works well. First off, you need a spark amplifier if you don't already have one, it allows you to use the bigger jets that come with the kit and not blow out the spark. In my case I used the 675 jet (the bigger of the 2 that come with the kit) and used the maf controller for the pump motor. It turns on around 2.5 volts and gradually increases water/meth flow from there. The a/f will fatten up about 1.5 points richer (at least that is what happened in my case). I already had the maf curve very accurate so the easiest thing to do was command a leaner a/f in the fuel stab OL tables to compensate. As a safeguard I have the act sensor mounted near the TB as far from the blower discharge as possible. The snow injector is mounted close to the discharge side so it travels a little distance before hitting the act sensor. With full flow I see act go from about 200 degrees down to 130 degrees which makes it easy to set up the act spark curve to advance timing a lot when the temp is down to 130 but it reduces spark aggressively when it goes higher. Since the act curve is rpm/load valued the big spark retard does not come into play during normal low load driving but has a big effect when under boost. So..if the water stops flowing under boost the act temp should rise dramatically and the spark in my case is retarded at least 10 degrees. Unfortunately I have'nt figured out how to get my a/f back in the 11's in that case since I am still commanding the leaner a/f to compensate for the richening effect of the methanol but I still think such low timing should prevent damage. BTW, a cheap way to get methanol is to go to Pep Boys and buy bottles of "HEET" the gas line dryer stuff. It is almost 100% methanol and you just have to buy a few bottle of the stuff and mix 50/50 in your meth container in the car. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Sep 25, 2006 7:49 am I'm having a similar issue, but mine isn't nearly as bad as yours nor am I forced induction (posting a new thread in a few min about it). However my suspicions as to why your KAMRFs jump to 1 when you hit the throttle are that it hasn't run long enough at anything but idle to learn anything about higher throttle and load conditions. The default is 1 until it learns otherwise. If it's running terribly rich, what you can do to get it under control for now is put larger injector values in for the high and low slopes until it gets into a range that's not so rich. You probably don't want to leave those values there once you get other things under control, but you may be able to use that technique to get you to where you can drive it and get more data about your setup. In my experience with the TwEECer, you want to use more global adjustments and determine if your setup is lean throughout the range (i.e. KAMRFs are always below 1) or if there are periods where you go above 1 for your KAMs. Once you dial in some slopes that give you a hodge-podge of values above and below, then you've done about as much as you can with global values. At that point, it'll be tweaking the MAF curve. Without a WB (Wide Band O2 sensor), you won't be able to do much with high load areas of the MAF curve. But you at least will be able to tweak the typical driving portions of the MAF curve to get better drivability. If you do have a WB, then a few WOTs at key RPMS should give you enough info to tweak the high-load parts of the curve. With the driving section roughed in using the KAMRFs to guide you in adjusting the curve and the top part of the curve roughed in using a WB & WOTs, you should be able to guesstimate what the curve looks like in the middle by looking at the shape of similar MAF curves. It won't be perfect, but it beats the cost of a dyno unless this car is a competition money-maker, in which the $600 for a dyno tune is almost a no-brainer. To help you with your endeavors, I'd highly recommend you purchase EEC Analyzer . It will help out A LOT in making heads-or-tails of your datalogs. It's WELL worth the money. I'm sure there are other analyzer softwares out there, this is just the one I use and have been very happy with it. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

With the MAF Transfer in particular most stock MAF's peak just below 5 volts and if for some reason the MAF voltage exceeded this second row value the eec would still return the maximum airflow value. It's a similar thing to having duplicate first/second and last/penultimate entries for the rows and columns in the scalers (normalising functions). Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Sep 27, 2006 4:07 pm cgrey8 wrote: So why do the MAF curves always have "16" at the top of the curve and it's usually the same exact flow value as the number just under it, usually 5 or 4.99? The MAF itself can handle upto about 7.5 volts. It is the EEC that limits the voltage to 5. Now we all know that not all electronics are created equal. They always have variances built in. With that said lets just say that a EEC is capable of producing 5.02. If this happened and the EEC tried to look it up in the MAF table it would get the same result as 5.0. If the 16 volt entry was not there then it would step off the end of the MAF curve. The main reason for the 16 volt point is for those times the EEC goes off the end of the curve. If the 16 volts was not there then the EEC defaults to 0. You can imagine what would happen then. Now the next part of it is the scalar that dictates the Maximum MAF voltage. I believe this was added when the GFUB was created. The earlier stratieges did not have this. This is where I believe the 16 volt MAF point came from. When they finally put a clamp on it the 16 volt point was no longer needed. This becomes more evident when looking at the newer EEC-IV's where they do not have a 16 volt entry. It actually allowed Ford to have one more meaningfull point on the curve for better resolution. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Tue Sep 26, 2006 8:42 pm You can either modify the Fuel Table - Startup to change the commanded fuel (LAMBSE) at startup. If the AFR's are different than the commanded LAMBSE's, either your MAF curve is off, or the Thermactor is enabled and adding air, thus giving false AFR numbers. You can make the time that the Startup Fuel Table is used shorter by modifying the Scaling Fuel Table Time function (FN018) - but be careful, this will affect cold startups too! You can try lowering ECT Minimum for Hot Start, but I'm not sure what that does. Not sure you can avoid the Fuel Table - Startup as it is part of the Open Loop Fuel calculation - there is a timer to go closed loop after a hot start (NITMR3), but I can't access it and have no idea how long it is. 428w now Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Mon Sep 25, 2006 3:55 pm Just want to make a correction to what I said above (I deleted part of my earlier post because it was wrong). According to GUFB, lowering the lowest column in the table from 17 degrees/second to 10 degrees/second does nothing since AEFUEL is set to 0 if the Throttle Angle Rate (TAR) is less than AETAR (minimum Throttle Angle Rate for AEFUEL) which is 20 degrees/second. If you want to change the threshold for AEFUEL, you have to lower BOTH the lowest column in AEFUEL AND AETAR. So if you lower the first column from 17deg/sec to 10deg/sec, you should also lower AETAR from 20 to 13 or so. The AEFUEL is set to 0 below the minimum TAR value in the table, so AETAR has to be higher than this. If you weren't confused before, you are now. Here is how it's described in GUFB: TAE (8x7 table of fuel flow function) is used in the above logic diagram. The X and Y inputs to this table are TAR and Temperature. For throttle angle rates of change below that of the first column of the TAE Table (17 degrees/second), TAE is set to zero. For TAR values between AETAR and 17 deg/sec, AEFUEL should be constant (to avoid effects of TAR jitter. Note that AETAR is accessible in TunerPro A9L.xdf, but not in CalEdit, so this does not apply to most folks anyway. 428w now Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Tue Sep 26, 2006 5:16 pm Decel load is different than accel (tip-in) load and decel doesn't update anyway since low loads (decel) reference cell row8column2 (idle). I tried to "bias" the MAF curve exactly like you are - the damned adaptive control would thwart me every time. I re-read GUFB and I realized that the MAF control is for steady-state operation & that tip-ins were transient conditions. The Acceleration Enrichment FUEL routine is designed to handle this. There are two parts to this routine - one acts like an accelerator pump and the other has to do with intake manifold wall wetting. I haven't figured out how to deal with the second one yet, but I was able to get good results by making sure that AEFUEL was used for even light tip-ins and that it stayed rich long enough after the tip-in to transition to steady-state MAF control. One part of that was to make sure accel fuel was still being applied as the throttle is pressed further; Accel Enrichment Multiplier vs TP A9L TP MULT 4.98 0.00 4.16 0.00 2.21 0.30 0.98 0.95 0.00 1.00 My tune TP MULT 4.98 0.00 4.16 0.00 1.99 0.80 0.98 0.95 0.00 1.00 The formula for AEFUEL = AEM*TAE*FN331B*FN378/60 AEM is the scalar multiplier than most people adjust first. TAE is the Accel Enrichment Fuel table FN331B is the Accel Enrichment Multiplier vs TP function above & FN378 adjusts for BP (barometric pressure) I think it's difficult to dial this in without a wideband, but not impossible. It sure worked for me - once I had it down, I could go out for a drive and do a hundred tip-ins from decel and not have a single bog - it's extremely smooth. 428w now Top

There are very likely some good reasons such as I have no clue what the correct injector slopes for my injectors are or the right injector vs battery function should be. Now most people are going to be quick to fire back a 19.64/26.1 or something along those lines for an answer to the injector slope issue. The problem is with those settings, I get a stumbling start. If the injectors I'm running were typical EV1 generation injectors, I'd agree, those numbers should work fine. The problem is these injectors came with the 97 Explorer motor. They are shaped like EV6 injectors, but have an EV1 style connector so the Mustang harness plugs right to them. My suspicion is that the newer EV6 injectors behave differently and are the reason why I've had to change this setting to get the engine to crank without stumbling. If I do nothing but modify the low slope from 26.1 to 23, the cold-start issues all goes away. Over time working with EA and the old MAF curve, I fine tuned the high slope down to 19 as well. Each datalog gives me some varying difference from 17.9/24 to 19/22 depending on whether the datalog contains WOTs or not. The average has been 19/23 and that has run pretty good with no cold-start cranking side-effects and that's the same values I'm running with the new MAF...but that's not to say they couldn't be changed to work better with this MAF. But I'm not going to mess with them. I'm doing as Juice suggested and focusing on one tweak at a time, although I was guilty of changing the above settings AND modifying the MAF curve for this morning's tune. From this mornings tune, I could tell that the engine was no longer going lean right at throttle increase thanks to Cougar's Accel Enrichment Vs TP tweak, but as soon as I quit moving the throttle, the LAMBSEs are still taking over and running me lean until adaptive control gets them back down where my HEGOs switch again. I don't think this tweak will be beneficial once the MAF curve is dialed in, but does seem to be minorly beneficial in the meantime. The good news is the MAF tweaks I made brought the LAMBSEs down from the 19s into the high 16s and 17s. So my hesitation was still there, but didn't last as long (didn't have to adapt as far) and wasn't quite as bad (wasn't as lean). posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Sat Sep 30, 2006 10:28 am Your MAF may be off in that area and if you are not in that area of flow much, there may not be enough KAMRF data to correct it. Have you taken datalogs & tried to adjust the MAF curve richer in that region yet? Once you dial in the MAF, then you may also need to add more acceleration fuel. This is more complicated, but I have found that it is required with the KB and the large throttle body that you have. Here is a quick explanation why... The acceleration fuel is added based on how fast you press the throttle. With a large TB (75-90mm), you get MUCH more air with a MUCH slower press of the throttle(think about it). The larger the TB, the worse it gets - I was able to get mine dialed in without adding much acceleration fuel with the 75mm TB, but when I went to the 85mm TB, it bogged worse than it ever had before - exact same MAF curve! Add to that the KB compressing that air and stuffing it into the chambers faster than a N/A motor, and, well, you can guess that it will lean out rather quickly using the stock settings that are set-up for a 60mm TB & a N/A engine! For me it was worse when the engine was cold. I copied this from another thread posted here this week (talking about how to add fuel during acceleration): I dialed in the accel fuel using the Accel Enrichment Fuel table, the Accel Enrichment Multiplier vs TP & the AEM scalar. The AEM multiplier I just set to 1 to eliminate it from the calculation (multiplying by 1 changes nothing), the Accel Enrichment Fuel table I set to 6 from 1.5 @ the lowest TP rates (on upper left) & blended into the "8" in the "92" column without changing anything to the right of that column. The AE Multiplier vs TP function I changed to keep the multiplier closer to "1" in the 1-2 volt range since my engine can pull a lot more air at low throttle positions with the Kenne Bell. See here: Accel Enrichment Multiplier vs TP A9L TP__MULTIPLIER 4.98 0.00 4.16 0.00 2.21 0.30 0.98 0.95 0.00 1.00 My tune TP__MULTIPLIER 4.98 0.00 4.16 0.00 1.99 0.80 0.98 0.95 0.00 1.00 The real secret is to set the table, function & scalar at some starting point (preferably too rich) & then get version A10 of Tweecer + a wideband & go for a ride. Do a datalog that includes the logging of "Accel Enrichment Fuel" & frequently go from coast to tip-in and then look at the datalog. You will see where AEFUEL kicks in and you can see exactly how rich it gets and for how long. I was able to dial the Accelerator Pump (Accel Enrichment Fuel) in this way after a few short drives up & down the street. 428w now Top

posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Quote Post by boss96 » Wed Sep 13, 2006 8:38 am I probably will get the exact names wrong since I don't have the strategy in front of me but there are functions for act and ect retard that determine how much timing vs temp is applied. You then go to tables and use the act/ect multipliers to see exactly how much timing is being added/removed. For example, at 4000rpm at high load (.9) the multiplyer might be .99 which effectively means "1". If the function table says 4 degrees of timing retard is applied at lets say 120 degrees of act temp then the multiplier of "1" mean that you will see 4 degrees if retard. If the multiplier is less (.5) then you would see 2 degrees retard at that particular air temp and so on. Same goes for ect retard function/tables. Under tables, watch for spark adders that are based on OL a/f ratios, CDAN4 adds timing when you go below 14.7-1 a/f (they are assuming you are going OL under heavy load or wot. All of these modifiers can be very useful if you have the time to dyno every possible condition that the motor would be operated at but most of us can't do that. If you had a relatively stock 4.6 engine with a blower you could leave all those spark tables in place and just reduce overall timing at wot/high load and be safe but you have a completely different motor. title: Dashpot Decay Rate - thorough explanation - EECTuning.org

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Dashpot Decay Rate - thorough explanation Quote Post by rockin_rick » Thu Aug 25, 2005 6:27 pm [EDIT - this first post of mine is a bit confusing. Read down farther and I explain it more clearly and with the important points more emphasized. Rick] This is my understanding of dashpot decay rate after a thorough research of the CRAI8 strategy document. This info applies specifically to CRAI8, but I would guess that it also works this way for CBAZA, and other EEC-V's. This may also be the way it works in A9L, but I haven't verified. -------------------------------------------------- First - ISC operational explanation: The ISC strategy can operate in any one of four modes: DASHPOT PREPOSITION, DASHPOT, RPM CONTROL, or LOCKOUT. Regardless of which of the four modes is active, the strategy first calculates a total desired idle airflow, DESMAF. DESMAF represents the total engine airflow required for idle and is comprised of both feedforward terms, i.e DESMAF_PRE and DASPOT, and feedback terms, i.e DESMAF_PID. DESMAF is given by: DESMAF = DESMAF_PRE + DASPOT + DESMAF_PID Where the feedback term, DESMAF_PID, is given by: DESMAF_PID = IPSIBR + ISCKAM + ISC_A_PROP + ISC_A_DER There are slight differences in the calculation of DESMAF depending on which mode is active. These differences are summarized below. * ISCFLG = 0 DASHPOT PRE-POSITION In engine run/underspeed mode and when operating at part or wide open throttle the ISC system is placed in dashpot pre-position mode. In this mode the ISC duty cycle is incremented a calibratable amount in anticipation of a required dashpot action. Proper dashpot operation is essential on systems having speed density fuel controls in order to avoid tip in/tip out stalls and HC spiking on decels. DESMAF_PRE = Initial prediction, based on rpm, load, & temperature DASPOT = DASPTK * (DSTPBR - (RATCH + DELHYS)) + FN830 DESMAF_PID := IPSIBR = Fixed at last calculated value (not updated in this mode) ISCKAMn = KAM cell n, where n is selected by ISFLAG ISC_A_PROP & ISC_A_DER are both zero * ISCFLG = -1 DASHPOT CONTROL In engine run/underspeed mode and having just transitioned from part to closed throttle the system is placed in ISC dashpot control mode. The length of time the ISC system will remain in dashpot control is both hardware/strategy dependent (some applications have VSS; some manual transmission applications have gear and clutch switches). Regardless of the length of time required to enter RPM control, as long as closed throttle operation is maintained the amount of airflow specified by the dashpot pre-position (see dashpot pre- position logic) is decremented at a constant rate until exhausted (until DASPOT = 0). DESMAF_PRE = Initial prediction, based on rpm, load, & temperature DASPOT = old DASPOT - FN879(DASPOT) DESMAF_PID := IPSIBR = Fixed at last calculated value (not updated in this mode) ISCKAMn = KAM cell n, where n is selected by ISFLAG ISC_A_PROP & ISC_A_DER are both zero * ISCFLG = 1 CLOSED LOOP RPM CONTROL Typical Idle RPM control (not at issue here) * ISCFLG = 2 CLOSED LOOP RPM CONTROL (Lock-out entry to RPM control) 'Hanging' RPM control in neutral when coming to a stop. This is often a few/several hundred more RPMs than idle RPM. (not at issue here) ------------------------------------------- While at PT or WOT (DASHPOT PRE-POSITION mode), airflow is added to the DASPOT term to prepare for a deceleration. It is mainly determined from the ISC_Dashpot_Pre-Position function. Then when going to closed throttle mode, the ISC strategy changes to DASHPOT CONTROL mode, and the airflow which was previously added to the DASPOT term is bled away. I BELIEVE that FN879 (ISC_dashpot_decay_rate) decay value (Y axis) represents the amount of air (in lb/min) to subtract from the value DASPOT, per background loop when in DASHPOT CONTROL mode. DASPOT was previously built up in DASHPOT PRE-POSITION mode. I believe that the X axis value is actually the current DASPOT value (in lb/min), rather than 'time' as known in caledit. So you are then able to adjust the amount of air that is decremented from DASPOT, as DASPOT itself decrements. So IOW, whatever the DASPOT value is going into the function, that becomes the X value, and the corresponding Y axis value is then subtracted from it. Most calibrations start out decrementing air quickly, and then ramp down the 'drop' as time goes on. This seems to make the function's 'decay' values go from right to left as the RPM drops. The DASPOT value is clipped to 0 (not allowed to go lower than zero). Thus setting 'decay' larger will subtract more from DASPOT each background loop, making for a larger/faster drop in RPMs (ultimately due to a smaller DESMAF value). -------------------------------------------- I also believe that the ISC_Dashpot_Pre-Position function's axis labels are wrong. It should have 'RPM's' on it's X axis, rather than 'Time', and 'air' on the Y, rather than decay. ROM fox_type FN830; /* Dashpot preposition offset. Resolution: 0.000240 Base Value: Units: PPM Min. Value: 0.000000 Max. Value: 2.000000 Cal. Level: RCON/VECTR XY Pairs: 6 X Input: N X Input Units: RPM*/ I also believe that the ISC_dashpot_decay_rate function's axis labels are wrong. It should have 'DASPOT value' (or 'air') on it's X axis, rather than 'Time', and 'air' (or 'air decay') on the Y. ROM fox_type FN879; /* A background driven decrement to the dashpot preposition airflow register as a function of DASPOT. Resolution: 0.000244 Base Value: Units: PPM Min. Value: 0.000300 Max. Value: 0.500000 Cal. Level: RCON/VECTR XY Pairs: 7 X Input: DASPOT X Input Units: PPM*/ ----------------------------------------------- Looking at the function definitions, it lists the values of air as PPM. I believe that PPM isn't "parts per million" as commonly known, but that it is really "Pounds Per Minute" (lb/min), as commonly used in the strategy for air units. I found these (non-important to this discussion) ram locations and descriptions in the CRAI8 document. RAM F32 pcomp_ppm; /* PCOMP IN POUNDS PER MINUTE. Resolution: 0.000000 Units: PPM Init. Value: 0.000000 Min. Value:0.000000 Max. Value: 63.990002 Reg. Type: RAM*/ AND RAM F32 pgm_pcomp_w; /* Filtered PCOMP flow in pounds per minute. Resolution: 0.000002 Units: PPM Init. Value: 0.000000 Min. Value:0.000000 Max. Value: 0.124000 Reg. Type: RAM*/ I haven't tested out these decay values, does my description reflect the operational charastics observed by others? posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Sat Aug 27, 2005 5:56 pm Perhaps I didn't emphasize the point of this, or my post wasn't read or understood. While most everyone knows that larger 'decay' values = faster drop, and smaller values = slower drop, I have never seen it posted exactly what the values in that function actually mean or specifically do, nor does it seem that anyone really knows. Everyone seems confused. I believe that I have solved the mystery of this function. The Dashpot decay rate function's X axis value is NOT time, but rather the value in the RAM location DASPOT. The Y axis value (known as decay) is the amount of air (in lb/min) to be subtracted from RAM location DASPOT, per background loop. The function doesn't work based on time, although coincidently (or indirectly) it sorta does. ******************************************************* RAM location DASPOT is the amount of air (in lb/min) added to the ISC to prepare for the closing of the throttle while in PT or WOT mode. This value is mainly comprised of the dashpot pre-position. DASPOT is the amount of air above the amount required to maintain desired idle speed. Once the throttle is closed, the EEC bleeds off the extra air that DASPOT adds. To do this, it uses the Dashpot decay rate function to figure out how much to subtract. It looks to that function, the current DASPOT value is the X axis. Then it exits the function with the amount to be subtracted, the Y axis value. This occurs once per background loop. Then the next time the function is applied (the next background loop), the new (slightly reduced) DASPOT value is the X value this time, and the 'decay' rate (Y axis value) is output and subtracted from DASPOT. This then continues until DASPOT is zero. Once all of this is bled off, then the ISC is told to let the amount of air past to maintain the desired RPM. When the vehicle is in motion, DASPOT is not allowed to completely go to zero, there is another function that clips it to a minimum per vehicle speed. Then once the speed has dropped under that speed, the remaining DASPOT amount is allowed to be bled off. ******************************************************* So taking CManT1914's values posted: 0.3000500-----0.4499500-----0.649900-----0.929930-----16.00000 0.0039063-----0.0080566-----0.023926-----0.050049-----0.050049 Assume you are driving in PT mode and DASPOT = 0.929930, and you go closed throttle, the EEC goes to the daspot decay rate function to start bleeding off that 0.929930 air adder. The first time through, it will compute a 'decay' rate of 0.050049. It then subtracts that from the 0.929930 and the new DASPOT value is 0.879881. During the next background loop, it goes to the dashpot decay rate function and the X axis value used is 0.879881. It then computes a 'decay' amount of about 0.045 (interpolated). Then it subtracts that 0.045 from 0.879881 to get the new DASPOT value of 0.834881. This continues until DASPOT = 0, or DASPOT = min clip value due to VSS. With CManT1914's given function, as DASPOT get's smaller, the 'decay' also slows down. ******************************************************* I have also checked GFUB, and the dashpot decay rate function also works this way - with the X input being DASPOT, and the Y output being a subtractor. I realize that this information will not have much of an impact on everyone's tune, but is more intended to be another piece of the puzzle - to increase our understanding of the EEC. posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Thu Oct 05, 2006 10:53 am I was having a problem with declutch stall/oscillation & I increased the DASMIN scalar until it caught the engine during a declutch. This is the function that prevents the DASPOT from decaying to zero when you are above 6.5 MPH (A9L). It becomes active when you are going faster than 8.5 MPH (6.5 MPH + 2 MPH hysteresis - A9L). The engine sits at ~1100 RPM until I get below 6.5 MPH during a decel, so it's not really that noticable. Not sure if adding the larger TB (85mm) changed where this needed to be set or ?, but it works fine & my ISC works fine in closed loop at ~38% DC & +/- ~3 degrees timing max, so I think I am good... DASMPH = Minimum VSBAR for declutch Daspot Clip, mph. DASMHYST = Hysteresis for DASMPH, mph. DASMIN = Minimum Daspot Clip for declutch, ppm. 428w now Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sat Oct 07, 2006 6:16 am AFAIK the LOWLOD address is correct in TunerPro (the conversion isn't, I think it shoud be X*64/327.68 ). Because this, and the A/C Low Load Adder (aka ACLOD), are set to zero in the stock A9L the ecu always sets the ISC Mode Flag (aka ISCFLG) to 2 (rpm lockout mode). If you are in neutral (assuming have a gearbox that detects neutral, e.g. Transmission Type (aka TRLOAD) >= 3) the ecu will skip any decision making processes involving LOWLOD and set the ISC Mode Flag to 2 anyway. Top

posts.author: Mudog715
posts.content: Mudog715 Regular Posts: 63 Joined: Sun Oct 08, 2006 2:48 am table 'maximum_allowed_spark_table_cold_starts' questions Quote Post by Mudog715 » Sun Oct 08, 2006 5:10 am On my strategy and catch code, this table (FN2000) is set up to limit spark advance based on engine temp and time after startup. I don't recall seeing it described elsewhere so I suspect maybe it's not in the other common (ie Mustang, Lightning) strategies. Stock settings limit advance to 15° for the first 8 seconds at 80-120°F ECT & 20° until 22 seconds at the same ECT range. Advance is not limited at ALL after 36 seconds OR under 0°F/above 160°F! At 40°F it's really weird: limit to 40° advance for first 8 seconds then 30° advance up to 22 seconds, then no limit after that. I looked at some other AGANN strategy applications and they were both different from mine: DUO2 (302 truck) limits to 10° advance for first 5 seconds above 50°F ECT, then 12° advance up to 30 seconds. At 0°F ECT and below, it limits to 28° advance until 10 seconds, then 10° adv until 20 seconds, then 12° adv until 30 seconds. After 30 secs no limits at any temp. VUE3 (460 van) has no limits at any ECT/time points (ie. table is all '60')! So my question is what is the point of limiting advance after initial startup and why on my FEZ2 460 is it primarily limited in the 40°-120° range, but not above or below those temps? And why would the van 460 have no limits at all, but the truck 460 does? Incidentally, my engine stumbles a little and idles low (800-ish) when started mid-cold (I live in Mesa, AZ and it hardly ever gets below 40°F) regardless of the idle speed adders and scalars but after about 20-30 seconds the idle "magically" smooths out and climbs to the rpms I have set in the 'ISC Startup RPM vs ECT' function (FN826A). I have been trying to figure out WHY it does this and only when the engine is under 180°F and I suspect this is the cause. 2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Tue Oct 10, 2006 11:55 am WA2FAST, We have a similar setup and I wish I could report 514rwhp. The best we have done is 425. I am certain the cats and restrictive FRPP 2.5" exhuast is part of the problem. Anyway, we have played a lot with the WOT AFR. Our car goes from 11.68 as specified in the stabilized fuel table until the ACT climbs above 116 degrees. Then there is a multiplier in the CBAZA W4H0 calibration that kicks in and starts adding fuel and we see the AFR dive to around 10.0 until the very end of the run where we seem to run out of injector. So I pulled the function and consequently burned pistons.:-( This year I changed from the W4H0 calibration to the J4J1 calibration and here Ford did not use the function to richen AFR based on ACT rise, instead they dialed in an increasing amount of spark retard as ACT and RPM rise. Now at the end of the run we are seeing close to 11.7 AFR but the timing is down to 9 degrees! My point is that I think you need to consider both timing and AFR when trying to decide target AFR at WOT. I don't know if your A9* strategy has similar functions. By the way, I have a 2 core intercooler on the P1SC and the ACT is ambient at launch and around 175 at the finish 12 seconds later. Unfortunately on the 94/95's the P1SC gets its intake air from right in front of the brake booster and the air cleaner sits right over the driver side header, so the ACT is disadvantaged from the get go. I also think 11.5 AFR is good, but with how much timing? I think the J4J1 calibration is overly conservative in its spark retard, but after burning pistons I don't feel smart enough to add much timing back. I definitely do not like the other approach Ford had for the 94/95 that I mention above, i.e. richening the mixture as ACT climbs. Do you have either of these functions in your calibration? And do you have a MPH richening function as well? (J4J1 does and I have defeated it) 94 GT, CBAZA/J4J1, 347 (on a R302 block), F303 cam, Performer II Intake, 1.7 Crane RR's, 1 5/8 Shorties, 70MM BBK TB, C&L 85mm Tuner MAF, Pro-Charger D1SC, 60#'s, TKO 600. posts.content: WA2FAST Tuning Addict Posts: 713 Joined: Wed Sep 29, 2004 1:04 pm Location: MI Contact: Contact WA2FAST Website AOL Quote Post by WA2FAST » Tue Oct 10, 2006 12:14 pm Hey 2Shaker... I'm running 17* total advance at higher RPM's right now and like I said, I have stabalized the fuel to be pretty good around 11.0:1 through most of the curve till I max the injector duity cycle out and then it starts leaning out big time up top and gets as far as 12.2-12.4:1 towards 6k, so I try to keep it around 5800 or so for now. The A9L does have similar functions but you have to remember how the A9L does ACT vs. your car. I have the ACT sensor plummed into the lower intake manifold to start with, so although it does climb with boost, the computer doesn't see too much of it from a 2k-6k pull lets say. It does go up about 10* or so and at that point, it is pulling timing, but that's how these cars were designed... good or bad. Your car has the ACT in the airbox from the factory so it REALLY IS seeing ambient air temps unlike mine, so I can't even imagine what that will do to timing because of hot header air... WOW that's got to pull a ton. Mine will pull a degree or so right at 6k usually on a normal 70-75 degree summer day which is fine. My timing is very controlable, it's my fuel that's the trick! I'm running out of injector way early on so I'm trying my best to remedy it, but we'll see how well it goes. With the AFR towards 11.0:1 now, WOW did the car ever pick up a TON of power! The 514rwhp is no where near right now... I have a touch more timing in it and a lot less fuel and am still way safe compared to the last time it was on the dyno. I'm actually very happy with it, just am trying my best to not have to go with new injectors, fuel system, etc., quite yet... saving up for a wedding right now! If I were you, I'd look at your functions for ACT trim and work with those, there is no reason you should be running that low of timing, that's a bit rediculous... I wouldn't say defeat it, but I would log a bunch of normal driving and WOT blasts to see where the temps are and work with it accordingly. I know that EGR on those cars is really bad for detonation if you defeat the system physically and don't take the timing adders out. I noticed that right away on a friends 95 that he blocked the EGR passages in... that thing ALWAYS detonated at part throttle after that... this was about 8 years ago now though, before I knew what I know now. -Don- 87' GT, A9L, TwEECer RT, P1SC@12psi Non-Intercooled, AFM PP, 3" Pro-M#42, 70mm TB, GT-40 Intake, GT-40X Heads, B303, 1.6, BBK 1-5/8" Long Tubes, 306 Built Bottom End, Probe Block Girdle, TR3550, 3.55, PLX WB, Jan 07 Modified Mustangs Feature Car Top

I was wondering if you had changed the HEGO Bias, because if you change it too much, it will not be able to achieve closed loop as the O2 will spend too much time on one side & not switch enough or at all. You have leaned out your idle 8%! - the car is attempting to idle at an AFR of 15.8 and it cannot achieve this. I would not change more than 4% from stoich max. You have another issue - it appears that you have a turbo? This will likely change the exhaust pulse delay and can add to your issues WRT closed loop stability. Also, you have changed the injector timing to have the injector fire sooner with that E-Cam. It seems that if you were trying to keep gasoline from going directly out the exhaust, you would want to have the injector fire later. 428w now Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Tue Oct 24, 2006 1:12 pm 4% is still a lot - I'm only leaning it ~1% and it seems to actually idle smoother and I really haven't noticed the fuel smell lately. I don't know of anybody who has leaned their car this much - you're setting the trend here - you may want to consider the possible extra heat & life of your turbo if it is running excessively lean. The conversion simply converts the number in the memory register (which is a whole number) into a number that is related to real life. It's actually done in reverse - they take the number - .04 for instance & multiply it by a value based on the size of the memory register, the range of values that can be used in real life & the resolution needed. I really don't know how much injector timing will help - the turbo probably causes some backpressure which might minimize the problem anyway. You need to experiment with the injector timing and perhaps lean it slightly at idle until you are happy. If you really can't take the smell of benzene, toluene, xylene, ethanol & the other vile chemicals in gasoline these days then get a pipe with a catalytic converter in it! The neutral injector timing thing is just something I did because I could and like the idea that I can delay the timing in neutral a little more than the table even though I believe it prolly makes no difference at all. As far as overlap, when you check "exhaust close" it will not fire the injector until the exhaust valve is on the seat, so this will ensure no possibility of firing fuel into the exhaust. At higher RPM you can have it fire sooner to get the entire pulse into the intake opening event. Breakpoints - well, I just used the numbers Clint found for the Lightning which uses the Green Top injectors, then tweaked based on some datalogs. The low slope does't make as much difference as you might think & you will quickly compensate for it with either injector offset or MAF tweaks. 428w now Top

I try to keep my approach as simple as possible and make absolute minimum changes to get results. Fuel table base OL table. This is what the eec is going to target depending on ECT and load. I worked with the top right corner of the table to enter/adjust WOT target afr. Stock eec is set to 12.5, and that is too lean for confort on a blown app. Change the top 2 rows (90* and up) on this table to get your desired WOT afr. This is what I did. WOT fuel multiplier, I never messed with. As for throttle breakpoints, there is the "OL throttle breakpoint" scalar, I lower this one also to match the "WOT throttle breakpoint" scalar, both are at 2.7 volts from ford, 2 volts is recommended for blown apps. Once I set up all these scalars, tables, injector slopes, and injector offsets, I worked with the maf to get adaptive NOT to make much of an adjustment. I don't know how you would do this with forced open loop.(btw, my maf flow sheet is about dead on, I only had to adjust airflow rates at idle and just above idle) My question is to you and everyone else:WHen you disable adaptive like you did, is closed loop also disabled? posts.author: kickerscrt
posts.content: kickerscrt Regular Posts: 122 Joined: Wed Feb 02, 2005 4:41 am More weird EEC/tune happenings Quote Post by kickerscrt » Tue Oct 31, 2006 10:31 pm Alright fellas, I fixed the whole code 66 thing by changing my MAF min voltage to .11 as Juice said to do. Voila! No more check engine light and no more LIMP mode. Car ran good, good afr's, etc, etc. Good to go, right? NO! A few guys from my work wanted to check out the engine bay to see the installed ProCharger system. I started the car up for them and one of them noticed that I had forgot (stupid me!) to hook up the vacuum line that comes $off the side of the manifold right by the throttle body (Cobra Intake). According to my Chilton manual, it's the Fuel Vapor Return Hose. Ok, no biggie, I'll just hook it back up and everything will be fine. Now let me first say that with this line disconnected the car had a rock-solid idle, which seems extremely crazy as usually a vacuum leak will cause all sorts of idle issues. So after I hooked the line back up, the idle got even better than it already was! After about 1 minute of idling like that, the car stumbled and died. I go to start it back up and had to push the gas pedal to the floor to clear the flooding. It finally started, ran for like 10 seconds, and died again. Same situation repeated a couple of times. So I figured since the ecm got used to that line not connected I'd do a KAM reset so it could re-learn. Even after that, the car still absolutely WILL NOT idle, and when it does die, I always have to push the pedal to the floor. I knew I couldn't drive the car home like that, so I popped the hood and disconnected that line...runs close to a 100% stock Mustang. Can anyone explain to me why with that line connected the car goes soo rich? Any possible solution in the tune aspect so I can run the car with this line hooked up? Please help! 91 LX Coupe, A9P/A9M, Intercooled ProCharger P1SC (9 Psi), FMS 42lb, PMAS 3" ProTube (42lb N/A Curve), AFR 165 heads, E303, FRPP Cobra Intake, Bassani exhaust, 3.73, aod-t-5 conversion Top

posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Thu Nov 02, 2006 11:09 am Ok, I got it now! Here is what I would do: car idling with line disconnected, start a datalog. After some time, connect that hose from the canister. Log till the car dies. Post that log or send it to me, maybe I can see something in there. I only see 2 possibilites, idle is too rich and the vacuum leak allows your car to idle. Or, the idle is fine and the canister is dumping too much raw fuel vapors. Note: A KAMRF of 1.121 is telling me your too lean, so I'm kinda confused. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Wed Nov 01, 2006 9:08 pm LOADX is also known as Load Percent. This LoadX parameter is the actual engine load with corrections for the Barometric Pressure and it is scaled using the sealevel load function. This is used on a few select tables through out the EEC LOAD is the actual engine load not compensated for anything. This is the parameter that will tell you how much load on the engine is applied. The LOADX maybe mis leading because it is scaled. In your case I would look at the LOAD parameter to find out where you actually are. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Nov 08, 2006 2:47 pm Brian-Mc's right...this happens when you change your datalog payload. About the only way to fix it is to shutdown BOTH CalCon and CalEdit. Reopen CalEdit and your BIN/CCF. Then reselect your Payload options and click the Payload button. At this point, CalCon should launch without giving you that stupid error. Don't forget to redownload your payload to TwEECer. Also make sure you actually SAVE the payload selection so it shows up in the list. I suspect this CalCon error has something to do with selecting those checkboxes in the list of available points to datalog. However as long as my payload was saved, I've always been able to get rid of the error by shutting both programs down, relaunching CalEdit, then selecting a saved payload, clicking payload button, then downloading. Also make sure if you ever see the "Update Only" checkbox checked, unselect it. I've had bad experiences where having that checked caused more problems than it was worth. It works a lot of the time, but then suddenly it'll foul up and download corruption to the TwEECer which requires a complete download to correct. Granted, it is faster downloading when all you have to update is what you changed, but unless it works right, it's not worth it. Now that all I use is TunerPro to make my BIN tweaks, it's a moot issue. Another thing you DO NOT want to do is accidentially uncheck "datalogging" or your payload of datalogged points while in traffic, then redownload the TwEECer. When you download the changes, your engine has a high chance of suddenly running like crap until you turn off the ignition, let it sit a second or so. I don't know why, but I've found that to be true enough to learn not to ever do it again while I'm in stop-n-go Atlanta traffic. When you get deeper into tweaking, you'll want to start playing with the Adaptive Update table. When you 1st start tuning, you pretty much want everything set at 10...some people set the decel (bottom) rows referencing something like -82. But I've found if you reference "-89" too much, it also causes one of your two KAMRFs to report to .5 at idle which really runs the engine lean on 1/2 your cylinders. It's unmistakeable when it happens, the engine just runs terrible. When setting this table up once your MAF is all tuned in, either copy exactly what the ECM's bin has or don't use "-89" anywhere and you should be safe. Well that was more than you wanted to know about... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Nov 08, 2006 2:26 pm The injector timing is a 1-time thing...you run the numbers based on your datalog, and unless you make major changes, the numbers stay pretty much the same. EA will also calculate Injector Slopes based on your application's datalogs. You want to make sure you run this on a rather long datalog with lots of idling, cruising, moderate acceleration throughout the RPM range, and WOTs off-idle to redline so it can see all the various types of driving styles and calculate a slope that fits it all. I've spent a lot of time watching my injector slopes calculate and recalculate based on the changes I make in the tune. If I run it against a tune with only light cruising and no heavy acceleration, it does affect the calculation...so like I said, get a nice comprehensive logfile that represents all possible driving conditions. Once you've done this, you set it and never need to mess with it again unless you are just doing santiy checks to make sure nothing major has happened. The thing I use the most is the MAF curve tuner, datalog mapping, and custom graphs. The custom graphs feature allows you to view valve-over-time graphs of any parameter you've datalogged such as RPM, MPH, Spark, Injector Duty Cycle, etc etc. codedout wrote: ...Honestly I think it would be very hard to tune without this program... I agree. I was advised to get EA when I got the TwEECer by the company I bought the TwEECer from. I spent 1 day trying to make head-or-tails of what my datalogs were saying, and decided they were right...I needed EA. Unless you are a VERY expereinced tuner that just knows what causes what problems and can "smell" what needs to change or you have some other way of analyzing the data, you are going to need some help. Not to mention, the datalogs are written off to a database. Unless you have a tool to open Paradox databases (an outdated Coral/Borland POS database) and view your data, you can't really get to the info in those logs. posts.content: stang&2Birds Gear Head Posts: 41 Joined: Sat Nov 04, 2006 1:01 am Quote Post by stang&2Birds » Sat Nov 04, 2006 1:46 am Cougar5.0 and I agree. :) I'll go a little more in depth. I don't know what the EEC-V wants for a table for the MAF. (And, I don't really care. :)) But, all the EEC-IV's care about is the kg/hr vs volts of the MAF. Nothing more, nothing less. Okay, let's say by some wild imagination, someone figured out how to use the Internet and found the VOLTS KG/HR MAF transfer curve for the LMAF. :) Or, they had it flow tested. Then, they can take that MAF curve that has kg/hr vs volts and plug it right in to an EEC-IV. EVERY MAF varies from base-line a little. That includes the Ford OEM MAFs. That's one of the reasons for the multiple trim values in the 2 dimensional trim table. From an A9x point-of-view, for the MAF curve, it doesn't matter if the EEC is running at 5MHz, 10MHz, or 20 MHz. If, by some stretch of the imagination, that isn't true, can someone please explain to me how come what Tom Cloud wrote, what the Tweecer uses, and how people have used KG/HR in the A9x table have been wrong all of these years? From Technical Notes on the EEC-IV MCU by Tom Cloud: The MAF Transfer Function is located at 6DE2 for the A9L, is 120 bytes in length, unsigned, and is 2-byte/4096 “X” (MAF voltage) by 2-byte/4 (mass air flow in kg/hr). Table 31: MAF Transfer Function From GFUB: The strategy integrates the instantaneous airflow , MAF, over each PIP period. To calculate the average air charge, ARCHG, this integration is accomplished by summing the average MAF over a finite period of time. The air meter sample period starts at each rising PIP edge. Successive samples are then obtained at fixed intervals of approximately one msec. ... =========== So, if you manually input the MAF curve for the LMAF, that should work fine. But, as I understand , if you choose the "LMAF" as the MAF from the Tweecer menu, then the Tweecer will use the values (Lb/Mn) that the EEC-V MAF table wants. And, not the kg/hr units that the EEC-IV MAF table expects. However, there's no reason you can't use an LMAF curve that is specified in kg/hr and input those values as a custom MAF curve into your EEC-IV. Then, do the custom MAF tuning if needed/as needed. Many people don't use screens and they use cone air filters right on the end of the LMAF and into the engine bay. Both of those will effect the measurement (curve) of the LMAF. Maybe I missed something??? Top

I appreciate all the responses From what I am understanding above... Those who are 'modifying' their LMAF curve would modify any MAF curve. I guess what I am saying is that I would assume the MAF Transfer was more accurate than the injector settings. When I tune, I leave the MAF Transfer alone, and dial in the KAMRF's with the injector slopes, vBat, etc. There is going to be error in both the MAF and the Injectors. I have always assumed that since there is real airflow data available for most MAF meters, that the MAF Transfer would be more accurate than the flow ratings for injectors, which are seldom flow tested and flow data seems hard to find. But here goes. The bosch system of fuel injection as explained to me by a guy that has been tuing Merc, Porsche's and Beamers for years is this: Its all relative to fluid dynamics. It is much harder to control the flow of fuel with and on off type device such as the injector. So what the bosch system does is inject X amount of fuel then trim it with airflow (IAC). The IAC can respond to changes faster than the injector can. As the system learns it roughly adjusts the fuel flow via the KAMRF's and continues to fine tune with the airflow. So what this really means is that the injector slopes are pretty much a rough value, and the MAF transfer are also rough. I was told by him to get your injectors dialed in within +/- 10% then trim your MAF to compensate the rest. You are right on the injector flows, and one thing has always concerned me is the fact that the flow rates are spec'ed out at +/- 10% so if you have one on the high side and one on th elow side they could be 20% apart. So one piston could be at 12.5 AFR and the other could be at 15AFR. Now because the O2's monitor a bank of 4 cylinders, one would hope that if sort of averages out. Sorry to get off subject, but I think the answer here IS: You will never get it dead solid perfect. There are too many variables. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Nov 09, 2006 8:22 am That sounds like what was holding you back. Also keep in mind when datalogging KAMs/LTFTs, you don't really read the memory of the EEC to get the table of values. You kind of "catch" them as you pass by certain RPM/loads. Thus, if you never hit 3000RPM at 50% load, then when you map your datalog in EA, you'll see a "hole" in the map where that data wasn't available in your datalog. So when doing MAF tuning, you want as diverse of a log as you can possibly get...from idles, cruising, light/moderate/heavy throttle at as wide of an RPM range as you can get and WOTs from as low in the RPMs as you can get all the way to red-line. However if I may make a suggestion before you go tweaking away on the MAF curve. 1. Get your injector slopes solid. Run that same "diverse" datalog mentioned above, then let EA crunch you out some more accurate Injector Slopes and enter those into your tune. 2. Clear your KAMs in the EEC. This can be done by lifting the positive battery terminal OR downloading an invalid BIN to one of TwEECer's placeholders and flipping to that position momentarily (Clint taught me that trick) 3. Now go drive another "diverse" datalog and calculate your MAF curve. This will produce more user-friendly MAF curve if your Injector slopes are tuned in a little better. At some point, you might also want to tune your Injector offset as well. Here's a suggested procedure for that: 1. In the morning, datalog your engine idling with a high voltage. Colder mornings tend to produce higher voltages for some reason on my truck. So with as little electrical load as possible get a good 30 seconds of datalogging. 2. Start slowly turning things on like headlights (brights) 3. Slowly ramp up the speed on your blower motor (a good 30 seconds between speeds) 4. If you can, run the windshield wipers. Nobody thinks about it, but that motor is pretty stout and does pull a decent load. 5. If you have a loud-@$$ stereo, crank it up (assuming its not going to piss of the neighbors) 6. Turn off the engine and unplug your alternator. And then restart the engine with all those loads turned off 7. Then start 1-5 over again with no alternator. If you have a car with a lot of manual stuff and can't find other loads to put on the system, then you may have a big gap between the alternator plugged in and with it unplugged. So you may have to run a 3rd datalog after you've let the engine warm up and the alternator's voltage isn't as high as it would be on a cold start. By the end of this exercise, you can take all your logs and merge them together using EA. A neat feature that many don't know about because it was just added to EA is you can now select multiple log files from the Open window. Select your NEWEST log first, then select in order to the oldest file. Once all are selected, open them and EA will merge them together automatically and then you can run your Injector Offset calculation. Use CTRL-Click to select one file at a time, or SHIFT-Click to catch multiples in a row. If you've never used the "Click" features, stick with CTRL-click (that's left-mouse click) for now. I've found if you don't go through all this, you'll end up with a hump in your Offset curve which isn't going to be accurate or useful. However if you go through this procedure, EA will give you a pretty smooth hypothesized curve to put into EA. You may have to use your noodle to smooth out obvious anomalies, but I think you can manage. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Fri Nov 10, 2006 12:18 am Looks good chris. The only thing that pops to mind is if your injector slopes are unknow and the MAF is unknown then I would recommend setting both slopes to the rate size of the injectors and start tuning the MAF. This of coarse is only for starters. The best way I have seen this done is by eliminating one of the unknowns. This means put the stock MAF and air clearner box back in there stock locations if you can. Now tune for the new injector slopes with the good known MAF curve loaded. Once the slopes are dialed in, you can then work on tuning the battery offsets. After all that is done then never touch the slopes or offsets again. Just plain forget about them. Now install the MAF and tune that. I am a believer in the KISS method. One last thing, do not assume that the slopes from another EEC processor are going to work for you in your EEC processor just because they are rated at the same flow rate. The Accell, Dakota, Bosch and other injectors are all different. Also the EEC hardware for the EEC-IV and EEC-V have different injector drivers. This will cause the injectors to open at different voltages and different speeds. After that, you can start tweaking other stuff like the injector timing (based on your cam) and possibly Fuel tables. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Nov 10, 2006 12:52 pm If you are running a stroker, then yeah, you probably need to pay attention to those before even cranking the engine. As for the attention to the TB, that was a suggestion from some document I read on tuning. When I went through the exercise of calculating my TB's flowrate when closed, it came up to almost what the stock A9L/A9P had for a closed flowrate. If memory serves, it's .55lb/min. However that's not very helpful when your MAF curves are converted to kg/hr. I begged Clint to add a kg/hr calculator to EA so you don't have to go looking up formulas anymore. But what I did to "tune" the TB was pull the IAC (idle air controller) so the engine was forced to get all its air through the TB. I adjusted it as low as it would go. Most TBs when adjusted all the way down will choke the engine out, but my stock Explorer 65mm TB has ~1/16" hole in it and will still keep the engine running. So I let the engine idle with that for a while, got a MAF reading from it in kg/hr. Plugged that value into EA's calculator on the settings tab and got a lb/min value. If you don't have this calculator, update your copy of EA via the About Tab. It ended up being something like .53...not much difference from default, but I changed it anyway. I also readjusted the TPS to as close as I could get to .95v, but I've found close is good enough. The reading I get from the TPS ranges from .94v to .97v depending on temperature, but averages .955v...where the ECM wants it. I think as long as you are below .98 or .99, you are fine. The main focus of these two exercises are to fine tune the ECM's ability to idle smoothly assuming the engine can. From best I remember, setting these values gets the ECM in the ballpark. After seeing how close my 65mm TB was, I figure these steps are really only necessary for those guys running 75-90mm butterflies and wild cams that lope the engine hard at idle. In hindsight, it probably would've made more sense to tune the MAF, then perfect the idle since you are relying on your MAF to give you an accurate flow reading to convert in the 1st place. Good point 2shaker. On a sidenote, don't take everything I say as gospel. I'm still learning this stuff too. I'm just relaying my understanding of what I've been dealing with in hopes that it'll benefit others in some way. I usually type war-n-peace explanations of things in an effort to be as exact and precise as possible but its not my intention to come across as a "know-it-all" @$$ either. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Nov 10, 2006 3:51 pm According to what I've read in "How to understand, Service and Modify Ford Fuel Injection & Electronic Engine Control" By Charles O. Probst The ECM will run with the IAC wide open when you are at cruise. So if you take your foot off the gas suddenly, the engine doesn't just stall. However when at high RPM and the TPS is registering closed for a few seconds, the ECM will close the IAC to offer some engine braking. Since most ECMs feed fuel during decel, it makes sense that you'd want to choke the engine as much as possible to reduce the amount of fuel consumption on an obviously coasting condition. Next time you are going down a steep hill, keep the engine in a gear that'll engine-brake the car. You'll feel the IAC closing a few seconds into the decel down the hill by offering more resistance than it was previously. If you have a loud exhaust, you'll also hear the gurgling/bubbling get more apparent as well. As the RPMs lower, the IAC will open back up and you'll feel the engine braking almost go away into almost a free-wheeling coast. That's one reason I like the X3Z Cobra tune. It turns the injectors off at decel RPMs above 1500-1600. However, I wish it would open the IAC and the EGR wide open during this period so the engine didn't engine brake and I could coast further without having to give it gas. The engine braking is so strong that most of the time, I can't coast in gear for any length of time. However, I can turn the ignition off and push the throttle wide-open and it almost free-wheels. It sounds wicked too from the intake and the exhaust pipes pumping maximum air, but not burning any of it. But before you turn the key back on, you'll want take your foot off the gas. LOL But as for your comment...I think it depends on the throttle-body. I know my old 2.9L V6, I could adjust the TB to completely choke the engine out if the IAC isn't plugged in. It had a hole in it too, but it wasn't big enough to supply the engine. The basic rule of thumb I've always heard is open the TB only as far as you have to in order to get the engine to run...i.e. no more than 600 or so RPMs. This gives the IAC more control to adjust the RPMs as needed. However you could adjust it so low that the engine REQUIRES the IAC in order to maintain an idle. But the IAC may be nearly wide open just to maintain 900RPMs. During cold-start, the ECM may be programmed to target 1100RPMs for a few seconds until the ECT warms. If that's true, you are removing the ability for the ECM to control the engine properly. Will it hurt anything? I doubt it, but you are mothballing the ECM a little by not giving it all the control it needs to do its job. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Nov 10, 2006 8:25 pm Ever since I dropped the 302 into my Ranger, I've been a little disappointed with the takeoff right off-idle. From what I understand, 302s aren't exactly torque monsters in any stock form regardless of whether its a GT or Explorer motor. There are plenty of options out there for building big HPs with a 302, but very little for off-idle torque. To build that, I'd either have to go forced induction or stroked. So I looked into doing an Eaton supercharger. After looking at the prices of the Explorer Express's superchargers, I decided, I could do a lot better by stroking for the money. Since loosing low-end was my main concern, I investigated cam options as well. Fortunately, I've gotten a good bit of gains by tweaking the spark tables. A buddy of mine has an engine simulator that allows him to simulate all sorts of various engine combinations. He's run simulations with the Explorer cam (what I have now), the E303, the OEM Cobra cam, and the Crane PowerMax 2020 (pn 444211). The Crane cam has come out on top with producing low-end torque and maintaining it all the way to 5500 RPM. The E303 came out at the bottom of the stack for low-end torque. The Explorer cam had the E303 beat by leaps and bounds at 2500RPM. In fact, the E303 didn't overtake the Explorer cam until RPMs were above 4000. Since my main concern was maintaining torque, I decided then and there the E303 was not even a consideration since the OEM Explorer cam I have simulated better off-idle. I'm not saying the E303 can't give good torque at the bottom end, I'm just saying there are other cams better suited for that task. The E303 has its place, there's no doubt about it. Here are the simulation results: Crane PowerMax 2020 rpm_____hp_____torque 2500____184____386 3000____226____395 3500____270____405 4000____292____384 4500____295____345 5000____273____287 5500____235____225 OEM Explorer rpm_____hp_____torque 2500____181____380 3000____221____387 3500____259____388 4000____269____353 4500____259____302 5000____232____244 5500____190____181 OEM Cobra rpm_____hp_____torque 2500____169____356 3000____208____364 3500____249____373 4000____264____347 4500____262____305 5000____240____252 5500____200____191 FMS E303 rpm_____hp_____torque 2500____161____337 3000____205____359 3500____245____368 4000____268____352 4500____280____327 5000____263____294 5500____??? ____??? (he forgot to run this one) These were based on a 331 with stock GT40p heads, stock Cobra intake, and 65mm TB. I don't know exactly what he entered for headers and exhaust. From what I understand on these engine simulations, they are not far off from what you can expect but obviously there are too many variables the simulations can't take into account. However they are close enough give you a rough idea of what the engine is capable of. But the real value of the simulator isn't so much to tell you what the engine will do, but to allow you to compare the performance gains of various engine components...like cams. Thus the numbers indicated above may not be accurate to actual, but the difference between the various simulations (percentage wise) should be very close. As you can see, the E303 was at the bottom of the pile for low-end torque but came alive and was the clear winner when it comes to maintaining torque into the high RPMs. The main bottleneck in the simulations that kept the E303 from being the MAX HP winner was the GT40p heads. MAF Volt Maximum - 4.78516 you can set this to 4.99 and get a little more room out of your MAF sensor MAF Volt Minimum - .366211 This is the min the computer will look at the maf sensor. I set mine to .25 but my 408 idles at 1.2 volts PIP Filter - 961 This is the most important rev limiter in the EEC-IV. Do some searches and you will find the calculation for rpms. Basically 961 = 6250 rpms limit. ~700 = around 7500. The lower the number the higher the rpms limit. I have mine set to 200 Speed Limiter A - 127.5 Speed Limiter A ON/OFF - 127.5 Speed Limiter B - 127.5 Speed Limiter B ON/OFF - 127.5 Speed limiters are not used in the A9L, not totally sure in the A9P, but I don't think so. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Nov 07, 2006 10:38 pm As Juice said, the payload is completely separate from your CCF/BIN files. What you are saving when you "save" a Payload is the things you want to datalog. If you are like me, you have a few different configurations of datalogging options based on what you are trying to analyze. To keep you from having to click all those checkboxes every time you want to datalog something different, you can save off various configurations, then reset those configurations simply by clicking the saved payload and clicking the "payload" button. If you have a new custom payload of checkboxes you want to save as a new entry in your list, select the checkbox and then hit the payload button. With that checkbox selected, you'll be prompted to save your new setup with a new name. That name will appear in the list of payload options. The payload name doesn't have to relate in any way to the tune's saved name since these are two independent saves. When setting datalogging payloads on the Utilities tab, you'll get instances where CalCon goes stupid and gives you errors and won't datalog. In these cases, shutdown both CalCon and CalEdit. Relaunch CalEdit, go to the Utilities tab, click your desired payload, and click the Payload button. At this point, CalCon should launch without barfing error messages. In the background what you are doing is saving off what CalCon is supposed to be looking for to some file somewhere. But there are bugs in CalEdit that get that info saved all corrupted. About the only way to save a payload without saving it corrupted again is to close CalEdit, relaunch it, then re-save the payload off fresh so CalCon is happy. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Nov 13, 2006 9:34 pm If you can datalog the HEGOs, watch for their voltages to jump from 0-.6v when in CL. If you see the voltages floating around one particular voltage like .3 or .4, then you probably have a grounding problem. You can confirm this by watching your HEGOs and turn on your blower motor or headlights. If the voltage on the HEGOs goes up and down with loads you are turning on in the truck, then you almost definitely have a ground problem. I had this problem for longer than I want to admit before I realized that the problem was a ground. The ground ended up being the pigtail ground wire on the battery terminal. It was supposed to be landed to a body ground lug right behind the battery, but corroded off. After re-landing that ground wire, all my HEGO switching and over-rich problems were fixed. As for tuning a MAF without a WB being guess-work, yeah it is, but not impossible with EA. It tells you right where you are rich and lean in your curve, and lets you hone in on it. After running log after log, you can tune in a MAF pretty darn good without a WB...and what you can't hone in on the KAMs will adjust for. Without a WB, I have KAMs that are no lower than .98 and no higher than 1.04 and I'm pretty sure I could hone that 1.04 down if I really cared. But the engine runs so good as-is, there's no real incentive for me to bother. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

Then go to this web site http://www.hardcore50.com/members/calculators.htm and calculate the speedo correction factor. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Nov 18, 2006 7:25 am I don't have a WB, so I can't speak from 100% experience, however if I did have a WB, I can go through the things I would tune and in the order I'd do it. First, I'd adjust the Fuel Table OL (FN1307) for both the 60 and 75% load rows to be the fuel mix you want. Then go to the WOT Fuel Multiplier vs RPM (FN303) to all 1s if that's not what you meant by your statement above about 1s across the board. Then use the WB to tune your MAF curve (FN036) on the top-end so you get the AFR your tweaks are targeting. Then if you decide to modify the tables to 12.7, 13.5, or some other AFR, you have a much higher chance of hitting that target accurately. Since the EEC doesn't use a WB to trim-n-respond to WOT fuel mix, you have to use the WB to manually hone the tune to what it is actually doing. I'm curious to hear what others with a WB would do and how different it is from this strategy. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Mon Oct 23, 2006 11:03 am Well, it will take a lot of reading. On a stock motor, it probably would not do you much good. Most of us here have highly modified motors that require tuning to run correctly. It is really the mods that give us the HP, and the tunning that allows us to use the mods with the stock computer. As far as what you can access, pretty much everything depending on what processor you are using. The older the processor the better the knowledge on here, and the more you can access. However there is pretty good support for anything 98 and older. You really have to decide what you want to do with the vehicle and motor.... Make a plan and stick with it. Too many people fail because they change their design mid-build, and things dont work the way they want to. People with long tube headers have quite a few issues with CL driving, so if this is a daily drive and you want some economy I would advise against long tube headers. Short air intakes for people that drive in stop and go traffic create issues as well, that are difficult to tune out. The engine compartment gets very hot in stop and go traffic and the eec does wierd things to fuel and timing to try and prevent a blown motor. In all its a lot of work and reading, but if you are willing to do this then the rewards are definately worthwhile. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Nov 21, 2006 8:40 pm If you've done a lot of EEC tuning before, you could probably tune the MAF without EA. However if you have never tuned a MAF, you'll NEED EA to do it any justice. Otherwise you are shooting in the dark... Get EA and do it right. Even if your curve isn't close, if it'll at least run the engine, you can find the curve from there. It'll take quite a few rough drives, but eventually you'll get something that's close enough to work and then hone in from there. If I may suggest, keep it on the rich side as much as you can to get it close. Engines running rich are much more docile than engines running lean. A lean engine bucks, hesitates, and is just annoying to drive. Once you get your curve close, don't tune-n-drive anymore. Give the curve multiple days of driving, then tweak. Reset the KAMs. And give the new curve a few days of driving to settle it in again.
