I've read a lot on here but this is my first post. I have a 2000 Explorer V8 in a 94 Ranger using a 92 Mustang EEC. So compare to a stock 92 Mustang things are a little different. GT40P heads explorer GT40 intake explorer 65 mm throttle body C&L 73mm mass air with stock mustang electronics. explorer cam FMS explorer headers Now I did install Mustang fuel rails and stock 19lb injectors. I also converted it from the coil packs to stock Mustang distributor and use an MSD 6A box and coil. I'm using the A9P with a baumann transmission controller for the 4r70w. So my problem only exists in the winter as far as I can tell. Seems to work fine in the summer. The problem is that when I come to an idle after a few seconds (30 or so) it starts to stutter and almost feels like it's missing. The rpms also drop a little and if I let it sit like that for a while it starts to run really rough and sometimes will seems like it might die but it never does. If I get on the gas it's kinda boggy like it's flooded but soon clears out (by about 3000rpm) and then seems to drive fine. Also in the winter I get around 13 mpg but in the summer I get 16.5 to 17.5. Every so often I get codes 41 and 91 which means lean EGOs not switching. Since I don't have a tweecer yet I hooked up two DVMs (digital volt meters) to each EGO. When I take off driving I get readings anywhere from 0 to .8 volts. It jumps up and down crossing the 0.45 mark like I've read it should. When I come to an idle I seem to get readings. However after about 20 minutes of driving or so (from a cold start in the morning) suddenly it will just drop to 0 volts when I come to a stop. Immediately. In fact if I'm coasting down to a stop I'll see 0 volts before I even get to a stop. It will sit and idle at 0 volts on the EGOs and then suddenly it starts stuttering and idling horrible. At this point something happens (I assume the EEC goes into open loop mode) because from here on out the EGOs will stay at 0 volts while I'm driving. I'll get a momentary flash around .9 volts if I WOT and approach red line but basically 3/4 throttle and less will continue to read 0 volts on the EGOs till I turn the truck off and back on and then everything resets and I'll get readings on the EGOs till I stop and idle. I've checked that the EGOs have a good supply of 12 volts (14 when engine running) by running their own dedicated wire from the battery and relay (hot in run) and circuit breaker. I've monitored that supply with another DVM and made sure it's got a constant supply to keep the EGOs heated and it does. I also hooked up DVMs to the mass air and baro sensor. Off the mass air I got idle around .8 (sometimes .7) and WOT saw 4.2 volts before it shifted. My baro sensor shows around 2.7 to 2.73 volts while driving and around 5000 rpm WOT it saw 2.8 volts (in kansas city, about 1000 feet above sea level). Fuel pressure at idle with vacuum pulled is around 41 to 42 PSI and with vacuum is around 32 to 34 PSI or so. Vacuum at idle is 18 Hg. I've searched and hunted for vacuum leaks both with carb cleaner and propane and can't find any. I've cleaned the mass air sensor, cleaned the K&N and re-oiled it. Stock 19lb fuel injectors, fuel pressure regulator, and fuel pump (190 lph walbro) are all brand new. I also tried swapping out my A9P with an A9L just to see if it was a bad EEC and no it is not. I've also made sure everything has really good grounds. 4 gauge cable from the battery to the frame, frame to body, frame to motor (by starter motor), body to battery. I have a dedicated ground from the battery directly to the EEC. From the motor, frame etc. to the negative battery terminal I see a max of 50 mV difference. I'm out of ideas. What could make my EGOs drop to 0 volts at idle? I never tested the voltage in the summer but the problem goes away in the summer (this is my second winter like this). Assuming the EEC isn't learning, the 55mm MAF may give you a closer-to-actual reading...enough that the LAMBSEs can allow HEGO switching at idle. Looking in EA, I compared the clear-tube 73mm C&L's actual MAF curve to the A9L 55mm stock MAF. The C&L does run leaner with the A9L curve in the EEC. This said another way, for every voltage on the curve, the C&L is flowing more air than the 55mm MAF would (as you would kind of expect it to). Thus, if the EEC thinks X amount of air is coming in based on the stock MAF curve, there's actually more than that coming in and thus the MAF would be running the engine lean. So putting that 55mm MAF in may just cure the problem until you can get a tuner to hone the curve yourself. There is one place where the curves cross and the C&L actually runs richer, but it is around ~.46v...below the voltage that the engine idles at. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Nov 21, 2006 9:00 pm I know those pop-in sensors are nothing but thermistors. However thermistors come in various curves and base resistances. I don't know what the 03/04 is, however if you can get a BIN and strategy, you can compare that tune's ACT transfer against the A9L's transfer. If the transfer values are close, then you can probably get away using it. However if they are different, you might want to think 2nd before blindly transferring the values from the 03/04 BIN over to your A9L tune. A9L uses the same transfer function for both ACT and ECT. So if it isn't the same, you'll have to find a way to use the 03/04 ECT as well...assuming that the 03/04 EEC uses the same transfer for ACT and ECT. It wouldn't surprise me if the newer EECs break out the ACT and ECT transfers and use different curves for those sensors...something to think about. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Nov 21, 2006 10:34 pm Get both... TwEECer is the hardware that connects to your EEC. It comes with CalEdit and CalCon softwares. CalEdit allows you to edit your tune. CalCon allows you to datalog values. TunerPro is an editing software which shows quite a bit more detail than CalEdit does...and most importantly, it's free. So I'd recommend you get the TwEECer, then tune your BINs via TunerPro, not CalEdit. Use CalEdit ONLY for downloading the TwEECer hardware and setting up what points you want to datalog. Then CalCon will still be used to get the datalog. And finally, PLAN on buying EEC Analyzer with TwEECer. It's about $50 and it makes diagnosing your datalogs possible. Don't bother getting the TwEECer unless you can afford the TwEECer RT and EEC Analyzer. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: rockin_rick
posts.content: rockin_rick Tuning Addict Posts: 613 Joined: Sun Mar 07, 2004 10:30 am Quote Post by rockin_rick » Fri Apr 29, 2005 11:42 am While I don't really have a definitive answer, perhaps some of my thoughts will steer you towards a correct answer. Perhaps your 12Mhz EEC can't go over 6500 RPMs (regardless of allowed PIP and rev limit settings). That's a lot of calculations in a very short time with a slow EEC. There has to be a RPM (and thus window for calculations) limit somewhere . 6500 RPMs = 3250 RPMs per cycle = 54.167 Rev/sec = 18.46ms per cycle. Perhaps your injectors are maxed out and you are leaning out. What kind of duty cycle are you seeing? What is your A/F at 6500? Your PW's @ 6500 can't be more than 16.61 ms (90% duty cycle) I've heard that the EEC limits the DC to 90% (regardless if a higher duty cycle is needed). This, of course, decreases as RPMs increase. 6800 = 15.88ms max PW (@ 90%) 7200 = 15ms max PW (@ 90%) Perhaps your valvetrain weight is limiting you. Got titanium/lightweight valves/spring hardware? Are you certain that your setup will handle that RPM? Perhaps you do have a tuning issue and all this stuff I listed is not your problem. Good luck, Rick I no longer have (but what all my posts refer to): 94GT, 302NA, AFR165, FTI hyd cam, Performer, 24lb-hr @39PSI, 65TB, Pro-M 80 w/ NA 94-95 GT cal, long tubes, egr & smog delete, T-5 TwEECer RT v1.20b3, J4J1 base, PLX M-300 WB, EEC Analyzer Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Nov 29, 2006 4:19 pm I would agree with that. You'll need to drive the engine at some moderately high RPMs and high CLOSED LOOP loads to get the MAF curve tuned. Without a WB, WOTs aren't that useful here. If the EEC goes open loop, those log entries won't be useful because your LAMBSEs will go to a much lower than normal value. So try to keep your high RPM accelerations to closed loop conditions. You want as much air flowing through the MAF as possible in a condition where the narrow-band HEGOs can tell you if the MAF is rich, lean, or dead-on. If you are having trouble maintaining high loads without the EEC going open loop, try increasing the scalar that forces OL at high load. Personally, I have that scalar set to 30 seconds. While driving in the mountains, I noticed that climbing caused me to run OL in 5th when it really didn't need to be OL. So I increased that time and I stay CL on most any steep hill...until I hit the WOT/OL TPS breakpoint. If you've lowered those, you might also want to increase them back up to help you stay in CL longer too. But since you are running Forced Induction, you don't want to go too far with this. Once you get into boost, you'll NEED the added enrichment to keep the engine cool. Once you have the MAF tweaked as good as can be expected on the high-end, you can return those scalars back to whatever you had them at. Hope that helps... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Dec 02, 2006 7:19 am Ahh, I see where the confusion is now. There are 3 possible states: 1. OL (no HEGO monitoring, no learning, but fuel in adjusted based on learned KAMRF values) 2. CL, no Adaptive Learning (i.e. LAMBSEs switch HEGOs, but no KAMRF updates allowed, however old learned KAMRFs are used just like in #1) 3. CL with Adaptive Learning (i.e. LAMBSEs switch, and based on LAMBSEs, KAMRFs are allowed to update based on the Adaptive update table settings) When you start up, you are in OL. After 45-60 seconds, you go CL and this is indicated in the datalog if you are logging it. All this means is that the LAMBSEs are allowed to move to induce HEGO switching. However until the engine ECT is up to temperature, the EEC will not "learn" anything about the LAMBSE values. I think the EEC goes into adaptive learning mode around 170° by default. That's a scalar you can adjust in the A9* EECs. I'd assume it's there for other strategies as well. And of course, as I eluded to above, learning will only occur if ECT is up to temp and the Adaptive Update table has positive values in the RPM/Load cell your engine is currently in. For those that don't know, cells with negative numbers are referencing other cells for KAMRF values and thus are prevented from learning for themselves. When you have a negative number in the cell, the 1st number is the row, the 2nd number is the column. Rows and numbers start at 0. In TunerPro (and I think CalEdit too), the bottom row is 0 and the 1st column is 0. The very top row usually marked as 0% load is a special row that's the idle row. Thus 700RPMs@10% load is handled differently than idling at 700RPM@10% load. I don't know exactly what the EEC is determining "idle" to be, but whatever it is, it's not capable of being datalogged and creates some confusion if the idle row has learned a KAMRF value different than the normal row consistent with the same RPM/Load so generally you have the lower load rows reference something like the idle row OR have those rows AND the idle row reference the same thing so there's no confusion when you analyze the datalog. When tuning an EEC, it's important that MOST of these cells be 10s so you can see what the learned condition is at any of your typical CL driving conditions. 10 somehow indicates the amount of time the engine has to be stable in that RPM/Load before it allows itself to learn. I've only ever seen 10s and 100s for positive numbers. This is my understanding of what the EEC is doing. Someone that knows differently, please clarify and correct me if I'm wrong. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sun Dec 03, 2006 12:35 am If the TwEECer is not data logging then the TwEECer is not slowing down any processing. On the other hand is the TwEECer is data logging then I do believe that the TwEECer is slowing down the processing. The reason I say this is, the TwEECer has to ask for the logging registers, and if you are like me, I have all 16 parameters being logged. This means 16 requests every 100ms. This will definitely slow down the bus or communications between the processor and the memory. It will not slow down the process of the real world inputs and outputs. The processor will get the inputs from the real world and not know what to do with it until it can get the calibration data from the memory. This means the whole process slows down. So if the TwEECer is logging and slowing down the bus then it will slow the whole thing down. The older EEC-IV's are only 12 and 15 MHz. The EEC then divides this by three for different reasons internally. This means the actual speed is only around 4 MHz. This is also one of the reasons the EEC-IV is only good up to around 7000 or 8000 RPM. Past that point, the electronics can not keep up. This is another reason some people have been successful in over clocking the EEC-IV with a different crystal. The end result is the TwEECer or any other hardware attached to the J3 port will slow down the bus if it is requesting data for logging. Now on to another thought. If the TwEECer is passive and is only monitoring the bus and is waiting for addresses of particular parameter then the memory bus is not compromised at all. I can not see this being the case since the loggings is done every 100ms. Now the TwEECer could have holding registers that get populated when the TwEECer sees the address on the bus and then writes the holding registers out to the data logging PC whether or not the holding register has anything in it or not. This would also make it completely passive. This may also explain why we see so many garbage data points in the logs. Personally I do not rev my car that high to even notice this issue. Sorry for rambling. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Dec 04, 2006 12:49 pm It looks to me like the voltage just never got to the top so EA is hypothesizing up to the voltage point listed in the log (~4.5v). Any values beyond that were not hypothesized. But more importantly, you got EA set to calculate off "BOTH" OL and CL conditions. This is not what you want. Set EA to use only CL conditions in the datalog (radio buttons at the bottom that show OL/CL/BOTH). When you are OL, the EEC isn't paying attention to the HEGOs and thus isn't learning nor responding to maintain anything other than the fuel table. In addition, when you are OL due to high-load like at WOT, then the LAMBSEs will be lower than they would at CL and EA is going to misinterpret this as a lean condition that the EEC was compensating for with low values for LAMBSEs. That's why the line is so pulled away from the base line. Run EA with only CL values in effect and see if that doesn't get rid of that jagged-edge in there. Unless you have a WB, there's no reason to try to do calculations off OL rows. Also notice lower in the curve, there's a hump. I'm suspecting that shortly after that hump is where you went OL. However if there's still a hump in the calculated curve, go back and smooth those values so that you result in a smooth MAF curve, not a jagged one. Even the base curve has some jitters in it. As a suggestion to see things better, reset the 16v at the top of the MAF values to 5v and zoom to extents so more of the graph's viewable area will be seen. Right now, most of the graph's viewable area is showing that straight line from 5v to 16v...that's not helpful. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Dec 05, 2006 8:03 am It looks like you did a pretty good job of getting it smoother but with the 16v values still in there, most of your graph is still dominated. Unfortunately an idle-only datalog isn't going to tell you anything useful about your MAF. After about 3 days of driving, see what EA's suggestions show. You can run datalogs throughout the 3 days and throw each one into EA just to see how things are progressing, but don't make MAF adjustments until a good 3 days of varied closed loop driving. The last day's log will be the most important one and the one you want to make a MAF curve tweak against. For those 3 days, try to stay in CL as much as possible. WOTs don't help you tune a MAF unless you have a WB sensor...but they are fun so I couldn't blame you for throwing a few in. :) I mentioned a thread or two back of ways you can keep the EEC in CL longer in an effort to get more data about the MAF curve at the higher voltages. Most tunes have the EEC kicking in OL early and under normal circumstances, that's probably a better strategy for performance, but its not helpful with MAF tuning so you want to go in the other direction with these scalars. 1. TPS voltage for OL (set to 3.3v, A9L default is 2.7) 2. TPS voltage for WOT (set to 3.3v, A9L default is 2.7) 3. Time@High load to force OL (set to 30 sec, A9L default is 2 sec) Again, these are not numbers you generally want to roll with all the time, but they are very helpful in tuning a MAF curve on the high end. To get stabilized high end MAF readings, try to drive the engine at stabilized high RPMs, both cruising and CL moderate acceleration. Even if you could be in a higher gear, force lower gears for the sole purpose of getting high-flow CL MAF readings. The higher the RPM, the harder you have to be on the pedal before OL will kick in and thus you get more useful information of what's happening at the higher part of the MAF curve. After a few days of doing that and watching the results in EA for each run, you'll start to figure out what's causing the things you see in EA. Just as a reminder, have you tuned in your Injector slopes yet? If you haven't, you might want to do that before spending lots of time and gas on the MAF curve. Those injector slopes can directly affect your MAF curve, so if you haven't already, run a good 15-30 minute datalog INCLUDING WOTs for Injector slope analysis and let EA crunch on that to see if your injector slopes are close enough or if they need some adjustment. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

One thing that hasn't been mentioned yet is it's a good idea to open up the Adaptive Update table from default to allow more areas to learn than what's in the EEC by default. Many of the areas on the low-end all have negative numbers instead of 10s. With the exception of the bottom two rows (5% & 10% load), put them all at 10 so all areas of the RPM/Load range can learn and give you feedback as to where the MAF may need tweaking. With a new feature JUST ADDED to EA (run update to get it), you can map out what your MAF readings were at the various RPM/Loads. That's valuable for determining what RPM/Loads have the similar average MAF readings. That in itself doesn't tell you much, but on the 2nd graph, you can then run an average LAMBSE and/or Last Known KAMRF and see places where the same MAF readings were giving different driving conditions. For instance you might find that 150kg/hr is running the engine lean 50%@1300, but lean at 30%@3000. This could indicate MAF airflow problems like backflow. Everywhere the LAMBSEs went high but were low somewhere else with the same MAF readings would tend to indicate backflow in those regions where it ran rich. posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Thu Dec 07, 2006 2:21 pm I keep on saying this but here goes again :) Rescaling the axis of your tables is the only way to go if your engine is producing LOAD values greater than the stock table values (any boosted engine will fall into this category). You should be setting the 'Percent Load Switch' and ignoring the 'SeaLevel Load Scaling vs RPM' function. Using this function to bring LOAD% down to the range in your tables is a waste of time as only three tables use LOAD% as their input, the remainder use LOAD (I'm referring to A9L etc here). This function is used as part of the calculation determining LOAD%, not LOAD. Top

I have scaled the Sealevel function so that the tables that use that are not going too far over the top of the table (there's no issue with going over if you are happy with the top row value). For instance, I do not care that the load goes over the top of the OL fuel table as the top row is 11.7 AFR which is what I want for any load at the top of the table and above. I have also scaled other tables LOAD functions to allow for a wider load range where I though it might help. The scaling does NOT have to linear which is helpful if you do NOT want to mess with day-to-day drivability. Basically I have tried to align my scaling so that my cruising load rows are in the same place as a stock engine - why change something if you do not have to, right? Because of gearing and the load of the S/C, I needed some adjustments to get the cruising loads to align with the same rows as when stock. I then expand the scale more rapidly above normal cruising loads (two-slope scaling) so that the wider range of heavy loads can fit within the table. Like I said above, I don't care what happens above a certain point above the top row. Spark tables get handed off to WOT function in A9L anyway. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Fri Dec 08, 2006 7:17 am Ok, let me try to clarify this. If you want to run a 30# maf without making changes to the maf transfer in the tweecer, then you need to run 30# injectors. This skewed calibration will "trick" the eec. This can work, but there is no way to fine tune the setup without the tweecer. (this was the 'old school' method, maf&injectors only) Now, with tweecer (or any other tuning hardware/software that modifies the ford binary) you take the flow data for the meter your using, and enter it into your tune. Now the eec knows the actual air flow. But in order for this to work, now you have to change the injector slopes to let the eec know what injectors your running. Now your no longer relying on the maf calibration to trick the eec, and can use pretty much any injector with any maf. The big advantage here is you can make fine adjustments to specific parts of your tune where you are having issues. Makes sense? Both methods allow the eec to 'measure' more air than stock, and the larger injectors will deliver the additional fuel that the stock injectors could not. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Dec 08, 2006 12:13 pm 95gtSTANG wrote: Does the MAF actually feed some sort of a transfer function to the eec? No, the transfer function is programmed into the EEC. For factory equipment, Ford knows what the MAF transfer is for any given setup using the sensor they provide. They also program in the injector slope based on the injectors they provide. When you need a new MAF to replace the factory MAF because you replaced injectors, the MAF manufacturer has to design the MAF to deliver a modified voltage at any given airflow rate that will provide the proper amount of fuel for the size injector you've installed. This modified MAF behavior built into the MAF assumes the following: 1. The EEC is using the factory MAF curve 2. The EEC is using the factory injector slopes 3. You are using injector sizes that were designed for use with this MAF This works pretty good when you are upgrading to 24lb injectors in a close-to-stock budget setup where the only mods are some headers, ported stock heads, and mild cam. But once you start swapping heads and/or intake, and putting a high-RPM cam in there, things have gotten so far from stock that factory settings with a matched MAF isn't going to optimize your setup. This modified MAF behavior built into the MAF assumes the following: 1. The EEC is using the factory MAF curve 2. The EEC is using the factory injector slopes 3. You are using injector sizes that were designed for use with this MAF This works pretty good when you are upgrading to 24lb injectors in a close-to-stock budget setup where the only mods are some headers, ported stock heads, and mild cam. But once you start swapping heads and/or intake, and putting a high-RPM cam in there, things have gotten so far from stock that factory settings with a matched MAF isn't going to optimize your setup. Besides after that kind of sweat and money, get a tuner and do your setup justice. That all makes sense whent he air flow is below 900 kg/h. What about if you are pushing 1500 kg/h though the maf sensor. The factory curve only goes up to 900 kg/h. Does this mean it just uses 900 for flows>900. Thanks, I do not mean to beat this to death. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Dec 08, 2006 2:10 pm All the voltages are skewed by some amount. It's almost a multiplier amount, but not quite. Lets run through a scenario. With a factory MAF and factory 19lb injectors, the MAF voltage for 100kg/hr may be around 1.9v for instance. However with 24lb injectors, if the EEC believed there was 100kg/hr of air flowing, it would calculate a pulse-width too large for these injectors (still thinking the injectors are 19s). So a MAF tuned for 24lb injectors must fool the EEC into believing the airflow is lower. So, when the airflow is 100kg/hr actual, instead of sending 1.9v, the MAF sends somewhere closer to 1.5v. The EEC takes that info and calculates an injector pulse for 19lb injectors and if the MAF manufacturer did a good job at tuning the MAF, the resulting pulse-width will be what's required for 24lb injectors and 100kg/hr airflow. Even though the EEC didn't have the right curve nor injector slopes, it was fooled into calculating the right pulse...or at least close enough the KAMs and LAMBSEs could makeup for the error. As the injectors get larger, the more the MAF has to drop the voltage at any given airflow rate to decrease the pulse-width the EEC calculates. Again, you can guesstimate by how much the MAF will drop the voltage by figuring what size injectors you want to run divided by 19.64. Then multiply your EEC's factory curve flowrate by that value. So lets say you have 30lb injectors, that's 30/19.64= ~1.53. Lets say the factory curve has 4.7v = 867kg/hr. So 867 * 1.53 = 1326kg/hr. To follow the MAF curve 1 for 1, the top end of your MAF curve would be around 1326 at 4.7v. When looking in the curves for a C&L MAF tuned for 30lb injectors (green tube), it's no big surprise that 4.8v=1482kg/hr. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Fri Dec 08, 2006 4:28 am If you are using a stock bin then there is no reason for a checksum error unless the J3 is dirty, the bin is corrupted in the Tweecer (does happen sometimes) or the Tweecer is faulty (very rare). I clean the J3 by dry wiping any protective grease off with a soft tissue and then rubbing the contacts with a soft cloth wetted with acetone (pcb cleaner will do). Some boards also have a clear laquer which isn't too obvious, the acetone softens this so that is can be scratched away using your fingernail. Don't be tempted to use any tools as the contacts are only circuit board tracks and easily damaged. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Dec 09, 2006 10:05 pm 0-.45v HEGOs indicate a lean condition. .46-.48v is about perfect. And anything above .5v indicates a rich condition. Under normal Closed Loop operation, the HEGOs should switch between 0v and .5v. If you aren't seeing one of your HEGOs moving, then it's either bad, bad wire, or something's wrong with the way the engine is running. As for things to datalog, try this for starters: 1. MAFV 2. Load 3. LAMBSE1 4. LAMBSE2 5. KAMRF1 6. KAMRF2 7. Closed Loop Status 8. HEGO1 9. HEGO2 10. Spark 11. Speed 12. RPM 13. Inj PW1 14. Inj PW2 15. BAT Voltage 16. TPS, ACT, EGR Pos, or ECT I always datalog 1-15. However depending on what I'm looking for, I switch between which of the 3 I pick for my 16th choice. The KAMRFs are likely not changing because the Minimum ACT temp is still at the default of 100degF. You'll need to drop that scalar down to something like 40degF. You'll also want to change you Adaptive Update Table to put 10s in most of those positions instead of negative values so more of the positions will learn. During the tuning phase, it's valuable to know how each of these positions are running. However when you get a solid tune, you'll start locking some of those positions down. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Dec 10, 2006 8:59 am During Closed Loop operation, the HEGOs should bounce between 0v and .5-6v every 1/2second or so. It should be very rhythmic and recognizable that the EEC is adjusting to maintain the HEGOs bouncing between rich and lean. Since the HEGOs are narrow band O2 sensors, the EEC can't maintain a perfect .4v all the time. The best it can do is keep the mix as close as possible, and to do that it looks for the O2 readings to "switch" (jump between 0v & .5v). Sometimes they'll go as high as .6v during switching, it just depends on your setup. As long as they are moving up and down rapidly, you are good. However they will frequently go into the .7v and possibly the .8v during acceleration or if you enter a region of the tune that needs work. When the HEGO does this, the EEC will see it stuck in the high rich condition and will compensate until the HEGO begins switching again. Likewise if the HEGO sticks at 0v, the EEC will compensate until it starts switching again. You may never notice when the HEGOs go rich (high voltage). However when they go lean for any length of time, the engine won't run right. It'll hesitate then the EEC will compensate and suddenly the engine will surge with power and create some quite annoying drivability issues. HEGO1 is the passenger's side...I think. The side with #1 piston is usually your #1 Bank. Someone correct me if I'm wrong on that. Make sure you don't have a grounding issue that's preventing the EEC from seeing it switch. As a quick-n-dirty test to see if the problem is a bad ground, run a long 16-18 gauge wire from the exhaust pipe close to the HEGO up to where your EEC gets its closest ground. If the problem is ground, you'll see this HEGO suddenly start switching with much more voltage than it ever did before. For testing, it doesn't have to be a permanent thing. In fact, you wouldn't want to rely on this setup for any length of time. You'd want to fix the ground issue. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Dec 10, 2006 8:07 pm One thing at a time... The EEC determines when you are in Closed Loop. However while in Closed Loop, the EEC is trying to maintain fuel mix via the HEGOs, not strictly off of timing tables. Eventually if the HEGOs never switch the way the EEC wants them to, the EEC will revert back to OL and if driven this way for about 20 minutes, the EEC will throw a Check Engine light. At least that's the behavior I got out of my A9L and A9P. As for spark, the higher spark is beneficial to get you more power and better fuel economy. However once the spark gets too far, you either surge really bad or the engine pings. At idle, the EEC may choose to adjust timing to get a better idle if it can't maintain a smooth idle via the IAC. At idle, higher spark usually increases the RPM. Lowering spark, lowers RPM. My idle is around 18 just because I found that this gives me the most stable idle AND take-off. I've lowered the spark tables at the lower RPMs quite a bit, but raised them up higher from about 2000RPMs up at all loads to maximize fuel economy at cruising. I went too far a while back and introduced some pretty bad surging at cruise. I backed off the timing at the RPM/loads it was surging at until the surging went away. 40deg advance is ok at higher RPMs that are loaded. I wouldn't expect to see 40s anywhere near idle. You said you were seeing 40s in the 2-3k range. That'd be normal. You want the LAMBSEs in the 14s during CL and whatever the fuel tables say at OL. You use the LAMBSE values during Closed Loop to determine where the MAF curve needs to be tweaked to maintain LAMBSEs at 14. Ideally, KAMRFs of 1 and LAMBSEs at 14.5 all the time is what you want. However the engine is way too dynamic for that. So you aim for "close". Right now, my KAMRFs are within .03 of 1. Some places go above, others below. Unless the car is drivable, the KAMRFs aren't going to update. You have to stay in certain RPM/Loads for a given amount of time before that area will update. The concept is to get the injector to fire only when the intake valve is open as much as possible so you aren't wetting up the back of a closed intake valve. Until you get the engine up to running speeds, both cruising and light-to-moderate acceleration, that's not going to be terribly important right now. This is more of a fuel economy move. Unless you have some larger injectors and a larger intake duration on your cam, chances are the injector is going to fire against a closed intake valve at heavy acceleration up to WOT. I've heard that tweaking this table has been a big help to a number of people running cams other than factory. However I've found that using the numbers in EA actually makes my engine run rougher...noticeably rougher. Once I'm in the RPMs, it's not noticeable, but around idle up to about 1500RPMs, the engine doesn't run nearly as smooth as it does with factory numbers in the EEC. I don't know if there's something odd about my stock Explorer cam that causes this, but time and time again, I've tried a tune with EA's numbers and every time, I have to revert back to get the engine to smooth out. It's as though the engine wants the injectors firing on closed intake valves. In fact, looking at the Cobra X3Z tune, it has the injectors firing at 300° for every RPM/Load cell, where the A9L tune has it scattered from 352-464°. Even though I'm running the Cobra tune, my engine seems to run best with the A9L parameters for the Injector Timing table. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Dec 11, 2006 8:03 am Those EECs follow a different strategy so I couldn't just download an A9P with a different EEC's bin. Besides, I wasn't diagnosing a problem with the transmission strategy. I bought an A9P (EEC for Automatic Mustang) a long time ago and used it on my truck, even though I have a manual tranny. I was having other unrelated issues that I couldn't explain with the HEGOs not reading right. I thought perhaps it was a bad EEC so I decided to try replacing it to see if anything changed. Since I was replacing it, I decided to replace it with the A9L (EEC for manual Mustangs) which better matched my setup. Turned out the A9P was not at fault. The A9L behaved identically to what I was experiencing with the A9P. Long story short, it was a ground problem. But replacing the EEC was part of the diagnostic process...along with replacing perfectly good HEGOs. It wound up costing me more than it shoud've, but I at least knew what the problem wasn't. I chock it up to the price of education. But the point I was trying to make is I never noticed an appreciable difference between the A9P or the A9L when it came to how the engine drove with the manual tranny. Unless the newer 94-95 EECs have tranny controls in them like many of the EEC-Vs do, I wouldn't expect you'd have much trouble running a mismatch either. But without experience using those EECs, I couldn't say that with full certainty. I'm just passing along my experience. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

EGRs were originally an emissions-only device back in the 70s and early 80s and had to be taken off just to get the engine to run right...and that was right off the showroom floor. But after manufacturers started toying with the EGRs and controlling them with computer precision, they realized there was some positive benefits to having some EGR in the intake mix at most Closed Loop cruise and acceleration conditions. In a round-about way, it acts as an octane booster allowing for more timing...when it's controlled right. At idle and WOT, EGR isn't used so it poses no top-end performance issues at all. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Dec 17, 2006 7:50 am Fords were also very notorious for Torque Converter shudder when you accidentally replaced Mercon V with Dextron III/Mercon or when the fluid gets old. When it shudders, it feels like you went over a series of light bumps in the road. The first or second time it happens, you may not even pay it any attention. But it'll eventually get to where it is predictable, happening every time the TC locks up, and generally only when it goes into Drive or OD. One of the things Ford dealers will do when you get Torque Converter shudder is do a transmission flush on the system and regardless of whether your tranny requires the higher quality Mercon V or not, they put that in there (that's not a bad thing). As long as you don't let the TC do this too much, replacing the fluid will help. The downside is, when you drop the pan, you are only getting about 30% of the fluid in the tranny. The procedure the dealers and other tranny places do where they disconnect the radiator lines is far more effective. An article I read about the AOD/AODE/4R70w transmission also highly recommended the use of auxiliary tranny coolers on any performance vehicle (RV, towing truck, or hot street car), as well as an in-line tranny fluid filter for any vehicle with an automatic. He stated quite boldly that if auto manufacturers put a decent filter on transmissions from the factory, most tranny shops would be out of business. Since tranny fluid is so similar to engine oil, but with more detergents, you can use a standard oil filter relocator bracket and oil filter, with the right fittings to mate it to transmission lines. Check out TransDapt for the oil filter brackets. Most all TransDapt parts can be purchased at O'Reillys Auto Parts if you have one of them local to you. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Dec 18, 2006 8:24 am Dominick wrote: ...now when i change the filter in the tranny by dropping the pan i notice a lot of fine fine oily powder stuck to the magnet and i mean this thing is usually covered in it is this bad? That's pretty normal based on my very limited experience with automatics. Those fine particles are pieces of the clutch that have worn off. They aren't magnetic, so they float around everywhere and coat everything that the trans fluid comes in contact with. Like I said, ideally, you'd prefer they don't get into the oil, but since they do, a better filtration system would catch MOST of that stuff instead of letting it collect in the pan like that. The magnet will have everything from fine shiny particulate to slivers of metal that love to get stuck in your finger tips if you aren't using a rag or gloves to clean the magnet with. The factory's "screen" filter keeps large particles from getting into the tranny, but it's barely adequate for preventing that fine particulate from circulating throughout the transmission. As long as it is fine enough, it doesn't cause an immediate problem, but it is still clutch material...a friction material that is designed to resist wear, and thus causes wear on other stuff. Removing it from the circulation does have a long-term benefit. The manufacturer is only interested in installing a filter that'll get most of vehicles through the warranty period. Face it, it's not in their best interest to have their components last as long as possible. :( The two killers of automatics are heat and wear. The good news is you CAN do something about it with a fluid cooler, better filtration, and use of synthetic fluids. Note, Mobil1 Fully Synthetic ATF still does NOT meet the requirements of Ford's Mercon V ATF fluid standards. If you do add an auxiliary filtration system, you'll need to change the tranny filter about every other engine oil change (depending on your driving habits) to make sure it isn't getting clogged up with that clutch particulate and creating excessive resistance. It is a better filter, so it'll be catching more than the factory filter...thus it'll need to be changed more often. As for the fluid itself, light driving will go 40-50k easy. Most people don't know when to change it and often don't. However an aggressive driver or a vehicle that tows a lot will need tranny fluid changed out about every 15-25k. Obviously a truck meant for towing will have a tranny built for towing and won't need fluid changes quite as often, but will likely have a cooler and possibly an in-line filter from the factory. But a smaller truck or car that can tow, but wasn't meant to do it on a regular basis will definitely benefit by frequent fluid changes under those conditions. You might also consider the parallel-flow dual filter setup. Any filter you install will add a small resistance to the pressure in those lines. As I eluded to above, that resistance increases as the filter catches debris. Having two filters in parallel will reduce that resistance by 1/2. Likewise an in-line dual filter increases the resistance...better filtration, but overkill and not worth the pressure loss in transmission applications. Two filters will allow you to go longer between filter changes AND you'll have the added 1/2 quart of fluid in the system. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Dec 20, 2006 4:15 pm I looked up that MAF and it appears to be a 90mm and made specifically for 2000+ Lightnings. It's a bolt-on style and won't have the right plug for an A9L wiring harness. That's no biggie if you have the right harness to fit it and a soldering iron, but you'll have to find a bolt-on filter to fit the MAF. Looking on eBay, there's not many 90mm MAFs other than the SCT MAFs. However, I'm curious as to whether an 80mm or 85mm C&L would do just as good. I know More's law...a lot is good, More's better, but when you are looking for drivability & MAF sensors, that may not apply. With such a large 90mm cross-sectional area, that doesn't produce much air-velocity across the MAF pickup to get really accurate readings at idle and light-throttle conditions (where drivability is important). Besides, an 80mm MAF can support some pretty serious ponies. If you are expecting 560rwhp, that's probably around 600 at the flywheel. Assuming .65 BSFC, you are probably talking what, 2000-2300kg/hr max airflow from that engine (someone correct me on that if I'm low). Looking at some flow sheets of various MAFs, the C&L 80mm using the "tuner" tube and 55mm (stock Mustang) MAF electronics maxes flow out at 3074kg/hr@5v and is 2457@4.8v. On the low-end, it's 22@0.4v which would be where the engine would idle. That'd be about right for this engine combination. Using the A9L, you'd need to tweak the MAF min/max voltage scalars and put the C&L curve in, but that's all stuff you'd have to do anyway with a high-flow MAF this setup is going to require. But if you got the hardware to make the SCT 90mm work, then try it and swap it out later if you decide it isn't working for you. As for the 55lb injectors, that's going to be about right for forced induction making 600hp at the flywheel. posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue Dec 19, 2006 9:56 pm The EA will display 40+ values because not all EECs are created equal and some have more or less cells to place these values. This is why the EA has 40+ values. It is up to you to pick the ones that best suite your EEC. Another food for thought is the EA will display load as a whole number like 10 which represents 10% load whereas some Tuner software displayes the values in decimal format so the same 10% is represented as 0.10. posts.content: mikenstang Regular Posts: 138 Joined: Sat Oct 23, 2004 8:22 am Location: Connecticut Quote Post by mikenstang » Thu Dec 21, 2006 11:48 am Yea that's basically what I ended up doing. I learned something interesting though?? I thought that the timing needed a "curve" or ramp up through the RPM range, not the case... i.e for the load range (.79) the stock J4J1 timing was 22*@ 2500, then 23* @ 4000 and 26* max @5000. I was reluctant to put in a lower number @ 2500-3000 RPM range that was where I was detonating. I now have as follows: 2000 rpm 21*, 2500rpm 18*, 3000rpm 18, 4000rpm 23*, 5000rpm 36* As you can see I drop from 21 to 18 then back up to 23. It works great. Here is what I learned from running some logs. From 23* - 36* the timing does not "jump" up, it ramps up gradually from 23 to 36 as spark is needed. This is assuming you have all other tables disabled (55) as I do. 94 GT, 347 stroker running j4j1 Cobra cal, EA, BE, w/cbaza rev39. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Dec 22, 2006 8:00 am I don't know how linear the reading is as it moves, but I've heard that they are only good for about 1.5-2 points; .75-to-1 above 14.7 and .75-to-1 below 14.7. Thus right at 0v would be around 15.45-to-15.7 and .9v (if your HEGO will give you .9) would be around 13.7-to-13.95. I don't know how true that is, just what I've heard. I believe the EECs are programmed to maintain a switching average of about .45v on the HEGO where actual readings jump from .6v to 0v, then back to .6v. As long as the readings are bouncing/switching, then you are running close enough to perfect. However if readings hold at 0v or around high .7-.8v range, then the mix is off the scale for the narrow-band O2. Even when I know it's running rich (i.e. startup & WOT), the highest my HEGOs ever go is .77-.80 range. Occasionally, I'll see it spike as high as .84v. Point is, mix that gives you values on the extreme are where you need a WBO2 to know what the engine is doing. I've heard HEGOs can give all the way up to .9v. If that's true, then I assume my loss of that .1 volt is electrical resistance. The newer 4-wire HEGOs do a better job of maintaining actual voltage up to the EEC since two of the 4 wires are dedicated sensor lines as opposed to the older 3-wire versions that use the exhaust pipe as a signal return which forces the O2 voltage to go up the tailpipe, through the headers, into the block, out the heavy gauge wire bolted to the motor that goes to the battery, then to the body, then to the EEC. If any one of those have a bad connection, your O2 readings will be low and thus the EEC will run the engine rich trying to compensate. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

The strategy defines what scalars/functions/tables are in the EEC. Thus, the only differences between EECs that have the same strategy is parameters in those scalars/functions/tables. So downloading a W4H0 to a T4M0 is no different than you tweaking the T4M0's parameters to be like the W4H0. The same is true of the GUFB strategy. A9L (Mustang GT manual) and X3Z (93 Cobra) use the same strategy, so you can download the X3Z to get a 93 Cobra EEC tune into your A9L. This is helpful if you upgrade your 302 to 24lb injectors. Since the X3Z is already setup for 24lb injectors, you can start with a solid "factory" tune, and tweak from there. posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Mon Nov 20, 2006 11:51 am You can increase the timing curve in the WOT Spark Advance vs RPM function, then adjust the WOT Spark Advance vs. ACT to make sure timing is pulled if the air gets too hot. Just be very careful as detonation can blow a head gasket (or worse) in a heartbeat. I am leaning toward the WOT Fuel Multiplier vs. RPM as I can dial in the percentage of fuel pulled versus how much I am adding - I think it will make it easier to see what's going on. This isn't how most people have done this, but I am wanting to try something new as who wants to redial the MAF curve whenever you change the nozzle or meth % of your mixture? Say you are adding the equivalent of 10% of your fuel from the meth, you would simply change the multiplier at the RPM's where the meth is active to 1.10 (above 1 leans mixture). See how this makes the calculations easier? You can also more easily take into account that stoich for methanol is like 9:1 AFR & only subtract like 3/4's of the amount of extra fuel from the meth. Say you are adding 10% of fuel from meth, you would multiply by 1.075 in the WOT vs RPM multiplier. Seems complicated but it's actually easier if you look at it this way. 428w now Top

The Tip-in is a little less than the Sealevel just to back-off the torque a tad so the clutch/tranny can get completely shifted without having to take the brunt of full load during the slippage. In the earlier EECs, this helped smooth out the shifts. But the amount of timing pulled during tip-in on GUF* strategies is minimal. It's just enough to slightly smooth the shifts. However with the newer strategies, the timing has REALLY been pulled to save the trannies so Ford wouldn't have to warranty-replace them...and they could put weaker trannies in. It's pathetic how much timing has been pulled during shifts on the new Taruses to make the shift glossy smooth. But from a performance standpoint it SUX. It doesn't accelerate the car at all during WOT-shifts. As it relates to your CBAZA, I've heard they have a built-in timing removal that you can't tweak out. But I don't know that for sure since I don't have a CBAZA EEC. posts.content: Bilford Gear Head Posts: 18 Joined: Wed Aug 09, 2006 5:44 am Quote Post by Bilford » Tue Dec 26, 2006 10:19 pm Adam McLaughlin wrote: What do I have to do for the KAMFR values to leave 1.000? I drove 25 miles today after I had tweaked down my MAF transfer function and Idle settings, and yet I had NO KAMFR adjustments either logged or seen on the screen. KAMFR values are Long term Fuel trims. 1 volt is a good thing. If it goes above its lean and below its rich. If you make adjustments to the tune clear the KAM before you rewrite it. "everytime" Adam McLaughlin wrote: Another issue I had seen was the O2s not fluctuating well. Mumber 1 seemed to range from 1.39 to .4 volts, while the passenger side went from .0 to 1. This of course made the LAMBSE values go all to heck. One side would read 13.9 and the other something like 19.1.... Don't know what's going on with that, both of these sensors are new with under 100 miles on them. Make sure you don't have an exhaust leak or intake leak etc. Maybe try swapping o2's to see a change. Since you said your car idle's smoothly I'd try to leave the MAF transfer alone for now. Did you change your inj offset vs bat voltage function? You need to if you didn't already. Lowering these numbers will help bring light on the short term fuel trims. After making proper adjustments to the inj offset vs bat voltage you can slowly make changes to your inj slopes and breakpoint. Remember if you input a larger value in the field for inj slopes it will be more lean, lower number would make it more rich. Hope this helps some. Bill DHG 01 Bullitt 4693 DSG 03 Lightning Top

The adaptive update rate table is what you would change for the KAMF. It has values that basically count how many times the eec see's something in a certain spot and makes changes after seeing something that amount of times occur in that specific spot. So if you put in a lower number it will update faster or vise versa. Maybe that doesn't make sense, but that's about as good as I can explain it. LOL Bill DHG 01 Bullitt 4693 DSG 03 Lightning Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Dec 30, 2006 9:35 pm In my EEC, that HEGO delay is degres of rotation on the crank. As for your stalls on cold mornings, I recommend you go out and turn the key ON for a good minute before cranking the car. This will allow your HEGOs to warm up BEFORE you crank. After a good minute (more if you have time), turn the key off, then back on again. Setup CalCon for datalogging, and crank the car. Pay special attention to what the HEGOs are doing when the car stalls. As well, pay attention to what the LAMBSEs are saying. If the mix is going from rich to lean, but the LAMBSEs stay about the same, then there's a problem with the crank enrichment function. Enriching these is what fixed my cold-start problems. I could see a very clear the exhaust was leaning out about 2-3 seconds after the engine started...and this coincided with when the engine would start sputtering and stumbling. The engine would stumble, often conking itself out. If the engine could stay running long enough, this sputtering would subside after about 5 seconds and run normal for the rest of the day. I can't explain why this was happening since the LAMBSEs weren't changing during this time. But increasing the Fuel Startup table's fuel adder fixed this and it cranks beautifully now. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Fri Dec 29, 2006 6:07 am You basically have to drive the car at as many different airflow levels as you can. You need to stay in closed loop (read: as little throttle as possible) and maintain a steady throttle. Use lambse, KAMRF, and WB feedback to see where your at. The biggest problem you will run into is this method will really only work for you up to about 300Kg/hr flow rates. Thats where you will pretty much just accelerate to illegal speeds. So to nail down the "top part" of your maf, you will need to be able to open up the car and log (or have a readout of) A/F ratio. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Jan 01, 2007 7:54 am Indirectly, he's right...but under certain conditions, you are both right. During Open-Loop, the EEC follows a set of Load/RPM tables. Load is calculated by the RPM and the amount of air coming into the engine either by measured amounts from a MAF or by Speed-Density vacuum tables. There's no feedback of how accurate these tables are in OL. It does what it does, and hopes for the best. In Closed-Loop, the EEC is using the HEGOs to tweak the mix. It does this in two ways. First it makes quick responses to mix needs by adjusting the LAMBSEs (aka Short Term Fuel Trim or STFT). The LAMBSE is the EEC's guesstimating of AFR. Adjusting this up and down allows the EEC to hit the target as indicated by the HEGOs. This quick adjustment isn't instantaneous. It happens in a matter of 1/4 second to a few seconds depending on how off-base the LAMBSEs were to start with. Hence, if the EEC was running the engine really lean during this period of time, you get noticeable hesitation and possibly surging until the LAMBSEs adjust. So LAMBSEs alone are not good enough. The EEC needs a tactic for "learning" it's own inaccuracy and compensating so the driver doesn't have to experience drivability problems in the future. So, if the EEC discovers that it takes a 12:1 LAMBSE to get the HEGOs to switch, it knows it was running lean because it is having to compensate towards the rich direction to get the mix right. To prevent this in the future, the EEC has the ability to learn this "error" for most Load/RPM positions the engine would ever be in at Closed Loop. The learned adjustment value for any given Load/RPM is called the KAMRF value. The KAMRFs (aka Long Term Fuel Trim or LTFT) are stored in non-volatile KAM (Keep Alive Memory). The KAMRFs are the EEC's adjustment to the base AFR mixes to better hit the mark without having to compensate by adjusting the LAMBSEs. Over time, the KAMRFs will gradually learn their way up or down in to get the LAMBSEs closer to the 14.5-14.7:1 range. The hope is that once the KAMRF values have settled in, the engine will no longer be overly rich or overly lean for any learned CL condition in the future. The part that gives CL some influence in the OL states is that KAMRFs are used in OL calculations so OL can take advantage of what has been learned. So lets say you are in some light-throttle OL condition (i.e. startup), if the EEC is aiming for 13.5:1 as per the OL fuel table, but the EEC also remembers that there was an error for the current RPM/Load, then it applies that adjustment to the actual fuel delivered in hopes that it really is hitting 13.5. Now once the engine has warmed up, the EEC should stay in CL for any cruising to mid-acceleration condition, but as soon as the Load/RPM hit a certain point, the EEC will kick out of CL and enter OL. In the A9L (and similar EECs), this decision is based on 2 things: 1. The TPS voltage. If the TPS is above the scalar to force OL, then the EEC runs OL. Any RPM/Loads hit above this TPS voltage never get any benefit from Closed Loop learning. 2. Load. There's a scalar that forces OL during high load for X amount of time regardless of the TPS. If this value is set to 1 or 0 seconds, you'll never get any CL exposure for "high-load" but not WOT conditions, and thus you'll never learn during these RPM/Load conditions. I don't know what load value the EEC determines is "high-load" but I guess it to be anything above 60%. Thus, if this scalar is set to something like 10-30 seconds, then CL has a chance to learn something and thus OL can benefit when it is forced. So, yes CL can affect OL operation via the KAMRFs. But it can only do so for OL conditions where CL is sometimes allowed. Thus any high load or WOT condition will never benefit from CL learning. The only way to accurately tweak these OL-only fuel regions is using a Wide-Band O2 sensor. Make sense? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Jan 01, 2007 10:28 am 2shaker, you bring up another point. The Adaptive Update table defines what RPM/Loads are allowed to learn and which aren't. Since high loads will never have CL exposure, it makes sense to reference those RPM/Load locations that would represent the same "error" as Closed-Loop RPM/Loads. So RPM/Load regions that are prevented from learning, are actually referencing another RPM/Load's KAMRF value. It's up to the tuner to choose an RPM/Load that properly represents the referenced region. The factory does a good bit of work in this area and for a factory 5.0L, using factory injectors, and factory MAF curve & MAF, they've determined that 2500RPM/50% load represents most locations fairly well. So if in doubt about what to reference at high load, choose 2500RPM/50%...and that might work ok for slightly modified configurations as well, but no promises. However if you have a WB, keep that location as a "learning" region. Since you'll never enter CL to learn anything, the KAMRF value will remain at 1, which nullifies the effects of the KAMRF contribution. This leaves you free to tweak the mix via the MAF curve or SD tables...depending on the EEC. Some people get a little confused with the difference between OL and WOT and rightfully so since WOT does assume OL. However you can have OL without WOT. WOT for the A9L and similar EECs is a little different than other EECs, I think (Since I only know about the A9L and A9P, I limit my explanation to include only them). Just like there's a TPS scalar to enter OL, there's another scalar that defines what TPS voltage to enter WOT strategy. For factory settings, the TPS voltage for forcing OL and forcing WOT is kept to be the same TPS voltage, but could easily be set to two different values which might prove useful in supercharged applications. However being at OL and being at WOT are quite different in the A9L. Being at OL simply means you are following normal operation, just following the fuel tables without the feedback from HEGOs...but you are still following the normal operation Spark tables, EGR tables, and whatever other normal operation tables that would be in effect at CL. However when you jump to WOT, you introduce WOT fuel contributions and special Spark functions. I'm sure there are times when it would be beneficial to nullify these tables so there's only one place you need to tweak to make adjustments. But since I don't have a WB, I'm guessing at best on these tables. To maximize CL, I've increased these voltages pretty high. Default is 2.7v, I've put them up to 3v to stay in CL longer...this allows for more learning in areas that wouldn't be learned before so I can get more of my MAF curve tuned without a WB. I don't recommend others with boost do this since boost requires enrichment, not for power production, but for cooling purposes. Since I have an all-stock motor, I'm not terribly concerned about overheating at high-loads, but maybe I should...I don't know. For those that don't know, I'll also note that the TPS voltage I'm referring to is a reference voltage, or the voltage ABOVE idle voltage. So if you have your scalars set to 2.7v, and you idle at .95v on the TPS, then the actual TPS trip-point voltage is .95+2.7=3.65v. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jan 02, 2007 11:34 am To hone the MAF curve, what I do is save my current MAF in EA. Calculate a new MAF based on the recent datalog. Then Update my Current MAF curve (1st column in EA) by exactly 1/2 of the difference between what EA suggests & the saved curve. I find that when you start getting really close, EA overcompensates. Moving the curve by 1/2 the amount seems more effective and even then, sometimes I go over. Also note, there are times when a particular MAF voltage is lean and other times when that same MAF voltage is rich which plays hell with tuning a MAF curve since you ASSUME that at any given flow, it'll always be rich or lean, not rich sometimes and lean others. But there's usually an explaination for this and I'll get to that in a minute. First, you need to know how to identify this phenomenon is happening. You can identify this by going to the Mapping function in EA. Map your average MAF in one map and the average LAMBSE (doesn't matter which) in another. Also setup to map only Closed Loop values, not BOTH. Then start comparing cells with similar MAF values and see if they are indicating about the same in the LAMBSEs. If you find cells that are strong lean at lowerRPM/higher loads (LAMBSEs are low to compensate), but are strong rich at higherRPM/lowerLoad (LAMBSEs are high to compensate), then that's a problem AND that will affect your MAF tuning and possibly drivability. If you find that this is, indeed, happening, it's probably MAF backflow at low loads. This is seen with LAMBSEs well above 16 at low loads, but LAMBSEs below 14 at those same MAF voltages at higher loads. What you want is for the higher loads to produce LAMBSEs in the 14s. So you have a couple of options here. 1. Filter your datalog to only include loads from 20% and up then recalculate your MAF and see if it is substantially different. If it is, start tuning for this. 2a. Fix the MAF Backflow problem. 2b. This is sometimes easier said than done. So the EEC should have a Fuel Table for correcting MAF Backflow. On the A9L, putting in smaller numbers decreases the amount of fuel being delivered. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jan 02, 2007 3:15 pm I'm basing this on absolutely nothing concrete, but just looking at the two manifolds, the Cobra manifold is "bigger" which would tend to suggest there's more air-mass inside the Cobra manifold as compared to a GT or std 5.0L intake. So what does that mean? I'm not sure, but running through it logically, this is the way I see it. A bigger intake manifold would mean "manifold filling" affects would increase. What affects does manifold filling cause? Well...at idle or light throttle, the engine is pulling a vacuum because the Throttle-Body is holding back atmosphere from rushing into the cylinders of the engine. But, as soon as you snap the TB open, in rushes atmosphere through the air filter, past the MAF, through the TB, and into the intake manifold. Well all this inrush of air fills the space BEFORE it enters the cylinders. Thus some of the measured air the EEC sees is NOT going into the cylinders yet ...it's just filling the void of intake manifold vacuum. So, my GUESS is that this scalar is a time-delay that should be increased as the intake manifold volume increases to delay the effects of the "accelerator pump" contribution to fuel delivery. Otherwise you might dump too much fuel into the first few cylinders that are aspirating right after you transition from closed throttle to WOT. Again, that's just a guess. But I wouldn't be surprised if I'm wrong. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Thu Jan 04, 2007 1:07 am The A9L is not as load dependent as the CBAZA therefore any change to load such as any cam or scaled MAF will screw up a CBAZA faster than any GUFB or GFUC. There is alot of info out there about the GUFB which makes it easier to tune. The CBAZA is more difficult to tune because of the load dependency but that is not to say with the right tuning software they can be programmed to perform the same. With todays tuners it is a toss up, but I still lean toward the A9L because ofd the wealth of public information. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sat Dec 30, 2006 5:36 am MBT spark advance and the advance at which pinging occurs do not coincide (there might be the very odd occasion when they look like they will but I expect the effects of the pinging result in a power drop thus negating the coincidence). You can run more advance than is required for MBT and still not get pinging. Conversely you can sometimes get pinging at advances less than what is required for MBT. People tend to forget that you only want to run as much advance as is required for the best power and not the most advance the engine will take without pinging. On a CBAZA type strategy if you want to eliminate some spark tables to concentrate on one alone I would suggest setting the Altitude, Sea Level and MBT tables to all 55's because the borderline spark calculation has a few more correction factors applied (e.g. for lugging and ACT). If you do this, then you need to think of the borderline spark table simply as the 'spark table' as you won't be using it for it's intended purpose anymore :) Top

First off, the functions/scalars/constants listed in TunerPro all depend on the definition (XDF) file you have for that strategy of processor. XDF is a proprietary format invented by Mark Mansur (the creator of TunerPro), and therefore these definition files must be created by someone (either him or the community). TunerPro has the ability for editing its own definition files to create custom/new definition files (either for a new strategy, or to add/edit/delete a function/scalar/constant). The only definition files I am aware of, are the ones he has linked to on his site . Considering he drives a GM car, that explains why there are more definition files for them (and why they are more thorough/filled out as well). If a definition suitable for your bin is not listed, you have one of 3 options - create your own, ask Mark to make on for your strategy, or find someone else that already made one. As for the P_6XXX and P_7XXX, those are just unlabeled functions/scalars/constants, they are address locations in the binary that have been found, but don't have any information about what they are or do. posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Mon Aug 07, 2006 5:37 pm When starting out with an "unkown" maf transfer, I suggest the following: 1 Always clear KAMRF after a tuning change. If this is less than one (like in your example above) your rich and the eec is "pulling" fuel. Above 1 and its adding fuel based on O2 sensor feedback. But KAMRF is somewhat slow to show you what you got. The range from observation is 0.890 to 1.121 or plus/minus 12%. And strange things happen when adaptive gets pegged. 2 Watch lambse closely right after a reset of KAMRFs. (batt disconnect) Lambse is commanded afr as seen by the eec and based on O2 sensors' feedback it should run in the 14 range cruising/light loads and around 12 WOT. But don't worry about WOT at this time. In your case, I expect to see lambse up high (over 15) since your KAMRFs posted says your rich. So the eec will command a lean afr to actually get 14.xx as seen by the O2 sensors. Once KAMRFs (adaptive builds up, lambse will/should be in the "good" range. (12-15 roughly speaking) 3 Don't bother working on warmup/startup, log and tune with engine fully warmed up. 4 change one thing at a time, work in small steps. I prefer to dial in the maf transfer. 5 make sure your fuel pressure is 40 psi vacuum line off. I helped 2 guys now to find wrong fuel pressure and trying to "tune around" it. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Mon Aug 07, 2006 11:55 pm I am not an SC guy or A9L, but the load scale was from a similar car. The load scale would be a good starting point.. I set my min inj pulsewidth to 0.0001. I just set it as low as I could I am sure there is some math behind this value. I would probably get the car running then figure out what your lowest pulsewidth is and set it slightly below that. One technique of tuning that I learned from a friend it to set the spark global adder to -10 which pulls 10 deg of timing. Use this until you get your A/F mixture close then bring it back in 2-3 deg at a time. Your A/f will change some but not too drastically. This will help reduce the chance of detonation. As far as load scaling if you figure you are at 327 CI and the stock eec is designer for 302 CI, then you can safely increase the load scale by 10%. On my 331 NA stroker I increased the load scale by 25% and that got me close. Now being SC, once you start getting boost you will have to increase it even more at boost. I would use the Pro-M calibration and start with you injectors at 41 HS and 46 LS. If you are unsure of your maf calibration, trust me its worth the 35 bucks to send it in and get it re-calibrated. when you do ask for a 30 point sheet with it. I also dont understand why you would change the inj offset vs battery. You should not have to change this unless you have EA, and are fine tuning it. This table is to compensate for low voltage conditions. Under lower voltage the injectors dont fire as hard and as fast, so it accounts for slop in the injectos based on voltage. This is just a guestimate for now. Each time I tried something new I starteed with a fresh bin. then made the changes I wanted to. posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Tue Aug 08, 2006 12:57 am Couple of comments here. There is no minimum injector pulsewidth setting in A9L as far as I can tell - and I've looked specifically for it. When you say it wouldn't even start, you mean to say it wouldn't even run since the MAF has no effect during cranking. Also, I can't imagine that if you add the right transfer in Caledit and slopes & burn it that the car will not even run at all. You'd have to be off by more than 25% for this to happen - weird. I have a KB and my load scaling is: 16383 1.00 5000 1.20 3500 1.20 2000 0.86 1350 0.84 1000 0.80 00 0.78 This is probably as good a starting place as any. I would also lower the FN320A - (Open Loop Load Limit vs ECT) so it goes into open loop sooner. Make sure Time at HL to Force OL is "0". Don't be afraid to treat the upper part of the MAF curve different than the bottom - the upper part will mostly be open loop and you need to see 11:1 AFR's for now until you get it dialed in. Don't be afraid to add acceleration fuel. Change Accel Pump Multiplier to "1" to start with. Reread my "egg head" posts on the accel fuel until you get something out of it - all of this bogging bucking backfiring pinging etc I hear people complaining about can be 90% fixed by having the accelerator pump be large enough for the fuel these hopped up motors can gulp on a tip-in. The pinging after tip-in is dialing in the upper part of the MAF curve. You don't really need a SC calibration since you can do the same thing in 10 minutes with the TwEECer. You really need to get it running somewhat OK in closed loop though. Are you putting in a 30 pt curve or something else? With the right slopes (I use 43 & 46.8 ) & right MAF curve it HAS to run. I've run my car with the wrong sample tube (1 injector off) in my C&L it and it still ran OK in closed loop (but not when I got on it). Something is not right here but I can't tell so far what. Oh, and injector offsets can have an effect even at normal voltages since it's added to the pulsewidth. At idle it can be a large percentage of the pulsewidth. Here is what I'm using: 15.94 0.72 14.00 0.78 13.00 0.91 12.00 1.03 11.00 1.19 10.00 1.41 9.00 1.69 8.00 2.13 7.00 3.13 6.00 4.72 5.50 7.00 0.00 7.00 428w now Top
