But you can't get it to run so I would say experiment with the crank pulse width and start up tables. Lean them 50% or more, it's easy to undo this and you are just experimenting. I'm a CBAZA guy so I don't know what these functions/tables are called in A9L. But I can tell you I had all of the typical rich issues when I went to 42's. Hard start when hot (crank PW), surge at idle before it went into CL (start up fuel table), stalling when it went into OL (had to lean the stabilized fuel table too) and so on. And I had the MAF calibrated by Pro-M and they provided the MAF flow sheet when I got it back. Using EEC analyzer and lots of logs I am convinced my MAF curve is right. I wound up leaning crank and start up by 19/42. Now in your case these changes may just be masking an incorrect MAF function because you don't have the real flow sheet and what you are using is perhaps wrong. It sounds to me like the MAF chart you have is incorrect. But you gotta make some progress here... It has to be very frustrating - you been on it since August :-( If it were me, I would solve the crank/start up first, then watch what happens when it goes to CL. If it seems fine until it is in CL for a while then gradually looses control and drops out of CL, I would lean the MAF curve in increments of 1% to see if this solves it. After these experiments perhaps we can help you some more. By the way, the MAF is not a factor in crank. And I also subscribe to the theory that you need a 0 volt at the low end of the MAF and a 16 volt at the top end. I also had this issue and had to cut the stock value in half. Remember that min PW is what EEC will command if the internal computation calls for something less at any given instant in time. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Nov 30, 2006 8:06 pm Any datalog you intend to use with EA should include a wide range of driving conditions from cruising at various speeds and gears as well as moderate accelerations and maintained loads. With that, you select the MAF curve that describes what's in your tune. If you have a custom curve in your tune, manually enter the Voltage/Flow values into EA and save them. You might want to save them as dated names so you can keep all the MAF tweaks straight. You'll also find it useful to do the same with your datalogs, name them with a date. With the MAF curve entered into EA, you can now open your datalog using EA. If you opened the datalog prior to setting the MAF, reopen it. The MAF curve will need to be selected BEFORE opening the datalog so that all related calculations get calculated correctly. CalCon also has a number of flaws that cause it to save erroneous data into the datalog. Use EA's filters to filter the datalog so you don't calculate against corrupt data that's in your log. An average 8MB log will have anywhere from 4 to 40 lines that get filtered out...that's how bad CalCon is. You can set EA to apply these filters at the load of your datalog, but in case you don't have that set, run the filter manually. With the datalog filtered and in EA, click Calculate from the MAF tab and notice the orange curve that results. This is a suggested curve based on where EA noticed the MAF curve needed work. I don't recommend you take the calculated line verbatim. What I do is modify the 1st column's numbers in such a way that it brings the blue line closer to the orange, but in a way that keeps the blue line as smooth as possible. Often the calculated line isn't very smooth. Until you get a finely tuned curve, you want to maintain a curve that's as smooth as possible. This is why I say manually modify the values in the "blue" curve. Also don't bring the blue curve all the way to the orange curve. If there is a BIG difference between them, modify the blue curve by 1/2 the distance between the blue and orange curve. Once you have a modified blue curve that is relatively smooth, save it and transfer that curve over to your tune. Download the modification to your EEC and clear the KAMRFs by either pulling the battery cable or downloading an invalid BIN if you have a selectable tuner like TwEECer (neat trick). Run this MAF curve for a few days. DO NOT go run the MAF curve for 10-15 minutes, then take that log and calculate a new curve. You'll chase your tail doing that. While running the new curve whether datalogging or not, make sure you spend a good amount of time at all the various cruising RPMs and loads. This means, even if you could be in 4th, run the tranny in 3rd or even 2nd to get some time at high RPMs, not just at the RPMs you'd normally cruise at. Eventually after hours of analyzing and understanding how EECs work, you'll get good at this. But until then, these are the basic steps. If you don't already have it, get TunerPro and make all your tune edits through that. It's much easier to transfer back and forth between EA with TunerPro than CalEdit. But before you worry about all that, get comfortable with the procedure. You can worry about streamlining your procedure once you get more practiced. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Jan 08, 2007 3:53 pm codedout wrote: Basically from my knowledge anything with a cam that has overlap will not pass emissions, which is why I went back down to the E303 from the X303 Generally speaking, you are right. The problem is that the overlap allows some of the incoming Air/Fuel to fly out the exhaust during lower RPMs. If you have large enough injectors, you can setup your tune to delay firing of the injectors until AFTER the exhaust valve has closed for RPM/Loads that are used in the emissions tests. This may make the engine run rougher, but may be enough to pass the test since all the fuel sprayed is done while the exhaust valve is closed. As soon as you get your certification in hand, flip back to a tune that drives better and be done with it. The catch is, your injectors have to be large enough to get the squirt complete before the intake valve closes. If the intake valve closes before the injector is done, some fuel will be sprayed on the backside of the closed intake valve and will get sucked in on the next stroke...and now you have raw fuel out the exhaust again. Unfortunately even with sufficiently large injectors, some amount of raw fuel may go out the exhaust anyway. Even if the injectors quit firing before their intake valve closes, the valve is most likely going to still be wet with fuel when it closes. That wetness will evaporate off with the heat of combustion and will be part of the next intake stroke's incoming payload of air. And that will be what goes right out the exhaust if there's sufficient overlap & exhaust scavenging. So if your overlap is bad, you may still fail. This is where really good CAT converters help. Even having a smog pump would help here...not to help the CATs burn off the fuel, but to "dilute" the exhaust with outside air so your Parts-Per-Million count of pollutants goes down. The more air you can pump into the exhaust to dilute the exhaust mix, the better your numbers will look even though the engine is ejecting the same amount of pollutants. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue Jan 09, 2007 7:43 am cgrey8 wrote: Are the Function/Scalar/Tables "labelled" by their documented names within the BIN? If only it was that easy It basically boils down to recognising the individual sub routines within the code. e.g. this is the altitude and sea level spark table lookup from a 1995 (ish) COSY ecu; Code: Select all ; ;first find sea level spark value ; AD3W L0038,OFFSET_D31E,#15Ah ;table = SPARK_SEA_LEVEL_TABLE CALL SPARK_TABLE_LOOKUP ;call SPARK_TABLE_LOOKUP LDB TEMP_DATA_4_LO,L003B ;TEMP_DATA_4_LO = result ; ;find altitude spark value ; AD3W L0038,OFFSET_D31E,#1BDh ;table = SPARK_ALTITUDE_TABLE CALL SPARK_TABLE_LOOKUP ;call SPARK_TABLE_LOOKUP LDB TEMP_DATA_4_HI,L003B ;TEMP_DATA_4_HI = result ; ;interpolate between the two tables ; CALL BYTE_LOOKUP_MAIN ;call BYTE_LOOKUP_MAIN DCW 8150h ;table = SPARK_MAP_BIAS DCW KAM_BAP_HI_BYTE ;input = KAM_BAP_HI_BYTE LDB L0037,L0038 ;L0037 = result (always 253 in ;this ecu) LDB L0036,L0037 ;L0036 = result (always 253 in ;this ecu) LDB L0035,TEMP_DATA_4_LO ;L0035 = [base spark] CLRB L0034 ;L0034 = 0 LDB L0033,TEMP_DATA_4_HI ;L0033 = [altitude spark] CLRB L0032 ;L0032 = 0 CALL UNSIGNED_A-D_FILTER_#1 ;call UNSIGNED_A-D_FILTER_#1 ASRW L003E,#2h ;\ LDW TEMP_DATA_1,L003E ; TEMP_DATA_1 = result / 4 By recognising a similar routine in another ecu you can quicky find the two spark tables as you find Ford tend to use very similar routines (if not identical) in most eec-iv’s of that age. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue Jan 09, 2007 10:07 am A .dir file is like a .xdf in that it is unique to the strategy. e.g. a A9L.dir will work on A9L, A3M, A3M1, S0Z and X3Z bins or a T4M0.dir will work on T4M0, W4H0, U4P0 and J4J1 bins (providing the .dir is renamed to match the bin or vice versa). David Claflin wrote: I need some schooling please.... what exactly is bin disassembly?? Thanks Here's computer theory 101 in a nutshell. Any computer program is made up of 1s and 0s. We've heard that most of our lives. Well the 1s and 0s are better "seen" in HEX format so to compress them into a format that's easier for our eyes to deal with, HEX editors take all those 1s and 0s and organize them into numbers. However even that is meaningless unless you know what it means. Well that's where the assembly code comes in. Each possible instruction a processor can run is hard-coded into a processor and given a unique ID, as well as published in documents for humans to write compilers. To the processor, this ID is a number. To humans writng Assembly code, it is a word (called a Opcode). Words are easier for us to deal with when we are trying to read and write code. So to compile assembly into it's proper unique ID values, you need a compiler which converts this written Assembly Language code into those 1s and 0s that the processor can deal with. However since Assembly is so closely related to the raw binary code the processor uses, it can be reversed back to assembly relatively easily. However what's missing is all the commentaryand intuitive variable/subroutine names the original programmer included in his original code. Since the computer doesn't care what you called a subroutine, only what the subroutine is doing, all that is boiled off during the compiling process...making the results of a decompiled BIN file much more cryptic. In a nutshell, that's what decompiling is. Need more? posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Tue Jan 09, 2007 10:42 am sailorbob wrote: Set the 'load scaling switch' to 1 so that your load = loadx, it makes tuning easier as you don't have to worry about which tables use load or loadx. Just be careful if you do this - Fuel Table - Base OL (FN1307) & OL Load Limit vs ECT (FN320A) use %Load - you will have to shift the OL Fuel rows about 1 down to compensate (just an approximation!). i.e., with load = load (not load % - load switch set to '1') - a 55% load @ 5000 RPM (open loop) will demand a 14.64 AFR! Using the load switch = 0, the %Load (using A9L stock scaling) would be 70% and demand an AFR of 13.04 ! In other words, will run lean if you just change the switch and don't then edit the OL Fuel Table cells individually. Also, when you lug the engine (going uphill in 4th at like 2000 RPM), a 55% Load will be 76% %Load (stock settings) and will force Open Loop (look at FN320A - greater than 70% %Load forces open loop). With the load switch set to 1 you will need to set FN320A lower and you will not have the advantage of the "normalizing" that the %Load function provides here. In other words, the engine will not be forced into open loop when it should be and you will "load up" and wonder why you are not going anywhere and you will keep pressing down on the accelerator until the OL/WOT TPS voltage threshold is hit. This may be confusing, but that is my point - changing Load to %Load does not necessarily make things easier to figure out - there is a reason that the Ford engineers added what seems on it's face to be an unnecessary complication to just 2 tables and one function. posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Sat Aug 26, 2006 12:25 pm The experiment I just did shows that the HEGO Bias table is off by a factor of two. So if you want to know the offset, take 1 & add 2x the number in the table. For numbers above the stock 20% load line (all 0's), you need to first subtract .125 from the number in the table, then multiply by two, then add then negative number to 1, then multiply by 14.64 to get commanded LAMBSE!! Example: Upper right number in table is .11719 - subtract .125 from this. .11719-.125 = -0.00781 - this is what should be in the table. This is off by a factor of two based on my experiments so -0.00781 * 2 = -0.01562 This subtracts from LAMBSE so commanded AFR equals: 1 - 0.01562 = 0.98438 * 14.64 = 14.41 This richens up the mixture when cruising at heavy load and closed loop. At light load it leans the mixture up to 1.4%. Pretty cool huh? 428w now Top

Keep in mind that the slop in the screw holes is generally enough to allow you to slightly loosen the TPS sensor, and move the sensor enough to get it to .95 without touching the throttle screw. I've never had to do this, but I've heard of people that didn't have enough slop needing to drill the holes out a little bigger or take a dremel to oval the holes a bit. What concerns me a little is why the values are as different as they are. Perhaps with 42lb injectors, that's common? I always though you didn't want your KAMRFs to be more than +/-.03. I've heard more than indicates some air/fuel balance problem between the left and right side of the motor. The KAMRF1@idle has topped out at 1.121. You need to fix that. Just out of curiosity, with the KAMRF all the way at 1.121, what is the LAMBSE1? There are a number of reasons why you may be running lean here and there are a number of ways you could correct for it as well. In case you don't know what they are, here's my thoughts: 1. Lower your injector low-slope. That'll bring the lower PWs down, enriching them. However since the higher PWs are obviously a little rich, this will further enrich them. You'll need to respond by raising the high-slope to compensate. You might also need to adjust the Injector Breakpoint function. However as a suggestion, do not get your low-slope too far away from your high-slope, otherwise you'll SEE the breakpoint in your logs as PWs flutter around the breakpoint. With 42lb injectors, I don't think this will be a problem for you, but since I have never run injectors that large, I can't say that for sure. 2. The more popular way of fixing these problems, adjust the MAF curve so idle doesn't starve. 3. Enrich the RPM/Load that needs it with the MAF Backflow table (numbers above 1 enrich, numbers below 1 take fuel away). I wouldn't do this until you've determined that other ways are not working for you or are causing side-effects you don't want to deal with. 4. Prevent idle from learning a KAMRF value that high by using the Adaptive Update table and reference the idle row at your idle RPM. Since you appear to be in the 800s, you may want to reference both the 700 and 900 RPM range. The idle row is the one listed as 0.00 Load. In TunerPro, it's the top row. If your table already is referencing another RPM/Load for the 700/900@idle, then your idle may simply need to be pointed at something else OR allowed to learn. But the fact that you have 1.121 for a KAMRF value still indicates a problem. FYI, positive numbers in the Adaptive Table indicate learning is allowed. Negative numbers indicate the cell is referencing another cell for KAMRF values. The 1st number is the row number starting at the bottom with 0. The 2nd number is column number starting at the left with 0. -57 is 2500@50%. See what other people say, but hopefully this is at least something to chew on if you get nothing else useful. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Jan 11, 2007 10:56 am The Shredder wrote: ...I also noticed that my LAMBSE1 value is 15-16 during part throttle/cruise operation. This would be a commanded lean which should help with gas mileage, right?... Not exactly. Seeing 15-16s in the part throttle range just means more work could be done with the injector slopes or the MAF curve. Run the car up to around 4000-4500 with moderate throttle (not enough to go WOT). Keep it in Closed Loop and see what your LAMBSEs are. Try to get some light to moderate acceleration in every RPM range then use EA to map out your average LAMBSEs. If you are rich across the board, then your injector slopes could use some work. However if you have regions of richness, and other places where your LAMBSEs are averaging lean, then your slopes are probably about as close as you'll get them...start tweaking the MAF to compensate. Keep in mind, when you are using the mapping function, it's only as useful as your logs are. So you need a decent amount of time in the log at each RPM/Load. If you only "passed by" an RPM/Load, you could see a LAMBSE value for that location that's not indicative of what's really going on there. Adaptive strategy needs time to do its thing and thus you need even more time in the log to average out the LAMBSEs that don't really represent your stabilized driving conditions at each RPM/Load position. Thus, you aren't going to learn as much from a datalog with only 1 run as you would from a datalog that has a series of accelerations at lots of different loads and RPMs. If you have a hilly area, that will help get you good logs. Up the hills, you can get yourself deep in the load and the hill will help keep you in those RPM/Load conditions longer so you get more data....and again you DO NOT want to be at OL or WOT for these logs unless you have a wideband. Without a wideband, You want to maintain in closed loop as much as you can. On A9* EECs, there are TPS voltage scalars that define when you go OL and when you go WOT. Increasing these will allow you to get deeper in the accelerator and still maintain CL. There's a 3rd scalar that forces OL at high load for X number of seconds...you might want to increase that as well...at least during MAF tuning. After that, return them to whatever you want. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Jan 11, 2007 1:48 pm Getting the Injector slopes, injector breakpoint, and MAF tuned in will help with fuel economy in that very minor amounts of fuel won't be wasted on needless enrichment. But noticeable fuel economy savings are made once you get everything running and you start tweaking the spark tables. The more spark you can get into the motor before exceeding MBT or causing detonation, the better. Most people focus on this only at WOT where performance matters to them. But to get better fuel economy, you have to focus on this in the midranges of your spark tables too. Think about it, the more torque you can get from your fuel, that's less fuel you have to inject so you push on the throttle a little less to maintain whatever speed you are trying to maintain while cruising. So whats the catch? Unfortunately, finding the max spark without exceeding MBT is not a straight forward thing to do. Without a dyno, it's more trial-n-error with vague feedback called "Fill up at the gas station and see if you got better fuel economy on that tank." Most people tune to the point that they get ping. But as discussed in another thread a while back, MBT and Borderline detonation are two different things. MBT (Max Brake Torque) is the max advance you can put on the engine before more advance is either not getting you more torque OR you actually loose torque. This one requires a dyno to accurately fill out and my suspicion is that only tells you what that day's best advance numbers are which is likely related to fuel, engine temp, air temp, engine mood, position of the moon & stars, rolling of eyes, and what-not. Another day on the same dyno may produce different results...but at least you are closer than you were at least for that day. Borderline ping is the max advance the engine can handle before detonation occurs. You can tune this one yourself...just use your ears. And again, fuel, air temp, engine mood, moon&stars, etc also affect this one too. But at least you can tweak if next week's new moon position makes your car ping more than last week. (BTW, I'm kidding about the moon-n-stars affects...I hope that much was obvious) Moving forward, for any given RPM/Load, these don't always exist at the same place. Thus at some RPM/Loads, it's possible to exceed your advance for Max torque, but not be pinging yet. Likewise at other RPM/Loads, you may ping, but if you advanced a little further anyway, you might could get a little more torque out of'er while upsetting small children with the pinging noise and loud mufflers. In an ideal situation, you don't want to exceed either of these. Since they don't occur at the same degrees of advance, but are in the same general vicinity, most do-it-yourselfer tuners tune to Ping since that's something that doesn't require a dyno. FYI, the CBAZA (94-95 Mustang) EEC strategy includes Borderline and MBT spark tables in the tune. Since the factory was lucky enough to have a dyno they could test a car on, they decided to put it to good use and create accurate MBT and Ping tables in their CBAZA EEC tunes. The EEC calculates the spark advance based off these tables, and chooses the table that results in the lower advance (since they didn't want to exceed either MBT or Borderline). That's probably more than you wanted to know, but I felt the need to hear the sound of my own.....keyboard. So, there you go. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Thu Jan 11, 2007 1:50 pm Load is the key to fuel milage (and your right foot ) You want to be in the 40-50% load at your desired highway speed, steady throttle, level road. This is roughly the range the eec will command the most timing and lean mixture. The easiest way to get the most milage out of your tune is to have a vacuum guage hooked up, and run so you get the most vacuum possible at said highway speed. Generally speaking, you should see 10" or more vacuum cruising. (I'm running 12-15" maintaining 65~70 mph on a flat road.) The easiest way to lower load is to raise the CID scalar. While some ppl frown on messing with the CID scalar, it is easy to change and does work. Try 10 cube/inch increments to bring you load down into the 4x% range. Note: I picked up MPG going from the tweecer to a moates chip and I still am not sure why(same tune). cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Jan 11, 2007 10:33 am If you have someone else running that same MAF with no problems, use their MAF curve as a starting point. At least then you can put MAF towards the bottom of the list of possible problems and diagnose other stuff like why you can't get the idle lower than 1100. Basic things like idle should get at least a little under control before you get too deep into it. As for your puffs of black because you are running too rich, that's far better than the alternative especially with forced induction. Things to check: 1. Verify fuel pressure is at 39psi with no vacuum connected to the regulator. With an adjustable regulator, you could easily be running too high of a pressure which would explain the over-rich condition 2. Verify the Injector slopes are entered correctly. If your buddy is running the same injectors you are, get his slopes AND injector breakpoint function values, and port that to your A9P. 3. Verify timing (not that this would cause what you are seeing...just a good idea to do) 4. Unplug the Idle Air Controller (IAC) and see if the engine still idles high. If it does, then your Throttle Body (TB) is allowing too much air past and needs to be adjusted back OR you got a leak somewhere. With the IAC unplugged, you should be able to run the engine down to about 600RPMs...with tighter TBs, you should be able to starve the engine of any air and stall it out. But generally you want the TB adjusted to idle the engine around 500-600 so the IAC can do its job. I read here recently what percentage the IAC should be at idle, but I forgot the number. 5. You mentioned that you thought the charger was holding the IAC open...unless the IAC is bad, that shouldn't happen. Verify the IAC isn't bad by putting it on another vehicle (if possible) and see that it is working. If you get the same high idle on the other vehicle, you found your problem. On pre-94 IACs, you can generally get away with dumping a bunch of oil down inside them to free them up if they get gummed up. That only works on the IACs that look like this: The newer style are shorter and I don't believe you can get away with this. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Jan 11, 2007 2:16 pm Things to look forward to with 4.10s: Everything said right above Good off the line tire control assuming you have some wide, sticky tires and an automatic with a moderate stall. Good towing ability assuming you have a tight stall converter and preferably lockup ability or a manual. Pathetic gas mileage unless you have some really tall tires. And potential for driveshaft bounce felt as a vibration at high cruising speeds due to the higher RPMs created on the driveshaft to get the same speed as a lower gear ratio. If this is to be a problem, it'll be most noticeable at speeds above 80mph. Take this with a grain of salt, but it has been my observation that 4.10s and 4.55s are only useful when all you care about is racing and 1/4 mile times...all side-effects are of no consequence. However on 4x4 trucks with taller tires (even factory), 4.10s can be beneficial, but most general purpose trucks are optimal at 3.55s or 3.73s depending on the application and the transmission used. For instance, most 4x4 Rangers and V6 manual tranny 2wd Rangers run a 3.73 gear. Automatic 2wd Rangers typically have a 3.55 (8.8") or 3.46 (7.5"). There are some exceptions out there, but these were the "typical" setups. The most popular exceptions were some 4x4 Rangers that did come factory with 4.10s, and generally it was because they were equipped with taller tires and really needed the extra gearing to turn those tires over. Perhaps 4.10s in an F150 would do fine. You'll have to ask someone that actually has that setup to know for sure. If you find someone, be sure to get pertinent info like their tire size (i.e. 295/60R18) and their transmission gearing both at 1st and OD. You get more torque at the expense of a lower speed. So every gear will shift at a lower speed. And off the line, you'll have some serious pull and will be able to break the tires loose without much trouble, BUT with a lower gear (higher ratio number), you'll be able to control the wheel spin to keep the engine just barely spinning the tires until you need to shift. Where as with a higher gear, say a 3.08, you'll loose torque in each gear, but your shiftpoint speed will be much higher. A high-end gear like a 3.08 is good for fuel economy. It keeps the RPMs low at cruising. And if the engine is built for low-end torque, you'll get better fuel economy with a lower RPM loaded a little harder than you will with a higher RPM running with less load. But 3.08s are not going to be impressive off the line. Off the line, you either can't brake the tires loose OR you break them loose and get them spinning too fast and loose control of the spin. Like I said, most trucks do best with 3.55s or 3.73s, where 3.73 is the sportier option, and 3.55 is the economy option. Notice from my signature, I have 3.27 gears. Since this truck is my daily driver and at the time, I was driving 70+miles a day to and from work, I was very interested in fuel economy and I went overboard. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Mon Jan 15, 2007 6:44 pm cgrey8 The 0x2000 is there for a couple of reasons, earlier versions of TunerPro would calculate the checksum incorrectly when using an offset and also for the DIY chip burning brigade it just simplifies their chip reading and burning. The padding that you see at the end of the bins can be unused memory as you say but it can also be garbage that the Tweecer (or other eec reading device) ends up pulling out because they assume there's a 64k EPROM fitted (or multiple banks of 64k). Not all eec-iv's have EPROMs that cover the full addressable range of the processor, 32k and IIRC 16k EPROMs were used on the early ecu's. garsten AFAIK the GUF1.xdf from the TunerPro site is the most up to date. A new version should be posted soon. This will have the error you found fixed and a few more items identified. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Sep 25, 2006 1:30 pm You got it...both *.BIN and *.CCF files can be opened by CalEdit. But only CCFs can be saved in CalEdit. If you've never messed with TunerPro, you'll need an XDF file which is the alignment file that details the BIN for you. For those that may not know, the BIN is the binary executable that runs in the ECM. But it doesn't contain any detail with regard to parameter description, where in the BIN the function/table parameter resides, the scaling (units of measure conversion) it uses, or any of that. Somebody has to figure all that out. Since those are the proprietary details of the manufacturer, all that must be reversed engineered by people that know a little bit about how ECMs are programmed (or have inside connections to get their hands on proprietary documentation). From what I understand, they actually follow the bin file logic out and determine what parts of the BIN are executing code, and what parts are the parameters the execution code is using. Once they figure out all this wonderful stuff, they write an XDF file that maps those locations in the BIN file to tables, charts, and scalar description labels so that it makes sense to us. In addition, the XDF may describe data conversions so the values you see and modify are in units that make sense, not values that the ECM is expecting. For instance values from 0-5 volts may literally be represented in the BIN file as 0-255. What voltage is 192? Well a good XDF would convert 192 to the appropriate value between 0-5 so you didn't have to think about it. All TunerPro is doing is providing an environment that knows how to display charts, graphs, and scalars. The advanced version of TunerPro has some ability to simulate an ECM, but I've never needed to know how to use that. All I ever used TunerPro for is modifying my tune. There's also an *.rdt file format which is the same thing as *.xdf. I'm assuming there's some similar product out there that uses *rdt files so TunerPro is compatible with their format as well. I have A9L/X3Z and A9P/A9M XDF files. If your ECM doesn't follow these strategies, then you'll need to get the XDF and BIN file that represents your ECM to begin tweakin' in TunerPro. The best way I know to get those is to ask around. If there's a repository for those files, that would be awesome. Once you get a tune you are 100% happy with, you can take that same BIN you loaded into CalEdit and burn it to a custom chip, pull the TwEECer off, and use your freshly burned chip instead. Then you can reuse your TwEECer on another vehicle to begin tweakin' away at it. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website TB vs HP Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Jan 17, 2007 2:13 pm When sizing components for an engine, it's important to size everything to the capacity of the engine. Oversizing can often be just as detrimental to the overall performance of an engine as undersizing...in many cases, it's worse. Sizing MAFs is just a matter of getting one that'll service the flow ranges you expect based on CID, heads, cam, and intake. Sometimes that's not an easy number to come by, but there's some guessing room here. As for injectors, I've seen breakdowns of how to size injectors vs the expected HP like this: Injector Size ___ Supercharged ___ Naturally Aspirated ___19 lb.__________276 hp_________338 hp ___24 lb.__________349 hp_________427 hp ___30 lb.__________436 hp_________533 hp ___36 lb.__________553 hp_________640 hp ___42 lb.__________611 hp_________747 hp ___55 lb.__________800 hp_________978 hp ** These numbers appear to be ratings with 0% safety and assuming an adjustable regulator set at 43.5PSI. Personally, I'd drop each of those HP estimates down by a good 25%. However I've never come across a ThrottleBody sizing chart that breaks out the various size TBs like the injector sizing chart above. Are there any rules-of-thumb, guidelines, or charts that other people know of that answer this? Or is it called Ask the Manufacturer ? cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jan 23, 2007 9:28 pm Keep in mind that narrow-band O2s are just that...narrow. A little change in fuel delivery will sway the O2s from lean to rich and back. It's not like the EEC is switching the HEGOs between 12 and 17:1. I don't know the exact mix that the engine is at when the O2s transition between 0v & .6v, but it's safe to say that very minute changes in fuel delivery is all it takes to sway them from .6v to 0v and back. So if the EEC can float a mix that keeps the O2s jumping, it knows it's "close enough" to perfect to pass the smog tests. To be honest, I don't think the older style EECs are precise enough to maintain any better control of the fuel delivery. It would be like asking you to walk a tight-rope drunk without one of those long poles to steady yourself. The slightest foot movement is going to throw you to one side or the other with very little control. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

You are likely going either really rich or really lean during cold starts. Do you see this behavior in like the first minute after startup? I made some adjustments to the Startup Fuel (FN1306) table at cold temps because of behavior like this. Granted, you would think that if your Injector Slopes, Offsets and MAF were all 100% accurate for 42's that you wouldn't have to do this, but since it's only during cold starts, it's easy to just adjust a few cells in the cold start table. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sat Jan 27, 2007 11:18 am The values in the 'Fuel Startup Table' (FN1306) are AF ratio and are subtracted from the 'Fuel Base Table' (FN1307) returned lookup value to richen the mixture during the first 45 seconds of running. You don't modify this table by the ratio of the injector change after an injector swap (in theory you shouldn't have to change it at all providing you injector slopes, breakpoint and offset are correct). What you might find is that some of the engine modifications require a small area of the table to be tweaked as per Cougar5.0's experience. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Jan 27, 2007 11:45 am I'm not running 42s, but I do have 19s with this problem. However my engine setup and the particular injectors I have wouldn't work with the factory A9L or A9P tune. The factory settings were way too lean at startup. When I 1st got the TwEECer, I figured out that lowering the injector low slope fixed the startup problem. As I got more informed about the power at my finger tips with the TwEECer, I learned that adjusting the Fuel Startup table was the more "correct" way of fixing this problem. Since then, I've found I can raise my injector slopes back to factory values and it cranks fine. The tweaks I made were to enrich the mix within the 1st few seconds of startup. I don't know the exact units of the values in the startup table's cells, but it SEEMS as though these are offsets of the Fuel OL Table. Thus if you have 13.8 for a particular ECT in the Fuel OL table, then a 2 in the startup table for that same ECT location, the result will be 11.8 LAMBSE. For the 1st few seconds, I have the engine running with 3s across the board for the bottom two rows (1sec & 6sec). After the engine gets on its feet (about 4-5 seconds) then it runs fine. So factory values for the rest of the rows above the 6-second row work fine for me. However even with this setting, I still see the EEC leaning my mix out during crank. About 2 seconds after the engine cranks, I see the HEGOs drop to lean, then immediately pop back to rich and pretty much stay there until CL kicks in. I'm pretty sure that lean dip is being caused by some strategy transition in the EEC, I just don't know what. I couldn't even tell this until I got the idea to turn the ignition on to allow the HEGOs to heat up for a good minute or so first. Then crank the engine. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Nov 09, 2006 8:53 am Also keep in mind, don't treat your tools like they are your brain. Your tools give you eyes and ears into aspects of ECM tuning that you couldn't access before. That being said, you shouldn't blindly copy/paste everything EA suggests over to the BIN without running it through your own thought process to determine if it makes sense. You have to be willing to think for yourself and decide what pieces and parts of what EA suggested make sense to transfer. As an example, when tuning a MAF curve, it's common to get all sorts of humps and curves into the hypothesized line especially when the MAF isn't dialed in even close. Until you start getting a very finely tuned MAF curve, you want to make every effort to fit your tune's MAF to EA's hypothesized curve while keeping the curve as smooth as the numbers will allow. This can be quite a challenge until you spend some serious time with it and just "see" what needs to be adjusted and by how much. There's no doubt about it, ECM tuning is as much an art as it is a science...that's the polite way of saying there's lots of guessing involved. Once your KAMs are within +/-.03 of 1, you may find that a natural hump really does occur in your MAF. I can show you a screenshot of my MAF and it has a very slight hump in it, but every datalog I've run shows this is what the engine wants. The KAMs and LAMBSEs are happy with this, so until someone says I need to be tweaking something else like my HEGO bias values or some other table I haven't learned about yet, I'm leaving it like that. The only other piece of advice I can give you about MAFs is...be patient. Don't make a datalog, then go tune the MAF. Clear the KAMs and make another datalog to tune it again. Unless the MAF curve you calculated is just causing too many problems to deal with (as compared to a previous curve), you want to run the tune for a good 3 or so driving hours in diverse driving conditions before downloading an updated curve. The KAMs take time to adjust. And in order for them to "learn" where they should be, you have to maintain in each load/RPM condition for extended periods of time so they have a chance to learn. If you can safely look at the datalog while you are driving, you can tell whether there's more learning to be done or not. If you are in CL and your LAMBSEs are below 14.6, the KAMs need to learn up. If above 14.6, then the KAMs need to learn down. That might help a little... If you aren't patient, you'll be chasing your tail...believe me, been there, done that...T-shirt has holes now. :) ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

To make dialing in the MAF tranfer easier on myself I changed all the A/F numbers in my fuel table to the same thing, since your NA 13.0 would be just fine, I used 12.0 since I am boosted. posts.author: yellowmustang
posts.content: yellowmustang Gear Head Posts: 4 Joined: Thu Jan 16, 2003 6:48 pm Quote Post by yellowmustang » Sun Jan 28, 2007 10:44 pm I don;t want to deviate too far from the stock warmup a/f and I would like to re-enable CL once i'm dialed it for economys sake. As such I'm thinking I need to tune for Stoich at most low loads before I work on WOT. I'm just not clear on where to start. Once you force open loop your EEC is no longer targeting 14.64 using your stock O2 sensors, it is aiming for a certain A/F ratio based on your A9l's fuel tables. The only way it can accurately do this is if your MAF function is correct. In open loop, if your MAF function is correct your wideband should read whatever A/F ratio is in the fuel table at what ever RPM and Load your currently driving at........problem is the fuel tables have all sorts of different A/F ratios at different points, this makes it difficult to use the wideband to tune in your MAF function as the EEC will quickly change A/F ratios under different driving conditions. The only reason I change all the numbers in the fuel tables is becauses it makes it very easy to know if your MAF function is too rich or to lean at a certain Kg/Hr since your only dealing with one targeted A/F ratio. This works great to tune in your MAF function at ANY load or rpm. Once your MAF function is dialed in you can change your fuel tables back to stock and make small changes from there, except now that the MAF is correct your A/f ratios will be very close to whatever your fuel tables want them to be. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jan 16, 2007 10:40 am When I did the V8 conversion on my Ranger, I used a 97 Explorer motor which had very little in common with a Mustang as far as sensors and connectors. What I had to do was replace all the sensors with Mustang sensors. However that didn't solve all the problems. Some sensors/controls were not in the same place so I had to do quite a bit of wire stretching in places to get things to connect. Then to make matters worse, whoever sold me the wiring harness didn't get it from a V8 Mustang. They got it from some other Ford SFI V8 such as a Cobra or Thunderbird. Most of my wire colors didn't match the Mustang wiring diagrams and my harness had connectors on it that the Mustang diagrams didn't show. So this meant a point-to-point check of EVERY SINGLE WIRE in that harness to verify where the ends were. Since I was going to be modifying wire lengths anyway, I wound up unravelling the whole wiring harness and working with the bare wire. This made it much easier to trace out. While I was at it, I went to a junkyard and clipped the engine wire harness connectors from other Rangers so I could literally plug my modified V8 harness up to my Ranger's chassis wiring as though it was made for it. Once I was done with all my terminations, I used about 3 rolls of Scotch 3M electrical tape to bind the wiring harness back together. That's when I found all the places I'd either grossly overestimated the amount of wire I needed or slightly underestimated, which made more solder-points in the harness, but I eventually got it all done, taped, and rebound inside black wire loom so it looks like factory again. My point is, as long as your Ford V8 wiring harness has all the same sensors and actuators (MAF, SFI injection support, 2-channel HEGOs, etc) as the EEC you plan to use on it, you can use it. Just plan on some manual intervention to get the wires to reach where they need to go. I will have to admit, all the sensor/actuator wires went to the same pins on my EEC. So whatever car it came from was close-enough to an 89-93 V8 Mustang setup to work. Most of the rewiring was getting the Ranger-specific connectors onto the main harness and relocating connectors to where their corresponding sensor/actuator was located on my setup. I expect retrofitting a 5.0L harness to fit a 460 will be much of the same. The good news is it's not rocket science, but it is intimidating looking at a birds-nest of wires strewn everywhere. You just drudge through it, wire by wire. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Nov 12, 2006 8:56 am I've had the opposite issue with my engine. It cranks fine warm, but was sputtering badly at cold-starts. My fix was to enrich the Startup Fuel Table in the temp ranges that were affected. But since your situation is so different, we need more details as to what is happening during crank. Get a datalog of a hot-crank attempt. But before cranking, let the key sit ON for a good 30 seconds before attempting to crank. This will get the HEGOs warmed up a little so we can get a better idea what the fuel mix is during start. All starts regardless of hot or cold should be on the rich side. If you are finding that throughout your crank attempts, the HEGOs indicate lean, then this may be an easy fix in that Startup Fuel Table. However if it is rich, then other diagnostics will probably be required. Even hot, I wouldn't think it possible to over-rich it by enough to keep the engine from starting at all. But I guess it is possible. So notice what your LAMBSEs are during crank. Just for informational purposes, get your crank timing as well...just to make sure it isn't going to some wildly advanced or retarded value. If the engine never cranks after a few seconds on the starter datalogging. Kick your pedal so the datalog will hopefully show you a difference between what it was doing and what the pedal did for you. If you aren't logging it, log TPS so we can see right when the pedal got kicked. Also note, if your TPS voltages are not reporting between .93-.97 (target is .955), then THAT could be your problem, although I've never heard of a misaligned TPS causing this. I doubt any of this will solve your problem, but it should be a good start at getting the diagnostic info you need to determine what the problem is. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

2Shaker Tuning Addict Posts: 2087 Joined: Thu Jul 22, 2004 9:24 pm Location: Dayton Ohio Quote Post by 2Shaker » Sun Nov 12, 2006 11:00 pm cgrey8, Well I'm no expert here either, and I have no proof it ignores the MAF on crank, but logic tells me it doesn't need to read MAF on crank, nor could it reliably. Imagine how low the voltage would be with so little air passing over the sensor. The EEC knows the RPM on crank is very low (what is it, maybe 100 RPM?), and it can't go any faster so the engine is going to injest a known amount of air no matter the throttle setting. So with known amount of air all it (EEC) needs to do is set the pulsewidth based on ECT and ACT. I can say in CBAZA that the crank PW vs ACT is a table to which the crank PW multiplier vs ECT function is applied. No where does "Load" or RPM figure into these calculations (at least that I can see in all of the TwEECer viewable items). Now as soon as you release the key it goes to the startup program where RPM, MAF and load definitely play a role. But if you can't get it to fire without holding the peddle to the foor, which tells the EEC to turn off the injectors because a flooded engine is assumed, the thing to do is lean the crank function/table. These are all assumptions on my part, but it worked. Car would not start hot, and then ran very rich and surged before going to CL after a minute or so. I leaned the crank function/table and it started by just tapping the key (like stock!), but then it would surge and run rich after it was running. I had to fix that by changing the startup fuel table. So in my mind there are 3 states here that need to be tuned separately: 1)crank; 2) startup; and 3) CL idle. And troubleshoot them in that order. Anyone disagree with that? No I understand it to be like this in the A9L: When initial cranking the MAF is ignored and FN348 is used along with FN306 After PIP is sycn'd up the startup routine activates. This uses FN1307 and FN1306. You can simply subtract FN1306 from FN1307 to get the target AFR for the predetermined time. There are other factors but most of them are nulled out by the calibration. You will notice the top row in FN1306 is 45 second which eliminates the modifier of the OL fuel table after 45 seconds has been reached. This timer does not get reset until the key is cycled. Once the startup routine is done the OL fuel control is in affect. This soley uses FN1307. This will stay operative untl the O2's switch for the first time. This is when CL idle control is entered. So, if you are tying to change startup then use FN1306 and FN1307. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Jan 16, 2007 4:34 pm It sounds like you are on the right track with the passenger side tires in the grass. Don't get me wrong, I'm not that much closer on the road, but here's my story. You are right to set your injector slopes to the size injectors you have. However you also need to adjust the low-slope to some value slightly higher than what your injectors are. Since I have no experience with monster injectors like 42s, I can't suggest a good starting point. Others may be able to help you out there. However the Injector offset and breakpoint aren't scalars in A9L. They are functions. The Injector offset is a fuel trim based on battery voltage. As voltage goes up, the speed at which the injectors open increases, which means you get slightly more fuel with higher voltages than with lower. As voltage sags below 12v, this becomes more and more pronounced. EA has the ability to help you calculate an offset curve based on your datalogs. The Injector Breakpoint is also based on voltage, but I can't figure out why. Every use of this breakpoint function, the value is always the same from top to bottom so voltage is taken out of the equation. However the values you put into this function affect the way the EEC transitions from injector low-slope to injector high-slope. I have vague understanding of it, but the intricate details still aren't clear. One explanation I've heard is that that the A9* EECs have a fixed (hardcoded) 2ms PW breakpoint. But to smooth the "edge" as the fuel delivery traverses this breakpoint area, the breakpoint function defines a constant fuel contribution for any given PW that has recognizable affects at lower pulse-widths, but becomes an inconsequential contribution at higher pulse-widths and thus the more you contribute here, the higher the PW has to be before it's inconsequential. However at the low-end where the steeper low-slope may be too steep, this constant contribution to the calculated PW keeps the mix from being too lean. Then I've heard other explanations that say this somehow defines the exact time (in ms) that the EEC uses to determine what PW the EEC should quit calculating the injectors based on low-slope and start using high. Thus you could fill the breakpoint function with 0s and this would completely disable the low-slope from being part of the PW calculation. To be honest, I don't know which is right. At this point, injector slopes and breakpoints are a trial-n-error guessing game for me. I'd be happy for someone that knows this stuff better than I to explain how the EEC deals with the low-slope and the breakpoint function. As for tweaking the MAF to get your idle leaner, that's one way to do it, however the other way is to get these injector slopes close...then massage the MAF curve into shape the rest of the way. I've also found the Fuel Table - MAF Backflow correction table useful for helping me get rid of rich low-loads as well...but I wouldn't start tinkering with that until you have things roughed in a little further. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue Jan 16, 2007 5:30 pm Regarding 'Injector Breakpoint' in the GUFB and GUF1 strategies I have not found anything to substantiate the statement that the minimum injector pw is hard coded at 2 mSecs. What I have determined is that the returned lookup value is multiplied by the rpm / 2 to determine the intersection point of the two injector slopes. If the desired fuel flow for a bank is less than or equal to this calculated value then only the 'Injector Low Slope' is used for the calculation of the injection pulsewidth otherwise both injector slopes are used. At no point is the 'Injector High Slope' used on it's own. The best use of the 'Injector Breakpoint' is to correct the AF ratio at idle when the Long Term Fuel Trims indicate adjustment is required by increasing the value to reduce fuel from the final calculated fuel pulsewidth. The breakpoint has a diminishing effect from idle up to approximately 1500 rpm. title: Fuel Pressure Regulator not holding pressure - EECTuning.org

posts.content: cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Fuel Pressure Regulator not holding pressure Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Feb 02, 2007 10:19 pm This not 100% on topic with tuning, but is related. If this thread needs to be moved somewhere else more appropriate, please do so. I recently bought an adjustable Fuel Pressure Regulator to boost the pressure on my injectors. I've boosted the pressure to about 43.5 PSI, however once the fuel pump shuts off, it takes about 1 second for the pressure to bleed off. It appears the FPR is simply flowing a small amount of fuel below the pressure setpt. I know the factory regulator didn't do that. It maintained pressure on the rails for hours after the engine had been turned off. Is this typical behavior of aftermarket adjustable FPRs or is this an indicator that I have a bad part? If that's normal, so-be-it. However a noticeable side-effect of this is that it takes running the starter a good second longer to allow pressure to build when I crank the truck. With the OEM regulator, the engine would crank in about 1-2 seconds turn of the key. Now it takes noticeably longer. Once pressure has built, the engine cranks and runs fine. My concern is that the FPR will flow too much fuel during peak fuel demands and allow the pressure to drop below the setpt causing a lean condition at a very bad time. If my 155lph pump hadn't gone out, I'd probably never notice this. But the stock Ranger 88lph is what's in the tank now (I was stranded and had to make do with what I had). Perhaps I should invest in another 155lph pump. Would that cure the problem? In the meantime, I've been tuning the key on to let the pump prime, then turning the key back off and back on again...then cranking. That helps, it's just cumbersome and a bit of a pain. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sat Feb 03, 2007 12:06 pm My fuel pressure also bleeds off rather quick. I looked into fixing it once but never did. At one point in time, I had a 155 lph pump installed. It did the same thing. I now have a 255lph high pressure pump installed and it does the same thing. I almost want to be that it is my pressure regulator. I have a BBK unit. As for the too much flow issue, it can be a problem if the engine is not consuming a lot. This means that you are circulating a lot of fuel. Everytime the fuel goes threw the pump it gets heated a little more. As time goes on you will see that the temperature of the fuel rises. Fuel boils at something like 95 degrees. Once this happens then you will experience vapor locks. I have yet to ever experience this but this is why Ford went to a returnless system. They only deliver the fuel that they need no more no less. Kenne Bell has a nice article on there web site about this topic. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Wed Jan 31, 2007 11:53 am Yes they are addresses, from the eec's rom. Editor-wise, I tend to favour TunerPro, there's a CDAN4 definfition file (XDF) available from the download section of the TunerPro site. There's not an incredible amount of items defined but you can at least add things as you go along. The two EGR items above aren't included in the xdf but it's a simple process to add them in. I need to caution you though, there are differences in the way some editors and CalEdit use bins resulting in offset address errors of 0x2000, once you know how the xdf is set up this can be adjusted and made to suit the Tweecer. posts.author: joesgt281
posts.content: joesgt281 Regular Posts: 148 Joined: Fri Dec 13, 2002 12:55 am Quote Post by joesgt281 » Sun Feb 04, 2007 10:15 pm Wow guys, this is REALLY embarassing..... Such a NEWB mistake..... Somewhere along the line I had switched over to Position 5 without realizing what the implication of that was. I'm sure everybody here knows it, but I'll restate it again, if for no other reason than so I'll never forget it again. Position 5 has your car running directly off of the EEC. If you haven't flashed your EEC, this is the original bin file (hmmm, wondered why my detonation was back :( ). The thing that compounded the misunderstanding is the fact that you can have your switch set to 5 and when you do a Read Tweecer, it actually reads Position 1. If you did a Read EEC, you'd see the original bin file. But reading Tweecer diverts you to Position 1. AND if you do a write Tweecer, it will take your changes and write it to Position 1. And if you want to verify what you had written, you can Read Tweecer and it will definetly be there.....you just won't get any affect from it because you just read Position 1 but you are running on Postion 5. That is unless you were to switch over to Position 1 So, long story short.....YES, changing the Ck Eng Lite Swiitch to zero WILL turn off your CEL. Thanks to everybody that tried to help. And special thanks to Mike Glover for finding out what I was doing wrong. 97 Cobraleen GT - SOLD 94 Saleen S-351, forged, Vortech 08 GT-500, auto swap 67 GT-500 Tribute, 427 stroked 351 79 Indy Pace Car, 331, Vortech, AODE Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Feb 02, 2007 10:39 pm CalEdit calling the GUFC strategy "A9M" in the very beginning was a mistake. Until CalEdit 1.30B3, GUFC has been represented by "A9M", even though you can't use that strategy on a real A9M EEC...you need to use the GUFB strategy (called A9L in CalEdit). Then to add further confusion, CalEdit 1.30B3 now has a separate strategy for A9L and A9M. They represent the same strategy...GUFB. But as you can see by flipping between A9L and A9M, there are things exposed on one and not the other. Why CalEdit has continued to NOT call these two strategies by their strategy names instead of by the popular processor catch code that uses it is beyond me. You don't see the CBAZA strategy called T4M0 in CalEdit. It's called CBAZA since that's the name of the strategy. (For those that don't know, T4M0 is an EEC follows the CBAZA strategy.) But then again, there are a lot of things that baffle me about CalEdit. I guess Mike (the developer of CalEdit) didn't figure this tuning business was complicated enough, so he took it upon himself to inject confusion and really screw with the newbies. If that's not what it is, then he's simply a pathetic tester of his own code. posts.author: staticstang
posts.content: staticstang Gear Head Posts: 18 Joined: Tue Apr 08, 2003 4:57 pm Location: Northern Indiana Quote Post by staticstang » Tue Feb 06, 2007 11:07 am Directly from the "getting started.pdf" Hope this helps. Which Firmware do I have? The Setting Bank Mode section is only valid for units with the 00E firmware, which supports 2 or 4 banks. You can check your board revision by performing a read or write of the TwEECer or a read of the EEC. Every time one of these operations is performed the board rev is displayed at the bottom of the CalEdit screen. The last 3 characters are the firmware and if they are not 00E then your board ONLY supports Four 2 bank programs. You may send your board in for a free firmware update and you only pay shipping both ways. STKR - firmware upgrade 6311 Holly Canyon Court Katy, TX 77450 Include your return shipping payment or a return airbill, etc and contact info. Do I have a Base or RT? The 5th Character in the board revision denotes Base or RT with a B or R respectively. The first 2 characters are hardware revision and the next two denote the build number. Setting Bank Configuration Driver must be installed first -- For 99.99% of the applications the Four 2 Bank Program mode will be the choice needed and the TwEECer is shipped this way by default, requiring no action by the user. Your TwEECer must have the 00E firmware to have this feature; otherwise CalEdit will report this feature unavailable. If you have a 98 or newer EECV based vehicle and need access to parameters in the two highest banks, then you will need to select the Two 4 Bank Programs. Go to the utilities tab in CalEdit, at the bottom of the page you will see the “Configure Banks” button with two (2) radio buttons. *The position of this radio button does NOT indicate the current setting, but CalEdit remembers the state of the button when the application was last exited. This procedure is best performed with the TwEECer out of the vehicle and NOT connected to the EEC. The EEC can store a voltage and keep the TwEECer from completely discharging power and not completing the process. Select the radio button for your case, with the TwEECer connected to the laptop but without the switch connected, and click the Config Banks button. Disconnect the TwEECer from the USB cable and then click OK. Your bank mode is now set. You can perform this operation as many times as you want, switching from 2 to 4 bank support and back, though most will not ever use this option and those that do only need to do it once. If the TwEECer is installed in the vehicle, you will need to disconnect the battery and discharge it by pressing the brake pedal several times. All power must be removed for this operation to complete successfully. When using the Two 4 Bank Program configuration, switch positions 1 & 3 are duplicate and 2 & 4 are duplicate. Your two available calibration switch positions are 1 and 2. 1993 SSP Notch DSS 306, TW heads, X303, RPM Intake, Quick Time 70mm Turbo Kit, A9L, etc. Top

posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Wed Jan 31, 2007 5:07 am The 'Part Throttle Breakpoint' value is checked against the relative throttle value (actual throttle position A-D counts minus closed throttle position A-D counts) in the same way the WOT breakpoint is used. posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Wed Jan 31, 2007 10:50 am sailorbob wrote: The 'Part Throttle Breakpoint' value is checked against the relative throttle value (actual throttle position A-D counts minus closed throttle position A-D counts) in the same way the WOT breakpoint is used. This means that the actual closed position value isn't too critical for the part and wide open breakpoints to still work. Thanks for posting this. I sometimes find it difficult to get folks to understand the "relative" way the TPS function works. I have explained to people on other sites a dozen times in the past year that it matters not where you set the TPS, so long as it doesn't go outside of the relatively huge window that Ford gave it (0.5 - 1.25V). Wherever the TPS hits the stop - that is "0". 0.04 volts (8 A/D counts) above that is "part throttle". WOT is whatever number of volts above "0" that you set it at. If you adjust the TPS down while the car running, the ECU will use this new value as "0" and the ISC will try to adjust to the new setting. If you adjust the TPS up (more than 0.04V) while the car is running, the car will think it's at part throttle from that point onward and will run strangely until the key is recycled off - on. Too many people adjust the thing and don't realize that the difference in operation they see is due to the ISC function trying to adapt to the new idle airflow since most folks aren't real careful about setting the throttle stop per procedure and don't have a tuning device. Anyway, "8" is the right number of A/D counts for PT. 428w now Top

posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Thu Feb 01, 2007 12:15 pm codedout wrote: Ok now this posed another question. Is this value supposed ot be AD counts or Volts? Is Caledit correct or TunerPro? You won't like this answer - it's personal preference. :D The ECU uses A/D counts because that's what it understands. The value as stored in the binary is A/D counts*64. If you divide the stored number by 64, you get the A/D counts - which is typically 8. If you divide the counts again by 200, you get volts. 8/200 = 0.04 volts. This is because the A/D conversion is 200 counts/volt. If you "Edit Item XDF Info" (F2) for the TPS Breakpoint Voltage for Part Throttle (Part Throttle Threshold) in TunerPro and go to the "conversion" tab, you will see that the conversion is X/12800. This is actually X/64*200. Caledit for some reason used a conversion of X/64 to convert to counts in this particular definition (dat file) - in other DAT files he converts to volts. It's all a matter of preference - the definition files (xdf for TunerPro, dat for CalEdit) convert the info in the bin into real-world understandable numbers. In TunerPro you are allowed to change the conversion to whatever you like, CalEdit does not let the user change these (good for most, bad when they are inaccurate or you want to add a new parameter). Sorry the answer was long, I hope this helps. 428w now Top

As long as it is getting power it will read and write, but if a couple of key circuit board fingers are not touching then the EEC may not be getting the right data to and from the PCM. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Mon Feb 12, 2007 5:14 am WOT_Multiplier (aka FN310) is a WOT fuel multiplier based upon time in WOT mode (using the WOT_Timer (aka WOTTMR) to determine this). FN310 is only used between the rpm range defined by WOT_Multiplier_Min_RPM (aka WOTRPL) and WOT_Multiplier_Max_RPM (aka WOTRPH). Top

posts.author: Mudog715
posts.content: Mudog715 Regular Posts: 63 Joined: Sun Oct 08, 2006 2:48 am Quote Post by Mudog715 » Mon Feb 12, 2007 5:33 am So if the timer for FN310 hasn't expired, this is multiplied against commanded fuel (FN1360) along with FN303, FN301, FN300, FN325 & FN396A ? If so then the name "WOT fuel mult for WOT enleanment" is misleading because the way it is currently calibrated the multiplier is 1.0 until 44 seconds at wot passes, then the multiplier becomes 0.96875 essentially richenening things more after the 44 second delay. I guess this is to keep engine temps down and prevent detonation? -Mudog 1967 Kaiser-Jeep M-715 '5-Quarter' Army truck 521 stroker, 9.5:1, ported F3 heads 2.19/1.76, 278/284 Hyd Roller Cam, Banks headers, 2x62mm TB, 90LMAF, 60#Dekas EEC-V (FOU1-CNAB1) mass-air/SFI/OBD2, integral EDIS w/ custom CKP & CID sensors, twEECer RT E4OD heavily modified, 2200rpm stall triple lock billet Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Mon Feb 12, 2007 7:54 am Mudog715 wrote: So if the timer for FN310 hasn't expired, this is multiplied against commanded fuel (FN1360) along with FN303, FN301, FN300, FN325 & FN396A ? I'm not sure if the WOT_Timer does expire, I'd expect it to reach a maximum value and stay there until you droppped out of WOT mode long enough to reset the timer (there would probably be a delay to allow for momentary changes in throttle position during gear shifts). FN310 is multiplied against the result of the WOT_Multiplier_vs_RPM (aka FN303) lookup. Mudog715 wrote: If so then the name "WOT fuel mult for WOT enleanment" is misleading because the way it is currently calibrated the multiplier is 1.0 until 44 seconds at wot passes, then the multiplier becomes 0.96875 essentially richenening things more after the 44 second delay. I guess this is to keep engine temps down and prevent detonation? Fuel multipliers less than 1.000 typically richen the AF ratio and, so yes, it would appear it is it is titled a bit misleadingly but to know for sure you would need to look at the code. Top

But even the 42#'s could see duty cycles of 85%-90% at high RPM's meaning the injectors could be staying on most of the 720 degrees of crank rotation. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Feb 11, 2007 9:54 pm :) My point was only that with that many cubes, making 450HP will be easy. With a 1/2 way decent set of aluminum heads (and TFs are plenty decent) & an aftermarket intake, a 0 degree overlap cam would give much better drivability & fuel economy as well as a MUCH better chance passing emissions without worrying about injector fire timing. As long as the engine is not supercharged, you could safely run the 30s, but if the 42s are already purchased, you could get away with them as well. But I doubt they'd see more than a 60% duty cycle with 400hp. If the stick hasn't been purchased yet, check out the Crane Cam Grind 2020 (pn 444211). This is a roller cam for 302 HO or 351s (I'm assuming when you say 410w, that's a 351w bored and stroked). This stick has got lots of lift, it's emissions complaint, and it has superior low-RPM performance for a cam as big as it is that's. Because it has such high lift, it's also a solid pull well above 5500RPMs on a 302. With a 410, I'd expect it to begin rolling off just above 5000RPMs. If you want something that's going to roll to 6000RPMs, I can recommend you to a guy that makes custom grind cams. The name of his company is LAZER cams. Unless you are doing some serious racing with this motor, I'd highly encourage you to keep with a hydraulic roller setup if at all possible. An engine that big is going to be difficult to keep together above 6000RPMs, so without a forged crank and some serious balancing, I wouldn't count on RPMs in the 7000s. But if you are sinking that kind of money into it, then you will need some overlap in your cam to maintain pull into those RPMs, but the sacrifice will be in the lower RPMs. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Feb 11, 2007 1:04 pm It doesn't matter how tuned up the car is, without CATs, you are failing the sniff tests. Older OBD-I and prior CATs work by capturing as much O2 from the exhaust that didn't get burnt and using it to break down the NOx (Nitrogen Oxides caused during high-temp lean conditions), and HC/CO (Hydro-Carbon/Carbon Monoxide caused during rich conditions). During lean conditions, there's an abundance of Oxygen it can capture and use during the rich conditions. The newer OBD-II compliant CATs have a greater O2 capturing capacity so the smog pumps aren't needed. So putting an OBD-II compliant CAT on OBD-I vehicle goes even further to help guarantee that the sniff test isn't going to give you a problem, especially with a tune that cleans things up. But without CATs, even a 14.7:1 (perfect) burn, there are still CO and HC emissions. In a perfect world, there wouldn't be, but this isn't a perfect world. As the burn gets towards the end, the chances of having an O2 molecule next to a gasoline molecule gets less and less so the burn gets imperfect even with a perfect stoich mix of air & fuel going into the chambers. So again, my point is you will NEED CATs to have a chance of passing the sniff test even if they don't notice the missing CATs on the visual inspection. Maybe someone else has a different experience, but its my understanding that to pass any state's sniff tests (even really lenient tests), you HAVE to have CATs. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Feb 12, 2007 4:56 pm If you find that there's one particular RPM/Load range that's not running as you'd like, adjust the values back towards factory for those RPM/Loads. Those injector timing numbers aren't rocket science numbers so you can play around with them to get a drive that you like. In fact, the only time they are critical is if you run a cam with overlap. You want the injectors firing only after the exhaust valve has closed so the early part of your injector fire isn't wasted out the tailpipe. Otherwise, set the values to what runs best with your setup. As a point of reference, look at the injector timing of an A9L, then look at how dramatically different an X3Z is (all values are 300).
