posts.author: Mudog715
posts.content: Mudog715 Regular Posts: 63 Joined: Sun Oct 08, 2006 2:48 am Quote Post by Mudog715 » Mon Feb 12, 2007 8:10 pm I am trying to tune my Injector Timing also. I have a cam with a moderate amount of overlap and have some theories on how it interacts with the injector timing and A/F ratio. By definition there will be a point in the intake-exhaust valve open overlap period where air in the intake is drawn straight through the combustion chamber (CC) and out the exhaust. My guess is this happens just after TDC on the exhaust stroke while there is still velocity present in the exiting exhaust gasses creating a slight vacuum in the CC. This vacuum is sucking intake straight through and out the exhaust. Soon thereafter the piston begins traveling downward on the intake stroke and once enough vacuum is created by this action to overcome the vacuum on the (open) exhaust port the intake air stops flowing out the exhaust and is drawn into the CC instead. Some reversion of the exhaust gasses (mostly air now) will also occur, drawing some of that air back into the CC. A llittle later the exhaust valve closes (at 382 in my case) and only intake air can enter the CC, On mass air vehicles ALL the air entering the engine is metered, even the "bypass air" that passes straight through during this overlap period. Right off the bat that would cause the A/F mix to be a little rich. If the injectors are fired AFTER the "bypass" period then no fuel will be wasted but the extra air in the exhaust will not be complimented by extra fuel to burn. The extra air in the exhaust will be misinterpreted as a leaner A/F than what the actual A/F is. The EEC will richen to compensate (in closed loop) and combined with the fact that there was metered air that didn't actually stay in the CC will push things even richer. Now if the injectors fire during this air bypass period so that some of the fuel passes out the exhaust with the extra air, this mixture should burn once it hits the the rest of the hot exhaust gases (just what AIR injection attempts to do) and since (theoretically) the extra air AND fuel are consumed there is no excess oxygent left to confuse the O2 sensor, cause a false-lean EGO reading and drive the mix rich. The problem with this is that fuel is going to be wasted in the process. Now the question is what is the best solution to the problem? Inject early and waste a small amount of fuel but keep the EGO accurate or inject after the overlap and compensate for the extra air in the exhaust causing the EGO to read a leaner A/F than what it actually is? Is this perhaps one of the purposes of HEGO bias? -Mudog 1967 Kaiser-Jeep M-715 '5-Quarter' Army truck 521 stroker, 9.5:1, ported F3 heads 2.19/1.76, 278/284 Hyd Roller Cam, Banks headers, 2x62mm TB, 90LMAF, 60#Dekas EEC-V (FOU1-CNAB1) mass-air/SFI/OBD2, integral EDIS w/ custom CKP & CID sensors, twEECer RT E4OD heavily modified, 2200rpm stall triple lock billet Top

The EEC then calculates a required fuel to go along with that measured air. When the exhaust port is open during overlap the mixture can escape out the exhaust. Again this is a mixture, meaning both fuel and air exit the exhaust not just air. The catch is that the fuel is not burnt therefore the O2s can not read it. The HEGO only read gass not liquid. It has to be in gas form not liquid form for the readings. The only difference is the amount of liquid fuel which is undetectable by the O2s anyways. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Feb 15, 2007 2:25 pm With a TwEECer RT, I'd log the following: 1. OL/CL indicator 2. HEGOs (both) 3. KAMRFs (both) 4. LAMBSEs (both) 5. MAFv 6. Injector PW (both) 7. Timing 8. Load (not LoadX) The main thing I'd look for is if the CL is going OL right as it starts misbehaving. Also notice what your KAMRFs are at and the LAMBSEs. If the KAMRFs have bottomed/topped out, then the EEC is forcing OL because it has hit the endpoints of both LAMBSEs and KAMRFs and assumes there's a problem it isn't going to fix so it gives up and starts running off limp-mode tables. If that's happening, you'll notice the EEC go OL and all KAMRF RPM/Load positions will read 1.000 regardless of what they were before. Turning the key on and off will reset things until the EEC forced OL again. I had this happen to me when my ground issue was causing low HEGO voltages and thus the EEC was running the engine VERY rich because it could never enrich the mix enough to see a HEGO switch above .48v. This may be way off base from what your problem is, but these are the things I'd want to see in a datalog. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Mon Feb 05, 2007 6:26 am The CBAZA strategy doesn't have 'on' and 'off' rev limits like the GUF* strategies. There are four rev limits that are for half fuel and no fuel depending on whether the vehicle is in drive or neutral. These are (in the order there are in the eec's rom in); Rev_Limit_Stage_3_Drive (aka NLMTHI) Rev_Limit_Stage_2_Drive (aka NLMTLO) Rev_Limit_Stage_3_Neutral (aka NLMTNEUHI) Rev_Limit_Stage_2_Neutral (aka NLMTNEULO) The cancellation of any rev limiting action is determined with a Rev_Limit_Hysteresis (aka PIPLIMHYT) value that has it's units in clock ticks. Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue Feb 13, 2007 8:22 am Adam, for the GUF* ecu's use the following; sailorbob wrote: Rev Limit Half Fuel On (aka NLM_SH) - Always set higher then the 'Rev Limit Half Fuel Off'. Instigates every other injector not to fire. Fuel delivery remains cut in half until the engine speed drops below the 'Rev Limit Half Fuel Off'. Rev Limit Half Fuel Off (aka NLM_CL) - Always set lower then the 'Rev Limit Half Fuel On'. Fuel delivery remains cut in half until the engine speed drops below this limit. Rev Limit No Fuel (aka NLMT) - Very harsh limiter, cuts all fuel delivery, always set higher than 'Rev Limit Half Fuel On'. Rev Limit No Fuel Hysteresis (aka NLMTH) - Hysteresis rpm for 'Rev Limit No Fuel'. Please ignore what I wrote above, following some more digging I've concluded; Rev Limit Set RPM (aka NLM_SH) - Always set higher then the 'Rev Limit Clear RPM'. Fuel delivery remains cut until the engine speed drops below the 'Rev Limit Clear RPM'. Rev Limit Clear RPM (aka NLM_CL) - Always set lower then the 'Rev Limit Set RPM'. Fuel delivery remains cut until the engine speed drops below this limit. Rev Limit No Fuel (aka NLMT) - Very harsh limiter, cuts all fuel delivery, always set higher than 'Rev Limit Half Fuel On'. Does not appear to be used in GUF* ecu's. Rev Limit No Fuel Hysteresis (aka NLMTH) - Hysteresis rpm for 'Rev Limit No Fuel'. Does not appear to be used in GUF* ecu's. EDIT: Changed because I previously made assumptions based upon the calibration data rather than walking through the code to see how the limits were used. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sun Feb 25, 2007 4:01 am The 'Do Adaptive Learning Vector' parameter is there to allow you to disable the adaptive learning whilst making your changes. Make sure you have the 'Item 'Comments' window open (press F10) to see the values you need to enter. If you fancy being experimental you could try adding a new xdf item; Title - Force Full Time OL Description - Normally this is set to 0xD7, change to 0x20 to prevent the ecu going into closed loop mode. Units - n/a Address (hex) - 4274 Size - 8 bit Visibility level - Always Output type - Hex Digits Significant digits - 1 Category A - Miscellaneous Category B - Any category All other boxes are left blank and leave the conversion and ALDL assoc items alone. This changes a conditional jump into a non conditional jump and *should* result in closed loop mode no longer being attainable. EDIT: Changed last sentence to avoid any ambiguities over what is being changed. Last edited by sailorbob on Sun Feb 25, 2007 9:42 am, edited 1 time in total. Top

While I don't know if this is the solution, maybe the 'transmission time before in drive' function needs tweaking. This function is to compensate for the delay from when you move the gear select lever (the PRNDL switch changes state) to when the trans load changes (goes into drive). In the EEC this defines the delay before the change from the neutral airflow to the drive airflow functions. If the 'trans time before in drive' function is too low (changes to the drive air too soon - before the trans load changes (aka - goes in gear)) then PERHAPS this is causing your troubles. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Feb 25, 2007 2:21 pm The most important question is "Is this causing drivability problems when you see the WB go high?" As mentioned above, what are the HEGOs and LAMBSEs doing when the WB says things are lean? The engine will run like crap, sputter, hesitate, and surge if the mix gets much over about 15.3:1. If your WB is saying you are above that and the engine is still running fine, my bet is the WB is telling lies and the Narrow-Bands are controlling like they are supposed to. Short of locating the WB after the CATs, I have no clue what could cause this. In the event the engine really is running bad like it is running lean, then that would tend to indicate the narrow-band HEGOs are running too high of a voltage. Generally when HEGOs go bad, they loose voltage (indicate lean), which runs the engine rich trying to compensate. In this case, it seems as though the HEGOs are reporting too high of a voltage running the engine too lean upon Closed Loop operation. You can try to decrease the HEGO Amplitude to see if that will drop the EEC's interpretation of the voltage. You can also decrease the HEGO Bias to the negative. Set all the cells to whatever your top line is. After doing this, see what your WB is telling you. I don't think this will be your fix, but it might be a good diagnostic to determine what the problem is. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Feb 27, 2007 9:56 am I agree, voltages higher than 1v from the HEGOs would certainly force lean running. My guess is that your datalog is accurate in that you are datalogging what the EEC is seeing as well which perfectly explains why the EEC is leaning things out. Make sure you didn't do something like put the HEGO heater return line as the the sensor line into the EEC. 12v going through a heater coil would probably result in a voltage around 3-4v at the EEC. Just to be thorough, check your grounds as was already mentioned. Make sure to verify the heavy gauge pigtail from the battery negative terminal to the body is secured without corrosion. On my truck, when that broke off, that caused my HEGO voltages to always be low. In fact, loads like the headlights and blower motor directly affected the HEGO voltages read by the EEC. I had a hell of a time tracking that one down. Since then, the HEGOs haven't had any trouble switching and accurately indicate lean conditions as I've found from my lean tip-in issues (different thread). Since then, Ford has gone to the 4-wire HEGOs which don't use the chassis ground for O2 sensor return, but rather give a direct return value to the EEC. I guess this was a common problem Ford struggled with. Point is, bad grounds are easy to look over and have a bigger affect on things than you'd think. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

Instead, I'd recommend you start using BinEditor to tweak your tunes. And doing data analysis using EEC Analyzer (both are written by the same guy). BinEditor is a free download. However EEC Analyzer is licensed. It's around $55, and well worth the money. If you are just beginning your venture into tuning, you NEED this software. If you are a seasoned tuner, then you may have similar tools or simply know what you are looking for and how to fix it without it. In either case, with EA (or Excel for that matter), you can input your 9pt MAF curve, see it visually in the graph. Then make your own 30pt (or however many point) curve to follow/track the 9pt exactly how you think it should be. With only 9pts, there's lots of "flat" places that hardly look like a curve. There's always going to be error in the MAF curve. But you have the greatest potential for error if your actual flow happens to be somewhere dead between two datapoints. The further away the closest datapoints are, the greater the chance for error. So having 30pts as opposed to only 9, puts each datapoint closer together, which decreases the chance for error. As well, you have much better resolution to tune the MAF curve with more datapoints. A lot of this, you are probably already aware of or you'd be fat-fingering in the 9pts and not even asking. As for how you should distribute your 30 points out, there's two different thoughts here. 1. Equally distribute. If you have 9 points ranging from 0-5v, then you have 8 regions. If you make 9 of your 30pts the same 9 as the original curve (not a bad idea), then that leaves a good 21 pts to spread over 8 regions. So put 2-3 additional datapoints between the 9pts defined in the original curve to evenly distribute out the values. This is the method most of the 9-to-30pt MAF calculators use...however I'm not sure they actually preserve the original 9 as part of the new curve or not. 2. Put a stronger concentration of points towards the area of your curve you plan to use most often. If this is a daily driven vehicle, then your engine runs at partial throttle more than WOT...so concentrate more points in the area from 0-3v. Anything above 3v is going to be a harder acceleration and you are likely to be in OL by then anyway. As long as the curve is "close", your OL tables will have you deep in the rich so even if things aren't dead-on, you'll still be safe. If you have a WideBand O2, you can tune in this section of the curve to be closer so you aren't needlessly overrich or running too lean...otherwise, most of your time will be spent at the lower parts of the curve to get drivability. In addition, if you find that at WOT, your engine never gets the MAV voltage above say 4.2v, there's no reason in consuming more than 3 of your 30 datapoints above that. In that case, you'd put your last data point around 4.4v or 4.5v (just to cover yourself) then the next point at 5v. And for traditions sake, you could put the very last point at 16v and make it the same value as what you have at 5v. This 16v entry is just in case there's some blip that runs the "detected" voltage above 5v, the computer doesn't freak out and not have a value to calculate. Personally, I haven't found it that necessary to jump right into the 2nd MAF curve-making strategy mainly since EA already has a MAF curve for my MAF. The EEC is quite resilient and is designed to respond to error. So I think the 2nd strategy is a little overkill for my setup. I'm still running stock equipment. However perhaps this is a better way to go to get better drivability if you are running some super-built motor that has 42lb or larger injectors and a huge-mouth MAF that measures 3000kg/hr of air. I'll have to yield to others that actually have that setup and see what they think. Either method you use, don't be terribly concerned if you are getting the curve exactly right. As long as it is a close resemblance of the 9pt with some added "curve" in between the 9pts that is a smooth transition from beginning to end, the engine should run well enough you can get some datalogs to start fine-tuning it based on closed loop feedback OR Wideband feedback if you have one. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Thu Feb 22, 2007 8:53 am I battled this problem a lot, and I posted something way back, cant seem to find the thread right now. So I will try and remember as much as possible. If you have a bigger cam than stock, especially if it close to having overlap or has overlap, then at a low idle what happens is that you have a surge in your vacuum, this in turn will cause the fuel pressure to surge (I really dont like the vacuum port on the regulator). Thus causing the engine to surge, the EEc tries to compensate with IAC but fails, and drops back to timing control. And the cycle startes all over again. When the car starts to lope, the vacuum starts to drop thus increasing fuel pressure hence goes rich. The IAC adds air to correct the mixture but this increases the rpm. It then cuts the air to get back to where it is commanded to be, starts to lope again vacuum drops again, and it becomes a vicous cycle. My solution was to bring up the idle to a point where I wasnt getting the surge in vacuum. Then I dialed everything in MAF, TB airflow, injectors. Once I had it dialed in then I dropped my idle at 25 RPM increments till I got the lowest idle without any vacuum surging. With the E303 cam I have a rock solid idle at 725 RPM, which may be a little high for an auto tranny. I have dropped it to 700 but on cold mornings I get a surge for abouut 60 secs so I bumped it back up. It was during this phase that I decided to go to this place http://www.glowshiftdirect.com/index.as ... ProdID=287 I picked up a vacuum gauge and a fuel pressure gauge, both gauges and shipping were less than $100. It really helped in getting it dialed in. You can also visibly see the vacuum and fuel pressure follow your surging. I remember back in the old carb days we used to dial it in using vacuum. So I went back to the basics. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Feb 23, 2007 8:01 am Well, I narrowed down what caused the hunting idle...FKARCH (Air Charge Manifold Filling Model Slow Filter Constant). The A9L has dramatically different numbers than the X3Z and I was experimenting with using the A9L numbers instead. The A9L has 13107, but X3Z has 64881. I tried it at 30000 and 55000. Both slowed down the idle surge but to get rid of it, I had to return all the way to X3Z default. So point being, for others that want to calm a hunting idle, try increasing this number and see if this will allow you to run a lower RPM. It might not work, but it's worth a try...assuming you run a GUF* EEC. posts.author: samseed101
posts.content: samseed101 Regular Posts: 98 Joined: Tue Feb 13, 2007 9:41 pm Car won't start at all now. With or without tweecer Quote Post by samseed101 » Thu Mar 01, 2007 9:09 am I have a 1995 GT auto. After installing the Tweecer, my car wont start. Here’s what happened: I removed the EEC and installed the tweecer (with the battery disconnected of course.) After that I reconnected the wire harnesses and did a "read" from the tweecer to get my stock settings. After that I reconnected the battery and tried to start the car. All it did was crank and crank until the battery started to choke out. Didn't fire up. So I disconnected the tweecer and tried again with nothing but the stock EEC..same deal. I double checked all the wire harnesses and noticed that I screwed up (not sure how badly yet.) Near the bottom of the wire harnesses and closest to the firewall (compared to the other bolts) there was a green bolt that held a red and black wire under it. It bolted directly to the side of the car. I can only assume it was some sort of ground wires. Well I somehow screwed up and managed to forget to put that back on. I screwed it back down and tried several more times but no luck. The tweecer could read the EEC, but the car would just crank both with and without the tweecer installed. So now I have no idea what the problem is. I checked the fuses (in the engine bay and under the dash) just for the hell of it and everything seemed fine. When I turn the key to the on position, I hear the fuel pump kick in. I don't know what the problem is but I'm starting to think I fried the computer by screwing up and forgetting that one screw / bolt. I can't think of anything else that could be causing the problem. I am correct in thinking that the green bold near the three wire harnesses was the ground correct? And by being a dumbass and leaving it off, there's a good chance I fried it? Any ideas what I can do to fix this? If it is the computer, where can I get a replacement besides a junkyard? Thanks for any help. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Mar 01, 2007 10:15 am I seriously doubt leaving a ground bolt off would cause this. There are multiple-redundant grounds for the EEC so that any sensor at any location can get a solid ground reading back to the EEC. Leaving that bolt off at worse would've only thrown the reading the EEC receives from sensors, but shouldn't have had anything to do with frying it. Generally EECs are fried by pulling the TwEECer off the J3 port or wiggling it while it is on the port with the ignition ON . You did right by disconnecting everything during any manipulation of the TwEECer. However if you didn't re-secure everything back up before trying to crank the motor, any little disruption that would've bumped the TwEECer or caused it to move while the ignition was on would explain why your EEC isn't acting right now. The discouraging part is you say you can read from the EEC, but it just won't crank. That indicates memory is working and powered. And by all rights, the processor should be too. Make sure there is no metallic debris on the edge-connectors both in your TwEECer and on the board. If there is, that "could" potentially halt the processor. But first, lets get back to the fuel pump turning on. Is the fuel pump turning on, then going off after 1 second or is it staying stuck ON and never shutting off until you turn the key? Staying ON is typical behavior when the TwEECer first gets connected and hasn't been downloaded with the right tune yet. However once you've downloaded all your BIN positions with what's currently uploading from the EEC, all should work and the fuel pump should act like it does without the TwEECer connected, with only a 1 second ON time when the key is turned. Without the TwEECer if the fuel pump is staying ON, that would lead me to believe the processor isn't running. The only other suggestion I can think of is to make sure you got the wiring harness bolted to the EEC right. Make sure as you turn the bolt, the harness is being drawn into the EEC. With the harness disconnected, visually notice how long the pins are on the EEC. That's about how far you should see the bolt drawing the harness to the EEC before it gets tight. Just for something to try...unplug the EEC from the harness and let it sit a good 10 minutes. Then try connecting it back to the harness without the TwEECer and see if this "revives" it. If not, you may have fried the EEC, but based on how you described things above, I'm not sure how. But I'm not willing to blame your failure to bolt the ground screw to the body either. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: samseed101
posts.content: samseed101 Regular Posts: 98 Joined: Tue Feb 13, 2007 9:41 pm Quote Post by samseed101 » Thu Mar 01, 2007 8:07 pm Well I'm not really sure what happened... but here's the rundown of the night. On the way home I grabbed some more autolite 24s figuring that my plugs maybe fouled. I figured worse case scenario, I'd have some extra spark plugs for the future. As soon as I got there, I spalled on my code reader I bought earlier at auto zone and all I got was an EGR code, which was expected because the EGR is sitting in a box in the garage. I then pulled a random spark plug to see if it was founed (#6 plug) It looked fine although there was a strong fuel smell. I then had my sister crank it while I grounded the plug to get a spark. It had a spark too so I put it back in. Then for the hell of it, I tried to start it using the Clear Flood method (WOT while cranking to keep teh injectors from spraying.) and the son of a bitch fired right up. I turned it off and on a few times and it fired up with no problems. So I disconnected the battery, put the twecer back on, reconnected the battery and tried again and she fired right up. I switched to position 2 on the tweecer and after about 1 second, my idle increased about 200 RPM. (which is what I set position 2 for.) As I left the engine running I could switch back and forth from the positions and second later, you coudl ehar the change in the engine. So in the end, I still ahve no clue wtf was wrong. if I had to guess, I would say that I must have flooded the engine and fouled the plugs with fuel (not sure how.) Overnight they must have dried off enough to get a spark, and the Clear Flood / Flood start took care of the rest. Finally the tweecer is on and working as good as expected. Now I can finally move forward with this and get a good tune going. Thank you everyone for your help and suggestions! As always everyone has been a great help. I guess I'll keep the mustang for another day... Until i get pissed off at my tune and decide to torch it Top

Perhaps it is cheaper for Ford to write one program with selectable sub-routines that covered many vehicles and years rather than trying to write a separate program for each one. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 05, 2007 1:10 pm I doubt there's supposed to be 8 degrees difference in advance between 87 and 89 octane. It sounds more like bad or old gas causing the premature pinging the 1st time. I'm not sure I'd expect quite 8 degrees between 87 and 93. Back when gas was $1.30/gallon, it was tough to talk yourself into premium. But with gas prices the way they are now, it's cheaper to get 93 vs 89 or 87 especially if you can get better fuel economy using it (and with a tuner, you should be able to do that). With a TwEECer RT, as your sig now indicates you have, I'd say forget the global timing. Use the timing tables and the WOT timing function to dial in your timing. The global is nice for rough adjustments and when you are a dyno tuner getting paid by the minute, it helps to have shortcuts. But as a do-it-yourselfer who has plenty of time to do it right, I'd say do it right and keep global timing at 0. So with it set to 0 and the distributor at -10 base, where do you start? Start with the WOT timing vs RPM function. Run the car a few times and keep increasing these numbers until you aren't getting any ping or aren't getting any additional pull/torque (whichever comes 1st). Once you got the WOT table advanced to the limit you like, set the sealevel spark table's top row to those same numbers less maybe a degree or two (this table is used during CL operation so you will most likely need a slightly lower timing value since you don't have the additional enrichment to help). If you set your TPS scalars for WOT/OL low enough, you'll never actually hit the top row of your timing table in CL, but for completeness, you need to put something in there. As you work down the table in load, you can tune out any mid-throttle ping you might get. With the global timing set to 0 and the spark table set with all stock values except for the top row, you shouldn't have any ping. But if during experimenting you develop some, notice at what RPM and Load (not LoadX) you are at while pinging and adjust that RPM/Load location in your timing table down about 2 degrees. Since you were getting pinging at what you are calling light-WOT, I'd say there's a good chance you were still in Closed Loop. You'll want to datalog your closed loop status, RPMs, TPS, as well as your timing (amongst a dozen other things) so you know exactly what the motor was doing during the pinging condition and you know where to try responding in the tune. That should keep you busy for a while. :) The good news is once you get it all right on the bleeding edge of ping, it all changes on the next fillup of gas. The numbers could either go up or down depending on what's in there now and what you get next time. My recommendation is once you find the bleeding edge of ping for every RPM/Load location, back off by 2° so you sacrifice minimal torque (if any) and don't get annoyed by quality differences in each fillup causing ping. Keep in mind, Max torque (aka MBT) and Ping do not always happen at the same advance value. Often, you hit MBT before the engine starts pinging so don't be afraid to back off a degree or two to save yourself the ping headache. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Mon Mar 05, 2007 2:32 pm I'm not sure if I understand your question correctly. So, let me add my .02. While I'm not too familiar with the 95s, I can tell you that 10* base + 8* global does NOT equal 18* of total timing. Total timing also varies with load. WOT timing for example is usually around 26* with the 5.0 cars. That is with base timing of 10* PLUS what the computer adds to it. Now if you go add 8* global your total timing is around 34* WOT. Part throttle timing will be around 40* for cruising with a light load. Thats with a 10* base plus what the computer adds. Once again, you go adding 8* global you have around 48* during part throttle/light load. These are the 2 conditions where you will see the most (part throttle) and least (full throttle) timing. I would stay away from using the global scalar, this is the equivalent of turning the distributor. So a global advance of 8* equals setting the distributor at 18* base and 0* global adder. I used general figures to illustrate my point, based off the A9* strategy. The 95 I'm sure is slightly different, but should be close (as far as total advance is concerned). You have 3 different tables that serve as the timing lookup tables for your eec. YOu need to figure out how your strategy uses them. Then make your changes in those tables at the specific rpm and load range you want to change the factory calibration. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 05, 2007 4:34 pm Naturally aspirated, you aren't going to tear up the engine unless you ignore some really bad indicators that the engine is not doing what it is supposed to. Supercharged motors are more temperamental and are notorious for tearing themselves up on their maiden voyage due to bad tunes (usually with fuel being too lean). So to answer if 18° base timing is too much, I say hell yes. But not because it'll tear something up, but because it just makes things too damn confusing and doesn't take into account any additional advance calculated by the EEC. You also have to forgive us since we don't talk about base timing here since we set the distributor to 10°BTDC, and leave the global at 0°. When we talk with others, we assume a 10°BTDC base timing on the distributor and let the various timing tables & functions which are far more granular and configurable sort out the details. Thus, when you talk to us about timing, we talk in terms of total timing as is datalogged or measured. Since the EEC assumes you have the distributor at 10°, any numbers you type into the timing tables will be in total timing not "additional" timing above the base 10°. So when you tune your tables, forget about what the base timing is and type in the timing you want at that RPM/Load. Does that make sense? Believe me, I know where you are at. When I 1st came on board with the TwEECer, the 1st thing I wanted to do is start messing with that global timing setting just to save myself the hassle of breaking out the timing light to get that little extra. But after talking to the others on the board, they convinced me that this isn't the way to do things. The power at your fingertips is wasted trying to mess with such a global value. After many months of learning from these guys, I am here to tell you...they were right. So now I'm spouting to you what was spouted to me many moons ago. BTW, you have to use underscores to get things aligned into tables since spaces are "absorbed" by the forum code for whatever dumb reason. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Mar 06, 2007 8:04 am samseed101 wrote: ...So if I get a larger (say 80mm) MAF calibrated to 19# injectors and use the FMU to spike the pressure, will that perhaps help keping the MAF from getting pegged?... You must've been posting your 2nd comment when I was typing mine. I didn't see it until this morning. However to answer this, you'll be wasting your time. You will increase the capacity of the MAF slightly. But what's holding you back is the MAF being calibrated to 19#. With a tuner, forget about MAF-to-injector tuning. Size the MAF slightly larger than the airflow you are pulling down. Even though the 80mm can physically flow way more than your stock MAF, when tuned to 19# injectors, it's only capable of reading slightly more air before you are back maxed out at 5v again. To increase the measurable range of the MAF, you need it to measure more air. This hurts the resolution by stretching 0-5v across a wider range of airflow, but not nearly enough to be of concern as long as you don't go overboard (i.e. install a MAF that can measure 3000kg/hr across the 0-5v range). I also don't think that an 80mm is going to be as good of a fit for the particular vehicle you are talking about here. Will it work? Yes, but I doubt it'll be the most economical choice. The 80mm MAFs are a good bit more expensive unless you stumble across a good deal. It's not because they are "better." It's just because there are far fewer people out there that need them and so there are fewer of them. The 73mm aftermarket MAFs are quite versatile and flow more than most people give them credit for. Is a 76mm better? 76s usually cost more. And they are only better if you need what 76mm can give that 73mm can't. Same true with 80mm. It's a classic case of diminishing return. So again, my point is size the MAF to the airflow you believe you will be taking down. Being that this motor is all stock except for the supercharger and exhaust, it's a safe assumption that IF the MAF is maxing out, it's just barely maxing out or your motor would probably be in pieces or the FMU is really saving your butt. Since you believe you are maxing out your factory MAF, start there. What airflow does your factory MAF max out at? Once you know that, then start looking at other MAF curves in a program like EEC Analyzer and find a curve that puts your MAF's max flow value in the 4v range (+/- .2v). This gives you MORE than plenty of buffer room for whatever extra your engine is sucking down as well as options on MAFs that'll work for you. Without knowing your MAF's flow values off the top of my head, I guesstimated that a MAF tuned for 24# injectors (i.e. C&L 73mm with blue tube) would drop your engine's max flow back down between 4-5v. Keeping your max MAF readings above 4 but below 5 saves you from maxing the MAF and optimizes the MAF resolution as much as possible (giving you a good 0-4.x volt range). An oversized MAF would put your engine's max airflow voltage in the mid 3v range (i.e. 3.6v) which wastes the resolution range from 3.7-up that you could be using to get more accuracy & fuel control. In addition, with injectors sized to handle the extra horses your engine is making with the supercharger, I'd guess you can get away without the FMU, then tune your AFR & accel enrichment functions to do what the FMU was doing for you. It would help you out a lot if you could get your hands on a WB for the time you'll be tuning. With that, you can force the EEC to OL, replace a factory HEGO with your WB, and dial your MAF curve right in and control your AFR to exactly the mix you want/need@WOT. Once you are done with the WB tuning, use it on your other car and replace the narrow-band HEGO & allow the EEC back into CL. Being that I've never tuned for a supercharger, I can't say that I got my strategy exactly right. You'll have to run that by some of the other guys that do have superchargers and get their opinions on ways to proceed. They may have some other tips they can share as well. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Mar 07, 2007 12:10 pm It sounds to me like you are running into "bugs" in the CBAZA strategy of CalEdit. Try this procedure to verify that what you are witnessing is a scaling problem: 1. Take the CBAZA bin in BinEditor and rename it to CBAZA_test.bin or whatever. 2. Go to the spark tables that are showing differently and for the 1st row, put in 1,2,3,4,5,6, and so on. 3. Go to one of the other similar spark tables and put 11,22,33,44,55,66 and so on for the top row (just to be different than the 1st). Any other spark tables put backwards numbering in. 4. Save in BinEditor 5. Load that test bin into CalEdit and see what the numbers are. This will indicate if there is a scaling difference between BE and CalEdit as well as it'll indicate if some of the spark tables have been mislabelled. If they are mislabelled, you'll be able to see the pattern (even if scaling is off) and determine which table in CalEdit is what table in BE. Like I said, it wouldn't surprise me if you found a problem here. I found a similar problem in the GUFB strategy. I am really wondering HOW the TwEECer works. does it actually flash the EEC? or does it store info on some separate chip and then the EEC reads this during its funtioning and overlays the tweeked code? or is is when you select a calibration, it pushes that cal to the EEC memory and then it runs from there? cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: looking at getting TwEECer.... some questions Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Mar 07, 2007 2:01 pm CrimsonWolf-II wrote: ...I want to know if it will work with my car. I have a 93 Tbird 5.0. at present... That's a common year and make of vehicle. I think it will, but to know for sure, it's helpful to know your EEC's code. The code is written on the connector that the wiring harness bolts to. CrimsonWolf-II wrote: ...second, if it does work, what features/adjustments will I be able to make? will I have full access to all the EEC(PCM) parameters?... Yes. You will have as much access to the BIN control as you will need to keep you busy learning about EEC tuning for quite a while...assuming your particular EEC code and strategy are supported. CrimsonWolf-II wrote: ...Will I be able to use all 4 calibrations on the switch with this car?... Yes, 1993 would put you at an EEC-IV era EEC which only has 64k of total addressable memory. So you will be able to use all 4 positions. Issues with not being able to use all the positions are only with the newer EECs that have 256k of addressable memory. CrimsonWolf-II wrote: ...does it actually flash the EEC? or does it store info on some separate chip and then the EEC reads this during its funtioning and overlays the tweeked code? or is is when you select a calibration, it pushes that cal to the EEC memory and then it runs from there?... No, the TwEECer disables the on-board ROM chip and assumes the role of the ROM. When you pull the TwEECer off the EEC, the EEC is back running the factory tune. CrimsonWolf-II wrote: ...are software upgrades hardware dependant? what about hardware upgrades?... Software upgrades to TwEECer are few and far between. Most people that are serious about tuning don't use the CalEdit software that TwEECer comes with to make their tunes. CalEdit is only used to download and select your datalogging payload. This also assumes your EEC is supported by the open source tuners like BinEditor and TunerPro. If they aren't, you may find it easier on yourself to find a Mustang A9L or A9P and replace your EEC. Believe me, working with BinEditor to tune your BIN files is easier than trying to use CalEdit. Ultimately, CalEdit works with all the various TwEECers that have ever been made (i.e. Parallel Port & USB port). CrimsonWolf-II wrote: ...what happens if a new version of the hardware is released? That hasn't happened in a long time. Nobody knows. The last upgrade of hardware was when the TwEECer went to USB. No major changes have been made because the hardware is relatively simple. The power of the TwEECer is the software. On a side note, I'll also include that you do not want to mess with the non-datalogging version of TwEECer. If you are going to bother, get the RT version. It's more expensive, but to try to tune without datalogging on EEC-IV processors AND deal with the learning curve of tuning is not practical. If you can't swing the RT version right now, save your money until you can. While you are saving it, also plan on another $50 on purchasing EEC Analyzer (aka EA). There are a couple of threads talking about EA and how powerful of a tuning tool it is. It's worth the money. As soon as you find out what your EEC's code is, post that and someone can look up what strategy it falls in and then can tell you whether that's a CalEdit Only EEC or whether you can use other BIN editors like BinEditor and TunerPro. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Mar 02, 2007 5:57 pm As far as I know, it can be used. From a technical standpoint, it's just a matter of clipping the stock MAF connector you currently have and soldering the 90mm MAF connector back on. Next, put the 90mm curve in your tune. Then download the new tune with the new MAF curve to your tuner chip. With a custom tuner like TwEECer, that's a relatively straight-forward procedure. The more challenging part will be finding the plumbing pieces to make it fit. Although, if you haven't bought it yet, I'd imagine a 76mm C&L would do everything you need it to. Even the 73mm C&L with green tube (36lb injector tune) will measure more airflow than the 90mm Lightning MAF will, but I'm not sure it could do it with the same low differential pressure (lower dp is better). Point is with a 93 Mustang, there are far easier plug-n-play type MAFs designed to replace the factory MAF than the 90mm Lightning MAF. You'd probably do better to find a used 73, 76, or if you are looking to make big HP numbers, an 80mm C&L, ProM, or equivalent. Then install a cold-air intake. Cold-air intakes can be found on eBay for about $50 with shipping. The nice part about C&Ls is they don't wear out or loose value unless somebody has damaged the housing in some way so they are just as good used as new. The electronics reuse factory stuff so if the unit goes out, go junkyard diving for a new one from a similar year Ford or go to eBay. They aren't terribly difficult to find. Although, I don't think ProM or any of the other brands have a problem with burning out anyway, so that may be a moot point. So, tell us a little about the car. What type of mods and what's the expected hp output? Accuracy is why I will be switching to the LMAF. Haven't yet, though, so I can't offer any feedback... I can agree that the C&L can only be so accurate when it comes to perfectly replacing the factory MAF on the stock tune. The whole concept and design of the C&L is amazing that it works as well as it does. But even if the C&L delivers the wrong voltage for the air flowing, as long as it is consistently delivering the wrong voltage, the EEC can learn this error and adapt with long-term fuel trims. However, there's nothing in the design that would lead me to believe that the MAF would not be consistent in delivering the same voltage for the same airflow every time. With a tuner, it seems you could tune out any of this inaccuracy/error to get it tuned into the value the HEGOs say without relying on the KAMRFs. However, if you are saying that C&L has a problem with precision...that's a completely different case. A problem with precision would indicate that C&Ls don't result in the same voltage for the same airflow each an every time (i.e. it's not consistent). This would be defined as "slop" in the MAF. And there's little to no way to tune out slop. It's like trying to do a front-end alignment on a vehicle with slop in the tie-rods. If the slop is greater than the allowed error, it's simply a bad part. So which do you believe C&Ls are? As a C&L MAF owner, I sure hope their only problem is accuracy, not precision. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

Man, I really dropped the ball on this one. Sorry it took so long to respond... Here goes, My experience with the C&L has been fairly decent. However, after seeing how sensitive these meters are to things like Air Temp and inlet bends, I won't be using one with my rebuild. ALL MAF meters will be impacted by a 90* bend just before the sensor inlet, but the C&L design seems to be more sensitive than others. I have not read many posts where folks have had to 'clock' their PMAS or LMAF meter to get the signal to stabalize. If there are known problems in extreme conditions, then it stands to argue that there will be issues in less extreme conditions as well. This is my main reasoning for replacing the C&L. The second reason is that I had a hard time getting my KAMRF's to stabillize while using the C&L. posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Re: amount_to_reduce_spark_for_tip_in_Cntrl Quote Post by sailorbob » Tue Jan 16, 2007 5:45 pm Mustang95_302 wrote: I used the base table for all ignition-timing adjustments and the other tables are all set to 55. You shouldn't do this with CBAZA as the eec interpolates between the base (sea level) and altitude tables, e.g. if you have 10 degrees in one table and 30 degrees in the matching cell of the other table the eec will use an advance value of 20 degrees. You are best to use the borderline spark table for your adjustments and set the base (sea level) and altitude to 55's if you want to tune this way. Mustang95_302 wrote: The lowest number in the base table is 10 degrees so how does the timing go below 5 degrees? There are a few adjustments that the eec applies to the result of the table lookup (e.g. for ECT, ACT etc) that can reduce the final value. Also, there are other spark tables (e.g. maximum brake torque) and the eec always uses the lowest calculated spark from the various lookups. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Mar 09, 2007 7:05 pm Someone please correct me if I'm wrong, but as long as the TB isn't oversized for the engine, the only thing the EEC cares about is the airflow when closed (the TB flow scalar). Problems with TB oversizing are with tip-in enrichment. For every degree you open the TB, you let in more air than was expected at lower TB positions, but don't let in as much air at the top-end because the engine isn't pulling down as much air as the TB is trying to allow to flow. So you wind up running the engine at a higher load at lower TPS positions. That in-and-of itself isn't a big deal because the MAF will get the load right as soon as the airflow is detected, but the initial acceleration enrichment that is done before the MAF detectes the new airflow won't be quite right. So you over-enrich tipins at higher TB movements, and don't enrich enough at the lower TB positions. But as long as the tip-in doesn't go lean, it doesn't really matter and you may not even notice. The potential lean tip-in will only affect one maybe two cylinder fires before the MAF catches up with what's going on. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Mar 09, 2007 8:19 pm With an A9L, you have a scalar (ITHBMA) that tells the EEC how many lb/min the TB flows completely closed. To find this value, you have to: 1. Have the MAF dialed in good enough at idle to give you LAMBSEs in the mid 14s & KAMRFs at 1.000 2. Have the engine able to run with the ISC valve unplugged. The RPMs should be as low as possible without conking the engine out, even if it just barely holds on. This is done with the idle screw. 3. Just for completeness, loosen the TPS sensor mounting screws just slightly so the TPS can be moved around and get the voltage on the TPS to between .94-.98v. Anything below 1v should be fine, but this is the recommended range. Others say get the voltage as low as possible and let it ride at that and don't waste time as long as you can get it lower than 1v. Depending on how much the idle screw had to be pushed in, you may have to drill/wallow out the TPS sensor mounting holes a bit. 4. Once all this is done, get the MAF reading (in kg/hr) and convert it to lb/min. Lb/min is the unit of measure used by the ITHBMA Throttle Body Airflow scalar. I believe the default is .55lb/min. I don't remember the exact formula to convert it, but search the forum for it. If you have EA, there's a calculator built-in just for this purpose. 5. Turn the ignition off for a few seconds and re-crank the engine with the TPS reset and the scalar set in the tune. At this point, you can download the EEC and plug the ISC back in to see if this stables out your idle a bit. If it doesn't, make sure these things have been done before moving forward with trying to stabilize your idle. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Mar 09, 2007 10:09 pm It depends on what kind of engine building you are aiming for. If all you care about is WOT power, then all you need is a custom chip that'll let you adjust the various scalar/function/tables and a Wideband O2 sensor to let you tune your AFR to exactly what you need. The need for a wideband is even more important if you have a supercharged engine. However if this is going to be a street driven vehicle, you are going to need drivability. To get drivability, you NEED datalogging. To get datalogging, you need a TwEECer RT or similar device AND you'll need some software to help you analyze the data you get from the datalog. So, what kind of engine building are you planning on? MAX power, high torque off the line, smooth driving, emissions, fuel economy? You obviously can't have it all, but it is possible to get some pretty impressive performance while passing emissions and getting acceptable fuel economy. The KEY is to size components to work together and compliment each other. The place where people always fall short is with the heads. The heads are the component that increase in price with quality. However intakes, cams, and injectors are about the same price for mild or radical. So people get the "bigger" component thinking they will be missing out on some power by going with something smaller. So they end up with cheap heads, a big @$$ cam, RPM intake, 50lb injectors, then expect 500hp from the engine. If you can't afford AFR heads, don't expect AFR performance from ported E7s or Victor Jrs. You'll do much better sizing all the other components smaller than expected. Even the "smaller" high performance parts are better than stock and much better sized for street performance. Unless you are trailer-hauling this car to the track, the smaller components are going to serve you much better. Without some more specific questions, that's about all I can tell you about how to plan for an engine and plan for tuning. As for writing threads here, these are the important points to remember: 1. Make descriptive titles that reflect what you are discussing in your thread 2. Include only closely related questions in threads. Don't ask 6 unrelated questions in the same thread (i.e. a question about injectors, then another question about trannys). Start 6 threads to ask 6 unrelated things so you can adhere to #1. 3. Create a signature from your profile that includes your vehicle, engine, mods if any, EEC code, and tuning device. Other details are also helpful like supercharger type & pressure, tranny type, and rear-end ratio. 4. Be descriptive. Hope this gets you going in the right direction and welcome to the site. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

The weakest point is the Explorer stock cam. It's a mild cam, not a performance cam by any means and starts laying down around 4000RPMs like clockwork. To get better performance with that setup, look at LAZER cams. The Crane PN 444211 is also an excellent choice for what you are looking for. I'd avoid the E303 though. It's a good performance cam, but it doesn't kick-in until upper 2000RPM range. There are plenty of other cams out there that give you off-idle torque AND maintain right into the 5000RPM range. The E303 is better for people looking to get into the 6000RPM range which isn't a good match for the GT40p heads. As for 270hp, that's quite doable with those heads in stock form. However I would upgrade the valve springs since the GT40p springs aren't particularly strong and will float relatively easy with a larger-than-stock lift cam. I'm assuming you'll go with the MAC headers made for GT40p heads? If you go with those, you'll sacrifice the EGR. If you want/need to maintain the EGR, then look into the FMS Explorer headers or the Torque Monster headers. They have a provision for you to run a tube up to the EGR. I've got a 94 Cobra and a Tweecer RT. I'm using the CBAZA/J4J1. The motor has been rebuilt (306), has some aftermarket cam in it (no idea which one though), 24lb injectors (that's stock right?), ProM MAF, Prof. Products TB, some crappy shorty headers and x-pipe, and flows. AC, Smog, EGR deletes too. The MAF says Pro FLow, Professional Flow Technologies. In the MODEL box it says, 75mm 19cxm. In the CALIBRATION box it says 19cxm. I can't make out the X character.....looks like either a C, G, maybe a O. I believe the MAF I picked in Tweecer was just Prom_19.maf. So far I have loaded the MAF transfer for my meter from the files in Tweecer, changed CID, changed idle, rev limiters, speed limiters, took care of the smog/egr crap, pulled the SPOUT and set timing to 10, and I think that's it. I've read SOOO much stuff now about the Tweecer and all that. I'm kind of tired of reading and was just ready to ask some of my own questions. Nothing I read really pinpointed what I'm looking for. Well I'm trying to fix my idle problems and really get everything dialed in. I was messing with the ISC neutral airflow trying to help the idle. The ISC duty cycle is around 40-55% and I was trying to get it around 35 or so. I got to thinking though, and it is pointless to mess with that when I haven't verified that my MAF transfer is correct. The MAF transfer is pretty much the first thing that has to be dialed in, in order for anything else to be correct......right?? How can I verify that it IS correct? Other things I've noticed......at idle, the car will go into closed loop, LAMBSE 1 & 2 will slowly creep down and stop at something like 10.90, then the car will idle pretty decent for a minute or two, then the RPMs will raise to about 1100, it'll go into OL and LAMBSEs jump back to 14.xx, then goes back into CL and repeats. I have the idle set to 750 and it generally hovers around 800-850, not sure if that's normal. Also it seems like if I tap the gas, it doesn't respond until about a second later, then the RPMs jump up much higher than expected. What else.......idle hangs around 1500-2000 quite often until I come to a complete stop. Sometimes it feels like it's hanging while in gear.....feels like a cruise control and I can take my foot off the gas. Cold starts it doesn't like to idle at all. KAMRFs I've noticed always go above 1 when they do change. Based on the KAMRFs and LAMBSEs, if I'm getting all this correct, the car is lean so it's commanding richer mixtures to try to compensate, correct? I'm just really not sure where to start since it seems like so many things are acting based on data from other things. I'm also not sure about how to set spark. I mean I've read tons of crap about HOW, but I guess it's figuring out how much spark I want a certain rpm/load. How are spark figures determined I guess. Advance it everywhere till you hear detonation then back off?? That really doesn't sound like a great way to go about it. Anywho right now I just want to fix the idle/drivability issues. If anyone can help me out I'd appreciate it. Sorry for the long post, too. -Blaise I'm new to the tweecer and am completely lost. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 11, 2007 8:25 am It sounds like you are on the right track. The MAF sounds lean. The EEC certainly thinks this is the case by dropping the LAMBSEs to the 10s, but it's too early to make the assessment that this IS what's happening...yet. You are running the CBAZA strategy which I know much less about. I pickup tidbits here and there, but it's not the same as having to work with it on your own vehicle. However my guess is that if you are seeing your LAMBSEs go to 10.80, next the EEC goes OL & returns the LAMBSEs to 14s, then goes CL just to repeat the cycle, you are hitting the endpoints of your LAMBSE tuning range and the EEC is recognizing this and "resetting" itself. GUF* doesn't do this. Once it locks itself out for an error like this, it goes OL limp mode and stays there until the ignition is turned off. What you need to do at this point is verify if you really are running lean or if this is a sensor issue with your HEGOs simply not registering right. The tell-tale sign is to hang out at the tailpipe while the LAMBSEs are down near 10s. If you see visible signs of rich burning and the distinct smell of fuel, then your HEGO readings are not reliable. However if the exhaust looks and smells clean, then you may very well be lean. The next question, do you ever see the HEGOs switching above .5v? The HEGOs should read rich in the 30-45 seconds during OL right after cranking and during WOT. How many volts do they jump to during these conditions? If you are seeing them go into the mid .7s, you are probably good here. Otherwise, you "may" have a grounding problem. It is possible that the tune is so far lean that you never see the HEGOs switch high even at WOT, but I'd think you'd have to be experiencing some BAD lean-bogs and terrible performance at WOT. If the engine otherwise runs fine at OL conditions (WOT and otherwise) then that would lean to a wiring/grounding issue. If you've cleared that the problem is not the HEGOs and you can see them switch above .7v when they want to, then we can assume they are not telling you lies about the AFR. So next you need to know if the MAF curve is lean across the board. This could indicate you need to adjust your injector slopes. Injector slopes are a fast way to affect the whole MAF curve IF the whole MAF curve is off by about the same %. However if some areas are lean and others are rich, leave the slopes alone and just do what it takes to get the MAF dialed in. If you don't have EEC Analyzer, get it. It will help you here. With some of these questions answered, you'll have a better idea of what the problems are, where they are, and how to proceed. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 11, 2007 2:19 pm J4J1, that's a CBAZA strategy (Mustang 94-95) EEC. You have a choice of a number of different BINs you can put into that EEC: T4M0 W4H0 J4J1 U4P0 ZA0 If you are using a J4J1, that would tend to indicate you have a Cobra. How do I know that? Familiarity with the BINs. Stick around here long enough, and you'll learn them too. So where do you put them? Wherever you want. But I'd recommend a folder in the CalEdit folder. Download BinEditor and install it in the CalEdit folder as well just to keep all your tuning paraphernalia together. Once you get it on the Harddrive, open CalEdit. Set your "strategy" to CBAZA. Click the folder icon at the top-left in CalEdit and navigate CalEdit to where you downloaded your BIN. Once it's loaded in, you can download it to the TwEECer. To download each BIN position, you'll need to flip to all positions and download to the TwEECer using the Write TwEECer icon (looks like a square box, with a cord coming out of it). Float over any of those icons at the top of CalEdit, and a "mouse-over" label should tell you what the icon does. I see you have some details of engine mods you've performed. May I suggest you update your signature with your vehicle year/model, EEC code, tuning device, and all engine/performance mods you've applied including injector sizes and MAF. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 11, 2007 3:49 pm jared_blown5.0 wrote: o do i have to download cbaza too? i just downloaded the u4p0 bin file and tried to open it through caledit and it wouldnt open. Is it giving you an error? Do you have the strategy selection box at the bottom of CalEdit set to CBAZA? CBAZA is not something you download, CBAZA describes a particular organization of info in your BIN file. However, a definition file describes a particular strategy and is what "translates" the BIN from computer HEX info to English descriptions & values that make sense to us humans. The BIN file by itself is only useful to the EEC. However with the accompanying definition file, you can view and adjust the BIN settings using an editor like CalEdit or BinEditor. In CalEdit, the various supported strategies are incorporated as part of the software and are selectable using the drop-down combo-box labelled Strategy. In BinEditor, you manually choose the definition file. Look for the CBAZA definition file in the c:\...\BinEditor\DEF\CBAZA directory. With the CBAZA.XLS file and the U4P0.bin file, you have access to all the settings that have been mapped in the definition file and can save those settings back off as another BIN file name (possibly named by the time/date). You really don't want to save over your original BIN file. You'll want to keep it around to revert back to if you end up with a tune that's gotten too far out of whack that you just want to get back to where you were. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sun Mar 11, 2007 7:55 pm Chris I think the first option that you described is the best not the second. The second option means that you are relying on the internet for a tune which in my opinion is not good. The only sure way to get the correct tune is to read back you stock tune from the EEC. Then download that to all positions like you stated. Also keep in mine the J4J1 is a calibration that is for the Cobra not the stock mustang. It had 24 pound injectors. The J4J1 is 94-95 cobra equivalents to the 93 X3Z tune. jared_blown5.0 Keep in mind that there is few catch phrases tossed around a lot on this forum. One is the word "strategy" and the others are "calibration", "catch code" and "Tune". The correct two phrases are "Strategy" and "Calibration". Strategy refers to the instructions that the EEC knows how to perform. This can also be thought of as firmware. The best way to relate to this is it is just like the BIOS of a PC. The Calibration is data that the strategy uses to perform its job. This is like the data that you enter into the BIOS of a PC. For example the boot sequence of a PC is the calibration. So to put this in perspective of the EEC the engine idle set point is part of the calibration. The strategy then uses that set point and then performs calculations that the EEC can understand. posts.content: Adam McLaughlin Tuning Addict Posts: 618 Joined: Fri Sep 22, 2006 8:43 pm Location: Santa Rosa, California Fuel Startup Table Quote Post by Adam McLaughlin » Sun Mar 11, 2007 1:14 am Hey Everyone, I am almost certain that I have a starting problem that is correlated to my base fuel table. Whenever I hit that key to start the motor, be it from a cold start, or a warm start, or from *any* kind of starting condition, the car runs like crap until it clears the specified amount of time that the Fuel Startup F(x) dictates. I have noticed that if I stall the car in the driveway, and I then hit the key to start it again, the engine will buck and surge at an idle. It will dip to 500, and then buck to 1500, in a style identical to when the MAF curve was waaaaaay too rich. If I try to ease the clutch out slow, and gently apply load to the motor, it will die much too easily. Once I have cleared the required amount of time to be spent in the Fuel Startup F(x), the LAMBSE values return to 14.64 and everything is just fine and dandy. The car is easily drivable, and responds well to all inputs. I have performed this inspection of all of the operating parameters with the O2s pre-heated for 2 mins. I do not yet own a wideband O2. I have extensively tuned the Ba-Jesus out of the MAF curve, especially at and idle point. When the engine is warm and in closed loop, it purrs like a dream. I have been directed that to keep the engine happy at startup, the O2s need to see >.65 Volts. Ok... When I start the engine while cold, they peg close to 1.00. I think we can all agree that this is very rich. Other consultation with pro tuners have told me that some engines need to be choked down to 10:1 AFR to get them going in the cold mornings. My gut feelings are that I have too much choke in the motor. Does anyone have any suggestions to point me in the right direction to clear up the Fuel Startup issues I am experiencing? cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 11, 2007 8:04 am When you crank, the HEGOs go to nearly 1v. That's good in that you are getting a solid signal from your HEGOs and that you are running rich during crank. So what are the HEGOs doing when the engine is running good (after the 45 sec startup)? What are your LAMBSEs during the startup time when the engine is running badly? As for how to adjust this regardless of whether the engine is running rich or lean, that's going to be the fuel startup table that lists the LAMBSE reduction vs ECT over time. The column is time since crank The rows are ECT. This indicates the amount of enrichment that is applied during start. If you find the enrichment you are getting is bogging the engine, you can back off of these values and see if that helps. You can also adjust the Fuel Base OL table if you feel like there's too much enrichment being placed in these tables by default. Engines are very different and I don't know the pattern as to what makes one engine run better than another with the same mix. Some engines dyno their best WOT torque at 13:1, others it takes 11:1 to get max torque. Ultimately, you want it as lean as possible without going much over 13.5:1@WOT. For the mid-throttle positions, you usually set these just lower than 14.6 just to make sure the engine is maintained a little rich, not a little lean during OL conditions. A lot of the effectiveness of this is going to be based on how close your MAF curve is. As you've already mentioned, you want your LAMBSE values in the mid 14s and KAMRFs at 1 +/-.03. If you can dial your MAF in to do this, you've done good. EEC Analyzer will help you in this area if you don't already have it. Getting the KAMRFs to work for you during tuning is also a tweak you'll want to look into. The scalar Min ACT for Adaptive Control (AFACT1) can be lowered from the default of 100°F to something more like 40°F. This will allow the KAMRFs to learn in colder temps. There's also a table you'll want to familiarize yourself with that directly affects KAMRF behavior. This is the Adaptive Control & Update Rate Table (FN1325). This table indicates all the RPM/Load positions that KAMRF learning is allowed in. You'll notice there are positive and negative values in this table. Positive values indicate time (don't know the units) to be in an RPM/Load before learning and adapting to what the LAMBSEs are indicating. Negative values indicate that these cells aren't allowed to learn and thus they harness from the learning done in another cell. The number indicates what cell they are referencing for the KAMRF value. The first number is the column, the 2nd is the row. Numbering start at 0 and counts up and over. Thus -57 is 2500RPM@50% load. If you are looking at the table, you'll be able to count up from the bottom, starting at 0, up to 5 and you should be on the 50% row at the count of 5. Same thing with the row. The scheme you see by the factory setting works fine for a tuned vehicle, but during the tuning phase, this setup just gets in the way and can slow down your efforts to tune a MAF. What you want is for most all these cells to be allowed to learn individually except for maybe the idle and light load rows. Notice the very top row labelled 0.00 load is a reserved row. This is the idle row. The EEC can learn idle separately from the rest of the tune. This can work for you or against you. There are a number of different ways to setup this table. I personally null the idle row from learning by referencing the idle row to the 20% row of the same column. I do the same thing for the 5% and 10% load rows. This way the KAMRF doesn't jump around as I go from idle to a loaded condition. In the meantime, you might want to modify your Cold and Hot start time delays that dictate cold, medium, and warm start times to stay in OL (OPCLT1, OPCLT2, & OPCLT3). When cold, you need to stay in OL until the engine gets at least 60 seconds of run time. In the very low temp climates, this number could be much longer. However for hot-starts (i.e. you drove home, turned the engine off for 5 min, then crank it back up), you don't need to wait any longer than about 45 seconds. Technically, you could start right into CL. The HEGOs are still hot and even if they aren't, they'll get hot again in about 5 seconds. However for the sake of tradition, I'd say keep it at 45 sec. Check out this thread for more details on adjusting these parameters and other related parameters: What quickens Closed Loop? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Feb 27, 2007 10:19 pm Unfortunately, I don't know your EEC but making a few guesses, I'm going to assume that an 86 F-150 is using a Speed-Density system (as opposed to a MAF). This means you won't be tuning a MAF curve, but rather a fuel delivery table that indicates how much fuel to inject vs vacuum (as detected by the MAP sensor) and RPM. With mods to the motor, the engine will be taking in more air than what the EEC is expecting for the same vacuum and it needs to know how much fuel will accompany this. So you'll want to run the engine at each RPM/Load position in this fuel delivery table on your dyno with the wideband to indicate what the mix actually is. So you aren't fighting with the computer, you'll need a way to disable Closed Loop operation so the EEC isn't trying to use the O2 sensors to meet the fuel requirements. But you don't want to disconnect them either. If you do, you'll force the EEC into "limp mode" which means you are likely to work off a completely different set of fuel and spark tables. I don't know that for sure, but that's the typical strategy of even MAF based systems when the MAF is disconnected or the O2s are disconnected. There are a few people on the forum that know Speed-Density systems far better than I do. You'll need to get your detailed tips from them, but that's the concept behind what you are doing. As for tuning spark, you'll want to get the fuel dialed in by forcing each of the RPM/Load positions, then go back and dial in the spark for each one of those. You can do them at the same time if you want. So once you get the fuel sorted out, then start bumping the spark up and watch your dyno for torque effects. You want to increase timing until torque quits increasing (Max Brake Torque) OR when it starts pinging. If you hit ping, drop back by 2 degrees and leave it there. If torque begins dropping off but you aren't yet pinging, leave the timing at what gets you max torque. Now most EECs generally have a WOT mode where they follow a different set of tables or functions. WOT is generally defined by TPS position. These are usually listed as such with WOT in the name of the scalar/function/table. Tune at WOT in the same way you would for non-WOT. The only difference with WOT is you aren't forced to maintain 14.64 AFR since you are running Open Loop in WOT. So for starters, get fuel at each RPM location in your tune to about 13.5:1 using the WB. Next, start increasing the spark advance until you don't get any more torque increase OR the engine begins pinging. If you hit ping BEFORE torque quits increasing, then see if enriching the mix gets rid of the ping. If it does, then increase the advance and see if torque goes up. If it does and you start pinging again, enrich the mix. Ultimately what you are after here is the spark advance that results in MAX torque without pinging while using as little fuel as possible. Some motors run better at 13:1. Others get better torque at 11:1. The dyno helps you find where you get the best performance. That's the basics as far as I know them and that's based on absolutely no personal experience so take it with a grain of salt. Someone with real dyno experience can give you some real-world tips on what engine combos will most likely result in what. But by far, the best tools would be to get that TwEECer upgraded to an RT version and buy EEC Analyzer. It can help you tune your Speed-Density fuel tables without the dyno. The dyno is most useful for WOT tuning than closed loop tuning although it can be used to tune there too, just not nearly as easily as it would be with datalogging. More advanced features in the EEC will define things like acceleration fuel contributions, transient fuel, spark tip-ins, and a number of other stuff that helps drivability. Your options here are purely based on what is available in your EEC. The only way to know what those options are is to go through the list and get an idea as to what all is available. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top
