cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 12, 2007 2:57 pm When you don't have a tuner, the answer is obvious. Match the injectors and MAF calibration so the computer will be sufficiently fooled. However with a tuner, my recommendation is size the MAF to the air intake you expect from the motor. If you've done a good job at estimating your motor's capacity, then your sizing of injectors and MAF will match them pretty good anyway and in the case of the aftermarket MAFs, you'll end up with a MAF that just happens to be calibrated to your injectors. However in the case of reusing OEM MAFs from higher performance cars, you aren't likely to get a MAF that'll be calibrated for anything expect the EEC it was designed for...the Lightning MAF comes to mind. In the case of using the LMAF, you'll have to program your MAF's curve into the EEC along with your injector slopes to even get close. So how do you know if you've sized right? People with experience building motors know about how many horses a particular setup should be able to yield so they can come pretty close guesstimating what MAF and injectors will be needed. But ultimately it takes running the combination to know if the chosen components are satisfactory. If you are not even breaking the 4v range of your MAF@WOT, then you've over-sized it. If you are hitting the mid 4.4-4.7v range, then you have it sized about perfect. However if it is sustaining flow ratings above 4.7v, then you are getting into the part of the MAF curve that's not nearly as accurate and you might do well to get a larger MAF or in the case of C&L MAFs, get a tube better suited for the airflow you are taking down to put your high RPM WOTs in the 4.4-4.7v range. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 11, 2007 1:11 pm At this point, check your MAF voltage with the ISC valve disconnected. If it is less than the Min MAF voltage scalar, then adjust the scalar to be less than what you get with the ISC disconnected. Also make note of what average voltage you are getting from the MAF and convert that to a kg/hr value. Convert it to lbm/min and type that into the Throttle Body Flow scalar. Note, the scalar doesn't take kg/hr values, but rather lb/min values. While you still have the ISC disconnected, wait the EEC into CL, and note what the LAMBSEs settle out to. If it is in the mid 14s, then you should be good at this point. However if the LAMBSEs are way off 14 (i.e. 12s or 16s), then you got some MAF tuning to do. Get the MAF airflow tuned in. Start with the airflow you are at with the ISC disconnected. Don't forget to clear the KAMRFs if your EEC winds up learning something other than 1. May I suggest to make one of your MAF datapoints equal to the voltage you get with the ISC disconnected. Once you get that airflow for that voltage so that you have KAMRFs at 1 and LAMBSEs at 14s in Closed Loop, eye-ball the MAF datapoints above and below this datapoint you just found. At this point, try plugging the ISC back in and see if it surges back up or if it settles in at this point. BTW, all this assumes you are running a GUF* processor like an A9L or A9P. If you are running a CBAZA, the procedure may be slightly different. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 04, 2007 11:48 am A9L is GUFB strategy. Look inside the c:\<installed>\BinEditor\Def\GUFB directory, you'll find the GUFB Rev 6.XLS file as well as the A9L.BIN and X3Z.BIN As soon as you make a tweak to the original file, you'll want to immediately save as a different name so you don't accidentally save over the original. I'd even go as far as to say to set all those files as "Read Only." As has been mentioned earlier, it makes a lot of sense to date your various BIN revisions. So that it sorts correctly, you'll want to name your BINs with year-month-day-etc.BIN so your BIN files might look like this: 2007-01-03.bin 2007-01-03b.bin 2007-01-03c.bin 2007-01-04.bin etc You may also want to keep a manual log of what all has changed. I've asked Clint to consider some kind of audit logging functionality to keep up with a particular BIN's mods. Such an audit log might list what changed (inc the file name), when it was changed (time/date), what it changed from and to, and would be done at File Save. As long as you start a BIN from a base-bin like an A9L.bin or X3Z.bin, such an audit log would list every tweak since its conception from the base-tune. Another common audit-log entry in industry is an additional field that indicates why a parameter was changed ( 21 CFR Part 11 compliance). But that's probably overkill for our purposes... To do this will require a separate log file that accompanies every BIN. As long as the log continues to append and rename itself along with the BIN renaming, I think this would suffice for most of our logging needs. I could even be in XLS format so if we wanted to manually put our "why" in the log, we could. TunerPro tried to do some of this, but reset the log file every time it was re-saved. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 05, 2007 7:37 pm EEC Analyzer's biggest benefit is the MAF transfer suggestions it makes to help you hone your MAF curve based on your datalog. For the speed-density guys, there's also a fuel table calculator which is the speed-density version of a MAF curve. You can also calculate new injector timing values based on your cam parameters & datalog of Injector PWs. This has the most benefit for cams that have overlap and need to pass emissions. EA will help you time the injectors so that they don't fire until AFTER the exhaust valve closes so you minimize unburned air/fuel out the exhaust due to overlap scavenging. For cams that don't have overlap, you can still tune your injectors to begin fire at a very specific cam position. For light throttle, you can setup the injectors to fire on the backside of the intake valve while its closed so it atomizes better. But for moderate acceleration, you want to limit the closed-valve injector firing so the fuel doesn't pool. With EA, you can calculate all these various things. EA also calculates injector slopes to help you hone those in if you don't like yours. You can calculate new Injector offsets based on engine voltages. There's a mapping function so you can map out KAMRF, LAMBSE, MAF, Inj PW, and a number of other datalogged parameters. The mapping allows you to map out min/max/avg/last-known values for each RPM/Load condition in your datalog. There's also a number of little calculators that you'll find useful like injector size calculator, fuel pump calculator, kg/hr to lb/min calculator (useful for tuning the TB airflow), kg/hr to cfm calc, etc etc. And there's a custom graphing function so you can map out up to 4 of your datalogged values onto a graph. EA is well worth the money to me. I couldn't imagine trying to tune without it. As for how useful it is to others, it's as useful as you make it. And if there's a new feature you think would be useful that can be calculated using datalogged info, Clint will consider your suggestion. EA is actively maintained and works very well with BinEditor now that it has a lot of the table/function copy-n-paste options to allow you to move info from EA to BinEditor and back very quickly (no fat fingering into CalEdit). cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Mar 08, 2007 3:28 pm Depends on how much overlap you got. Generally firing on the backside of the intake valve while it is closed smooths idle out, but does seem to take away some power if you fire on it too much...at least that's what I've found messing around with my stock Explorer cam which is super mild. However when I setup my injectors to only fire when the intake valve is open, my idle gets rougher and light throttle takeoff isn't nearly as smooth & consistent. So what I do is use EA to calculate timing values that'll allow the intake valve to be fired on, but only so much (say 100° before the intake valve begins to open). At lighter loads, most of the injection is done with the valve closed. But as the injector PW and/or RPMs increase, more of the injector fire time is with the intake valve open. Eventually, the RPMs increase to the point that the PW exceeds the amount of time the intake valve is open and thus if I want the injector to get the complete fire in before the intake valve closes, the injector has to start firing earlier than 100° at higher WOT RPMs. I found that allowing the injector to continue to fire past when the intake valve closes causes the engine to jerk when I nail the throttle. The 1st intake of air after nailing the throttle on each cylinder doesn't get all the fuel it needs because the injector is still firing when the intake valve closes, so the first 8 fires of a quick WOT run lean. The fuel that continued to spray after the intake valve closed was part of the next intake charge and thus ran the next explosion fine. Setting timing values that guaranteed the injector fired a complete charge before the intake valve closed too much improved that quick-WOT hesitation. But keep in mind, these are my findings with a stock cam with FAR from overlap conditions. With a lot of overlap in your cam, firing the injectors before the exhaust valve closes causes raw fuel to go out the exhaust, wasting fuel. The assumption is anybody installing a heavy overlap cam isn't interested in fuel economy...just high RPM HP. The other problem with this type cam is at lower RPMs, no matter when you fire the injectors, some unburned intake air is going out the exhaust which I'd think would play hell with your HEGOs and if your HEGOs sample when the raw intake charge goes out the exhaust, your computer will compensate by adding for fuel which isn't going to fix the problem, only run the engine too rich. But he's right, having raw fuel in that mix will make the HEGO's response time even more sluggish. The larger the overlap, the higher the RPMs have to be before this isn't an issue. The playing field is so different with an aggressive cam with overlap. I'm curious to hear from those who successfully tuned for a heavy overlap cam how they did it or what the sacrifices are (i.e. what you'll just have to live with running this type cam). Bottom line, I doubt you are going to smooth out much by messing with injector firing since you don't really want injectors firing until the exhaust valve is closed to .050" OR until the engine is above the RPM where intake charge isn't scavenging out the exhaust anymore. The cam company might be able to tell you about what RPM that'd be for your particular setup. I highly doubt it is a hard-n-fast number since the scavenging effect is dependent on your headers, heads, and intake pressure (i.e. naturally aspirated or forced induction). In addition, depending on what RPM that is (i.e. how much overlap you have), you'll need a larger injector than you would need with a no-overlap cam producing the same HP. The larger injector will fire more fuel in the same amount of time which is what you need in order to get all the required fuel to the cylinder from the time the exhaust valve closes to the time the intake valve closes. With EA and knowing that RPM, you can determine what your Injector timing table should be as well, you can determine if your injectors are too small to meet that criteria. Without EA...well, have fun with that. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Thu Mar 08, 2007 11:36 pm Chris did a good job of explaining it. The only thing I can add is, be careful when deciding the injector size. The reason I say this is the EEC has a pretty good resolution on the PW but the smaller the PW gets the harder it is to control. This is most evident in idle situations. Trying to control a system with 42s is harder than a system with 24s, especially at an idle. This is the main reason the Mega Squirt control systems have some problems. The Mega Squirt systems only have a resolution of 0.1 which means the calculated PW can overshoot or undershoot their target fairly easily at the lower PWs. This just goes to show you the issue. I am not to sure of the EECs resolution, but I would hope that it is greater than 0.1. I know our logs show better resolution but this could be a rounding error on the TwEECer side or some stupid thing like that. I just can not verify it. I just know that the lower the idle PW the harder it is to tune. You may not think that 0.1 is a lot, but at an idle it can mean a lot to the AFR. This is amplified when the latency delay of the injector is added to the mix. Most injectors take a full millisecond to open fully from a closed position. Let’s just take an example of a 2.0 ms idle PW on a setup with 42s and a idle PW of 3.8ms on a stock 5.0 mustang. When you subtract the latency of 1ms the EEC only has control over the 1ms on the 42 and 2.8 on the stock setup. Now if the resolution is only 0.1 then that is ten percent on the 42 setup and 3.5 percent on the stock setup. This is like swinging your AFR 10 percent or 3.5 percent around your target. The 10 percent is too much if you ask me. This may sound counter intuitive but if the fuel pressure is lowered a tad then the idle PW will increase to compensate for the resolution issue. This is the reason I think FORD uses 39 psi rather than 43.5psi. Most other car manufactures use 3 bar or 43.5 psi. Lowering the PSI to 39 allowed my idle PW to increase to 2.6, which is better. Lowering the pressure made the injectors rating change to 39.8. Take a look at the Lightning tune and you will see that this is closer to what Ford has the injector size set to. Like Chris also stated, the fuel may exit threw the exhaust as raw fuel. The HEGO will not detect raw fuel since they only read oxygen. This would then tell the EEC to richen the mixture. This only complicates things when the injector timing is on trailing edge. With the trailing edge firing the PW has to end by the given point in the calibration table. In the above example the EEC will command a larger PW caused by the lean reading from the HEGO. This would cause the injectors to start firing earlier since the PW has to stop firing at the same point. This means more raw fuel will exit the exhaust. The EEC would still since the lean condition and more fuel would be added again. Get the picture, now the EEC goes into KAMRF runaway. It will eventually run the KAMRF up to its limit and cause a check engine light. This is why the injector timing is so important on big cams. It not so much of a performance modification, but rather a stability modification. If the EEC was a leading edge triggered tune, than the issue would not be as bad because the PW would get larger and the PW end point would increase. At some point the extended PW would be after the Exhaust would close event and the fuel would finally get burnt. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

Move the most important stuff over to BinEditor like the MAF curve, injector slopes/offset/breakpoint, and any fuel/timing tables. If you have a really mature tune, you'll find stuff for the next 2 weeks that you forgot to move over. But once it's moved, you'll have a base tune to start from and won't have to save another CCF. All your tunes will be *.BINs. Just discipline yourself to NOT make "quick" mods using CalEdit just because you can. You'll have to remember to make that same tweak back in BinEditor and the chances of forgetting are high. It takes a little more time, but by far the best practice is to make ALL tune tweaks in BinEditor so you know you got'em and won't loose'em. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 11, 2007 8:40 am Sounds like your 1st problem is getting your datalogging to work. Make sure you are following this procedure: 1. Select 16 things to datalog 2. Save those selections by clicking the save checkbox and then clicking payload. This will prompt you to give this combination of 16 things a name 3. Set the dial to a position OTHER than the factory tune. If you can't remember whether "TwEECer disabled" is on the far CW or CCW, then switch to a center tune and download your tune and payload. 4. Launch CalCon with Datalogging checked 5. Start datalogging with the ignition turned on an the RT light illuminated in CalCon. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Mar 15, 2007 11:11 am Unless you have a supercharger, you may not even need the wideband O2. In the closed loop conditions, you can tune most everything purely based on the factory narrow-band HEGOs. The Widebands are only required when tuning for OL conditions like WOT where you expect the fuel to be much richer (in the 11:1-13.5:1 ranges) and running lean at WOT (i.e. 14:1) is still richer than what you'd run at Closed Loop (14.5-14.7:1). That doesn't mean they won't be useful at the Closed Loop loads. It's always nice to get a 2 sensor readings (the narrow and wideband readings) to confirm conditions. It just means widebands are not required for tuning for drivability in the closed loop conditions. Make sense??? As for tuning, make sure you get the RT version of the TwEECer. You can't do justice with tuning without getting datalogs of what's happening so you can do deep-level analysis after you've run the car. As well, you'll want to plan on purchasing EEC Analyzer. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Mar 15, 2007 8:35 pm It sounds like you got the idea... As for your HEGOs...130kmiles, I'd say you got your money's worth from those HEGOs. However if you are going into the project with the WB, you'll know whether they are good or not. Narrow band HEGOs generally fail with less voltage generation. Since high voltage from an O2 sensor means rich, a failing HEGO usually indicates lean even when the mix is really rich so the EEC starts overcompensating to get the HEGO to go back up to the voltage it expects which runs the engine rich all the time. I imagine this O2 sensor behavior is by design since manufacturers don't want HEGOs failing and causing lean conditions. A little rich doesn't hurt too much. Under light loads, you may never notice anything's wrong. A little lean, and you have drivability problems. As for getting WOT datalogs, what I find works pretty good is go as slow as I can, put it in 3rd (I have a manual T5) and WOT it from 1200 RPM to red-line. With 3.27 gears and an aftermarket T5 with higher gear ratios (lower numbers), 3rd at 5500 puts me well into 90MPH. So yeah, I need a good stretch of road. If I can't get it all the way to red on third, I pull as far as I can, then I do another run in 2nd. With EA analyzing your datalogs, you can analyze all the data so as long as you got the engine into all the RPM ranges you want to WOT tune for, it doesn't matter what gear you are in. But 3rd and 4th does work better for getting better, more stabilized low-RPM WOT readings than 1st or 2nd. Believe me a few months of talking on this forum and running datalogs, you'll get the hang of it. There's a lot to learn, but fortunately tuning WOTs is a relatively straight forward thing with a wideband. It's drivability issues that are the pain to deal with and hunt down. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Fri Mar 16, 2007 11:20 am The units in TunerPro are displayed as mSecs as the result of the table lookup is checked against a millisecond timer (Time_Since_Last_Advance). There is actually an error in the conversion which should be X*16 (not X/16 as in the GUF* xdf versions up to and including 172007). The table will be renamed in the next xdf release as "Knock Advance Rate vs RPM" to properly indicate it's use as part of the knock control strategy. The description will be along the lines of; "This limits the rate at which the spark returns to the calculated spark advance following retardation due to knock control in order to avoid pinging. This value is the number of milliseconds that must pass since the last spark increment before the next increment is allowed to occur. Decrease to improve throttle response. When allowed, the spark is advanced a 1/4 of a degree each time at a maximum rate of a 1/4 quarter of a degree between each firing event." NB This is for the GUF* strategy ecu's. Top

posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Thu Mar 15, 2007 8:20 pm What are your rings gapped at. I built my motor for use with NOS so my rings are gapped at 0.025 which is about 0.010 more than stock. this is to allow for ring expansion caused by the extra heat from the nitrous. This is the reason I get so much blowby, especially when its cold. Once it gets up to running temps its not too bad. you actually shouldnt have any breathers. The pass side should be sealed, the drivers side should have a vent tube from the front of the valve cover to the intake tube, and the PCV should be hooked up to a direct vacuum port on the intake manifold. This way any air drawwn through the motor is also drawn through the MAF, Its not much air but its enough to throw your tune off. I used to use oil separators but found they clogged very quickly and then there was no flow in the motor. I could always tell when it clogged as it would leak oil lilke crazy. Now I just let the oil go into the intake I know its not good but its better than leaking a quart aa week. Most of the info above comes from an article, but I cant remember where I read it. The only real oil separator I have foudn that works is here http://www.aircraftspruce.com/catalog/e ... oilsep.php but I cant afford this. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 18, 2007 7:46 am First thing that'll help us out is to know what EEC you are using. I'm assuming an A9L based on your year and tranny, but that's not always the case. If you plan to be a regular visitor of this site posting questions, you'll find it a lot easier to take all your car info and type it into your profile's signature. Every post you make from that point on will include your car's details so you don't have to retype it every time you post a question. Good signatures will contain year/make, EEC code, tuning device (i.e. TwEECer RT), engine, all mods to the engine (stroked, intakes, cam, TB, supercharged, etc), MAF, injectors, headers, tranny, and rearend ratio. So about your problem, if changing the TPS voltage to go WOT was the only thing he changed to kill the motor, then it seems logical, you could switch that back (I'm assuming you did that). However, when someone talks about their car mysteriously not cranking anymore, we all get a little worried. If the TwEECer is pulled off the EEC while the ignition is turned ON, the chance of frying the EEC increases. If you are pretty sure the EEC is working, the engine just isn't running, then you can probably start over with a stock tune and tweak the things you need just to get the car running. It may not run great, but it should run good enough to get it moved. I'm assuming your MAF is tuned to the size injectors you actually have. If that's true, then you can get away with not changing the MAF curve or the injector slopes in the stock tune for now. This isn't the way you want to run the car for a long period of time, but it should get the engine at least to crank and run. Then you at least know the problem isn't with the EEC. And under these conditions, you be able to drive it just to get it moved, but I wouldn't trust it not to conk out on takeoffs and sitting at idle. But once it's rolling, it should do OK. After all, those tuned MAFs are designed to prevent people from "needing" to tune their car. Once you get the car moved and you can settle down about the car not running, then you can learn how to tune the car for real, which means replacing the factory MAF curve with your MAF's actual curve and replacing the injector slope values with your injector sizes. As well, you can increase the timing tables to get a notable amount more torque (but you want to leave the distributor at 10deg BTDC). And then of course, learning how to tweak out the cold crank and drivability problems that may still linger. There'll be a ton to learn, but if you are into that sort of thing, it's a fun challenge seeing your car run better after punching buttons on the computer. If you hate computers and learning about cryptic "computer crap" then you are better off going to a reputable dyno shop and having it tuned by someone that knows what they are doing. But from everybody I've ever talked to, the only thing the dyno shops can really get you that you can't do for yourself is optimizing WOT. Tuning drivability problems is something that takes time, diligence, and constant trial-n-error based on some new condition that your engine has never been in before. That is to say, some problems you may run into are climate based. The engine may run and crank fine in the summer, but as soon as the winter months roll around, you realize you have cold-cranking problems or some other weird issue that wasn't there before. I tell you, I have a lot of respect for the original Ford programmer/engineers that thought up all the tables and controls a car EEC would need to run an engine in all drivable climates. I can't imagine the years of development time that even a 1989 EEC represents, to say nothing of the EECs used in brand new cars today. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Mar 15, 2007 12:39 pm I don't know that the stock timing of the injector firing puddles the fuel but rather "coats" the valve. However I do agree if you fire the injectors too early, you do start pooling. I've played around with injector timing at the lighter loads and it seems that starting injector fire 100° before the intake valve opens works very nicely. Any more than that, and the engine starts running sluggish (presumably because it does start pooling). So what I did was set EA to calculate injector stop times such that the injector starts firing around 250° (since my valve opens at 350°). As the RPMs and injector PW increase, the injector is firing while the valve is opening. As the PW and RPM continue to increase into the high RPM/Load conditions, the injector is still firing when the intake valve is closed. So to prevent that, I manually clip all the injector stop-times to the mid 500s which pushes the injector start fire before 250°, but at the higher RPM/Loads, the entire injector payload of fuel is delivered so it doesn't run quick-WOTs lean for one cycle. That's my take on injector timing. Your results may vary... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL Me and the dyno tonight Quote Post by boss96 » Sat Feb 03, 2007 4:18 am I finally got to dyno the car tonight, it's been a long time coming. I thought I had the tune pretty well set up but there were some surprises. First off, my water injection pump quit, first run the a/f was around 13-1 which is what I command in the stab OL table because once the WI kicks in the a/f gets in the mid 11's normally. This caused me to burn 4 plugs but no damage to the engine. We replaced the pump and tuned from there. I had always thought you should lean out the a/f to overcome the water/methanol richening the a/f but it worked better to not do that. I ended up commanding 11.7 a/f and leaving it at that. Timing was able to run anywhere from 19-21 degrees with the WI. The next problem I had was the hp was going flat above 5200 rpm, it ended up that the belt was slipping, boost is supposed to go to 15 at 6k rpm, instead it would hit 11 and then drop to 9lbs. Even so, with 9lbs of boost it made 503hp/495tq, and that was on a Mustang Dyno, not a dynojet. I'll be looking into fixing the belt slip :D Oh, I should mention, I use a UEGO wideband, we ended up just watching the WB itself as the transfer was way off on Calcon such that it made it seem like it was running richer than we thought. I'm sure I could adjust the transfer function but it was'nt worthwhile tonight. posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Mon Mar 05, 2007 10:22 am Yeah that would be good, caps by themselves are not effective unless you know the frequency you are trying to filter out. The higher the frequency the smaller value cap you have to use. 10uF would be too big. A 0.1 or 0.01 would be much beter. I will do some calculations tonite and see if I can get close on the spark frequency, and injector frequency. Once I get this I can at least try and come up with a good number to start with. Also there is alternator whine that has to be considered. The way caps work, is that at a certain frequency they effectively become a short for that frequency, for eg 80Mhz-108mhz a 180pF capacitor is a short, So if you have equipment that works around radio stations, then those pieces of equipment use a lot of 180pF caps to eliminate the radio frequency. Also keep in min that even though the leads are pretty short the leads themselves act as an inductor, and could potentiall eliminate the need for a coil. The probelm we have is that we do not know the impedence of the EVP port and what circuitry is on the inside of the EEC. Also you have the harness hanging our there which acts aas a big coil as well. The best way to hook it up woudl be to cut the evp wire as clost to the eec as possible and hook your WB directly into the eec and eliminate the rest of the wiring from that pin. The other thing to keep in mind most of the WB the highr the voltage the lower the AFR, so by default calcon would be less susceptable to noise at the lower AFR's. I dont know if this all makes sense or just confuses the issue more. Bob One thing to remember about boosted applications is this. You have to account for injecting into a boosted chamber. You are not injecting into a vacuum anymore. So if you have 14lbs of boost, or 21, etc... you have a positive pressure acting against the injector trying to get fuel into that intake. For instance a fuel system and injector squirting into normal atmosphere has to work twice as hard to get into 14lbs which is double normal. You can't just size an injector for HP only. You have to size for how much pressure you are working against too. I never realized that until I John Kolivas told me the way he discovered it back early in his racing efforts. He just ran 8.02 @175.57 mph on Drag radials at the last NMRA event with a turbo setup. He won last years NMRA and set a new world record in doing so. Of course he and one other just shattered those records the first race of the year so far. Also between supercharing and turbo he didn't have to run near as much boost to get the same ET when he made the switch. He is running a 359 cubic inch engine but 5.0 based after market block. Dart I think. Risks that go with splitting blocks, (which I have seen a few) is snapping off the crank snout from belt pressure. I would not expect over 500hp reliably from a stock short block or even a Level 20 DSS block which I am running with beefed main girdle. A 351 is stronger but I don't think 600HP should be approached often. There is a twist here though. We are talking drag racing. Launch loads are extremely high on these blocks. If road racing and high rpm the car is moving and the stress is less than moving 3000+lbs in 8 seconds to 175mph as in drag racing. Those are just my observations. -Patrick. 90Stang Kenne Bell/ ExplorerGT40P/HOCAM/1.7RR/36lbinj/ 5spd -CBAZA 06Stang 4.0 dual exhaust. Stock. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue Mar 20, 2007 5:24 pm We are getting off topic here. The injector PW maybe off if you consider the battery offset. The EEC will calculate a given PW which is accurate. When you compare that to RPM Cal Con will report the correct injector Duty Cycle. What we are forgetting is the Injector battery offset and propogation delays. This is not added into what is logged. So for most of us, this means the PW logged represents the time from when the injectors are Fully open until the time closing starts. This is not from open seat to close seat. You may also remember in the older posts that we said the EEC will limit the output to something like 90%. This prevents the injectors from going into saturation (full open all the time). Cal Con will report higher than 100% because it is solely dependent on the PW and RPM. As RPM increase so will duty cycle. I would not go past 90%, just for saftey reasons. On a cold day I can hit 88% with 42s. I am no were near 500hp. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Re: Tweecer scalar definitiions?? Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 25, 2007 1:31 pm While you are on Clint's site (posted in his signature above), get BinEditor. If you want more clarity on the various scalar/functions/tables, then download BinEditor and do all your tuning through that. BinEditor includes notes about most all the scalars. If there are some that don't have comments, you can add your own to the def file so your comments show up. There are far more comments, and more useful comments in BinEditor than any other def files I've found. As for your specific questions, here we go... cobradvm wrote: ...WOT TPS Breakpoint Voltage - what is breakpoint, and what is the effect of altering this value?... The TPS OL voltage (THBP5) and WOT (THBP2) voltage scalar are the voltage above baseline that will force OL or force WOT conditions. So for instance, if you crank the engine and the TPS is reading .95v and you have 2.7v for the TPS WOT voltage, then the actual TPS voltage has to be 2.7+.95= 3.65v before WOT is forced. Most people drop the stock value down to about 2.5v. However for the purposes of tuning my MAF curve as high in the flow rates as possible (I don't have a wideband), I've increased these values. Generally these are at the same value so when you go OL, you go WOT at the same time. Since WOT also has some functions specific to it, you generally want OL and WOT to go into effect at the same time when you leave Closed Loop for high loads to optimize performance. On a side note, I also increased the scalar that forces OL at high load (HLCTM) to about 30 seconds. This scalar forces OL even if the TPS isn't high enough to force it. When cruising in the mountains, I found that I was going OL when the engine really didn't need to. Increasing this from 2 sec to 30 seconds fixes this. cobradvm wrote: ...Spark tip in - Maximum advance... The Spark Tip-in is the spark value the engine will advance to while your throttle is increasing. This makes shifting and accelerations smoother before the actual defined spark in the Sealevel/Alt spark tables goes into effect. At lower loads, this can make things shift a little smoother as long as it's only a slight difference. Otherwise, you may notice a distinct "kick in" shortly after the throttle position stops moving as tip-in transitions to full advance. At higher loads, the tip-in lightens the brunt on the transmission during the shift of stick-shift trannys. Since you are usually pushing the accelerator while letting the clutch out, the tip-in will be in effect. I've also heard (and experienced) that a tip-in like action is implemented more heavily for EECs that CONTROL electronic automatic transmissions so the trans has a chance to shift under a lighter torque. The difference here is that this is more of a spark-retard-at-shift, than a tip-in because with an automatic, your throttle may not be moving when the tranny shifts. Once the shift is complete, the EEC implements full advance. This saves the transmission, decreases in-warranty trans failures, and decreases performance. Most people with tuners tune the tip-in out and accept that the tranny will take the full load of the engine. With a built tranny, this shouldn't be a problem or at least isn't as big of a concern as it obviously is to a manufacturer. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Mar 25, 2007 8:36 am It's OK to have the 0 rows at the bottom, but those are rows you could be making use of to get a little more accuracy out of your MAF curve. Theoretically, if the MAF were actually used from 0v to 5v, it would make the most sense to evenly distribute the voltage points up and down the 0-5v range. So, before you know what the "usable range" of your MAF is based on your engine's capabilities, you run with an evenly distributed MAF curve that represents the entire 0-5v range. However once you get a better handle on what you can expect from your engine, there's no reason why you can't identify and reallocate "unused" rows into voltages your engine will use in an effort to gain more accuracy from your MAF. Depending on your MAF and your engine, you may never run the car below .5v on the MAF (idle or decel). Therefore any voltage readings below say .45v are not being used including all the 0 rows. Likewise if the max sustained MAF voltage at WOT that your engine can produce is 4.3v, then anything above say 4.4v is can also be reallocated. So if your MAF curve has 4.4v, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, 4.9, 5.0, & 16.0, then you can take the 4.5, 4.6, 4.8, 4.9 rows and use them as usable parts of the curve (you might want to leave the 4.7v just in case you happen across some power-adder to bump you above 4.4v. To keep the curve looking smooth (i.e. all voltages increasing as you go up the curve), you'd simply shift the curve upward. Now that EA has the ability to copy/paste, this shouldn't be too difficult. With some new rows to work with, start looking down the voltage range and identify any two voltages that are noticeably further apart than most of the other voltage jumps. Then use one of your newly acquired rows here to define a new voltage row between the two you identified. I'd also concentrate my efforts of re-integrating these rows into the MAF voltage range that's seen during Closed Loop conditions. The voltages attained only during WOT conditions are already running rich so they will be much more tolerant of error in your MAF curve and thus will not benefit as much from the added accuracy. But the closed loop areas typically between .6v-3v are the areas that generally are benefited by a more accurate curve and thus will promote better drivability. Likewise, be aware of voltages that are uselessly close to a neighboring voltage. To make my point, I'm going to exaggerate the numbers here. But lets say you have a MAF curve with the following voltages: . . . 1.6 1.5 1.33 1.3 1.0 0.9 0.8 . . . In this case, there's no benefit in having 1.3 and 1.33. They are so close to each other, they don't really help smooth the curve much. They would serve better if 1.3 were 1.17 just to spread the distance between 1 and 1.5. So now your curve would look more like: . . . 1.6 1.5 1.33 1.17 1.0 0.9 0.8 . . . Notice how the differences have been spread out more? If you have extra rows to add here, you might even eliminate this by adding two rows to represent 1.1 and 1.4 so the .1 offset pattern can be followed. But that's up to you. Those decisions have to be made looking at the entire MAF curve, not just a little piece of it like we have here. So, you can either let EA handle doing a MAF fitting for you, or what you can do is display up your current MAF curve, then using the 2nd MAF column in EA, overlay your custom voltage ranges that better represent your engine's usable MAF voltages, then start finding what flows put your MAF voltages close to the existing curve. Once you got your custom curve roughed in to what the old curve represents, run the curve in your tune and start tweaking it like you normally would. So is all this necessary? That depends on you. If you are identifying some drivability problem that you've linked to the MAF curve being in error at a specific spot every time and the error is so great that the KAMRFs can't properly correct for it, then yes, this might be necessary. But personally, I think of doing this more as optimization, rather than a required step. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 26, 2007 8:49 am It appears this is a scaling discrepancy between BE and CalEdit. The same value in the BIN is being converted to different values to us. I can open the same BIN in CalEdit and in BE, and get two different values. The value in the BIN is the same. What's different is the scaling of that value into terms we, humans, want to see it in. I tend to trust BinEditor's scaling much more than I do CalEdit purely based on previous experience with other F-ups in CalEdit. However, CalEdit may be right in this case. The reason I say that is because the stock MAF curve only goes to about 4.77v before it flat lines to 16v. Thus if you are going to have a trigger point for a shorted MAF or a MAF overflow, I'd think it would be around the MAF's max value in the transfer. So having this at 4.79 makes a lot of sense. That doesn't mean that the EEC really flags a MAF short at 4.79v. It just means it makes sense that it would. The good news is, it's only ~.1v off AND this is only a trigger point to turn on the MIL/CEL light and flag a MAF over-volt condition in the codes. Generally, this indicates a shorted MAF wire. But with a built motor running a stock MAF, this could also be an indicator that your MAF is undersized. So what about aftermarket MAFs? Should this value be upped? Most aftermarket MAFs are good to 5v. But in my opinion if you are running your MAF over 4.7v, you really should get a bigger MAF or in the case of a C&L, re-tube it for higher flow. So perhaps this scalar should stay right where it is and be an indicator to you when/if you are undersized on the MAF? That's purely a personal choice. Also think about it this way, I tend to agree with Ford's philosophy that whatever your MAF flow is at 4.7v should be considered the max your MAF can accurately measure. Whether you reuse the stock electronics in a C&L or buy an aftermarket MAF with it's own electronics like ProM or Granatelli, the max voltage the MAF "should" give is 5v. Thus that's all you can rely on to be delivered. If there was 0 resistance between the MAF and EEC, then that might be OK. But that not being the case, either the MAF would need to be able to deliver just over 5v to ensure the EEC sees 5v OR you need to consider that when the MAF sends 5v, your EEC is going to see 4.9x volts. Hopefully the engine is running rich enough in this condition it won't matter. But the MAF curve gets pretty steep at the top-end because airflow has to increase exponentially to get the voltage to raise at the same rate. Thus the difference between 4.95v and 5v is pretty big and pretty dangerous if there isn't enough fuel going into the engine to cover for that error. It's certainly a greater error than it would be at 4.65 and 4.7v. That's why I say the smarter thing to do is put a larger MAF in that'll keep that max MAF voltage in the 4.5v neighborhood. The difference in airflow between 4.5v and 5v is huge, so even quick spikes of high airflow going into a built motor shouldn't be a problem if you size the MAF to never sustain over 4.5v. But back to the original question...ultimately, you'd either have to look at code to find out how it "tests" this value against the MAF reading or test the operation of the EEC by feeding it controlled and monitored voltages and watch when you get a CEL. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

Last year the car was really dialed in, at startup, idle/cruise in closed loop, and WOT. Over the winter we added AFR 185's in place of the Ford X303 heads, replaced the GT40 intake with the new Perfomer II, and removed the cats. We started it for the first time on saturday and I noticed it was running ragged because it was lean while on the startup table. Then when it went to CL it smoothed out but I could see by the wide band it was on the lean side most of the time. I reasoned that the engine must be moving more air through it, but why wouldn't the MAF "see" that and adjust accordingly? I want to believe the thing is just flowing a lot better, but at this point I don't know if what I am seeing is good or bad. Any thoughts? cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Mar 29, 2007 5:13 pm Depends on how you have your Wide-band O2 connected. If you are using the EGR position sensor to connect to your wideband, then you'll datalog the EGR position. If you are using a DataQ, then the Wide-band will connect to the DataQ, then the DataQ will connect to the computer (USB or 232, I don't know which connection the DataQ uses). If you are just trying to datalog what the EEC thinks AFR is, then that's the LAMBSEs. But unless your tune is close, your LAMBSEs may not reflect actual AFR. Having your LAMBSEs track AFR accurately is the intended effect of tuning your EEC. But the moderator of the site tries to get them deleted off as often as he can. As for technical advertising, there are a few different products that frequently come up that you'll hear people boosting. For instance the TwEECer RT vs the TwEECer (plain). The Moates chips you can burn yourself. BinEditor (which is free) and EEC Analzyer (which is ~$55). Then you hear people boosting the particular brand of MAF they use. But none of the people you hear boasting about these products are making a dime off those comments...at least not that I'm aware of. Those are unsolicited comments of support for products they've found to be useful. In fact the only regular to the board that has a product for sale is 86GT (Clint). He's the developer of EEC Analyzer and BinEditor. And the only thing you'll hear from him is how-to types of feedback. You'll never hear him "pushing" his product. He doesn't have to. We all have our opinions, ways of doing things, suggestions, and what-not. Some give better advice. Not to mention, these HEGOs are heated to stabilize the temp as the exhaust passes by them. I know I can turn my ignition on and leave it on for about a minute before cranking to let the HEGO heaters heat them, and I get a rich mix indication right at crank, when I know the exhaust has to be cooled quite heavily with a cold engine, cold exhaust port, cold header, cold pipes, etc. Maybe that's just because my HEGOs are relatively new and are still very responsive??? I always heard the issue with long-tubes and HEGOs was the delay in pickup due to the longer distance the gas has to travel AND the added volume the long-tubes can hold vs exhaust manifolds & shorties. I've also heard the EEC waits a certain amount of time (or is it crank rotations?) before reading the HEGO and associating the reading with a particular cylinder/bank. But I always thought that was more significant with batch-fire systems that use 1 HEGO to read both sides of the engine and thus the EEC needs an accurate account of which bank is running lean or rich and thus which LAMBSE to adjust. In the case of dual HEGOs, I wouldn't think HEGO sensory delay would be as big of a deal. Perhaps its the added delay itself that's causing the problems people see with long tubes. Added delay could make the adaptive strategy "hunt" too much...which results in way overshooting the LAMBSEs rich-n-lean. Thus the EEC is responding too quickly and needs to know how long to wait before assuming its adjustments have settled and been sensed before making another LAMBSE adjustment??? cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Mar 31, 2007 2:53 pm The stock pattern is right. And I too have seen what you are describing, but EA does that when you datalog isn't diverse enough and thus some RPM/Loads were never hit in your log so it is having to guess...and is guessing in the wrong direction. there is logic behind the guessing, but if there are too many blanks around the areas it is trying to guess for, it'll often guess a number that makes no sense. It usually indicates the numbers it is guessing by bolding them as opposed to normal font numbers being the ones it had a datalog to base off of. Are the numbers you see decreasing as load and RPM go up bold? Depending on your injector sizes, I'd go high 200s to low 300s at the lower RPM/Loads and have the values not exceed 580-600 on the higher RPM/Loads. For the higher RPM/Loads, my general rule of thumb (based on absolutely nothing concrete) is to have the injector stop before the crank is in the last 1/3rd of the intake valve duration regardless if EA calculates numbers higher. Why? 1. If you have a fast-lift and fall on your cam lobes (most aftermarket cams are a faster lift than stock), you don't want the injector still firing when the intake valve is just about closed. 2. With an aggressive, long-duration intake lobe, at lower RPMs, the cam may actually be allowing aspirated air from the cylinder to be pushed back up into the intake because the piston is moving upward with the valve still open. Long duration is beneficial at higher RPMs, but at lower RPMs, it can cause backflow. You'd prefer not to have that backflow blowing your fuel charge meant for the combustion chamber back up into the intake throwing your AFR mix. 3. At higher RPMs, you may not get the entire fuel charge for the air you are taking in if you don't limit when the injector stops firing. EA could calculate a stop time that's after the intake valve has closed (usually shows up as red numbers). EA does this trying to honor your desire to fire the injector at your defined start time. But in these cases, it's better to let the injector fire start time be earlier to ensure a complete charge of air mixes with the air being aspirated. If you don't care about emissions, none of this applies. But, if you have a slight overlap cam and you are trying to maintain emissions, then you'll want to make a tune to drive with, and another for passing the smog tests. The smog test tune would start the injectors AFTER the exhaust valve has closed. You do this so that any exhaust scavenging doesn't suck unburned intake air-fuel out the exhaust which shoots your hydrocarbon (HC) PPM counts up. Since smog tests are running the engine at mild to moderate cruising loads at lower RPMs, you should have no problems getting your entire injection pulse complete between when the exhaust valve closes and when the intake valve closes. However doing this does tend to run the engine a little rough due to less-than-optimal atomization time. With a no-overlap cam, it's generally preferable to fire the injector about 100° before the intake valve opens...that assumes 19-24lb injectors. That'd be much less with larger injectors like 42s. If you fire too early, you risk puddling which causes droplets of fuel to enter the combustion chamber and they don't atomize as well as the fuel being squirted during the air-charge. So you are back to a slightly rough or sluggish engine at lower RPMs. So if your overlap is only a degree or two, you might try running a tune like a 0-overlap cam would be run (firing on intake valve before it has opened). Make sense? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

My overlap is 1deg at .05, but about 30deg at absoute. I believe EA is calculating absolute closure when you choose that option. However when overlap is calculated, it's only calculated at .050" valve lift, not cam lobe lift. Like I said earlier, all cams have overlap. But unless the cam and rockers has the valves open wider than .050" at the same time, the overlap is considered negligible and to not exist. Cams with 1° overlap and 1.6 rockers, indicates there is 1° of crankshaft rotation where the exhaust and intake valves are both open wider than .050". If you look at the E303. It's a zero overlap cam with 1.6 rockers...but just barely. There's a theoretical moment when the intake and exhaust are at .050" but because it's only a single position, it's considered not to exist. However, if you run the E303 with 1.7 rockers, the E303 suddenly becomes an overlap cam because the same cam lobe lift will be exaggerated into a slightly higher valve lift which means with 1.7 rockers, there is more than just a crank position, but rather a range of crankshaft rotation where the valves are open greater than .050" (thanks to the added lift). I just wish EA showed this. But the way EA is setup, the values in the list are independent of rocker ratio with the exception of lift. I wish Clint could marry the values for each cam to a 1.6 ratio rocker, then in the background calculate actual cam lobe lift. Then with those number, when you switch to another rocker size like 1.7, you'd see that the duration increases (both at .006" advertised and .050") AND thus the calculation for overlap & lobe separation would increase as well. Currently to "see" this you have to do the math yourself and enter a custom cam configuration. Maybe that should be a feature request to upgrade EA to allow you to see the overlap/duration effects of increasing your rocker. EA does effectively recalculate the max lift, but it doesn't recalculate the duration, overlap, or .050" events. title: Calc/Est cam duration/events when changing rocker ratio - EECTuning.org

posts.content: cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Calc/Est cam duration/events when changing rocker ratio Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 01, 2007 4:59 pm Generally when you get a cam, it's got a series of values that describe the cam such as duration, overlap, lobe separation, etc etc. With the exception of max lift points, most of those values assume a specific rocker ratio since most of those values are measurements with respect to the valve, not the cam lobes. So, when you increase the rocker ratio (i.e. 1.6 to 1.7), then this increases the effective cam duration @ measured valve openings like @.006" & .050". So likewise, it is possible that a cam with 0 overlap using one rocker may have some overlap with a higher ratio rocker. But is there a calculator out there that easily recalculates these cam values as you change the rocker ratio? This topic came up in a different thread which got me to thinking more about it. I started looking around the Internet for a calculator or some formula that would allow you to "recalculate" a cam's parameters assuming a new rocker ratio. But I couldn't find anything. So I thought I'd start it as a new discussion and see what others know. The example being used over there was an E303, which is a 0-overlap cam (but just barely), will have overlap when using 1.7 rockers. With 1.6 rockers, there's only 1 theoretical engine position (abstracting out engineering tolerances) per cylinder that the intake and exhaust valves are open @.050" at the same time. With the E303, at this position they are BOTH exactly at .050" thus any movement forward or backward and one of the valves will be less than .050" and thus "effective overlap" doesn't exist. However if you put 1.7 rockers in. The intake and exhaust valve will be open further for any given crank position. Thus with the same cam, there's a region of rotation that the intake and exhaust valves are now open above .050" using the E303. However many degrees that region is will be the overlap value. What I want is a formula or an online calculator that'll take in a cam's 1.6 rocker-based values and recalculate (even if it's only an approximation) to what the duration, overlap, and lobe separation would be using 1.7 rockers. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 01, 2007 7:55 pm I agree, knowing the exact rate of the lift between .006 and .050 would be critical in getting a perfectly accurate number. I agree that the events points at which the valve begins and ends lift is the same regardless of rocker ratio. I also agree that the rate of lift will be increased. But once lift has begun, any given lift position on the cam results in lift on the valve at a direct proportion defined by the rocker ratio. If the cam lift is multiplied by the rocker ratio to give valve lift, and duration, overlap, and all that good stuff is defined by the valve lift (i.e. @.050"), not cam lobe lift, then that means with a greater rocker ratio, the valve will get to .050" quicker than it would with 1.6 rockers AND will take longer to get to .050" on the downside. So again, if things like overlap are also based on valve position, then rocker ratio will have a direct effect on what a cam's overlap value is. Thus if the E303 has a 220degree duration with 1.6 rockers. That means that there are 220degrees of crank rotation with the intake valve at or greater than .050" lift (open). If you put 1.7 rockers on, then 220degrees describes the crank rotation that the valve will be open at or greater than .0531", not .050". I got that number by taking .050", divide by 1.6 to get the cam's actual lift, then multiply by 1.7 to get the valve lift with 1.7 rockers. .050" valve lift / 1.6valve to cam ratio = 0.3125" cam lift .03125" cam lift * 1.7 valve to cam ratio = .053125" valve lift So, what I'm wanting to know is what the duration would be with a 1.7 rocker @.050". The difference between .053" and .050" is a few degrees at least. If you ASSUME the ratio between advertised and .050" lift is linear (which it isn't), then lets start with a cam lobe that's 220@.050" and 283@.006" using 1.6 rockers. 283 - 220 = 63 degrees between .050" and .006" valve lift .050 - .006 = .044" difference in lift between .050" and .006" valve lift So then you could say a flat-line ratio is 63 degrees per .044" (i.e. 63/.044= 1432 degrees/inch). Keep in mind, that's the average degree/inch ramp rate between .006" & .050" valve lift not the effective ramp rate. What I don't know is how much the error between effective and average throws my duration calculation (coming up). Also keep in mind at other locations on the cam lobe, this ramp rate value is different like as you approach the max lift. This value has to eventually reach 0, then increase again as the valve closes. So anyway, multiply 1432 deg/inch *. (.053125" - .050") = 1432 * (.003125") = 4.475 degrees difference between .053125" and .050". This is the duration increase of upgrading the rocker. So 220 degrees using 1.6 rockers + 4.475 additional duration using 1.7 rockers = 224.475 total duration with 1.7 rockers@.050". In the case of E303 cam, which was right on the bleeding edge of overlap, if both intake and exhaust durations are increased by the same amount of duration, then there are a few degrees of overlap now @.050" valve lift. But it's still 0-degree overlap cam if you consider overlap to only exist when both intake and exhaust valves are open at or above .053125" at the same time. I don't know the overlap math quite as well, but my gut feeling is the E303 would calculate to 4.475 degrees overlap@.050"...which is not a negligable amount of overlap. The only reason the overlap value is the same as the duration increase is because: 1. The intake and exhaust valve duration of the E303 are the same 2. There was EXACTLY 0 degrees of overlap on the E303 cam For other cams that are not nearly as close to overlap as E303, it would be nice to know how many degrees away from being an overlap the cam it is (i.e. what's the negative overlap value). Nice conservative cams like stocker cams, putting 1.7 rockers on may still give you no overlap@.050". But it'd be nice if there was a calculator out there to tell you stuff like this. Does all that make sense or have I completely fallen off my rocker with all that math? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

Lets exaggerate THAT a little further just in case my estimate of 10% is not as high as I thought and just double the potential error to a full +/-1° potential error just to cover ourselves. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Mar 31, 2007 5:55 pm I think I already know the answer, but I want to ask JUST IN CASE I'm wrong. If I'm wrong, I wanna know it. Does location in the pipe have any effect on WB accuracy? Obviously you'd want to be before CATs, but as far as distance from the headers, is there any difference? I've heard claims that the distance from the EM/header with narrow-bands has an effect on their accuracy. Some have even said it has to do with running the O2 cold. But to be honest, I just don't buy that they are going cold. The heater in HEGOs heats and maintains the tip at or above 600°F. Exhaust burns upwards of 2300°F (source Emission Controls - Demystifying Oxides of Nitrogen ) if it isn't enriched or "cooled" by things like EGR gases. However, depending on the engine is more in the range of 1000-1600°F for Closed Loop operation with proper EGR. That number goes up if you are running higher compression, forced induction, don't have the benefit of EGR, or just running really lean. So, can the exhaust cool to drop below what even the HEGO's heater can't maintain? MAYBE on a cold day at a pig-rich idle. But under sustained closed loop cruising loads? I have a hard time believing that it would. Sure, exhaust cools on it's way out the exhaust ports and through the header pipes, but that gas is moving FAST and is constantly being followed up with gas just as hot. I just don't see the gas getting the O2 sensor "cold". But I've been wrong before. As far as I know, any issues related to narrow-band exhaust placement would have more to do with pulse delay (i.e. when running long tube headers). That's my thinking, but like I said, I just wanted to ask since we were on the subject. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Feb 21, 2007 6:58 am If you are using an actual A9P EEC, you'll need to use the A9P strategy in the beta versions of CalEdit. It was a SNAFU that the earlier versions of CalEdit called the GUFC strategy A9M to start with. A9M doesn't even follow the same strategy that A9P does. A9M and A9L are part of the GUFB strategy. But A9P had to use the strategy wrongfully named A9M in the previous versions...that much is true. Like I said it's a ClusterF... However you may be having trouble datalogging if you chose all your datalogging choices were done with CalEdit set to A9M. Try switching to A9P strategy, make all your datalogging choices, click the Save checkbox, then click Payload button. At that point, you'll be prompted to save your choices. THAT will be what you want to use from now on until you come up with a different combination to datalog, then save that as a different payload name. Any other payloads you may have saved with CalEdit selected to a different strategy can be deleted to get them out of your list. I don't know why CalEdit doesn't disappear inappropriate payloads when it knows they aren't compatible with the selected strategy...But I could go on and on about the goofiness of CalEdit... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Apr 07, 2007 7:19 am At first, I used the accel fuel functions and table to enrich fuel on tip-in. The problem is this fuel contribution is only active while the throttle is moving. Not the second or two after it stops moving where lean tip-ins are most noticed. So adjusting these tables is going to do nothing but waste gas on throttle movements when it is probably already being compensated plenty for. What you want to do is attack the "time" after tip-in. In GUFx strategies, the Transient Fuel works pretty good for this. I don't know if it exists for CBAZA or not. You can also use the HEGO Bias to make the computer respond quicker to lean conditions. On GUFx, making the HEGO Bias negative, makes it favor rich conditions by speeding up the EEC's response to lean conditions but be a little more relaxed/slower/sluggish at correcting rich conditions. The further negative you go, the quicker it is to respond to lean and the less responsive it is to correct for rich. If you go too far, the EEC will start flagging HEGO switching codes because it isn't seeing the HEGOs switch fast enough. Same is true if you go positive, except the same behavior favors a lean condition and is quick to correct a rich condition on the HEGOs...never what you want except MAYBE at idle (hence why factory settings have positive values for the bottom row). What I did to help this was to adjust the transient multiplier scalars, and the transient fuel tables (set the 180 and 210 column equal to the 150 column except for the bottom two rows where idle is) as well as send the HEGO bias a little more negative during Load/RPMs that are more susceptible to lean tip-ins. You just don't want to go too far with those transients. The effects of transient fuel contribution is done AFTER the LAMBSEs are calculated. So if you over-compensate, the transient contribution is in effect for too long and you'll notice at times like idle, the LAMBSEs will adjust high trying to make up for too much transient compensation. Then they'll gradually drop back down as the transient fuel is being removed over time. It's weird. I just wish there was a more straight-forward way to compensate for lean tip-ins. However what I've found though is that having a MAF transfer or injector slopes that are off can cause lean tip-in conditions. In fact, what I do is purposely run my tune such that idle keeps the LAMBSEs in the low 13s and 12s. But loaded conditions stabilize the LAMBSEs in the 14s where they are supposed to be. The effect is when I tip-in, the LAMBSEs are already rich for the loaded tip-in, then adjust up to where they are supposed to be. This causes the engine to run lean on decel and for a few seconds at idle, but who cares if it's lean at decel? As long as the engine doesn't conk out at idle from being too lean, that strategy works for me. And under unloaded conditions like idle (I have a manual tranny), running a little lean doesn't seem to cause the engine any ill effects. But with an automatic where the engine does experience some load even at idle, this strategy may not be an option. Something to think about... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Apr 04, 2007 11:03 am It sounds like you are using an old version of CalEdit. Your "strategy" is actually GUFC. But as has been discussed 1000 times, CalEdit sux and has misnamed that strategy. Even the A9M processor doesn't use the A9M strategy in CalEdit 1.30A9...that's how lame it is. Point being, here's what I recommend, dump CalEdit as your tuning software. You are unfortunately stuck with CalEdit to setup your datalogging payload and to download your tune to the TwEECer, but you don't have to use it to make the actual adjustments nor do I recommend that you try. The GUFC (lamely called A9M) strategy coverage in CalEdit is poor. Instead, use BinEditor. With BinEditor, you can open up the GUFB strategy and then open the X3Z tune. Then copy/paste fuel injector info from the X3Z tune over to your GUFC/C3W1 tune. Since BinEditor doesn't come with a C3W1.bin, just start with the A9P.bin. It's REALLY close to a C3W1. You can also download the C3W.bin from here: Ford Fuel Injection BINs The A9P, A9T, C3W, and C3W1 are all going to be VERY similar since they all follow the GUFC strategy, so it doesn't matter which you start from in BinEditor. With your setup though, you will be adjusting the same parameters regardless of which one of those tunes you begin with. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 08, 2007 7:42 pm Widebands are good for a 2nd opinion on exhaust O2 conditions, but to be honest you can tune out most anything with the narrow bands for closed-loop tuning. The Widebands come into play when running open loop like at WOT. In these conditions, you are running the engine MUCH richer than you would in Closed Loop. Since the narrow-bands are only good to about 14-15.5 (or somewhere in that neighborhood), you can't use the narrow bands for WOT. You need a wideband to tell you what's happening when you expect the mix to be in the 11-13 AFR range. With a naturally aspirated engine, you can get away without a wideband and just "guess" at enrichment. If you ever go to a dyno, they can find what AFR and timing gets you max power at all the various WOT RPMs. Then you can program that in. As you continue to tune, it might be nice to have a wideband just to make sure what you are tweaking isn't throwing you away from what the dyno's confirmed is optimal for your engine setup. However if you have a supercharger, things are much more critical that you maintain a heavy enrichment. Going 13.5 AFR while at full boost could be a problem. A lot of the extra enrichment with a supercharger is often recommended/required, not for max power, but for combustion temp control so you don't do things like melt piston tops. In the case of a supercharger, I'd always recommend someone get a wideband. However if your WB is saying 13.6 and the EEC is switching the Narrowbands(NB) in CL, that would lead me to believe your WB transfer isn't quite right. When people say NBs are not accurate, what they mean is that they are no good outside their detection range (i.e. telling you if you are at 11.5 or 13.5 AFR). But within their "narrow" detection range, I'd think they should be accurate unless the NB is old. Personally, I'd use the NB as a gauge to indicate whether your WB transfer is tuned in or not. Others with correctly tuned WBs should be able to tell you exactly what AFR a NB reaches 0.0024v and about what AFR it's at .6v (generally what the EEC runs it up to during CL). As you get above .6v, the accuracy of the NB does diminish due to voltage losses. I've heard of some NBs getting into the .8s and .9v. But mine typically stay in the high .7s at WOT occasionally touching .8v, but I've never seen mine come close to .9v. Since the EEC never uses the NBs when they are "that" rich, it doesn't really matter. All the EEC cares about is that the NB goes above and below .45v. and it tries to maintain a fuel delivery that keeps the NBs going above and below .45. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top
