cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Apr 09, 2007 2:45 pm LAMBSE is what the EEC thinks the fuel being delivered should be creating for an AFR. So yes, it is a commanded value. When all is perfect, the AFR and LAMBSE values will be very close to the same. However LAMBSE and actual separate, not glide together when the tune is out. Thus if you are running 15 AFR and the EEC thinks you should be at 14.5 for the conditions, the EEC will eventually get wind of the lean condition via the HEGOs and start dropping the LAMBSE value in an effort to command more fuel until the actual AFR indicates rich via the HEGOs. Once the HEGOs hit rich, the EEC backs off until the HEGOs go lean. It will continue to enrich/lean causing the HEGOs to switch from lean to rich on a regular basis. The EEC never settles out with the HEGOs at a given voltage. Even though you are receiving a modulating voltage value from the HEGOs, the EEC doesn't treat them as "analog signals" but rather as digital inputs that are ON or OFF based on whether they are above or below .45v. I imagine the EECs today have the ability to hone in on the AFR a little tighter than they do, but this is actually done for emissions reasons. The CATs need oxygen to do what they do. So every "switch" the engine is run just lean enough to let oxygen slip into the exhaust to feed the CATs. But then the mix is enriched again. The oxygen sent down is then used to prevent the slightly rich mix while the HEGO was at high voltage from actually making it out the tailpipe. CATs are extremely efficient at cleaning up the exhaust as long as you don't veer far from 14.64 AFR (which the NBs don't). Once you start getting into the 13s, you start producing too many Carbon Monoxide (CO) and Hydro-Carbon (HC) molecules for the CATs to burn off. Both the CO and HC need stored Oxygen to finish off the combustion into Carbon Dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). So when the EEC is going lean, it's giving the CATs that oxygen to work with. Likewise as you go deep into the lean side of things, say high 15s and 16s, the engine starts producing Nitrogen Oxide (NOx) molecules which need to be broken back down into Nitrogen (N2) and Oxygen (O2). In the days before OBD-II, the smog pumps were designed to give the CATs the oxygen they needed. But after further development, they came up with better, more efficient, and more expensive CATs that can store a LOT more oxygen and don't require smog pump support. These higher quality CATs were needed to implement OBD-II since part of what OBD-II's effort was directed to adding those 2nd set of HEGOs that go after the CATs to make sure the CATs are working. Having smog pumps would mess up the reading the EEC got from the 2nd set of HEGOs so from what I understand, no engine from 96 up has smog pumps. This holds true with my 97 Explorer 302. The 96 Explorer 302 was the first EFI 302 to ever come from the factory without a smog pump. They didn't do so hot their 1st year passing emissions so Ford rushed a GT40 head redesign known now as the GT40 p head. There was no way around it, they had to move the spark plug to get a better burn hence why GT40p heads don't take MOST SBF headers. But with the relocation of the plug, removal of the EGR and smog pump bumps in the Exhaust flow, they actually made a better head. In fact, the GT40p head is the best flowing production cast iron head ever made by Ford for the 302! Go figure, it took emissions requirements to get Ford to make the head better. Later FMS came out with the GT40 turbo swirl aluminums and they beat the GT40p in flow by a good margin, but they should. They are aftermarket for one. They have bigger ports, bigger valves, and a bigger price tag. I think FMS also made a GT40x head but I don't know much about them. And like usual, I digress... ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sun Apr 08, 2007 2:37 pm For the most part the EEC does use LOAD and not LOADX. LOADX is also referred to as pecent load or preload. The LOADX will affect FN072A, FN1307 and FN1328. It is ideal to get the loadx down to a 100% level so that the three tables that use it do not have to be rescaled to 0-200. You can see that you will shoot right off the top of the table pretty easy when you are hitting 140 on the LOADX. If you have the EA installed you can goto the help files on the hard drive and the Load Matrix is in there as an excel. I forgot that I made it part of the installer of the EA. So to answer the question the LOADX will affect OL fuel. You can either do one of two things. You can set the preload scalar to bypass the LOADX calculation and then rescale the tables to 0-200 and move the data around in the tables or two get the SLL function dialed in to bring down the LOADX to within the 0-100 range so the tables are correct. Either way you go I do not think this is the root of the WOT AFR being so rich. I would tend to look at the WOT fuel multiplier and set it to 1.0 across the board and then use the fuel table to dial in what you want. Then do a few logs and dial in the MAF to get the WB to equal what you have in the table. I hope all of that makes sense. Which EEC are you using with what tune? The X3Z tune will cause lean decels and this is normal. If it is an A9L then that is a different story. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 08, 2007 8:55 pm If you run the X3Z tune, you'll see the PW go to 0.00ms on decel. It completely shuts off fuel...HEGOs and Wideband will go full lean because the engine is doing nothing but pumping air so the exhaust sees unburned intake air. As for your load being related to the MAF, it's related to a lot of things. Load is the direct result of airflow vs RPM compared to theoretical MAX (the CID). Sufficive to say MAF is not directly related to Load. Thus a any given MAF reading will give you a higher Load value at lower RPMs because the EEC knows that the higher the RPMs, the theoretical MAX air the engine can take in is higher. In reality, a naturally aspirated engine should never be able to hit 100% load because of inefficiencies that slow airflow down (i.e. MAF, TB, intake, head, exhaust restrictions). However, with a forced induction system, the supercharger can shove more air into the engine than the engine could pull in on its own thus emulating a higher CID engine and a higher compression engine all at the same time. So it's quite possible the engine is being fed more air by the supercharger at high loads than the CID@atomospheric pressures could possibly support. The EEC registers this surplus of intake air as Load above 100%. As for Load% (aka LoadX), it's my understanding that Load% takes Barometric pressure into account in an effort to indicate the engine's actual MAX power producing capacity as 100%. Thus in high altitudes, the amount of air registered by the MAF will be less than it would be at sealevel which lowers the actual Load for any given throttle/RPM condition. But Load% is supposed to compensate for this, taking into account the "thinner" air condition and report 100% when the engine is doing all it can under the conditions it's at. Some formulas the EEC is calculating need that. But most formulas just need to know how much air is coming in. However with the supercharger, you still want Load% to indicate actual engine MAX, not engine MAX relative to theoretical MAX (air intake and RPM vs CID). I think I got that right. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

So at 141%, you should be OK. A typical stock naturally aspirated engine will WOT around 75-80% LOAD. With a few external mods (exhaust, cold air intake system, K&N filter, bigger MAF, etc) you can bump that number up a a tad or two. But to get the number into the 90s, you have to replace major parts like heads, intakes, cams, and exhaust manifolds. But even then, THEORETICALLY, you still won't hit 100% load. In actuality, I think it can be done with tuned parts. If the intake runners are tuned , the exhaust has good scavenging, the TB and MAF as free-flowing as possible for the amount of air the engine can pull down, and cam is selected to match the other components, you can probably get bursts above 100%. But I have no clue by how much over... As for using the CID value to artificially lower the LOAD, that's a "hack" way of doing it. If you are paying $100/hr to be on a dyno, and doing that fixes a problem in a matter of a few seconds, then it makes a lot of sense to do things like that to save money especially if the tuner's just installing a generic burnt chip onto the EEC. But in your case, you are the tuner and have time, desire, and ability to tune it "right." Not to mention, you are looking at datalogs based on your tune mods, and then doing analysis on those datalogs. If you fake-out the system, then your logs will reflect this. That means, leave the CID to true, and tune the parameters around your engine to get the desired results. It can be done, and the guys on here with superchargers that have been through all this can help. As for me? I'm still running an all-stock motor so I'm not much help at all on the nitty-gritty of tuning for forced induction. And I have to agree, values in the 8:1 AFR ratio is TOO rich. posts.author: davidnc
posts.content: davidnc Regular Posts: 65 Joined: Sat Jun 04, 2005 4:26 pm Quote Post by davidnc » Mon Feb 26, 2007 9:05 pm I assume you have a fox style TB, since the 94/95 style TB has an iac air bypass screw to set the idle. I will recommend what I did with my 351w with a fox TB. Basically, the stock fox TB is set up for the idle airflow of a 5.0, whereas our stroked 347's and 351w's require more air at idle than a stock 5.0. I added the IAC plate with air bleeder screw (see timing advice needed thread). With this plate in place, I adjusted the TB blade stop screw to the correct position and got .97tps volts. I then adjusted the new air screw to get proper idle speed (disconnected spout and iac). Then did datalogs to get my idle air flow number (.997 in my case). Even if you do slot the TPS, the TB blade will be opened more than you want, and this will give an abrupt acceleration. Before adding the plate, I'd just touch the throttle and the tires would break loose. No I hav a much smoother and controllable throttle application, w/o the torque snap. 95 GT vert, 351w bored 30 over, forged dished pistons, 185AFR heads, mild cam (similar to e303, but with slight valve overlap), GT40 lightning intake, 70mm TB Fox conversion, LMAF, tko500, LT's, 180 deg stat TwEECer RT, full emissions. But based on the numbers I saw in these tables AND the numbers as they differ between A9L and X3Z, it seems that these functions were to blame for the hunting idle AND why the hunting went away as soon as you pull the Spark Block on the distributor. posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Sun Apr 08, 2007 8:56 am If you are going to negate all the values in the idle spark modifier tables then you'll need to reduce the spark in your tables accordingly. If there is no drift from your desired idle rpm these modifiers reduce the spark by some 25 - 30% so you ought to be reducing the last row/first few columns accordingly. Bear in mind that the spark idle modification is there because the spark can help stabilise the idle quicker than the ISC valve can and if you eliminate these tables there may be stalling issues or rough idling when the extra load from accessories is encountered. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 01, 2007 4:57 pm Wow, it sounds like there are quite a few unknowns there. Here's just a brain dump of what my plan of attack would be in this situation. The 1st thing you need to do is get under there and measure what the O2 voltages are and verify that what they are reading is what you are reading in the datalogs. If there's a significant discrepancy, then the issue is clear. You have some electrical issues either with the wire or with the EEC itself. However if the O2 sensor really is showing low voltages (indicating lean), then you can try swapping the two HEGOs and see if the problem follows the HEGOs or stays with the side of the engine. If the problem follows the HEGO, the problem's obvious. Replace the bad one. If the problem doesn't follow the HEGO, then I'd start thinking something else is wrong. My 1st thought here would be an exhaust gasket leak. When exhaust gaskets go bad, exhaust doesn't just go out, it also scavenges in outside air which obviously plays hell with an O2 sensor. Even if none of these are the problem, at least running through all this will give you more info about the problem than you got right now. The one thing you mention about the other HEGO though. You say it's staying at about .5v. Is it bouncing and averaging .5v or is it just stuck at .5v? In closed loop operation, it should bounce between 0-.6v. You'll see some intermittent voltages from time to time but for the most part, it should bounce (aka switch). ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 01, 2007 5:27 pm The timing increasing t0 40 then backing down is part of your timing table. Look in your tune at the timing table and you'll see what the timing will be for any given RPM/Load position. When you don't have a tuner, your only control over timing is twisting the dizzy. But with a tuner, you should ALWAYS keep the distributor at 10°BTDC because this is what the EEC expects for base advance. All values you use in the tuner will be actual with the EEC compensating as needed for that built-in 10°. The popping is generally the engine running lean. What you may have is one side of the engine running lean. With that one HEGO stuck at .5v, that would tend to lean that side of the motor while the other HEGO enriches the other side making some really weird and untypical stuff happen. My guess is you have multiple problems. But the only way to know what's what is to start verifying what the TwEECer is datalogging to see if the problem is the sensor or the wiring between the sensor and the EEC. Have fun with this. Having multiple problems ALWAYS complicates the diagnostic process. If you need further help, there are plenty of people on here that do a pretty good job of analyzing a datalog. Since you have a TwEECer RT, here's a list of the things I'd recommend you datalog. Others may suggest slightly different things, but this will get MOST of what anybody'd want to see: 1. MAF (not MAFV) 2. Closed Loop Indicator 3. LAMBSE1 4. LAMBSE2 5. KAMRF1 6. KAMRF2 7. Inj PW1 8. Inj PW2 9. HEGO1 10. HEGO2 11. Timing 12. TPS 13. Actual Load (not LoadX or Load%) 14. BAT voltage 15. RPM 16. Engine Coolant Temp Get as diverse of a log as you can, from cold-crank, light throttle, moderate acceleration from low to high RPMs (trying to stay in Closed Loop), and then a few solid WOTs from low in the RPMs to red-line. A decent datalog should be at least 10 minutes of driving. When you mail that log to someone, winzip it to compress it and include the BIN file you were running. If you aren't using BinEditor to tune your EEC, get it. Avoid trying to use CalEdit for doing the actual tuning. It doesn't save in *.BIN format, only it's proprietary *.ccf format. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

FYI, In my logs I saw O2 volts less than .1 upto a bonafied 1 volts when things were right. Normal closed loop swing was .2-.8 volts. From the description, your VERY lean, and my gut feeling is its lean enough to be outside of the eec's range to correct for it. Even though WOT seems to run ok, I bet its still lean there too. Why no check engine light with yours for the O2 sensors. I think here that you didn't drive it long enough to meet the criteria for tripping the O2 faults. I've seen this before on many cars. (totally stock) Now, what is causing the lean condition. Check the ECT (engine temp sensor), maf output (in the logs), fuel pressure. How are you checking fuel pressure? Static/idle is somewhat meaningless, you really need to check it when its popping/while your driving. Finally, the one piece of the puzzle, your stock injectors. How long have they been sitting? They could be gummed up. I assume you have 42s that you ran with the blower. You have a tweecer, I'd put them back in for testing purposes, with the stock maf. All you really should need to do is set high/low slopes in the scalars. (40.6/47 works well for me) This will put you slightly on the rich side, but once you confirmed if its the 24s that are the problem, you can just tweak the injector offset vs batt volts. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Mar 10, 2007 11:36 am As far as I know, the best way to get your injector offset right, you need EEC Analyzer to analyze a datalog on your system which has voltages that range from the highest to lowest running conditions. You usually get the highest voltages right after cranking in the morning. Once the engine has run for a while, the voltage is usually backed off a tad. With it backed off, turn on every electrical load in your vehicle (i.e. blower motor, windshield wiper motor, head lights, etc etc)...all while datalogging. Once you got a datalog with voltages from crank to fully electrically loaded (i.e. highest to lowest running voltages), then let EA calculate a new Injector Offset curve. Smooth out the curve where you didn't get voltages (i.e. below 10v and above 15v) and run with that. Without EA, I have no clue how to get this tuned in. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Mar 26, 2007 10:37 am If you never see your HEGOs go above .45v, then that'd be why you never go into CL. The EEC knows that it should be running very rich during crank and the 45 seconds after crank. So it expects to see the HEGOs go from 0v to something above .45v. In your case, the HEGOs are stuck at 0v, either due to a wiring issue or due to a tuning issue. You said the exhaust seems to "smell" rich which would tend to indicate this is not a tuning problem but rather something physical preventing the HEGOs from getting their signal to the EEC. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Mar 27, 2007 11:44 am The A9L was designed for 3-wire HEGOs. You have 4-wire HEGOs. The difference is the 3-wire HEGOs use the exhaust pipe as the HEGO sensor return, where the 4th wire in the 4-wire HEGOs is the sensor return and the exhaust isn't used for anything except to physically hold the HEGO. Ford found that using the exhaust, block, and chassis as a sensor return was problematic. I can't believe they ever thought that was a good idea, but whatever. That's the system you are using with an A9L processor. If you abandoned the 4th wire, then that would PERFECTLY explain why you have no readings at your EEC. Make sure you have the negative side of your O2 sensor wire wired to the ground lug the EEC is using for HEGO voltage feedback. If in doubt, run those two wires up to the EEC, and ground them on the ground lug the EEC uses right next to it. Use a wire thicker than what the HEGO uses to minimize resistance losses. If memory serves, the HEGO wires are similar colors thus it's difficult to tell which wire is what unless you have a wiring scematic and can tell which wire is what via the HEGO's connector. In the event you clipped the connector, you'll want to run the truck for a few minutes and use a volt meter and find which 2 wires have voltages around the .8v range. Then figure out the polarity (which is positive and negative). The other two wires will be the heater wires. I don't believe polarity really matters for them. As for the long tubes, yes you will need to do some tuning for the long-tube headers. That's the HEGO delay time (time to delay before associating a HEGO reading to a particular cylinder). But that's fine-tuning. First we gotta get you in the ballpark so you can get to fine-tuning. That means you need to get the HEGOs registering a voltage at the EEC during OL when you know the engine is rich. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Mar 28, 2007 10:53 am The good news is your HEGOs are indicating .8v at idle. That means they are working AND you are running rich. Now, you just need to find out what it's going to take to get the EEC to recognize that voltage. Again, what I'd do is take the positive wire you measured giving you .8v and run that into the EEC. Take the other wire and just to verify the concept, run a temporary line and run it from the negative wire on the HEGO up to the EEC's ground lug and hold it there with your finger (this is not a precise procedure obviously). But while datalogging, what you are looking for is the datalog to jump to the voltage you were getting with the meter. To do this test, the HEGO heaters don't need to be running. The heaters are only there to stabilize the tip temperature AND get the tips hot, quicker on cold starts so the EEC can go into CL sooner (it's mostly an emissions thing). But for this test, as long as the engine has been running for a few minutes and you got .8v on the meter, that should be more than enough for you to verify the EEC can detect the HEGO as described above. With all this setup, you should be able to touch the O2 negative to the ground lug and immediately see one of the datalogged HEGO voltages jump just as if you landed those wires to a volt meter. You can even confirm which pin is which by watching which HEGO updates in CalCon. title: SEFI vs Batch-Fire TFI distributors - EECTuning.org

posts.content: cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website SEFI vs Batch-Fire TFI distributors Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Apr 16, 2007 11:38 am Before MAF, all Ford injected engines used a Speed-Density method of fuel delivery. This method used the intake vacuum, RPM, intake air temp, TPS, and engine temp to determine how much fuel to deliver. These systems also used "banks" of injectors that fired together instead of firing each injector independently. With the advent of a MAF sensor, Ford also added the ability to fire injectors independently and called this system a Sequential Fire EFI or SEFI. One of the key things that helps the SEFI EECs to know "when" to fire the injectors is the distributor. In all TFI distributors, there are bars or fingers that pass by a Hall sensor (aka pickup) and create a square-wave PIP (Profile Ignition Pickup) signal that's used by the TFI module and the EEC. On SEFI controlled engines, the bar for the #1 cylinder is thinner than the other cylinders and thus creates a shorter wave than the other cylinders. This is how the SEFI EEC knows where the crank is and thus when to start firing the injectors. So my question is, do all TFI distributors (even ones on SD-equipped 302s) have the #1 finger/bar thinner than the others so any TFI distributor from a 302 roller block can be used on an SEFI EEC? I know there is a tip-in enrichment that is only contributed when the throttle is moving, and the rate of enrichment is related to the rate of movement on the throttle. However that's just tip-in. You assume you will be accelerating when you do this, but this is more emulating the result of a carb's Accelerator Pump Function, not really adding fuel as the car accelerates. This is what BinEditor has for details on this function: BinaryEditor wrote: FN1303 = Acceleration enrichment desired fuel flow table. Output = AE desired fuel flow. TAE is its synonom. X-input = Normalized throttle angle rate - FN019B Y-input = Normalized ECT - FN020B TAE (FN1303) = An 8x7 table of fuel flow as a function of throttle angle rate of change (TAR) and temperature. The temperature input can be ECT or ACT as defined by the combination [FRCTAE*ACT +(1-FRCTAE)*ECT]. The normalizing function for TAR is FN019B. The normalizing function for the ECT/ACT temperature combination is FN020B. So my question is, is this Accel Enrichment Fuel table (FN1303) a tip-in table or is this based on actual acceleration of the vehicle? If it truly is a vehicle accel fuel contribution, is it related to RPM acceleration or MPH acceleration? What about the Accel Enrichment vs TP function (FN331B)? Part of the AEFUEL equation: AEFUEL = AEM*TAE*FN331B*FN378/60 Input - throttle position (volts) Output = Multiplier According to this, the Accel scalar(s) play into the Accel function. I have previously posted the logic here, but AEFUEL basically is active until the TPS stops moving from a tip-in (is below threshold rate) or load stops increasing. posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Fri Apr 13, 2007 12:26 pm I think you're on the right track. As far as tip-in and larger TB's - here is my logic: AEM - increased from 0.39 - 0.6-0.8 just because engine has higher VE FN331B - increased the 2V multiplier from about 0.4 to 0.8 - this compensates for the huge increase in airflow an 85mm TB can provide down low FN1303 - I lowered AETAR from 20 to 15 so AEFUEL will activate at a lower TP rate. I then lowered the lowest column in FN1303 to 10 deg/sec from 17 so AEFUEL will have a look up in the table at the lower TP rate - again these changes are due to the larger TB. After you get the fuel in there and AEFUEL shuts off, then Transient Fuel (EFTRFF) is there to provide an orderly "decay" back to stoic AFR. The logic is much more complicated and mathematical, but if you can imagine a spike in AFR caused by AEFUEL, EFTRFF (transient fuel) is there to create an exponential decay back to stoic so that you do not get a lean undershoot after an accel since a very fast closed loop system will "chase it's tail" if not properly compensated. Transient Fuel is the needed compensation. INTENT The Transient Fuel Compensation Strategy (TFC) augments the closed/open loop fuel control to keep cylinder events at the desired air/fuel ratio during all engine transients. The goals are: . To eliminate lean air/fuel excursions during accelerations. . To eliminate rich air/fuel excursions during decelerations. The formula for accels is: EFTRFF=EFTR*60*MEFTRA where EFTR is: EFTR = KFT * [(EISF * MTEISF) - AISF)/(EFTC * MTEFTC)] The values of EISF & EFTC are derived from the values in the tables FN1321 & FN1322 respectively. I have changed the values in EISF by doubling the values in the 180F column in FN1321. This adds fuel (lengthens the decay) as this is on the top of the equation. You could also lower the values in FN1322 to increase the EFTR multiplier as they are on the bottom of the division in the equation. Yes, this affects decels since the decel formula is: EFTRFF=EFTR*60*MEFTRD I haven't experienced any issue with decels - in fact I think they are more stable and less likely to oscillate now. You could treat the lower load columns differently to deal with decels if you wanted. 428w now Top

In that case, transient contribution on tip-in-accelerations is like a ramp starting at TB tip-in and gradually decreasing to zero where CL is maintaining things from there. But you can't simply say "more fuel". With such a ramp, there are two ways fuel can be added: 1. How much fuel is being compensated with initially (the vertical height of the ramp) 2. How long to decay for (the horizontal aspect which is time) So when you say give it more fuel or take it away, you have to speak in terms of whether you are increasing the height of the ramp or the length of the ramp. In my case, the lean tip-ins only happen maybe 1-2 seconds after tip-in. So I don't think I need 6 seconds of decay, maybe 3 just to ease back into CL. That's on acceleration. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Apr 17, 2007 8:50 am LAMBSE is the EEC's expectancy of what the AFR will be ASSUMING the MAF curve and it's expectation of injector behavior are correct. When they aren't, you need a wideband to help you bring the tune in closer to what the components will actually do so the EEC's expectancy will be close, within reason, to what's really happening...at WOT. At Closed Loop conditions, you can use stock HEGO feedback to tune by. As far as where the LAMBSE comes from, there are two places you set this. 1. The OL Fuel Table 2. The WOT Functions that are a multiplier to add even more fuel under WOT conditions...based on RPM I believe if you are GUFx. My concern is that you were 16AFR at WOT and you were modifying the MAF to get your 11.98. The problem may have also been corrected by injector slopes. The high slope has a very direct effect on enrichment at WOTs. If it's too steep, the EEC will expect more fuel to be dumped than is actually being dumped by the injectors. But to be honest, when it comes to "using" the top end of the MAF curve to bring things in tighter, there's probably no reason not to. Unlike the lower parts of the curve that can be hit at various different RPM/Loads, the higher parts of the curve are generally only hit AT WOT so it doesn't really matter how you get it tuned in as long as it's tuned in...and certainly not giving you 16 AFR. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Apr 17, 2007 9:50 am I didn't answer your timing question. Again, this is done in two places. Go to your sealevel timing table and start setting the upper part of the tables to higher values. I think the 60-75 load rows are around the 21 degree area. Bump those up to about 27-28ish. If you are doing all this in BinaryEditor, select-drag the whole table, and copy it, then paste it in as the Altitude Spark table...overwriting whatever's there. I wouldn't increase these numbers much more. This is the table that's used to define timing when you are running Closed Loop. The chances of you being in CL at the top row are thin, but it could happen. So you don't really want to push these numbers too much. Then go to the WOT Spark Advance vs RPM function, and set it to be a degree or two above whatever you put into the table for each of the RPM ranges. That should get you right back where you want to be. With your setup and able to advance 9 degrees. Start bumping the WOT numbers up and up, 1 degree at a time until you start pinging the engine. AT that point, back off by 2 degrees in the RPMs you pinged and hold tight with that. You can continue to advance the other RPM ranges that didn't ping to see if they'll go any higher. But once you ping, back off that value by 2-2.5 degrees. If you don't you'll find that some tanks of gas will ping and others won't. Or that certain humidity & temp conditions will ping the engine even though you can find the edge of not pinging on the day you do these runs. When you get that close to ping, backing off a degree isn't going to make or break you. If you were on a dyno, what you'd do is enrich the fuel from your 11.98 down to 11.5 and see if that got rid of the ping before backing off the timing. As well, you'd also find if continuing to advance was actually giving you more power. Since ping is your only feedback of "too much timing", most people use this to gauge if they have gotten all the spark they can from an engine. But, there is a point at which advancing further isn't getting you anything more regardless of whether you are pinging or not. That point is referred to as MBT (Max Brake Torque). In the newer CBAZA EECs, there's an MBT spark table that defines the spark point that this occurs that's independent of ping. A dyno can find that spark point, but without it, the best you got is the ping feedback, datalogs, and the seat of your pants. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: stang&2Birds Gear Head Posts: 41 Joined: Sat Nov 04, 2006 1:01 am Quote Post by stang&2Birds » Mon Apr 16, 2007 3:24 am The PMAS guy can correct me if I'm wrong. :) All ProM/PMAS MAFs are calibrated to the same *base* curve for an specific curve (example 30# Fox scaling ). They then go a little further and calibrate the MAF for a specific filter setup (example, the IMHO, foolish cone file in the hot engine bay, or the smarter cold air kit). Also, they'll go a step further for forced setups and make it so that the MAF would run the EFI a little richer at the high end. Then, they give you a flow sheet for your unique MAF! Okay, now some more fun. :) The OLD style ProM MAFs can vary ~10%+ more from the base-line. The NEW style PMAS MAFs are similar to Ford OEM and can vary ~4% from the base-line. Of course, that's with the MAF calibrated for a specific filter setup . So, you really need the flow sheet for a ProM , and know what filter it was calibrated for. EEC: Electronic Engine Controller ECM: Electronic Control Module or Engine Control Module ECU: Electronic Control Unit MCU: Microprocessor Controlled Unit (generally a Mazda term, but it bleeds over to Ford occasionally) I've also heard of the TFI (Thick Film Ignition) Module referred to as the ECM or ECU. It's not really an ECM, however I do have to agree, there is some intelligence in that device. The EEC tells the TFI module what spark advance to apply using a PW communication method. Thus the EEC doesn't directly dictate when the coil will fire. That's left to the TFI module to do by monitoring the distributor PIP (Profile Ignition Pickup) and the spark advance being commanded by the EEC, then making it happen. The EEC does get to monitor the actual PIP signal though. This is particularly important when running a Sequential EFI system. SEFI distributors have a "thinner" bar that creates the PIP signal for the #1 cylinder which produces a shorter PIP signal when #1 comes up to bat. With that, the EEC knows where the crank is at and thus can time the injectors right. Batch fire Speed-Density systems could care less... Now I'm just rambling. If we calibrate a maf for a fox gt (mt1) 19lb injectors we adjust our maf to behave exactly like the stock maf attached to the stock airbox. Even if you have a velocity with filter attached, 75mm with cold air, protube with elbow in front of the maf.. we make them all act like the stock maf and airbox. if you buy it calibrated for 38lb injectors the curve will be the same shape as the stock but it will be twice as much air at the save voltage output (38/19=2). This we feel makes tuning much more simple for you guys. back in the day you always needed to put in the pro-m transfer function because the mafs were all over the place (10% or so.) not only did they not repeat from maf to maf, but they didn't match the stock curve shape very well. This was because of the sample tube style of metering the air. This is the reason we changed all of our mafs to the tonsil style elements. We also changed the way we calibrate. On other point is that Pro-m only used a couple of "curve shapes" fox, cob, 96+, and 96+cob. They would then screw with the calibrating to match all the different shapes, (focus,truck,02-04 gt, etc.) if you look at a pro-m flow sheet under the er/abs colum you will see error numbers like +20....-30 and so on. It made absolutely no sense, and it was impossible to tell if the maf actually matched the curve it was supposed to.. Example a fox maf flow sheet was supposed to be +6 at the bottom and +2 at the top. when a tuner would look at this he had no idea what car was supposed to look like what. What we do is have a separate curve for every car and airbox. If you look we have mt1,mt2,mt3,mt4 etc... Now you look at a pmas flow sheet and the error column, all zero's would be a perfect match to the stock curve in the pcm. Obviously we can't make all of our housings match the stock curve shape perfectly but you can at least look at our flow sheet and if you see something like +7% at 150 kg/hr you know that our maf deviates from the pcm curve by 7% at the point. One thing I should point out is that you can buy 50 velocity mafs with the same cal and all 50 will be within 4% of each other ( all having the +7% at 150 kg/hr). The 30 points on our site are the mean transfer functions for all our maf housings. But no maf we have will be more that 4% of those numbers. Hopefully this all makes sense and helps you guys out and explains why it was always so hard to tune Pro-M stuff. PMAS GURU Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Wed Apr 18, 2007 12:33 pm Just remember that the offset is called an offset because it is correcting for electro-mechanical delays in the injector. This is why the values change with battery voltage as obviously the solenoid in the injector will operate faster with more voltage applied across it (thus the offset is lower at higher voltages). So when you have an offset of 1mS and a duty cycle of 1mS, you are really only delivering fuel for 1mS, the other 1mS is lost due to the electro-mechanical delays in the injector. Obviously there is a "grey area" of what is "open" since some fuel is delivered during the transitions from closed to open and open to closed. The offset is definitely most critical at idle as if it is off significantly, fuel delivery could be significantly different than calculated by the ECU. People running underdrives will see voltage variations at idle as well making the values closer to 12V important as well. 428w now Top

The reason that the offset can't be specified knowing just the injector specs is that the offset delay is also a function of the injector drivers within the ECU. The injector has an input impedance (resistance) and the drivers have an output impedance (resistance). Holding the battery voltage constant, the current flowing through the injector's solenoid coil will vary based on the output impedance of the drivers within the ECU. This is why using the Lightning Offset curves for 42# Green Tops is questionable as the driver in the Lightning truck is likely different that the one in the ECU you are using. Even knowing the part number of the output driver device in the A9L, I can't even find a cross-referenced replacement part no matter how long I search - and I work with MOSFETs/bipolar transistors daily as a power design engineer! I think Ford used a custom part or custom part number, though perhaps someone has figured it out since (was a thread on the Yahoo TwEECer board about this). I could design a new driver in a heartbeat that could drive low-impedance injectors though - lol. 428w now Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Apr 19, 2007 3:51 pm First of all, I'd recommend you get BinaryEditor and don't try to do any tuning through CalEdit. Use it to download and set payload info only. If you have the $55 to upgrade your copy of BinaryEditor, you can get the ability to do datalogging and downloading right through BinaryEditor. If I were a newbie at tuning, I'd want as few tools and softwares to have to learn and get used to, so having a single tool like BinaryEditor would be worth the investment. BUT if cash is tight (when is it ever not?), then you can still get a good bit of benefit from the free version of BinaryEditor simply because it's not buggy like CalEdit, it's got common features like click-drag, right-click menus that are useful, etc etc. But to answer your question about what things you can do to your tune to get immediate results...that's probably going to begin and end in the spark tables&functions. This will allow you to run the distributor at 10° and get the WOT advance you want without creating driveability problems at the mid/light throttle conditions. The amount you can increase the spark is going to depend heavily on the fuel you run, the condition of the engine, etc etc. Just keep in mind that just because you aren't pinging doesn't mean you will get more power by further advancing. There is a point at which advancing timing further isn't getting you more power, regardless of whether the engine is audibly pinging or not. To a lesser extent, you can also play around with the fuel mix at WOT. I don't know enough about engines to know when a naturally aspirated engine runs better at 11:1 and when it runs better at 13:1 other than to say that higher compression engines, like forced induction (super/turbo charged) engines need additional enrichment. But I do know differnet engines crave different amounts of fuel to get optimum output. High compression and super/turbo engines genearally like a very rich mix, not so much because they make more power with more fuel, but to cool the combustion (richer mix burns at a lower temp). With a cooler burn, detonation isn't as quick as it would be with a higher temp so a little more advance can be gotten. I don't know if there's enough heat buildup in a stock motor to benefit from over-enrichment. The stock A9L (89-93 Mustang) tune enriches pretty liberally at WOT anyway. The OL fuel table is around 12.35 and the WOT multipliers get down into the .95s which gets you into the high 11s in places. But like I said, the HEGOs do stay low for longer on light throttle tip-in than they would under stabilized conditions. I think what's happening is Accel Enrichment action gives enrichment right at tip-in which throws the HEGOs high. And it's that second or two after tip-in when the CL action gets tires of seeing the HEGOs high and wants the HEGOs to switch. Since they are rich, it has to switch low. It just happens that when it is trying to see a low-switch by raising LAMBSEs is when they would've gone low anyway if CL hadn't been so impatient. So whatever causes the lean condition along with CL raising the LAMBSEs sometimes overshoots into the lean enough to cause hesitation. I tell you, it would be so nice if manufacturers would put wide-band or even moderate-band HEGOs on cars instead of narrow-bands. Then they could switch the HEGO at .3v and .6v. This way the EEC gets a sense of rich/lean severity, not just a binary Rich/Lean. If the condition went below say .2, they'd know to more aggressively correct for that lean condition and could possibly learn what driving conditions to expect lean tip-ins based on previous conditions where it had to respond more aggressively. But I'm sure that'd require a more involved programming and a faster processor and what they have works for a 100% stock application so there's next to no chance that'll ever happen. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Fri Apr 20, 2007 11:46 am Just a couple more comments. 1) you will inevitably see a little ring-out under certain conditions no matter how carefully you tune the transient fuel. It's not too big a deal if it's below the drivability threshold. 2) transient fuel, not accel fuel, is designed to minimize the negative overshoot after an accel by setting the AFR close to stoich on a gradually decaying slope (until the min threshold (TFCDED) is hit.) This is done specifically to combat the CL desire to quickly bring the mixture back to stoich (causing an overshoot). I know this concept is more difficult for the average tuner to grasp, but it is very powerful when understood and properly implemented as I have discovered. I spent over a year fighting the lean at/after tip-in bug - now I have no issue at all. Remember what I said in that other post about how changing the scaling for load (FN071) unintentionally messed up the alignment of rows in FN1321 - a critical table for transient fuel? You may not have changed your scaling, but there is still something to be learned from this... 428w now Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue Apr 10, 2007 2:22 pm garsten wrote: ...is there still a limit of only 16 parameters which can be datalogged?... Yeah, Clint worked on trying to get more parameters out of the TwEECer, but the 16 is a TwEECer limitation, not a software one. Until a better hardware solution comes out, 16's what you got. From what I understand, even with a 12MHz processor, 16 parameters updating as fast as they do saturate the USB bandwidth pretty good. An interesting tidbit of trivia is that the datalogging parameters are actually being stored as part of the BIN file upon download. I would've figured the TwEECer would its own memory to store what all it is datalogging. But evidently, memory was such a hot commodity at the time the TwEECer was developed, that unused space within the actual tune was commandeered for datalogging which terribly complicates the programming process that Clint had to go through to get datalogging to work...not to mention, it wasn't a very intuitive way of doing things. But then again, I'm sure Mike G. wasn't exactly interested in making an interface to his hardware easy and intuitive to others. The Tweecer's datalogging works by copying the payload variables from the 8061's internal ram and the eec's ram to the Tweecer so once you start copying large numbers of the variables you are going to affect the eec's operation by taking up cpu time. I'm not so sure about that. See when datalogging, the TwEECer isn't reading the EEC's memory directly. Since the MBus (the 8-bit bus the RAM and ROM are on) is shared, a J3 device like the TwEECer disables the on-board ROM and emulates that ROM with whatever tune you download to it. As a beneficial side-effect of being a member on the bus, a J3 device can eavesdrop on what the EEC is reading and writing to its RAM. Thus any piece of info stored in RAM such as the LAMBSEs, Timing, Voltage, etc, is "listened" for, not actively read by the TwEECer. So the throughput of datalogged info is as fast as the EEC is reading/writing to RAM. Most of the time the EEC is reading the ROM, but even at that, the frequency at which the EEC's processor touches RAM (for reads or writes) is not slow. I THINK there's also some filtering or some grouping of data going on at the hardware J3 level as well. The TwEECer doesn't send data just as fast as it hears it. If I understand correctly, it sends data in blocks (whole rows of the datalog). However at the MBus level, I'd think the EEC is actually accessing some pieces of info much more often than others. For instance airflow, HEGO values, ACT, or any of the other inputs are monitored by the EEC on some frequency and saved to memory as well as referenced when needed. However calculated values like the LAMBSEs and timing may be calculated and recalculated at a higher frequency depending on what the status of the engine is at (i.e. idling, at WOT, cruising Closed Loop, etc). But my GUESS is that all the values are "refreshed" to RAM on a minimum frequency which guarantees that you'll get a complete datalog row at that same frequency, even if some values in that row were actually updated more than once before being sent to the PC as a datalogged value. I don't know this to be true, but I could see it being potentially true. Given this, theoretically ANY read/write to memory could be relayed up to the PC if the bandwidth between the PC and the hardware is fat enough to support the data transfer plus the overhead required to transfer it (i.e. the packet of surrounding data explaining to the PC what is being sent to it). Thus nothing says the hardware has to wait for a row of data to be completed before sending it up to the PC...it could relay everything it hears to the PC as fast as it can IF the connection AND the J3 device can keep up with that. All those protocols and details have to be worked out. But I'm confident it can be done. It just needs to get done. Finding the time to do it and the expertise to mentor me along to be able to do it is another story. Anyone who has turned the distributor while the car is running will tell you that reducing timing will make the engine run slower. You will also notice your exhaust pipes heating up as one of the things the ECU does during warm-up is reduce timing to fire up the cats. posts.content: boss96 Tuning Addict Posts: 836 Joined: Thu Mar 06, 2003 3:02 pm Location: Ft Lauderdale Contact: Contact boss96 AOL OBD2 test switch settings Quote Post by boss96 » Wed Apr 25, 2007 5:21 pm This is from Mike Glover. Click on the obdII_MIL_sw scalar, then click the NOTES button in the lower right corner of caledit, there are notes regarding this parameter. It is a bit position flag, each position represents a specific obdII test: Bit Test 0 CAT_MIL_SW 1 CCM_MIL_SW 2 PURG_MIL_SW 3 SAIR_MIL_SW 4 FUEL_MIL_SW 5 EGO_MIL_SW 6 EGR_MIL_SW 7 MIS_MIL_SW Each bit position represents a value to reduce the scalar value Bit value 0 1 1 2 2 4 3 8 4 16 5 32 6 64 7 128 Default value of 247, changing to 246 turns off the cat temp mil. changing from 247 to 215 should turn off the EGO mil. you will need to do the same for the obdII_test_sw. 96 GT, Vortech Si trim,Procharger 3 core intercooler, forged bottom end, MAC longtubes, ported PI heads , Edelbrock intake, Crower cams-.580lift/234dur@.050, 80lb injectors, CDAN4/GGL4 processor. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Apr 25, 2007 8:10 pm You have Spark Idle Multipliers that are in effect as well. I don't think any are 1 by default. So whatever spark you define is getting reduced by those multiplier functions. What I did was reduce the multipler range AND put the top-end of the multiplier at 1. That way, your multiplier actual will be closer to what you see in the Spark Idle vs RPM Error. As well, I highly recommend you adjust your spark tables to be very close (within a few degrees) of what you see at idle. Otherwise, when you "tip out" of idle and into drive mode and start following the spark in those tables, you don't jump from 10-12 up to 28 which will cause a serious surge making any takeoff where you push on the gas even the slightest amount very jerky. An automatic has a better chance of absorbing this, but if you got a manual, it'll be almost impossible to get a smooth takeoff from a "rolling idle." cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu Apr 26, 2007 8:33 am This is what I have for each of the things that affect Spark Idle: Idle Drive RPM Scalar (DRBASE) set to 672 Idle Neutral RPM Scalar (NUBASE) set to 672 Spark Idle Mult vs Dashpot (FN839): 3.98_____1.000 0.09_____1.000 0.00_____0.898 0.00_____0.898 Spark Idle Mult vs Drive RPM Error (FN841D): 8192._____1.000 150.0_____0.977 0.000_____0.953 -150._____0.953 -8192_____0.953 -8192_____0.953 -8192_____0.953 Spark Idle Mult vs Neutral RPM Error (FN841N): 8192._____1.000 150.0_____0.977 0.000_____0.922 -150._____0.891 -8192_____0.852 -8192_____0.852 -8192_____0.852 Spark Idle Neutral vs ECT (FN180): 255_____0.00 0.0_____0.00 0.0_____0.00 0.0_____0.00 0.0_____0.00 0.0_____0.00 (basically this function is nulled out and I think it's that way by default) Spark Idle vs RPM Error (FN111): 8192._____23.00 350.0_____22.00 0.000_____21.00 -350._____20.00 -8192_____20.00 As well, I have my Sealevel and Alt Spark tables from 500-1100RPM/0.06-.30Load set to around 22 so that tipping out of idle (the above functions), into drive (the spark tables) doesn't give me a jolt as the spark advance transitions. Keeping these functions and the tables close in value has improved the transition dramatically. It used to be I would almost refuse to drive-idle the truck because I hated having to transition by pressing the throttle. EVERY TIME it would jerk and buck in 1st gear when I ever-so-slightly moved the throttle because the idle timing was around 18 and my tables were still at default 28. That's a 10 degree jump...and that's going to create a power differential. And when it happens suddenly with the truck in 1st gear, it was down right annoying. But now, I can press the throttle with no jerks or rough transitions at all. If I press lightly, I get a smooth acceleration and spark doesn't change more than about 2-3 degrees between idle (~19-20°) and drive (~22°). The increase of 2 degrees is probably a good thing as load is increasing. But not 10°... The only negative part to this is the engine is capable of producing much more torque for the fuel being used. But I have to mothball that capacity in order to get better drivability off-idle and get an unloaded idle-RPM that's reasonable (~675 RPM). And my daily commute includes idle-driving so idle performance is important to me. It's typical Atlanta rush-hour traffic...and this morning was no exception. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Thu Apr 26, 2007 10:46 am Well, if your after a flow sheet, the LMAF won't help. You don't get a flow sheet with it. Not having a flow sheet makes tuning a bit more difficult, but its not impossible. Having a flow sheet specific to your meter does not guarantee you won't have to tune the maf transfer. You shouldn't have to, but, thats not the case in real life. Most of the time small changes are necessary to get things right. SC cal vs N/A cal. The difference is about 15% between the two. The SC maf is actually cal'd LEANER since its meant to run without a chip/tune. This produces a higher voltage at lower flow rates when compared to the 42 N/A cal resulting in a richer mixture. (tricking the eec) Theoretically, you could load the 42 N/A transfer (provided by the tweecer software) and lean the entire curve by 15%. That should get you a drivable starting point. You will need a wideband to dial everything in, unless your really good at reading plugs. posts.author: JuiceSC
posts.content: JuiceSC Tuning Addict Posts: 1628 Joined: Tue Apr 27, 2004 1:50 pm Location: PA Contact: Contact JuiceSC ICQ Quote Post by JuiceSC » Sat Jun 17, 2006 9:34 am The cut over to WOT values is right around 75-80% load. As you noted, the eec uses the load to read from the different parts of fuel and timing tables. What happens when you put in a larger maf calibration is the load calculation gets jacked. Before I scaled down my load, I saw my combo hit 200% load. You want to NOT hit 200% laod. 330 CID works really well for my combo. I see max load of 140%, cruising load aroun 45%. Its safe to have the load error to the high side. The TPS breakpoint I belive will override the load calculation and force WOT. (this can cause hesitation obviously as you get into the throttle) The "Sealevel load scaling" function is the other way to alter calculated load. But working with this function you need to be very carefull. A small change makes a pretty big impact on calculated load. By raising the values you reduce calculated load. With this function you can target parts of the RPM range, where the cid scalar will shift the the load in the entire rpm range. For the most part, not changing either CID or sealevel load scaling will work. But as you suspect, it will command richer mixtures and less timing sooner than you need it. Killing the fuel economy, if there is such a thing on a forced induction car. 91 GT, A9P, systemax II, 75mm tb, AFP, 75mm Pro M, 42#, Vortech S trim, GT40 crate 5.0, BBK catted X, flows, Tremec 3550, Pro 5.0, 3.27 gears. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Apr 27, 2007 12:48 pm There are a few different things that affect fuel delivery and thus would cause commanded LAMBSEs to not be in sync with actual measured AFRs. 1. MAF Transfer 2. Injector slopes (both low and high) 3. Injector Breakpoint (as a function or scalar depending on your strategy) 4. Injector Offset The Injector Offset is generally only an issue at lower load conditions where the injector PWs are low. However any of the other 3 will affect the EEC's ability to predict the amount of fuel that is needed and thus command the proper injector PW to produce the intended AFR (as indicated by the LAMBSEs). If you are only interested in getting the LAMBSEs closer to actual during WOT pulls, then adjust the MAF curve in the airflow regions you identify are leaner than LAMBSE command. Personally, I wouldn't mess with the voltages. I'd increase the airflow values at the current voltages defined...and yes, increasing by the percentage difference you want is a good way to start. With a WB, you should be able to dial in the MAF to get you what you want at WOT. It's the Closed Loop fuel delivery conditions that are generally the bear to tune for because you have different PWs for different airflows depending on the part throttle RPM/Load condition. In those cases, the Slope/Breakpoint/Offsets matter more. The problem is, if you mess with injector slopes/breakpoint, you are messing with your WOT fuel delivery as well. So you gotta ask yourself, do you want to tune for WOT and ignore driveability, or do you want to tune for driveability, get that solid, THEN focus on WOT? Or do you want to tune for driveability, knowing that tweaks there are going to require retesting and redialing in of WOT every so often? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri Apr 27, 2007 1:21 pm If you repalced the stock MAF with a higher flowing MAF, it's pretty normal to get the MAF undervolt codes...particularly on deceleration. In the GUFB strategy, that's easily fixed by lowering the MAF Min Voltage scalar so the EEC doesn't throw a code about your aftermarket MAF reporting a lower voltage than what the factory MAF would've for the same condition. I assume CBAZA has the same scalars that can be modified. There's also a MAF Max Voltage scalar as well that can be increased, but to be honest, if you are pushing over 4.8v on your MAF, you might want to seriously consider a higher flowing MAF. Once you get this high in the voltage range, the MAF gets really inaccurate since very small bounces in voltage equate to really large differences in registered airflow. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: stangfreek94 Regular Posts: 210 Joined: Fri Jul 16, 2004 1:41 am Location: Eastern shore Maryland Quote Post by stangfreek94 » Mon Apr 30, 2007 2:24 am If you are running a blow thru setup, I'm not sure if this info will help or not. If you are draw thru, read on. Sounds like your bypass is backwashing your maf meter. Happened to me once. A word of advice, don't get into any boost, until you get it sorted out. You will most definately blow a head gasket. Now, I have a vortech. I installed a Mondo bypass. My meter was actually 13 inches in front of where I had my bypass plumbed back into the 4 in inlet pipe. When I was running the standard bosch type bypass, I never had any problem. When I was getting the backwash. My car would read lean on the wideband at idle, and super rich as soon as I touched the throttle, when it was actually super lean. The meter was getting bad airflow, due to the mondo returning so much more air. The bypassed air was just flooding my inlet pipe, running back thru the maf meter. I had to make a spoon shaped deflector, and weld it inside of the 4 inch inlet pipe, to divert the bypassed air toward the blower inlet. This was my only option, as I already had the bypass return as close the the blower inlet as possible. It wirked like a champ. First time I fired it up, everything straightened out. Not sure how your setup is, but you might try moving the bypass return as far away from the meter as possible< or rig up a deflector. Like, I did. When this was happening, and I was researching what could cause this. I couldn't believe that the maf could get backwashed like that. But, apparently I was mistaken. posts.author: Cougar5.0
posts.content: Cougar5.0 BIN Hacker Posts: 1880 Joined: Thu Mar 17, 2005 3:16 pm Location: New Hampshire Quote Post by Cougar5.0 » Sat Apr 28, 2007 7:56 pm The key thing about load scaling is how it EXPANDS or CONTRACTS the Y-axis (load) of the table it modifies (OL Fuel) based on RPM. This means that the Y-axis at low RPM's has MORE resolution where you need it at low RPM's (expanded) where loads can't possibly get to 100% (e.g. 0 - 70% load = 0 - 1.0 scaling) and LESS resolution at higher RPM's where loads can easily go closer to 100% (in my case: 0 - 120% load = 0 - 1.0 scaling - scale is compressed). This is a really cool idea as it makes the two-dimensional table a 3 dimensional table. Base OL table thus includes ECT, Load & RPM using % load scaling (FN035). Unfortunately this concept is difficult for most people to understand. Here is the list of tables that use loadx versus load again: If you eliminate load scaling you cannot use the enrichening cells at low RPM's as the load won't get high enough. Load scaling lets you make use of all of the cells in the Open Loop Fuel table - a good thing! Imagine that the top row is 1.0. If you set the Load Scaling vs RPM to the highest volumetric efficiency of the engine at each RPM point, you can take advantage of all the rows from 0 - 1.0 in the Base OL fuel table. This means the engine will always be able to enrich the mixture the same amount based on the PERCENT of it's capability at that RPM. Also, the OL Load Limit versus ECT (FN320A) will have a fixed load point for OL at all RPM's versus a varying trigger point for OL based on RPM when the Load Scaling function (FN035) is used. Does this make sense? Anybody see this function differently? 428w now Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Apr 30, 2007 8:34 am It's not intuitive that this is necessary, but the payload of things you want to datalog is actually a part of your tune. So, just as you'd modify a setting on a scalar/function/table, when you choose payloads, those are changes to what gets downloaded to the TwEECer. In the background, what you select is a list of things you want the EEC to relay from it's internal resources out the TwEECer, and the TwEECer relays that info up to the PC. If what the TwEECer is relaying up is different than what the PC is expecting, then you have a payload-mismatch and you get garbage for data...or no data in the case that the EEC was never told to relay anything. posts.author: 86GT
posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Tue May 01, 2007 3:27 am JuiceSC wrote: Just want to clarify, the datalog payload makes changes in Caledit and not your .ccf or .bin files. The payload stays with Caledit. So once you have your payload setup, you don't have to mess with it each time you load a new tune to the tweecer. (unless you want to change what your datalogging) This is not true. Cal Edit actually inserts bytes of data into the CCF before it is downloaded to the TwEECer. This byte information is what tells the EEC to monitor and push to the TwEECer. The TwEECer then sends this out the USB port. The PC then scales the data to a readable format. Ford used what they called a Calibration Console, hence the name of Mikes CalCon to monitor data. Mike figured out how ford did it and then put his own data in for the monitoring. When I read back the EEC with the BE it has the payload information in it. With the BE you can have four tunes each with different payloads and the BE can read back the payload information and start logging. Cal Con on the other hand uses a file called Payload.db that is used by CalCon to determine what is in the TwEECer. This same file is used no matter what switch setting you have the TwEECer on. This is why if the tunes have different payloads in them you will get garbage on one or more of the switch setting. 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

The details of what payload are chosen are kept separate from the "tune". That's true of both CalEdit and BinEditor...but that's by design. It doesn't have to be that way. In CalEdit, your payload choices are saved in the Payload.db file as Clint mentioned. So no matter what *.ccf or *.bin you open in CalEdit, the choice of payload will be independent of the tuning parameters we know of as scalars/functions/tables. What Clint was saying is that from the TwEECer's standpoint, the payload is part of the tune (the BIN file). In the background, CalEdit and BinEditor are actually modifying your tune's executable code in order to make datalogging possible. Literally the modifications are telling the EEC processor (i.e. 8061/8065) to read certain inputs (like the TPS, ACT, MAF, etc) and get various run-time values (LAMBSEs, KAMRFs, Inj PWs, RPMs, etc) and send those values to the TwEECer so the TwEECer can relay them up to the PC. This is not behavior the processor would've done otherwise. There also seems to be a TwEECer limitation of 16 payload items. Derek and Clint tried to hand-modify a BIN to give them 17 datalogged items just to see if it could be done and the TwEECer didn't like that. I take it, the TwEECer has some kind of internal buffer that only holds 16 things and can't handle more, even if the EEC processor is sending it. Point is, the tune modification to include payload only has to be done at download time so it can be kept separate from the actual *.BIN file. As I said before, that's by design so you can use that BIN file for other tunable platforms like Moates chips that don't yet do datalogging and could possibly be freaked out by the processor trying to send it info in a way it wasn't expecting. I also suspect that the performance differences people recognize between running a TwEECer and their same exact tune in a Moates chip is the EEC processor overhead that's having to go on to make datalogging work. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: Davin
posts.content: Davin Regular Posts: 82 Joined: Wed Sep 08, 2004 9:53 pm Quote Post by Davin » Fri Apr 27, 2007 10:48 am First read the "Getting Started" doc from files, its very helpful..next Bank Count = 1 update only - unchecked This might go without saying, but if you are going to mess with the injector slopes, I would make sure that the MAF Transfer function table is modified to reflect your C&L MAF sensor too (assuming this is calibrated for 24# inj). The timing should be set back to 10*. One thing I am learning, though is that just b/c you add timing to the global scaler or a table, does not mean that your EEC will run with that setting. I don't think that the scaler is added on top of the timing curve the same as manually setting it. Here is a simplified version of what I mean: EEC thinking... 1. Look at load and RPM and choose timing number from spark_bdln_table. 2. Adjust timing based on a/f, ECT, and/or ACT multipliers and functions if neccessary. 3. Add on global scaler value. 4. Compare this to the spark_base_table value based on load and RPM. 5. Take lower value. So if one of the tables has a lower value than the one you want, then it doesn't matter what you are trying to add with the timing scaler. I think this is why many people "55" out other tables so the EEC does not have a choice. 94 GT (J4J1/CBAZA): 347 (CHP 9.3:1), AFR 185 Heads, RPM II Intake, Edl 70MMTB, ProM30# MAF, 30# Inj, AFM B-21 cam, MAC LTs, Fluidyne Rad, MSD dizzy, etc... posts.content: Toy 94 GT Regular Posts: 180 Joined: Thu Apr 21, 2005 6:39 pm Quote Post by Toy 94 GT » Sun Apr 29, 2007 3:49 pm A MAF is not calibrated to injector size as it is to a specific max airflow. Now a specific size injector or larger will be needed to support that specific max airflow. If you maxed out your MAF it is because your engine requied more air then the MAF could measure. So you did the right thing by buying a new larger capacity MAF. With the Tweecer you can use any MAF with any injector size as long as they are not to large or to small for your engines requirements. I used a MAF for 19# injectors wiht my 24# injectors for a while but it was close to being maxed out. I swapped for a 24# MAF then upgraded to 42# for the blower. I am still using the 24# MAF but it is close to being maxed out. I have a PMAS 42# MAF that needs to be repaired. You should always configure the EEC (using Tweecer) for the specific MAF and injectors you are using. 1) Enter the info from the flow sheet included with your MAF into the MAF transfer function 2) Enter a new high slope, low slope and break point scalar for the new injectors. To give people a VERY crude, quick-n-dirty way of upgrading injectors without having the EEC tuned. 2. Give a good guideline of what MAF will support the airflow needed for the injectors being installed. See, running a MAF that is cal'd to 19lb injectors will MAX out (approach 5v) before a MAF cal'd to 30s. So if you installed 30lb injectors and you have an engine that can run them near capacity, your MAF will have maxed out long before...thus it's undersized. However if you installed 30s because you got a good deal on them, but your engine is better suited for 19 or 24s, then it makes better sense to size the MAF for 24lb injectors and tune the differences. I, myself, have an Explorer 302 in my Ranger that came with EV6 19lb injectors. The engine's been retrofitted back to 89-93 Mustang sensors and EEC. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed May 02, 2007 11:44 am For this setup, I'd recommend you figure on at least .65 BSFC, not .60. Even if the engine really is in the low .6s, you want to calculate worst case scenarios here. If you are running high boost (above 10 psi), you'll want to push that on up to about .68. Others with SCs, what are yall figuring BSFC to be? But besides, you might want to go straight to 42lb injectors and get that 42lb MAF. If you are maxing the injectors and MAF out that quickly, then this won't be that bad of an overkill. With the 42s, you can also loose the FMU. The 42s should be plenty big by themselves...they won't need help. From what I understand, 42s are often cheaper than 30s. As for your confusion over the MAF, you are right. You cannot change the MAF's reading without retubing it. I don't know anything about ProTube MAFs but it sounds like they use the same concept that C&L does, retube it to give a different reading. The way ANY MAF works is, it sticks MAF pickups (heated wires) into the airflow and measure the amount of current it takes to maintain the wire at a certain temp. The more air that flows, the more current that has to flow through the wire to keep it at the temperature setpt. This directly correlates to the mass of air passing through the MAF. Now the way the "adjustable" MAFs like C&L work is they vary the size of the bores in the tubes the pickup hangs in. In the case of C&L tubes, there are actually two different diameter bores in these tubes...an inlet bore and an exit bore. The pickup is always in the exit bore. You can make the pickup more or less sensitive to airflow by changing the diameter-ratio of those bores. For a MAF sized for larger injectors, there'll be a much larger exiting bore than incoming bore. So literally what you are doing to increase the calibration from say 19lb to 24lb injectors is slowing down the air that passes over the MAF pickups. So for the same amount of air passing through the MAF, you get a lower voltage with tube cal'd for 24lb injectors than you do for a tube cal'd for 19s. As a consequence of this slower airflow, you have to flow MORE air through the MAF before the sensor is maxed out at 5v which gives the same MAF frame a different MAF transfer (airflow vs voltage). So lets start there. 1800kg/hr = 3968lb/hr of air Assuming an AFR of 12:1 ratio, that's 3968/12= 331lb/hr of fuel Divide 331lb/hr by 8 injectors = 41.3lb/hr for each injector This means the 1800kg/hr MAF is better sized to 42lb injectors with 0% safety factor, not 60s. However if you figure on a 30% safety factor, this means the 60lb injectors won't put out but about 44-45lbs. As long as the engine won't max out the 1800kg/hr, then I'd say you sized about right. Assuming a .65 BSFC, the 60s will be a perfect fit for an engine putting out 500-550hp with 30% safety factor. Your calculations tie very well to what we saw on the dyno last year. We were running a different intake and different heads then, the blower had not been upgraded (now is a D1SC) and we still had the cats. With the 42's we read 430 rwhp. Assuming about 50HP lost due to drivetrain, and maybe it took another 30HP to drive the 9lbs boost we can conclude the motor was putting out just over 500HP at the crank. As it approached 6000RPM the injecotrs reached saturation (DC close to 100%) and as it went over 6000RPM the AFR crossed over into dangerous 14.0+ : 1 territory. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Apr 25, 2007 12:29 pm Timing tuning without a dyno is simple. Advance until you ping. Then back off 2 degrees. The only feedback us without dynos have is "ping" and without a knock sensor to monitor, you can't detect ping in a datalog. That's about as good as you'll get without a dyno. Unfortunately, MAX Brake-Torque (MBT) production and ping happen at different degrees of timing. Some engines may produce more torque with more advance and were pinging 4 degrees ago. Other engines may quit producing more torque with advance, but not ping for another few degrees. But generally speaking, MBT and Ping are within a few degrees of each other. So as long as you are 2 degrees from ping, you are probably about as close as you'll get without shelling out dollars to measure your output. However with a dyno, you simply advance until the torque quits increasing OR you start pinging (whichever comes 1st). It's more tedious than it is interesting. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top
