cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sun Apr 22, 2007 12:44 pm The computer isn't really trying to "control" fuel pressure. You see fuel pressure rise and lower as vacuum in the intake rises and lowers. The computer is relying on the injectors to deliver a very defined amount of fuel at any given RPM/Load condition (as defined by injector slopes/offset/breakpoint). Well, as the pressure in the intake lowers, the injectors would deliver more fuel because the differential pressure across the injector is greater. To keep the differential the same, a pressure regulator lowers line pressure by the same amount as what drops in the intake. My guess as to why you are seeing higher fuel pressure with adaptive control is that the effect of that is less vacuum. Perhaps the EEC was over-enriching the mix causing the engine to bog and pull in more air to maintain the idle which would explain the lower vacuum. I don't have a good explanation of why you are seeing something different at WOT. Another thing I want to point out is the difference between adaptive control and adaptive learning. Adaptive control is what we casually refer to as Closed Loop control. This uses HEGO feedback to adjust LAMBSE controls. Adaptive learning is the EEC's ability to learn stabilized mix control and adjust for it so it can "predict" mix conditions based on previous conditions. This is what defines KAMRFs. So when you refer to disabling adaptive, are you referring to disabling Closed Loop control or learning? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Wed Apr 25, 2007 10:46 am Your test of the FPR is good. For every PSI you put into the FPR, you should see the fuel line pressure raise by the same amount. Likewise, as you pull a vacuum on the FPR, you should see the fuel line pressure drop by the same amount. However what this doesn't take into consideration is that at lower vacuum conditions (i.e. hard acceleration and WOT), fuel consumption is higher than it will be during your pressure test with the car sitting still. Point being, if your pressure tests come out indicating that your FPR is working as designed with the engine idling, then the problem may be undersized fuel pump or too much restriction in the lines caused by undersized fuel lines or dirty fuel filter. I don't know at what point stock fuel lines become incapable of supplying the fuel needed to run the car, but it seems people rip out their stock lines for larger diameter lines and high-flow fuel filter when they install injectors larger than ~30lb/hr. Does that sound about right? If you do find you are running into fuel delivery issues and you replace your lines, use ethanol-resistant lines. Even if you never plan to run E85, which is rather destructive to most rubbers, you will most likely run E10 and soon E20 through your system. Since 1988, car manufacturers have been required to design vehicles to be tolerant of concentrations of ethanol up to E20. However if you replace stock components, you'll just need to keep this in mind and make sure you aren't installing a line that will break down over time as ethanol concentrations in our pump gas rise in the next few years. I think it goes without saying that rupturing a rubber fuel line right on top of a nice, hot header would probably end in disaster. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Fri May 04, 2007 10:19 am I would've figured for a mild motor with all-stock equipment on it like mine, that I wouldn't have ever had an idle problem, but due to whatever I've tweaked in my tune (and starting with a Cobra tune) set things off enough that the engine was surging at idle. What I was seeing is that the timing would go up as RPMs dropped. When this happened, this extra timing gave the engine more torque so the engine raised in RPM, which caused timing to go down. So the engine dropped in RPMs. From that point on, it was a snowballing effect that if left alone would have my RPMs bouncing from 700-950RPMs. It was though the Spark Idle strategy was overshooting adjustments. So what I did was restricted the range of adjustment it had as well as set the Spark Idle multipliers closer to 1 so when I tipped out of idle into a drive strategy, the timing was closer and didn't cause the engine to surge with power on takeoff. Here are 2 threads that might help: A9L - what determins idle timing exactly? New Tweecer user needs help getting rid of surging idle These were discussions of idle control techniques using the A9L. I don't know if CBAZA has the same functions. But I'd imagine there are some, at least, similar functions to play with. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: codedout Tuning Addict Posts: 691 Joined: Sun Mar 26, 2006 11:49 am Location: Hollywood/tampa, FL Contact: Contact codedout Website Yahoo Messenger AOL Quote Post by codedout » Fri May 04, 2007 12:53 pm Yup..... you dont have your idle dialed in correctly, it is failing over to timing control. You need to work some more on you MAF and you ISC idle airflow. Start with the MAF, then fine tune with the ISC idle airflow. Its a pin in the A$$, you have to do it at cold start and hot start, and then average them to get it nailed. Have some patience and you will get there. ---edit---- Also make sure you dont have too much timing in at idle this will do the same thing. Good way to check this is to use a vacuum gauge and make sure you are not getting surging vacuum at idle, if you are then bump up the idle till it goes awaay before you start tuning. If you are getting surgin vacuum, It will affect fuel pressure, and will be next to impossible to get it dialed in. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue May 08, 2007 8:27 pm If it was dropping to 9 at WOT, then your program is calling for a constantly enriching mix, not reacting to a condition. The EEC isn't responding to a lean condition for two reasons: You are in OL which ignores HEGO feedback Stock HEGOs are narrow band so even a 14:1 mix, which is considered lean at WOT would register as being rich with the stock HEGOs Without a wideband, it's very difficult to know how accurate your MAF is at the top-end. You can get close to finding out and that's by allowing CL to stay active for longer. This is done with a combination of tweaks: You need to increase the TPS voltage scalars that force OL and WOT from the stock 2.7v to somewhere around 3-3.2v Increase the seconds to force OL at high load to something like 30 seconds With this, you'll be able to press the accelerator further, for longer before the EEC forces OL. If you can get the EEC to stay in CL up into the 500kg/hr range, then you can get an idea as to whether your MAF is accurate at that range. IF it isn't, adjust it till it is. THEN when your EEC commands 12:1, it'll be much closer to actually being 12:1. Right now, you know what it is trying for via the LAMBSEs, but without a wideband, you really don't know where it is. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Sat Apr 14, 2007 12:35 am Whe I start from scratch I tend to put both slope to the same and eliminate the breakpoint for starters. I then enter in the known good MAF. Sometimes this requires going backwards and placing the factory airbox and MAF back in. This allows for only one change which is th injectors. I then use the EA to dial in the injector offset curve to get the slopes close. Say within +-3 percent. Then use EA to get the slope calulation within +- 1 or 2 percent. Lastley tweak slopes and breakpoint to get the rest of the curve dialed in. Once all that is done then you can place you new MAF in and only deal with the MAF curve. (startup hot&cold, part throttle drivability, fuel milage, etc.) You need to let the tune "mature". (this doesn't apply if adaptive is disabled) You should not ignore KAMRFs. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Apr 14, 2007 9:43 am I haven't had much luck at all with EA calculating injector slopes that make sense. I feel like the calculations EA is using make sense theoretically and "should" be right, but I don't think the outcome is right. When I use EA's suggestions, it always is in the direction that will enrich things when my tune is already running too rich. What's to blame for that? I have no clue. So what I do is put in a MAF curve that represents my MAF as close as possible (i.e. what the mfg said the MAF flows) then I start adjusting the injector low slopes and breakpoint. With everything set the way "it should be", my system runs rich at all locations...more so at lower loads which causes lean tip-ins like you wouldn't believe with the LAMBSEs compensating for the very rich condition at idle and lower loads, then having to adjust down for higher loads. To compensate, I adjust the breakpoint and low slope to get my low load close to Stoic. In fact, I rather prefer my lower loads (idle loads) to run just SLIGHTLY on the lean side (low 14s and high 13 LAMBSEs) so that as I transition into higher loads, the LAMBSEs are on the rich side and enter into potential lean tip-ins slightly prepared. To prevent the engine from learning out my attempts via the KAMRFs, I have those RPM/Load locations reference in the Adaptive Table so they can't learn. If you are reading this and don't know what that means, check out this thread that talks about setting up the Adaptive Learning table (FN1325) and using positive and negative values. Since the low slope and breakpoint do have an effect on the way the top end, just not nearly as much as high slope, and high slope has very little effect on low load conditions, I always start with them. I believe this is even more recognized with larger injectors than with stock sized injectors that idle in the range controlled by the high slope. With big injectors, it's possible that idle fuel delivery is completely unaffected by high slope (someone correct me if I'm wrong there). After the low slope and breakpoint are working for me and transitioning to high slope smoothly, I run some hard, but Closed Loop accelerations at various RPMs from idle up to 4500RPMs and see if the injector slope I have is giving me rich or lean conditions on the high end of the MAF curve. Since I don't have a wideband, I set the EEC scalars that control when I go OL to delay going OL as long as possible so I can keep the HEGOs switching as far up the MAF curve as possible so I know where I'm at. Based on whether CL hard accelerations are rich or lean, I adjust accordingly to get to stoic at these hard-acceleration conditions. After doing all this, it won't be perfect when you are done. In fact, you know you are close when some places are lean and others are rich as opposed to the entire spectrum being rich or lean. Once you get some places lean and others rich, that's about the best you'll get with the injector slopes. Leave'em where they are and start dialing in the MAF to massage out the rest. The X-factor in all this is the Injector Offset. I haven't found a really, really good way to handle this one. I can't decide whether it makes more sense to tune this in before or after the slopes/breakpoint or the MAF. If I ever come up with a good procedure that works, I'll let you know. But for now, I'm "trying" to ignore the injector offset and get the slopes/MAF dialed in, then I just "check" the offset to see what's changing. Sometimes I get weird spikes in it that are obviously not right. Other times, it makes a smooth curve. When it is smooth, it is usually lean everywhere. I think EA was indicating all locations were rich because the whole spectrum was rich last time I did an offset calculation. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Sat Apr 14, 2007 9:28 pm Adjusting the slopes in closer to actual will bring the KAMRFs in closer together. You can't fully tune out bad slope values using the MAF. The reason is you can get the same MAF reading at different PWs. For instance, a high RPM at light load will give you particular flow at a particular Injector PW. At a lower RPM/higher load, you may get the same MAF flow reading, but the PW will be different. The problem comes in that if your injector slopes aren't close, then when you go to tune your MAF, you may find that at any given flowrate, certain RPM/Loads that flow is too rich. At other RPM/Loads that same flowrate is too lean. Thus you can't tune that out. Your only hope is to let the KAMRFs adjust to make up the slop and learn where the lean and rich positions are. So if you are having problems getting your KAMRFs to stay around 1 but your MAF curve looks dead-on from EA or is constantly either lean or rich and you can't get it dialed in...it just keeps jumping around, inaccurate injector slopes may be the problem. The good news is you have KAMRFs to absorb the slop. So if you don't get the injector slopes perfect, the KAMRFs can help. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Apr 16, 2007 1:27 pm The EEC calculates how much fuel to deliver based on the MAF and based on the injector slope/breakpoint/offsets. In the case I was referring to, it is possible to have the same MAF reading at different RPM/Loads. And in these different RPM/Load conditions, the MAF looks like it is reporting too much air is flowing causing things to be rich and in other RPM/Load conditions the MAF looks like it isn't reporting enough air is flowing causing things to be lean. The actual airflow in each instance is close to the same. What's different is the amount of fuel the EEC was expecting the injectors to deliver based on injector slope, breakpoint, & offset. Lets just use some numbers so we don't get all twisted up. Assume the MAF is pulling in 100kg/hr of air for both these scenarios (I'm using my datalogs and the Mapping function in EA to come up with these examples and I've rounded the numbers so not to get bogged down in the details). For the 1st RPM/Load condition lets say RPMs are 900 and load is at 40%. PW might be 10ms (these are 19lb injectors). For the 2nd RPM/Load condition lets say RPMs are 1500 and load is at 20%. The MAF may read 100kg/hr for both these conditions, but the engine is spinning much faster at 1500RPMs than at 900RPMs, so there are more injector pulse-events at 1500 than at 900. Since it is the same amount of air, it makes sense that the pulses are going to have to be smaller to ultimately deliver the same amount of fuel. So lets say the PW is now 5ms. Well if the EEC is calculating the expected behavior of the injectors wrong because of bad slope/breakpoints, then it may expect less fuel than actual from the injector at 10ms than what they are actually delivering. As well, it may expect more fuel than actual at 5ms. Given that, the LAMBSEs will appear rich for one condition and lean for the other...but it's the same flowrate measurement from the MAF thus you won't fix this problem by adjusting the MAF curve. If you try, you'll correct one RPM/Load condition, but make the other possible condition for this same airflow further off. In this case, fixing the EEC's expectancy of Injector behavior (adjusting slopes&breakpoint) is the only way to make things more consistent so that if the MAF is indicating too much air, it'll indicate too much air for all possible RPM/Load conditions that flow that particular amount of air. Under that condition, adjusting the MAF curve fixes something. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Mon Apr 16, 2007 10:26 pm You got it. With the same MAF flowrates, the injector PWs can be different and thus if the EEC's expectation of what the Injectors will deliver is not right, the LAMBSEs could appear rich in places and lean in other places with the same flowrates. As for setting the injector slopes the same, I'd say that's probably a good place to start if you have no clue. That at least gives you a starting point to start tuning from. But I don't think that's how you want to run on a regular basis unless there's some dynamic to this strategy I'm not aware of. It's also possible it ends up that this just works with no issues. As for the comment about entering the MAF curve and completely tuning using slopes/breakpoint and offset, I'd say that's probably the best way to start, but not the best way to end. In a perfect setup with a custom MAF curve (i.e. a MAF's measured flow curve, not a generic curve), I'd say starting with that and trying to fit slopes/breakpoint/offset info to get the LAMBSEs as close to stoic as possible is the BEST way to start . But ultimately, there's only a limited amount of control you have with injector slopes and breakpoint. Get as close as you can with these. Use EA's mapping (averaging) function to verify that MAF readings are yielding very close LAMBSEs for any given flowrate (i.e. you don't have 13s in one place and 15s for the same flowrate at a different RPM/Load). Once your MAF flows are consistent (even if rich or lean) at different RPM/Loads , this means the EEC has the injector behavior solid. At this point, start honing in on the MAF curve to get the LAMBSEs to 14.64. With some luck, it'll be mid 14s at all locations once you get the MAF curve tuned in. At this point, you've tuned in stable running. If there are any transient issues, you can easily attack these with injector/MAF dialed in. But you are right, it takes some time to wrap your mind around the dynamics of this. I stared and stared at my datalogs trying to figure out why my MAF never would get dialed in. I asked Clint to add MAF & PW to EA's mapping list, and that's when I was able to see it clear as day. And it was obvious, MAF tuning wasn't going to fix my problems because the MAF was rich AND lean for the same flowrates. It was going to require injector slope work to get things right. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.content: 86GT BE/EA Developer Posts: 5145 Joined: Sat Feb 22, 2003 11:19 pm Location: Dixon, California Contact: Contact 86GT Website Quote Post by 86GT » Mon Apr 23, 2007 4:59 pm Not to sure how you got from 45 down to 41.37 but the formula is as follows: When the base fuel line pressure is different than the rated injector pressure, then the injectors will flow differently than rated according the following formula. FN = F0 x SQRT(PN/P0), where FN equals the new flow rate when the differential fuel line pressure is PN and the injector has a rated flow rate of F0 at a rated pressure of P0. The differential fuel line pressure (psi) is the difference between the actual line pressure and the boost pressure in the manifold. Our cars are designed to maintain a 43 psi differential pressure. This means the 45 lb/hr at 43.5psi is equal to 43.152 at 40psi not 41.37 1967 Mustang Build Up Using EDS2 Calibration Owner/Creator EEC Analyzer & Binary Editor Core Tuning Strategies Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu May 10, 2007 1:06 pm Yes. The EEC has a desired RPM it is trying to target. I think it is based off of the idle RPM scalars, but there's other math that goes into the actual number that defines the idle RPM setpoint. The computer uses this setpt value to determine an RPM Error (the difference between setpt and actual). The Spark Idle functions will adjust spark based on the amount of RPM Error. When the engine is running faster than setpt, it pulls timing to get the RPMs to come down. If the engine is lower than setpt, the spark is allowed to increase. The problem is if you give the EEC too much control, it'll overcompensate and have your engine hunting at idle where it is constantly going above and below setpt. So what I did to get control of idle was to take some of that leeway to adjust spark away from the EEC so it couldn't change spark quite so much, so fast...and that calmed my idle. This gives the engine time to respond to the changes. It idles and accelerates off-idle quite smooth now, smoother than it EVER did before I played with those Spark Idle functions. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu May 10, 2007 1:40 pm No when you pull the wire off the IAC valve, it should close. As for your EEC metering all the air...not necessarily. In closed loop, if extra air was getting in, the HEGOs would tell it to adjust and the EEC would regardless of whether it was metering the extra air or not. It'll adjust the LAMBSEs all the way to their endpoint to keep the HEGOs switching. Thus if you KNOW for a fact that your MAF curve is accurate at the idle airflow rates, then leaking air explains why you are seeing LAMBSEs in the 13s. More air is getting in than what the EEC is expecting, so it is having enrich more than it expected to keep the HEGOs switching. However in the case of my tune, I purposely run my idle air flows in the 13s so tip-ins will be rich not lean. I also prevent the EEC from learning the LAMBSEs back up to the 14s in the idle RPM/Loads. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu May 24, 2007 2:51 pm I don't have a forced induction system, so take this with a grain of salt. But if I did, this is what I'd do. I'd get a Wideband O2 sensor so I'd know exactly where my AFR is. With that in hand, I'd crank the engine and get it driveable. Then drive it around lightly while watching the WB on light accelerations. Once I got it driving around the neighborhood without any surprises, I'd verify that it isn't going lean on me at light throttle (no boost) on an open road. To do this, I'd make sure to get it high in the RPMs with light acceleration to get the most airflow through the MAF as possible so I could tell if I had any AFR issues with my MAF/Injector Slopes. I'll need high RPMs to get into the mid part of the MAF curve without heavily loading the motor. Next, adjust as necessary to get my LAMBSEs to give me what the WB is saying things actually are. Up to this point, all my runs may be in Closed Loop since the engine won't be pressed hard enough to warrant OL/WOT. Once I got things giving me the AFR I expect at sub-boost manifold pressures, then I'd start easing into the boost area at lower RPMs while watching the WB like a hawk to make sure I'm not going lean. I'd expect at the lower RPMs in light boost, the MAF will be measuring in the airflow range already verified at high RPMs and no boost. So what happens if the WB indicates you are going significantly leaner than the datalogged LAMBSEs at low RPM boost conditions? Verify the MAF is reading at or below flowrates that you verified were good at high RPM/Light Loads earlier. If you are significantly leaner than the LAMBSEs for the same MAF flowrates as you verified earlier, then you likely have some other problem (i.e. Injector Slope/Breakpoints aren't close, loosing fuel pressure, etc). If you have the injector slopes pooched, you'll see the effects at higher loads more readily because the injector PWs will be higher. The higher the PW, the more evident error in injector slopes. But to guarantee that you start off being too rich instead of too lean, I'd say lower your Injector High Slope and/or Injector Breakpoint to a value below what they are. You will be running 42lb injectors which typically take a low-slope of 50. I can't remember the breakpoint. Set the breakpoint really low. Doing this reduces the effect of the low slope. If you are REALLY paranoid, set the high slope to 40. Any one of those "should" over-enrich things to give you a pseudo-safe place to tune from. Again, I'm shooting from the hip with these comments since I don't have a boosted application. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu May 24, 2007 3:56 pm Somewhere there's a fairly detailed explanation of Injector Slopes/Breakpoint, but I'll see if I can fat-finger it in again. The quick-n-dirty answer that doesn't really tell you much about injector slopes is lower values get you longer PWs for the same amount of air. But the longer explanation goes something like this. The EEC knows how much air is coming in via voltage from the MAF. It correlates that voltage to a measured airflow via the MAF transfer (a curve that could be flawed and will likely need to be tweaked). Then based on a number of other conditions and calculations, it calculates how much fuel needs to go with that amount of air. But ultimately what delivers that fuel are pulse-outputs to the injectors. So it needs to correlate a calculated amount of fuel to a Pulse-Width (PW). That's done with the Injector Slopes, Injector Breakpoint, and Injector Offset function. The Injector Slopes define an expected behavior of the injectors so the EEC has some basis for calculating that PW. An interesting phenomenon of most injectors is they act larger than they really are at lower pulse-widths since the act of opening and closing an injector allows more fuel to be released than what is released when the injector stays open. But once the injector is open, the flow of fuel stabilizes out. So you need more than a single slope (fuel delivery vs inj PW time period) to define the injector behavior. You need low-slope to define the injector behavior up until it starts stabilizing out. Once the PW holds the injector open long enough, you need a 2nd slope line to define that stabilized behavior. Then you need a breakpoint to define what PW the injector starts acting stable. But because there's always an open and close event with every PW (even big ones), that added fuel defined by low-slope is always part of the PW calculation. That's injector slopes and breakpoint in a nutshell. So what happens if the defined behavior is different than what the injectors are actually doing? The EEC will give too much or not enough fuel for a given fuel demand. Then how do you know if your defined injector behavior matches your actual injector behavior? You may never know...but you can at least get close enough for all practical purposes. The easy way is to buy Clint Garrity's EEC Analyzer program that will help you see what your calculated PWs are and based on performance, what they should be. But without that, the way you do that is you compare various MAF airflow rates against different PWs. Some people might say, "It sounds like I can ignore injector slopes and just tune the MAF to fit actual conditions". And if you find that when the MAF reads, for instance 100kg/hr, the EEC is always lean or always rich, then you can safely tune the MAF accordingly and fix that problem. But what if at high RPMs/Low Load, 100kg/hr is super rich, but at lower RPM/High Load, that same 100kg/hr reading from the MAF is super lean? At that point, you either fix one condition and throw the other even further off OR you change the EEC's tune of expected injector behavior to better-match what the injectors will actually do. Will you ever get it perfect? Hell no. One of the biggest reasons is because most injectors of supposedly the same size will behave slightly different than another that's supposed to be just like it. In addition, I've found injector behavior changes as the air temp changes, as the fuel temp changes, as the fuel quality changes, you get the idea. So the best you can do is get it close and let your KAMRFs (learning adaptive strategy) sort out the rest, that's what they are there for. To fix the mis-matched injector behavior problem, they do sell "matched" injector sets. These are injectors that someone has tested and categorized the behavior of hundreds of different injectors, then grouped the ones that have similar behavior together and sold them as matched sets. That helps, but for typical "budget" street applications, it's not necessary. Those are for people that get paid thousands of dollars to win races and REALLY care if they are getting 12.1:1 instead of 12:1 AFR ratios. For most street applications, as long as you are at or below 13:1@WOT, you are good. Then dyno test to find out if 12.5:1 or 12:1 gets you anything more. Of course, if you are forced induction (as you are), you'll want to enrich WOTs to the 12:1 or lower. Hopefully at this point (if you are still reading), you can now answer your own question of whether setting high and low slopes equal to each other is a good idea. To start off, it could (and most likely will) cause your lower PWs to be richer than they need to be which could cause driveability problems but for starting off, it won't hurt much. Would you want to leave them that way? I can't say. You'll have to decide that as you tune, drive the car, and analyze the logs. The X3Z tune comes from the factory with high and low slopes the same. So it can't be that bad. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

posts.author: sailorbob
posts.content: sailorbob BIN Hacker Posts: 1767 Joined: Tue Jul 12, 2005 6:10 am Quote Post by sailorbob » Thu May 24, 2007 1:39 pm The airmass value that the eec uses at idle can either instantaneous airmass (aka AM) or filtered airmass (aka FAM). The filtered airmass is an averaged value that's used when the eec thinks the instantaneous airmass is fluctuating too much to allow a steady idle. The filtered airmass region is when the throttle position, desired and actual idle rpms indicate that filtering (i.e. averaging) is required. I think the stock A9L never uses a filtered airmass value in it's fuelling calculations because the 'FAM Multiplier' (aka DELTAM) parameter is set to zero. This is because I believe the zero value causes the eec to use the instantaneous airmass instead of the filtered airmass even though the eec has decided that filtering should be used. Top

cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Thu May 10, 2007 12:49 pm There's a little magic when dealing with Cam/Injector timing. This is a place you can spend a fair amount of time just piddling...and it won't affect the rest of your tune much as you play around. But to begin, you do need a rather long and diverse datalog. In fact, I would recommend you load multiple datalogs into EA, to do this calculation. The more data you have at varying load/RPMs AND other conditions, the better. You can load multiple datalogs at the same time in EA by holding the CTRL button while click/selecting your datalog file). Next you need to configure the Injector table to have the same Load row values and RPM column values as your tune. Double click one of the values to bring up a dialog box to edit them all. If you got a small window that only seems to modify the one you double-clicked, you need to update EA. Once you got EA configured and loaded with either 1 really good diverse datalog OR a multitude of different datalogs that together are diverse (and preferably were all from the same tune/BIN), then you can configure the Cam Specs tab settings. Depending on your engine and injector size, you may find you can use the "Intake Open" option and get black numbers across the board. Being that I've never run an engine with larger-than-stock injectors, I can't offer real-world advice here. But based on what I know about what I've learned from my own tuning experience, I'd say choosing the "Intake Open" option is best for people running 36-42# injectors on a street-driven car. If you are running 19-30# injectors AND your build can run them into the 75% duty cycle range, you will get red numbers in the top-right corner. To reduce that some and smooth out the engine at the lower RPMs, try setting a custom injector start time that's before the intake valve opens. This will spray the backside of the intake valve some so that you cool the intake valve as well as boil off some of the fuel into the air that's in the intake runner before it is aspirated into the combustion chamber. You don't want to give too much time here or you'll wind up forming droplets, or worse puddles...which at lower RPMs cause the engine to feel boggy & sluggish like the mix is too rich even though the HEGOs are indicating all is well. For starters, say 50-100 degrees less than when EA indicates your intake valve opens (look at the Cam Events chart in EA). For most street cams (stock and aftermarket) running 19-24# injectors, entering a value of 275 is a good starting point. Larger injectors would take less degrees since they spray more fuel. My current tune, I have RPM/Load columns 1500 RPMs and below, firing the injectors 50 degrees before the Intake Valve opens since lower RPMs, each degree represents a larger amount of time than at higher RPMs. From 2000-3000, the values are firing injectors around 75 degrees before. And 3500-up, timing events are firing at least 100 degrees before. Since my stock Explorer cam has a VERY slow ramp rate, I want the injector to stop firing well before the intake valve closes. So I clip all the injector values toward the top-right to around 60 less than when my intake valve closes (gets to .050" closed). For my cam, that's 550 degrees. So regardless of whether the calculated value was red or black, if it calculates above 550, I limit it to 550. What this does is ensure that all the air that's taken into the cylinder has all the fuel that's supposed to go with it. If the injector is allowed to continue firing after the intake valve has closed, then guess what? The air and fuel are not together, so the 1st time this happens, that air-charge will be lean. This will cause QUICK WOTs to bog for the first round of fires since they will all be running lean. The next round will only be slightly lean since they will get the benefit of the fuel that was meant for the combustion that was lean. Make sense? ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top

Of course, one thing I forgot to mention is if you are running a cam with overlap and you need to pass emissions, you HAVE to time your injectors to NOT fire until after the exhaust valve has closed so that any scavenging of unburned intake air that gets pulled out the exhaust doesn't pull fuel out with it and fail the sniff tests due to excessive HC at low RPMs. The sacrifice with doing this is the engine will run pretty rough as compared to firing the injector before the intake valve opens, but if you are using an overlap cam, you probably don't care about drivability a whole lot in the 1st place since overlap cams are generally only for all-out HIGH RPM performance. Another detail that ALMOST goes without saying is you will need injectors large enough to fire the complete fuel load in the time between when the Exhaust valve closes and when the Intake Valve Closes WITH some extra time left over to "dry" the intake pathway so you minimize the amount of raw fuel that does get pulled out the exhaust on the next stroke. cgrey8 Administrator Posts: 11298 Joined: Fri Jun 24, 2005 5:54 am Location: Acworth, Ga (Metro Atlanta) Contact: Contact cgrey8 Website Quote Post by cgrey8 » Tue May 15, 2007 11:10 am To be honest, I'm not sure. However if you are leaning out, that would tend to indicate that firing your injectors before the exhaust valve closes is scavenging some of your fuel out the exhaust (hence why it is burning a little lean now). If you want your fuel economy back, you may have to revert to recalculating all these values for AFTER the Exhaust Valve has closed so you minimize the amount of fuel escaping out the exhaust. That's the unfortunate disadvantage to overlap cams. Even the E303 scavenges a little and will cause KAMRF differences as you play with these numbers. But stock cams and other aftermarket cams that are pretty far from overlap shouldn't have this problem. If this is a daily driver, you might want to reconsider your cam choice at some point in the future. There are plenty of cams out there that get some impressive street performance without overlap. Although, you do sacrifice top-end performance since top-end is where the overlap cams accel. But with an overlap cam, you sacrifice driveability, which is of pretty high importance in a daily driven vehicle (at least it is to me). That doesn't mean you can't cruise around with overlap cams. It just means there are other cams that are better suited for fuel economy, emissions, and lower RPM daily driving. Although if this is a HOT street/strip car and all you are trying to do is get a little smoothness on the rough edges and can accept the side-effects, then there's no reason to change at all. ...Always Somethin' 89 Ranger Supercab, 331 w/GT40p heads, ported Explorer lower, Crane Powermax 2020 cam, FMS Explorer (GT40p) headers, aftermarket T5 'Z-Spec', GUFB, Moates QuarterHorse tuned using BE&EA Member V8-Ranger.com Top
